In the context of base 10, Kaprekar investigated this problem during the 1950s and 1960s, specifically seeking $K(n)$, the smallest $u$ for which the equation $u = v + s(v)$ admits exactly $n$ solutions. He established $K(2) = 101$ and $K(3) = 10^{13} + 1$, while conjecturing that $K(4) = 10^{24} + 102$. In 1966, Narasinga Rao provided an upper bound of $10^{1111111111124} + 102$ for $K(5)$, along with bounds for $K(6)$ through $K(16)$. This paper introduces a set of recurrences that determine $K(n)$ for any base $b$, confirming the validity of Kaprekar's conjectured values. Central to this methodology is a novel recurrence for $F(u)$, which counts the number of solutions to $u = v + s(v)$. The authors demonstrate the approach by calculating $K(n)$ for $n \leq 16$ and bases $b \leq 10$, revealing that $K(n)$ increases as a tower of height proportional to $\log_2(n)$. Notably, the base-5 case is governed by the classical Thue-Morse sequence, prompting the definition of generalized Thue-Morse sequences applicable to other bases.

This paper introduces a Python package for rule-based sentence boundary disambiguation that operates immediately for 22 languages. Our goal is to deliver a realistic segmenter capable of producing logical sentences even when the input text's format or domain is unclear. We have adapted the Golden Rules Set—originally a Ruby gem known as pragmatic_segmenter—into Python, incorporating additional enhancements and features. PySBD achieves a 97.92% pass rate on English Golden Rule Set exemplars, representing a 25% improvement over the next best open-source Python tool.

False data injection attacks (FDIAs) constitute a significant threat class designed to compromise measurement integrity by injecting erroneous data into smart metering devices within power grids. To the best of the authors' knowledge, no prior research has endeavored to create a detector that automatically learns the underlying graph topology and spatially correlated measurement data of smart grids to enhance cyber attack detection. This paper offers two primary contributions toward detecting and mitigating FDIAs. First, it introduces a generic, localized, and stealthy (unobservable) attack generation methodology along with publicly accessible datasets, enabling researchers to develop and evaluate their algorithms. Second, the authors propose a scalable, real-time Graph Neural Network (GNN) based detector for FDIAs. This approach effectively integrates model-driven and data-driven strategies by leveraging the inherent physical connections of modern AC power grids and utilizing spatial correlations in measurement data. Experimental validation, which compares the proposed GNN-based detector against existing FDIA detectors found in literature, demonstrates that the algorithm surpasses the best available solutions by 3.14%, 4.25%, and 4.41% in F1 score for standard IEEE testbeds comprising 14, 118, and 300 buses, respectively.

An interactive error-correcting code ($\mathsf{iECC}$) is an interactive protocol ensuring that a receiver can accurately recover the sender's message despite noise. This concept extends the standard error-correcting code ($\mathsf{ECC}$), which functions as a non-interactive $\mathsf{iECC}$ with a maximum erasure resilience of $\frac12$. While \cite{GuptaTZ21} achieved the first construction of an $\mathsf{iECC}$ resilient to more than $\frac12$ adversarial erasures, their approach required communication complexity quadratic in the message size. In contrast, our work presents the first positive-rate $\mathsf{iECC}$ capable of withstanding more than $\frac12$ adversarial erasures. Specifically, for any $\epsilon > 0$, our $\mathsf{iECC}$ tolerates up to $\frac6{11} - \epsilon$ adversarial erasures while maintaining a size of $O_\epsilon(n)$.

This paper explores the identification of community counts and the detection of community structures within complex networks. The block model, recognized as a practical and visual approach, has proven effective for uncovering these structures. To evaluate the quality of the block model, we introduce an objective function termed the WQ value. Utilizing the GSA algorithm enhanced by random keys, we optimize the WQ value to derive the block model B of a given network. By subsequently applying the Adding Ones (AO) and Removing Ones (RO) procedures to block model B, the number of communities in the network can be clearly identified. Additionally, leveraging the block model's inherent feature where node ordering aligns with community ordering, we propose a novel fuzzy boundary algorithm for community detection, which has been successfully tested on several representative networks. Finally, experimental outcomes confirm the feasibility of the proposed algorithm.

Like most machine learning systems, recommender systems are usually assessed using performance metrics calculated on held-out data. However, real-world behavior is complex, necessitating ad hoc error analysis and deployment-specific tests to guarantee desired quality in actual production environments. This paper introduces RecList, a behavioral-based testing methodology that categorizes recommender systems by use case and offers a general plug-and-play process to scale behavioral testing. We validate its effectiveness by examining established algorithms and black-box commercial systems, and we release RecList as an open-source, extensible package for the community.

This correspondence examines the rotating magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) of a thin astrophysical plasma layer. By employing the shallow water approximation, we model a thin plasma layer with a free surface situated in a vertical external magnetic field. The inclusion of this vertical field significantly alters the dynamics of wave processes in the plasma compared to both neutral fluids and plasma layers under toroidal magnetic fields. In this specific scenario, three-wave nonlinear interactions occur. Utilizing an asymptotic multiscale approach, we derived equations governing nonlinear wave packet interactions, specifically involving: three magneto-Poincaré waves, three magnetostrophic waves, two magneto-Poincaré waves and one magnetostrophic wave, and two magnetostrophic waves and one magneto-Poincaré wave. The study predicts the existence of decay instabilities and parametric amplifications. Four distinct types of decay instabilities were identified: the decay of a magneto-Poincaré wave into two magneto-Poincaré waves, the decay of a magnetostrophic wave into two magnetostrophic waves, the decay of a magneto-Poincaré wave into one magneto-Poincaré and one magnetostrophic wave, and the decay of a magnetostrophic wave into one magnetostrophic and one magneto-Poincaré wave. Furthermore, four mechanisms of parametric amplification were discovered: the amplification of magneto-Poincaré waves, the amplification of magnetostrophic waves, the amplification of magneto-Poincaré waves in the presence of magnetostrophic waves, and the amplification of magnetostrophic waves in the presence of magneto-Poincaré waves. The respective growth rates for these instabilities and amplification factors were calculated.

The Quantum Symmetric Simple Exclusion Process (Q-SSEP) models the quantum stochastic dynamics of fermions hopping along graph edges with Brownian noisy amplitudes, driven out of equilibrium by injection and extraction at specific vertices. We provide a solution for the invariant probability measure of the one-dimensional Q-SSEP in the infinite-size limit by deriving the steady-state correlation functions of the system's density matrix and quantum expectation values. These functions encode a complex structure of fluctuating quantum correlations and coherences. While our approach does not employ standard integrable systems techniques, it relies on a significant interplay between permutation groups and polynomials. Additionally, we highlight a potential combinatorial interpretation of these Q-SSEP correlation functions through an unexpected connection to geometric combinatorics and associahedron polytopes.

This note, intended as an input for the Snowmass studies, offers a high-level overview of the physics potential of future colliders, dependent on their center-of-mass energies and luminosities. Rather than depending on precise physics reach projections that are often unavailable, we concentrate on straightforward benchmarks of physics yields, such as the number of Higgs bosons produced. We provide more detailed considerations for lepton colliders due to various recent proposals, and we also include a brief summary for hadron colliders based on simple scaling estimates of physics reach.

This study examines a network of sensors designed to capture environmental data and transmit a limited selection to a central fusion center for state estimation. The objective is for these sensors to select the most informative measurements to maximize estimation accuracy. The problem is modeled as a submodular maximization task, typically solved using a greedy algorithm where sensors sequentially pick measurements from their local pools and inform subsequent sensors. In this work, we introduce the capability for sensors to share measurements with peers, thereby expanding each sensor's available decision set. We investigate how this enhanced communication can optimize the performance of the standard greedy approach. Our findings demonstrate that this measurement exchange can improve the quality of the final measurement set by a factor of up to $n+1$, where $n$ represents the total number of sensors.

Crowd estimation remains a formidable challenge. Although recent research has attempted to leverage auditory data to assist visual models, performance has been constrained by ineffective methods for feature extraction and integration. This paper introduces a novel audiovisual multi-task network designed to overcome critical hurdles in crowd counting by efficiently combining visual and audio inputs to enhance modality association and feature extraction. The proposed architecture incorporates auxiliary and explicit image patch-importance ranking (PIR) alongside patch-wise crowd estimates (PCE) to generate a dynamic third modality. These three modalities—audio, visual, and the derived run-time modality—are processed through a transformer-inspired cross-modality co-attention mechanism to produce the final crowd count. To capture rich visual representations, the system employs a multi-branch structure featuring transformer-style fusion. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art networks across all evaluation settings, achieving improvements of up to 33.8%. Furthermore, analysis of the vision-only variant confirms its empirical superiority over previous methods.

Due to the wide range of stellar masses and orbital dimensions in binary systems, along with the intricate interactions among stars and planets, it has proven challenging to completely characterize planetary systems within such environments. This study presents high-precision astrometric data for the low-mass binary GJ 896AB, which confirms the existence of a Jupiter-mass companion, GJ 896Ab. This planet orbits the primary star, GJ 896A, with a mass of approximately 2.3 Jupiter masses and an orbital period of 284.4 days. By combining optical and infrared relative astrometry from multiple telescopes with absolute radio astrometry from the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), we have, for the first time, fully mapped the three-dimensional orbital orientation of both the binary pair and the planet. The analysis reveals that the planetary and binary orbits are retrograde and exhibit a significant mutual inclination of 148 degrees. Understanding the 3D orbital architecture of such systems is crucial for studying planet formation, as it can distinguish between formation via disk or turbulence fragmentation and explain spin-orbit misalignments. Moreover, since the majority of stars reside in binary or multiple systems, insights gained from systems like GJ 896AB will significantly advance our general comprehension of how planets form.

While strongly correlated systems and graphene have been the primary focus of electronic solid-state theory, the latter's Dirac bands, composed of $sp^{2}$-electrons, lack the strong Hubbard repulsion ($U$) and Hund's rule coupling ($J$) necessary to generate novel interaction-driven physics at Dirac points. To address this, we introduce GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ (Ga-substituted herbertsmithite) as a correlated Dirac-Kagome metal that integrates Dirac electrons with robust interactions and frustrated magnetism. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal its crystallographic and electronic characteristics, confirming the presence of symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level. This material exhibits a rich many-body landscape, potentially hosting charge, magnetic, and superconducting instabilities. By employing various many-body techniques, we investigate symmetry-breaking phase transitions, including Mott-Hubbard, charge or magnetic ordering, and unconventional $f$-wave superconductivity within this compound.

Multivariate functional or spatial data are typically analyzed using multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). Two recent methodologies extend Gaussian graphical models (GGM) to multivariate GPs, where each node signifies a full GP over a continuous domain and edges denote process-level conditional independence. The functional GGM approach employs a basis function expansion for multivariate processes, modeling the resulting vector coefficients via GGM. In contrast, Graphical GP directly constructs valid multivariate covariance functions by "stitching" univariate GPs, ensuring strict adherence to a specified graphical model while maintaining marginal properties. We unify these two seemingly distinct frameworks by demonstrating that any partially separable functional GGM utilizing a specific covariance selection model constitutes a graphical GP. Furthermore, we establish that the finite term truncation of functional GGM is equivalent to stitching with a low-rank GP, a technique known to oversmooth marginal distributions. These theoretical insights facilitate the development of new algorithms for functional data that precisely align with a given inter-variable graph and preserve marginal distributions.

Driven by the proliferation of vast datasets and escalating computational capabilities, data-driven artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed across various sectors, demonstrating significant potential. Nevertheless, a critical limitation persists: many of these systems fail to communicate the rationale behind their decisions to users. This opacity poses a substantial drawback, particularly within critical fields like cybersecurity, where understanding decision-making processes is essential. Addressing this gap, this paper offers three key contributions: first, it proposes and discusses essential criteria for explaining outputs from AI-based cybersecurity tools; second, it conducts a comparative analysis of existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches, evaluating them against both the proposed criteria and other standard assessment dimensions; and third, it presents a comprehensive architecture designed as a roadmap to guide future research. This roadmap uniquely integrates multiple research strands to address the distinct challenges inherent in developing explainable AI for cybersecurity.

Applying neural sequence models like Transformers to music generation requires representing musical pieces as sequences of tokens from a finite vocabulary, which typically includes diverse token types. For instance, describing a musical note necessitates distinct tokens for its pitch, duration, velocity, and onset time. Although these token types possess different characteristics, current models generally treat them uniformly, similar to how words are modeled in natural language. This paper introduces a distinct approach that explicitly accounts for token types, such as notes and metric units, by proposing a new Transformer decoder architecture featuring specialized feed-forward heads for different token categories. Additionally, we utilize an expansion-compression technique to group neighboring tokens into compound words, thereby significantly shortening the token sequence length. We demonstrate that this model functions as a learner operating over dynamic directed hypergraphs and apply it to generate full-length, expressive Pop piano compositions (involving up to 10,000 tokens per song) under both conditional and unconditional settings. Experimental results indicate that compared to state-of-the-art models, our approach converges 5–10 times faster during training—achieving this within a day on a single 11 GB GPU—while maintaining comparable generation quality.

PSR B0950+08 is a luminous non-recycled pulsar known for significant variability in its single-pulse fluence. By analyzing observations from two distinct frequencies—55 MHz using NenuFAR and 1.4 GHz using the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope—we have examined the characteristics of these individual pulses. Our findings indicate that they resemble standard radio pulses rather than the rare, intense Giant Pulses seen in only a few other pulsars. We propose that fluctuations in the interstellar medium along the line of sight, specifically the varying decorrelation bandwidth caused by diffractive scintillation, play a crucial role in the observed fluence variability. Additionally, we identify intriguing structures in the low-frequency single-pulse spectra that mimic the "sad trombones" characteristic of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), though upward frequency drift is also commonly observed in PSR B0950+08. We attribute these spectral features to radius-to-frequency mapping, employing a model similar to that proposed by Wang et al. (2019) for FRBs. Finally, we suggest that the microsecond-scale fluence variability within the broader pulsar population is currently underexplored, and investigating it may provide valuable insights into the origins of FRBs.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) functions as an independent global collaboration dedicated to standardizing the extraction of image biomarkers from acquired imaging data to facilitate high-throughput quantitative image analysis, commonly known as radiomics. A primary obstacle facing this field is the lack of reproducibility and validation in high-throughput quantitative image analysis studies. This issue stems partly from the scarcity of consensus-based guidelines and definitions required to translate raw imaging data into high-throughput image biomarkers. Consequently, the IBSI aims to establish nomenclature and definitions for image biomarkers, provide benchmark datasets and values to verify image processing and calculation methods, and develop reporting guidelines for high-throughput image analysis.

The publish-subscribe model offers an efficient communication framework characterized by strong node decoupling, making it particularly suitable for large-scale deployments. It inherently supports highly dynamic environments and is applied across diverse real-world domains, such as finance, smart cities, healthcare, and IoT sensor networks. Many of these applications demand increasingly robust security measures due to the sensitivity of exchanged data and the privacy requirements of clients and stakeholders. MQTT, a lightweight, topic-based publish-subscribe protocol, has become a de facto industry and research standard, especially in edge and IoT contexts. However, because MQTT brokers must process data in plaintext, they present a significant attack surface. This paper introduces MQT-TZ, a secure MQTT broker that utilizes Arm TrustZone, a trusted execution environment (TEE) prevalent even on affordable devices like Raspberry Pi units. We establish a mutual TLS-based handshake and implement a two-layer encryption scheme for end-to-end security, employing the TEE as a trusted proxy. Our experimental evaluation, which includes micro- and macro-benchmarks alongside real-world industrial workloads from a MedTech scenario, highlights various trade-offs associated with using TrustZone TEEs. We also document key lessons learned during the system's development and assessment. The MQT-TZ source code is now released as open-source.

This thesis centers on applying the quantum tunneling mechanism to investigate black holes. It establishes a general framework for existing tunneling approaches, specifically the radial null geodesic and Hamilton-Jacobi methods. Regarding the radial null geodesic approach, the study examines how back-reaction and non-commutative spacetime effects modify the tunneling rate, Hawking temperature, and the Bekenstein-Hawking area law. The Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) method is first reformulated, leading to a proposed close link between quantum tunneling and gravitational anomaly mechanisms in explaining the Hawking effect. A key advantage of this reformulated HJ method is its ability to directly derive the emission spectrum from the black hole's event horizon—a feature absent in previous literature. Furthermore, this method addresses the quantization of a black hole's entropy and area. Another significant portion of the thesis introduces a novel global embedding of curved spacetime into higher-dimensional Minkowski space (GEMS), which offers a unified description of the Hawking and Unruh effects. This approach simplifies and generalizes conventional embedding techniques. The analysis extends beyond spherically symmetric spacetimes to include the Kerr-Newman black hole. Finally, utilizing the aforementioned concepts and the definition of the gravitational partition function, the thesis demonstrates that entropy extremization yields Einstein's equations of motion. Within this framework, a relationship linking black hole entropy, energy, and temperature is established, identifying energy as the Komar expression. Notably, this relation constitutes the generalized Smarr formula. In this analysis, the GEMS method serves as an intermediate step to derive the law of energy equipartition.

This paper outlines two methods for constructing explicit presentations of Dehn quandles based on the presentations of their underlying groups. The first method provides finite presentations for Dehn quandles associated with specific Garside and Gaussian groups. The second method applies to general Dehn quandles where the centralizers of the generators of the underlying groups are known. The results are illustrated with several examples, including Dehn quandles derived from spherical Artin groups, surface groups, and the mapping class groups of orientable surfaces.

Driven by recent trends in urbanization and e-commerce, businesses are increasingly adopting efficient systems to reduce supply chain expenses. Vendor Managed Inventory (VMI) stands out as a widely adopted strategy for managing multi-party supply chains, yet its implementation necessitates solving the Inventory Routing Problem (IRP). This study addresses a multi-product, multi-period IRP involving a supplier, multiple customers, and a heterogeneous vehicle fleet. Given the IRP's complexity, we devised a Modified Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (MAGA) to efficiently resolve various problem instances. We benchmarked our approach against results from Cplex software and an existing efficient heuristic from prior literature. Through extensive computational experiments on randomly generated instances using diverse metrics, we demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms the alternative approaches.

Accurate numerical solutions for most wave propagation problems depend heavily on reliable and efficient domain truncation. The perfectly matched layer (PML) offers a convergent truncation scheme with increasing layer width or damping, provided it remains stable. However, the primary challenges with PML stem from stability issues, which may arise at the continuous level or be induced by numerical approximations. Consequently, the mathematical and numerical analysis of PML for hyperbolic wave propagation has become a focal point of active research. Current advancements enable the construction of stable, high-order accurate numerical solvers by combining wave equations with PML and approximating them using summation-by-parts finite difference methods, as well as continuous and discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods. This review summarizes progress from mathematical, numerical, and practical standpoints, highlights remaining open problems, and outlines future directions. It further presents numerical experiments on model problems that support theoretical findings, alongside real-world wave propagation simulations demonstrating significant impact. Notably, stable and parallel PML implementations within high-performance computing packages like WaveQLab3D and ExaHyPE allow for a substantial reduction in the computational domain for seismological applications, requiring only a few grid points or elements near the boundaries where the PML is active. This approach can save up to 96% of the computational resources needed for three-dimensional seismological benchmark problems.

This paper outlines general principles for extracting knowledge from large datasets or graphs characterized by pair-wise connections, such as causal relationships. It operates with minimal assumptions, requiring only that data can be represented as relationships between objects or events. These relationships facilitate the mining of patterns to create a reduced, more compact representation of the dataset. The resulting symbolic structures, which encode the graph's topology via a generative grammar, are formally identified as sheaves. Consequently, this work introduces the foundational concepts of sheaf theory to the field of graphical data analysis.

By employing a geometric framework for the 2HDM, we categorize CP invariants into three independent sectors: the scalar potential, Yukawa interactions, and the CKM matrix. The thermal effective potential of the 2HDM is computed using a basis-invariant approach. We demonstrate that while CP violation within Yukawa interactions contributes to the effective potential at the one-loop level, the CP phase inherent in the CKM matrix fails to influence the effective potential at any order. Furthermore, in a 2HDM model with a softly broken Z₂ symmetry, the dominant thermal corrections tend to restore CP symmetry at elevated temperatures.

With the growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence as a Service, safeguarding well-trained models as intellectual property has become crucial. Two primary protection strategies exist: ownership verification and usage authorization. This paper introduces Non-Transferable Learning (NTL), an innovative method that secures exclusive data representations within a model and limits its generalization to specific domains, thereby addressing both verification and authorization needs. Specifically: 1) Regarding ownership verification, while watermarking is standard, it often fails against advanced removal techniques. In contrast, our NTL-based verification offers robust defense against state-of-the-art removal methods, as demonstrated by extensive testing across six approaches on the digits, CIFAR10, STL10, and VisDA datasets. 2) Concerning usage authorization, existing solutions typically restrict access to specific users but allow them to apply the model to any data. Our NTL-based approach instead enforces data-centric protection, termed applicability authorization, which significantly degrades model performance on unauthorized inputs. The efficacy of this method is further validated through experiments on the mentioned datasets.

In network design tasks like compact routing, the objective involves routing packets between nodes along approximated shortest paths. A key advantage of these routes is minimizing the number of hops, which enhances reliability and lowers transmission expenses. Building on the widespread success of stochastic tree embeddings in algorithm design, Haeupler, Hershkowitz, and Zuzic (STOC'21) investigated Ramsey-type metric embeddings into trees with hop constraints. Specifically, an embedding $f:G(V,E)\rightarrow T$ exhibits Ramsey hop-distortion $(t,M,\beta,h)$ (where $t,\beta,h\ge1$ and $M\subseteq V$) if for all $u,v\in M$, the inequality $d_G^{(\beta\cdot h)}(u,v)\le d_T(u,v)\le t\cdot d_G^{(h)}(u,v)$ holds. Here, $t$ represents distortion, $\beta$ represents hop-stretch, and $d_G^{(h)}(u,v)$ signifies the minimum weight of a path between $u$ and $v$ containing at most $h$ hops. Haeupler et al. developed an embedding where the subset $M$ includes a $1-\epsilon$ fraction of vertices, achieving $\beta=t=O(\frac{\log^2 n}{\epsilon})$. They leveraged this embedding to create several bicriteria approximation algorithms for hop-constrained network design issues.

In this work, we first refine the Ramsey-type embedding to achieve parameters $t=\beta=\frac{\tilde{O}(\log n)}{\epsilon}$, while also extending it to arbitrary distortion values $t$ (at the expense of reducing the size of $M$). This improved embedding directly yields polynomial enhancements for all approximation algorithms derived by Haeupler et al. Furthermore, we develop hop-constrained clan embeddings (in which each vertex possesses multiple copies) to construct bicriteria approximation algorithms for the group Steiner tree problem, thereby matching the current best results for the unconstrained variant. Finally, we apply our embedding findings to build hop-constrained distance oracles and distance labeling schemes, most notably delivering the first hop-constrained compact routing scheme with provable guarantees.

We introduce a numerical approach for simulating noise within Stimulated Brillouin Scattering (SBS), specifically designed for dynamic scenarios involving optical pulses and incorporating both thermal noise and phase noise from input lasers. By utilizing this model, we analyze the statistical characteristics of optical and acoustic power in both pulsed spontaneous and stimulated SBS regimes, examining how gain and pulse width influence noise levels. Our results indicate that thermal noise significantly shapes the statistical behavior of the fields, while laser phase noise affects the SBS interaction when the laser's coherence time aligns closely with the optical pulse duration. This algorithm supports arbitrary waveguide geometries and material properties, offering a flexible tool for noise-based SBS simulations that are crucial for advancements in signal processing, sensing, microwave photonics, and opto-acoustic memory storage.

Rare electromagnetic decays of charmed mesons serve as valuable experimental grounds for investigating hadronic state structures and photon-meson interactions, validating chiral perturbation theory within the flavor sector, and probing for new physics such as dark photons. This study computes the relative branching fractions for electromagnetic Dalitz decays ($D_{(s)}^\ast\to D_{(s)}\ell^+\ell^-$) compared to their radiative counterparts ($D_{(s)}^\ast\to D_{(s)}\gamma$), along with dileptonic invariant mass spectra and leptonic angular distributions, utilizing the Vector-Meson Dominance model. The calculations cover transitions involving $D^\ast(2007)^0$, $D^\ast(2010)^\pm$, $D^\ast(2640)^\pm$, $D_s^{\ast\pm}$, $D_{s1}^\ast(2700)^\pm$, and $D_{s1}^\ast(2860)^\pm$, incorporating the relevant transition form factors.

We determine the precise conditions governing the embeddings between Wiener amalgam spaces $W_{p,q}^s$ and several classical function spaces, such as Sobolev spaces $L^{s,r}$, local Hardy spaces $h_{r}$, and Besov spaces $B_{p,q}^s$. These findings partially refine and broaden the primary results presented by Guo et al. in J. Funct. Anal., 273(1):404-443, 2017. Furthermore, we provide a complete characterization of the inclusions between Wiener amalgam spaces $W_{p,q}^s$ and $\alpha$-modulation spaces $M_{p,q}^{s,\alpha}$. Notably, for the case where $\alpha=0$ (yielding $M_{p,q}^s$), we establish the sharp conditions for the most general embedding scenario. Additionally, when $0<p\leqslant 1$, we derive the sharp embedding criteria between Wiener amalgam spaces and Triebel spaces $F_{p,r}^{s}$.

Existing quantum processors suffer from noise, restricted coherence times, and imperfect gate operations, meaning only algorithms fitting within the total coherence window can run successfully. An effective quantum compiler must therefore optimize input programs into their most efficient equivalents to maximize hardware utility. This study introduces novel deterministic algorithms capable of compiling recurrent quantum circuit patterns in polynomial time. Specifically, these patterns are prevalent in circuits designed to calculate molecular ground states via the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) method, utilizing the RyRz heuristic wavefunction Ansatz. We demonstrate that our pattern-focused compiling techniques, when paired with a robust swapping strategy, generate output programs generally comparable to those from state-of-the-art compilers regarding CNOT count and depth. Notably, our approach yields superior, unmatched results specifically for RyRz circuits.

This research examines diffusive particle systems with heterogeneous, mean-field interactions defined by a graphon, alongside their finite-particle counterparts. Assuming appropriate conditions, we derive exponential concentration bounds within a finite time frame for both the 1st and 2nd Wasserstein distances between the empirical measures of the finite systems and the averaged graphon law, thereby generalizing previous findings by Bayraktar and Wu.

This study examines the central force problem within the framework of special relativity. We derive the relativistic analog of the Binet equation to describe orbital motion. Subsequently, we analyze the trajectory of a planet in a solar-type system where the gravitational potential includes an additional term proportional to the inverse square of the radial distance. By applying a perturbative approach, we determine the explicit form of the orbital function. Finally, we investigate the resulting orbital precession and compare it with predictions from general relativity.

Although the beta distribution is a primary choice for modeling data within the unit interval, it fails to adequately represent bimodal patterns. To address this limitation, we introduce a bimodal beta distribution developed using an approach grounded in the alpha-skew-normal model. This paper examines key characteristics of the new distribution, including its bimodal nature, real moments, entropy measures, and identifiability. Additionally, we present a novel regression framework based on this distribution and analyze its residuals, with parameter estimation achieved through maximum likelihood. A Monte Carlo simulation evaluates the performance of these estimators in finite samples, and an empirical application demonstrates the distribution's effectiveness in handling bimodal datasets.

This study introduces a semi-supervised approach for clustering short texts, utilizing neural networks to generate distributed vector representations and leveraging limited labeled data to guide the clustering intent. We develop a new objective function that integrates representation learning with k-means clustering, optimizing it iteratively using both labeled and unlabeled data through three stages: (1) assigning each short text to the nearest centroid based on its current neural network representation; (2) re-estimating cluster centroids according to the assignments made in step (1); and (3) updating the neural networks via the objective function while keeping centroids and cluster assignments fixed. Experiments across four datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms several other text clustering techniques.

We examine the deposition of thin Fe films on MgAl$_2$O$_4$(001) and MgO(001) substrates via dc magnetron sputtering. Results indicate that Fe layers grown on MgAl$_2$O$_4$ exhibit significantly superior crystal quality compared to those on MgO substrates. The influence of these differences in crystallinity on the magnetic and electronic transport characteristics is analyzed.

We address the challenge of solving high-order semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for nonconvex polynomial optimization problems (POPs), which frequently possess degenerate rank-one optimal solutions. Rather than relying solely on the SDP, we introduce a novel algorithmic framework that integrates global descent derived from the convex SDP with local search informed by the nonconvex POP. Specifically, we develop a globally convergent inexact projected gradient method (iPGM) for the SDP as the foundation of this framework. We then enhance iPGM's performance by incorporating long, safeguarded rank-one steps produced by rapid nonlinear programming solvers, maintaining global convergence for the SDP. To handle the iPGM subproblem of projecting points onto the SDP feasible set, we propose a two-phase approach: the first phase employs a symmetric Gauss-Seidel based accelerated proximal gradient method (sGS-APG) to generate a high-quality initial point, while the second phase utilizes a modified limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) method to achieve an accurate solution. We analyze convergence for both stages and demonstrate a new global convergence result for the modified L-BFGS that functions without requiring twice continuous differentiability of the objective function. Numerical experiments on second-order SDP relaxations from various POPs show that our framework achieves state-of-the-art efficiency, scalability, and robustness in solving degenerate rank-one SDPs to high precision, even when dealing with millions of equality constraints.

We establish that for a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, the property of being $(\epsilon,\delta)$ in Jones' sense is equivalent to being an extension domain for $\text{bmo}(\Omega)$, the non-homogeneous analogue of the space of functions of bounded mean oscillation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these conditions are equivalent to local versions of two other criteria characterizing uniform domains: one concerning the existence of length cigars between proximal points and the other a local formulation of the quasi-hyperbolic uniform condition. Our findings indicate that the definition of $\text{bmo}(\Omega)$ is intrinsically linked to the geometric structure of the domain.

Models like BERT, XLNET, and XLM-R have demonstrated state-of-the-art results in numerous NLP applications, particularly in detecting hate speech and offensive language on social media platforms. This paper introduces fBERT, a BERT variant retrained on SOLID, the most extensive English corpus for offensive language identification containing over 1.4 million labeled instances. We assess fBERT's effectiveness across multiple English datasets and experiment with various thresholds for selecting data from SOLID. The fBERT model will be released freely for public use.

Differential cross sections for Higgs boson (H) production serve as sensitive indicators for physics extending beyond the standard model. New phenomena could influence the dominant gluon-gluon fusion loop at the LHC, appearing as discrepancies from standard model predictions. This study presents combined spectra for the H $\to$ $\gamma\gamma$, H $\to$ ZZ, and H $\to$ $\mathrm{b\overline{b}}$ decay modes, along with the inclusive Higgs production cross section, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Analysis of the transverse momentum spectrum allows for constraints on Higgs couplings to top, bottom, and charm quarks, as well as its direct interaction with the gluon field. No significant deviations from the standard model were found in any differential distribution. The measured total cross section is 61.1 $\pm$ 6.0 (stat) $\pm$ 3.7 (syst) pb, and the precision of the differential cross-section measurement for the Higgs transverse momentum has improved by approximately 15% compared to using only the H $\to$ $\gamma\gamma$ channel.

We extend the world line EFT framework to incorporate parity-violating finite size effects. Our analysis provides results for the potentials and radiating moments of a binary inspiral within the parity-conserving sector, confirming consistency with prior calculations while deriving new findings, specifically the current quadrupole moment arising from finite size gravitomagnetic effects. Additionally, we offer novel insights into parity-violating sources, potentially stemming from beyond standard model physics, demonstrating that these generate gravitational wave signals characterized by a unique signature: the current moment emerges at a 0.5PN order earlier than the mass moment in the post-Newtonian expansion. Parity violation further introduces a distinct potential proportional to $\textbf{S}\cdot \textbf{r}$. Lastly, we derive new results for the dissipative force acting on parity-violating constituents, revealing the unusual signature of a force oriented normal to the orbital plane.

Measurements of global spin polarization in hadrons from heavy ion collisions conducted by the STAR experiment have opened new avenues for studying the hottest, least viscous, and most vortical fluid ever created in a laboratory. This work introduces an alternative perspective on spin polarization beyond conventional methods: a topological realization achieved via quantum vortex formation during Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) collisions. This approach relies on the concept that vortices act as topological excitations in superfluids possessing local orbital angular momentum (OAM), serving as an analogue to spin degrees of freedom. Using a large-scale parallel algorithm on Graphics Processing Units (GPU) to achieve high precision, the study solves the Gross-Pitaevskii Equation to investigate vortex and vortex-antivortex pair formation. In rotating environments, primary vortices with a winding number of one remain stable against perturbations due to their minimal energy and fixed OAM, whereas vortices with higher winding numbers are unstable and decay into primary vortices by redistributing energy and vorticity. Additionally, OAM injection can occur in non-central collisions of self-interacting condensates, where initial OAM induces vortex formation through the concentration of energy and vorticity density around topological defects. Unlike hydrodynamical descriptions, the interference of the wave function critically influences the transport of energy and vorticity, highlighting the quantum nature of the process. Ultimately, examining vortex formation may provide insights into the nature of particle spin and spin-orbit couplings within the strongly interacting matter produced in heavy-ion collisions.

We introduce FlameNEST, a framework that enables explicit likelihood assessments in noble element particle detectors by leveraging data-driven models from the Noble Element Simulation Technique. FlameNEST facilitates statistical analysis of real-world data without relying on large, computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations. Instead, it calculates likelihoods on an event-by-event basis by convolving analytic probability elements into a single TensorFlow multiplication. Additionally, this robust framework opens avenues for straightforward inter-collaborative analyses, which will be essential for the future of experimental dark matter physics.

**Motivation:** Understanding which specific attribute combinations drive the adoption of software technologies is vital for developers, as it dictates which tools gain broad community support and which risk abandonment, potentially wasting developer investments. **Aim and Context:** This study models software adoption to identify attributes linked to greater visibility among competing technologies. **Approach:** Utilizing social contagion theory and statistical modeling, we empirically define and test measures influencing adoption. Specifically, we analyze a vast dataset of open-source version control repositories to build dependency chains for R language files. We employ logistic regression to examine the technological attributes driving the selection between competing data frame implementations (tidy and data.table), quantifying both key project attributes and the characteristics of the developers making these choices. **Results:** Our findings indicate that higher adoption correlates with rapid issue response times, a larger volume of overall deployments, and a greater number of high-quality StackExchange questions. Decision-makers tend to favor technologies that are proximate within technical dependency and author collaboration networks while satisfying performance requirements. **Future work:** We anticipate that our methodology, which integrates social contagion to capture both rational and irrational preferences and extracts key metrics from extensive version control data, offers a general framework for enhancing visibility, fostering better-informed decisions, and promoting more sustainable, widely adopted software.

When evaluating the short-term health impacts of air pollution, researchers typically analyze pollutants individually due to their strong correlations. Recent multi-pollutant approaches attempt to address this by aggregating pollutants into air quality indexes or clustering them before assessing their collective effects; however, a significant limitation of these methods is the inability to isolate the specific health impact of each individual pollutant. This paper introduces a Bayesian hierarchical framework utilizing a two-component model to handle multi-pollutant data. The model first estimates the "true" concentrations for each pollutant and subsequently links these values to health outcomes within a time-series context. We validate the model's performance through simulations and apply this framework to examine the influence of six specific pollutants on cardiovascular mortality in Greater London during 2011–2012.

Log-logistic distribution parameters are typically estimated using classical techniques like maximum likelihood estimation, yet these approaches often yield significantly biased results when outliers are present. This study examines various alternative estimators that feature closed-form expressions and exhibit robustness against specific levels of data contamination. We assess the robustness of each estimator by analyzing its breakdown point. The finite sample performance and efficacy of these methods are evaluated via Monte Carlo simulations and an application to real-world data. Numerical findings indicate that the proposed estimators perform comparably to the maximum likelihood estimator in clean data while offering superior performance when data contamination exists.

Drawing from the empathetic principle of "walking a mile in someone else's shoes," which encourages imagining the struggles others endure, we propose a novel machine learning criterion for counterfactual fairness at the group level. Rather than asking how an individual from a non-protected group (e.g., a Caucasian convict) would be treated if they belonged to a protected group (e.g., were Black), we examine how entire groups would fare under the conditions of another. Specifically, we investigate how the average outcomes for all White convicts would shift if they possessed the protected group's status while retaining their original White characteristics, such as the same number of prior convictions. We formally define this problem and evaluate it empirically across various datasets. Furthermore, our methodology offers a resolution to the issue of covariates being correlated with sensitive attributes.

**Context.** In radial velocity-based exoplanet searches, the Bayes factor and false alarm probability (FAP) are the primary statistical metrics. Although both are valuable, they do not explicitly determine if an exoplanet detection warrants a claim. Additionally, there is ambiguity regarding the appropriate detection threshold and the robustness of findings against model misspecification. **Aims.** This study seeks to establish a detection criterion that precisely conveys the necessary information to validate an exoplanet discovery. We evaluate this new metric against existing ones regarding sensitivity and robustness. **Methods.** We introduce the false inclusion probability (FIP), a significance metric derived from the posterior probability of a planet's existence. Using the nested sampling tool Polychord, we compute posterior distributions. We demonstrate that defining priors on linear parameters as Gaussian mixture models substantially accelerates calculations for both FIP and Bayes factor. The performance of FAP, Bayes factor, and FIP is assessed through simulations and analytical reasoning, first under the assumption of a correct model, and then by testing sensitivity to variations in prior and likelihood choices. **Results.** Beyond other attributes, FIP provides mechanisms to verify the reliability of significance levels, effectively handles aliasing, and enables the exclusion of planets with high confidence. Our simulations indicate that FIP outperforms current detection metrics. Furthermore, we observe that planet detections are sensitive to priors on period and semi-amplitude, and that allowing noise parameters to vary freely yields superior results compared to fixing a noise model based on ancillary indicators.

Recent advancements in average-case analysis for optimization techniques offer a more nuanced and representative assessment of convergence compared to traditional worst-case bounds. However, this approach necessitates a more specific assumption regarding the data generation process, specifically the requirement to know the expected spectral distribution (ESD) of the problem's associated random matrix. This study demonstrates that the clustering of eigenvalues near the boundaries of the ESD dictates the asymptotic average complexity of a problem. Relying on prior knowledge of this eigenvalue concentration proves to be a more realistic assumption than possessing complete information about the entire ESD. This concept of approximate concentration serves as a balanced compromise between the oversimplification of worst-case convergence and the overly restrictive nature of earlier average-case studies. Furthermore, we present the Generalized Chebyshev method, which is asymptotically optimal under hypotheses concerning this concentration and achieves global optimality when the ESD adheres to a Beta distribution. By comparing its performance against standard optimization algorithms like gradient descent and Nesterov's scheme, we establish that, within the average-case framework, Nesterov's method is universally nearly optimal in the asymptotic limit.

This research examines one-dimensional lattices featuring imaginary-valued Aubry-Andre-Harper (AAH) potentials. These systems support edge states characterized by purely imaginary eigenenergies, distinguishing them from those in the Hermitian AAH model and ensuring their stability through non-Hermitian particle-hole symmetry. Such edge states emerge specifically when the period of the imaginary potential is an integer multiple of four lattice constants. Originating from topology, they can appear at domain walls separating lattices with varying modulation periods and phases, as indicated by a bulk polarization invariant. Notably, these states maintain their localization even when the real line gap closes. These properties offer potential applications in laser arrays for selecting topological lasing modes under spatially extended pumping conditions.

Enabling robots to deduce human intentions is a fundamental requirement for successful collaboration. While most computational methods model intent as a probability distribution conditioned on the robot's perceived state, they typically rely on pre-existing, task-specific intent labels. To address this limitation, we introduce the Disentangled Sequence Clustering Variational Autoencoder (DiSCVAE), an unsupervised clustering framework designed to learn intent distributions without prior labels. This framework utilizes recent unsupervised learning techniques to disentangle latent representations within sequence data, distinguishing between time-varying local features and time-invariant global attributes. As an innovative extension, DiSCVAE infers a discrete variable to create a latent mixture model, facilitating clustering based on these global sequence concepts, such as high-level intentions. We validated DiSCVAE using a real-world human-robot interaction dataset gathered from a robotic wheelchair. Our results demonstrate that the inferred discrete variable aligns with human intent, indicating significant potential for collaborative applications like shared control.
This note demonstrates in just eight lines that a finitely generated convex cone is closed, and subsequently derives Farkas' lemma using standard, well-known arguments.

Graph-structured data is prevalent in real-world applications and is typically handled via graph neural networks (GNNs). Following the implementation of regulations guaranteeing a "right to be forgotten," the challenge of removing data from graphs has gained considerable significance. To tackle this, we present the inaugural framework for \emph{certified graph unlearning} within GNNs. Unlike standard machine unlearning, complex graph data introduces distinct analytical and heuristic hurdles. Specifically, three categories of unlearning requests must be addressed: node feature removal, edge deletion, and node unlearning. Furthermore, establishing provable performance guarantees requires overcoming difficulties related to feature mixing during propagation. Our theoretical analysis focuses on simple graph convolutions (SGC) and their generalized PageRank (GPR) variants, establishing a foundation for certified GNN unlearning. Empirical evaluations across six benchmark datasets reveal superior performance-complexity trade-offs compared to full retraining and methods ignoring graph structure. For instance, unlearning $20\%$ of nodes on the Cora dataset results in merely a $0.1\%$ drop in test accuracy while achieving a four-fold speed-up over complete retraining. Additionally, our approach surpasses graph-agnostic unlearning methods by delivering a $12\%$ improvement in test accuracy at comparable computational costs.

This work investigates the local well-posedness of the Einstein-Yang-Mills equations within the constant mean extrinsic curvature spatial harmonic generalized Coulomb gauge (CMCSHGC). Under this gauge selection, the full Einstein-Yang-Mills system simplifies into a coupled elliptic-hyperbolic framework. Leveraging the methodology introduced by Andersson and Moncrief \cite{andersson2003elliptic}, we demonstrate the existence of a unique solution that is both local and continuous in time. This result provides an "in time" continuation criterion for the solutions, intended for future application in proving an enhanced continuation criteria for this coupled system by employing Moncrief's light cone estimate technique.

Droplet-to-droplet interactions are fundamental across numerous fields, spanning from medical diagnostics to the optimization of liquid jet propulsion. This study utilizes an experimental approach in which a laser pulse induces optical breakdown within a micron-sized droplet. By precisely controlling the interaction between a nanosecond laser pulse and an isolated spherical droplet, we manipulate the deformation and fragmentation of droplet arrays. We demonstrate how fluid dynamic responses—including drop-drop and shock-drop interactions—can be regulated and optimized by adjusting laser pulse energy and its relationship with the liquid target's optical density. A novel "butterfly" breakup mode is identified, facilitating controlled and efficient fragmentation of outer droplets in an array. Furthermore, the spatio-temporal properties of laser-induced breakdown determine how shock waves and fragments from a central droplet affect surrounding droplets. The laser energy levels and pulse durations used in this research are representative of various industrial processes, such as surface cleaning, nano-lithography, and microelectronics, as well as medical procedures like intraocular microsurgery.

Analyzing how social determinants of health influence health outcomes necessitates data reflecting the specific neighborhood characteristics where individuals reside. Yet, estimates of these attributes are frequently aggregated across space and time, reducing their effectiveness. For instance, data from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) aggregates figures for small municipalities over five-year intervals, while one-year estimates are restricted to areas with populations exceeding 65,000. Although researchers aiming to characterize neighborhood-level exposures in population health studies might utilize ACS data, the five-year estimates fail to accurately capture temporal shifts or synchronize with other study data, and the limited spatial granularity of the one-year estimates hampers their ability to define neighborhood exposure. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a modeling framework designed to disaggregate proportion estimates derived from sampling surveys, explicitly incorporating survey design effects. We demonstrate the model's practical value by applying it to ACS data to generate poverty estimates for Michigan at a high spatio-temporal resolution.

The BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider has, for the first time, investigated the process $e^+e^-\to 2(p \bar{p})$ using data collected at 23 center-of-mass energies ranging from 4.0 to 4.6 GeV, with a total integrated luminosity of roughly $15$ fb$^{-1}$. Measurements of the Born cross sections for this reaction reveal no significant structures in the lineshape. Furthermore, the invariant mass spectra for the baryon pairs ($pp$ and $\bar{p}\bar{p}$) align with phase space expectations, indicating that no hexaquark or di-baryon state was detected.

This work examines limits and colimits within the category $Part$ of partial groups, algebraic structures originally defined by A. Chermak. We establish that $Part$ is both complete and cocomplete, and further demonstrate that the full subcategory consisting of finite partial groups is finitely complete and finitely cocomplete. These cocompleteness properties are subsequently employed to define quotients of partial groups. Additionally, we identify a category that is richer than $Set$ (the category of sets and set-maps) and construct the free partial groups over its objects. This process generates a broader class of free partial groups, ultimately enabling the proof that every partial group can be expressed as a quotient of a free partial group.

We introduce a method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) utilizing a collection of neural networks termed Neural Basis Functions (NBF). This framework represents a new adaptation of the POD DeepONet operator learning strategy, where a set of neural networks is regressed onto a reduced-order Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) basis. These networks, paired with a branch network that accepts the parameters of the specified PDE, generate a reduced-order approximation of the equation. We apply this methodology to the steady-state Euler equations under high-speed flow regimes (Mach 10–30), specifically analyzing 2D flow around a cylinder that generates shock conditions. Furthermore, we utilize the NBF predictions as initial conditions for a high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) solver (CFD++) to demonstrate accelerated convergence. Additionally, we will share insights regarding the training and implementation of this algorithm.

We present the third-order $1/N$ correction to the four-point correlator of the stress tensor multiplet in large 't Hooft coupling $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang--Mills theory, which maps to two-loop four-graviton scattering in the dual $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times\mathrm{S}^5$ supergravity. This result is derived by bootstrapping an informed ansatz grounded in intuitions from the hidden 10-dimensional conformal symmetry.

This survey paper reviews prominent deep learning techniques applied to Natural Language Processing (NLP) and source code over the past 35 years. It further examines the applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in source code, encompassing Code Intelligence (CI) and Programming Language Processing (PLP). By analyzing over 287 publications, the authors introduce a software-engineering-centric taxonomy for CI, categorizing each study based on its specific contribution to the software development lifecycle. Additionally, the paper explores conversational assistants and their roles within software engineering and education. Finally, it identifies research opportunities where AI for code intersects with conversational assistants and outlines future directions for developing conversational assistants with integrated CI capabilities.

We present a framework equipped with tools and metatheorems designed to facilitate end-to-end verification of security protocols, effectively bridging the divide between automated protocol analysis and code-level proofs. This system automatically converts Tamarin protocol models into sets of I/O specifications formulated in separation logic. Each specification delineates the intended input/output behavior of a protocol role, serving as the benchmark against which the corresponding implementation is verified. Our soundness theorem ensures that any verified implementation retains all security (trace) properties established for the Tamarin model. Consequently, our framework allows researchers to harness the extensive existing verification efforts in Tamarin to validate both new and current implementations. By permitting the use of any separation logic code verifier, the approach offers flexibility concerning the target programming language. To demonstrate the viability and scalability of our method for real-world protocols, we successfully verified a significant portion of the official Go implementation of the WireGuard VPN key exchange protocol.

This research investigates admissible observation operators within perturbed evolution equations through the lens of maximal regularity. Initially, we demonstrate that maximal $L^p$-regularity remains invariant under non-autonomous Miyadera-Voigt perturbations. Subsequently, we prove that the admissibility of observation operators is also preserved under this specific class of perturbations. To conclude, we provide two illustrative examples: one involving a non-autonomous parabolic system and another concerning an evolution equation featuring mixed boundary conditions alongside a non-local perturbation.

Target-specific stance detection on social media, which involves categorizing textual content like posts or comments regarding a specific issue, has emerged as a significant area within opinion mining. A practical application of this technology includes addressing vaccine hesitancy during the coronavirus pandemic. However, current methods often rely solely on individual data points, failing to fully capture the nuanced stance expressed toward a target. To address this limitation, we introduce conversational stance detection (CSD), a new task that infers stances toward a specific target by analyzing both a data instance and its associated conversation thread. We developed a benchmark CSD dataset annotated with stance labels and conversation thread structures, drawn from six major social media platforms in Hong Kong. To solve this task, we propose Branch-BERT, a model designed to leverage contextual information from conversation threads alongside the primary data instance. Extensive experiments on our dataset demonstrate that Branch-BERT surpasses all baseline models that ignore contextual information. Notably, it achieves a 10.3% improvement in F1 score compared to the state-of-the-art method from SemEval-2016 Task 6. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating rich contextual data for detecting target-specific stances on social media and suggest a more practical framework for future stance detection research.

A novel explicit high-order semi-Lagrangian technique is proposed for resolving Lagrangian transport equations within Eulerian-Lagrangian frameworks. To maintain consistency between the semi-Lagrangian approximation and an explicit Eulerian discontinuous spectral element method (DSEM) discretization, Lagrangian particles are initialized at Gauss quadrature collocation points inside each element. These particles advance explicitly in time to compute an advected polynomial solution at the corresponding Gauss locations. Subsequently, this solution is mapped back to the Gauss quadrature points via a semi-Lagrangian least-squares fit, incorporating constraints for element boundaries as well as optional mass and energy preservation. The semi-Lagrangian approximation employs explicit time integration compatible with the grid-based DSEM solver, ensuring that particles seeded at Gauss points remain within element boundaries. Consequently, the method is local and parallelizable, enabling the solution of the Lagrangian formulation without the grid intricacies or parallelization hurdles typical of particle-mesh approaches. Numerical experiments on one- and two-dimensional advection equations demonstrate exponential convergence. Furthermore, the application of mass and energy constraints can enhance accuracy, contingent upon the precision of the time integration.

Scene classification is a prevalent and critical challenge in remote sensing, essential for tasks such as identifying natural hazards, retrieving geographic images, and monitoring environmental conditions. While recent advancements in this domain depend on supervised learning methods that require labels, this approach is incompatible with the vast 35 petabytes of unlabeled satellite imagery available in the NASA GIBS archive. To address this limitation, we introduce CELESTIAL, a self-supervised learning framework designed to efficiently utilize sparsely labeled satellite data. This pipeline adapts the SimCLR algorithm, which first extracts image representations from unlabeled data before fine-tuning with available labels. Our findings demonstrate that CELESTIAL achieves comparable accuracy to supervised methods using only one-third of the required labels on a test dataset. The initial unsupervised stage facilitates applications like reverse image search for NASA Worldview, enabling the retrieval of similar atmospheric phenomena across years of unlabeled data with minimal samples, while the subsequent supervised stage substantially reduces the need for costly data annotation. Moving forward, we aim to extend the CELESTIAL pipeline to diverse data types, algorithms, and application areas.

We introduce a symmetric monoidal category designed to represent fuzzy concepts and reasoning based on G\"ardenfors' framework of conceptual (convex) spaces. By modeling fuzzy concepts with log-concave functions, we demonstrate that this is the most general option meeting G\"ardenfors' criteria while maintaining strong compositional properties. Furthermore, we extend this approach to define a category of log-concave probabilistic channels between convex spaces, which facilitates the modeling of fuzzy reasoning under noisy conditions and offers a new instance of a Markov category.

Recently, Salkuyeh et al. introduced an alternating positive semi-definite splitting (APSS) method for nonsymmetric block three-by-three singular saddle point problems derived from the Picard iteration of a mixed finite element scheme (D.K. Salkuyeh, H. Aslani, Z.Z. Liang, Math. Commun. 26 (2021) 177-195). This study investigates the semi-convergence properties of the APSS method when applied to this specific class of problems. Furthermore, the APSS-induced preconditioner is utilized to enhance the semi-convergence performance of the flexible GMRES (FGMRES) algorithm. Experimental outcomes validate the theoretical findings, demonstrating that the proposed preconditioner significantly improves efficiency compared to using FGMRES without preconditioning.

Machine learning (ML) is extensively applied in software engineering literature to automate various tasks, yet its results can be highly sensitive to randomization within data sampling and learning processes. To investigate how researchers address these threats, we surveyed 45 recent studies focusing on three predictive tasks: defect prediction (DP), predictive mutation testing (PMT), and code smell detection (CSD). Our findings reveal that fewer than 50% of these papers tackle threats associated with randomized data sampling through multiple repetitions, only 8% address the inherent randomness of ML, and merely 18% report parameter values. To evaluate the severity of these issues, we performed an empirical study using 26 real-world datasets typical for the three tasks, employing eight common supervised ML classifiers. We demonstrate that different data resamplings during 10-fold cross-validation result in extreme variability in performance metrics. Additionally, randomized ML methods exhibit significant variability across different random seeds. Concerningly, both performance and variability differ inconsistently across implementations of the same ML method in various libraries, a finding supported by multi-dataset pairwise comparisons. To mitigate these critical threats, we offer practical guidelines for validating, assessing, and reporting results from predictive methods.

This study addresses the challenge of estimating the total search volume and query count within a specific domain over a defined timeframe. Our statistical framework posits that search distributions adhere to Zipf's law, accounting for biases in observed sample volumes across three distinct scenarios. These premises align with empirical findings, industry keyword research standards, and existing approximate algorithms for frequency counting. We develop and test several parameter estimators tailored to the characteristics of empirical and simulated datasets. For continuous data, we advocate for nonlinear least squares regression (NLS) applied to top-volume queries, utilizing the Clauset, Shalizi, and Newman (CSN) method to establish volume bounds. For binned data, we suggest a Chi-square minimization approach limited to top-volume queries, employing the binned CSN method for bounding. Subsequently, we derive estimates for both the total number of queries and the aggregate population volume, complete with statistical error margins. The proposed methods are applied to Italian recipe and cooking queries from 2017, utilizing Google Trends for continuous data and SearchVolume for binned data. We compute the estimated totals and volumes for both scenarios and present a comparative analysis and discussion of the results.

This study addresses the estimation of the mean vector $\theta$ for a $d$-dimensional spherically symmetric random vector $X$ using balanced loss functions defined in two forms: {\bf (i)} $\omega \rho(\|\de-\de_{0}\|^{2}) + (1-\omega)\rho(\|\de - \theta\|^{2})$ and {\bf (ii)} $\ell\left(\omega \|\de - \de_{0}\|^{2} + (1-\omega)\|\de - \theta\|^{2}\right)$, where $\delta_0$ serves as a target estimator, and $\rho$ and $\ell$ are increasing, concave functions. For dimensions $d\geq 4$ with the target estimator $\delta_0(X)=X$, we introduce Baranchik-type estimators that dominate $\delta_0(X)=X$ while remaining minimax. These results extend the work of Marchand & Strawderman (\cite{ms2020}) along two axes: {\bf (a)} shifting the scope from scale mixtures of normals to the broader class of spherical distributions with Lebesgue densities, and {\bf (b)} generalizing the requirements from completely monotone derivatives to concave $\rho'$ and $\ell'$.

We present a $q$-deformation that unifies prior research on classical and enriched $P$-partitions into a single framework. Specifically, we construct a new family of power series dependent on a parameter $q$, which smoothly transitions between Gessel's fundamental functions at $q=0$ and Stembridge's peak quasisymmetric functions at $q=1$. We demonstrate that this family forms a basis for $\QSym$ whenever $q\notin\{-1,1\}$. Additionally, we develop corresponding monomial bases parametrized by $q$, which encompass our earlier findings on enriched monomials and Hoffman's essential quasisymmetric functions.

This paper investigates three two-species Lotka-Volterra competition models defined on finite connected graphs, incorporating Dirichlet, Neumann, or no boundary conditions. Our findings indicate that as time approaches infinity, the outcome is either the extinction of one species with the survival of the other, or the coexistence of both, depending critically on the strength of species competitiveness and initial population sizes under Neumann and no-boundary conditions. One of our results partially addresses a question posed by Slavík in [SIAM J. Appl. Dyn. Syst., 19 (2020)]. The primary techniques employed in proving our main results are the method of upper and lower solutions, which are developed herein for weakly coupled parabolic systems on finite graphs.

We analyzed 40 high-resolution, high signal-to-noise quasar spectra spanning redshifts 2.1 < z < 4.7 to investigate the HI Lyalpha forest signature of the proximity effect. By comparing the effective optical depth near each quasar with the expected value, we confirmed the proximity effect in both the combined sample and individual quasars. The distribution of observed proximity effect strength (PESD) is skewed toward weaker effects, and we demonstrate that this is not merely due to gravitational clustering around quasars. Comparing simulated PESDs with observations suggests that standard averaging methods for determining the UVB intensity $J$ are heavily biased toward high values due to this asymmetry; using the mode of the PESD instead yields an unbiased estimate. For our sample, the modal value is $\log(J) = -21.51 \pm 0.15$ (in units of erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ Hz$^{-1}$ sr$^{-1}$) at $z = 2.73$. We also quantified the excess HI absorption caused by gravitational clustering. On scales of approximately 3 Mpc, only a minority of quasars exhibit overdensities increasing the effective optical depth by a factor of a few, and these are precisely the objects showing the weakest proximity effects. Excluding them, we recalculated the UVB intensity to be $\log(J) = -21.46^{+0.14}_{-0.21}$. This represents the most accurate measurement of $J$ to date. We introduced a new diagnostic based on the PESD shape that strongly supports the conclusion that no systematic overdensity bias affects the proximity effect, thereby resolving the inherent degeneracy between UVB intensity and overdensity. Finally, we estimated the redshift evolution of $J$ and found tentative evidence for a mild decrease with increasing redshift. Our results align excellently with predictions for the evolving UVB intensity, supporting the idea of a significant contribution from star-forming galaxies.

We employed two covariant isobar models to examine the impact of nucleon and delta resonances possessing spins of 11/2, 13/2, and 15/2 on the kaon photoproduction reaction $\gamma + N \to K + Y$. The theoretical framework for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians was derived from studies by Pascalutsa and Vrancx et al. Unknown amplitude parameters, specifically coupling constants and hadronic form factor cutoffs, were determined by fitting calculated observables to experimental data. In the $K\Lambda$ channels, adding the $N(2600)I_{1,11}$ and $N(2700)K_{1,13}$ resonances markedly enhances the alignment between theoretical predictions and experimental results while diminishing the dominance of Born terms through an increased hadronic form factor cutoff. Additionally, these inclusions reduce the number of resonance structures in cross sections, notably eliminating the feature in the $K^0\Lambda$ differential cross section near $W\approx 1650$ MeV, potentially indicating a narrow resonance. For the $K\Sigma$ channels, incorporating $N(2600)I_{1,11}$, $N(2700)K_{1,13}$, $\Delta(2420)H_{3,11}$, $\Delta(2750)I_{3,13}$, and $\Delta(2950)K_{3,15}$ states also significantly refines the model and raises the hadronic form factor cutoff for Born terms. Contrary to the $K\Lambda$ results, however, introducing these high-spin resonances in the $K\Sigma$ sector generates additional resonance structures within the $K^+\Sigma^0$ differential cross section. This study demonstrates that the second and third peaks in the $K^+\Sigma^0$ differential cross section arise from the $\Delta(2000)F_{35}$ and $N(2290)G_{19}$ resonances, respectively. Furthermore, we assessed resonance properties at pole positions and via the Breit-Wigner method.

Heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) are a common feature in numerous extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics. This study examines the potential of the NA62 experiment at CERN to tighten existing constraints on the HNL mixing angle $|U_e|^2$ by conducting a missing mass search for $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays of particles in flight. We demonstrate that, using currently available data, a limit of $|U_e|^2 \simeq 2\times 10^{-6}$ can be achieved within the 125 -- 144 MeV mass range, an area that is presently under-sampled by production-based searches. Furthermore, with future data collection, a specialized trigger system, and enhanced rejection of out-of-acceptance photons, this sensitivity could improve by an additional order of magnitude.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) has garnered significant academic and commercial attention due to the increasing need for natural communication solutions. However, general-purpose ASR systems often struggle when applied to domain-specific languages. To mitigate these errors, researchers have employed various strategies, including modifying language models with contextual information and applying post-processing corrections. This article investigates the application of evolutionary processes to create optimized contexts tailored to specific application domains, alongside correction techniques grounded in phonetic distance metrics. The findings demonstrate that a genetic algorithm is a viable tool for context optimization; when combined with post-processing corrections based on phonetic representations, this approach effectively reduces speech recognition errors.

Deep neural networks have significantly improved decision-making systems across various domains, such as image recognition, with additional performance potential offered by ensemble methods. Nevertheless, constructing ensembles of deep networks often yields limited benefits due to the prohibitive training time or marginal gains in performance. This paper examines the Error Correcting Output Coding (ECOC) framework as an ensemble strategy for deep networks, proposing novel design approaches to balance accuracy and computational complexity.
