Validation through two simulated and two real-world datasets demonstrates that this new method outperforms standard BSL in terms of accuracy when the assumed model is misspecified.

Federated learning (FL) represents a machine learning framework that ensures data privacy while enabling distributed clients to collaboratively train models. In an FL scenario, a task publisher compensates the FL server financially, which then distributes the task to participating clients. Designing appropriate incentives for these clients is difficult because the training process remains private. This paper introduces a contract theory-based FL training model aimed at minimizing the incentive budget while ensuring that clients are individually rational (IR) and incentive compatible (IC) in every training round. We propose a two-dimensional contract model that formally defines two private client attributes: data quality and computational effort. To effectively aggregate the trained models, a contract-based aggregator is developed. The paper analyzes both feasible and optimal contract solutions for this model. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework and contract model effectively enhance the generalization accuracy of FL tasks when contract-based aggregation is utilized.

Reactive synthesis aims to automatically construct system implementations from specifications describing reactive, non-terminating input/output behaviors. Typically, these specifications are expressed as logical formulas or automata operating on infinite signal sequences ($\omega$-words), while implementations are modeled as transducers. Traditional approaches assume a finite signal set, whereas this paper investigates data $\omega$-words, which involve an infinite alphabet. In this framework, both specifications and implementations are defined using automata and transducers augmented with a finite collection of registers. The study examines various scenarios based on whether the specification is deterministic, universal, or nondeterministic, and whether the implementation's register count is fixed or unbounded. For unbounded scenarios, undecidability is demonstrated for both universal and nondeterministic specifications, though decidability is achieved in the deterministic case. In bounded settings, undecidability persists for nondeterministic specifications but can be resolved by prohibiting tests on input data. The technique developed to prove this latter result also enables a reproof of existing findings regarding the decidability of bounded synthesis for universal specifications.

This paper details the methodology for pre-processing 55,134 images from the non-commercial MORPH-II dataset. After the introduction, the second section provides an overview of the pre-processing pipeline's individual steps. The third section elaborates on each stage, specifying all calculations performed and linking them to the corresponding OpenCV functions. Finally, the paper concludes by discussing potential enhancements to the pre-processing pipeline identified through retrospective analysis.

This study examines the angular distributions of the triple differential cross-section (TDCS) for the (e,2e) ionization process in noble gas atoms—specifically He (1s), Ne (2s and 2p), and Ar (3p)—using both plane wave and twisted electron impact models. The theoretical framework is established within the first Born approximation. We compare the TDCS outcomes for twisted electrons, varying the orbital angular momentum quantum number $m$ and the beam's opening angle $\theta_p$, against those obtained from plane wave interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the TDCS for macroscopic atomic targets to assess how the twisted beam's opening angle $\theta_p$ influences the cross-section. Our findings indicate that peaks in both the binary and recoil regions shift away from the momentum transfer direction. Additionally, for larger opening angles, peaks associated with $p$-type orbitals in the twisted beam split into double-peak structures, a phenomenon absent in the corresponding plane wave results for the specified kinematics. Finally, the angular profiles of the averaged cross-section reveal a dependence on the opening angle that differs significantly from plane wave TDCS.

We conduct high-precision calculations of disconnected fermion loops on Graphics Processing Units to determine various nucleon matrix elements derived from lattice QCD. Among the quantities evaluated are isoscalar electromagnetic and axial vector form factors, sigma-terms, momentum fractions, and helicity. We analyze the relationship between these disconnected contributions and connected ones, highlighting the physical implications for nucleon observables that investigate its internal structure.

To enable rich and detailed discussions regarding data, we introduce a hands-free method for directly interacting with visualizations during remote presentations. By integrating dynamic charts superimposed on a presenter's webcam stream with continuous bimanual hand tracking, we enable interactions that highlight and manipulate chart elements in the foreground. These gestures serve both functional and deictic purposes, with certain actions allowing for "rhetorical flourish"—expressive movements used when discussing quantities, categories, and time intervals. We assessed this approach through two studies involving professionals who regularly present and attend data-focused meetings. The first study examined the presenter's experience, with 12 participants delivering remote presentations using our system. The second study focused on the audience, involving 17 participants who attended presentations supported by our environment. Finally, we analyze observations from both studies and discuss their implications for engaging remote audiences in data conversations.

The integration of large pre-trained models via transfer learning has significantly transformed natural language processing (NLP). The recent release of Optimus, a variational autoencoder (VAE) that merges BERT and GPT-2, demonstrates promising results when paired with generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create novel, highly human-like text. This VAE-GAN synergy circumvents the challenges of applying GANs to discrete text data and mitigates the exposure bias inherent in standard maximum likelihood approaches. Our methodology involves training GANs within the latent space while fine-tuning Optimus's decoder for single-word generation, thereby capturing both high-level sentence features and low-level word-by-word generation. We further refine the model using reinforcement learning (RL), leveraging GPT-2's architecture and incorporating entropy-based intrinsic rewards to balance text quality with diversity. Benchmarking this VAE-GAN model across three standard text generation datasets reveals that our RL-fine-tuned approach substantially outperforms the current state-of-the-art in generating high-quality text.

The recent identification of the ferroelectric nematic phase ($N_F$) raises critical questions regarding the stability of its uniform state against the formation of domain structures typical of solid ferroelectrics or space modulations of the polarization vector $\mathbf{P}$ (and its coupled nematic director) common in liquid crystals. This study employs Landau mean-field theory to examine the linear stability of a minimal model supporting both the conventional paraelectric nematic ($N$) and $N_F$ phases. Beyond standard gradient and polarization terms, the model incorporates the director flexoelectric coupling ($f$), which is standard in liquid crystal theory, as well as the flexo-dipolar coupling—a symmetry-equivalent term often neglected in literature. Our findings indicate that for easy-plane anisotropy, the uniform $N_F$ state becomes unstable toward one- or two-dimensional modulations; however, when $f \neq 0$, the threshold for 2D modulation always exceeds that of 1D. If the dipole-flexoelectric coupling is ignored, no instability occurs. Conversely, in the easy-axis case, the instability thresholds for both modulation types are identical, and instability can arise even without flexo-dipolar coupling. We speculate that these 1D or 2D modulated phases correspond to the single splay or double splay nematics discussed by Rosseto and Selinger (Phys. Rev. E 101, 052707, 2020).

Unsupervised point cloud completion focuses on reconstructing a full point cloud from a partial one without paired supervision, representing a critical yet difficult task due to the absence of direct partial-complete training data. This study introduces a new framework that learns a unified, structured latent space capable of encoding both partial and complete point clouds. Specifically, the approach maps a sequence of related partial point clouds into multiple pairs of shape and occlusion codes, which are then fused to generate representations within the shared latent space. To ensure the latent space remains structured, the method employs several constraints, including structured ranking regularization, latent code swapping, and distribution supervision on the input partial clouds. By establishing this unified and structured representation, the method achieves superior partial-complete geometric consistency and higher shape completion accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on both synthetic ShapeNet and real-world datasets such as KITTI, ScanNet, and Matterport3D.

The project addresses ongoing debates regarding Net Neutrality and the policies implemented by various network service providers, which often result in increased network congestion. By analyzing congestion traffic data, the study examines correlations between different service providers and message requests across various Autonomous Systems (AS). It evaluates the Round Trip Time (RTT) derived from time-series data to determine if specific websites receive preferential treatment. Furthermore, the project employs time-series prediction techniques to forecast future network conditions several hours or days ahead based on historical patterns.

Linear algebra operations, which involve matrices and vectors, are typically executed by invoking highly optimized kernels from libraries like BLAS and LAPACK. Since a sequence of these kernels constitutes an algorithm, and due to factors such as associativity, algebraic identities, and kernel multiplicity, a single expression can often be evaluated through numerous distinct algorithms. Although all these methods are mathematically equivalent and yield identical results in exact arithmetic, they frequently exhibit significant differences in execution speed. High-level tools and languages, including Julia, Armadillo, and Linnea, currently resolve algorithm selection by choosing the one with the lowest FLOP count. This paper investigates the reliability of FLOP count as a metric for dense linear algebra algorithms by examining "anomalies"—specific problem instances where the fastest algorithm does not correspond to the one performing the fewest FLOPs. We analyzed relatively simple expressions to determine when and why these anomalies arise, discovering that they do exist and often cluster within large, contiguous regions. Our findings show that anomalies can be either rare or abundant depending on the expression. We conclude that FLOP count is an unreliable discriminator for selecting optimal algorithms, even when using highly optimized kernels, and that most anomalies persist even after accounting for inter-kernel cache effects. We hypothesize that integrating FLOP counts with kernel performance models will substantially enhance our capacity to select the best algorithms.

Natural Language to SQL (NL2SQL) seeks to convert natural language inputs and database schemas into executable SQL queries, a capability essential for many practical internet applications. A core challenge in this domain is the joint encoding of the database schema and the user's question, a task often approached by modeling the input as a heterogeneous graph. However, this method struggles to generate effective word representations for the question text, which is critical for building a robust NL2SQL system. To address this, we introduce a Relation-aware Semi-autoregressive Semantic Parsing framework (MODN), designed to be more adaptable for NL2SQL tasks. This approach first learns relation embeddings by connecting schema entities and question words using predefined schema relations, leveraging ELECTRA and a relation-aware transformer layer as its backbone. Subsequently, it generates the SQL query using a semi-autoregressive parser guided by predefined SQL syntax. Empirical results and case studies demonstrate the model's effectiveness in enhancing word representation learning within the NL2SQL context.

We establish a semi-analytic criterion for identifying chaos in compact, eccentric multiplanet systems. Above a specific minimum semimajor-axis separation, we demonstrate that chaos onset is driven by the overlap of two-body mean motion resonances (MMRs), mirroring the behavior in two-planet systems. In this regime, secular evolution adiabatically modulates MMR widths, causing the chaotic boundary to form where resonances overlap at their maximum extent. For tightly packed two-planet systems, a near-symmetry dampens this secular modulation, accounting for the qualitative differences in chaotic boundaries compared to systems with more planets. Leveraging these findings, we develop an enhanced angular-momentum-deficit (AMD) stability criterion, defining the critical AMD below which stability is assured. This new approach introduces an exponential factor based on interplanetary separations to the Laskar and Petit (2017) formula, lowering the AMD threshold for tightly packed configurations by a factor of several. Additionally, we have released routines to calculate these chaotic boundaries to the public via the open-source SPOCK package.

In recent years, quantized graph neural networks (QGNN) have garnered significant research and industrial interest owing to their robustness and minimal computational and memory costs. However, these performance benefits have yet to be fully realized on modern GPU architectures. To address this, we present QGTC, the first Tensor Core (TC)-based framework designed to enable any-bitwidth QGNN computation on GPUs. Our approach features a novel low-bit arithmetic design utilizing low-bit data representation and bit-decomposed computation. Furthermore, we developed a CUDA kernel specifically optimized for Tensor Cores by integrating 3D-stacked bit compression, zero-tile jumping, and non-zero tile reuse techniques to systematically enhance performance. We also implemented an effective subgraph packing strategy that optimizes bandwidth to maximize data transfer efficiency between the CPU host and GPU device. By integrating QGTC with PyTorch, we ensure improved programmability and extensibility. Extensive experiments show that QGTC delivers an average 2.7x speedup over the state-of-the-art Deep Graph Library framework across various configurations.

Given a graph $\Gamma$ with at least one edge, we seek a non-zero $(0,1)$-vector within the row space of its adjacency matrix $A(\Gamma)$. Akbari, Cameron, and Khosrovshahi conjectured that for any such graph, there exists a non-zero $(0,1)$-vector in the real row space of $A(\Gamma)$ that is not identical to any row of the matrix itself. This conjecture holds trivially for complete graphs, which have a diameter of $1$. In this paper, we confirm the conjecture for all graphs with a diameter of $4$ or greater. Additionally, we present partial progress supporting the conjecture for the remaining cases where the diameter is $2$ or $3$.

We investigate the parameter space of the phenomenological Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (pMSSM), focusing on a light neutralino thermal dark matter candidate ($m_{\tilde{\chi}_1^0} \leq m_h/2$) under both positive and negative higgsino mass parameter ($\mu$) scenarios that satisfy existing collider and astrophysical constraints. Our analysis indicates that recent data from the LHC and direct detection experiments by LUX-ZEPLIN effectively exclude the $\mu>0$ case, whereas the $\mu<0$ scenario permits only a very restricted region containing light electroweakinos. This viable region lies well within the capabilities of the LHC's Run-3, and dedicated efforts to explore it are strongly warranted.

We introduce a comprehensive optimization framework for hybrid quantum-classical circuits incorporating classical parity logic. Although standard quantum algorithm optimizations typically address only pure quantum segments, there is a growing need for global optimization strategies in fields like quantum error correction and assertions. Building upon the pure-quantum circuit optimization method by Duncan et al., our approach utilizes an extended formal graphical ZX-calculus known as ZX-ground to represent hybrid circuits, enabling granular optimizations beneath the quantum-gate level. We establish a translation from hybrid circuits to diagrams possessing the graph-theoretical focused-gFlow property, which is essential for reconstructing the circuit. Subsequently, we develop several gFlow-preserving optimization rules for ZX-ground diagrams that decrease graph size and create a strategy to identify optimization opportunities by rewriting diagrams guided by a Gauss elimination process. Finally, after extracting the circuit, we outline a general method for identifying segments of circuit-like ZX-ground diagrams that can be realized using classical gates. We have realized this optimization procedure as an extension to the open-source Python library, PyZX.

We demonstrate that for any linear ordering of $[2]^n$, a large subcube exists where the ordering follows a lexicographic pattern. Leveraging this finding, we infer that every lengthy sequence possesses a long monotone subsequence supported on an affine cube. More broadly, we establish a comparable result for linear orderings of $[k]^n$: for any such ordering, we prove the existence of a large subcube on which the ordering coincides with one of approximately $\frac{(k-1)!}{2(\ln 2)^k}$ specific orderings.

The Stackelberg equilibrium represents a solution concept where a leader commits to a publicly announced strategy, prompting a follower to respond optimally. This study addresses the computation of Stackelberg equilibria in sequential games with finite or indefinite horizons, specifically when players employ history-dependent strategies. By utilizing an alternative framework known as strategies with memory, we demonstrate that strategy profiles requiring polynomial memory can be represented efficiently. We prove the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the Strong Stackelberg Equilibrium in sequential games defined on directed acyclic graphs, where strategies rely solely on memory states from a set linear in the graph's size. This finding is further extended to general directed graphs that may include cycles. Additionally, we examine the scenario involving approximate Strong Stackelberg Equilibria in games featuring chance nodes.

We introduce ReproducedPapers.org, an open digital repository designed to teach and organize machine learning reproducibility. This study evaluates the impact of reproduction projects on students and the utility of an online repository for AI researchers, utilizing anonymous self-assessment surveys with 144 respondents. The findings indicate that students engaged in reproduction projects place greater emphasis on scientific replication and develop stronger critical thinking skills. Furthermore, both students and AI researchers concur that the proposed online repository holds significant value.

The LHCb experiment analyzed a dataset from 7 TeV $pp$ collisions with an integrated luminosity of 0.9 fb$^{-1}$ to search for the rare decay $D^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$. The observed event count aligns with background predictions, yielding an upper limit of \mbox{${\cal B}(D^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-) < 6.2(7.6) \times 10^{-9}$} at \mbox{90%} \mbox{(95%)} confidence level. This finding improves upon prior measurements by more than a factor of twenty.

As the Internet of Things (IoT) evolves, the proliferation of connected devices in daily life continues to expand. This surge influences not only overall network traffic but also the specific communication quality standards, such as Quality of Service (QoS), required by IoT applications. The emergence of dynamic network management and programming technologies, notably Software-Defined Networking (SDN), enables the customization of traffic handling and QoS to address specific use cases. We introduce PSIoT-SDN, a publish/subscribe QoS-aware framework designed to orchestrate IoT traffic and manage resource allocation between IoT data aggregators and pub/sub consumers. By leveraging publish/subscribe orchestrator capabilities at IoT aggregators, the PSIoT framework facilitates edge-level QoS control, while its integration of SDN features with a bandwidth allocation model enables network-wide QoS management. Consequently, the framework's synergy with SDN allows it to dynamically adapt to bandwidth sharing orchestrated by the SDN controller, thereby optimizing bandwidth distribution and enhancing link utilization for IoT traffic.

El-Kassar and Chehade initially defined the generalized group of units for the ring modulo $n$, denoted as $U^k(Z_n)$. This concept enables a novel extension of the Euler phi function $\varphi(n)$, where $\varphi^k(n)$ represents the order of $U^k(Z_n)$. This paper introduces this newly defined function, deriving its explicit formula and investigating properties analogous to those of $\varphi(n)$. Furthermore, we explore various generalized equations involving $\varphi^k(n)$, providing complete solutions for selected cases by addressing both general and specific scenarios.

The Lovász Local Lemma (LLL) is a fundamental theorem in probability theory frequently employed within the probabilistic method to demonstrate the existence of combinatorial structures. Its basic formulation asserts that given $n$ "bad" events, each occurring with probability at most $p$ and being independent of all but $d$ other events, there exists a positive probability of avoiding all such events provided specific conditions on $p$ and $d$ are met. Although the initial proof was purely existential, significant research has focused on the algorithmic LLL, aiming to construct algorithms that assign values to random variables to successfully avoid all bad events. A landmark contribution by Moser and Tardos [JACM '10] established an efficient distributed algorithm with a round complexity of $O(\log^2 n)$. For cases with low $d$, Fischer and Ghaffari [DISC '17] further optimized this to $O(d^2+\log^{O(1)}\log n)$, a breakthrough that has become pivotal in distributed complexity theory (Chang and Pettie [SICOMP '19]).

This paper presents an enhanced algorithm for the Lovász Local Lemma that balances the tightness of the $p$ and $d$ criterion against distributed round complexity. Specifically, within the same parameter regime as Fischer and Ghaffari's work, we reduce the round complexity to $O(\frac{d}{\log d}+\log^{O(1)}\log n)$. Conversely, at the opposite end of the spectrum, we achieve a round complexity of $\log^{O(1)}\log n$ applicable to a significantly broader range of instances than previously possible.

As a primary application, we introduce the first distributed algorithm capable of $\Delta+o(\Delta)$-edge coloring a graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ in $\log^{O(1)}\log n$ rounds. This represents an almost exponential leap forward compared to prior work; notably, no algorithm with a round complexity of $\log^{o(1)} n$ had been established even for $2\Delta-2$-edge coloring.

The XENON1T experiment has observed an excess of electron recoil events, which has been attributed to either axion-like particles (ALPs) originating from the Sun or the Milky Way's dark matter halo, or alternatively to trace tritium contamination. We evaluate the support for solar and dark-matter ALP hypotheses by combining XENON1T data with various astrophysical indicators, such as horizontal branch stars, red giants, and white dwarfs, while also briefly examining the effects of ALP decays and supernova cooling. Although the datasets show significant tension regarding solar ALPs, they can be reconciled if ALPs constitute a sub-dominant fraction of dark matter. However, this scenario necessitates tuning several previously unknown parameters; consequently, our Bayesian analysis, given the chosen priors, finds no compelling evidence favoring the ALP explanation over the background hypothesis.

This research investigates the separability of mixtures of Dicke states, specifically focusing on Diagonal Symmetric (DS) states. We demonstrate that determining separability for DS states in $C^d\otimes C^d$ (symmetric qudits) can be recast as a quadratic conic optimization problem. This bridge enables the cross-pollination of concepts between quantum information theory and mathematical optimization; notably, copositive matrices emerge as indecomposable entanglement witnesses for DS states. Consequently, we establish that the Positive Partial Transposition (PPT) criterion is both necessary and sufficient for separability when $d \leq 4$. For $d \geq 5$, we construct analytic examples of PPT-entangled states. Additionally, we derive new sufficient conditions for separability that extend beyond the PPT limit for bipartite DS states. Finally, examining $N$-partite DS qubits—where PPT is already known to be necessary and sufficient for separability—we introduce a family of nearly DS states that remain PPT across all partitions yet retain entanglement.

The paper explicitly investigates the Hitchin system constrained to Higgs fields within a fixed very stable rank 2 bundle for genus 2 and 3. The resulting families of quadrics connect to the geometry of Penrose's twistor spaces and various classical findings.

Cities represent critical focal points for climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies. To analyze, forecast, and enhance urban energy efficiency, researchers employ numerical models that simulate interactions between cities and the atmosphere across various scales via heat and moisture exchanges. This review highlights recent breakthroughs in statistical physics, which extend established path-integral methods to non-linear coupled systems, alongside the technological revolutions in computer graphics from the last decade. We contend that this unique convergence of advancements in mathematics, physics, computer science, and engineering offers significant potential for urban climate modeling. We demonstrate this potential through coupled heat transfer simulations within complex urban geometries under diverse atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, we underscore the broader applicability of these methodologies for addressing the core challenges of the energy transition that societies must master.

This study introduces two fundamental queueing models for service platforms within the digital sharing economy, differentiated by their respective platform matching information policies. We demonstrate that these models can be formulated as level-independent quasi birth-and-death (QBD) processes. Leveraging these QBD frameworks, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the platforms, examining system stability, the average steady-state counts of seekers and idle owners, the expected sojourn time for arriving seekers, and the anticipated profits for both the platform and individual owners. Furthermore, numerical examples are utilized to validate our theoretical findings and illustrate how key system parameters impact platform performance metrics. We contend that the methodology and results presented here not only facilitate the development of a wide range of service platform queueing models but also pave the way for innovative research in performance evaluation, optimal control, and queueing-game dynamics within the context of service platforms and the digital sharing economy.

This paper presents a Zariski-like topology defined on the spectrum of all proper ideals within a ring. We demonstrate that this space is T_0 and quasi-compact, with every irreducible closed subset possessing a unique generic point. Additionally, the space is strictly weaker than a spectral space, and if the ring contains a non-trivial idempotent element, the space includes a closed disconnected subspace.

This paper investigates several formulations of the uncertainty principle concerning the windowed Opdam–Cherednik transform. Specifically, we demonstrate the validity of the uncertainty principle for orthonormal sequences, as well as Donoho–Stark's, Benedicks-type, and Heisenberg-type uncertainty principles, alongside a local uncertainty inequality for this transform. Furthermore, we derive a Heisenberg-type uncertainty inequality by employing the $k$-entropy of the windowed Opdam–Cherednik transform.

The emergence of blockchain technology has spawned numerous research opportunities and dialogue platforms. Nevertheless, technology transfer to the general public has not yet occurred, preventing widespread access to secure, decentralized software. Currently, most blockchain solutions focus on financial applications and monetary transactions, which often fail to benefit or remain accessible to the general public, particularly those at lower income levels. Medi-Chain is a people-centric medical blockchain featuring an intuitive desktop application and interface that leverages advanced blockchain technology and BFT consensus protocols to guarantee highly secure and private medical records. This paper seeks to shift the perception of blockchains-as-a-service and demonstrate that the adoption of new technologies should primarily depend on usability and ease of integration.

The Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) is currently mapping the entire sky north of $-40^{\circ}$ in the S-band ($2<\nu<4\,$GHz), achieving an angular resolution of $2''.5$, which is the highest among all-sky radio continuum surveys to date. The survey is divided into three distinct epochs, with the first now fully completed. Utilizing Quick Look images from this initial epoch, we have compiled a catalog containing $1.9\times10^{6}$ reliably detected radio sources. However, limitations in these Quick Look images result in flux density underestimations of approximately $15\,\%$ for components with $S_{\text{peak}}>3\,$mJy/beam and reduced reliability for fainter sources. We employ this catalog to conduct statistical analyses of the radio sky at $\nu \sim 3\,$GHz. Comparisons with the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty cm survey (FIRST) indicate that the typical spectral index, $\alpha$, between $1.4$ and $3\,$GHz is roughly $-0.71$. By cross-matching with FIRST and the LOFAR Two Meter Sky Survey, we investigate the color-color distributions of both point and extended sources. The resulting VLASS source counts, $dN/dS$, align with prior observations at $1.4$ and $3\,$GHz. Enhanced resolution compared to FIRST reveals excess power in the VLASS two-point correlation function at angular scales below $7''$, and causes $18\,\%$ of active galactic nuclei previously identified as single FIRST components to be resolved into multiple sources by VLASS.

Forecasting traffic time series is difficult because of intricate spatio-temporal dynamics: distinct locations often exhibit unique patterns, and patterns within a single time series can fluctuate over time, such as showing stronger temporal correlations during specific daily periods. While recent deep learning models have shown promise, they remain spatio-temporal agnostic. These models utilize a shared parameter space regardless of location or time period, assuming that temporal patterns are uniform across locations and static over time—an assumption that is often inaccurate and leads to sub-optimal performance. This work proposes a framework designed to transform spatio-temporal agnostic models into spatio-temporal aware ones. By encoding time series from various locations into stochastic variables, we generate location-specific and time-varying model parameters that better capture spatio-temporal dynamics. We demonstrate how to integrate this framework with canonical attention mechanisms to create spatio-temporal aware attentions. Furthermore, to mitigate the computational overhead introduced by generating these parameters, we introduce a novel window attention scheme that reduces complexity from quadratic to linear, ensuring that spatio-temporal aware attentions remain highly efficient. Empirical results on four traffic time series datasets show that the proposed spatio-temporal aware attentions surpass state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and efficiency. This is an extended version of "Towards Spatio-Temporal Aware Traffic Time Series Forecasting," scheduled for publication in ICDE 2022 [1], which includes additional experimental results.

Solids featuring an internal angular degree of freedom are described by Cosserat, or micropolar, elasticity. This study investigates a natural extension of these materials that incorporates chiral active components and odd elasticity. We determine the static elastic properties of such a solid, demonstrating that the static response to rotational stresses generates strains influenced by both Cosserat and odd elasticity. Subsequently, we calculate the dispersion of linear solutions in the overdamped regime for these odd Cosserat materials, identifying the existence of \emph{exceptional points} within the dispersion relation. We find that these exceptional points delineate a distinct boundary between a Cosserat-dominated regime characterized by complete wave attenuation and an odd-elasticity-dominated regime allowing for wave propagation. Finally, we examine how both Cosserat and odd elastic terms affect the polarization of Rayleigh surface waves.

Currently, there is no unified agreement on how to characterize out-of-equilibrium phenomena in matter triggered by ultrashort light pulses. We examined pulse-induced dynamics in the layered Dirac semimetal SrMnBi2 using pump-and-probe photoemission spectroscopy. At approximately 1 ps, increasing the pump power resulted in a slowdown of electronic recovery, a bottleneck-like behavior anticipated by the two-temperature model (TTM), despite contradictory trends previously reported in graphite and cuprates. Later, around 100 ps, an unconventional power-law cooling emerged, suggesting that spatial heat diffusion remains ill-defined at this timescale. We determine that the sequential dynamics preceding the onset of heat diffusion represent a canonical implementation of the TTM scheme, and we also outline the criteria for the model's applicability.

Assessing the trustworthiness of a Bitcoin wallet presents a significant challenge. Currently, there are no rating systems that supply exchanges with valuable data regarding the potential taint of incoming funds. This absence of information leaves exchanges vulnerable to liability if they process stolen or illicitly obtained bitcoins. This paper addresses that issue by proposing a metric called TaintRank, which evaluates a wallet's history based on all addresses it has interacted with over time. This ranking system offers exchanges critical insights into the counterparties they are dealing with.

OptControl.jl (OptControl) is a Julia-based system that models optimal control problems using symbolic algebra and automatically generates corresponding numerical optimization scripts to solve them via Julia packages. Instead of defining a specific data type, OptControl processes Julia strings to create and execute solution scripts on demand, while also offering functionality to save these script files. Additionally, it supports component-based modeling, facilitating the construction of optimal control problems for complex systems. All dependencies for OptControl are drawn from the Julia ecosystem.

Active materials like cytoskeletal filaments, bacterial colonies, and epithelial layers display unique orientational coherence, typically defined by nematic order and topological defects. In contrast, positional coherence—specifically, how a concealed dynamic framework arranges chaotic movement—remains poorly understood, despite being a key and observable trait. By integrating dynamical systems theory, experiments with two-dimensional microtubule-kinesin mixtures, and hydrodynamic simulations, we have characterized positional coherence in active nematics. These structures manifest within Lagrangian dynamics as moving attractors and repellers that regulate complex motion. Examining the interplay between positional and orientational coherence regarding defect dynamics, our analysis of both simulations and observations reveals that +1/2 defects migrate and distort these attractors, effectively serving as control hubs for collective behavior. Furthermore, areas surrounding isolated +1/2 defects experience significant bending with minimal stretching or shearing, aligning with local stress patterns where stress is lowest at the defect itself. Conversely, high differential stress along the defect's orientation drives folding. This study provides a novel framework for describing self-organization in active fluids, with implications for multicellular systems.

Time-dependent driving offers the potential to achieve dynamical phenomena that are impossible in static systems. In this work, we present a correlated random driving protocol that establishes a spatiotemporal order unattainable even through periodic driving, thus broadening the scope of time-translation symmetry breaking to include randomly driven systems. Our findings reveal a synergy between temporally disordered microscopic motion and prethermal stroboscopic spatiotemporal long-range order. This order proves robust against generic perturbations, exhibiting an algebraically long prethermal lifetime whose scaling exponent is highly sensitive to the perturbation's symmetry—a relationship we explain analytically.

We introduce a metric tensor tailored for Riemann manifold Monte Carlo, specifically designed for non-linear Bayesian hierarchical models. This tensor is constructed from the newly proposed symmetric positive semidefinite log-density gradient covariance (LGC) matrices, which quantify the joint information and dependency structures between a random variable and its parameters. The methodology is highly automated and effectively leverages sparsity inherent in specific models. When combined with a Riemann manifold adaptation of recently developed numerical generalized randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithms, this approach proves highly competitive, especially when dealing with the complex target distributions typical of Bayesian hierarchical models.

Deep neural networks serve as potent statistical learners, yet they operate without revealing the rationale behind their predictions. To address this opacity, researchers are developing explanation techniques; we introduce OLM, a new approach tailored for natural language processing classifiers. By integrating occlusion—a core explainability technique—with language modeling, a fundamental NLP method, OLM generates explanations that are both theoretically robust and accessible.

Our work advances the theoretical framework of explanation methods by exploring axioms as a means to understand foundational principles and derive new techniques. We propose a novel axiom, elucidate its underlying intuition, and demonstrate how it conflicts with an established axiom. Furthermore, we highlight theoretical limitations inherent in current gradient-based and certain occlusion-based methods within NLP. We also present a comprehensive argument regarding the challenges associated with evaluating explanation methods. Experimentally, we compare OLM against existing approaches to highlight its distinctiveness and finally examine its edge cases to discuss validity and potential refinements.

This paper introduces a method for synthesizing dynamic 3D facial expressions starting from a neutral 3D face and an expression label. The approach addresses two core challenges: modeling the temporal dynamics of expressions and deforming a neutral mesh into an expressive one. We capture the temporal evolution of expressions through the motion of a sparse set of 3D landmarks, which are learned via a manifold-valued GAN called Motion3DGAN. To effectively encode expression-induced deformations while separating them from identity information, the generated motion is expressed as per-frame displacements relative to a neutral configuration. To produce expressive meshes, we train a Sparse2Dense mesh Decoder (S2D-Dec) that translates these landmark displacements into dense, per-vertex displacements. This enables the learning of how sparse landmark movements influence overall facial surface deformation independently of identity. Experiments on the CoMA and D3DFACS datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches in both dynamic expression generation and mesh reconstruction, while maintaining strong generalization to unseen data. The source code and pretrained models will be released publicly.

Historically, theoretical investigations of magnetism have focused primarily on classical spins or the quantum extreme of spin-1/2. Nevertheless, magnets composed of spin-1 moments hold distinct intrinsic value, particularly due to their ability to sustain both dipole and quadrupole moments at individual sites. Consequently, spin-1 models are widely examined as prototypes for quadrupolar (spin-nematic) ordering in magnetic insulators and Fe-based superconductors. However, the presence of quadrupoles means the classical limit of a spin-1 moment does not conform to an $O(3)$ vector, a nuance that must be incorporated into their characterization. This Article introduces a simulation framework for spin-1 magnets grounded in $u(3)$ algebra, treating dipole and quadrupole moments equivalently. This methodology supports both classical and quantum computations, enabling the calculation of thermodynamic properties via Monte Carlo simulations and classical low-temperature expansions, as well as dynamical properties through "molecular dynamics" and multiple-boson expansions. As an illustrative case study, we provide detailed analytic and numerical findings regarding the thermodynamics and dynamics of ferroquadrupolar order on a triangular lattice. We demonstrate that, at low temperatures, it is feasible to correct for classical statistical effects in simulations to extrapolate toward the zero-temperature quantum results predicted by flavour-wave theory.

Current deep video quality assessment (VQA) techniques often incur significant computational expenses when processing high-resolution footage, a limitation that impedes the acquisition of superior quality-related representations through end-to-end training. While existing methods typically employ naive sampling strategies—such as resizing and cropping—to mitigate these costs, such approaches inevitably degrade quality-related information, making them suboptimal for robust representation learning. Consequently, there is a critical need to develop a novel sampling scheme that preserves quality. To address this, we introduce Grid Mini-patch Sampling (GMS), which samples raw-resolution patches to capture local quality and utilizes uniformly grid-sampled mini-patches to encompass global quality through contextual relationships. These mini-patches are temporally aligned and spliced into fragments. We further develop the Fragment Attention Network (FANet), specifically tailored to process these fragments. The resulting framework, FrAgment Sample Transformer for VQA (FAST-VQA), facilitates efficient end-to-end deep VQA and learns highly effective video-quality representations. FAST-VQA enhances state-of-the-art accuracy by approximately 10% while reducing FLOPs by 99.5% on 1080P high-resolution videos. Additionally, the learned representations demonstrate transferability to smaller VQA datasets, improving performance in those contexts. Extensive experiments confirm that FAST-VQA maintains high efficiency and strong performance across various input resolutions. Our code is available at https://github.com/timothyhtimothy/FAST-VQA.

The Fermi surface in cuprates presents an anomaly, manifesting as disconnected segments known as arcs rather than the traditional closed contours of gapless excitations. Previously, the observation that these arcs grow linearly with temperature in the pseudogap phase suggested a nodal liquid state emerging below T*, interpreted as a result of d-wave pairing interacting with strong scattering. However, this study employs a novel method analyzing the temperature dependence of the density of states to detect energy gaps with enhanced sensitivity. We demonstrate that the arcs form abruptly at T* and maintain a remarkably constant length across a broad temperature interval between T* and Tarc, indicating an ordered state exists below T*. These arcs correspond to fixed momentum-space points that define specific wave vectors, serving as the distinctive signatures of the ordered state responsible for the pseudogap.

Cut selection serves as a critical subroutine in contemporary mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers, aiming to identify a subset of generated cuts that maximize solver efficiency. Given the vast number of parameter combinations available in these solvers, they are ideal candidates for parameter tuning. Typically, cut selection scoring rules function as weighted sums of various metrics, where the weights act as tunable parameters. This paper introduces a parametric family of MILPs accompanied by an infinite set of valid cuts; while some cuts can yield integer optimal solutions immediately upon application, others cannot, regardless of how many are added. We demonstrate that for a specific selection rule, any finite grid search over the parameter space inevitably fails to identify parameters that select integer-optimal-inducing cuts across an infinite subset of our problems. To address this, we propose a modification to existing graph convolutional neural networks adapted for learning cut selection parameters. Furthermore, we present a reinforcement learning framework for cut selection, training our design on the MIPLIB 2017 benchmark. Our results indicate that adaptive cut selection significantly enhances performance across diverse problem instances, though deriving a single universal function for such rules remains challenging. Reproducible code for all experiments is hosted at https://github.com/Opt-Mucca/Adaptive-Cutsel-MILP.

Distribution shifts between training and test datasets often degrade the performance of deep learning models. Recently, significant research has focused on domain generalization (DG) to handle scenarios where the target domain is unseen and distribution shifts occur. Despite advancements in algorithm design, two fundamental aspects have historically been overlooked: 1) the optimization strategies for regularization-based objectives, such as distribution alignment, and 2) model selection methods for DG, given the lack of access to target domain knowledge. This paper introduces Mixup-guided optimization and selection techniques for domain generalization. Regarding optimization, we employ an adapted Mixup approach to create an out-of-distribution dataset that guides preference directions and facilitates optimization through Pareto techniques. For model selection, we generate a validation set with a distribution closer to the target, enabling it to more accurately represent the unseen data. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights supporting our proposals. Extensive experiments across one visual classification benchmark and three time-series benchmarks demonstrate that our optimization and selection methods significantly enhance the performance of existing DG algorithms, achieving new state-of-the-art results.

This study examines how dynamo action is influenced by the combination of anisotropic electrical conductivity and anisotropic magnetic permeability. The resulting dynamo is fully axisymmetric and relies on only a simple differential rotation, a configuration that significantly challenges established dynamo theories. An entirely analytical stability analysis yields an explicit formula for the dynamo threshold. The findings reveal a competition between the anisotropies of electrical conductivity and magnetic permeability; specifically, the dynamo effect becomes impossible when these two anisotropies are identical. Furthermore, while Cowling's neutral point argument precludes an azimuthal current component in cases of isotropic electrical conductivity, it does not rule out the dynamo effect provided the magnetic permeability remains anisotropic.

Driven by growing concerns over the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of computing, major cloud providers have committed to reducing their environmental impact. Data centers possess a distinct capacity to redistribute computational tasks across various regions, creating geographic load flexibility that can mitigate emissions. This paper introduces a model where data centers adjust their loads independently of Independent System Operators (ISOs). Initially, we examine load shifting strategies guided by locational marginal carbon emissions ($\lambda_{\text{CO}_2}$), a sensitivity metric that quantifies the effect of incremental load changes. Compared to prior data center shifting models, our approach offers greater accuracy and incorporates more realistic assumptions about data center operations and electricity markets. Additionally, we propose a new benchmark model where data centers possess complete power system information to identify optimal shifts for the current period. Validated on the IEEE RTS GMLC system using five-minute load and generation data for a full year, our results demonstrate that the proposed $\lambda_{\text{CO}_2}$-based shifting model is highly effective, outperforming the benchmark model.

The Lerche-Newberger formula streamlines harmonic sums involving Bessel functions and has been utilized in the study of plasma physics and frequency-modulated quantum systems. This paper offers a rigorous proof of the formula and broadens its scope to a class of multi-dimensional extensions of single-variable Bessel functions, known as generalized Bessel functions. Because existing definitions for these functions fail to handle arbitrary complex orders, we introduce an auxiliary set of functions termed generalized Anger functions to demonstrate that the single-variable result remains valid in multiple dimensions for specific parameter choices. The study concludes with applications of these findings to physical systems.

Federated learning offers a promising solution for privacy-preserving machine learning by linking multiple computational devices into a decentralized network to overcome data silos. This paper focuses on Vertical Federated Learning (VFL), designed for situations where collaborating entities share the same user base but possess disjoint feature sets. While current VFL approaches are primarily suited for static environments where data availability remains constant for both active and passive parties, real-world data often undergoes dynamic changes. To address this limitation, we introduce DVFL, a novel VFL method that utilizes knowledge distillation to adapt to shifting data distributions. DVFL prioritizes data security and model efficiency by keeping the majority of computations local. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DVFL achieves performance comparable to existing VFL methods in static settings while successfully adapting to dynamic data distribution changes.

This article leverages specific characteristics of the transform $\mathscr{C}_{M,m}(A)=(M\mathbf1_{\mathcal{H}}-A^*)(A-m\mathbf1_{\mathcal{H}})$ to derive fresh inequalities concerning bounded linear operators $A$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Specifically, we establish novel relationships involving $|A|,|A^*|,|\mathfrak{R}A|$, and $|\mathfrak{I}A|$. Additionally, we present further inequalities regarding the numerical radius that generalize several established results.

This paper introduces a compact and precise technique for addressing problems where infinite power series solutions diverge or where series coefficients are known only up to a finite order. The approach requires only that a power series solution (or a truncation thereof) and the solution's asymptotic behavior away from the expansion point be available. We formalize the method of asymptotic approximants, which has recently shown promise in analyzing thermodynamic virial series, where typically only a few to a dozen coefficients are known. By applying a few established rules of series manipulation, we derive simple recurrence relations to construct these approximants. The resulting approximant connects two asymptotic regions of the unknown exact solution while maintaining accuracy in the intermediate range. A general algorithm for constructing such approximants is presented. To illustrate the method's versatility, we apply it to three nonlinear problems in mathematical physics: the Sakiadis boundary layer, the Blasius boundary layer, and the Flierl-Petviashvili monopole. In each case, the power series solution is underspecified because, without numerical simulations, one lower-order coefficient remains unknown, rendering all higher-order coefficients dependent on it also unknown. The constructed approximants successfully predict this missing coefficient and other key properties of each problem. Furthermore, the approximants yield new benchmark values for the Sakiadis boundary layer and align with recent numerical results for the properties of the Blasius boundary layer and the Flierl-Petviashvili monopole.

This work introduces a Hessian geometric framework for chemical thermodynamics applicable to chemical reaction networks (CRNs) possessing equilibrium states, without relying on the ideal gas assumption or mass action kinetics. We derive the conditions for the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium states by leveraging the intrinsic Legendre duality of the Hessian structure. The entropy production occurring during relaxation toward equilibrium is quantified using Bregman divergence. Moreover, the equilibrium state is defined by four distinct minimization problems of this divergence, derived from the generalized Pythagorean theorem within the context of dual flatness. In the specific case of an ideal gas, we demonstrate that our existence and uniqueness conditions entail Birch's theorem and that the divergence-based entropy production aligns with the generalized Kullback-Leibler divergence. Additionally, when applied under mass action kinetics, our general framework recovers the local detailed balance condition.

This study examines a UAV-assisted wireless communication framework incorporating energy harvesting, in which the UAV supplies energy to users via either half-duplex or full-duplex modes, while users harvest energy to transmit data back to the UAV. The primary objective is to reduce the UAV's total energy consumption while satisfying the minimum data transmission requirements of the users. The initial optimization challenge is divided into two subproblems: trajectory planning and energy minimization with a fixed trajectory. For the trajectory planning phase, the optimal visiting sequence is determined using the dual method, and the path is refined through successive convex approximation. Regarding the energy minimization phase with a fixed path, the optimal data transmission time allocation and transmission power for each user are first derived. Subsequently, this subproblem is significantly simplified and efficiently resolved using a one-dimensional search approach. Simulation outcomes are presented to validate the theoretical results.

It is established that the split Cayley hexagon of order two admits two distinct, non-equivalent embeddings into $\mathcal{W}(5,2)$, the binary symplectic polar space of rank three, termed classical and skew. By assigning labels to the 63 points of $\mathcal{W}(5,2)$ via the 63 canonical observables of the three-qubit Pauli group, in accordance with the symplectic polarity derived from the group's commutation relations, both embedding types exhibit sensitivity to quantum contextuality. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that the complement of a classically embedded hexagon lacks contextuality, while the complement of a skewly embedded one possesses it.

We report the discovery and high-cadence monitoring of SN 2018ivc, an atypical Type II supernova occurring in NGC 1068 at a distance of 10.1 Mpc. Its light curve exhibits a piecewise-linear decline with frequent slope shifts, including four distinct changes within the first 30 days, suggesting that ejecta interaction with circumstellar material significantly drives its evolution. This hypothesis is reinforced by a robust X-ray detection. Spectral analysis reveals rapid evolution dominated by emission lines from hydrogen, helium, and calcium. Notably, we detected a rare high-velocity blueshifted feature at approximately 7800 km/s across multiple lines (Ha, Hb, Pb, Pg, HeI, CaII), persisting from day 18 through day 78, which may indicate an asymmetric explosion or progenitor. Based on similarities to SN 1996al, the equivalent width of the parent HII region's Hα line, and pre-explosion Hubble Space Telescope archival constraints, the progenitor mass is likely under 12 Msun, though it could reach up to 52 Msun. SN 2018ivc underscores the critical value of early detection and rapid follow-up of nearby supernovae for understanding their physical mechanisms and origins.

The Donate Speech initiative has successfully compiled roughly 3,600 hours of natural, conversational Finnish speech for the "Lahjoita puhetta" corpus. This dataset features more than 20,000 speakers representing every region and age group in Finland. The project's main objectives were to establish a large, representative resource for analyzing spontaneous spoken Finnish and to speed up advancements in language technology and speech services. This paper details the data collection methodology and the resulting corpus, demonstrating its flexibility through various applications. These applications include automatic speech recognition for spontaneous speech, as well as the detection of age, gender, dialect, and topic, alongside metadata analysis. We offer performance benchmarks for these tasks and provide downloadable, trained baseline systems with open-source code to ensure reproducibility. Additionally, the corpus serves to validate its own metadata and transcripts, while also generating artificial metadata and transcripts for segments where such information is missing.

Building upon our prior research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we explore the potential formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) during a secondary inflationary phase driven by curvaton oscillations. By leveraging the instability inherent in the Mathieu equation, the power spectrum can be comprehensively modeled using a $\delta$ function. Accounting for the running of the curvaton mass allows us to simulate PBH abundance across nearly the entire mass spectrum, with three specific scenarios examined. In one scenario, the PBH abundance reaches approximately $75\%$, potentially accounting for dark matter. Furthermore, at late times, the relic of the exponential potential stabilizes to a constant value comparable to the cosmological constant, effectively functioning as dark energy. Consequently, this model offers a phenomenological unification of dark energy and dark matter. Finally, the study provides fresh insights into Higgs physics.

Prior research underscores the critical need for both global and local adjustments in image enhancement. Nevertheless, current convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer-based architectures struggle to balance the efficiency and effectiveness of utilizing global-local information. Specifically, most existing approaches rely on a unidirectional global-to-local fusion, neglecting the significance of bidirectional interactions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel Mutual Guidance Network (MGN) that facilitates efficient bidirectional exchange between global and local information within a compact framework. Our design employs a two-branch structure: one dedicated to capturing global relationships and the other to processing local details. Furthermore, we implement an attention-based mutual guidance mechanism across the entire framework to enable bidirectional interactions, allowing both branches to benefit from aggregated information. Additionally, to further refine the MGN's output, we propose a new residual integration strategy based on a divide-and-conquer philosophy. Extensive experiments confirm the method's efficacy, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on various public image enhancement benchmarks.

This paper presents a rigidity conjecture that connects deep diagonal pentagram maps with Poncelet polygons. Furthermore, it proves a specific instance of this conjecture: the application of a 3-diagonal map to a convex 8-gon possessing 4-fold rotational symmetry. This particular case is resolved through a standard analysis of an elliptic curve pencil.

We introduce a message passing algorithm designed for localization and tracking in environments with significant multipath interference, which inherently accounts for obstructed line-of-sight conditions. This adaptive probabilistic data association method determines a mobile agent's location using multiple anchors by leveraging the delay, amplitude, and associated uncertainties of multipath components (MPCs). By implementing a nonuniform clutter model, the algorithm allows MPC-derived position data to support agent localization without requiring precise knowledge of the environmental geometry. Furthermore, the method dynamically adjusts in real-time to fluctuations in signal-to-noise ratio and the probability of line-of-sight availability for each anchor. Numerical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm maintains reliable performance in scenarios with strong multipath propagation, even when all anchors are temporarily blocked simultaneously.

[abridged] We report new scattered light and millimeter observations of the protoplanetary disk surrounding LkH$\alpha\,330$, utilizing SPHERE/VLT and ALMA, respectively. The SPHERE scattered-light data uncover an asymmetric ring approximately 45 au from the star, alongside two spiral arms originating at similar radial distances around 90 au. ALMA millimeter observations, with a resolution of 0.06''$\times$0.4'', primarily detect an asymmetric ring at 110 au; additionally, two faint symmetric rings appear at 60 au and 200 au. CO isotopologue lines ($^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, and C$^{18}$O) show reduced abundance in the inner disk (resolution 0.16''$\times$0.11''). The $^{13}$CO peak aligns with the inner SPHERE ring, indicating it is optically thick and traces temperature variations rather than gas density changes, whereas the C$^{18}$O peak sits slightly further out at roughly 60 au. Comparing our data with hydrodynamical simulations involving gas and dust evolution, we conclude that a 10 $M_{\rm{Jup}}$ planet on an eccentric orbit ($e=0.1$) at 60 au qualitatively accounts for most observed structures. Circular orbits produce narrower millimeter emission concentrations, while higher eccentricity creates a very eccentric cavity and causes the outer spiral arm's pitch angle to vary due to eccentricity and vortex interaction, potentially manifesting as two distinct spirals. These findings identify LkH$\alpha\,330$ as a prime target for detecting embedded eccentric planets and studying planet-disk interactions.

Beyond standard class labels, numerous practical methods exist for annotating datasets used in machine learning classification. These approaches are valuable because they can streamline the annotation collection process without significantly compromising model performance; collectively, they are often referred to as weak labels or annotations. However, the relationships between these various alternatives remain ambiguous. This paper introduces a framework designed to categorize weak supervision settings, aiming to (1) assist dataset owners and annotators in selecting appropriate annotation strategies within the weak supervision landscape and (2) inform machine learning practitioners about existing dataset annotations to clarify their impact on the learning process. To achieve this, we pinpoint the defining characteristics of weak supervision and establish a set of dimensions to classify the majority of current approaches. We demonstrate how prevalent settings in the literature align with this framework and explore its practical applications.

This concise overview examines techniques and applications for modeling exoplanetary atmospheres. We explore various advanced self-consistent and retrieval models in both 1D and multi-dimensional contexts, emphasizing open questions and short- and long-term objectives within the discipline. Expertise previously cultivated in modeling cool stellar and solar system planetary atmospheres has proven highly beneficial and will remain so. We outline forthcoming opportunities to advance our understanding of atmospheric systems and conclude with the field's primary challenges.

Let $\Omega$ denote a function that is homogeneous of degree zero and vanishes on the unit sphere $\mathbb {S}^n$. This paper examines the limiting weak-type behavior of the singular integral operator $T_\Omega$ linked to a rough kernel $\Omega$. We demonstrate that if $\Omega$ belongs to $L\log L(\mathbb S^{n})$, then for any non-negative function $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, the following limit holds:
$\lim_{\lambda\to0^+}\lambda|\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:|T_\Omega(f)(x)|>\lambda\}| =
n^{-1}\|\Omega\|_{L^1(\mathbb {S}^n)}\|f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)}.$ Furthermore, when $\Omega \in L\log L(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, the quantity $n^{-1}\|\Omega\|_{L^1(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})}$ serves as a lower bound for the weak-type norm of $T_\Omega$. Additionally, we have derived corresponding results for rough bilinear singular integral operators defined by the form $T_{\vec\Omega}(f_1,f_2) = T_{\Omega_1}(f_1)\cdot T_{\Omega_2}(f_2)$.

Single-person human pose estimation enables markerless motion analysis in both sports and clinical settings; however, current state-of-the-art models often fail to satisfy the demands of real-world scenarios. While the rise of deep learning has spawned numerous advanced methods, recent progress has also led to increasingly complex and inefficient architectures, driving up computational requirements significantly. To address these issues of complexity and inefficiency, we introduce EfficientPose, a novel convolutional neural network architecture that leverages EfficientNets to provide scalable and efficient single-person pose estimation. This family of models utilizes an effective multi-scale feature extractor and computationally streamlined detection blocks based on mobile inverted bottleneck convolutions, all while enhancing pose configuration precision. Thanks to its low complexity and efficiency, EfficientPose allows deployment on edge devices by minimizing both memory usage and computational costs. Experimental results on the challenging MPII single-person benchmark demonstrate that EfficientPose substantially surpasses the widely adopted OpenPose model in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, our best-performing model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MPII dataset using low-complexity ConvNets.

This study examines how neutrino self-interactions, shock wave propagation, and matter effects influence the neutrino-process within core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe). Our hydrodynamic simulations employ two approaches: a simple thermal bomb model and a specific hydrodynamic model tailored for SN1987A. The pre-supernova structure is based on an updated model refined to match SN1987A observations, incorporating recent advancements in $(n,\gamma)$ reaction rates for nuclei near the stability line ($A \sim 100$). Regarding neutrino luminosity, we utilize both equivalent and non-equivalent models; the latter derives from synthetic analyses of CCSN simulation data that quantitatively integrate results from various neutrino transport schemes. Reaction rates for neutrino-induced processes are computed using a shell model for light nuclei and a quasi-particle random phase approximation for heavy nuclei. For each configuration, we report the abundances of light nuclei ($^7$Li, $^7$Be, $^{11}$B, $^{11}$C) and heavy nuclei ($^{92}$Nb, $^{98}$Tc, $^{138}$La, $^{180}$Ta) synthesized via the neutrino-process. Our findings indicate that light nuclei abundances are highly sensitive to the Mikheyev-Smirnov-Wolfenstein (MSW) effect in the O-Ne-Mg region, whereas heavy nuclei are predominantly formed before this region. Detailed analysis reveals that neutrino self-interaction is a crucial component alongside the MSW effect for comprehending the neutrino-process and resulting nuclear abundances. Furthermore, the normal mass hierarchy aligns better with meteorite data. We also provide an in-depth investigation of the primary nuclear reactions for each nucleus.

This study explores mutual scattering, defined as light scattering involving multiple incident beams with specific phase relationships, as a technique for retrieving structural data from opaque objects. Specifically, we examine the sensitivity with which the displacement of an individual scatterer can be detected within an optically dense medium containing up to $N=1000$ similar scatterers. Through exact calculations on ensembles of point scatterers, we contrast mutual scattering (utilizing two beams) against the conventional differential cross-section method (using one beam) to assess their responses to the positional shift of a single dipole amidst a randomly distributed array of similar dipoles. Our numerical results indicate that mutual scattering generates speckle patterns exhibiting an angular sensitivity at least tenfold greater than that of traditional single-beam approaches. By analyzing the "susceptibility" of mutual scattering, we establish the feasibility of determining the original depth of the displaced dipole relative to the incident surface within an opaque sample. Additionally, we demonstrate that mutual scattering presents a novel method for determining the complex scattering amplitude.

Utilizing topological current theory, we investigate the internal topological architecture of vortices within a two-dimensional (2D) XY model and identify the topological current associated with the order parameter field. By introducing a scalar field, $\psi$, via this theoretical framework, we re-examine the interaction energy of vortices in a 2D XY model. Our analysis covers the dynamical evolution of vortices and establishes the branch conditions for their generation, annihilation, crossing, splitting, and merging. Near the limit point during vortex growth or annihilation, we derive the dynamical scaling law for the relevant length scale in a 2D XY model as $\xi(t)\propto(t-t^*)^{1/z}$, assuming a dynamic exponent of $z=2$. This scaling behavior aligns with renormalization group theory, numerical simulations, and experimental findings. Additionally, we observe that during vortex crossing, splitting, or merging, the relevant length follows the scaling law $\xi(t)\propto(t-t^*)$. However, when vortices remain stationary during splitting or merging, the relevant length's dynamical scaling law becomes constant.

We investigate sudden quench dynamics across quantum phase transitions in diverse systems to elucidate the role of the long-time average of the Loschmidt echo in characterizing nonequilibrium quantum phase transitions. Although dynamical quantum phase transitions are marked by zero points appearing at critical times during evolution, we show that nonequilibrium transitions can be identified through nonanalyticities in the long-time averaged Loschmidt echo. These nonanalytic behaviors manifest as sharp changes in the average echo or its associated rate function, or as divergences in the second derivative of the rate function when the quench parameter crosses critical points. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the second derivative of the rate function and fidelity susceptibility.

Measurements of the differential cross section for the quasi-free photoproduction process $\gamma n\rightarrow K^0\Sigma^0$ were conducted at BGOOD/ELSA, spanning from the reaction threshold up to a center-of-mass energy of 2400 MeV. Data indicate a rise in the cross section at forward angles exceeding 2000 MeV. Although limited statistics hinder a precise characterization of this trend, the observation aligns with models featuring dynamically generated vector meson-baryon resonances—similar to those that predicted the $P_C$ states discovered by LHCb. Validating this connection would suggest a parallel between the strange and charmed quark sectors.

Message passing serves as a core mechanism for graph neural networks within the domain of graph representation learning. Relying on the homophily assumption, existing approaches typically aggregate features from connected nodes, akin to graph Laplacian smoothing. However, real-world graphs are often noisy and non-smooth, causing the homophily assumption to fail frequently and resulting in sub-optimal performance. To address this, a refined message passing strategy must preserve each node's discriminative power while aggregating neighbor information. Accordingly, we introduce Memory-based Message Passing (MMP), which decomposes a node's message into a self-embedding component for discrimination and a memory component for propagation. Additionally, we implement a control mechanism and decoupling regularization to manage the ratio of message absorption versus exclusion within the memory for each node. Crucially, MMP functions as a versatile module that can be added as an extra layer to enhance the performance of traditional GNNs. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets with differing homophily ratios confirm the method's effectiveness and robustness.

This paper extends the work of Y. Fittouhi and A. Joseph on Weierstrass sections for the parabolic adjoint action in type $A$. Let $G$ be an irreducible simple algebraic group with a Borel subgroup $B$, and let $\mathfrak n$ denote the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $B$. Consider an irreducible subgroup $P$ of $G$ that contains $B$, and let $P'$ be the derived group of $P$. Denote by $\mathfrak m$ the Lie algebra of the nilradical of $P$. According to Richardson's theorem, the algebra of $P'$ semi-invariants on $\mathfrak m$, denoted $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$, is multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety $e+V$ is defined as a Weierstrass section for the $P'$ action on $\mathfrak m$ if the restriction map creates an isomorphism between $\mathbb C[\mathfrak m]^{P'}$ and $\mathbb C[e+V]$. In this type $A$ setting, such a section is constructed in a superior form compared to that in Section 4 of the cited work. However, the primary distinction lies in shifting the focus entirely from the construction of the section to its applications.

Let $\mathscr N$ represent the nilfibre associated with this action. The construction of the Weierstrass section $e+V$ demonstrates that $e$ belongs to $\mathscr N$, and consequently, the orbit $P.e$ lies within a unique irreducible component $\mathscr C$ of $\mathscr N$. Utilizing the structure of $e+V$, an explicit description of $\mathscr C$ is provided as a $B$-saturation set, specifically in the form $\overline{B.\mathfrak u}$, where $\mathfrak u$ is a subalgebra of $\mathfrak n$. This subalgebra $\mathfrak u$ is not necessarily complemented by another subalgebra in $\mathfrak n$; therefore, $\overline{B.\mathfrak u}$ is not always an orbital variety closure (and thus not necessarily Lagrangian), although it may be.

Furthermore, it is established through purely theoretical analysis that $\mathscr C$ does not necessarily contain a dense $P$ orbit. This phenomenon occurs for a specific parabolic subgroup in $A_{10}$, which appears to be the simplest example. In this specific instance, $\mathscr C$ is confirmed not to be an orbital variety closure.

Recent studies indicate that self-supervised pre-training enhances performance on difficult visual recognition tasks compared to supervised learning. CLIP, a novel method utilizing language supervision, has shown promising results across numerous benchmarks. This research investigates whether self-supervised learning can bolster the effectiveness of language supervision in visual representation learning. We present SLIP, a multi-task framework designed to integrate self-supervised learning with CLIP pre-training. Following pre-training using Vision Transformers, we rigorously assess representation quality and compare performance against both CLIP and self-supervised methods under three scenarios: zero-shot transfer, linear classification, and end-to-end finetuning. Evaluations across ImageNet and several other datasets reveal that SLIP significantly boosts accuracy. We further corroborate these findings through experiments involving varying model sizes, training schedules, and pre-training datasets. Our results demonstrate that SLIP achieves the best of both worlds, outperforming self-supervision by +8.1% in linear accuracy and language supervision by +5.2% in zero-shot accuracy.

While the drainage and spreading of thin liquid films on substrates have garnered significant attention over recent decades, research into three-dimensional scenarios remains scarce, largely restricted to flat or axisymmetric surfaces. This study leverages differential geometry to examine these processes on general curved substrates. We first analyze drainage and spreading on spheroidal and paraboloidal surfaces using asymptotic expansions near the pole and self-similar methods, revealing that film thickness distribution is governed by the substrate's metric and tangential gravitational components. Specifically, spheroids with a high height-to-equatorial-radius ratio exhibit increasing thickness away from the pole, whereas the opposite occurs for flatter shapes. Furthermore, asymmetric coating on a toroidal substrate demonstrates that the inner region achieves greater thickness and faster spreading compared to the outer region. An ellipsoid with three distinct axes serves as a test case for three-dimensional dynamics, revealing modulations in the drainage solution and varying thickness profiles along different axes. By enforcing mass conservation, we derive an analytical expression for the average spreading front, which aligns well with both numerical simulations and experimental data from coating curing polymers on various substrates.

This paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of weak solutions for a general class of Kirchhoff equations within magnetic fractional Orlicz-Sobolev spaces.
