Our approach enables the learning of effective, domain-specific modulation parameters that integrate into a shared, domain-agnostic network. By adjusting different configuration sets, the generator can produce high-quality images tailored to specific modalities. Furthermore, this method can synthesize missing modalities across various data centers, facilitating modality completion tasks. Downstream models trained on these synthesized multi-modal samples outperform those trained on data from a single real center and achieve performance nearly equivalent to models trained on complete real-world datasets.

In this paper, I present my ongoing Ph.D. research at the University of Potsdam, supervised by T. Schaub. My primary focus is action description within Answer Set Programming (ASP), specifically investigating how to model actions with durations across various contexts. Currently, I am concentrating on Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) to analyze the representation of speeds for different agents and scenarios.

Prior to addressing duration, I aimed to explore and compare diverse representations of action execution in ASP. I initiated this by comparing several simple encodings for the MAPF problem. Even in straightforward implementations, specific choices and assumptions are inherent to their design. My objective is to demonstrate the impact of these design decisions on both performance and knowledge representation, a topic that, to my knowledge, has not yet been researched.

Additionally, I am investigating alternative methods for representing duration and solving associated problems. I intend to evaluate these methods using the same comparative approach described earlier, with the goal of identifying innovative and effective strategies for handling problems involving duration.

Gossip-based distributed algorithms are extensively employed for decentralized optimization in multi-agent systems, yet they remain susceptible to data injection attacks by internal malicious agents due to the lack of authorized oversight during local direction estimation. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) to identify such internal threats. We demonstrate that general neural networks are exceptionally well-suited for detecting and pinpointing malicious agents, given their ability to capture the nonlinear relationships within collected data. Furthermore, we suggest leveraging a state-of-the-art federated learning technique—specifically, a collaborative peer-to-peer machine learning protocol—to train these neural networks through gossip exchanges. This advanced method is anticipated to enhance model robustness against challenges related to limited training data or data distribution mismatches. Simulations involving a least-squares problem validate the feasibility and efficacy of these AI-driven approaches. The results indicate that the proposed AI-based methods significantly outperform score-based techniques in detecting and localizing malicious agents, confirming the resilience of the peer-to-peer neural network model.

We introduce unbiased estimators with finite variance for energy derivatives in real-space diffusion Monte Carlo simulations under the fixed-node approximation. The computed derivative $d_\lambda E$ remains fully consistent with the energy dependence $E(\lambda)$ obtained using the same time step. To resolve the problem of divergent variances caused by wave function node variations, we employ two regularization strategies: one based on wave function parameter gradients from variational Monte Carlo, and another utilizing a coordinate transformation. We illustrate the core divergent variance issue through a particle-in-a-box toy model and demonstrate the proposed algorithm within this framework.

This paper tackles the minimum-time steering problem for a drone modeled as a point mass with bounded acceleration and subject to gravity, navigating through a sequence of desired waypoints. Initially, we present a method to determine the minimum-time control input for steering a point mass between two waypoints using a continuous-time formulation solved via Pontryagin's Minimum Principle. Next, we compute the time-optimal trajectory across the entire set of waypoints by discretizing the time domain and formulating the problem as a nonlinear program (NLP). The velocities at each waypoint derived from this discretized NLP solution serve as boundary conditions to extend the two-point solution across the multiple waypoints. We apply this planning strategy to execute a surveying task that minimizes the total time required to fully explore a target area or volume. The study includes numerical simulations and theoretical analyses of this novel methodology, with results compared against traditional polynomial trajectories, such as minimum snap planning.

This paper outlines our methodology for tackling the EACL WANLP-2021 Shared Task 1, titled Nuanced Arabic Dialect Identification (NADI). The objective of this task is to create a system capable of determining the geographical origin (country or province) of an Arabic tweet, whether written in Modern Standard Arabic or a dialect. Our solution comprises two main components: the first involves pre-processing the dataset through cleaning, enrichment, and text segmentation, while the second entails conducting experiments with various versions of two Transformer-based models, AraBERT and AraELECTRA. Our final approach yielded macro F1-scores of 0.216, 0.235, 0.054, and 0.043 across the four subtasks, securing second place in the MSA identification subtasks and fourth place in the dialect identification subtasks.

We have investigated the transport coefficients, specifically shear viscosity and electrical conductivity, as functions of density within dense nucleonic and quark matter. By employing a simple massless limit for the quark phase and two distinct effective models for the hadronic phase, we calculated these coefficients for each phase individually. The density profiles of these coefficients were analyzed by dividing them into two components: the phase-space contribution and the relaxation time contribution. Furthermore, by computing the ratio of shear viscosity to density, we examined the conditions under which quark and hadronic matter behave as nearly perfect fluids.

The Goldbach conjecture posits that every even integer is the sum of two prime numbers. Let $D(N)$ represent the count of such prime pairs for an even number $N$. An established upper bound for $D(N)$ is given by $D(N) \leq C^* \Theta(N)$, where $\Theta(N)$ is defined as $\frac{N}{\log^2 N}\prod_{\substack{p|N, p>2}} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{p-2}\right)\prod_{p>2}\left(1-\frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\right)$, and $C^*$ is Chen's constant. While it is conjectured that $C^*=2$, Wu demonstrated in 2004 that $C^* \leq 7.8209$. In an effort to replicate Wu's calculations, we developed a refined approximation of the Buchstab function $\omega(u)$, governed by the differential equations $\omega(u)=1/u$ for $1\leq u\leq 2$ and $(u \omega(u))'=\omega(u-1)$ for $u\geq 2$, building upon the work of Cheer and Goldston. They utilized Taylor expansions centered at $u=j+1$ for the interval $[j,j+1]$; conversely, we expanded about $u=j+0.5$. This approach ensured that evaluations of $\omega(u)$ remained within a distance of $0.5$ from the expansion center, yielding significantly tighter error bounds.

Complications with applying these Taylor expansions to the necessary integrals led us to solve the differential equation directly for $\omega(u)$ before integration. Although our resulting values were lower than Wu's, we proceeded to refine his methodology by discretizing his integrals with greater precision. The resulting adjustments to Chen's constant were negligible, as anticipated by Wu. This outcome offers experimental support, though not a formal proof, suggesting that computing Wu's integrals over smaller intervals with exact forms would similarly yield negligible improvements. Consequently, achieving a substantial enhancement of Chen's constant likely demands a fundamentally different approach than the one provided by Wu.

By treating a nested sequence of topological spaces as a filtration and the emergence and vanishing of features as events, persistent homology enables the application of simple event history methods to topological data analysis. We introduce a Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard estimator, adapted for comparing topological features within random fields and testing parametric assumptions, alongside a Cox proportional hazards framework for analyzing embedded metric trees. The Nelson-Aalen approach is demonstrated using globally distributed climate data and neutral hydrogen distribution in the Milky Way, while the Cox method is applied to compare vascular patterns in fundus images from patients with diabetic retinopathy against those of healthy individuals.

Using data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and subsequent follow-up observations, we report the identification of a transiting mini-Neptune orbiting TOI-1201. This target is a moderately young ($\sim$600-800 Myr), relatively bright early M dwarf ($J \approx$ 9.5 mag) situated within an equal-mass binary system separated by approximately 8 arcseconds. The planet, TOI-1201 b, has an orbital period of 2.49 days and is classified as a warm mini-Neptune with a radius of $R_\mathrm{b} = 2.415\pm0.090 R_\oplus$. High-precision radial velocity measurements from CARMENES corroborate this detection, yielding a planetary mass of $M_\mathrm{b} = 6.28\pm0.88 M_\oplus$ and a derived bulk density of $2.45^{+0.48}_{-0.42}$ g cm$^{-3}$. Spectroscopic analysis further reveals a 19-day signal alongside a long-period variation of unknown cause. Combining these findings with ground-based photometry from WASP-South and ASAS-SN, we suggest the 19-day signal corresponds to the stellar rotation period ($P_{rot}=$ 19-23 d), though the possibility that photometric variations stem from the nearby binary companion remains unruled out. We have also determined precise stellar parameters for both TOI-1201 and its companion. With a transmission spectroscopy metric of $97^{+21}_{-16}$, the transiting planet is an ideal candidate for atmospheric characterization using the James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, its spin-orbit alignment could be measured via the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect using current high-precision spectrographs capable of sub-meter-per-second radial velocity accuracy.

Cartesian-tree pattern matching is a recently developed technique designed to identify fragments within a sequential data stream that share the structural characteristics of a query pattern. Formally, this approach aims to find all substrings $S'$ of a text string $S$ where the Cartesian tree of $S'$ is identical to that of a query pattern $P$. This paper introduces a novel indexing structure for this problem, termed the Cartesian-tree Position Heap (CPH). Let $n$ represent the length of the input text $S$, $m$ the length of the query pattern $P$, and $\sigma$ the alphabet size. We demonstrate that the CPH of $S$, denoted as $\mathsf{CPH}(S)$, facilitates pattern matching queries in $O(m (\sigma + \log (\min\{h, m\})) + occ)$ time while utilizing $O(n)$ space, where $h$ denotes the height of the CPH and $occ$ represents the number of pattern occurrences. Furthermore, we detail a method to construct $\mathsf{CPH}(S)$ in $O(n \log \sigma)$ time using $O(n)$ working space. The study also extends this problem to scenarios where the text is represented as a labeled tree, specifically a trie. For a trie $T$ containing $N$ nodes, we show that its CPH, denoted $\mathsf{CPH}(T)$), supports pattern matching queries in $O(m (\sigma^2 + \log (\min\{h, m\})) + occ)$ time with $O(N \sigma)$ space. Additionally, we present a construction algorithm for $\mathsf{CPH}(T)$ that operates in $O(N \sigma)$ time and requires $O(N \sigma)$ working space.

Proxy Means Testing (PMT) and Community-Based Targeting (CBT) represent two dominant approaches to social assistance targeting in developing nations. This paper introduces a hybrid methodology that merges CBT's focus on local knowledge and community preferences with PMT's dependence on verifiable indicators. We detail a Bayesian targeting framework similar to PMT, where beneficiary selection relies on a weighted aggregate of sociodemographic traits. However, we propose calibrating these weights using preference rankings derived from community targeting exercises, ensuring the weights mirror how potential beneficiaries themselves prioritize different sociodemographic features in decision-making. The discussion includes several practical extensions, such as accommodating multiple community rankings, adjusting for elite capture, integrating auxiliary beneficiary data, and implementing a dynamic updating mechanism. Additionally, we offer an empirical demonstration using data from Burkina Faso and Indonesia.

Neural networks (NNs) and linear stochastic estimation (LSE) are established as potent instruments for fluid-flow regression. This study examines the core distinctions between these approaches by addressing two benchmark fluid dynamics challenges: first, deriving high-order proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) coefficients from lower-order counterparts in a flow around a two-dimensional cylinder, and second, estimating the state from wall properties in a turbulent channel flow. In the cylinder scenario, the performance of LSE is contrasted with that of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), whereas the channel flow case leverages a convolutional neural network (CNN) as a nonlinear architecture capable of managing high-dimensional data. Across both scenarios, nonlinear NNs surpass linear methods due to the presence of nonlinear activation functions. Furthermore, we conduct error-curve analyses focusing on estimation error and internal weight responses. This investigation visualizes robustness against noisy perturbations within the error-curve domain while uncovering the fundamental differences between these regression tools for fluid flows.

Port Knocking is a technique used to authenticate clients via a closed firewall and authorize their access without exposing any ports, allowing servers to serve authenticated users while maintaining security. However, increasing complexity in design has hindered the effectiveness of existing port knocking solutions. This paper introduces a novel approach called Crucible, a secure authentication method that offers high usability, stealth, and the ability to keep servers and services hidden and protected. As a stateless solution, Crucible requires clients to memorize only a command, the server's IP address, and a password. It serves as a defense mechanism against various threats, including port scans and zero-day exploits. To function as a random oracle for both the client and server, the system generates cryptographic hashes using chaotic systems.

This study examines the nonlinear elliptic equation $-\Delta u = \frac{\lambda}{(a-u)^2}$ defined on a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. Originating from Micro-Electromechanical Systems (MEMS) where an elastic membrane touches a ground plate at the boundary, the analysis focuses on minimal solutions for $\lambda > 0$, assuming the function $a: \bar{\Omega} \to [0,1]$ satisfies $a(x) \ge \kappa \, {\rm dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^\gamma$ for some $\kappa > 0$ and $\gamma \in (0,1)$. The findings elucidate the influence of boundary decay on both the solutions and the pull-in voltage $\lambda$.

In Bayesian learning, Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) serve as a model prior that leverages the expressive potential of function composition. Although DGPs provide versatile modeling options, their inference remains difficult due to the intractability of marginalizing over latent function spaces. By applying Bochner's theorem, a DGP utilizing a squared exponential kernel can be interpreted as a deep trigonometric network featuring random feature layers with sine and cosine activations, alongside random weight layers. Under the wide limit with a bottleneck constraint, we demonstrate that the weight-space perspective yields identical effective covariance functions to those derived previously in function space. Furthermore, altering the prior distributions of network parameters corresponds to employing distinct kernels. Consequently, DGPs can be reformulated as deep bottlenecked trigonometric networks, facilitating exact maximum a posteriori estimation. Notably, this network representation allows for the investigation of the DGP's neural tangent kernel, potentially illuminating the mean of the otherwise intractable predictive distribution. From a statistical standpoint, unlike shallow networks, deep networks of finite width exhibit covariances that diverge from the limiting kernel, where inner and outer widths may influence feature learning differently. Numerical simulations are included to validate these conclusions.

Finite Mixture of Regressions (FMR) models are a prevalent method for addressing heterogeneity in regression analyses, yet they often fail to account for existing group structures in the data. In scenarios where clustering entire groups of observations is preferable to clustering individuals, current FMR approaches fall short. This study extends the FMR framework to incorporate such group structures, introducing the Grouped Mixture of Regressions (GMR) model. We develop a rapid fitting algorithm utilizing the Expectation-Maximization (EM) principle and demonstrate that leveraging group structure enhances prediction accuracy by sharing information within groups, as evidenced by the posterior predictive density under GMR. The efficacy of this approach is evaluated through both synthetic datasets and a real-world case study.

The study of all valid restrictions for the maximal operator within a Hilbert space is presented. A specific class of these correct restrictions is identified, characterized by a transformation whose domain aligns with that of a fixed, correct restriction. This derived theorem is then utilized to investigate the $n$-order differentiation operator featuring singular coefficients.

This study benchmarks a zero-dimensional (0D) global model (LoKI) against a one-dimensional (1D) radial fluid model simulating the positive column of oxygen DC glow discharges within a 1 cm radius tube across pressures from 0.5 to 10 Torr. By utilizing identical input data for both models, the comparison isolates the impact of dimensionality. While the models show strong agreement on primary discharge parameters, with relative differences under 5%, the match for average species number densities (both charged and neutral) is less precise. These discrepancies grow with pressure, ranging from 11% at 0.5 Torr to 57% at 10 Torr. Consequently, the effectiveness of the 0D global model in capturing these plasmas via volume-averaged quantities diminishes as pressure increases, driven by the narrowing of radial profiles. Therefore, within the investigated conditions, volume-averaged models are recommended only for pressures up to 10 Torr.

Speech enhancement serves as a foundational element for key technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, making it a vital field within audio signal processing. This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for speech enhancement that integrates a comprehensive attention mechanism into a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach. By leveraging latent information following each focal frame, this model extends earlier attention-driven recurrent neural network methods. The proposed bidirectional attention architecture demonstrates superior speech quality, as measured by PESQ, when compared to OM-LSA, CNN-LSTM, T-GSA, and the unidirectional attention-based LSTM baseline.

We introduce a semi-supervised autoencoder framework designed to classify perceived human emotions based on walking styles derived from video or motion-capture data, represented as sequences of 3D poses. The encoder hierarchically aggregates joint motions in a bottom-up fashion, adhering to the human body's kinematic chains, while constraining its latent embeddings to reflect psychologically grounded affective features inherent in gait. The decoder then reconstructs joint-specific motions at each time step in a top-down manner from these latent representations. For labeled data, a classifier is trained to map latent embeddings to emotion categories. Our semi-supervised method achieves a mean average precision of 0.84 on the Emotion-Gait benchmark, which includes both labeled and unlabeled gaits from diverse sources. We surpass current state-of-the-art algorithms for emotion and action recognition from 3D gaits by 7% to 23% in absolute terms. Notably, we enhance average precision by 10% to 50% for classes comprising less than 25% of the labeled Emotion-Gait dataset.

Zariski's local uniformization, a partial form of resolution of singularities, establishes that any valuation ring containing $\mathbf{Q}$ is a filtered direct limit of smooth $\mathbf{Q}$-algebras. For an immediate extension of valuation rings $V\subset V'$ over $\mathbf{Q}$, we demonstrate that $V'$ is a filtered direct limit of smooth $V$-algebras. This finding corrects our previous work \cite{Po1}, in which we erroneously believed that the problem could be reduced to cases with finitely generated value groups. To achieve this correction, we employ an infinite tower of ultrapowers constructed using results from model theory.

Satellites, crewed missions, and stations in low-Earth orbit (LEO) are highly susceptible to atmospheric drag, with their lifespans and orbital tracking becoming increasingly uncertain during magnetic storms. Given the anticipated surge in government and private LEO assets, there is an urgent need for precise density predictions to facilitate collision avoidance and optimize satellite lifetimes, especially during extreme events, which necessitates broad international cooperation. Furthermore, long-term solar activity models and historical records indicate a significant rise in solar activity over the coming years and decades. This article briefly reviews key advancements in understanding the thermosphere's response to extreme magnetic storms, particularly in the context of numerous new satellites equipped with state-of-the-art accelerometers capable of determining high-accuracy densities. Our findings indicate that empirical models utilizing data assimilation outperform those without it across all phases of extreme storms. We propose two avenues for improving forecasting models: first, leveraging historical extreme storm datasets to refine density predictions, and second, enhancing the assimilation of large-scale thermosphere data sets expected from future events. Consequently, this subject is of critical importance to the scientific community, government agencies operating satellites, and the private sector with LEO assets.

The effectiveness of multi-messenger astronomy hinges on gravitational-wave observatories such as LIGO and Virgo issuing immediate alerts for mergers involving neutron stars, encompassing both binary neutron star and neutron star–black hole systems. This capability critically depends on the low-frequency sensitivity of LIGO, as binary neutron star signals typically remain within this band for several minutes. Currently, LIGO's sub-60 Hz sensitivity has not met its design specifications, with excess noise exceeding an order of magnitude below 20 Hz. This limitation stems from nonlinearly coupled noises originating from auxiliary control loops, which are also nonstationary and complicate the development of realistic early-warning pipelines. However, machine-learning-based neural networks offer a solution to simultaneously enhance low-frequency sensitivity, address nonstationarity, and identify gravitational-wave signals in real time with minimal computational delay. Our proposal involves feeding both the primary gravitational-wave readout and essential auxiliary witness data into a compound neural network. Utilizing simulated data that mirrors actual LIGO detector characteristics, our networks reduce nonlinearly coupled noise by approximately a factor of five. This improvement enables the detection of typical binary neutron star and neutron star–black hole mergers up to 100 seconds and 10 seconds, respectively, prior to coalescence at distances of 40 Mpc and 160 Mpc. Furthermore, if noise levels can be reduced to the fundamental limit, these networks could extend detection ranges to 80 Mpc for binary neutron stars and 240 Mpc for neutron star–black hole systems. These results demonstrate that employing machine-learning-based neural networks is a promising avenue for the timely detection of electromagnetically bright coalescing sources in the LIGO/Virgo network.

Gender bias is a widely recognized and pervasive issue. This paper examines the depiction of gender roles in English cinema, a medium that significantly shapes societal beliefs and opinions. We began by collecting scripts from various film genres and extracting sentiments and emotions through natural language processing. These scripts were then transformed into vector embeddings for analysis. Our investigation revealed specific patterns in the personality traits of male and female characters that align with societal stereotypes. Additionally, by applying mathematical and machine learning methods, we identified biases where men are portrayed as more dominant and envious, while women are depicted with more joyful roles. To the best of our knowledge, this study introduces a novel method for converting dialogues into arrays of emotions by integrating Plutchik's wheel of emotions. Ultimately, our research aims to foster reflection on gender equality in filmmaking and enable other researchers to analyze movies automatically rather than relying on manual methods.

This article presents a physically-inspired, model-based assist-as-needed semi-autonomous control (ASC) algorithm designed to enable safe vehicle navigation (specifically for a power wheelchair) amidst static obstacles. Once deployed online, the algorithm demands minimal computational resources and utilizes pre-computed offline maps, or look-up tables. These tables are generated via policy iteration, which minimizes the expected time to safely terminate near an obstacle by accounting for (i) vehicle dynamics and (ii) driver intentions represented by three distinct stochastic processes: the expert driver, the naughty child, and the blind driver models. Empirical studies involving healthy participants demonstrated that the ASC approach significantly outperforms a baseline rule-based control system.

We present a new, explicitly invertible approximation for the normal cumulative distribution function, $\Phi(x)$, defined for $x \ge 0$ as $\Phi(x) \simeq 1/2 + 1/2\sqrt{1-{e}^{-x^2\frac{17+{x}^{2}}{26.694+2x^2}}}$. This formula maintains an absolute error below $4.00\cdot 10^{-5}$ and a relative error magnitude under $4.53\cdot 10^{-5}$. Designed primarily for practical application, it is significantly simpler than a previously published formula; although slightly less precise, it still achieves four decimal places of accuracy. Its computational complexity is comparable to the approximation of $\Phi(x)$ directly derived from Winitzki's approximation of erf$(x)$. Compared to that baseline, our method reduces the absolute error by approximately 36% and the relative error by about 28%, thereby surpassing the four-decimal precision threshold.

Building on earlier findings by Godefroy and Shapiro, we identify the conditions under which conjugate multipliers are hypercyclic, mixing, or chaotic within certain reflexive spaces of analytic functions.

The SDSS-IV MaNGA survey's spatially resolved spectroscopy has identified a prevalent class of quiescent early-type galaxies known as "red geysers," which may harbor large-scale active galactic nucleus-driven winds. Because these galaxies play a significant role in suppressing late-stage star formation, corroborating evidence that winds drive the red geyser phenomenon is essential. This study utilizes follow-up observations from the Keck telescope's Echellette Spectrograph and Imager (ESI) to examine two red geysers (z < 0.1). By employing multiple long-slit positions to map various regions within each galaxy, our data achieves a spectral resolution (R) of approximately 8000, representing a fourfold improvement over MaNGA. This enhanced resolution allows us to resolve ionized gas velocity profiles along the suspected wind cone with an instrumental resolution of σ = 16 km s⁻¹. The Hα and [NII]λ6584 line profiles exhibit asymmetric shapes that vary systematically with position: extended blue wings appear on the redshifted side, while red wings are found on the opposite side. We developed a simple wind model demonstrating that our findings align with geometric projections of an outflowing conical wind directed toward the line of sight. Conversely, an alternative hypothesis attributing the asymmetry to "beam-smearing" from a rotating, ionized gas disk fails to adequately match the observed line profile asymmetries. Although this investigation focuses on only two sources, it strengthens the hypothesis that red geysers are indeed the product of galaxy-scale winds.

This work establishes the existence of $\mathbf{m}$-fold simply-connected V-states near the unit disc for Euler-$\alpha$ equations, deriving these solutions as implicit bifurcation curves from circular patches. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of time-quasi-periodic vortex patches in proximity to Rankine vortices, provided the scale parameter $\alpha$ resides within a specific Cantor-like set of almost full Lebesgue measure. The methodology employed relies on techniques adapted from the Berti-Bolle theory regarding KAM for partial differential equations.

Iron-based superconductors have been extensively investigated using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), with significant attention directed toward the LaFeAsO family due to its high transition temperatures. Prior ARPES studies on this material revealed Fermi surfaces significantly larger than those predicted by bulk theoretical models, a discrepancy previously linked to surface states that depend on termination. In this work, we employed nano-ARPES, utilizing a sub-micron focused beam, to probe the electronic structures of both LaO and FeAs terminations in LaFeAsO. Our findings demonstrate distinct band dispersions and core-level spectra for these different surface terminations, indicating that earlier macro-focus ARPES measurements were incomplete. These results provide direct evidence for a surface-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure in LaFeAsO, specifically the formation of termination-dependent surface states at the Fermi level. Furthermore, this newly demonstrated experimental technique proves highly effective for analyzing this prototypical compound and can now be applied to investigate various materials with differing surface terminations.

Distributed optimization has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its extensive applications across diverse domains. This study re-examines the convergence behavior of decentralized gradient descent [A. Nedić-A.Ozdaglar (2009)] over the entire space defined by $$ x_i(t+1) = \sum^m_{j=1}w_{ij}x_j(t) - \alpha(t) \nabla f_i(x_i(t)), $$ utilizing a stepsize of $\alpha (t) = \frac{a}{(t+w)^p}$ where $0< p\leq 1$. Assuming strong convexity for the aggregate cost function $f$ while allowing local cost functions $f_i$ to be non-convex, we demonstrate that the sequence converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $O(t^{-p})$, provided that the parameters $a>0$ and $w>0$ are appropriately selected.

In sequential hypothesis testing, Generalized Binary Search (GBS) is a strategy that greedily selects the test yielding the maximum information gain at each step. It is established that GBS achieves an optimal query cost of $O(\log n)$ for problems meeting the $k$-neighborly condition, where any pair of tests can be linked by a sequence of tests that differ on at most $k$ hypotheses between neighbors. This paper introduces a more relaxed requirement termed "split-neighborly," which stipulates that for any set of hypotheses on which two adjacent tests disagree, there exists a test capable of splitting that subset. We demonstrate that four specific problems, which do not satisfy the $k$-neighborly condition for any constant $k$, are indeed split-neighborly. This property enables us to achieve the optimal worst-case query cost of $O(\log n)$ for these problems.

This study aims to develop a Deep Learning approach for classifying protein structures. Our Artificial Intelligence system was trained to identify complex biomolecule structures derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) database and converted into images. To extract meaningful features and achieve accurate classification, we conducted various tests using pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks, including InceptionResNetV2 and InceptionV3. Consequently, a comparative analysis of the performance of these different networks will be presented.

To overcome the "meaning conflation deficiency" inherent in word embeddings, various models have attempted to embed distinct word senses. Although these methods were initially effective for word sense induction (WSI), they have since been surpassed by task-specific techniques that leverage contextualized embeddings. However, sense embeddings and contextualization do not have to be mutually exclusive. We present PolyLM, a method that frames the learning of sense embeddings as a language modeling problem, thereby enabling the application of contextualization strategies. PolyLM relies on two core assumptions regarding word senses: first, that the probability of a word appearing in a specific context equals the sum of the probabilities of its individual senses; and second, that for any given word occurrence, one sense is significantly more plausible in that context than the others. Evaluation on WSI demonstrates that PolyLM outperforms prior sense embedding approaches and matches the current state-of-the-art specialized WSI method despite utilizing six times fewer parameters. Code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/AlanAnsell/PolyLM.

This paper introduces a sparse spectral-Galerkin scheme designed to solve second-order partial differential equations on arbitrary tetrahedra. We define generalized Koornwinder polynomials on the reference tetrahedron as basis functions, investigating their recurrence relations and differentiation properties. The resulting approach generates well-conditioned, sparse linear systems; entries are computed directly using the orthogonality of these polynomials for constant-coefficient differential equations or efficiently via a recurrence algorithm for variable coefficients. Additionally, Clenshaw algorithms are developed to evaluate polynomials within the generalized Koornwinder expansion, enhancing the method's efficiency. Numerical experiments are subsequently performed to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed Koornwinder spectral technique.

We propose a weak concept of $2\times 2$-minors for the gradients of a specific subset of $BV$ functions. For maps belonging to $BV(\mathbb{R}^2;\mathbb{R}^2)$, this concept generalizes the standard Jacobian determinant definition to include non-Sobolev maps. Leveraging this distributional Jacobian, we establish a compactness and $\Gamma$-convergence theorem for a novel model that captures the emergence of topological singularities in two dimensions, aligning with Ginzburg-Landau and core-radius methodologies. In this framework, the order parameter is an $SBV$ map $u$ with values in $\mathbb{S}^1$, and the energy comprises the squared $L^2$ norm of $\nabla u$ plus the length of the jump set of $u$ (specifically its closure) scaled by $\frac 1 \varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon$ represents a length-scale parameter. We demonstrate that within the $|\log\varepsilon|$ regime, as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$, the Jacobian distributions converge to a finite sum $\mu$ of Dirac deltas with weights that are integer multiples of $\pi$, while the resulting effective energy equals the total variation of $\mu$.

High-speed photography was used to investigate the vertical drop impacts of ferrofluids onto glass slides within a non-uniform magnetic field. The results were categorized according to the behavior of the fluid-surface contact lines and the development of peaks (Rosensweig instabilities), which influence the height of the spreading drops. Similar to crown-rim instabilities observed in conventional fluid impacts, the most prominent peaks nucleate at the spreading drop's edge and persist for a prolonged duration. The study examined impact Weber numbers between 18.0 and 489, with the vertical component of the magnetic field (B-field) adjusted from 0 to 0.37 T at the surface by varying the height of a 25 mm diameter disc magnet positioned below. The falling drop was aligned with the magnet's vertical cylindrical axis, resulting in Rosensweig instabilities without any splashing. At elevated magnetic field strengths, a stationary ring of ferrofluid forms roughly above the magnet's outer edge.

The Matrix Pair Beamformer (MPB) functions as a blind beamforming technique that leverages the temporal characteristics of the signal of interest (SOI) by performing generalized eigen-decomposition on a pair of covariance matrices. Distinguished from other blind algorithms, MPB relies exclusively on second-order statistics. Previous studies have operated under the assumption that both matrices share identical interference statistics; however, this condition often fails in scenarios involving multipath propagation or specific "smart" jammers, a phenomenon termed "matrix mismatch." This paper investigates the performance of MPB under such mismatched conditions. Initially, we introduce a comprehensive framework that encompasses current methodologies and derive the normalized output SINR. The analysis demonstrates that matrix mismatch induces a threshold effect driven by "steering vector competition." Furthermore, applying matrix perturbation theory reveals that when infinite generalized eigenvalues exist, the threshold can increase without bound as interference power rises, a scenario likely to occur with multiple periodic interferers. Finally, simulation results are provided to validate the theoretical findings.

This paper presents a general effective theory for two coupled copies of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, featuring a time-dependent bilinear interaction. Addressing a quantum quench scenario initialized with a thermofield double state, we demonstrate that the system's evolution is governed by a classical Hamiltonian acting on a complex reparametrization field. We analyze correlation functions within this framework and contrast the large-$q$ formulation with the bulk low-energy effective theory. A key focus is the "rescued black hole" scenario, where a precisely tuned time-dependent coupling drives an evolved thermofield double state into the ground state of a coupled SYK system. In the low-energy regime, this corresponds to a holographic dual geometry transitioning from an eternal black hole to a global AdS$_2$ vacuum. This geometric family enables access to the black hole interior region without requiring the rescue mechanism. By comparing the large-$q$ and low-energy descriptions, we observe that deviations from the low-energy theory become significant if the rescue process initiates late, suggesting the bulk low-energy effective theory breaks down near the black hole's inner horizon. Finally, we highlight a potential link to a two-dimensional analogue of higher-dimensional black hole singularities.

SinGAN demonstrates remarkable proficiency in learning internal patch distributions even with a constrained effective receptive field. We aim to understand how a translation-invariant convolutional generator can capture global structures using only spatially independent and identically distributed inputs. By examining SinGAN and StyleGAN2, this study reveals that this capability largely stems from implicit positional encoding introduced by zero padding within the generators; such encoding is crucial for achieving high-fidelity image generation. This phenomenon is also present in other architectures like DCGAN and PGGAN. Furthermore, we observe that zero padding creates an unbalanced spatial bias with ambiguous location relationships. To establish a superior spatial inductive bias, we explore alternative positional encodings and evaluate their impacts. Leveraging an explicit positional encoding, we introduce a novel multi-scale training strategy, demonstrating its efficacy in the state-of-the-art unconditional generator, StyleGAN2. Additionally, this explicit spatial inductive bias significantly enhances SinGAN's performance for more versatile image manipulation tasks.

Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a cornerstone of contemporary recommender systems. While existing approaches, evolving from early factorization machines to recent deep learning architectures, primarily aim to capture feature interactions and uncover behavioral patterns, they face significant limitations: label sparsity due to the vastness of the feature space relative to interactions, label noise within collected data, and insufficient utilization of domain knowledge regarding sample correlations. To tackle these issues, we introduce the Multi-Interest Self-Supervised (MISS) learning framework, which enriches feature embeddings through interest-level self-supervision. This framework employs two novel CNN-based multi-interest extractors to discover self-supervision signals by comprehensively addressing diverse interest representations (point-wise and union-wise), dependencies (short- and long-range), and correlations (inter- and intra-item). Consequently, contrastive learning losses are applied to augmented interest representations, substantially enhancing feature learning. Moreover, MISS functions as a plug-in module compatible with existing CTR models, boosting their performance. Extensive evaluations across three large-scale datasets demonstrate that MISS surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 13.55% improvement in AUC, while maintaining strong compatibility with representative deep CTR architectures.

In interior point methods (IPMs), iterative techniques are typically used to solve linear systems, with a primary focus on accelerating convergence through the design of suitable preconditioners. However, these linear solvers are often treated as black boxes employing standard termination criteria that demand a sufficient reduction in the linear system's residual. This conventional approach frequently results in unnecessary "oversolving." This paper introduces and analyzes an IPM that utilizes an inner termination criterion independent of the linear system's residual. Furthermore, new indicators for early termination are derived from a comprehensive understanding of IPM requirements. This novel technique has been adapted for the Conjugate Gradient (CG) and Minimum Residual (MINRES) methods within the IPM framework. Extensive computational testing on quadratic optimization problems—including those involving compressed sensing, image processing, and partial differential equation constraints—compares the new criterion against standard residual tests with variable tolerances. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the number of inner linear iterations, leading to substantial savings in overall IPM solution time.

Speech separation models are essential for isolating individual speakers across various speech processing applications, with deep learning approaches currently achieving state-of-the-art performance on numerous benchmarks. Among these, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have demonstrated significant promise for speech separation; however, they are limited by a fixed receptive field (RF). Recent studies in speech dereverberation indicate that the optimal RF for a TCN should vary depending on the reverberation characteristics of the signal. To address this, this work introduces deformable convolution to enable TCNs to possess dynamic receptive fields that adapt to different reverberation times for effective reverberant speech separation. On the WHAMR benchmark, the proposed models achieve an average scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SISDR) improvement of 11.1 dB over the input signal. Furthermore, a compact deformable TCN model with only 1.3M parameters is presented, delivering separation performance comparable to larger, more computationally intensive models.

We derive a partial rectifiability result concerning the free boundary of a $k$-varifold $V$. Specifically, we first enhance a theorem by Gr\"uter and Jost by demonstrating that the first variation of a general varifold with a free boundary constitutes a Radon measure. Subsequently, we establish that if the mean curvature $H$ of $V$ belongs to $L^p$ for some $p \in [1,k]$, then the set of points where the $k$-density of $V$ is either undefined or infinite possesses a Hausdorff dimension no greater than $k-p$. Leveraging this finding, we prove that, under appropriate conditions, the component of the first variation of $V$ characterized by positive and finite $(k-1)$-density is $(k-1)$-rectifiable.

Spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) is a fundamental mechanism driving numerous natural phenomena, ranging from Turing patterns in biological systems to intricate patterns in brain dynamics. This study examines whether a network of coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators can exhibit SSB when linked via dissimilar variables or conjugate coupling. Our findings reveal the emergence of SSB states characterized by coexisting distinct dynamical behaviors within the parameter space, illustrating the system's transition from symmetry breaking to out-of-phase synchronized (OPS) states while maintaining multistability. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of the feedback factor on SSB, oscillation quenching, and demonstrate that a decreasing feedback factor entirely suppresses both SSB and oscillation death. Notably, we observe that while the feedback factor eliminates symmetry breaking oscillations and standard oscillation death (OD), it leaves the nontrivial amplitude death (NAD) state unaffected. Finally, we derive analytical stability criteria for in-phase and out-of-phase oscillations, as well as for amplitude and oscillation death states.

Building upon the algebraic structure of additive conjucyclic codes over F_4 established by Abualrub et al. (Finite Fields Appl. 65 (2020) 101678), this paper aims to extend their theoretical framework. By utilizing an isomorphic mapping, we establish a canonical bijective correspondence between F_q-linear additive conjucyclic codes of length n over F_{q^2} and q-ary linear cyclic codes of length 2n. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this proposed isomorphic map preserves orthogonality under the alternating inner product. Leveraging the factorization of the polynomial x^{2n}-1 over F_q, we derive the enumeration of these F_q-linear additive conjucyclic codes. Additionally, we present the generator and parity-check matrices for these q^2-ary additive conjucyclic codes of length n.

Contextual lexical substitution serves as a highly potent technology underpinning numerous NLP tasks, including word sense induction, extraction of lexical relations, and data augmentation. This paper introduces a comprehensive, large-scale comparative analysis of prominent neural language models and masked language models (such as context2vec, ELMo, BERT, and XLNet) within the domain of lexical substitution. We demonstrate that state-of-the-art results can be further enhanced by appropriately injecting information regarding the target word, and we evaluate various methods for this injection. Furthermore, we offer an analysis of the semantic relationships between target words and their generated substitutes across different models, shedding light on the specific types of words that models produce versus those provided by human annotators.

Understanding Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) relies heavily on investigating heavy quarkonium production. This note presents measurements of the cross sections for J/ψ, χ_c, and double charm production, alongside an analysis of the prospects for measuring J/ψ polarization at LHCb.

The spatial arrangement of galaxies at small scales holds key information regarding the nature of dark matter. We introduce a new approach to describing halo distributions using persistent homology summaries, which break down point collections into clusters, loops, and voids. Applying these techniques alongside hypothesis tests to dark matter haloes within Milky Way-analog regions of CDM and WDM Copernicus Complexio $N$-body simulations, we find statistically significant distinctions (p-values $\leq$ 0.001) between the structures of the two models. The functional summaries derived from persistence diagrams identify differences at scales distinct from other spatial point process summaries, such as the two-point correlation function. These model differences are most pronounced at filtration scales of approximately 100 kpc, where CDM produces more unconnected halo clusters while WDM forms loops. Although this study focused on dark matter haloes generally, future research will extend these methods to realistic galaxy catalogs.

Ride Hailing Services (RHS) have gained widespread popularity, raising significant privacy concerns for both drivers and riders. ORide, a privacy-preserving RHS introduced at the USENIX Security Symposium in 2017, leverages Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption (SHE). In its protocol, a rider and all drivers within a specific zone transmit their encrypted coordinates to the RHS Service Provider (SP). The SP calculates the squared Euclidean distances between these points and sends them to the rider, who decrypts the values to identify the nearest driver. However, this work reveals a location-harvesting attack where an honest-but-curious rider, submitting just a single request, can pinpoint the exact coordinates of approximately half the responding drivers despite receiving only distance data. The attack's significance lies in exposing driver locations that the protocol is designed to keep hidden. We validated this attack through experiments across zones of various sizes in randomly selected major cities. The methodology involves enumerating lattice points on a circle with a sufficiently small radius and filtering solutions based on application-specific constraints. Finally, we propose a modification to ORide designed to neutralize this attack, demonstrating that it effectively maintains driver anonymity while preserving ride-matching accuracy.

Mobile Crowdsourcing (MC) offers a powerful method for mobilizing large numbers of smart devices to execute remote tasks by utilizing their inherent capabilities. This approach has garnered significant interest within smart city and urban computing sectors for delivering decentralized, rapid, and adaptable ubiquitous services. While most prior research has concentrated on non-cooperative MC schemes in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, there is a growing need for advanced collaboration strategies to harness MC potential for more intricate tasks. In this regard, Collaborative Mobile Crowdsourcing (CMC) allows requesters to engage groups of IoT users who must interact and coordinate their operations to complete complex assignments. This paper introduces and examines the novel CMC paradigm within IoT, followed by a comprehensive taxonomy of the system's constituent components. Furthermore, it explores the challenges associated with designing CMC tasks and evaluates various team formation strategies that involve both the crowdsourcing platform and designated team leaders. The study also assesses and compares the performance of specific CMC recruitment algorithms, concluding with an analysis of open research avenues to enhance CMC service design.

Topological frameworks offer a fresh avenue for advancing phonon physics, yet unlike the extensive literature on topological electronic excitations, research into topological phonons remains scarce. In this work, we introduce KMgBO3 as a novel material exhibiting the simultaneous presence of various multifold and multidimensional topological phonon modes, safeguarded by both spatial and non-spatial symmetries. These include zero-dimensional double, triple, and quadratic Weyl phonon nodes, one-dimensional nodal lines or loops, and two-dimensional doubly degenerate nodal surface states. Specifically, the nodal lines or loops originate from spin-1/2 phonon nodes, whereas the two-dimensional doubly degenerate nodal surfaces result from the interplay of twofold screw rotational and time-reversal symmetries. Applying strain disrupts C3 rotational symmetry, eliminating the spin-1 double Weyl nodes while retaining other topological characteristics; notably, strain also generates two additional single Weyl nodes that maintain the total chirality. Conversely, alloying breaks specific symmetries, largely eradicating the material's topological phonon features. Consequently, KMgBO3 emerges as a promising candidate hosting diverse Weyl points, extensive Fermi arcs, a pristine phonon spectrum, and tunable topological phonon excitations, making it an ideal subject for future theoretical and experimental studies in topological phononics.

A novel data acquisition system has been created for the high-resolution magnetic spectrometer at the superconducting Darmstadt electron linear accelerator (S-DALINAC), enabling inclusive and coincidence electron scattering experiments with event rates reaching up to 10 kHz.

Let $k$ and $d$ be integers where $k \ge d+2$. Given two $k$-colorings of a $d$-degenerate graph $G$, it is possible to transform one into the other by recoloring a single vertex at each step while maintaining a proper coloring throughout the process. Cereceda et al. confirmed this possibility, noting that the required sequence of recolorings can be exponentially long. Specifically, when $k=d+2$, some graphs require a quadratic number of recolorings, whereas if $k=2d+2$, a linear transformation is always guaranteed. In this work, we demonstrate that for all $k \ge d+4$, any two $k$-colorings of chordal graphs can be transformed into one another using at most $f(\Delta) \cdot n$ steps, where $\Delta$ represents the graph's maximum degree. Our proof is constructive, yielding a linear-time algorithm that, given two $k$-colorings $c_1$ and $c_2$, computes a linear transformation between them.

Recent research across various disciplines has employed gamification to enhance users' flow experiences. Nevertheless, the diversity of existing studies and the scarcity of secondary analyses, such as systematic literature reviews, make it challenging to establish the current state of the art in this domain. To address this gap, we performed a systematic literature review aimed at identifying: i) the gamification design methods utilized in research combining gamification and Flow Theory, ii) the specific gamification elements applied in these studies, iii) the methodologies used to assess flow experiences within gamified environments, and iv) the impact of gamification on user flow. Our findings indicate a rising interest in this field, evidenced by an increasing number of publications, with the most significant focus being on education. However, there remains no consensus on preferred research methodologies or the specific effects of gamification on user experience. Consequently, our results underscore the necessity for new experimental studies that examine how gamification influences flow across diverse settings, applications, and domains.

Instance-level alignment is a prevalent technique in person re-identification, encompassing methods such as spatial, latent semantic, and triplet alignment. This study explores an alternative alignment modality: cluster-level feature alignment across the entire dataset. Unlike traditional approaches that rely solely on local mini-batches, our method utilizes distilled anchors to expose the model to the global feature distribution of the full dataset. To achieve this, we introduce an anchor loss and examine various cluster-level alignment strategies, characterized by iterative aggregation and alignment derived from a dataset-wide perspective. Extensive experiments indicate that our methods yield consistent and substantial performance gains with minimal additional training effort, particularly after conventional training has plateaued. Both theoretically and empirically, our approach facilitates more stable and directed optimization, leading to superior representations and generalization through well-aligned embeddings.

We introduce the inaugural intensive continuum reverberation mapping investigation of the high accretion rate Seyfert galaxy Mrk 110. This source was observed nearly daily for over 200 days using Swift's X-ray and UV/optical instruments, complemented by ground-based data from Las Cumbres, the Liverpool Telescope, and Zowada Observatory, thereby broadening spectral coverage to 9100 \r{A}. Significant variability was detected across all wavelengths. Intraband lag analysis reveals two distinct behaviors based on timescale: for periods under 10 days, lags relative to the shortest UV band ($\sim1928$ \r{A}) grow with increasing wavelength, peaking at roughly 2 days for the longest band ($\sim9100$ \r{A}), aligning with standard disc reverberation models. Conversely, on longer timescales, the g-band lags Swift BAT hard X-rays by approximately 10 days, with the z-band following the g-band by a similar margin, a pattern that defies simple accretion disc reprocessing explanations. We attribute this to an interaction between accretion disc emission and diffuse continuum radiation originating from the broad line region.

Work-stealing is a widely adopted method for achieving dynamic, distributed load balancing. In this model, each process maintains its own queue of tasks, acting as both the provider and executor of work. While a process can add tasks to its queue or retrieve them for execution, it may also adopt the role of a "thief" to fetch tasks from another process's queue if its own becomes empty. Consequently, work-stealing algorithms define three core operations: Put and Take, restricted to the queue owner, and Steal, accessible only to thieves. A primary design goal is to optimize the simplicity and efficiency of Put and Take. However, it has been demonstrated that within the standard asynchronous model, these operations inevitably rely on costly atomic Read-Modify-Write instructions or expensive Read-After-Write synchronization. To address this, prior research introduced idempotent work-stealing, which eliminates atomic Read-Modify-Write and Read-After-Write patterns; yet, this approach still requires fences between writes during Put, and fences alongside Compare&Swap or reads during Steal. Furthermore, in the TSO (Total Store Order) model, where writes and reads are individually non-reorderable, fully fence-free algorithms have been developed that maintain similar properties for Put and Take, though Steal still necessitates Compare&Swap or a lock.

Recent investigations into complex language models have uncovered significant insights regarding linguistic and semantic patterns within their learned representations. This study focuses specifically on BERT to analyze and quantify the relational knowledge it encodes. By employing knowledge base completion tasks—including ranking, question answering, and named entity recognition (NER)—we examine every layer of both pre-trained and fine-tuned BERT. Our results demonstrate that knowledge is not exclusively stored in the final layers; instead, intermediate layers contribute substantially (17-60%) to the model's total relational knowledge. Furthermore, probing these intermediate layers highlights how different knowledge types emerge at varying rates. Upon fine-tuning, relational knowledge is partially lost, though the degree of forgetting depends on the fine-tuning objective rather than dataset size. We observed that ranking models experience the least forgetting and preserve the most knowledge in their final layer. Our code for replicating these experiments is available on GitHub.

We introduce a spectral viscosity method (SVM) to approximate incompressible Euler equations influenced by multiplicative noise, demonstrating that the SVM solution converges to a dissipative measure-valued martingale solution. These solutions are weak in the probabilistic sense, meaning the probability space and the driving Wiener process constitute integral components of the solution itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate a weak (measure-valued)-strong uniqueness principle and establish that approximate solutions converge strongly to the regular solution of the limit system, at least within the lifespan of the latter, leveraging the weak (measure-valued)-strong uniqueness principle inherent to the underlying system.

Vortices, characterized by closed elliptic streamlines, represent exact nonlinear solutions to the compressible Euler equation. This work employs differential geometry to establish the transformations between Cartesian and elliptic coordinates, demonstrating that within the elliptic framework, a flow with constant vorticity simplifies to $\dot{\mu}=0$ and $\dot{\nu}={\rm const}$ along the streamline $\mu_0$, which corresponds to the vortex's eccentricity.

This study presents a sub-percent precision determination of the scale using the omega baryon mass and gradient-flow techniques. The analysis utilizes 22 ensembles of $N_f=2+1+1$ highly improved, rooted staggered sea-quark configurations produced by the MILC and CalLat Collaborations. M\"obius Domain-Wall fermions serve as the valence quark action, applied to these configurations following a gradient-flow smearing procedure with a flowtime of $t_{\rm gf}=1$ in lattice units. The dataset covers four lattice spacings ($0.06 \lesssim a \lesssim 0.15$ fm), six pion masses ($130 \lesssim m_\pi \lesssim 400$ MeV), and various lattice volumes. For each ensemble, the gradient-flow scales $t_0/a^2$ and $w_0/a$, along with the omega baryon mass $a m_\Omega$, are calculated. These dimensionless products are extrapolated to the continuum and infinite volume limits and interpolated to the physical light, strange, and charm quark masses under the isospin limit. This process yields $\sqrt{t_0}=0.1422(14)$ fm and $w_0 = 0.1709(11)$ fm, incorporating all statistical and systematic uncertainties. The primary source of uncertainty is stochastic in nature, establishing a clear trajectory toward achieving a few-per-mille precision, a benchmark recently met by the Budapest-Marseille-Wuppertal Collaboration.

Consider an arbitrary positive selfadjoint operator $A$ acting on a separable Hilbert space $H$. This study examines inverse problems aimed at identifying the function $f(t)$ and the term $\phi$ within the non-local boundary value problem defined by $D_t^{\rho} u(t) + Au(t) = f(t)$ for $0 < \rho < 1$ and $0 < t \leq T$, coupled with the condition $u(\xi) = \alpha u(0) + \phi$ for $0 < \xi \leq T$, where $D_t$ denotes the Caputo derivative and $\alpha$ is a constant. The over-determination condition $u(\xi_1) = V$ is imposed for both inverse scenarios. The paper establishes existence and uniqueness theorems for these problems and analyzes how the constant $\alpha$ affects solution properties. A notable phenomenon is observed: while the forward problem may lack uniqueness for certain values of $\alpha$, the corresponding inverse problem yields a unique solution $u(t)$ for the same parameter values.

This study introduces a novel model, drawn from galactic disk structures, to describe three-dimensional Bernstein-Greene-Kruskal (BGK) modes within a plasma characterized by a uniform, finite background magnetic field. These modes represent exact nonlinear solutions to the steady-state Vlasov equation, featuring electric and magnetic potential perturbations that are localized across all three spatial dimensions while self-consistently satisfying both the Poisson equation and Ampere's Law. The existence of such solutions is demonstrated analytically for small perturbations linked to the disk species and numerically via an iterative approach that remains convergent even under moderately strong field disturbances.

In 2014, Darmon and Rotger introduced the Garrett-Rankin triple product $p$-adic $L$-function, connecting it to the image of specific diagonal cycles via the $p$-adic Abel-Jacobi map. We present a novel variant of this $L$-function and demonstrate that it adheres to symmetry relations upon permuting the three families of modular forms. Furthermore, we offer computational evidence supporting its cyclicity when these families are evaluated at even weights, while also presenting counter-examples for odd weights. To achieve this, we have extended the algorithm from arXiv:1310.4421 to accommodate ordinary projections of nearly overconvergent modular forms—rather than restricting them to overconvergent forms—and to handle certain projections over spaces of non-zero slope.

This study examines a two-species reaction-diffusion system featuring a trapping reaction ($A + B \to A$) and coagulation/annihilation processes ($A + A \to (A,0)$), where both particle types undergo Lévy flights characterized by a control parameter $0 < \sigma < 2$, resulting in superdiffusive dynamics. It is established that the density and correlation function of target particles $B$ scale with nontrivial universal exponents when the spatial dimension $d$ does not exceed the critical dimension $d_c$. Utilizing the renormalization group approach, we determine these exponents for the superdiffusive regime below the critical dimension $d_c = \sigma$. Additionally, numerical simulations were conducted for the one-dimensional case. The analytical findings regarding the decay exponent for the density of surviving $B$ particles align closely with the quantitative estimates from the simulations. Specifically, the analysis reveals that the survival probability of target particles in a superdiffusive environment exceeds that observed in systems governed by ordinary diffusion.

Epilepsy represents a highly varied and prevalent group of chronic neurological conditions, characterized by seizures, which are defined as excessive or synchronized neuronal activity. Signal processing of electroencephalograms (EEGs) is crucial for both detecting and forecasting these seizures. This paper presents a novel approach for seizure detection that leverages wavelet properties. Specifically, we employ the Maximum Overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform to minimize signal noise. By analyzing the variance within the resulting wavelet coefficients, we establish connectivity and measure communication efficiency among electrodes, noting that these metrics vary distinctly between seizure and non-seizure states. We construct an attribute space using fundamental statistical parameters derived from the denoised reconstructed signal, electrode connectivity, and information transfer efficiency. Our method was evaluated using publicly available datasets, demonstrating performance that significantly surpasses several existing approaches.

This study addresses time-domain fluorescence diffuse optical tomography (FDOT), aiming to reconstruct fluorophore distributions within biological tissue from boundary measurements. Leveraging the Laplace transform and principles of complex analysis, we establish a uniqueness theorem for this inverse problem. Subsequently, we examine numerical reconstruction methods, proposing both a non-iterative inversion approach based on peak detection and an iterative algorithm grounded in a regularizing framework. Finally, we present multiple numerical examples in a three-dimensional setting to demonstrate the efficacy of these proposed inversion strategies.

We introduce an inflationary model where the inflaton corresponds to a potential valley, a mechanism that generates $CP$ violation within the Standard Model (SM). By employing singlet scalars with appropriate nonminimal couplings to the Ricci scalar, we derive a viable inflationary trajectory along a valley formed by these scalars. An analysis of the scalar dynamics during and post-inflation indicates that the process can be effectively modeled as single-field inflation. Furthermore, if these scalars interact suitably with Standard Model components, vectorlike fermions, and right-handed neutrinos, the model can induce a CKM phase and facilitate successful leptogenesis, even at relatively low reheating temperatures.

High-performance primitives designed for mathematical operations on sparse vectors must address challenges such as skewed degree distributions and memory constraints that are rarely encountered in dense operations. We demonstrate that a sparse semiring primitive offers sufficient flexibility to support a broad spectrum of essential distance measures while preserving both performance and memory efficiency on GPUs. Furthermore, we show that this primitive serves as a foundational element, enabling numerous neighborhood-based information retrieval and machine learning algorithms to process sparse inputs. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural work to unify the computation of several critical distance measures on the GPU under a single, flexible design paradigm; we hope it establishes a robust baseline for future research in this domain. Our implementation is fully open source and is publicly accessible as part of the RAFT library of GPU-accelerated machine learning primitives (https://github.com/rapidsai/raft).

This study reveals a previously unreported characteristic of splashing drops on solid surfaces, identified by extracting image features via a feedforward neural network (FNN). Experiments involved dropping ethanol with an area-equivalent radius of approximately 1.29 mm from heights between 4 cm and 60 cm onto a hydrophilic surface, where the splashing threshold was observed at 20 cm. Images captured at the moment the drop reached half-impact were labeled as either splashing or nonsplashing to train the FNN, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 96%. By visualizing the weight matrix of the trained network, researchers identified that the contour height of the main drop body serves as a critical differentiator between splashing and nonsplashing events—a finding absent in prior literature. This feature proved significant throughout the impact process, even when 1.25 of the drop had contacted the surface. To validate this finding, the FNN was retrained to classify based solely on the main body, ignoring ejected secondary droplets; the accuracy remained above 82%, further confirming the contour height's importance. Finally, various aspects of drop impact were analyzed to explore the mechanisms behind the differences in contour height between splashing and nonsplashing scenarios.

Recommender systems are essential as they shape daily choices and behaviors through personalized suggestions. Major platforms like Netflix, YouTube, and Kindle rely on these systems to enhance user satisfaction and boost revenue. However, despite their widespread use, these systems often mirror and magnify real-world biases. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle that degrades user experience and leads to increasingly homogeneous recommendations over time. Additionally, such biased outputs can cement gender or ethnic stereotypes, thereby strengthening existing filter bubbles. This paper tackles gender bias in recommender systems that utilize explicit feedback. We introduce a model designed to measure gender bias within book rating datasets and the subsequent recommendations generated by these systems. Our primary contribution is a principled framework for mitigating bias in recommendations. Theoretically, we demonstrate that this approach yields unbiased recommendations even when the underlying data is biased. Empirical analysis using public book rating datasets confirms that the model significantly reduces bias with minimal impact on accuracy. Our method is model-agnostic, making it applicable to any recommender system. To validate its performance, we present results across four algorithms: two from the K-nearest neighbors family (UserKNN and ItemKNN) and two from the matrix factorization family (Alternating Least Squares and Singular Value Decomposition).

Topological quantum computing depends on a protected degenerate subspace to facilitate complex, noise-resistant operations. Hybrid systems utilizing non-Abelian quasiparticles, such as parafermions, offer significant potential in this regard. These particles are expected to arise at the boundary of fractional quantum Hall states and superconductors, creating a natural interface with superconducting qubits. In this study, we investigate a parafermionic fluxonium circuit and demonstrate that topological states induce a distinct periodicity within the qubit energy spectrum. Furthermore, unique signatures in the microwave spectrum reveal various parafermion coupling modes linked to the multiple tunneling of fractional quasiparticles. While finite parafermion coupling can partially lift the full degeneracy of the non-Abelian manifold, we show that this specific configuration allows for the evaluation of the system's residual protection.

Current state-of-the-art self-supervised learning (SSL) methods typically learn features by contrasting image instances or by clustering images before contrasting those clusters. In contrast, we present a straightforward mean-shift algorithm that learns representations by grouping images without relying on contrastive losses or strong prior assumptions about cluster structures. The method simply shifts each image's embedding toward the average of its neighbors. Since the nearest neighbor in our setup corresponds to an augmentation of the same image, our approach becomes identical to BYOL when configured with a single nearest neighbor rather than the five used in our experiments. On the ImageNet linear evaluation using ResNet50 after 200 epochs, our model achieves 72.4%, surpassing BYOL's performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/UMBCvision/MSF

Although neural networks have achieved significant success in computer vision and natural language processing, their application in stock market trading has been limited. To demonstrate their potential in this domain, we developed a single-layer neural network designed to recommend buying or selling stocks. This network analyzes year-long historical data by comparing the highest prices of 10 consecutive days against the subsequent 10 days. A chi-squared analysis confirmed that the model can accurately determine buy or sell decisions for specific stocks, proving that neural networks are capable of making straightforward market predictions.

Over recent years, the job market for High Energy Physics (HEP) faculty has remained stagnant, failing to keep pace with the growing number of PhDs and postdocs entering the field. Physicists pursuing careers outside traditional academia encounter significant obstacles; those hired at Predominantly Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs) and community colleges often struggle to maintain research productivity due to heavy teaching loads and limited funding. Similarly, individuals seeking industry roles may find themselves underprepared despite possessing marketable skills. However, new opportunities leveraging HEP-developed expertise are emerging in data science, machine learning, and quantum computing. Since the majority of graduates transition to industry, it is essential to reinforce current pathways and create new methods to facilitate this shift, a process that could be accelerated through stronger engagement between HEP institutions and their alumni. Concurrently, those remaining in academia at PUIs or community colleges must be empowered to continue research with adequate support and funding guidance. These institutions serve as vital gateways for inclusivity, offering an early entry point into the pipeline that can address diversity gaps and increase participation from underrepresented groups beyond national labs and traditional research universities. This report outlines a study examining these challenges within the HEP community and presents corresponding findings and recommendations.

For certain Maltsev conditions $\Sigma$, verifying that a finite algebra $\mathbf A$ satisfies $\Sigma$ on subsets of bounded size is sufficient to determine its global satisfaction. This local-global principle serves as the primary known source for tractability results regarding the decision of Maltsev conditions. This paper examines the local-global property specifically for the existence of a $G$-term, defined as an $n$-ary term invariant under variable permutations dictated by a subgroup $G \leq$ Sym($n$). Our findings demonstrate that all cyclic loop conditions, as defined by Bodirsky, Starke, and Vucaj, possess this property and are therefore decidable in polynomial time, whereas symmetric terms of arity $n > 2$ do not exhibit the local-global property.

Numerous adversarial attacks now target natural language processing systems, with most succeeding by altering individual document tokens, a strategy we term \textit{token-modification} attacks. Each such attack is characterized by a unique combination of foundational \textit{components}, including adversary constraints and specific search algorithms. Building on this insight, we conduct a survey of existing token-modification attacks to isolate their constituent components. By employing an attack-independent framework, we organize this survey to provide an effective categorization of the domain and facilitate straightforward comparisons between components. We anticipate that this survey will assist new researchers in entering this field and inspire further investigation into individual attack components.

The study investigates a warm pseudoscalar inflation model \cite{Kamali:2019ppi} within a high dissipative regime, assuming an approximately constant dissipation parameter $Q$. This analysis utilizes an intermediate solution for the scale factor, which describes the accelerated expansion of the Universe and aligns with observational data from the standard (cold) inflation framework. The authors identify a region within the model's free parameter phase-space that is notably consistent with recent observational findings. Furthermore, it is argued that the model satisfies the swampland criteria across a broad range of parameter space, while also being compatible with the TCC within a more limited parameter domain.

This extended abstract outlines the initial phases of research dedicated to in-painting techniques for art reconstruction, using M.C. Escher's "Print Gallery" lithograph as a case study. This specific artwork features a central void and adheres to a complex mathematical structure that must be maintained by the in-painting process. We detail our current progress and outline our future research directions.
