Estimating the occupations of microblog authors based on their short text offers significant advantages for numerous applications, yet it faces several hurdles. Primarily, brief text is rife with excessive lexical noise, complicating inference. Second, cognitive semantics are often obscure, with crucial linguistic features remaining latent within short content. Third, establishing a correlation between these cognitive semantic aspects and occupation-specific traits is difficult. We contend that utilizing multi-aspect cognitive features is essential for accurately linking short text to specific jobs and identifying suitable candidates for careers. To address this, we propose a novel framework that simultaneously infers short-text content and leverages cognitive features. Furthermore, this framework integrates various innovative algorithms—including curve fitting, support vector machines, and boosting modules—to enhance occupation prediction accuracy. Finally, an estimation module constructs an $R^w$-tree using coherence weights to optimize the inference outcome. Comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world Twitter data demonstrate that our cognitive multi-aspect model outperforms existing approaches in career estimation, highlighting the necessity of accounting for contextual user semantics.

This article introduces a general boundedness criterion for function pairs $(F, f)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ within the framework of weighted Lebesgue, Lorentz, (Lorentz--)Morrey, and variable Lebesgue spaces, utilizing a two-weight approach. The authors apply this criterion to provide a unified proof of the two-weight boundedness for Calderón--Zygmund operators, Littlewood--Paley $g$-functions, Lusin area functions, Littlewood--Paley $g^\ast_\lambda$-functions, and fractional integral operators across these spaces. Furthermore, by leveraging the established criterion, the study derives two-weight boundedness results for Riesz transforms, Littlewood--Paley $g$-functions, and fractional integral operators linked to second-order divergence elliptic operators with complex bounded measurable coefficients on $\mathbb{R}^n$ within the same functional settings.

We will conduct a detailed examination of the scalar potential within the Supersymmetric $SU(3)_{C}\otimes SU(3)_{L}\otimes U(1)_{N}$ Model, analyzing the masses of the standard scalar sector both with and without the inclusion of the anti-sextet.

We present a three-qubit waveguide QED architecture designed to emulate the strong coupling regime of a probe qubit situated within atom-like mirrors, a setup recently achieved experimentally in cavity-QED. Extending this framework into the deep non-Markovian domain, we highlight the critical influence of retardation on dressed resonances. This effect enables substantial enhancements in polariton lifetimes (across multiple orders of magnitude), precise resonance tuning, the emergence of Fano-like resonances, and concurrent coupling to various cavity modes. We provide exact Green function solutions for spectral resonances and simulate quantum dynamics using matrix product states, further illustrating how chiral probe qubits offer additional control over the cavity-QED system.

Quasi-Newton methods are established approaches for large-scale numerical optimization, utilizing approximations of the Jacobian for nonlinear systems or the Hessian for optimization tasks. Within the Interior Point framework, these algorithms generate low-rank updates to the matrix governing Newton systems, avoiding the computational expense of recalculating it from scratch at each step. This study demonstrates that a simplified quasi-Newton primal-dual interior point algorithm for linear programming achieves polynomial worst-case iteration complexity. The analysis covers both feasible and infeasible scenarios and examines the most prevalent neighborhoods along the central path. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first effort to establish such polynomial complexity bounds for these specific methods. Although the worst-case complexity derived from quasi-Newton directions is inevitably inferior to that achieved with exact Newton directions, quasi-Newton updates remain highly desirable for large-scale optimization, where the cost of matrix factorization significantly exceeds the cost of solving linear systems.

This study investigates the probability of fermionic particle-antiparticle pair creation within $(d+1)$-dimensional noncommutative Moyal space. By employing Seiberg-Witten maps to relate noncommutative and commutative field variables up to the first order in the noncommutative parameter $\theta$, we calculate the probability density for Dirac particle vacuum-vacuum pair production. The analysis examines and discusses scenarios involving constant electromagnetic fields, as well as electric fields that vary with time and space.

Next-generation spectrographs designed for exoplanetary atmospheric research demand highly accurate atmospheric models to properly interpret observed spectra. Enabled by space missions, these observations span a broad wavelength range from visible to mid-infrared with greater precision than previous instruments, unveiling intricate features originating from various atmospheric layers. For hot and ultra-hot Jupiters (HJs and UHJs), spectral complexity primarily stems from thermal and chemical disparities between the day and night sides. Consequently, one-dimensional plane-parallel retrieval models may fail to capture this intricacy. Furthermore, Bayesian frameworks are computationally demanding, hindering the use of full three-dimensional self-consistent models for atmospheric retrieval. We introduce TauREx 2D, a retrieval code that employs two-dimensional atmospheric models as an optimal balance between computational efficiency and accuracy for characterizing the atmospheres of the hottest planets. This tool utilizes a 2D parametrization across the limb to compute transmission spectra under the assumption of azimuthal symmetry and incorporates a thermal dissociation model for multiple species. We demonstrate that TauREx 2D effectively reduces biases between retrieved and true atmospheric parameters when applied to input observations. Additionally, we show that incorporating prior knowledge regarding the relationship between local temperature and composition is crucial for inferring atmospheric temperature structures. Finally, applying this model to a synthetic spectrum derived from a General Circulation Model (GCM) simulation of WASP-121b illustrates how two-dimensional forward models across the limb can eliminate parameter biases.

We demonstrate that chiral spin liquids can spontaneously arise in Kitaev materials that are partially amorphous, polycrystalline, or subjected to ion irradiation. In these systems, the spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry results from a non-zero density of plaquettes containing an odd number of edges, denoted as $n_{odd}$. This mechanism generates a substantial energy gap at low $n_{odd}$ values, a range consistent with typical amorphous materials and polycrystals, or it can be triggered via ion irradiation. Our findings indicate that this gap scales linearly with $n_{odd}$, reaching saturation around $n_{odd}\sim 40\%$. Through exact diagonalization, we observe that the resulting chiral spin liquid exhibits stability against Heisenberg interactions comparable to Kitaev's honeycomb spin liquid model. Consequently, our results identify numerous non-crystalline systems capable of hosting chiral spin liquids without the need for external magnetic fields.

Calculating the covariance matrix for fitted model parameters is an often overlooked task in statistics. This work presents algorithms to determine accurate covariance matrices, both by numerically differentiating the Hessian matrix and by analyzing the posterior distribution of model parameters. Assessments on two datasets, where the Hessian could be derived analytically, demonstrate that the numerical differentiation approach yields high accuracy.

Interpretable regression models are vital across various fields because they enable experts to discern variable relationships even when data is sparse. Symbolic regression tackles this challenge by exploring the entire space of potential free-form equations built from basic algebraic functions. Although this method can rediscover explicit mathematical functions, the estimation of unknown numerical constants during the search process has frequently been overlooked. We introduce a novel multi-objective memetic algorithm that leverages a differentiable Cartesian Genetic Programming representation to optimize constants throughout evolutionary iterations. Our results demonstrate that this approach matches or exceeds the performance of machine-learned black-box regression models and manually engineered fits in two space-related applications: estimating thermal power for the Mars Express mission and determining stellar ages via gyrochronology.

This work investigates the König type property within non-simple polyominoes. Specifically, we demonstrate that for closed path polyominoes, their associated polyomino ideals possess the König type, thereby generalizing the findings of Herzog and Hibi regarding simple thin polyominoes.

We present an infinite family of polynomials possessing roots modulo every positive integer yet lacking rational roots. Every polynomial within this family consists of monic quadratic factors that lack a linear term.

We calculate the flow field disturbances arising from point viscosity variations in a heterogeneous fluid under a background flow, assuming negligible fluid inertia. The resulting disturbance matches that of a force-dipole known as a stresslet. By combining theoretical analysis with numerical simulations, we demonstrate how point viscosity variations modify the hydrodynamics of active rigid particles and how this mechanism can be utilized to manipulate and steer them within microfluidic environments.

Assessing automatically generated text summaries remains a difficult challenge, as existing methods often fail to match the accuracy of human evaluations. We introduce RISE, a novel evaluation framework that adapts techniques from information retrieval. RISE is initially trained as a retrieval task using a dual-encoder architecture, allowing it to assess generated summaries against input documents without requiring gold-standard references. This makes RISE particularly effective for new datasets where reference summaries are unavailable. Extensive experiments on the SummEval benchmark demonstrate that RISE achieves a stronger correlation with human judgments than many previous approaches. Additionally, RISE exhibits data efficiency and generalizability across different languages.

This study introduces an AI-driven approach designed to enhance traditional retinal disease management and assist ophthalmologists in boosting diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. The proposed framework consists of a deep neural network (DNN) module, which features a retinal disease identifier and a clinical description generator, alongside a DNN visual explanation component. To train and validate this DNN-based system, we developed a large-scale dataset of retinal disease images. Furthermore, we provide a manually labeled retinal image dataset by ophthalmologists to serve as ground truth, enabling a qualitative demonstration of the method's effectiveness. Experimental results confirm that the approach is both quantitatively and qualitatively effective, capable of generating clinically relevant visual explanations and meaningful descriptions of retinal images.

This paper investigates the primary decomposition of the edge ideal associated with the join of graphs, expressed through data from weighted oriented graphs. Furthermore, we examine the depth and regularity of both ordinary and symbolic powers of these edge ideals. We explicitly calculate the depth and regularity for the ordinary powers of edge ideals formed by joining two graphs of isolated vertices and establish upper bounds for the regularity of their symbolic powers. For joins of two graphs where each contains at least one oriented edge, we derive exact formulas for depth and regularity, along with upper bounds for the regularity of ordinary powers. Examples demonstrate that these upper bounds are attainable but may be strict.

Combining a lexical retriever with a neural re-ranking model has achieved state-of-the-art results on large-scale information retrieval benchmarks. While this pipeline is effective for question answering and navigational tasks, it often falls short in information-seeking scenarios where users provide relevance signals through clicks or explicit feedback. To address this, our work investigates directly integrating relevance feedback into neural re-rankers using few-shot and parameter-efficient learning methods. We propose a kNN strategy that re-ranks documents based on their similarity to both the query and the user-marked relevant items. Additionally, we examine Cross-Encoder models pre-trained via meta-learning and fine-tuned per query using only the feedback documents. To assess these approaches, we adapted four existing IR datasets to the relevance feedback setting. Extensive experiments confirm that embedding relevance feedback directly into neural re-rankers boosts performance, and fusing lexical ranking with our top-performing neural model surpasses all other methods by 5.2 nDCG@20.

The goal is to sample nodes from a large, unknown graph through crawling in order to precisely estimate a specific metric. To achieve high efficiency, we design a random walk on a weighted graph that prioritizes crawling nodes and edges containing more information about the target metric. The method starts by using stratification theory to determine optimal node weights for a given estimation problem within an independence sampler. However, because these weights may be impractical for graph crawling due to structural constraints, the edge weights for our random walk must be selected to create an equilibrium distribution that balances approximating the optimal independence weights with rapid convergence. We introduce a heuristic strategy called the Stratified Weighted Random Walk (S-WRW) to meet these objectives while relying on limited data regarding graph structure and node attributes. We validate the technique through simulations and an experiment collecting samples of Facebook college users. Results demonstrate that S-WRW achieves the same estimation accuracy as a simple re-weighted random walk (RW) using 13 to 15 times fewer samples across various metrics.

In the $U(1)_X$ extension of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, we investigate a two-stage cosmological phase transition. The initial stage occurs at high temperatures, evolving from the origin along the z-coordinate axis, followed by the electroweak phase transition (EWPT). This second stage is characterized as a first-order transition featuring a barrier between two minima. We examine the necessary conditions for this specific type of phase transition to take place, anticipating a strong first-order EWPT. Using assumed parameters, we illustrate the universe's evolution through the provided figures.

Although robotic manipulation has seen major progress recently, managing non-rigid objects like clothing remains an unsolved challenge due to the uncertainty and complexity of their physical interactions. Leveraging sample data to extract useful information could significantly enhance modeling accuracy, yet training such models is difficult because of the high dimensionality of state representations. This paper introduces the Controlled Gaussian Process Dynamical Model (CGPDM), a method designed to learn high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics by projecting them onto a low-dimensional manifold. A CGPDM consists of a low-dimensional latent space with associated dynamics where external control inputs operate, along with a mapping to the observation space; the parameters for both mappings are marginalized using Gaussian Process priors. Consequently, the CGPDM reduces a high-dimensional state space to a more manageable latent space, enabling the learning of system dynamics from training data. The model's effectiveness was validated in both simulated and real-world settings, demonstrating its ability to generalize across diverse movements and accurately predict cloth motions from previously unseen control sequences.

Neuromorphic hardware relies on Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) cells to store model parameters as resistance states. However, these cells are prone to read disturb, a phenomenon where repeated access during inference causes the programmed resistance to drift, potentially degrading inference accuracy. Mitigating this issue typically requires periodic reprogramming of parameters, which incurs significant overhead. This study investigates read disturb failures in NVM cells, revealing strong dependencies on model characteristics—specifically synaptic activation and criticality—as well as the read voltage applied during inference. To address this, we propose a system software framework that leverages these dependencies to optimize parameter programming on neuromorphic hardware. Our approach utilizes a convex optimization formulation to assign synaptic weights with higher activation rates and criticality to NVM cells subjected to lower read voltages, thereby maximizing the time between necessary reprogramming events. Evaluation using various emerging inference models on a neuromorphic hardware simulator demonstrates that our framework significantly reduces system overhead.

Contemporary steganography must withstand attacks from both feature-based and convolutional neural network (CNN) steganalysis. This paper introduces a new scheme called ITE-SYN, which stands for Iteratively adversarial perturbations onto a SYNchronized-directions sub-image. The method embeds security data using synchronized modification directions to boost security, followed by iteratively increasing perturbations on sub-images to minimize the loss regarding the target CNN classifier's cover class label. The process begins by using an existing steganographic function to calculate initial costs. The cover image is then split into non-overlapping sub-images. After embedding each sub-image, costs are refined based on the clustering of modification directions, allowing the next sub-image to be embedded with these updated costs until all secret data is inserted. If the target CNN fails to classify the stego image as a cover, the costs are modified adversarially according to the signs of gradients back-propagated from the CNN. A sub-image is then re-embedded using these altered costs. This adversarial intensity is iteratively increased until the resulting stego image successfully deceives the target CNN. Experimental results show that this approach effectively strengthens security against both traditional feature-based classifiers and CNNs, including non-target models.

Bayesian model selection offers a robust framework for directly comparing models using observed data, independent of ground truth. However, the necessity of computing the marginal likelihood (model evidence) presents significant computational hurdles, often restricting its application in high-dimensional Bayesian inverse problems. Focusing on Bayesian imaging applications where images inform decision-making under uncertainty, this work introduces proximal nested sampling. This methodology adapts nested sampling—a Monte Carlo technique designed for model comparison—by leveraging proximal Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to efficiently scale to large problems and handle log-concave, non-smooth models, such as those involving $l_1$ or total-variation priors. The approach is computationally viable for problems with dimensions on the order of $10^6$ and higher, making it ideal for high-dimensional inverse imaging tasks. Validation is performed on large Gaussian models with analytically available likelihoods, followed by illustrations across various imaging scenarios to evaluate different dictionary and measurement model choices.

Real-world internet traffic is often disrupted by internal and external factors, causing sudden shifts in flow that are classified as outliers. Although deep sequence models are established for predicting complex IP traffic, their specific efficacy in handling anomalous traffic remains under-researched. This study evaluates various deep sequence models for predicting such anomalies. We implemented multiple models to forecast real traffic both with and without outliers, demonstrating the critical role of outlier detection in accurate prediction. First, anomalies were identified using two techniques: the Three-Sigma rule and Isolation Forest. Second, these abnormal data points were corrected using the Backward Filling method prior to model training. Finally, we compared the performance of different models on both raw and adjusted traffic datasets. Our experiments identified LSTM_Encoder_Decoder (LSTM_En_De) as the top performer; after adjusting outliers, it reduced the deviation between actual and predicted traffic by over 11%. Other models—including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), LSTM_En_De with an Attention layer (LSTM_En_De_Atn), and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU)—also showed improved accuracy post-adjustment, with prediction errors decreasing by 29%, 24%, 19%, and 10%, respectively. These results confirm that outliers significantly degrade prediction quality, indicating that detecting and mitigating them helps deep sequence models better learn general trends and generate more accurate forecasts.

This study introduces a new lowest-order conforming virtual element method (VEM) for planar linear elasticity under pure displacement/traction boundary conditions. The core innovation involves treating a generic polygon $K$ as an augmented polygon $\widetilde{K}$ by adding interior edge points as new vertices, thereby defining the discrete admissible space using a $V_1$-type virtual element space based on the partition $\{\widetilde{K}\}$ rather than $\{K\}$. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method achieves uniform convergence with optimal rates in both $H^1$ and $L^2$ norms relative to the Lamé constant $\lambda$. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the proposed VEM's efficacy and corroborate the theoretical findings.

This work investigates the potential of utilizing Machine Learning (ML) to characterize Dark Matter at particle colliders, specifically within the monojet and missing transverse energy (MET) channel. We establish a suite of benchmark models for analysis, including a standard WIMP candidate (SUSY neutralino), an Axion-Like Particle acting as a pseudo-Goldstone impostor, and a light Dark Matter impostor interacting via a heavy mediator. These models are evaluated against one another and the dominant Standard Model background ($Z$+jets). Our approach leverages both leading-order kinematic features and information from an additional hard jet. We examine various data representations, ranging from simple event samples of kinematic variables processed by Logistic Regression or Fully Connected Neural Networks, to data transformed into probability distribution images analyzed by Deep and Convolutional Neural Networks. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of our methodology against detector effects, the omission of kinematic variables, and variations in the number of events per image. For signals involving multiple hard jets and greater combinatorial complexity, we employ Principal Component Analysis to identify the most critical data features. Comparing all tested methods reveals that utilizing 2D images representing the combined information of multiple events substantially enhances discrimination performance.

The Hirota-Miwa equation, alternatively referred to as the discrete KP equation or octahedron recurrence, is a bilinear partial difference equation involving three independent variables. Its integrability is characterized by its emergence as the compatibility condition of a linear system, known as a Lax pair. This equation possesses an infinite family of plane wave-type reductions, defined by triples of integers or half-integers and including a quadratic exponential gauge transformation, which yield bilinear ordinary difference equations of the Somos/Gale-Robinson class. The text details the derivation of Lax pairs and presymplectic structures for these reductions to establish the Liouville integrability of certain associated maps, some of which correspond to reductions of the discrete Toda and discrete KdV equations.

We examine a specific class of matrices characterized by a rank-1 interconnection structure and establish a straightforward necessary and sufficient condition for their diagonal stability. This underlying Lyapunov function is subsequently employed to derive sufficient conditions for the diagonal stability of systems with approximately rank-1 interconnections. We then utilize this primary result as a pivotal component in a broader stability analysis concerning power systems control. Specifically, we present the inaugural theoretical stability analysis of Automatic Generation Control (AGC) within an interconnected nonlinear power system. Grounded in singular perturbation theory, our work offers theoretical validation for the established belief that AGC is stabilizing under typical operational time-scales. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our core analytical findings can be applied to gain deeper insights into the tuning and dynamic performance of AGC.

Open-domain Question Answering (ODQA) has yielded impressive outcomes through supervised learning; however, the extensive data annotation required for open domains presents an insurmountable challenge. Although unsupervised approaches for Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) or general Question Answering have been explored to some extent, unsupervised ODQA remains an unaddressed area to our knowledge. This study pioneers the field by formally defining unsupervised ODQA and introducing a suite of essential data construction techniques. Our findings demonstrate that unsupervised ODQA can achieve performance levels reaching up to 86% of those attained by supervised methods.

We examine a process $\{X_t\}_{0\leq t\leq 1}$ belonging to a fixed Wiener chaos $\mathcal{H}_n$. We derive certain non-degenerate characteristics and associated findings for this process. As an application, we demonstrate that the solution to the stochastic differential equation driven by $\{X_t\}_{0\leq t\leq 1}$ possesses a density. Our methodology depends on the interaction between Malliavin calculus and analysis on Wiener space.

Spatial and spatio-temporal model checking techniques are widely utilized across various domains, including large-scale distributed systems and signal and image analysis. Within the latter field, automatic and semi-automatic contouring in medical imaging has emerged as a highly versatile and promising application, significantly aiding professionals by enhancing explainability, facilitating easy replication, and enabling the exchange of analysis methods. Recent efforts have applied these model-checking techniques to contour tumors and associated edema in 3D magnetic resonance brain images. This current study focuses on contouring 2D images of nevi. A primary challenge in processing nevi images is their significant variability in shape, color, texture, and size. To address this, we employ a texture similarity operator alongside spatial logic operators. We evaluate our approach on a large public dataset, comparing the generated results against ground truth segmentations provided by domain experts.

This work investigates the reaction-diffusion behavior of Fibonacci anyons within a one-dimensional lattice. Beyond their spatial degrees of freedom, these anyons possess a non-Abelian internal degree of freedom described by a fusion tree. Initially, we examine pure-reaction dynamics driven by this internal DOF, starting from either an "all-$\tau$" or "completely random" fusion tree configuration. These two states represent unstable and likely stable steady states, respectively, for the internal DOF, and we derive the exact decay rates for the anyon number in both scenarios. Extending the analysis to full reaction-diffusion dynamics using the same initial conditions, we observe a distinct interplay between classical and quantum effects. While the fusion trees maintain their roles as unstable and stable steady states for the internal DOF, the position DOF dynamics map onto a hybrid classical system involving $A+A\rightarrow 0$ and $A+A\rightarrow A$ reactions. The relative rates of these classical processes are dictated by the state of the nonlocal internal DOF. At late times, the anyon density follows the scaling law $\rho(t)=\frac{c}{\sqrt{8\pi}}(Dt)^{-\Delta}$, where $D$ is a non-universal diffusion constant, $\Delta=1/2$ is a superuniversal exponent, and $c$ is a universal constant determined exactly by the fusion tree structure. Specifically, $c$ takes the values $\frac{2\varphi}{\varphi+1}$ for the all-$\tau$ case and $\frac{2(4\varphi+3)}{5(\varphi+1)}$ for the completely random case, with $\varphi=\frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}$ denoting the golden ratio. Furthermore, we analyze the two-point correlation functions.

Driven by concerns regarding interpretability, computational efficiency, and the need for principled inductive priors, researchers have sought to develop sparse neural architectures for natural language processing. If sparsity is indeed crucial for NLP, do well-trained models inherently exhibit approximate sparsity? Employing the Taxi-Euclidean norm to quantify sparsity, our analysis reveals that frequent input words correspond to concentrated activations, whereas frequent target words are linked to dispersed activations but concentrated gradients. Furthermore, even when controlling for word frequency, the gradients associated with function words remain more concentrated than those of content words.

This study offers a reanalysis of the publicly available, network-calibrated EHT 228 GHz data for M87 using conventional hybrid mapping methods. We investigated how various initial models—including point sources, disks, annuli, Gaussians, and asymmetric double Gaussians—influence the resulting images. Regardless of the starting model, the reconstructions converge on an extended source measuring approximately $44~\mu$as. Initiating the process with annulus or disk models yields images characterized by minimal noise, reduced off-source artifacts, and improved closure residuals. These results depict the source as a ring or edge-brightened disk with greater surface brightness in the southern hemisphere, aligning with prior findings. Models other than the annulus or disk produce images of similar size featuring an internal depression, though they lack the distinct ring-like clarity. An analysis of visibility amplitudes relative to UV-distance suggests a roughly circularly symmetric structure with a scale of $\sim 50~\mu$as and a sharp edge, inferred from a prominent minimum in the UV-distribution; notably, the amplitude of the secondary peak in the UV-plot favors an annular model over a flat disk. Further processing reveals a potential modest extension from the ring toward the southwest, a direction consistent with the southern jet limb observed in 3mm VLBI images at larger scales. However, since this extension aligns with a principal sidelobe of the synthesized beam, it necessitates verification through enhanced UV-coverage.

This paper offers a theoretical examination of two-photon absorption involving both classical and squeezed light, applicable when one-photon absorption to an intermediate state is either resonant or far-detuned, covering both low and high intensity regimes. While focusing on continuous-wave excitation, the methodology developed remains broadly applicable. We compute the energy extracted from an incident field using standard experimental parameters, analyzing limits where photon pairs are either narrowband or broadband relative to molecular linewidths. Our findings indicate an enhancement of two-photon absorption driven by resonant contributions from the extensive bandwidth of large squeezed light and by photon bunching under low-intensity conditions. Nevertheless, for the selected parameters, one-photon absorption remains the dominant process within the parameter space where significant two-photon absorption enhancement occurs.

Recent years have seen significant interest in automatically categorizing non-melanocytic skin lesions based on pigmentation status. However, factors such as inconsistent skin textures, irregular lesion shapes, varying degrees of depigmentation contrast, and fluctuating lighting conditions impede robust feature extraction, thereby reducing classification accuracy. This paper introduces a novel deep neural network designed to leverage input data for enhanced feature extraction. Specifically, we examine the convolutional network's field-of-view behavior to identify optimal locations for deep supervision. The process begins with activation mapping to create an object mask that isolates input regions most critical for generating classification outputs. Subsequently, the network layer whose layer-wise effective receptive field aligns with the approximated object shape in the mask is selected as the target for deep supervision. We validate the efficacy of this approach by applying various convolutional feature extractors and classifiers across three melanoma detection datasets and two vitiligo detection datasets.

We present an algorithm that identifies a minimum cut in a directed graph with edge weights, $n$ vertices, and $m$ edges within $\tilde O(n\cdot \max(m^{2/3}, n))$ time. This result surpasses the 30-year-old $\tilde O(nm)$ bound established by Hao and Olin. Our primary approach involves reducing the directed mincut problem to $\tilde O(\min(n/m^{1/3}, \sqrt{n}))$ invocations of any maxflow subroutine, which, when combined with current state-of-the-art maxflow methods, achieves the aforementioned runtime. Furthermore, our methodology enables efficient approximation algorithms for minimum cuts in directed graphs. Specifically, for both edge-weighted and vertex-weighted graphs, we provide $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation algorithms with a running time of $\tilde O(n^2 / \epsilon^2)$.

This study provides an in-depth evaluation of deep learning architectures—including CNNs, LSTMs, GRUs, their combinations, and various shallow classifiers—applied to sentiment analysis of Arabic reviews. The assessment also incorporates advanced models like the transformer architecture and the pre-trained araBERT. The research utilizes two of the largest publicly available multi-dialect Arabic review datasets, specifically for hotels and books. Contrary to findings in existing literature, the results indicate that deep learning methods surpass shallow learning techniques for both binary and multi-label classification tasks. This divergence is attributed to dataset size, which demonstrates a proportional relationship with deep learning performance. Model efficacy was measured using accuracy and F1 scores. Among shallow methods, Random Forest achieved the highest performance, followed by Decision Tree and AdaBoost. Deep learning models exhibited comparable results with standard embedding layers, whereas the transformer model yielded superior outcomes when enhanced with araBERT.

Open quantum systems form a fundamental theoretical framework for advancing new quantum technologies, as real-world quantum systems invariably interact with their surroundings. While Lindblad master equations describe the impact of Markovian environments, closed quantum systems can be analyzed using flow equations equipped with a particle-conserving generator. We extend this generator to accommodate non-Hermitian matrices and open quantum systems driven by Lindbladians, benchmarking our approach against recently suggested generators by Rosso et al. (arXiv:2007.12044). Our comparison reveals that the proposed generator yields an efficient flow with high accuracy, even when truncations are applied.

Weighted monadic second-order logic (WMSO) serves as a weighted extension of monadic second-order logic that precisely characterizes the behavior of weighted automata, with its semantics defined relative to a specific semiring. While Gastin and Monmege (2018) introduced abstract semantics to provide a general and modular proof of the equivalence between WMSO and weighted automata, this work focuses on that abstract framework. We present a complete axiomatization for both the full logic and a fragment excluding the general sum operation, offering a more granular insight into the system. Furthermore, we examine how standard decision problems for logical languages adapt to the weighted context, demonstrating that many remain decidable but retain the poor complexity characteristics of underlying first- and second-order logics. Notably, we establish that satisfiability becomes undecidable for the logic when employing abstract interpretation.

Recently, biochemists and biologists have increasingly embraced mathematical techniques and computer science applications for modeling biological systems. These computational and mathematical approaches hold immense promise for representing the structures of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). The application of automata theory to model the secondary structures of DNA and RNA has notably influenced computer science. Consequently, it is a logical objective to model RNA secondary biomolecular structures using quantum computational models. In the context of language recognition, two-way quantum finite automata featuring classical states have proven more dominant than their two-way probabilistic counterparts. The primary aim of this paper is to utilize two-way quantum finite automata with classical states for the simulation, modeling, and analysis of ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequences.

The graph fused lasso, a method that encompasses the one-dimensional fused lasso as a special case, is commonly employed to reconstruct piecewise constant signals on graphs, where adjacent nodes typically share identical values. This study addresses the problem of testing for mean differences between two connected components estimated via the graph fused lasso. A standard z-test for mean differences fails to control selective Type I error in this context because the hypothesis itself depends on the data. To resolve this, we introduce a novel testing procedure that maintains control over selective Type I error while conditioning on less information than current methods, thereby achieving significantly higher statistical power. We validate our approach through simulations and by analyzing datasets concerning drug overdose death rates and teenage birth rates across the contiguous United States. Results demonstrate that our method identifies more significant findings in both datasets.

A recent study by Liu et al. [Phys. Fluids 29, 116105 (2017)] established a universal framework for calculating aerodynamic forces on bodies in three-dimensional steady viscous and compressible flows, spanning from incompressible to supersonic conditions. This theory posits that the total force can be derived exclusively from the vorticity distribution on a single wake plane situated in the steady linear far field. Although this finding is crucial, its practical validity and performance remained unexplored until now. This paper addresses this gap by conducting Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulations of subsonic, transonic, and supersonic flows over a three-dimensional wing. We compared the aerodynamic forces predicted by the universal theory with those calculated using standard wall-stress integrals. The strong agreement between these methods provides the first confirmation of the theory's validity in three-dimensional steady viscous and compressible regimes. The theory's robust performance stems from the fact that turbulent viscosity in the wake significantly exceeds molecular viscosity, thereby substantially reducing the required distance to the steady linear far field. To further validate the theory, we compared wake plane flow structures derived from analytical results against numerical simulations and elucidated the physics behind the theory's universality by identifying distinct sources of wake vorticity.

This research investigates the asymptotic behavior of orthogonal polynomials in the complex plane linked to a specific normal matrix model. Depending on a given parameter, the model exhibits a transition in the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution at a critical value, characterized by the emergence of a corner-type singularity. Near this transition, within the double scaling limit, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the orthogonal polynomials using a solution to the Painlevé IV equation. Furthermore, we calculate the associated Fredholm determinant numerically along the real line and demonstrate that the corresponding Painlevé transcendent remains free of poles on a semi-infinite axis.

The proximal alternating linearized minimization method (PALM) is highly effective for addressing block-structured optimization problems, which are prevalent in practical applications. When subproblems lack closed-form solutions, often due to intricate constraints, infeasible subsolvers become necessary, leading to the development of infeasible inexact PALM (PALM-I). While extensive research has focused on feasible PALM, PALM-I has received little attention, resulting in a lack of theoretical guarantees for its application. The primary analytical challenge lies in the nonmonotonicity of the objective value caused by infeasibility. This study investigates the convergence properties of PALM-I by constructing a surrogate sequence to address the nonmonotonicity issue and formulating a practical inexact criterion. Leveraging these tools, we demonstrate the stationarity of any accumulation point and prove iterate convergence along with asymptotic convergence rates under the Lojasiewicz assumption. Numerical experiments on problems from quantum physics and 3D anisotropic frictional contact highlight the significant computational efficiency advantages of PALM-I in terms of CPU time.

This study investigates the convergence of Gradient Descent (GD) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in mildly parameterized neural networks initialized randomly. We establish an "early stage convergence" result across a wide variety of models and loss functions, including standard square and cross-entropy losses, demonstrating that the loss decreases significantly and rapidly during the initial phase of training. Additionally, for exponential loss functions under specific data assumptions, we prove global convergence of GD. Rather than depending on extreme over-parameterization, our approach utilizes a microscopic analysis of neuronal activation patterns to derive stronger lower bounds for the gradient. These findings on activation patterns, termed "neuron partition," offer valuable intuition regarding neural network training dynamics and hold independent significance.

Achieving accelerated controlled thermodynamic processes necessitates an auxiliary Hamiltonian to guide the system toward instantaneous equilibrium, inevitably incurring additional energy costs during finite-time operations. Our recent work introduced a geodesic method to minimize this energy expenditure in shortcuts to isothermal processes. However, standard auxiliary controls often include momentum-dependent terms that are difficult to realize experimentally due to the need for continuous speed monitoring. In this study, we utilize a variational auxiliary control devoid of momentum-dependent forces to approximate the exact control strategy. Adhering to the geometric framework, we derive an optimal control protocol that achieves the minimum variational energy cost. We illustrate the construction of this protocol using a Brownian motion model with a controllable harmonic potential.

We examine a stationary Markov process representing specific queueing systems characterized by bulk service of a fixed capacity $m$. We derive an integral representation for the transition probability function using specific multi-orthogonal polynomials. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence of a simultaneous quadrature scheme to develop an algorithm for evaluating this integral expression.

Muon colliders offer a distinct pathway to achieve high-energy collisions, facilitating both precision measurements and discovery searches that deepen our comprehension of fundamental physical laws. The design strategy targets maximum energy reach while maintaining favorable costs, power requirements, and timelines compared to other proposed facilities. Consequently, a new international collaboration has been established to advance design concepts and performance studies for this machine. The primary objective is to deliver a ~10 TeV center-of-mass (CM) energy configuration to investigate the physics energy frontier, potentially utilizing lower-energy options as an intermediate step. Currently, a 3 TeV CM stage is under consideration, alongside other possibilities such as an s-channel Higgs Factory at 125 GeV CM. This document outlines the current status of research and development and design efforts for such a machine and presents a roadmap to mature these concepts into a valuable tool for the high-energy physics community.

This paper establishes guidelines for central banks on selecting monetary-policy rules when addressing multiple objectives, including the output gap and anticipated inflation. It specifically examines whether policy instruments are predetermined or forward-looking. By employing a New-Keynesian Phillips curve coupled with a cost-push shock transmission mechanism, the study demonstrates that a forward-looking framework results in severe deficiencies in the robustness and credibility of stabilization efforts. Conversely, in a backward-looking scenario, simple-rule parameters can align with the outcomes of Ramsey optimal policy under limited commitment. Consequently, the authors recommend explicitly modeling the policymaker's rational behavior through Ramsey optimal policy, rather than relying on simple rules with ambiguous assumptions that yield advice lacking both robustness and credibility.

Garc\'ia-Fritz and Pasten demonstrated that Hilbert's 10th problem is undecidable in the rings of integers of number fields of the form $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{p},\sqrt{-q})$ for a significant proportion of primes $p$ and $q$. We enhance these proportions and broaden their findings to include number fields of the form $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{p},\sqrt{Dq})$, where $D$ is a member of a specific family of positive square-free integers. This advancement is achieved by employing multiple elliptic curves and substituting their Iwasawa theory-based arguments with a more straightforward approach.

This study reports a measurement of $W$ boson polarisation derived from $t\bar{t}$ decays, specifically reconstructed in events containing a single high-$p_{\mbox{T}}$ lepton and a minimum of four jets. Data were gathered from $pp$ collisions at the LHC operating at $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV, accumulating an integrated luminosity of 20.2 fb$^{-1}$. The sensitivity to $W$ boson polarisation arises from the angle $\theta^{*}$ defined between the $b$-quark from the top quark decay and a direct $W$ decay product within the $W$ rest frame. Polarisation analysis employs two distinct decay products: the charged lepton for leptonically decaying $W$ bosons and the down-type quark for hadronically decaying ones. The highest precision in measuring $W$ polarisation via the $\cos{\theta^{*}}$ distribution is achieved using the leptonic analyser combined with events where at least two jets are identified as $b$-quark jets. The resulting fitted fractions for longitudinal, left-handed, and right-handed polarisation states are $F_{\mathrm{0}}= 0.709 \pm {0.019}$, $F_{\mathrm{L}}= 0.299 \pm {0.015}$, and $F_{\mathrm{R}}= -0.008 \pm {0.014}$, representing the most accurate measurements of these fractions to date. Additionally, constraints on anomalous couplings at the $Wtb$ vertex are established.

Modern civilization relies on extensive human cooperation, yet understanding the underlying mechanisms has remained a centuries-old challenge. A critical oversight in previous research is the assumption that real-world games are played in isolation; in reality, they are typically simultaneous and interactive. This study introduces the concept of interacting games, where distinct games coevolve and mutually influence decision-making. We demonstrate that as game-game interactions intensify, the phase transition toward cooperation significantly improves, leading to high levels of cooperation across all involved games when interactions become strong. A mean-field theory reveals a new mechanism, termed \emph{dynamical reciprocity}, which acts as a counterpart to the well-established network reciprocity to promote cooperation, a finding supported by detailed analysis. This reciprocity proves robust against variations in game types, population structures, and updating rules, with the number of interacting games generally correlating with higher cooperation levels. These findings highlight the potential for achieving high cooperation in real-world scenarios where issues are interconnected, even under extremely adverse conditions.

Split signature enables global twistor constructions for conformally self-dual (SD) gravity and Yang-Mills, generating solutions from twistor data defined by free functions devoid of gauge freedom. This approach is extended to asymptotically flat SD gravity, providing a fully nonlinear description of asymptotic gravitational data via a real homogeneous generating function $h$ within real twistor space. The recently identified $Lw_{1+\infty}$ celestial symmetries, when considered real, function locally as passive Poisson diffeomorphisms on this space. The twistor data, represented by $h$, induces an imaginary Poisson transformation that constructs the gravitational field by shifting the real slice of the twistor space. Twistor chiral sigma models, whose correlators produce the tree-level S-matrix for Einstein gravity, are recast as theories of holomorphic discs in twistor space with boundaries constrained to the $h$-deformed real slice. While real $Lw_{1+\infty}$ symmetries act geometrically on the S-matrix formula with vanishing Noether currents, imaginary generators produce graviton vertex operators that create gravitons in the perturbative series. The text also briefly explores a generating function for all-plus 1-loop amplitudes, the analogous framework for Yang-Mills, potential Lorentz signature interpretations, and related open string formulations of twistor and ambitwistor strings in four dimensions under split signature.

Few-shot prompting proves to be a remarkably effective method for leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) across diverse tasks; however, its efficacy diminishes as task complexity grows or when the intrinsic reasoning steps are difficult to master, particularly within intricate contexts. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Decomposed Prompting, a novel strategy that addresses complex challenges by breaking them down—through prompting—into manageable sub-tasks assigned to a library of specialized prompting-based LLMs. This modular architecture enables each prompt to be finely tuned for its specific sub-task, allows for further decomposition if needed, and facilitates easy substitution with superior prompts, trained models, or symbolic functions. Our findings demonstrate that the flexibility and modularity of Decomposed Prompting enable it to surpass previous few-shot prompting approaches when using GPT-3. Regarding symbolic reasoning, we can recursively split sub-tasks that challenge LLMs into even simpler, solvable components. When complexity arises from input length, the framework recursively divides the task into identical operations with reduced inputs. Furthermore, evaluations on textual multi-step reasoning tasks reveal significant gains: on long-context multi-hop QA, separate sub-task prompts allow for more effective instruction, while on open-domain multi-hop QA, integrating symbolic information retrieval within our decomposition framework yields improved performance.

This study introduces a new pipeline that illustrates the potential of integrating state-of-the-art techniques. It specifically proposes the R2-D2 (Rank twice, reaD twice) framework, which combines a retriever, passage reranker, extractive reader, generative reader, and a straightforward method for integrating these components. Unlike prior works that often require massive external document indexes scaling to tens of GiB, this approach offers a simple pruning strategy. This allows the entire open-domain QA system, including the index, OS, and library, to fit within a 6 GiB Docker image. Despite retaining only 8% of the original index, the system maintains performance by losing just 3% in exact match (EM) accuracy.

We propose a new, dual-purpose framework that simultaneously performs all-optical enantioselection and sorting of single multipolar chiral microspheres, utilizing optical pulling forces generated by two non-collinear, unstructured, circularly-polarized light sources. This chiral resolution technique allows for external control by adjusting the angle between the incident wavevectors, enabling precise tuning of the chiral index range for selection. Enantioselectivity is realized by selecting specific angles that ensure only particles matching the handedness of the light sources experience pulling forces. Consequently, this approach facilitates the all-optical sorting of chiral microspheres with arbitrarily small chiral parameters, surpassing the capabilities of existing optical methods.

It is widely accepted that the helical edge states of quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulators are exceptionally stable because of topological protection provided by time-reversal symmetry. In this study, we present the first experimental detection of an edge-dependent quantum (pseudo-)spin Hall effect using two Kekulé electric circuits featuring molecule-zigzag and partially-bearded edges, where the chirality of circulating currents within the unit cell simulates electron spin. We observed that the helicity of topological in-gap modes reverses in opposite parameter regimes for the two distinct edge geometries. These results are explained through the concept of a mirror winding number defined in the unit cell, which is determined solely by the edge morphology. Our findings provide deeper insight into how boundary effects influence the QSH phase and open new avenues for investigating spin-dependent topological physics in electric circuits.

This study identifies signatures of episodic accretion in young stellar objects (YSOs) arising from protobinary systems formed during gravoturbulent gas collapse. In the majority of these protobinary systems, strong accretion bursts occur between the two companions with a recurrence period of approximately 1 kyr. Typically, the accretion rate onto the secondary star surpasses that of the primary, reaching peak values of $2 \times 10^{-2}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ for the secondary and $6 \times 10^{-3}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ for the primary. We suggest that the more active secondary companion, particularly in gas cores with subsonic velocity dispersion, offers promising observational avenues for detecting traces of episodic accretion in the gas surrounding embedded binary YSOs. In contrast, protostars evolving as single objects in similar environments exhibit fewer accretion bursts and a more steady mass growth history. Furthermore, prestellar cores with subsonic velocity dispersion display accretion bursts roughly an order of magnitude more intense than those with supersonic dispersions. In the latter case, some protobinaries form where the primary acts as the more active accretor, potentially evolving into extreme mass ratio systems. Additionally, YSOs in binary configurations characterized by small semi-major axes ($a \approx$ 50 au) and high mass ratios ($q > 0.7$) support phases of intense episodic accretion. However, eccentricity appears to play no significant role in the occurrence of these accretion bursts.

Decentralized settlement involving the exchange of data and digital assets presents several legal hurdles, most notably the necessity to comply with privacy laws (such as data protection regulations) and copyright statutes. To empower software platform providers in managing these assets effectively and granting owners greater oversight, usage control technologies can ensure that consumers adhere to privacy preferences, licensing terms, and regulatory mandates. This research proposal investigates the deployment of usage control within decentralized settings, specifically focusing on challenges regarding the definition of usage policies, their enforcement, and the user-friendliness of the administrative tools involved.

Hyperspectral imaging systems gather and analyze data from distinct wavelengths throughout the electromagnetic spectrum. Researchers have leveraged the combination of multi-spectral bands within the visible range to enhance face recognition capabilities compared to traditional broad-band images. This chapter introduces a novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) framework that utilizes structural sparsity learning to identify the most effective spectral bands, thereby maximizing face recognition accuracy. In this approach, input images from all bands are processed by a CNN, where the first-layer convolutional filters are regularized using a group Lasso algorithm to eliminate redundant bands during training. Unlike existing methods that rely on manual selection or greedy strategies to identify useful bands, our technique automatically selects optimal spectral bands to achieve superior recognition performance. Furthermore, experimental outcomes show that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art band selection techniques across various publicly available hyperspectral face image datasets.

This study determines the branching fractions ${\mathcal{B}}$ and $CP$ asymmetries ${\mathcal{A}_{{\it CP}}}$ for the decays $B^+ \rightarrow \pi^+ \pi^0$ and $B^+ \rightarrow K^+ \pi^0$. These findings rely on a dataset of 198 million $b\bar{b}$ meson pairs, achieved through an integrated luminosity of $190\;\text{fb}^{-1}$ collected by the Belle II detector during energy-asymmetric electron-positron collisions at the $\Upsilon (4S)$ resonance. The measured values are ${\mathcal{B}(B^+ \rightarrow \pi^+ \pi^0) = (6.12 \pm 0.53 \pm 0.53)\times 10^{-6}}$, ${\mathcal{B}(B^+ \rightarrow K^+ \pi^0) = (14.30 \pm 0.69 \pm 0.79)\times 10^{-6}}$, ${\mathcal{A}_{{\it CP}}(B^+ \rightarrow \pi^+ \pi^0) = -0.085 \pm 0.085 \pm 0.019}$, and ${\mathcal{A}_{{\it CP}}(B^+ \rightarrow K^+ \pi^0) = 0.014 \pm 0.047 \pm 0.010}$, with the first uncertainties representing statistical errors and the second representing systematic uncertainties. These results represent an improvement over a prior Belle II measurement and are consistent with the current world averages.
I review our recent research regarding the verification of population protocols and their state complexity.

Recent scholarship has introduced formal methodologies for auditing algorithmic systems to identify bias and harm. Although these structured approaches have made significant strides, they frequently overlook critical flaws that only become apparent during routine real-world deployment. Consequently, numerous instances have arisen where everyday users uncover and highlight harmful behaviors encountered through daily interactions with these systems. Despite this, academic research has largely neglected these bottom-up, user-led auditing mechanisms. This paper introduces and examines the concept of everyday algorithm auditing, defined as a process where users identify, comprehend, and challenge problematic machine actions through their regular engagement with algorithms. We contend that everyday users are uniquely capable of exposing algorithmic issues that formal, centralized audits might miss, irrespective of their technical understanding of the underlying systems. By analyzing specific real-world examples of such auditing, we derive insights for designing future platforms and tools that support these behaviors. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at connecting formal auditing frameworks with the organic auditing practices that naturally emerge during everyday system use.

Social dialogue, which underpins our democracies, faces current threats from partisanship and disinformation, both of which disrupt individual and collective awareness while harming decision-making processes. While significant attention has been paid to the news sphere itself, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the nuanced interaction between information supply and demand. Consequently, a broader perspective encompassing both producers and consumers is essential for developing new tools to evaluate the health of the information ecosystem. This study integrates news supply—reflected in a largely comprehensive Italian news database, partially annotated for fake news—with news demand, captured via Google Trends data for Italy. The investigation examines the temporal and semantic relationships between news, disinformation, and search queries across various domains, including the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. Two primary findings emerge: first, disinformation is highly responsive to public interest and flourishes particularly when there is a disconnect between what the public seeks and what media outlets provide; second, a specific index can estimate the level of disinformation using only the available volumes of news and search data. Although the results primarily concern the Coronavirus topic, they offer indications of broader applicability. We argue that these findings serve as a valuable resource for informing anti-disinformation campaigns and providing news organizations and institutions with relevant strategic insights.

This study examines forward error in floating-point summation of real numbers using algorithms that avoid higher precision or specialized hardware. We derive explicit expressions and establish new deterministic and probabilistic error bounds for three algorithmic categories: general summation, shifted general summation, and compensated (sequential) summation. The probabilistic bounds for general and shifted general summation are valid to all orders. For compensated summation, we provide both deterministic and probabilistic first- and second-order bounds, including a novel first-order bound that differs from previous results. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these bounds are informative and confirm that, among the three methods, compensated summation is typically the most accurate.

This paper examines the production of light charged Higgs bosons through the $pp 	o  ar{t} bH^\pm$ process at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) within the Type-III Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM). We investigate the viability of detecting this production channel via the $H^\pm 	o \mu
u$ decay signature. In the Type-III framework, this signal may dominate significantly over the $H^\pm 	o 	au
u$ and $H^\pm 	o c ar{s}$ channels. Our analysis demonstrates that, across both standard and inverted mass hierarchy scenarios and after accounting for various theoretical and experimental constraints, the $pp 	o  ar{t} bH^\pm$ process followed by $H^\pm 	o \mu
u$ represents the most promising avenue for searching for light charged Higgs bosons at the LHC.

This study theoretically examines the topological characteristics of a dimerized quasi-one-dimensional lattice featuring multiple legs ($L$) and multiple sublattices ($R$). The system possesses both primary and secondary exchange symmetries. When analyzed in the basis of the latter symmetry, the lattice decomposes into $L$ distinct one-dimensional subsystems, each resembling a generalized $SSH_R$ model with $R$ sublattices and on-site potentials. Chiral symmetry is generally absent across these subsystems, occurring only when the main exchange symmetry axis aligns with the central chain. Our findings indicate that the system can support both zero- and finite-energy topological edge states. Specifically, the emergence of zero-energy edge states depends on a specific relationship between the number of legs and sublattices. Consequently, various topological phases protected by subsystem symmetry are identified, including zero-energy edge states within the main gap, their absence, and zero-energy edge states within bulk states. Although the overall system classification falls under the $BDI$ symmetry class, individual subsystems belong to either the $AI$ or $BDI$ class.

The Bañados-Silk-West (BSW) effect suggests that the center-of-mass energy ($E_{c.m.}$) of two colliding particles near a black hole can theoretically become infinite. While standard models typically assume particles follow geodesic or electrogeodesic paths, this study explores an alternative scenario. In this version, one particle remains stationary near a static, potentially distorted black hole, while a second particle (approaching from infinity) collides with it. This collision also results in an unbounded $E_{c.m.}$. However, the force needed to maintain the stationary particle's position diverges for nonextremal horizons, stays finite and nonzero for extremal ones, and approaches zero as the horizon is reached in ultraextremal black holes. Extending this to rotating black holes involves a particle that corotates without radial motion. In this context, the energy $E$ approaches zero when the angular momentum $L$ is zero, a condition that substitutes the fine-tuning of parameters required in the conventional BSW effect.

This article provides a comprehensive explanation of the Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) architecture and presents an enhanced auto-encoder variant named AE-ConvLSTM. Functioning as a sequence-to-sequence model, AE-ConvLSTM predicts the long-term evolution of dynamical systems by transferring hidden states between encoders. The network demonstrated strong performance in forecasting the dynamic evolution of unsteady 2-D viscous Burgers equations, whether trained on data or on governing equations alone (physics-constrained). Additionally, AE-ConvLSTM was applied to predict the time evolution of two unsteady Navier-Stokes problems involving coupled pressure and velocity fields with disparate magnitudes and temporal evolution rates. While the network successfully learned these dynamics from data, it failed to train effectively when using a physics-constrained approach based solely on governing equations.

The experimental study of rare $B$-decays began in 1993 with CLEO's measurement of $B \to K^* \gamma$, followed two years later by the observation of the inclusive decay $B \to X_s \gamma$, which serves as the field's benchmark. Since then, the research frontier has shifted to LHC experiments, particularly LHCb, which recently measured the branching fraction for $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ at approximately $10^{-10}$, the lowest value recorded to date. The high precision achieved in this domain has subjected the Standard Model to unprecedented scrutiny, with further tests anticipated soon. This overview examines key measurements in radiative, semileptonic, and leptonic rare $B$-decays, compares them with Standard Model predictions, and highlights several recent discrepancies. While these anomalies are too numerous to dismiss, none individually possess sufficient significance to invalidate the Standard Model. Rare $B$-decays currently stand at a critical juncture: they may signal new physics, but they might also simply demand a more refined theoretical framework within the Standard Model. An independent high-precision experiment like Belle II could play a crucial role in resolving these current experimental ambiguities.

Let $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be vectors in $\mathbf{R}^n$ with nonnegative entries. By reordering their coordinates, we may assume $a_1 \geq \cdots \geq a_n$ and $b_1 \geq \cdots \geq b_n$. We say that $\mathbf{a}$ majorizes $\mathbf{b}$, written $\mathbf{b} \preceq \mathbf{a}$, if the sums of their components are equal ($\sum_{i=1}^n b_i = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i$) and the partial sums of $\mathbf{b}$ are less than or equal to those of $\mathbf{a}$ for every $k \in \{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ ($\sum_{i=1}^k b_i \leq \sum_{i=1}^k a_i$). This paper establishes results by Hardy, Littlewood, Pólya, and Rado stating that $\mathbf{b} \preceq \mathbf{a}$ holds if and only if there exists a doubly stochastic matrix $P$ such that $P\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}$, which is equivalent to saying that $\mathbf{b}$ lies within the $S_n$-permutohedron generated by $\mathbf{a}$.

This research investigates the decays of $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_c(\to B_n f) \ell ^- \overline{\nu}$, where $\ell$ represents electrons, muons, or taus, and $B_n$ and $f$ denote the daughter baryons and remaining particles resulting from the $\Lambda_c$ cascade, respectively. Specifically, we analyze the complete angular distributions accounting for polarized $\Lambda_b$ states and lepton mass effects to identify time-reversal asymmetries. To illustrate experimental viability, we focus on the $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_c(\to p K^- \pi^+) \ell ^- \overline{\nu}$ channels. Our findings demonstrate that observables linked to these time-reversal asymmetries are valuable for probing new physics, as they vanish within the standard model. Explicitly, these observables exhibit sensitivity to right-handed currents originating from new physics and are potentially observable at LHCb.

Future radio interferometers designed to detect the 21\,cm signal from cosmological distances, utilizing arrays with $N\gg 1000$ antennas, may encounter substantial computational hurdles if they rely on traditional correlator architectures, where resource demands scale quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$. Since the primary output of these systems involves cross-correlating every antenna pair, the FFT-correlator architecture offers a more efficient solution by reducing this scaling to $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ via spatial Fourier transforms. However, the FFT-correlator's output is only valid if the input antenna voltages are properly gain- and phase-calibrated. Historically, interferometric calibration has depended on the $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ cross-correlations generated by standard correlators. This paper introduces two real-time calibration schemes capable of operating alongside an FFT-correlator, forming a self-contained $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ system suitable for scaling to large-N redundant arrays. An evaluation of these schemes' performance and scalability reveals that the variance in antenna gains diminishes according to a $1/\log{N}$ trend as the array size increases.

This research investigates word structures defined as $(D,<,P)$, where $D$ represents either the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ or the integers $\mathbb{Z}$, $<$ denotes the standard linear order on $D$, and $P$ is a subset of $D$ acting as a predicate. Specifically, we establish the following: (a) The collection of recursive $\omega$-words possessing decidable monadic second-order theories is $\Sigma_3$-complete. (b) Established characterizations regarding the decidability of monadic second-order theories for $\omega$-words are extended to apply to bi-infinite words. (c) We demonstrate that "tame" predicates $P$ exist within every Turing degree. (d) For any predicate $P \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, we calculate the quantity of predicates $Q \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ such that the structures $(\mathbb{Z},\le,P)$ and $(\mathbb{Z},\le,Q)$ are logically indistinguishable. Collectively, these findings highlight both the parallels and distinctions in the logical characteristics of infinite versus bi-infinite words.

This study examines the mathematical characteristics of a stochastic variant of the balanced 2D thermal quasigeostrophic (TQG) model, which governs potential vorticity dynamics. Designed to parametrize the dynamical generation of unresolved degrees of freedom in simulations of upper ocean dynamics, this model specifically addresses scenarios where horizontal buoyancy gradients and bathymetry influence behavior at the submesoscale (250m–10km). We employ the SALT (Stochastic Advection by Lie Transport) algorithm, as introduced in [25] and utilized in [11,12], for our modeling framework. The SALT method maintains the Kelvin circulation theorem and an infinite set of integral conservation laws for TQG. Its primary objective is to quantify uncertainty associated with the up-scaling or coarse-graining of fine-scale observed or synthetic data for application in coarse-scale computational simulations. This paper offers a rigorous mathematical analysis of the solution properties of the thermal quasigeostrophic equations incorporating stochastic advection by Lie transport (SALT) [27,28].

Vehicle shape data plays a critical role in Intelligent Traffic Systems (ITS). This study introduces a method for utilizing a training dataset comprising vehicles from various release years and captured from diverse angles. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how clustering enhances make/model classification, with both approaches yielding improved accuracy and robustness. A deep convolutional neural network built on the ResNet architecture was developed to train the classification model. Addressing the unequal class distribution in the training data, which creates a priori probability, the study employs bias removal and hard normalization of centroids in the classification layer to eliminate this issue, thereby boosting classification performance. Finally, a custom application was utilized to evaluate vehicle re-identification on video streams based on manual make/model and color classification. This research received partial funding under a specific grant.

This paper presents and investigates Rafael Sorkin's *evolving co-event scheme*, a theoretical framework designed to definitively determine which events occur and which do not within evolving quantum or classical systems. Built upon discrete histories and independent of any observer, the framework offers a promising setting for discrete quantum cosmology, quantum gravity, and standard discrete quantum systems. The theory rests on Quantum Measure Theory, an extension of classical measure theory that accommodates quantum interference among alternative histories, alongside a co-event interpretation that specifies whether events can occur and in what combinations, given a specific system and quantum measure. Unlike earlier co-event schemes, the evolving co-event scheme operates in stochastic stages without reliance on future stages, ensuring manifest compatibility with an evolving block view. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the co-event realities generated by this basic scheme remain unaffected by whether zero-measure histories are included or excluded from the history space, a result derived non-trivially from the scheme's fundamental rules. Finally, the study shows that when applied to classical systems, the evolving co-event scheme naturally reduces to producing classical realities.

Noise poses a persistent obstacle to generating and maintaining delicate quantum states. Recent studies indicate that spatial noise correlations can be exploited as a resource for mitigation by employing spectator qubits to gauge environmental disturbances. This research extends that principle from spectator qubits to a spectator mode: a photonic mode that continuously monitors spatially correlated classical dephasing noise and delivers a continuous correction drive to frequency-tunable data qubits. Our analysis demonstrates that utilizing numerous photon states allows spectator modes to overcome many quantum measurement limitations that restrict spectator qubit methods. We further discover that long-term dephasing of data qubits can be suppressed indefinitely, even in the presence of white noise dephasing. Additionally, by employing a squeezing (parametric) drive, the error in this spectator mode approach can achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling relative to the number of photons. We also establish that spectator mode noise mitigation can be executed entirely autonomously through engineered dissipation, eliminating the need for explicit measurement or processing of classical records. Consequently, our work positions spectator modes as a potentially robust alternative to spectator qubits for noise mitigation.

Filaments have been extensively analyzed via simulations and observations, with numerical studies individually examining the impacts of chemistry, diffusion, and magnetic field structures on gas dynamics. However, non-ideal effects remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) processes, alongside a simplified chemical model, influence the evolution and accretion of star-forming filaments. Using the one-dimensional (1D) non-ideal MHD code lemongrab, which incorporates chemistry, we modeled an accreting, self-gravitating, turbulent filament. We examined how non-ideal MHD, magnetic field orientation and strength, and cosmic ray ionization rates affect filament evolution, specifically focusing on width and accretion rates. Our findings indicate that filament width and accretion are governed by magnetic field properties, including initial strength, coupling with gas (regulated by cosmic ray ionization), and alignment relative to the accretion flow. Increasing the cosmic-ray ionization rate yields behavior more akin to ideal MHD; this reduces magnetic pressure support, thereby dampening accretion efficiency and broadening the filament. Conversely, lowering the initial magnetic field strength results in a narrower width and higher accretion rate for similar reasons. While these factors alter outcomes by roughly a factor of two, excluding non-ideal MHD effects causes significantly larger variations (up to a factor of seven). Consequently, incorporating non-ideal MHD and cosmic-ray ionization is essential for studying self-gravitating filaments and accurately determining critical observables like filament width and accretion rates.

The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a vital metric in machine learning, assessing average performance across all combinations of True Positive Rates (TPR) and False Positive Rates (FPR). Given that an effective classifier must balance a high TPR with a low FPR, we investigate a more generalized approach known as Two-way Partial AUC (TPAUC), which focuses exclusively on the region where $\mathsf{TPR} \ge \alpha$ and $\mathsf{FPR} \le \beta$. Recent research indicates that TPAUC is fundamentally inconsistent with existing Partial AUC metrics that restrict only the FPR range, highlighting a novel challenge to maximize TPAUC. Driven by this insight, this paper introduces the first attempt to optimize this metric. A primary obstacle in this endeavor is the difficulty of applying gradient-based optimization with end-to-end stochastic training, even when using an appropriate surrogate loss.
