To overcome this, we propose a general framework for constructing surrogate optimization problems that facilitates efficient end-to-end training with deep learning. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that: 1) the surrogate objective function achieves an upper bound of the original problem under mild conditions, and 2) optimizing these surrogates yields strong generalization performance regarding TPAUC with high probability. Finally, empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets confirm the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

This research investigates the evolution of Laughlin states under significant geometric deformations of the sphere and plane, specifically those governed by Mabuchi geodesics on the space of metrics possessing Hamiltonian $S^1$-symmetry. When considering geodesics driven by the square of the symmetry generator, the geometry of the sphere asymptotically approaches that of a thin cigar collapsing onto a line as geodesic time extends to infinity; concurrently, the Laughlin states concentrate on a discrete collection of $S^1$-orbits, which align with the Bohr-Sommerfeld orbits of geometric quantization. Furthermore, the elevation of these Mabuchi geodesics to the bundle of quantum states containing the Laughlin states is realized through generalized coherent state transforms, a process equivalent to the KZ parallel transport found in Chern-Simons theory.

This work presents a basic, calculus-free demonstration of Kepler's first law, confirming that bounded planetary paths are elliptical. Following the approach of earlier derivations, it employs conservation laws to formulate an expression for the orbit, which is then contrasted with the equation of an ellipse. Distinctively, the elliptical equation is derived using trigonometry based on two established properties of the ellipse, entirely bypassing calculus.

This paper generalizes the quadratic phase Fourier transform from complex-valued functions to quaternion-valued functions of two variables, a method we term the quaternion quadratic phase Fourier transform (QQPFT). Leveraging the connection between QQPFT and the quaternion Fourier transform (QFT), we derive a sharp Hausdorff-Young inequality for QQPFT. Furthermore, we introduce the short time quaternion quadratic phase Fourier transform (STQQPFT), analyzing its properties such as inner product relations and inversion formulas. We also examine the relationships between QQPFT, the two-dimensional quaternion ambiguity function, and the quaternion Wigner-Ville distribution, ultimately establishing Lieb's uncertainty and entropy uncertainty principles for these three transforms.

We introduce the Multi-Track Music Machine (MMM), a generative framework utilizing Transformer architecture to produce multi-track music. Unlike prior approaches that treat musical material as a single, interleaved time-ordered sequence, our method constructs a separate time-ordered sequence for each track before concatenating them. This structure leverages the Transformer's attention mechanism to effectively manage long-term dependencies. Furthermore, we investigate various representations to grant users significant control during generation, featuring an interactive demo that supports track- and bar-level inpainting, along with adjustable parameters for instrumentation and note density.

We introduce a novel workflow for background-oriented schlieren (BOS), called "physics-informed BOS," designed to derive density, velocity, and pressure fields from paired reference and distorted images. This approach employs a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to generate flow fields that concurrently adhere to both measurement data and governing physical equations. Specifically tailored for the high-speed flows examined in this study, we define a physics loss function grounded in the Euler and irrotationality equations. As a quantitative fluid visualization method, BOS characterizes high-speed flows by processing background pattern images through computer vision and tomography to map the density field. However, BOS inherently involves a series of ill-posed inverse problems that demand additional information beyond the images alone for accurate flow reconstruction. Traditional BOS workflows typically rely on image interpolation or penalty terms to enforce global or piecewise smoothness; yet, these methods often conflict with actual flow physics, resulting in density field inaccuracies. In contrast, physics-informed BOS utilizes a PINN that integrates both the BOS measurement model and governing equations to directly reconstruct all flow fields. This methodology enhances the precision of density estimates and additionally provides velocity and pressure data, capabilities previously unattainable. We validate our approach by reconstructing synthetic data derived from analytical and numerical phantoms, as well as experimental measurements. Our physics-informed reconstructions demonstrate significantly superior accuracy compared to conventional BOS estimates. Furthermore, to our knowledge, this study marks the first application of a PINN to reconstruct a supersonic flow from any type of experimental data.

This project report details the tuning of Focus[1], a video inference system designed for low cost and latency, achieved through a two-phase approach. We aim to reduce query time by caching the intermediate layer outputs of the neural network, employing a strategy that trades increased memory usage for faster execution. Using prototype systems, we demonstrate the efficacy of this scheme, which results in a 20% reduction in time. The code repository is available at https://github.com/iphyer/CS744FocousIngestOpt.

Neutron reflectometry analysis is fundamentally an ill-posed problem, meaning numerous distinct solutions can fit the experimental data with equal accuracy. Consequently, researchers employ model-dependent analysis, incorporating prior knowledge about the system into the evaluation process. This tutorial provides a brief overview of the mathematical foundations supporting the application of model-dependent analysis in neutron reflectometry.

Specific biochemical reactions are initiated only once enough particles bind to a designated target, such as an enzyme or protein sensor. This study examines the reaction time distribution, defined as the moment when all independently diffusing particles have attached to the target. In scenarios of irreversible binding, this corresponds to the first-passage time of the final particle to bind; however, reversible binding introduces significant complexity and alters the reaction time distribution substantially. We provide an exact analytical solution for this problem and explore both short-time and long-time asymptotic behaviors of the reaction time probability density. Furthermore, we evaluate the influence of the unbinding rate and particle count on the mean reaction time. Finally, our derived exact and asymptotic results are validated against Monte Carlo simulations.

The Quantum Search Algorithm significantly advanced the field by solving search problems for $N$-element sets in $O(\sqrt{N})$ steps. Although the asymptotic complexity cannot be improved, constant factor optimizations are achievable. This paper explores such enhancements for search tasks within sets characterized by known probability distributions. We demonstrate that a modified quantum search algorithm can reduce the expected number of iterations required for these specific sets.

This paper provides a survey of deep multiagent reinforcement learning. Recently, the integration of deep neural networks with reinforcement learning has gained significant momentum, gradually shifting attention from single-agent to multi-agent scenarios. Managing multiple agents presents inherent complexities due to (a) future rewards being contingent on the joint actions of all players and (b) an increase in computational demands. We outline the most prevalent representations of multiagent problems and their primary challenges, highlighting five key research areas that tackle these issues: centralized training with decentralized execution, opponent modeling, communication, efficient coordination, and reward shaping. Our analysis reveals that many computational studies depend on unrealistic assumptions or lack generalizability, often failing to overcome the curse of dimensionality or nonstationarity. Conversely, approaches drawn from psychology and sociology offer promising insights into relevant behaviors like communication and coordination, which can enhance agent performance in multiagent settings. We propose that for multiagent reinforcement learning to succeed, future research must adopt an interdisciplinary approach to address these challenges and unlock new possibilities.

We investigate the bending of light caused by time-periodic, spherically symmetric gravitational fields using both the geodesic method and perturbation theory. Under the assumption of a weak gravitational field, we establish general formulas for the leading-order deflection angle, which apply to both static and time-periodic metrics. Applying these findings to a spherically symmetric, oscillating distribution of a self-gravitating scalar field with a logarithmic potential, we determine that the resulting deflection angle remains constant with respect to time at the leading order.

This paper provides a concise overview of branch-cut cosmology and delves into previously unexamined areas. Beginning with the established concept of primordial singularity suppression, we introduce, for the first time, key themes crucial to comprehending the scope of this framework. Drawing on recent advancements, we enhance our understanding of the scenarios depicted in these formulations, as well as address fundamental issues in modern cosmology—specifically the flatness, homogeneity, and horizon problems—through the classical lens of branch-cut cosmology.

Obtaining slowly-scanned images progressively is advantageous for both real-time visualization and drift correction. While interlacing techniques are standard for managing data on rectilinear grids, we propose applying them to scanning-mode imaging modalities. In such scenarios, it is crucial to maximize the utility of sample points to accelerate scanning and minimize subject damage. Although the use of hexagonal scanning grids for optimal sampling of band-limited signals has been established for some time, this note introduces two novel methods for interlacing hexagonal grids. These approaches facilitate early full-field-of-view imaging with optimal sampling efficiency and achieve resolution doubling.

Over the past ten years, numerous visual analytics (VA) systems have been successfully applied across diverse fields, including urban analytics and explainable AI. Nevertheless, the research community has frequently questioned the rigor and contributions of these systems. To defend VA systems, we present two interview studies designed to gather critiques and responses to these challenges. First, we interviewed 24 researchers to document criticisms found in their review comments, which were then synthesized through an iterative coding and refinement process into a list of 36 common criticisms. Second, we interviewed 17 researchers to validate this list and collect their responses, facilitating a discussion on how to uphold and enhance the scientific value and rigor of VA systems. We emphasize that the resulting knowledge is deep and extensive yet also imperfect, provocative, and controversial, advising readers to approach it with both critical and inclusive perspectives. Ultimately, we hope this work offers foundational insights for future VA research and stimulates dialogue to advance the field with greater rigor and vitality.

Accurately characterizing noise environments responsible for qubit decoherence is essential for advancing robust quantum technologies. Although dynamical decoupling is a leading technique for noise spectral analysis, it relies on extensive sequences of $\pi$ pulses, thereby increasing experimental complexity and cost. In this work, we present a noise spectroscopy approach that depends solely on the Fourier transform of free induction decay data, eliminating the requirement for any $\pi$ pulses. We demonstrate that this method accurately reconstructs noise spectra, surpassing prior dynamical decoupling strategies while substantially lowering experimental overhead. Furthermore, we evaluate the experimental viability of our proposal and confirm its resilience against statistical measurement noise. Applicable across diverse quantum platforms, our method offers a streamlined route to more precise spectral characterization of quantum devices, enabling tailored strategies for mitigating decoherence.

Distributed learning tasks typically demand extensive communication, which severely hampers scalability and convergence speed in wireless settings. To address this, we propose Gradient Descent with Sparsification and Error Correction (GD-SEC) for a general worker-server architecture, aiming to boost communication efficiency. Inspired by diverse wireless learning scenarios, GD-SEC minimizes the bits transmitted per worker-server exchange without compromising the convergence rate order, thereby facilitating larger-scale model training without sacrificing accuracy or speed. In each iteration, rather than sending the full gradient vector, workers transmit a sparsified difference between their current gradient and a linear combination of previously sent gradients. A defining characteristic of GD-SEC is that gradient difference components are only transmitted if their magnitude exceeds a sufficient threshold. Additionally, an error correction mechanism at each worker offsets the inaccuracies introduced by sparsification. We demonstrate that GD-SEC guarantees convergence for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex problems, matching the convergence rate order of standard Gradient Descent (GD). Specifically, for strongly convex objectives, GD-SEC achieves a fast linear convergence rate. Numerical experiments confirm these convergence properties and highlight the significant reduction in communication bits. Compared to existing algorithms, GD-SEC substantially lowers the communication burden required to reach a target accuracy while maintaining the optimization speed.

The efficiency of a nuclear fusion power plant is evaluated, noting that under nominal conditions, it depends on thermodynamic efficiency and the fraction of recirculated power. However, because reactors typically operate below nominal capacity on average—even excluding long maintenance shutdowns—the capacity factor must also be included in the calculation. An expression accounting for both the recirculated power fraction and capacity factor is presented. The analysis demonstrates that a high recirculated power fraction combined with a low capacity factor leads to poor overall plant efficiency. This occurs because fusion reactors maintain high recirculated power levels even when output power is reduced. It is argued that this specific combination is probable for first-generation plants. The discussion includes worked examples based on the Power Plant Conceptual Study models and concludes by examining the implications for fusion's competitiveness in the energy market, emphasizing the need to develop plant designs with a low recirculated power fraction.

This study presents a method for swiftly computing the geometries and characteristics of quasi-axisymmetric and quasi-helically symmetric stellarators. The technique involves optimizing magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium and quasisymmetry equations expanded near the magnetic axis, following the formulation by Garren and Boozer [Phys. Fluids B, 3, 2805 (1991)]. By reducing the equations through this expansion, computational expenses drop to approximately one CPU-second, facilitating extensive, high-resolution parameter space scans. Unlike conventional stellarator optimization, this approach defines the cost function to maximize the volume where the expansion remains valid, with a critical term $|| \nabla\mathbf B ||$ used to enhance field scale lengths. Employing this methodology, a database comprising $5\times 10^5$ optimized configurations was generated and displayed. The results reveal that quasisymmetric configurations occur in continuous bands across varying ratios of magnetic axis length to average major radius. Additionally, several novel configuration types were identified, including quasi-helically symmetric fields featuring two or more than six field periods.

This study examines the expressive capabilities of the two primary categories of program logics identified in literature for handling complex, non-regular program properties: those extending propositional dynamic logic (PDL) and those extending the modal mu-calculus. This investigation is motivated by the recent identification of a decidable logic, Visibly Pushdown Fixpoint Logic with Chop, which integrates both the modal mu-calculus and PDL over visibly pushdown languages, thereby bridging two previously distinct pillars of decidable program logics. We demonstrate that this logic surpasses the expressiveness of both its individual fragments and even their combined union, effectively raising the decidability boundary for program logics. Furthermore, we finalize this analysis by establishing separation results among all PDL-based and modal fixpoint logics incorporating regular, visibly pushdown, and arbitrary context-free constructions.

We investigate the convergence rate of the randomized Newton-like method proposed by Qu et al. (2016) for smooth, convex functions, which employs random coordinate blocks of a Hessian approximation matrix $\bM$ rather than the exact Hessian. Analyzing this algorithm is difficult due to its intricate reliance on $\bM$'s structure. However, we demonstrate that if coordinate blocks are selected with probabilities proportional to their determinants, the convergence rate relies exclusively on the eigenvalue distribution of $\bM$ and takes an analytically tractable form. To achieve this, we establish a novel expectation formula for determinantal point processes. Furthermore, we show that determinantal sampling enables reasoning about the optimal block subset size based on $\bM$'s spectrum. Finally, numerical evaluations confirm that determinantal sampling yields performance that is either superior to or comparable with uniform sampling.

Although vaccines have been introduced, the Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) persists as a global challenge, with the emergence of new variants like Delta and Omicron. The standard testing method, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), is often costly, time-consuming, and inaccessible to many. In contrast, chest X-rays have been utilized since the early 1900s, offering a cheaper, faster, and typically insurance-covered alternative. By carefully selecting models, hyperparameters, and data augmentations, we demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve 83% accuracy in binary classification and 64% in multi-class classification for detecting COVID-19 from chest X-rays.

Lorentzian 4-metrics are formulated using spinorial coordinates, where the metric components decompose into a product of complex conjugates. This framework is employed to analyze the linearized theory and Einstein's vacuum field equations, alongside an examination of the connection between Lorentzian and complex 4-metrics.

The proposed Laser Und XFEL (LUXE) Experiment at DESY, Hamburg, is designed to investigate Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) within the strong-field non-perturbative regime. This unique environment will be achieved through collisions between high-intensity laser pulses and high-energy electron or photon beams originating from the Eu.XFEL facility. Beyond exploring QED, the experiment offers a distinctive chance to search for physics beyond the Standard Model. This proceeding details how the substantial photon flux produced at LUXE enables the detection of axion-like particles with masses up to 350 MeV and a photon coupling of $3\times10^{-6}$ GeV$^{-1}$. Such sensitivity in parameter space rivals the projected capabilities of future experiments, including FASER2 at the HL-LHC and NA62 operating in dump mode.

This paper introduces a new approach utilizing character sequence-to-sequence models to refine documents that have already undergone Optical Character Recognition (OCR). The primary contribution lies in a series of strategies designed to accurately handle strings significantly longer than those typically used to train sequence models, all while maintaining efficiency in terms of samples and resources, backed by extensive experimentation. The highest-performing strategy splits the input document into character n-grams, merges their individual corrections into the final output via a voting mechanism that functions as an ensemble of numerous sequence models. We also examine how to weight the contributions from each member of this ensemble. Our method was evaluated on nine languages within the ICDAR 2019 competition for post-OCR text correction, achieving new state-of-the-art results in five of them. The code for our post-OCR correction system is available at https://github.com/jarobyte91/post_ocr_correction.

This paper introduces an enhanced version of Wigner Distribution Deconvolution (WDD) designed for live ptychographic processing. This capability enables the gradual reconstruction and visualization of the specimen transfer function concurrently with the acquisition of diffraction patterns. To achieve this, we restructure WDD and integrate a dimensionality reduction method that lowers memory usage and accelerates computation. Numerical results demonstrate that this approach preserves the fidelity of reconstructed specimen transfer functions while simultaneously decreasing computational complexity during data acquisition. Although the current study focuses on Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) data, the proposed live processing algorithm is broadly applicable to real-time ptychographic reconstruction across various domains.

Most existing neural networks for surface reconstruction from point clouds disregard sensor poses and function solely on raw point coordinates. However, sensor visibility contains significant data regarding spatial occupancy and surface orientation. This paper introduces two straightforward methods to enrich raw point clouds with visibility metrics, enabling surface reconstruction networks to utilize this information with minimal modification. Our proposed enhancements consistently boost both the precision of the generated surfaces and the networks' generalization capabilities across unseen shape domains. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/raphaelsulzer/dsrv-data.

In recent years, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown exceptional performance in predicting visual fixations, yet their underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored, leaving them as opaque "black box" models. This study aims to illuminate the internal workings of these deep saliency models and identify the features they utilize for fixation prediction. We introduce a streamlined yet effective architecture composed of a single CNN processing a single resolution input, paired with a novel loss function designed for pixel-wise fixation prediction during natural scene viewing. Our findings demonstrate that this simple approach matches or surpasses the performance of more complex, state-of-the-art saliency models. Additionally, we propose a visualization technique inspired by saliency evaluation metrics to reveal the internal representations of these models. Our analysis suggests that human-like saliency likely integrates both low-level perceptual cues and high-level semantic knowledge. These results offer valuable insights for quantifying the discrepancy between current saliency models and human inter-observer models, facilitating the development of new models that bridge this gap.

Fibred semantics serves as the bedrock for the model-instance paradigm in software engineering. Software models are frequently formalized as objects within presheaf topoi—categories comprising entities that function as both algebras and coalgebras, such as directed graphs. The process of multimodeling necessitates the construction of model colimits, whereas decomposition is achieved through pullbacks. Achieving compositionality demands a precise interaction between these operations, requiring diagrams to satisfy the Van Kampen property. Nevertheless, algorithmically verifying the Van Kampen property directly from its definition is often infeasible. This paper introduces a necessary and sufficient, yet computationally efficient, condition for the Van Kampen property to hold within presheaf topoi. This condition relies on a uniqueness characteristic of path-like structures found within the congruence classes that constitute the colimiting cocone of the models. Consequently, this work extends the assertion by Heindel and Sobociński that "Being Van Kampen is a Universal Property" by demonstrating that the Van Kampen property also exposes a specific structural uniqueness inherent to the presheaf framework.

Numerous uncertainty propagation tools are available in various programming languages, yet few can manage functional correlations between variables. This paper examines a strategy for propagating uncertainties among functionally correlated quantities and introduces a new solution: the Julia package Measurements.jl. This software handles uncertain real and complex numbers, performs arbitrary-precision calculations, and supports mathematical and linear algebra operations on matrices and arrays.

This study evaluates malware detection methods utilizing static, dynamic, and hybrid approaches. We train Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) on both static and dynamic feature sets to assess detection performance across a wide range of malware families. Additionally, we examine hybrid scenarios where dynamic analysis informs the training phase while static techniques handle detection, and the reverse configuration. Our experimental results indicate that a fully dynamic approach consistently achieves superior detection rates. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for future hybrid malware detection strategies.

Generative diffusion models have become state-of-the-art for creating images and speech, yet achieving high performance with few denoising steps requires an expensive, specific tuning of noise parameters. This paper introduces a simple and flexible learning framework that can progressively adjust these parameters for any chosen number of steps, contrasting with prior methods that necessitate separate retuning for each step count. Moreover, by leaving the diffusion model's weights unchanged, we achieve a substantial boost in synthesis quality for low-step scenarios, all with negligible computational overhead.

Infrared dark clouds (IRDCs) serve as promising locations for the nascent stages of high-mass star formation (HMSF). This study presents a detailed examination of fragmentation characteristics within a selected sample of 10 IRDCs, recognized as prime targets for investigating HMSF in the Milky Way. Utilizing ALMA band 3 (3mm) observations, we acquired extensive mosaics of these regions, achieving high angular resolution (~3 arcsec or ~0.05 pc) alongside superior sensitivity in both continuum and spectral line data (~0.15 mJy/beam and ~0.2 K per 0.1 km/s channel at the N2H+(1-0) line). Analysis of the dust continuum revealed 96 gravitationally bound cores with masses spanning 3.4 to 50.9 M☉ (virial parameter α_vir = 0.3–1.3), which would necessitate magnetic field strengths between 0.3 and 1.0 mG to maintain virial equilibrium. By integrating these findings with a standardized literature catalogue, we reconstructed the hierarchical structure of these clouds across four orders of magnitude in spatial scale (0.01 pc to 10 pc). Supplementary high-resolution observations indicate that the smallest fragments (<0.02 pc) within this hierarchy currently lack the necessary mass and density to form high-mass stars. Nevertheless, the new ALMA data enabled the identification of 19 cores (6 quiescent, 13 star-forming) retaining >16 M☉ without further fragmentation. These massive cores exhibit trans-sonic non-thermal motions, are kinematically sub-virial, and require moderate magnetic fields to resist collapse. Pinpointing these potential HMSF sites constitutes a crucial advancement for testing theoretical predictions regarding high-mass star and cluster formation.

This study presents an adversarial approach designed to stress-test trained metrics used for evaluating conversational dialogue systems. By utilizing Reinforcement Learning, the method identifies response strategies capable of maximizing scores from these metrics. When applied to recently introduced trained metrics, the results reveal that all are vulnerable to assigning high scores to responses produced by relatively simple and evidently flawed tactics. Specifically, the method converges on strategies such as copying segments of the conversation context to generate replies, which achieve competitive scores or even surpass those written by humans.

Although the Markowitz framework has been widely applied to portfolio analysis over the decades, it prioritizes market uncertainty analysis over trend prediction. While generative adversarial networks (GANs) and conditional GANs (CGANs) have been utilized to generate financial time series and extract features for portfolio analysis, the CGAN approach is limited by its excessive focus on series generation at the expense of retaining useful features for the generator. This paper presents an autoencoding conditional GAN (ACGAN) grounded in deep generative models, which simultaneously captures market uncertainty, forecasts future trends, and learns the internal patterns within historical data. Evaluated on real-world datasets from both US and European markets, the proposed ACGAN demonstrates superior portfolio allocation and produces time series that more closely resemble actual data compared to traditional Markowitz and standard CGAN methods.

This paper details the matrix computation capabilities within the Apache Spark cluster programming framework. Spark natively offers abstractions and implementations for distributed matrices alongside associated optimization routines. When adapting single-node algorithms for distributed clusters, we found that a straightforward strategy is often sufficient: isolating matrix operations to be executed on the cluster while retaining vector operations on the local driver. Applying this principle to Singular Value Decomposition allows us to leverage cluster-scale computational power while executing code originally designed for a single core decades ago. Additionally, we present a Spark port of the widely used TFOCS optimization package, originally developed for MATLAB, enabling the solution of linear and various other convex programs. The discussion concludes with a comprehensive benchmark suite for JVM-based, hardware-accelerated matrix computations, a topic of independent interest given that many cluster frameworks rely on the JVM. The contributions outlined in this work have been integrated into Apache Spark, are available by default on Spark installations, and are commercially supported by numerous companies offering related services.

Maunakea stands as a premier global location for astronomical observations, hosting numerous telescopes that operate across optical and sub-millimeter wavelengths. Situated above 4,200 meters, its summit offers ideal conditions characterized by a historically dry and stable climate with minimal atmospheric turbulence. However, amid a shifting climate, this study investigates how summit conditions have evolved over the past few decades since the site's selection and assesses its resilience to future changes. By synthesizing data from in-situ meteorological records, radiosonde profiles, and numerical reanalyses, we have constructed a 40-year climatology for Maunakea. Our analysis examines both meteorological factors, such as wind speed and humidity, and image quality metrics, including seeing conditions. Results indicate that meteorological conditions remained largely stable throughout the period, showing few statistically significant trends but exhibiting quasi-cyclical inter-annual variability in key astronomical parameters like temperature and precipitable water vapor. Conversely, maximum wind speeds have risen over recent decades; specifically, the frequency of winds exceeding 15 m/s has increased by 1–2%, a change that could significantly affect ground-layer turbulence. Crucially, the Fried parameter has remained unchanged over the last 40 years, implying no increase in optical turbulence strength above the summit. Ultimately, the acquisition of additional data and profiling instruments is essential to maintain ongoing monitoring and to detect future alterations in the summit's climate.

In online Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) decision-making, it is essential to perform inference on the true mean reward of each arm using data gathered up to that point. However, because arms are selected adaptively, resulting in non-i.i.d. data, accurate inference becomes challenging. Specifically, simple sample averaging—employed by UCB and Thompson sampling (TS) algorithms—is suboptimal due to inherent bias and poor statistical properties, such as a lack of asymptotic normality. This paper argues that employing more advanced inference methods capable of accounting for the adaptive nature of sequential data can yield additional performance improvements, despite UCB and TS already being optimal in the worst-case scenario. We introduce "doubly adaptive TS," a TS variant that utilizes recent causal inference advances to adaptively reweight a doubly robust estimator for estimating each arm's true mean reward. Through 20 synthetic experiments and a semi-synthetic study based on real-world A/B testing data, we show that this adaptive inferential approach significantly enhances online decision-making while maintaining TS's exploration capabilities. The proposed DATS algorithm outperforms existing baselines (UCB and TS) in both regret and sample complexity for identifying the optimal arm. Furthermore, we derive a finite-time regret bound for doubly adaptive TS that matches the worst-case bounds of UCB and TS (up to logarithmic factors), confirming that its practical advantages do not compromise theoretical optimality.

Building upon \cite{Licollapsing}, this work investigates Calabi-Yau metrics that degenerate along a holomorphic fibration defined over a Riemann surface. Under the assumption that singular fibers are at most canonical, we establish a uniform diameter bound for all fibers under appropriate rescaling. This result yields significant implications for the geometric structure in the vicinity of these singular fibers.

Capturing images through glass windows frequently results in unwanted reflections that compromise photo quality. This ill-posed challenge has garnered significant research attention for over a decade, primarily due to the scarcity of real-world training data and the critical need to generate realistic synthetic alternatives. This paper introduces a single-image reflection removal approach utilizing context-aware modules and adversarial training to efficiently restore the transmission layer free of reflections. Additionally, we present a sophisticated data generation model capable of producing a vast training set featuring diverse reflection types. Our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior PSNR and SSIM scores on the SIR benchmark dataset.

Let ${\mathcal A}$ denote the class of functions $f$ analytic in the unit disk ${\mathbb D}$ satisfying the normalization $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+a_3z^3+\cdots$. For $0<\lambda\le1$, define the set ${\mathcal U}(\lambda)$ as $\left\{ f\in{\mathcal A}: \left |\left (\frac{z}{f(z)} \right )^{2}f'(z)-1\right | < \lambda,\, z\in{\mathbb D} \right\}$. This paper establishes sharp upper bounds for the first three coefficients of the inverse function $f^{-1}$ under the condition that $\frac{f(z)}{z}\prec \frac{1}{(1-z)(1-\lambda z)}$.

This paper continues the investigation into $(\mathrm{tw},\omega)$-bounded graph classes—hereditary families where large treewidth arises solely from large cliques—to determine the algorithmic consequences of this property for the Independent Set problem and similar challenges. Following our prior work introducing the tree-independence number, a min-max invariant linked to tree decompositions that guarantees polynomial-time solutions for Maximum Weight Independent Set in graphs with bounded independence number, this study examines six distinct graph containment relations. For each relation, we identify the specific graphs $H$ such that any $H$-free graph admits a tree decomposition with bounded independence number. Of particular significance is the induced minor relation: we demonstrate that excluding a $K_5$ minus an edge or the $4$-wheel ensures a tree decomposition where every bag consists of a clique plus at most three vertices, whereas excluding a complete bipartite graph $K_{2,q}$ yields a decomposition with an independence number no greater than $2(q-1)$. These constructive proofs leverage diverse tools, including $\ell$-refined tree decompositions, SPQR trees, and potential maximal cliques, leading to polynomial-time algorithms for Independent Set across an infinite family of graph classes. Notably, these findings apply to $1$-perfectly orientable graphs, thereby resolving a question posed by Beisegel, Chudnovsky, Gurvich, Milani\v{c}, and Servatius in 2019.

Multiple density estimation techniques have proven ineffective at identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) samples by incorrectly assigning high likelihoods to anomalous data. Energy-based models (EBMs), which are flexible and unnormalized, appear capable of overcoming this limitation. However, our comprehensive investigation into OOD detection using EBMs trained via various methods on both tabular and image datasets reveals that these models do not consistently offer advantages. We hypothesize that, despite possessing a discriminative structure akin to Normalizing Flows, EBMs fail to learn semantic features. To validate this hypothesis, we demonstrate that incorporating supervision and imposing architectural constraints enhances OOD detection performance in EBMs, regardless of the specific training methodology employed.

Neutrino physics represents a pivotal area within both cosmology and particle physics. Although numerous theoretical and experimental aspects of neutrino properties have been established, significant unresolved questions remain. This study proposes that gravitational perturbations inducing space-time deformation could significantly influence neutrino oscillations. Through analytical examination, we demonstrated that such deformations result in an anomalous cyclic pattern within these oscillations. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of this anomaly is directly correlated with the extent of space-time deformation. The implications of this anomaly for neutrino oscillations may be substantial, potentially linking the cyclic anomaly to other known neutrino irregularities, including constraints on mass, energy, oscillation length, mixing angles, and propagation speed. These cyclic anomalies could potentially be observed experimentally; their confirmation would necessitate a more profound reconsideration of current neutrino physics frameworks.

This article presents a modular framework designed to apply Reinforcement Learning to Optimal Trade Execution, prioritizing flexibility to simplify various simulation configurations. Instead of centering on agents or optimization techniques, the approach decomposes the environment into essential components for simulating trade execution under RL, including data preprocessing, observation construction, action handling, child order execution, benchmark simulation, and reward calculation. The authors provide examples for each component, examine implementation challenges and inter-component interactions, and discuss the phenomena each induces, particularly noting the divergence between simulations and real market behavior. The modular design is demonstrated through a setup where an agent, adhering to a Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP) schedule, places only limit orders; these are executed by iterating over Limit Order Book (LOB) snapshots, with rewards defined as the price improvement over a TWAP benchmark. Additionally, the paper introduces evaluation procedures involving iterative re-training and assessment across training intervals, mimicking continuous agent adaptation to new data and reflecting regulatory monitoring practices required of algorithm providers.

In federated learning, both malicious attackers and honest-but-curious servers risk stealing private client data through uploaded gradients. While existing protection strategies, such as additive homomorphic encryption, ensure system security, they incur significant computational and communication overheads. To address these costs, we introduce the \texttt{FedAGE} framework, allowing the server to aggregate gradients within an encoded domain without ever accessing individual clients' raw gradients. Consequently, \texttt{FedAGE} prevents curious servers from gradient theft while preserving prediction accuracy without adding communication expenses. Additionally, we provide a theoretical proof demonstrating that the proposed encoding-decoding scheme functions as a Gaussian mechanism for differential privacy. Finally, evaluations across various federated settings confirm the effectiveness of our framework.

This paper presents ExpertMatcher, an approach to automate deep learning model selection via autoencoders. The focus is on enabling inference across distributed client data sources by leveraging pretrained expert machine learning networks hosted on a central server. ExpertMatcher identifies the most pertinent model(s) on the server based on the client's data representation. This facilitates resource-limited clients in developing nations to access the most suitable ML models for their specific tasks without needing to assess every model's performance individually. The proposed method is versatile and advantageous in any scenario involving local clients and a large collection of centralized expert ML models.

We numerically investigate the confinement/deconfinement transition in the D0-brane matrix model, frequently referred to as the BFSS matrix model, along with its one-parameter deformation known as the BMN matrix model, utilizing lattice Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings align with general predictions derived from the dual string/M-theory framework under strong coupling conditions. Specifically, we detect the confined phase within the BFSS matrix model, a result that constitutes a nontrivial implication of the M-theory perspective. We propose that these models offer an optimal framework for examining the Schwarzschild black hole, M-theory, and the parameter regime governing the phase transition between type IIA superstring theory and M-theory. Furthermore, conducting a detailed study of M-theory through lattice Monte Carlo simulations of the D0-brane matrix model may be feasible with significantly fewer computational resources than previously anticipated.

Complex systems serve as ideal environments for investigating the fundamental interactions between components and their resulting emergent behaviors. Integrated photonics, through sophisticated design, provides a platform for complex nonlinear interactions that generate novel light patterns. Specifically, the standard Kerr-nonlinear resonator becomes unstable when subjected to strong traveling-wave excitation, leading to the formation of a Turing pattern consisting of a few interfering waves. While these resonators also sustain localized soliton pulses as a distinct nonlinear stationary state, Kerr solitons are highly adaptable for applications yet cannot arise from constant excitation. This study examines an edge-less photonic-crystal resonator (PhCR) that facilitates the spontaneous generation of a soliton pulse, replacing the typical Turing pattern. We engineered a PhCR within the single-azimuthal-mode regime to counterbalance Kerr-nonlinear frequency shifts, thereby favoring the soliton state in a manner analogous to how group-velocity dispersion balances nonlinearity. Our experimental results confirm that PhCR solitons function as mode-locked pulses through ultraprecise optical-frequency measurements, while also detailing their fundamental characteristics. This work demonstrates that sub-wavelength nanophotonic design broadens the possibilities for nonlinear engineering of light.

We demonstrate the application of the Recursive Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (RQAOA) to the MAX-$k$-CUT problem, which involves finding an approximate $k$-vertex coloring for a graph. This approach is evaluated against the most advanced existing classical and hybrid classical-quantum algorithms. Initially, we establish that standard (non-recursive) QAOA struggles to solve this optimization problem for most regular bipartite graphs at any constant depth $p$, achieving an approximation ratio barely superior to random vertex coloring. Subsequently, we develop an efficient classical simulation method capable of replicating level-1 QAOA and level-1 RQAOA across arbitrary graphs. These hybrid methods effectively function as efficient classical algorithms, implying no immediate advantage from quantum mechanics; however, they serve as an ideal testbed for evaluating hybrid algorithmic potential. Utilizing this simulation tool, we conducted large-scale experiments on ensembles of randomly generated 3-colorable constant-degree graphs, testing level-1 QAOA and RQAOA with up to 300 qutrits. Our results indicate that level-1 RQAOA is unexpectedly competitive, frequently outperforming the best known generic classical algorithms based on rounding SDP relaxations in terms of approximation ratios. This outcome suggests the promising possibility that higher-level RQAOA could prove useful for NISQ devices.

This study investigates drift estimation for linear stochastic evolution equations, particularly linear SPDEs, driven by additive fractional noise with Hurst indices between 0 and 1, utilizing a least-squares approach. Because the standard least-squares estimator involves stochastic integrals of divergence type, we tackle the challenge of evaluating it pathwise and robustly against observation errors by comparing it with Stratonovich pathwise integrals and leveraging their chain-rule property. Consequently, the resulting pathwise least-squares estimator is defined implicitly as the solution to a non-linear equation. We examine both its numerical characteristics (existence and uniqueness of the solution) and statistical attributes (strong consistency and convergence rates). The asymptotic properties are derived under a fixed time horizon with an increasing number of observed Fourier modes (spatial asymptotics), and we further conjecture the asymptotic normality of this pathwise estimator.

We present a source generating correlated atom pairs with opposite momenta and spatial modes that constitute a Bell state based solely on external degrees of freedom. The state of the emitted atom beams is verified through the observation of strong number squeezing, reaching -10 dB, within the correlated two-particle emission modes. Additionally, we demonstrate authentic two-particle interference by analyzing the normalized second-order correlation function $g^{(2)}$ of the emitted atoms.

Normalized harmonic centrality is a relatively recent metric within social network analysis. As a variation of closeness centrality, it calculates the sum of the reciprocals of the geodesic distances from each node to all others, assigning a value of zero if no path exists between nodes. This sum is subsequently normalized by dividing by m-1, where m represents the total number of nodes in the graph. This paper explores the harmonic centrality properties of several significant graph classes.

The discrepancy between standard model (SM) theoretical predictions and experimental data for $\mathcal{R}(D)$ in the semileptonic decay $B\to D\ell\bar{\nu}_{\ell}$ suggests the possible existence of physics beyond the SM. In studies of this decay using perturbative QCD factorization and light-cone QCD sum rules, the primary uncertainties arise from the $D$-meson twist-2, 3 distribution amplitudes (DAs): $\phi_{2;D}(x,\mu)$, $\phi_{3;D}^p(x,\mu)$, and $\phi_{3;D}^\sigma(x,\mu)$. Consequently, deriving more precise and physically sound behaviors for these DAs is crucial. Building on our prior research regarding pionic leading-twist DAs, we re-examine the $D$-meson twist-2 and twist-3 DAs. We propose novel sum rule formulas for the $\xi$-moments of these three DAs to enhance calculation accuracy. Furthermore, we refine the light-cone harmonic oscillator models for these DAs, determining their parameters via a least-squares fit to the $\xi$-moment values.

This study aims to conduct a thorough assessment of 32 cutting-edge Full-Reference Image Quality Assessment (FR-IQA) metrics using the newly released MDID database. This repository comprises distorted images generated from pristine reference images through various random distortion types and intensities, specifically including Gaussian noise, Gaussian blur, contrast variations, JPEG artifacts, and JPEG2000 compression noise.

Although dark energy has only begun to dominate cosmic evolution at a redshift of approximately $z\approx0.7$, its energy density already accounted for more than $5\%$ of the total as far back as $z\approx2.5$. By computing model-independent constraints on this fraction from upcoming galaxy surveys, we demonstrate that the emergence of dark energy could be detected with $3\sigma$ significance almost out to $z\approx2.5$.

By employing {\it ab initio} methods that integrate extended Hubbard interactions with phonons, we show that the intersite Coulomb interaction is pivotal in defining the distinct phases of paradigmatic charge-ordered materials like Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$AO$_3$ (where $A=$ Bi and Sb). We demonstrate that including self-consistently derived nearest-neighbor Hubbard interactions accurately explains key doping-dependent experimental observations, such as breathing instabilities, anomalous phonon dispersions, and the transition between charge-density wave and superconducting states. Consequently, this establishes a minimal requirement for reliably modeling spontaneous charge orders in solids.

The ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider has conducted a measurement of single top-quark production via the s-channel using proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This analysis utilized a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. Events were selected based on the presence of an electron or muon, missing transverse momentum, and precisely two $b$-tagged jets. To distinguish single-top-quark s-channel events from primary background sources—specifically top-quark pair production and jet-associated $W$-boson production—a matrix-element-based discriminant was employed. The analysis yielded an observed signal significance of 3.3 standard deviations (with an expectation of 3.9) against the background-only hypothesis. The resulting measured cross-section is $\sigma=8.2^{+3.5}_{-2.9}$ pb, which aligns with the Standard Model prediction of $\sigma^{\mathrm{SM}}=10.32^{+0.40}_{-0.36}$ pb.

Backwards reachability serves as a highly efficient zone-based method for verifying probabilistic timed automata against PTCTL specifications. However, existing implementations are limited to handling maximum probabilities within reachability properties. This paper details our novel implementation of backwards reachability integrated into the Modest Toolset, which extends support to both minimum and maximum probabilities for until formulas, making it the most comprehensive solution currently available. Furthermore, we evaluate its performance by comparing it with the experimental findings from the foundational papers introducing the backwards reachability technique.

Reconstructing a many-body Hamiltonian from its dynamical evolution is a cornerstone challenge in physics. This study introduces the inaugural algorithm capable of reaching the Heisenberg limit for learning an interacting $N$-qubit local Hamiltonian. Following a total evolution time scaling as $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$, the method efficiently estimates any parameter within the $N$-qubit Hamiltonian with $\epsilon$-accuracy and high probability. Notably, the approach remains robust against state preparation and measurement errors, avoids the need for eigenstates or thermal states, and relies on only $\mathrm{polylog}(\epsilon^{-1})$ experimental runs. By comparison, leading prior methods—such as those employing gradient-based optimization or polynomial interpolation—demand $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ evolution time and an equivalent number of experiments. Our technique leverages concepts from quantum simulation to separate the unknown $N$-qubit Hamiltonian $H$ into noninteracting segments, subsequently learning $H$ via a quantum-enhanced divide-and-conquer strategy. Furthermore, we demonstrate a matching lower bound to confirm the asymptotic optimality of this algorithm.

We demonstrate that the eigenvalues of a power hypergraph $G^{(k)}$ can be derived from the eigenvalues of signed subgraphs within the underlying graph $G$. This finding corrects an erroneous claim made in [Linear Algebra and its Applications, 590:243-257, 2020].

**Context:** The origins of hot exozodiacal dust and its relationship with outer dust reservoirs remain uncertain. **Aims:** This study investigates potential links between hot exozodiacal dust and warm dust reservoirs (>100 K) within asteroid belts. **Methods:** We employed high-precision near-infrared interferometry using VLTI/PIONIER to detect resolved emission at H-band around a selected sample of nearby stars. **Results:** Observations identified resolved near-infrared emission around 17 of the 52 stars; four cases were attributed to previously unknown stellar companions, while the remaining 13 H-band excesses are believed to stem from thermal emission by hot dust grains. Incorporating earlier PIONIER data and re-evaluating the warm dust content of all targets via spectral energy distribution modeling, we determined a detection rate of 17.1(+8.1)(-4.6)% for H-band excess around main-sequence stars hosting warm dust belts. This rate is statistically consistent with the 14.6(+4.3)(-2.8)% occurrence rate observed around stars lacking warm dust. However, after adjusting for sensitivity losses caused by partially unresolved hot disks—assuming they form thin rings at their sublimation radius—we find tentative evidence at the 3σ level that H-band excesses around stars with outer dust reservoirs (warm or cold) may be statistically higher than those around stars with no detectable outer dust. **Conclusions:** Our findings do not indicate a direct connection between warm and hot dust populations at the sensitivity level of these instruments, although they suggest a possible correlation between the magnitude of H-band excesses and the general presence of outer dust reservoirs.

Despite the widespread adoption of speech recognition, extracting emotion from speech signals remains a significant challenge. To tackle this, we introduce a Quaternion Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) designed for speech emotion recognition (SER), which encodes Mel-spectrogram features into an RGB quaternion domain. Our QCNN-based SER model surpasses existing real-valued approaches on the RAVDESS dataset (8 classes), achieving state-of-the-art performance with an accuracy of 77.87%. Additionally, the model delivers results comparable to current state-of-the-art methods on the IEMOCAP (4 classes) and EMO-DB (7 classes) datasets, attaining accuracies of 70.46% and 88.78%, respectively. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the quaternion unit structure effectively captures internal dependencies, leading to a substantially reduced model size compared to alternative methods.

This study aims to benchmark automatic polyp segmentation using a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework. By treating the challenge as an image-to-image translation task, the authors employ conditional GANs to produce masks based on input images, with both the generator and discriminator constructed using convolutional neural networks. The resulting model attained a Jaccard index of 0.4382 and an F2 score of 0.611.

Topic taxonomies organize text corpora into hierarchical structures, offering topical knowledge that improves various NLP tasks. To integrate emerging topics from new documents, recent research has attempted to expand existing taxonomies by inserting these new topics. However, current approaches rely solely on frequent terms and local topic-subtopic connections, resulting in poor term coverage and an inability to capture the global hierarchy. This paper introduces TopicExpan, a novel framework for taxonomy expansion that directly generates terms related to new topics. By utilizing the hierarchical context surrounding a new topic and the content of input documents, TopicExpan promotes the inclusion of important yet less frequent terms while maintaining relational consistency within the taxonomy. Experiments on two real-world corpora demonstrate that TopicExpan significantly outperforms baseline methods regarding the quality of the resulting taxonomies.

Theoretical models of evolutionary dynamics in spatially structured populations often depend on non-spatial frameworks. Biofilms represent such populations where a more precise theoretical understanding is valuable for uncovering new solutions to current challenges. In this study, we investigated how environmental geometry influences the evolutionary dynamics of expanding populations using the Eden model. Our findings indicate that fluctuations within sub-populations during range expansion in both 2D and 3D environments do not follow Brownian motion. Moreover, we observed that the geometry of the substrate disrupts the evolutionary dynamics of populations growing on it. Drawing inspiration from these results, we propose implementing periodically wedged patterns on surfaces susceptible to biofilm formation. On these patterned surfaces, natural selection becomes less efficient, making it more difficult for beneficial mutants to establish. Additionally, this modification accelerates genetic drift, resulting in biofilms with reduced genetic diversity. Both of these outcomes are highly desirable for managing biofilms.

We present an etale fundamental group incorporating a modulus and establish a reciprocity homomorphism mapping the Kato-Saito idele class group with modulus to this group. This construction serves as the K-theoretic counterpart to the cycle-theoretic reciprocity for the idele class group with modulus developed by Kerz and Saito, and it is pivotal in demonstrating the isomorphism between these two idele class groups. Furthermore, it offers a novel perspective on the etale fundamental group with modulus previously defined by Deligne and Laumon.

Although deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have significantly advanced face recognition, they frequently struggle in real-world scenarios where training images sourced from the internet differ from test images due to variations in lighting, pose, and image quality. These discrepancies create a gap between the source (training) and target (testing) domains, causing learned models to underperform in practical applications. Furthermore, the scarcity of labeled data in the target domain makes direct fine-tuning of pre-trained models both infeasible and impractical. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel clustering-based domain adaptation method tailored for face recognition tasks where the source and target domains share no common classes. Our approach effectively learns discriminative target features by globally aligning the feature domain while simultaneously distinguishing target clusters locally. Specifically, the method first generates more reliable representations for clustering by minimizing global domain discrepancies to bridge the domain gap. It then employs a simplified spectral clustering technique to produce pseudo-labels within a domain-invariant feature space, ultimately learning a discriminative target representation. Extensive experiments on widely used datasets, including GBU, IJB-A/B/C, and RFW, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach. Notably, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GBU dataset using only unsupervised adaptation from the target training data.

This study focuses on approximating fractional powers of self-adjoint positive operators. By leveraging the integral representation of these operators, we employ the trapezoidal rule alongside both single-exponential and double-exponential transforms applied to the integrand. For the single-exponential approach, our primary objective is to revisit theoretical foundations to optimize parameter selection for accelerated convergence. Regarding the double-exponential transform, we demonstrate improvements to existing error estimates for the scalar case and extend this analysis to the operator setting. Finally, we present numerical experiments to validate the reliability of the derived estimates.

Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) are prevalent in the centers of most intermediate-mass galaxies ($10^{9}$ M$_{\odot}$), though recent studies indicate they are uncommon in the least and most massive systems, with their occurrence rate rising in dense environments. However, the validity of this trend for field galaxies remains uncertain due to scarce data. This study presents findings on the nucleation fraction for 601 galaxies within the Local Volume ($\lesssim 12$ Mpc), representing the largest analysis of such galaxies in a low-density setting across more than eight orders of magnitude in stellar mass. We confirm a strong correlation between nucleation fraction and stellar mass, consistent with prior research. Additionally, for galaxies with $M_{\star} < 10^{9}$ M$_{\odot}$, early-type systems exhibit higher nucleation fractions than late-type ones. In the Local Volume, the nucleation fraction correlates independently with stellar mass, Hubble type, and local environmental density. By standardizing stellar mass calculations, we compared our data with results from galaxy clusters (Coma, Fornax, and Virgo). We observed significantly reduced nucleation fractions (up to 40%) for galaxies with $M_{\star} \lesssim 10^{9.5}$ M$_{\odot}$, aligning with earlier work. While our results strengthen the link between globular clusters and NSCs, the extent to which this connection explains trends related to Hubble type and local environment remains ambiguous. We further speculate that the correlation between nucleation fraction and cluster density diminishes in the most concentrated clusters, such as Coma and Virgo.

When a physical system evolves within a thermal bath at a fixed temperature, it eventually reaches an equilibrium state whose characteristics are independent of kinetic parameters and specific evolutionary pathways. This is generally not true for systems driven out of equilibrium; instead, they attain a steady state where properties rely heavily on the detailed dynamics, including driving noise and energy dissipation. Understanding how steady states depend on these parameters is typically a complex challenge. In this work, we address this broad issue using a minimal model of a two-dimensional nano-machine, the Brownian gyrator, comprising a trapped particle driven by fractional Gaussian noises—noises characterized by long-range temporal correlations and an anomalous diffusion exponent $\alpha$. When the noise differs across spatial directions, our fractional Brownian gyrator exhibits persistent rotation. Despite the noise's non-trivial nature with long-range time correlations, its Gaussian properties allow us to analytically characterize the resulting nonequilibrium steady state by calculating the probability density function, probability current, its curl, and angular velocity, supported by complementary numerical results.

Training denoising autoencoders typically demands pristine data, a condition that is frequently unattainable. To address this limitation, we propose a technique for training autoencoders exclusively on noisy datasets that contain both signal and non-signal examples. This approach enables the network to learn a segmented representation that isolates and reconstructs both signal and noise components independently. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by cleaning birdsong audio—readily available in uncontrolled noisy environments—using a convolutional autoencoder.

Starting with Pythia version 8.150, the basic isotropic decay model for tau-leptons has been superseded by advanced decay mechanisms. This document outlines the decays and spin correlations for tau-leptons within Pythia 8, covering the spin correlation algorithm, production processes, decay models, user interface, and implementation details.

For any graph $G$ and parameters $\alpha \ge 1$ and $\beta \ge 0$, a spanning subgraph $H$ is defined as an $(\alpha, \beta)$-spanner if the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ in $H$ satisfies $\dist(u, v, H) \le \alpha \cdot \dist(u, v, G) + \beta$. These structures, known as \emph{linear spanners}, serve as a generalization of both \emph{multiplicative} and \emph{additive spanners}. Following recent work by Fomin, Golovach, Lochet, Misra, Saurabh, and Sharma (IPEC 2020) on directed additive and multiplicative spanners, this paper extends that research to directed linear spanners. We demonstrate that the \textsc{Directed Linear Spanner} problem, when parameterized by the vertex count $n$, lacks a polynomial compression of size $\calO(n^{2 - \epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon > 0$, assuming $\NP \not\subseteq \coNP/poly$. Comparable lower bounds apply to the \textsc{Directed Additive Spanner} and \textsc{Directed Multiplicative Spanner} problems. Furthermore, these sparsification hardness results remain valid even for directed acyclic graphs and for any computable functions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ dependent on the approximated distance.

Data centers face significant congestion challenges due to the combination of bursty composite traffic, low bandwidth-delay products, and limited switch buffers, which traditional congestion control protocols like TCP fail to manage effectively. While previous efforts have attempted to resolve this by adapting TCP to fit data center dynamics—a strategy viable in private environments but prohibited in public ones—this work proposes a novel, switch-based queue management solution. This approach eliminates the need to modify TCP sender or receiver algorithms, facilitating seamless deployment in public data centers. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating the scheme's stability and efficacy. Furthermore, we detail three distinct implementations (a Linux kernel module and an OpenvSwitch extension), supported by numerical results from NS-2 simulations and real-world tests on a small cluster. These results confirm the method's ability to deliver high throughput, ensure fairness, and minimize flow completion times for delay-sensitive applications.

Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) are a critical component of Biosafety Levels (BSLs) in laboratories and infection-control hospitals, designed to contain deadly pathogens and prevent their escape. These rooms maintain internal pressure lower than the surrounding environment to ensure microbial containment. Currently, Building Management Systems (BMSs) rely on Differential Pressure Sensors (DPSs) to monitor and regulate this negative pressure. This paper presents a stealthy, non-invasive attack on NPRs by spoofing a DPS at its resonant frequency. Our key contributions are: (1) identifying that DPSs commonly used in NPRs possess resonant frequencies within the audible spectrum; (2) developing malicious music to induce resonance in these sensors, which causes their pressure readings to overshoot; and (3) demonstrating how this resonance can deceive BMSs into switching an NPR's negative pressure to positive, creating a risk of pathogen leakage. Through experiments on 8 DPSs from 5 manufacturers, we found resonance in 6 units, taking sampling tube length into account. Our attack can induce a 2.5 Pa pressure shift from approximately 7 cm away without a sampling tube, or from 2.5 cm away with a 1-meter tube. Additionally, we introduced an interval-time variation technique for adversarial control, allowing the forged pressure to range between 12 and 33 Pa. The attack is capable of targeting multiple NPRs at once. We successfully demonstrated this attack on a real-world, FDA-approved NPR in an anonymous bioresearch facility that adheres to CDC guidelines, and we also propose countermeasures to mitigate this threat.

During the LHC's first two operational runs, the LHCb experiment at CERN completed numerous physics measurements, relying heavily on Monte Carlo simulations for their analysis. As LHCb prepares for Run 3 with a major detector upgrade designed to handle five times the luminosity of previous runs, new simulation technologies are required to generate sufficiently large data samples within the allocated computing budget. Consequently, the collaboration is developing an enhanced version of the Gauss simulation framework. This updated system retains LHCb-specific features while integrating its general simulation infrastructure into the experiment-agnostic Gaussino framework. Gaussino merges the Gaudi core with the Geant4 toolkit, fully leveraging their multi-threading capabilities. Additionally, a prototype fast simulation interface is being built for Gaussino, offering a wide range of models, including emerging deep learning-based options.

The widespread success of pre-trained models has led to the broad adoption of the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm for source code understanding tasks. Yet, despite the high costs of training large-scale models from scratch, effective methods for adapting these pre-trained models to new tasks remain underexplored. This paper introduces a method to connect pre-trained models with code-specific tasks. By utilizing semantic-preserving transformations to increase the diversity of downstream data, we enable pre-trained models to learn semantic features that remain invariant to these equivalent changes. Additionally, we incorporate curriculum learning to arrange the transformed data in an easy-to-hard sequence for fine-tuning. When applied to various pre-trained models, our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance on source code understanding tasks, including algorithm classification, code clone detection, and code search. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that a natural language pre-trained model like RoBERTa, when fine-tuned with this lightweight method, can match or exceed the performance of specialized code pre-trained models such as CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT, even without extensive pre-training on code data. This indicates considerable potential for further improvement in code pre-trained models.

We propose an adiabatic long-range quantum communication scheme utilizing a quantum dot array. By adiabatically adjusting the external gate voltage, quantum information encoded in an electron is transported from one terminal dot to another. Through numerical solutions of the Schrödinger equation for a specific number of quantum dots, we demonstrate that this approach offers a straightforward and efficient protocol for the coherent manipulation of population transfer via appropriate gate pulses. We numerically analyze how the energy gap and transfer time vary with system parameters. Furthermore, we examine adiabatic passage in a more realistic scenario accounting for unavoidable fabrication imperfections. This methodology offers valuable guidance for future experimental implementations of adiabatic quantum state transfer.

This work introduces a novel approach to compute the Coulomb breakup of high-energy, unstable neutron-rich isotopes. Utilizing the eikonal approximation, the method incorporates a newly developed Coulomb dynamical polarization potential (CDPP). This potential is derived by solving the Schrödinger equation for the full trajectory of the exotic projectile, modeled as a two-body cluster under the adiabatic approximation while including continuum excitations. Comparisons of calculations for various exotic isotopes against experimental Coulomb dissociation cross-section data demonstrate strong agreement.

The synergistic relationship between ferroelectricity and photovoltaics in two-dimensional (2D) materials offers a promising pathway to enhance and control photovoltaic performance. This study utilizes 2D 3R bilayer BX (where X = P, As, Sb) as model systems to investigate the photovoltaic properties of intrinsic out-of-plane (OOP) ferroelectric materials, aiming to develop strategies for tuning photoelectric characteristics by adjusting ferroelectric polarization strength. The unique 3R stacking arrangement breaks spatial inversion symmetry, inducing spontaneous OOP ferroelectric polarization that can be switched via specific interlayer sliding. This ferroelectricity drives charge transfer between layers, facilitating efficient spatial separation of holes and electrons and establishing type-II band alignment. Furthermore, the perfect lattice matching between identical layers makes 3R bilayer BX more experimentally stable and feasible compared to traditional 2D heterostructures composed of different materials. These systems exhibit moderate band gaps, ultra-high carrier mobility, and strong optical absorption, resulting in nano-devices with high photocurrent, superior photon responsivity, and excellent external quantum efficiency. Crucially, all these photoelectric parameters are governed by the intrinsic OOP ferroelectric strength; by modifying the interlayer distance, the ferroelectric polarization can be effectively regulated to optimize photoelectric performance. Finally, we highlight the significance and universality of broken spatial inversion symmetry in layered materials beyond 3R bilayer BX for achieving the co-regulation of ferroelectric and photovoltaic effects.

Biological neural networks are frequently represented as systems of coupled, nonlinear ordinary or partial differential equations. As network size and the granularity of neuron and synapse modeling increase, so does the number of equations required. Consequently, scaling simulations demands robust computing infrastructure. Although numerous tools exist for numerically solving these equations, they are often limited to specific platforms. Furthermore, creating flexible, platform-independent code that leverages hardware acceleration on modern architectures like GPUs, TPUs, and distributed systems presents a significant challenge. While TensorFlow is a Python-based open-source library primarily for machine learning, it also serves as a scalable environment for diverse computations, including solving differential equations via iterative techniques such as Runge-Kutta methods. This article and its associated tutorials offer a straightforward introduction to numerical methods for solving ordinary differential equations using Python and TensorFlow. The curriculum comprises five Python notebook sessions that guide novice programmers from integrating simple one-dimensional ODEs to simulating large-scale systems of thousands of coupled conductance-based neurons using a highly parallelized and scalable framework. Additionally, the tutorials include a physiologically realistic model of an insect olfactory network, featuring multiple neuron and synapse types, which can serve as a template for simulating other neural networks.

Contrastive learning techniques utilizing the InfoNCE loss are widely adopted for node representation learning on graph-structured data. However, their dependence on data augmentation and quadratic computational complexity can result in inefficiency and inconsistency. To address these drawbacks, this paper presents a straightforward yet effective model called Localized Graph Contrastive Learning (Local-GCL). This approach incorporates two primary innovations: first, it generates positive examples for each node directly from its immediate neighbors, eliminating the need for carefully crafted graph augmentations; second, it introduces a kernelized contrastive loss that can be approximated with linear time and space complexity relative to the graph size. Theoretical analysis supports the validity and effectiveness of these proposed methods. Furthermore, experiments across diverse datasets of varying scales and characteristics demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, Local-GCL achieves highly competitive performance in self-supervised node representation learning tasks.

Robots require task planning to order and perform actions to reach their objectives. Conversely, Behavior Trees offer a mathematical framework for defining plan execution that is inherently composable, reactive, and robust. PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) currently serves as the standard language for describing plans to most systems. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that systematically converts PDDL plans into Behavior Trees for execution. The method leverages the plan's execution graph to construct the tree. A key contribution is an algorithm that generates a Behavior Tree optimized for execution by parallelizing actions; this applies to any plan while respecting causal dependencies between actions. We validate the performance improvements in mobile robot plan execution using the ROS2 Planning System framework.

We employed Bayesian model comparison to test for variability in the per-cycle annual modulation amplitude across the various phases of the DAMA/LIBRA experiment. Building on prior frequentist work by Kelso et al. (2018), which indicated a mild preference for time-dependent DAMA amplitudes spanning the DAMA/NaI phase and the initial DAMA/LIBRA phase across multiple energy bins, we first applied Bayesian techniques to show a moderate preference for exponentially varying amplitudes in the 2–5 and 2–6 keV ranges within the Kelso et al. dataset. We subsequently performed a comparable analysis on the most recent modulation amplitudes from the first two phases of the upgraded DAMA/LIBRA experiment and examined the single-hit residual rates provided by the collaboration to search for any temporal dependencies. Nevertheless, our Bayesian model selection yielded no evidence for variability in either dataset. All analysis codes and data utilized in this study are publicly accessible.
