However, since observables can be determined on an event-by-event basis in both experiments and simulations, we introduce a framework using the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) to infer the density-dependent nuclear symmetry energy through event-by-event analysis. Training data for this approach are drawn from ultrarelativistic quantum molecular dynamics (UrQMD) simulations. When tested against additional UrQMD data, the symmetry energy slope parameter extracted via LightGBM exhibits an average deviation of approximately 30 MeV from the true value and demonstrates robustness against model parameter variations. Furthermore, LightGBM can pinpoint the features most influential to the physics of interest, providing significant insights. This study indicates that the proposed framework serves as a powerful tool capable of establishing a new paradigm for investigating the underlying physics of heavy-ion collisions.

A commonly employed stochastic plate equation is the classical plate equation modified by an It\^o integral term. It has been established that this model lacks exact controllability, even when controls are active throughout the drift and diffusion terms as well as on the boundary. This limitation suggests that a critical aspect was overlooked in the original formulation. Consequently, a one-dimensional refined stochastic plate equation was introduced, and its exact controllability was proven in [28]. In this study, we utilize a novel global Carleman estimate to demonstrate the exact controllability of the multidimensional refined stochastic plate equation, employing two interior controls alongside two boundary controls. Furthermore, we present findings regarding the absence of exact controllability, indicating that the simultaneous application of two interior controls and at least one boundary control is essential.

Neutrinos traveling through dense environments, such as those found in core-collapse supernovae and neutron star merger remnants, can undergo rapid flavor conversions on scales far shorter than those predicted in a vacuum. A common class of these fast instabilities arises from neutrinos scattering backward off nuclei at significant distances from the supernova core. This study demonstrates that, despite being ubiquitous, such scattering-induced instabilities are unlikely to drive substantial flavor conversions unless the population of neutrinos moving in the backward direction is sufficiently large. In fact, these instabilities primarily affect neutrinos traveling backward, which constitute only a small fraction of the total neutrino population at large radii. We show that this limitation stems from the shape of the unstable flavor eigenstates, which are often extremely peaked toward backward angles.

We demonstrate that Rule-based Integration (Rubi) represents an advanced symbolic integration technique capable of solving numerous complex integrals that other computer algebra systems cannot handle. By employing Rubi, a wide range of integration methods become feasible. This approach utilizes step-wise simplification to break down integrals into composite forms, thereby revealing previously unknown integration rules even when the final solution is not yet identified. Our primary case study involves deriving the updated five-loop series expansion for the quark mass renormalization group equation (RGE). This expansion establishes the relationship between a light quark mass in the modified minimal subtraction ($\overline{\text{MS}}$) scheme at a specific reference scale, such as the tau-lepton mass, and an arbitrary energy scale $s$. Explicitly illustrating the renormalization scheme dependence of the running quark mass on the scale parameter $s$, this relation is crucial for accurately determining light quark masses at chosen scales, utilizing the five-loop QCD $\beta(a_s)$ and $\gamma(a_s)$ functions in the process.

Imitation learning offers a promising avenue for endowing robots with dexterous manipulation skills without relying on meticulously crafted rewards or substantial computational resources. Nevertheless, current methods depend on complex data collection setups and often fail to generalize beyond their training distributions. To overcome these challenges, one strategy involves collecting supplementary data that more accurately reflects the complete range of operating conditions. This study examines the attributes of such extra demonstrations and evaluates their influence on performance. Specifically, we analyze how corrective and randomly-sampled additional demonstrations affect the learning of a policy for a five-fingered robotic hand performing a pick-and-place task. Our findings indicate that corrective demonstrations significantly surpass randomly-sampled ones when the volume of additional data drawn from the full task distribution exceeds the number of original demonstrations from a limited training set. Conversely, when the original demonstration count is higher than that of the additional set, no statistically significant difference exists between the two types of supplementary data. These outcomes shed light on the fundamental trade-off between the effort needed to acquire corrective demonstrations and their comparative advantages over random sampling. Furthermore, we demonstrate that low-cost vision-based sensors, such as the LeapMotion, can substantially lower the expense of generating demonstrations for dexterous manipulation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/GT-STAR-Lab/corrective-demos-dexterous-manipulation.

Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) offer a non-parametric approach to function approximation, operating as a black-box technique that sums numerous trees. This method employs priors to regularize inference by limiting the learning capacity of individual trees, ensuring that the collective ensemble explains the data rather than any single component. This work examines BART within the framework of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs), treating it as a modular primitive for probabilistic models instead of an isolated tool. We introduce PyMC-BART, a Python library that extends PyMC to facilitate this integration. The discussion includes illustrative models constructed with PyMC-BART, guidance on hyperparameter selection, and a conclusion outlining current implementation constraints and potential avenues for future enhancement.

The balanced hypergraph partitioning task involves dividing a hypergraph into $k$ disjoint blocks of limited size to minimize the sum of hyperedges connecting multiple blocks. We introduce an enhancement to the flow-based refinement framework of KaHyPar-MF, which is currently the leading multilevel $k$-way hypergraph partitioning algorithm for generating high-quality results. This improvement leverages the recently developed HyperFlowCutter algorithm, which computes bipartitions of unweighted hypergraphs by solving a series of incremental maximum flow problems. Because vertices and hyperedges are aggregated during the coarsening phase, refinement methods in multilevel settings must accommodate both weighted vertices and hyperedges, even when the initial hypergraph is unweighted. Consequently, we extend HyperFlowCutter to manage weighted instances and propose a method for calculating maximum flows directly on weighted hypergraphs. We evaluated two configurations of our new algorithm against KaHyPar-MF and seven other partitioning tools using a comprehensive benchmark set covering application domains such as VLSI design, scientific computing, and SAT solving. The first configuration, KaHyPar-HFC, achieves marginally superior solutions compared to KaHyPar-MF with significantly reduced runtime. The second configuration, KaHyPar-HFC*, delivers substantially higher solution quality while remaining slightly faster than KaHyPar-MF. Additionally, both configurations outperform all other competing partitioners regarding solution quality.

Achieving phone-level pronunciation scoring remains a difficult challenge, as current performance lags significantly behind human annotators. Conventional approaches assign scores to individual phones within a phrase using models trained exclusively on native speech recognition (ASR) data. Although systems trained specifically for pronunciation scoring with non-native data demonstrate superior results, they are hindered by the scarcity and limited size of labeled datasets. This paper introduces a transfer learning strategy that adapts an ASR-trained model for the specific task of pronunciation scoring. We evaluate various design choices and benchmark our approach against a state-of-the-art Goodness of Pronunciation (GOP) system. On the EpaDB pronunciation scoring database, our final system outperforms the GOP system by 20% when utilizing a cost function that emphasizes minimizing unnecessary corrections.

This paper investigates multifractal analysis and large deviations within singular hyperbolic attractors, encompassing geometric Lorenz attractors. For singular hyperbolic homoclinic classes where all periodic orbits are homoclinically related and the space of ergodic probability measures is connected, we establish two key results: (i) level sets corresponding to continuous observables are dense within the homoclinic class and adhere to a variational principle; and (ii) irregular sets are either nonexistent or Baire generic while possessing full topological entropy. These conditions hold for $C^1$-generic singular hyperbolic attractors and $C^r$-generic geometric Lorenz attractors (where $r \ge 2$). Additionally, we derive level-2 large deviation bounds for weak Gibbs measures, yielding a large deviations principle specifically for Gibbs measures. The primary method employed is the horseshoe approximation property.

This study experimentally examines the behavior of pairs of silicon micromechanical oscillators that are doubly clamped, mechanically coupled, and driven by opto-thermal forces, while also numerically analyzing the corresponding lumped-parameter model. These coupled limit cycle oscillators display remarkable nonlinear dynamics and bifurcations as system parameters change. We demonstrate that input laser power affects the frequency detuning between two non-identical oscillators. By varying the laser power, we map various oscillation regimes—including synchronized, drift, and quasi-periodic states—at both low and high coupling strengths. For non-identical oscillators, we show that the synchronized and quasi-periodic states can coexist under conditions of high coupling and high laser power. Experimentally, this bistability appears as irregular oscillations where the system rapidly switches between the two states due to sensitive dependence on initial conditions in the presence of noise. Finally, we offer a qualitative comparison of experimental and numerical findings to clarify the system's behavior.

Detecting extensive air showers (EAS) via their radio emissions is emerging as a leading method for investigating cosmic rays and neutrinos at the highest energies. Designing, optimizing, and characterizing radio arrays, along with their reconstruction algorithms, requires tens of thousands of Monte Carlo simulations. However, existing simulation codes can take days to generate signals for a single shower, rendering the production of the necessary simulations impractical regarding time, cost, and environmental impact. This article introduces a technique to synthesize the complete time-trace signals at any location relative to the shower core, based on a limited set of simulated signals from a strategically arranged array of antennas that leverages specific features of the radio wavefront. This approach works equally well for electric fields or antenna responses across all three polarization directions. The resulting synthesized signals enable the evaluation of trigger conditions, fluence calculation, and shower direction reconstruction. Consequently, this allows for the creation of a single, reusable simulation library for array characterization and algorithm optimization, achieving results with only one-thousandth of the CPU time typically required.
We examine the equivalence principle within quantum mechanics using the frameworks of Newton-Cartan geometry and non-relativistic twistor theory.

This study employs numerical diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods to examine a $S=1/2$ quantum spin ladder system featuring anisotropic ferromagnetic exchange interactions on the rungs under an applied magnetic field. The analysis reveals that a nematic-spin-correlation-dominant Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) emerges at high magnetic fields, a phase characterized by the realization of a two-magnon bound state. For specific parameter sets, a field-induced phase transition occurs from this two-magnon-bound TLL phase to a single-magnon TLL phase, followed by a re-entrant transition back to the two-magnon-bound TLL phase, a phenomenon validated by DMRG magnetization curves. The work presents various phase diagrams mapping coupling anisotropy against both magnetization and magnetic field. Ultimately, these findings propose this system as a candidate for exhibiting a spin nematic phase without requiring biquadratic interactions or frustration.

This study introduces a feature-driven named entity recognition (NER) model that attains state-of-the-art accuracy for the Vietnamese language. The proposed Conditional Random Fields (CRF) framework integrates word and word-shape features, part-of-speech (PoS) tags, chunking information, Brown-cluster features, and word embeddings. Furthermore, we investigate how word segmentation, PoS tagging, and chunking outputs from various popular Vietnamese NLP toolkits influence the performance of this feature-based NER system. To our knowledge, this is the first work to conduct a systematic extrinsic evaluation of fundamental Vietnamese NLP toolkits on the downstream NER task. Experimental findings indicate that while automatically generated word segmentation proves beneficial, PoS and chunking data produced by Vietnamese NLP tools do not yield significant improvements for the proposed feature-based NER model.

Behavioral cloning for self-driving vehicles typically employs an open-loop approach that neglects how actions influence future states. Relying solely on Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) for training can harm real-world performance by biasing the policy network to mimic open-loop behaviors, resulting in poor closed-loop outcomes. This paper introduces an efficient and straightforward method named Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization (CW-ERM). This principle first uses a closed-loop evaluation to pinpoint training data critical for practical driving, then leverages these samples to reduce bias within the policy network. When tested on a demanding urban driving dataset, CW-ERM demonstrated a substantial decrease in collisions and improvements in other non-differentiable closed-loop metrics.

Detecting millikelvin signals from the 'Cosmic Dawn' demands exceptional sensitivity and rigorous systematic calibration. We present the theoretical foundation of a new calibration algorithm derived from the formalism established by the EDGES collaboration for 21-cm experiments. Our approach surpasses earlier methods by integrating a Bayesian framework and machine learning techniques. Specifically, we utilize Bayesian evidence to identify frequency variations in calibration parameters supported by the data, account for correlations between these parameters when estimating their values, and employ a conjugate-prior method that yields a rapid algorithm suitable for field application. Self-consistency tests using empirical data models of varying complexity demonstrate that our methodology successfully calibrates a 50 $\Omega$ ambient-temperature load, achieving an RMS error of 8 mK against the measured temperature—well within the 1$\sigma$ noise level. Although these methods are particularly suited for global 21-cm experiments, they can be readily adapted for other uses, such as with telescopes like HERA and the SKA.

We construct an infinite set of exact axisymmetric solutions within the framework of metric-affine gravity, specifically Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity, interacting with an anisotropic fluid. The solution-generating technique used is not exclusive to this theory but can be generalized to other Ricci-Based Gravity (RBG) models, which are constructed from contractions of the Ricci tensor with the metric. This approach leverages a mapping between the solution spaces of General Relativity and RBGs and remains independent of the problem's symmetries. In the specific scenario where the fluid corresponds to non-linear electromagnetic fields, we explicitly derive the associated axisymmetric solutions. Furthermore, we apply these findings to determine the metric-affine equivalent of the Kerr-Newman black hole under Maxwell electrodynamics. Our results suggest a promising new direction for testing novel gravitational phenomenology, particularly concerning gravitational waves and the shadows cast by rotating black holes.

The double copy has become a well-established link between amplitudes and classical solutions within biadjoint scalar, gauge, and gravity theories. However, no strongly coupled four-dimensional examples have been identified, and prior efforts using exact non-linear biadjoint solutions in Lorentzian signature were unsuccessful. Instead, this paper investigates biadjoint solutions in Euclidean signature, which may correspond to Yang-Mills or gravitational instantons. We demonstrate that spherically symmetric, power-like Euclidean solutions do not exist in exactly four spacetime dimensions. The reason for this absence involves the Eguchi-Hanson instanton, whose single copy structure proves to be more complex and intriguing than previously believed. We offer a broader prescription for double-copying instantons and show how our findings complement a recent non-perturbative double copy of exact solutions in two dimensions. Through this work, we illustrate how the substitution of color with kinematic Lie algebras functions at the level of exact classical solutions.

This survey examines various network modeling techniques and their relevance to precision medicine, specifically reviewing five centrality measures (degree, closeness, eccentricity, betweenness, and eigenvector-based prestige) and two controllability approaches (minimum dominating sets and network structural controllability). We apply these methods to three multiple myeloma patient disease networks, each constructed from protein-protein interactions centered on patient-specific mutated genes, standard-of-care drug targets, and multiple myeloma-specific essential genes. For each network, we illustrate how these techniques can identify personalized, targeted drug combinations uniquely tailored to the individual patient.

The existing picture of cosmic star formation history at redshifts greater than 3 relies mainly on UV-selected galaxies, such as Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs). However, recent investigations into H-dropouts suggest that significant star formation within massive galaxies at these redshifts has been overlooked. To bridge the gap between LBGs and H-dropouts, this study extends the H-dropout selection method to lower masses to identify optically-dark or faint galaxies (OFGs). Our selection criteria (H > 26.5 mag and [4.5] < 25 mag), paired with a de-blending algorithm, target both dust-obscured massive galaxies and typical star-forming systems. We identified 27 OFGs with photometric redshifts greater than 3 (median z = 4.1) in the GOODS-ALMA field, spanning a stellar mass range of log($M_{\star}$/M$_{\odot}$) = 9.4–11.1. Our analysis reveals that up to 75% of OFGs with masses between log($M_{\star}$/M$_{\odot}$) = 9.5 and 10.5 were missed by previous LBG and H-dropout techniques. Stacking analysis indicates that these OFGs possess shorter gas depletion times, slightly reduced gas fractions, and lower dust temperatures compared to average star-forming galaxies. Their total star formation rates (SFR_tot = SFR_IR + SFR_UV) vastly exceed UV-corrected rates (SFR_UVcorr), with a ratio of 8 ± 1, implying extensive hidden dust regions that absorb all UV light. Fitting a circular Gaussian model yields an average dust size of R_e(1.13 mm) = 1.01 ± 0.05 kpc. Furthermore, the contribution of massive OFGs to the cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) at z > 3 is at least two orders of magnitude higher than that of similarly massive LBGs. Ultimately, combining OFGs and LBGs results in a cosmic SFRD at z = 4–5 of 4 × 10$^{-2}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-3}$, representing a 43% (0.15 dex) increase over estimates based solely on UV-selected samples.

Tropical Newton-Puiseux polynomials, which act as tropical algebraic functions, are defined as piece-wise linear functions featuring rational coefficients in their variables. We present explicit formulas for these polynomials, specifically identifying them as the tropical zeroes of a univariate tropical polynomial that has parametric coefficients.

This paper investigates the computational complexity of minimizing makespan for non-preemptive scheduling of independent jobs across identical parallel processors. We introduce the \textit{Scheduling Solution Space Tree (SSST)}, a novel data structure designed to comprehensively explore the problem's combinatorial landscape. Through analytical findings, we formally characterize the properties of the SSST. Leveraging both the SSST and the \textit{Weighted Scheduling Solution Space Tree (WSSST)}, we devise a distinct method to demonstrate the problem's $\mathcal{NP}$ status. Furthermore, we propose the first non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, termed \textit{Magic Scheduling (MS)}, utilizing a reduction framework. Additionally, we introduce a new variant of multiprocessor scheduling that incorporates the user as an extra input parameter and rigorously determine its complexity class via reduction principles. The study concludes by identifying several promising open questions for future research.

This study reports hydrodynamic simulation results for Au-Au collisions spanning $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ from 7.7 to 200 GeV. The simulations incorporate three innovative elements: first, a Monte-Carlo initial state model based on the Linear EXtrapolation of Ultrarelativistic nucleon-nucleon Scattering to nucleus-nucleus collisions (LEXUS); second, a crossover equation of state applicable at finite baryon densities that excludes a critical point; and third, departure functions derived from quasiparticle theory to describe transport coefficients in hadronic matter under non-zero baryon density conditions.

We compare chemical patent word embeddings with established biomedical embeddings, demonstrating that the former surpass the latter in both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. Additionally, we illustrate that contextualized embeddings can generate predictive models with acceptable performance for this specific domain, even when relying on a relatively small gold standard dataset.

This study conducts on-the-fly non-adiabatic molecular dynamics simulations employing the symmetrical quasi-classical (SQC) approach, utilizing recently proposed molecular Tully models for ethylene and fulvene. We aim to establish benchmarks for SQC methods by evaluating both square and triangle windowing schemes, alongside a newly introduced electronic zero-point-energy correction known as the gamma correction. To facilitate direct coupling between diabatic SQC methods and adiabatic electronic structure calculations, we implement a quasi-diabatic propagation scheme. Our findings demonstrate a significant enhancement in accuracy through the application of trajectory-adjusted gamma corrections, which surpass the performance of the commonly used trajectory surface hopping method with decoherence corrections. Furthermore, these computations offer valuable, non-trivial tests for systematically assessing the numerical efficacy of diverse diabatic quantum dynamics techniques, extending beyond the simple diabatic model systems that have traditionally dominated the field. Concurrently, these benchmark studies are poised to stimulate the advancement of new quantum dynamics methodologies built upon these foundational techniques.

This work proposes a framework for investigating photon number amplification and discrimination by examining the interaction between a large ensemble of two-level atoms and a single-mode radiation field. Leveraging the conservation of the total number of photons and excited atoms inherent to the Dicke model during time evolution, we reallocate atom and photon counts. Our analysis yields three key predictions: the threshold time for initial photon exposure, the perception time (defined as the moment of peak detection probability), and the ability to distinguish among the first few photon states.

When dark matter interacts only weakly with the Standard Model environment, it can avoid stringent limits imposed by direct detection experiments, while simultaneously being generated through the freeze-in mechanism. This scenario becomes particularly compelling when thermal masses are incorporated for the particles involved. Including these thermal corrections enables dark matter production through channels that are kinematically forbidden in the standard freeze-in framework. Consequently, we examine freeze-in production within a minimally extended $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ model that aligns with recent muon $(g-2)$ measurements. In this framework, the dark matter candidate is a scalar field carrying a non-trivial charge under the additional symmetry, which acquires a thermally corrected mass at high temperatures provided the self-coupling is sufficiently large. Our analysis demonstrates that these thermal mass corrections significantly influence dark matter phenomenology.

We present spectroscopic ellipsometry (VASE) measurements of the reflection and transmission spectra for 2% doped Thulium Yttrium Gallium Garnet (Tm:YGG) across a wavelength span of 210 to 1680 nm (0.73–5.9 eV). By isolating the well-known Tm resonances from the combined dataset, we determined the previously unknown frequency-dependent complex refractive index of the host material. These findings are critical for various YGG applications in classical and quantum photonics, such as optical cavity construction, laser systems, and quantum information devices. A comprehensive database of the derived parameters is provided in the supplementary information.

The emergence of U-Net and subsequent fully convolutional deep neural networks has revolutionized medical image segmentation. Nevertheless, early observations highlighted a critical flaw: these methods' heavy reliance on pixel-level classification and regression. This dependency becomes particularly problematic when training on medical datasets with sparse annotations, often leading to artifacts like fragmented structures, topological errors, and isolated pixel clusters. Such issues are detrimental in medical imaging because segmentation typically serves as a prerequisite for downstream tasks such as surgical planning, visualization, shape analysis, prognosis, and treatment strategies. Despite the variety of these applications, a shared requirement exists: anatomical consistency. To address this, methods incorporating Markov/Conditional Random Fields and Statistical Shape Models have gained significant traction over the last five years. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent literature on integrating anatomical constraints into medical image segmentation, critically analyzing the limitations and potential of current approaches while outlining future directions. The paper covers studies published up to the submission date, with key details regarding methods, datasets, and performance summarized in tables for easy reference.

Geometric Deep Learning has recently gained considerable attention across numerous machine learning domains, particularly in document analysis. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential for various document-centric tasks due to their ability to reveal critical structural patterns vital for key information extraction. While prior literature has focused on task-specific models that fail to leverage the full potential of graphs, we introduce Doc2Graph, a task-agnostic document understanding framework built on GNNs designed to handle diverse tasks across different document types. We validated our approach on two challenging datasets involving key information extraction for form understanding, invoice layout analysis, and table detection. Our code is freely available at https://github.com/andreagemelli/doc2graph.

Recent proposals for weakly disentangled representations aim to loosen constraints inherent in traditional disentanglement definitions, thereby offering greater flexibility. However, currently, achieving weak disentanglement necessitates increasing supervision as the number of data variation factors grows. This paper presents modular representations for weak disentanglement, a novel approach that maintains a constant level of supervised information regardless of the number of generative factors. Experimental results demonstrate that models utilizing modular representations can outperform previous methods without requiring additional supervision.

Self-reinforcing feedback loops act as both the cause and effect of the over- or under-display of specific content within interactive recommender systems. This dynamic results in flawed user preference assessments, specifically the overvaluation of frequently shown items and the infringement upon the right to be exposed to all alternatives; we define a system as fair only when it respects this latter right. We examine two models, one that accounts for and another that neglects the systematic yet limited exposure to diverse options. Simulations reveal that failing to consider these systematic presentations leads to an overestimation of promoted items and an underestimation of censored ones. Addressing this bias effectively requires simply conditioning on the limited exposure.

We introduce a robust state estimation system that integrates data from multiple lidars, inertial sensors, and GNSS. The process begins by leveraging prior GNSS pose information, followed by real-time incremental motion estimation. This approach generates robust global frame motion estimates by fusing lidar and IMU signals with GNSS translation components within a factor graph framework. Additionally, we propose new synchronization and fusion mechanisms to handle signal loss. To validate the method, extensive tests were conducted on data gathered from Scania test vehicles across five sequences totaling approximately 7 kilometers. Our evaluations demonstrate an average 61% improvement in relative translation and a 42% reduction in rotational error compared to a state-of-the-art estimator that fuses a single lidar/inertial sensor pair.

In this work, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the c-Boomerang Connectivity Table for the Gold function within finite fields of even characteristic, utilizing double Weil sums. Furthermore, we extend a finding by Boura and Canteaut (IACR Trans. Symmetric Cryptol. 2018(3) : 290-310, 2018) concerning classical boomerang uniformity.

The silicon-tungsten electromagnetic calorimeter (SiW-ECAL) serves as the reference design for the ECAL within the International Large Detector concept, one of two proposals for the future International Linear Collider. Prototypes for this detector are being developed by the CALICE Collaboration, focusing on technical challenges such as integrated front-end electronics and compact layer and readout designs. In 2017, a seven-layer stack was assembled and tested at DESY's test beam facilities. This presentation outlines preliminary findings regarding electromagnetic shower properties, provides a roadmap for future steps, and demonstrates initial digitization concepts through simulations of the prototype.

Federated learning has gained significant traction for constructing models without direct access to raw user data, a capability particularly valuable in healthcare. However, in practical scenarios, distinct federations often fail to collaborate due to challenges like data heterogeneity and the lack of a trustworthy central server. To address this, we introduce MetaFed, a novel framework designed to enable secure federated learning across separate federations without relying on a central authority. By employing Cyclic Knowledge Distillation, MetaFed generates personalized models for each federation through a cyclic aggregation of knowledge, treating every federation as a distinct meta-distribution. The training process consists of two phases: accumulating common knowledge and achieving personalization. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks reveal that server-less MetaFed outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving superior accuracy (with improvements of over 10% compared to the baseline on the PAMAP2 dataset) while reducing communication overhead.

India achieved a significant breakthrough in space astronomy by successfully launching and operating its first space observatory, AstroSat. To expand India's presence in international space astronomy, the lessons from this success should be leveraged. Responding to a call for proposals from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), a detailed bid was submitted for the next-generation UV-optical mission known as the INdian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST). Featuring a large focal area and a straightforward, efficient optical design, INSIST is anticipated to deliver Hubble-quality imaging and moderate-resolution spectra of celestial objects. The mission's primary scientific goals cover a broad spectrum of topics, including galaxy evolution within clusters, the chemical dynamics and demographics of the nearby universe, accreting stellar systems, planetary systems, and both local and distant cosmology. Following the award of seed funding, the project has successfully completed two years of its pre-project phase. This document provides an overview of the proposed mission along with its current status.
We categorize connected graphs $G$ for which the binomial edge ideal is Gorenstein, employing techniques from prime characteristic in the proof.

This paper examines a communication game involving a sender and a receiver, where the sender possesses a collection of informative signals regarding a specific state of the world. The sender selects one signal, termed an "anecdote," to convey to the receiver, who then takes an action that generates utility for both parties. While both players value the true state of the world, they also hold distinct personal preferences, leading to divergent ideal actions. We analyze perfect Bayesian equilibria in a non-commitment setting, where the sender faces a "persuasion temptation" to choose a more biased anecdote to sway the receiver. Although anecdotes remain informative, this bias reduces precision, resulting in "informational homophily": receivers prefer like-minded senders because their signals are more precise. Specifically, we demonstrate that a sender with access to numerous anecdotes will typically report only the extreme values (minimum or maximum), even when a highly accurate anecdote close to the true state is likely available. Unlike the classic Crawford-Sobel model, where full revelation is a fragile equilibrium, even minor preference differences here trigger highly polarized communication and utility losses. Furthermore, for fat-tailed anecdote distributions, receivers may actually prefer less-informed senders with aligned preferences over knowledgeable experts whose preferences diverge. Finally, we show that under commitment, personal preference differences cease to distort communication, leading the sender to report the most representative anecdote closest to the posterior mean for common distributions.

We investigate low-resolution Spitzer infrared (IR) spectra spanning 5–14 microns from the diffuse emission along sight lines to a rigorously selected stellar sample. This sample consists of stars with precisely characterized ultraviolet (UV) extinction curves that are located beyond virtually all dust responsible for extinction and emission along their paths. Our selection encompasses lines of sight displaying a diverse range of UV curve morphologies, thereby sampling various interstellar environments. Consequently, this distinctive sample allowed us to explore the relationship between the extinction and emission characteristics of identical grains and assess their reactions to differing physical conditions. We characterize the emission features using the Draine & Li (2007) PAH model alongside a set of additional, non-PAH-related features. We then correlate the intensities of these Spitzer mid-IR features with the Fitzpatrick & Massa (2007) parameters defining UV to near-IR extinction curve shapes. Our main finding is a robust correlation between the area of the 2175 Å UV bump in the program stars' extinction curves and the strength of the primary PAH emission features in the corresponding mid-IR spectra.

We introduce two families of knots where the straight number exceeds the crossing number. For the second family, the straight number has been calculated explicitly. Additionally, we provide a general theorem concerning alternating knots, which states that adding an even number of crossings to a twist region does not alter whether the knot is perfectly straight or not.

This work examines the orthogonal separation of variables for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation on spaces of constant curvature, emphasizing significant contributions by Benenti. Central to this framework is a specific conformal Killing tensor, referred to as a concircular tensor. Initially, we demonstrate how to extend Benenti's original findings to intrinsically define all orthogonal separable coordinates in constant curvature spaces via concircular tensors, thereby establishing a unique class known as Kalnins-Eisenhart-Miller coordinates. Subsequently, we outline the Benenti-Eisenhart-Kalnins-Miller separation algorithm, which leverages concircular tensors to intrinsically identify these coordinates for a given natural Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Furthermore, as a novel application, we derive separable coordinate systems for two-dimensional constant curvature spaces, including Minkowski and (Anti-)de Sitter spaces. Finally, we utilize the aforementioned algorithm to investigate the separability of the three-dimensional Calogero-Moser and Morosi-Tondo systems.

Intracellular protein distributions govern essential cellular functions, including motility and division, processes frequently accompanied by dynamic alterations in cell morphology. These morphological shifts can reciprocally influence the behavior of pattern-forming proteins, establishing a complex feedback mechanism between chemical dynamics and cell shape. Although computational research has investigated these rich dynamics, the fundamental mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. To address this, we investigate a conceptual framework for cell polarity on a time-evolving one-dimensional manifold. By applying principles of differential geometry, we formulate equations describing mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems on evolving manifolds. Mathematical analysis of these equations demonstrates that membrane shape fluctuations can trigger pattern-forming instabilities in specific regions, termed regional instabilities. Furthermore, local geometric deformations can either suppress pattern formation within specific areas or spatially displace existing patterns. We interpret these results by extending and applying the local equilibria theory for mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems, which yields a straightforward criterion for the onset of geometry-induced instabilities linked to the system's phase-space structure. Consequently, the feedback loop between membrane deformation and reaction-diffusion dynamics generates a diverse array of patterns—such as oscillations, traveling waves, and standing waves—that are absent in systems with static membranes. This study highlights that the local configuration of membrane geometry serves as a critical control parameter for pattern formation in mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems.

While eigenstates in non-Hermitian lattices typically localize at open boundaries due to the non-Hermitian skin effect, we investigate another intriguing aspect of this phenomenon by predicting quasi-stationary solutions that are nearly time-independent. We demonstrate that the transition from these states to true eigenstates is markedly non-perturbative. Furthermore, we discuss how mathematically extending the boundary of an extended non-Hermitian lattice to infinity can yield nontrivial solutions. Finally, by examining a non-Hermitian modification of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, we forecast the existence of robust, non-topological quasi-stationary zero-energy modes.

Arago is a proposed space mission concept submitted to the European Space Agency's M7 science program, designed to address various stellar physics objectives, particularly the study of star-planet interactions. The architecture features a 1-meter class Ritchey-Chretien F/13 telescope mounted on an Ariel-type platform. The scientific payload comprises a shared polarimetric unit and two spectrographs linked by a dichroic splitter. The polarimetric system consists of six MgF2 plates arranged in pairs with optical contact, alongside a Wollaston analyzer. Each spectral channel utilizes an echelle spectrograph: the first operates in the ultraviolet range (119–320 nm) with a resolving power of R > 25,000. It incorporates an off-axis parabolic collimator, a quasi-Littrow-mounted echelle grating, a cross-disperser concave grating, and a CMOS camera. Notably, the cross-disperser grating functions simultaneously as a camera mirror; it is a holographic grating recorded with aberrated wavefronts on a spherical substrate, projecting the spectral image onto a d-doped CMOS detector. The second channel covers the visible spectrum (350–888 nm) with R > 35,000 using an immersed grating, with the image focused by a four-lens objective onto a CMOS detector. The optical design also includes a two-stage fine-guiding system. The initial stage acts as a projection system that tracks the image around the entrance pinhole and interfaces with platform actuators. The second stage receives the zero-th diffraction order from the visible channel's echelle and communicates with a tip-tilt mirror positioned before the dichroic. The first stage aims to enhance platform pointing accuracy from 8 arcseconds to 200 milliarcseconds to ensure star images align with the entrance pinhole, while the second stage further refines pointing accuracy and compensates for thermo-elastic deformations.

This study focuses on reconstructing minor fluctuations in a medium's electric properties, specifically permittivity and conductivity, using boundary data of the electric field at a constant frequency. The theoretical framework relies on the three-dimensional time-harmonic Maxwell equations governing the electric field. By conducting sensitivity analysis regarding these parameters, the research derives explicit connections between boundary measurements and perturbation characteristics through a suitable integral equation and comprehensive three-dimensional numerical simulations. The developed non-iterative algorithm efficiently determines the location and volume of these perturbations across diverse scenarios, ranging from ideal spheres to realistic human head models.

This work investigates the impact of quantum communication on attacks targeting quantum position verification (QPV). We present the first QPV protocol that is provably secure against unentangled adversaries using only classical communication, yet can be perfectly compromised via local operations combined with a single round of simultaneous quantum transmission, demonstrating that permitting quantum communication can undermine security. Additionally, we establish that any protocol secure against classical communication can be adapted to withstand quantum communication attacks. Furthermore, leveraging arguments rooted in the monogamy of entanglement, we demonstrate that Bell state discrimination cannot be performed locally with a single round of quantum communication, even probabilistically (accounting for potential signal loss), thereby introducing the first fully loss-tolerant QPV task resistant to quantum communication attacks. Finally, we note that any multi-round QPV protocol becomes vulnerable to attacks utilizing a linear amount of entanglement when signal loss is sufficiently high.

Centralized training with decentralized execution offers a promising avenue for value function factorization in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Among existing methods, QMIX has reached state-of-the-art status, achieving top performance on the StarCraft II micromanagement benchmark. However, QMIX's reliance on monotonic mixing of per-agent estimates limits the representable joint action Q-values, and its lack of sufficient global state information for single-agent value estimation often leads to suboptimal results. To address these limitations, we introduce LSF-SAC, a new framework that incorporates a variational inference-based information-sharing mechanism to provide additional state context, thereby aiding individual agents in value function factorization. Our findings indicate that sharing latent individual state information significantly enhances the capabilities of value function factorization while maintaining fully decentralized execution via a soft-actor-critic architecture. We evaluated LSF-SAC on the StarCraft II micromanagement challenge, demonstrating that it surpasses several state-of-the-art methods in demanding collaborative scenarios. Furthermore, we conducted extensive ablation studies to identify the key factors driving these performance gains. We believe this new perspective can inspire advancements in local value estimation techniques and variational deep learning algorithms. A demo video and implementation code are available at https://sites.google.com/view/sacmm.

We present an investigation into the magnetic phase transitions of Na$_2$BaMn(PO$_4$)$_2$, a two-dimensional triangular lattice antiferromagnet with a spin-5/2 system. Specific heat data indicate two magnetic transitions occurring at 1.15 K and 1.30 K under zero magnetic field. Furthermore, detailed AC magnetic susceptibility studies identify multiple phases, including a $\uparrow$$\uparrow$$\downarrow$ (up-up-down) phase observed between 1.9 T and 2.9 T at 47 mK when the field is aligned with the $c$ axis. These findings suggest that Na$_2$BaMn(PO$_4$)$_2$ behaves as a classical 2D triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet characterized by easy-axis anisotropy. Nevertheless, deviations from an ideal model are evident through a hysteresis region involving the $\uparrow$$\uparrow$$\downarrow$ and $V$-phases, as well as weak phase transitions. This study offers another experimental case for examining frustrated magnetism in 2D triangular lattice antiferromagnets and serves as a reference for interpreting the quantum spin liquid behavior and anomalous phase diagrams found in related systems such as Na$_2$Ba$M$(PO$_4$)$_2$ ($M$ = Co, Ni).

Standard analyses of high-speed boundary layer linear instability often assume static edge conditions, neglecting shock internal structures and potential instabilities within them. Recent findings reveal that the kinetically modeled non-equilibrium zone of straight shocks, away from solid surfaces, displays low-frequency molecular fluctuations. The dominance of these low frequencies, identified via the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method, is attributed to the bimodal probability density function (PDF) of particle energy inherent to shocks. This study derives particle energy PDFs for upstream, downstream, and shock regions, demonstrating for the first time that they follow non-central chi-squared (NCCS) distributions. A linear relationship is proposed linking the evolution of these analytical PDF shapes with Mach number ($3 \le M \le 10$) to the DSMC-calculated average characteristic low frequencies. At $M=7.2$, varying the upstream translational temperature ($89 \le T_{tr,1}/(K) \le 1420$) reveals a correlation between DSMC-derived low frequencies and changes in the most probable speed within the shock at the peak bulk velocity gradient. Utilizing these linear functions, average low frequencies are estimated across the specified Mach and temperature ranges, leading to a semi-empirical model for predicting shock low-frequency oscillations. This approach enables the generation of realistic, physics-based boundary conditions for receptivity and linear stability analyses regarding laminar-turbulent transition in high-speed flows.

Adjusting the behavior of pre-trained models—such as enhancing their performance on specific downstream tasks or reducing biases acquired during pre-training—is a standard procedure in machine learning system development. This work introduces a novel approach to steering neural network behavior, which revolves around \textit{task vectors}. A task vector represents a specific direction within the weight space of a pre-trained model, where moving along this direction enhances performance on a given task. These vectors are constructed by calculating the difference between the weights of a model after fine-tuning on a task and its original pre-trained weights. We demonstrate that these task vectors can be manipulated and combined using arithmetic operations like addition and negation to control model behavior. Negating a task vector degrades performance on the target task while leaving behavior on control tasks largely unaffected. Furthermore, summing task vectors can simultaneously improve performance across multiple tasks. Additionally, when tasks are related by an analogy (e.g., "A is to B as C is to D"), combining task vectors from three of the tasks can enhance performance on the fourth task, even without using any data from it during training. Our experiments across various models, modalities, and tasks confirm that task arithmetic is a simple, efficient, and effective method for editing neural networks.

Although quantum computers promise substantial performance gains over classical systems, pinpointing the inherently quantum attributes responsible for these advantages remains difficult. In the continuous-variable framework—a leading approach for achieving universal, scalable, and fault-tolerant quantum computing—contextuality and Wigner negativity have traditionally been viewed as separate resources. This study demonstrates that, within standard continuous-variable quantum computing models, these two concepts are actually equivalent. Our findings offer a unified understanding of the resources driving quantum speedups in this domain, facilitate future practical demonstrations of continuous-variable contextuality, and clarify the role of negative probabilities in phase-space representations of quantum mechanics.

Investigating condensed matter under extreme conditions facilitates a deeper understanding of microscopic structural mechanisms and the development of materials with novel mechanical properties. This study examines the structure and crystallization kinetics of the bulk metallic glass (BMG) Ni$_{62}$Nb$_{38}$. We demonstrate that this BMG undergoes rapid crystallization when subjected to the combined influence of shear deformation and ultrahigh pressure. A specific threshold pressure necessary to trigger the formation of a stable crystalline phase is identified. Both shear and pressure induce phase separation, resulting in two high-density, inhomogeneous crystal structures. Furthermore, the crystallization process occurs in two distinct stages, driven by the substantial disparity in growth rates between the Ni and Nb crystalline phases. These findings significantly advance the understanding of crystallization and amorphization characteristics in Ni-based BMGs.

Previous research indicates that Twitter users employ skin-toned emojis to signal their racial or ethnic identity. This study investigates whether such identity markers influence readers' judgments regarding the veracity of post content. In a large-scale, pre-registered controlled experiment (n=944), we manipulated the inclusion of skin-toned emojis and profile photos while participants evaluated obscure trivia facts (framed as tweets) as either true or false. Bayesian statistical analysis revealed that neither emojis nor profile photos affected how readers rated these facts. These findings offer reassurance to those worried about the manipulation of online users through the creation of deceptive profiles.

This study examines the impact of finite-temperature quasiparticle self-energy corrections on x-ray absorption spectra, employing the finite-temperature quasiparticle local density GW approximation for temperatures $T$ approaching the Fermi temperature. To streamline these computations, the quasiparticle self-energy is modeled using low-order polynomial fits. Our findings indicate that the temperature-induced reduction in electron lifetime significantly broadens the spectra near the edge as $T$ increases. Nevertheless, the quasiparticle shift exhibits its most pronounced modification in the vicinity of plasmon excitation onset.

Vehicular communication (VC) protocols significantly contribute to accident prevention by transmitting alert messages, a benefit that is particularly critical at road intersections due to their elevated collision risks. Concurrently, Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) has emerged as a promising technology for fifth-generation (5G) wireless systems. This paper introduces and evaluates an Adaptive Cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol designed for vehicular communications at intersections. The system facilitates transmission between a source and two destinations, subject to interference from vehicles distributed on the roads according to a Poisson Point Process (PPP). First, we derive closed-form expressions for the outage probability of the ACN protocol. Subsequently, we compare these results with existing protocols in the literature. Our findings demonstrate that the ACN protocol achieves a substantial reduction in outage probability compared to current solutions, especially within intersection scenarios. Furthermore, the ACN protocol exhibits superior performance relative to other protocols at high data rates. These theoretical conclusions are validated through Monte-Carlo simulations.

The growing emphasis on resource-efficient production necessitates that manufacturing firms establish a more dynamic environment featuring flexible machines and processes. To fully leverage the potential of dynamic manufacturing via automated production planning, formal skill descriptions of these machines are crucial. Yet, manually generating such descriptions is both labor-intensive and demands substantial domain expertise. This paper introduces an ontology-based, semi-automatic system for skill description that leverages production logs and industrial ontologies through inductive logic programming, and it evaluates both the advantages and limitations of this proposed approach.

Radiologists produce text reports detailing findings from medical images. Existing state-of-the-art computer-aided diagnosis systems rely on training with a fixed set of predefined categories automatically derived from these reports. This supervised approach restricts model capabilities, as they cannot detect anomalies outside their established categories, necessitating retraining with new data when encountering novel classes. In contrast, we explore direct text supervision to overcome this closed-set limitation. This method eliminates the need for noisy label extraction via text classifiers and integrates richer contextual information.

We utilize a contrastive global-local dual-encoder architecture to learn concepts directly from unstructured medical reports while retaining the ability to perform free-form classification. Furthermore, we examine key properties of open-set recognition in radiological data and introduce a method for leveraging currently weakly annotated datasets. Our approach is evaluated on large-scale chest X-ray datasets, including MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, and ChestX-Ray14, for disease classification. We demonstrate that, despite relying on unstructured report supervision, our method achieves performance comparable to direct label supervision through a sophisticated inference framework.

This study reports a numerical lattice quantum chromodynamics computation of nucleon isovector form factors and the initial moments of isovector structure functions. The simulation utilizes two degenerate dynamical flavors of domain-wall fermions, ensuring robust control over chiral symmetry breaking, with non-perturbative renormalization applied to the necessary quark currents. The lattice inverse spacing ($a^{-1}$) is approximately 1.7 GeV, employing degenerate up and down dynamical quark masses at roughly 1, 3/4, and 1/2 the strange quark mass within a physical volume of about $(1.9 \text{ fm})^3$. As the quark mass decreases toward the physical point, the ratio of isovector vector to axial charges, $g_A/g_V$, shows a slight downward trend relative to experimental data. We computed the momentum-transfer dependencies for the isovector vector, axial, induced tensor, and induced pseudoscalar form factors. The Goldberger-Treiman relation remains valid at low momentum transfer, yielding a pion-nucleon coupling constant of $g_{\pi NN} = 15.5(1.4)$, with the error representing only statistical uncertainty. Our findings indicate that, following linear chiral extrapolation, the flavor non-singlet quark momentum fraction $\langle x \rangle_{u-d}$ and quark helicity fraction $\langle x \rangle_{\Delta u-\Delta d}$ exceed their experimental values. We determined the transversity to be $\langle 1 \rangle_{\delta u-\delta d} = 0.93(6)$ in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme at 2 GeV, while the twist-3 polarized moment, $d_1$, appears small, implying that the Wandzura-Wilczek relation holds approximately. Finally, we address systematic uncertainties, focusing specifically on finite-volume effects, excited-state contamination, and chiral extrapolations.

Contracts form the foundation of most contemporary commercial dealings by specifying the duties and obligations of the involved parties. Ensuring these agreements are free of errors is vital for modern society, yet analyzing them demands a grasp of the logical connections between clauses to spot potential contradictions. Currently, this analysis relies heavily on human effort, which is prone to mistakes. This work presents a method to automate the extraction of logical relationships between contract clauses by framing the issue as a Natural Language Inference task to identify the entailment type between any two clauses. Ultimately, this approach aims to assist contract authors in identifying logical conflicts within their documents.

Like other machine learning models, reinforcement learning algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation that can degrade policy performance. This study examines Multi-task Federated Reinforcement Learning, where collaborative agents across diverse environments aim to maximize the cumulative discounted return despite the presence of malicious agents. We demonstrate that standard attack techniques do not reliably compromise Multi-task Federated Reinforcement Learning and introduce a novel adaptive attack strategy that yields superior results. Additionally, we refine the conventional federated reinforcement learning framework to effectively mitigate adversarial threats, ensuring robust performance whether adversaries are present or absent. Empirical evaluations on various small-to-mid-sized reinforcement learning tasks confirm that our proposed attack method outperforms existing general approaches, while the modified algorithm successfully achieves near-optimal policies even in adversarial settings.

Joint Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) is a growing field in audio signal processing that integrates spatial dimensions into acoustic scene analysis and sound event detection. A common method for jointly modeling SELD involves Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (CRNNs), where Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) extract high-level features from multi-channel audio, and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) capture temporal relationships within those features. However, RNNs suffer from limitations, including difficulty modeling long-term temporal dependencies and slow training and inference speeds caused by their sequential processing. Recently, some SELD research has adopted Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and related Transformer architectures, which have demonstrated state-of-the-art results across various domains. These models excel at capturing long temporal dependencies and allow for efficient parallelization. This paper investigates the specific impact of MHSA on SELD by replacing RNN blocks with self-attention layers. We analyzed the effects of stacking multiple self-attention blocks, utilizing multiple attention heads per block, and the roles of position embeddings and layer normalization. Evaluation on the DCASE 2021 SELD (task 3) development dataset reveals significant improvements across all metrics compared to the baseline CRNN used for the task.

Caribou is a versatile open-source data acquisition platform created and utilized within multiple collaborative initiatives, including CERN EP R&D, RD50, and AIDAinnova. It facilitates laboratory and high-rate beam testing while enabling the seamless integration of new silicon-pixel detector prototypes. By leveraging shared hardware, firmware, and software components across various projects, Caribou significantly lowers the development costs and effort associated with readout systems. This contribution details the recent integration of FASTPIX, APTS, and DPTS detectors into Caribou, outlining their specific requirements for waveform sampling and digital pulse timing. To address the constraints of prior oscilloscope-based readout methods, a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) was implemented within the Caribou FPGA. This component provides the high-precision timing over extended durations necessary for Time-of-Arrival, Time-over-Threshold, and position encoding in the asynchronous digital readout of FASTPIX and DPTS test chips. Following calibration, the system achieves a time resolution superior to 10 ps.

In this brief note, we demonstrate that $v(-\epsilon)=-v(\epsilon)$. Specifically, $v(\epsilon)$ denotes the speed of a one-dimensional random walk evolving in a dynamic \emph{reversible} random environment. This environment biases jumps to the right (probability $1/2+\epsilon$) or left (probability $1/2-\epsilon$) depending on whether the walker occupies an occupied or empty site, respectively. The result is established under any conditions where $v(\epsilon)$ and $v(-\epsilon)$ are well-defined, provided a weak Law of Large Numbers holds. The proof utilizes a straightforward coupling argument applicable exclusively to the discrete setting.

We establish semiorthogonal decompositions of Donaldson-Thomas (DT) categories for reduced curve classes on local surfaces as products of quasi-BPS categories and Pandharipande-Thomas (PT) categories, thereby providing a categorical counterpart to the numerical DT/PT correspondence observed in Calabi-Yau 3-folds. Central to this work is a categorical wall-crossing formula for DT/PT quivers—identified as Ext-quivers within the DT/PT wall-crossing framework—previously proven in our prior publication. Additionally, we investigate quasi-BPS categories concerning points on local surfaces and suggest conjectural K-theory computations that parallel existing formulas for three-dimensional affine space.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each cell to independently schedule uplink and downlink modes based on local traffic demands, though this introduces inter-cell interference. Consequently, the combined problem of power allocation and scheduling becomes a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a low-complexity, decentralized framework that decouples power allocation from scheduling. In this approach, power is distributed centrally, while transmission modes are determined via a non-cooperative game aiming for a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. We evaluate two payoff calculation methods corresponding to different cross-interference power models and their associated communication overheads. Simulation results in a dense outdoor small-cell environment demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly outperform static TDD configurations.

This paper introduces the solvable conjugacy class graph (SCC-graph), denoted as $\Gamma_{sc}(G)$, for a group $G$. The vertices of this graph represent the nontrivial conjugacy classes of $G$, with an edge connecting two distinct classes $C$ and $D$ if there exist elements $x \in C$ and $y \in D$ such that the subgroup generated by them, $\langle x, y\rangle$, is solvable. We examine various properties of the SCC-graph, including its connectivity, girth, and clique number. Among our findings, we establish that for any given clique number $d$, only a finite number of finite groups possess an SCC-graph with that specific clique number; furthermore, we explicitly identify all such groups when $d=2$.

This study examines inference techniques for the discrete Bilal (DB) distribution, originally proposed by Altun et al. (2020). Specifically, it addresses parameter estimation under randomly right-censored data using both maximum likelihood and Bayesian approaches. The analysis also incorporates a cure fraction within the model. The utility of this proposed framework is demonstrated through three applications utilizing real-world datasets. These examples indicate that the DB-based model performs comparably to, or better than, several established discrete distributions, including the DsFx-I, discrete Lindley, discrete Rayleigh, and discrete Burr-Hatke models. Additionally, R code is included in the paper's appendix to facilitate independent analysis by readers.

This research investigates how transformers can capture intra-frame relations by expanding their receptive fields. Specifically, we introduce a model integrating CycleGAN with a transformer to examine its performance in emotional voice conversion. During training, we implement curriculum learning to progressively increase frame length, allowing the model to learn from short segments up to full speech. We evaluated the proposed approach on a Japanese emotional speech dataset against several baselines, including ACVAE and CycleGAN, using both objective and subjective metrics. The findings indicate that our model achieves superior emotion conversion in terms of strength and quality.

Variational quantum algorithms present a promising approach for addressing partial differential equations on near-term quantum hardware. In this work, we introduce a variational quantum algorithm designed to solve general evolution equations by employing implicit time-stepping of the Laplacian operator. Utilizing encoded source states derived from previous solution vectors accelerates convergence relative to random re-initialization. Statevector simulations of the heat equation illustrate how the algorithm's time complexity for gradient estimation scales with the ansatz volume and how the time-to-solution depends on the diffusion parameter. Furthermore, our method extends cost-effectively to higher-order time-stepping schemes, including the Crank-Nicolson method. We also introduce a semi-implicit scheme for handling systems of evolution equations containing non-linear terms, such as reaction-diffusion and incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, validating the approach with proof-of-concept results.

Simulating colloidal suspensions that contain mesoscopic particles alongside smaller entities like ions or depletants poses significant computational hurdles due to the disparate length and time scales involved. This study introduces a machine learning (ML) framework where the degrees of freedom for microscopic species are integrated out, allowing mesoscopic particles to interact via effective many-body potentials. These potentials, fitted using symmetry functions dependent on all colloid coordinates, were applied to a colloid-polymer mixture. Notably, the resulting ML potentials proved to be effectively state-independent and suitable for direct-coexistence simulations. We demonstrate that this ML method lowers computational costs by several orders of magnitude compared to numerical evaluation while accurately capturing phase behavior and structural properties, even at state points where many-body contributions dominate the effective potential.

This analysis examines social learning within a dynamic environment. For society to remain responsive to shifts in the underlying state, agents must continuously act on new information; otherwise, the utility of social learning is constrained. In scenarios where the state is relatively stable, a consensus typically forms where the majority of agents select the same action. However, this consensus does not perfectly track the true state due to societal inertia following changes. Interestingly, when signals are highly precise, periods of inertia can actually extend, even if agents observe large historical samples. This occurs because high precision causes actions within those samples to become overly correlated, which diminishes their informativeness and ultimately lowers welfare.
In this note, we present an example of a domain where the $d$-balanced squeezing function fails to be plurisubharmonic.

We introduce a formula expressing the Poincaré dual of the equivariant fundamental class for any regular nilpotent or regular semisimple Hessenberg variety within the flag manifold as a polynomial involving specific Chern classes. Subsequently, we establish a type-independent proof of the Giambelli formula for the Peterson variety and apply this result to determine the intersection multiplicity between a Peterson variety and an opposite Schubert variety defined by a Coxeter word. Finally, we derive an equivariant Chevalley formula for the cap product of a divisor class with a fundamental class, alongside a dual Monk rule, specifically for the Peterson variety.

Humans exhibit the most advanced computational systems in the known universe, enabling them to comprehend and communicate using language of remarkable descriptive depth with great precision. Among the key drivers of interest in natural language are the properties of compositionality and structure dependence, both well-documented and offering extensive avenues for theoretical modeling. The initial step toward addressing these questions involves grounding linguistic theory in formal terminology. Drawing upon linguistics and set theory, the first half of this thesis presents a formalization of these concepts. It demonstrates that cognitive systems processing language must adhere to specific functional constraints, namely time-based, incremental operations defined within a structured domain. The insights derived from this formal framework are evaluated through a modeling exercise. Leveraging advancements in word embedding techniques, a relational learning model is simulated using a custom dataset to illustrate how a time-based role-filler binding mechanism fulfills certain constraints outlined earlier. The model's capacity to represent structure, combined with its symbolic-connectionist architecture, renders it a cognitively plausible implementation. Collectively, the formalization and simulation aim to identify constraints imposed by linguistic theory and investigate the potential of a cognitive model of relational learning to realize these constraints.

Differential-algebraic equation (DAE) systems are frequently generated automatically by modeling tools like Maplesim, System Modeler, and Modelica. Structural techniques play a critical role in lowering the index and uncovering hidden constraints within these DAEs, particularly for high-index nonlinear systems. While such analysis often succeeds for many dynamic systems, it can fail when the resulting Jacobian matrix remains singular due to symbolic cancellation or numerical issues. Although existing modified structural methods address some scenarios involving symbolic cancellation by assuming a Jacobian determinant is identically zero, this paper eliminates that assumption. Instead, it offers numerical approaches to analyze these degenerated cases using real algebraic geometry for polynomially nonlinear DAEs. First, a witness point method is introduced to generate points on all components, aiding in the detection of degeneration across the entire polynomial DAE system. Second, an implicit index reduction method is proposed to restore a full-rank Jacobian matrix for degenerated DAEs. Third, building on this implicit index reduction, an enhanced structural method is presented to numerically solve degenerated DAEs across all components. The paper includes examples demonstrating these methods and highlighting their benefits for handling degenerated DAEs.

Demazure crystals constitute subcrystals of highest weight irreducible $\mathfrak{g}$-crystals. This paper investigates the tensor products of a broader category of subcrystals known as extremal, offering a local condition that precisely identifies when the tensor product of Demazure crystals is extremal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the tensor product of Demazure crystals splits into a direct sum of Demazure crystals if and only if the tensor product is extremal; consequently, this establishes a necessary and sufficient local criterion for determining when such a tensor product remains a Demazure crystal. As a practical application, we prove that the primary component within the tensor square of any Demazure crystal is invariably Demazure.

We present a thorough diagrammatic framework for electrical circuits using string diagrams. Expanding on earlier, restricted case studies, we incorporate controlled sources and meters as fundamental components and introduce impedance calculus as a robust toolkit for reasoning about circuit diagrams. We illustrate the efficacy of this method by providing elegant proofs of standard textbook theorems, such as the superposition theorem and Thevenin's theorem.

Recent years have witnessed significant progress in pre-trained language models, including the release of non-English variants. As their adoption grows, numerous lightweight versions with fewer parameters have been introduced to accelerate training and inference. Nevertheless, such compressed models for languages other than English remain limited. This paper introduces ALBETO and DistilBETO, Spanish-exclusive adaptations of ALBERT and DistilBERT, respectively. We trained multiple ALBETO variants ranging from 5M to 223M parameters, alongside a 67M parameter DistilBETO version. Our models were evaluated on the GLUES benchmark, which covers diverse Spanish natural language understanding tasks. Results indicate that these lightweight models achieve performance comparable to BETO (Spanish-BERT) despite their reduced parameter counts. Specifically, the larger ALBETO model surpasses all competitors on the MLDoc, PAWS-X, XNLI, MLQA, SQAC, and XQuAD datasets, though BETO still leads in POS and NER tasks. Additionally, all models are made publicly available to support future research.

We illustrate the realization of an atomtronic SQUID using a toroidal Bose-Einstein condensate featuring a movable barrier. The barrier height, which functions as an analogue to an SNS junction, is critical, as are the specific protocols for increasing and decreasing it. If the barrier is too low, dynamic relaxation is inhibited because phase slips occur at a minimal rate. Conversely, a higher barrier suppresses phase coherence across the junction due to thermal fluctuations, a factor accounted for in our Truncated Wigner methodology. Additionally, we demonstrate that the ramp-up process can be optimized by first increasing the barrier's height and then its velocity. This approach can be further refined by tuning the ramp-up and ramp-down time scales, a consideration with immediate practical significance for current experimental efforts.

This study presents a likelihood analysis of Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) variants using MasterCode, where soft supersymmetry-breaking parameters are assumed to be universal at a scale $M_{in}$ below the supersymmetric grand unification scale $M_{GUT}$, a scenario applicable to mirage mediation and similar frameworks. These "sub-GUT" models extend beyond $M_{in}$ by incorporating the four CMSSM parameters: a common gaugino mass $m_{1/2}$, a common soft scalar mass $m_0$, a common trilinear mixing term $A$, and the MSSM Higgs vacuum expectation value ratio $\tan\beta$, under the assumption that the Higgs mixing parameter $\mu$ is positive. The analysis integrates constraints from approximately 36/fb of LHC data at 13 TeV regarding strongly- and electroweakly-interacting sparticles, alongside recent dark matter scattering searches from LUX, 2017 PICO, XENON1T, and PandaX-II, as well as established LHC and dark matter limits and comprehensive flavor and electroweak constraints. Results indicate a preference for $M_{in}$ ranging between $10^5$ and $10^9$ GeV, with $M_{in} \approx M_{GUT}$ being disfavored by $\Delta \chi^2 \sim 3$ due to the ${\rm BR}(B_{s, d} \to \mu^+\mu^-)$ constraint. Lower bounds on strongly-interacting sparticles are primarily driven by LHC searches and resemble those in the standard CMSSM. The analysis favors a Lightest Supersymmetric Particle (LSP) that is either a Bino or Higgsino with a mass around 1 TeV, achieving the required cold dark matter density through annihilation via heavy Higgs bosons ($H/A$), stop coannihilation, or chargino coannihilation. Furthermore, spin-independent dark matter scattering is projected to be detectable by upcoming LUX-Zeplin and XENONnT experiments. Finally, the impact of the $(g-2)_\mu$ constraint was examined, yielding consistent results regardless of its inclusion.

Analytical closed-form expressions, formulated as double sums of Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, are derived to evaluate bra-ket spherical harmonic overlap integrals for a broad range of trigonometric functions. These analytical results prove valuable in addressing non-separable wave equation problems—such as those in general-relativistic perturbation theory, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics—where such integrals emerge from the interaction between various angular modes.

We report the measurement of form-factor independent angular observables in the decay \mbox{$B^0\to K^{*}(892)^{0}\mu^+ \mu^-$}. This analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb experiment from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV.
