Four observables were determined across six bins of the dimuon invariant mass squared, $q^2$, spanning the range $0.1 < q^2 < 19.0$ GeV$^{2}$/c$^{4}$. The results align with Standard Model predictions for 23 out of the 24 measurements. However, a local deviation of $3.7$ Gaussian standard deviations was detected in one observable within a single $q^2$ bin. Assuming the 24 measurements are independent, the probability of observing a discrepancy of this magnitude or greater in at least one measurement is $0.5\%$.

Conventional classical sensors are nearing their peak sensitivity in numerous fields, yet they remain significantly distant from the fundamental limits imposed by quantum mechanics. Quantum sensors offer a significant advancement by leveraging the heightened sensitivity of quantum states to environmental factors. This work specifically addresses rotation sensing, a field with wide-ranging applications. Utilizing fundamental principles of estimation theory, we identify states capable of reaching the ultimate sensitivity limits for determining both the orientation of an unknown rotation axis and the magnitude of rotation around it. The substantial performance gains achieved with these optimal states suggest they will be an essential component in the emerging next generation of rotation sensors.

A formula for determining energy quantum fluctuations within small subsystems of a hot, relativistic gas is developed. Our findings indicate that these fluctuations rise as subsystem sizes decrease, yet they align with canonical ensemble predictions when the system is sufficiently large. Beyond relativistic heavy-ion collisions, this expression proves valuable for defining the limits of energy density and fluid elements, and it has broader applications across physics for studying high-temperature, high-velocity matter.

We calculate the differential decay widths for two- and three-body neutrino decays, treating neutrinos as Dirac fermions and accounting for non-zero masses of the decay products. We explore various hypotheses regarding the interaction mediating neutrino decay, focusing on scenarios where the masses of these daughters significantly alter the observable signatures across different experiments. Particular attention is given to decay daughters arising from right-chiral neutrino fields, where the daughter mass plays a critical role. As a specific illustration, we contrast the impacts of visible versus invisible antineutrino decays within the JUNO experimental framework.

Recovering coefficients within a diffusion equation constitutes a fundamental inverse problem. The most critical component is the diffusion coefficient, denoted as $a$ in the equation $u_t - \nabla(a\nabla u) = f$, which links spatial and temporal scales. This study aims to determine the unknown $a$ under the assumption that it is a function of the solution value, $a=a(u)$, at specific points. Such models underpin numerous physical processes, including nonlinear heat conduction, chemical mixing, and population dynamics. We examine two forms of overdetermined data to facilitate the recovery of $a(u)$: the time evolution $u(x_0,t)$ at a fixed boundary point $x_0 \in \partial\Omega$, or the value of $u$ along an interior curve $\Sigma \subset \Omega$. Practical examples include boundary temperature readings or population censuses in a specific region at a fixed time $T>0$. For the interior curve scenario, we demonstrate a uniqueness theorem that enables a constructive approach to recovering $a$. Furthermore, for both data types, we present reconstruction techniques utilizing the iterative algorithms detailed in this paper.

This paper introduces the design and analysis of a unified asymptotic preserving (AP) and well-balanced numerical scheme for the Euler Equations, incorporating gravitational and frictional source terms. The asymptotic behavior of the Euler system, particularly in the limits of zero Mach and Froude numbers alongside large friction, is defined by an additional scaling parameter. Based on the values of this parameter, the system transitions toward either a hyperbolic or a parabolic limit equation. Conventional Implicit-Explicit Runge-Kutta schemes fail to transition between these regimes. To address this, we propose a time semi-discretization that yields a unified scheme capable of remaining AP across both limits. A reformulation of this semi-implicit approach allows it to be expressed as a fully-explicit method where the mass update integrates both hyperbolic and parabolic fluxes. Within a finite volume framework, a space-time fully-discrete scheme is developed. To ensure the well-balancing property for hydrostatic steady states, the method employs a hydrostatic reconstruction strategy, upwinding of sources at interfaces, and a precise central discretization of parabolic fluxes. Several numerical case studies are provided to validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the scheme's robustness.

This paper introduces enhanced network architectures, data augmentation techniques, and training methodologies for the Webface and Insightface/Glint360K tracks of the ICCV2021 Masked Face Recognition Challenge. A primary objective is to ensure balanced performance across both masked and standard face recognition tasks. To mitigate overfitting in masked recognition, we limit masked faces to no more than 10% of the total dataset. Our proposed network modifications include a novel stem unit, drop block integration, face detection and alignment via YOLO5Face, feature concatenation, and a cycle cosine learning rate. These strategies collectively yield robust and balanced results for both recognition types.

This research investigates vector instabilities emerging in the post-inflationary Universe as a mechanism to amplify primordial magnetic fields. We posit a charged spectator scalar field, arbitrarily coupled to gravity, that exists in a vacuum de Sitter state during Inflation. Upon transitioning from Inflation to Reheating, gravitational particle creation converts this vacuum state into an excited many-particle system, which can be modeled as a real fluid. We construct a hydrodynamic framework based on second-order relativistic fluid theories, incorporating a relaxation time prescription for the collision integral. Given the high-temperature environment and vanishing scalar curvature characteristic of the Reheating epoch (a radiation-dominated era), the fluid behaves conformally. The rapid shift from inflationary to effectively radiation-dominated expansion generates large quantum fluctuations, which manifest as statistical variations producing charge excesses and anisotropic pressures within finite domains. The magnitude of these effects depends on the averaging domain size and the curvature coupling. We examine domains larger than the horizon at Reheating's onset but smaller than the current horizon, demonstrating that in a finite subset, the resulting anisotropy and charge excess create conditions favorable for Weibel instability. Furthermore, if the Reheating duration is shorter than the fluid's relaxation time, this instability can counteract or surpass the conformal dilution of primordial magnetic fields. Additionally, we find that any existing magnetic helicity, representing the non-trivial topology of the magnetic field, is also amplified.

This study presents neutron diffraction analysis of single-crystal CePtAl$_3$, supported by specific heat measurements under applied magnetic fields. Below the Néel temperature ($T_\mathrm{N}$) of 3 K, CePtAl$_3$ establishes incommensurate antiferromagnetic order characterized by a single modulation vector $\vec{k}$=$(0.676 \, 0 \, 0)$. The presence of residual magnetic scattering intensity above $T_\mathrm{N}$ and the broadening of the specific heat anomaly at $T_\mathrm{N}$ can be explained by a Gaussian distribution of transition temperatures with a standard deviation of $\sigma\approx0.5\,{\rm K}$. This variation in $T_\mathrm{N}$ is likely due to occupational and positional disorder between Pt and Al sites. Furthermore, magnetic field measurements show atypical changes in domain populations when the field is oriented along the $[0\,1\,0]$ direction, indicating a transition from cycloidal to amplitude-modulated magnetic order near 2.5 T.

Full-duplex (FD) communication offers a viable solution to overcome data rate constraints in underwater acoustic (UWA) channels. However, simultaneous transmission on the same frequency band causes the local transmitter's signal to generate self-interference (SI), which degrades the reception of the remote signal. To mitigate this, the local receiver must acquire channel state information for both the self-interference and the remote link to cancel the SI and equalize the clean signal, respectively. Given the rapid time-variability of UWA environments, real-time channel tracking is essential. This paper introduces a UWA-FD receiver that jointly tracks variations in both the SI and remote channels using a recursive least squares (RLS) algorithm driven by feedback from previously detected data symbols. By employing joint channel estimation, the proposed method achieves superior self-interference cancellation compared to receivers utilizing separate estimators. Furthermore, since real-time tracking is accomplished without relying on frequent training sequences, the system maintains high bandwidth efficiency.

This study tackles the longstanding and contentious question regarding the origin of superconductivity in cuprates, proposing that it stems from amphoteric defects located at vacancy sites within copper oxide planes. Local relaxation of the defect lattice creates a negative-$U$ binding energy, which traps two holes on these amphoteric defects in a donor configuration, forming preformed boson pairs. Thermodynamic equilibrium between defects in donor and acceptor states stabilizes the Fermi energy at the amphoteric defect's charge transition point, ensuring resonant coupling between free holes and these localized pairs. Model calculations indicate that the critical temperature is chiefly governed by the density of amphoteric defects in the donor configuration, which explains both the universal dome-like relationship between critical temperature and doping, as well as its dependence on superfluid density. Intentional chemical doping with acceptors or donors is neither a necessary nor sufficient condition for superconductivity; instead, the phenomenon is fully determined by amphoteric defects, whose concentration can be regulated through crystal nonstoichiometry. The sole function of chemical doping is to adjust the ratio of amphoteric defects between donor and acceptor configurations, thereby increasing superfluid density and the critical temperature for acceptor doping while decreasing them for donor doping. This mechanism accounts for the experimentally observed asymmetry in the dome structures resulting from acceptor versus donor doping. The unusual sensitivity of the critical temperature to external perturbations is attributed to the resonant nature of the coupling between free holes and preformed hole pairs. Furthermore, this work has broader applicability, potentially extending to other superconductors exhibiting a dome-like dependence of critical temperature on doping.

Stochastic precipitation generators (SPGs) represent a category of statistical models capable of producing synthetic data that mimics extended periods of both dry and wet rainfall. These generated time series are essential for climate projections, evaluating the impacts of extreme weather, and managing water resources and agriculture. We developed an SPG tailored for daily precipitation, defining it as a semi-continuous distribution at each location: this includes a point mass at zero to represent no rain and a mixture of two exponential distributions for positive rainfall amounts. Functioning as hidden Markov models (HMMs), our generators utilize underlying climate conditions as states. Specifically, we fitted a 3-state HMM to daily precipitation records from the Chesapeake Bay watershed along the U.S. Eastern coast, covering the wet season (July–September) between 2000 and 2019. Data were sourced from the GPM-IMERG remote sensing dataset, and we extended existing variational HMM methodologies to accommodate semi-continuous emission distributions. To address the data's high spatial dimensionality, we employed a stochastic optimization approach to enhance computational efficiency. Using the Viterbi algorithm, we identified the most probable sequence of latent states and characterized the distinct weather regimes linked to each state. The synthetic data produced by this HMM successfully replicates both monthly precipitation statistics and the spatial dependencies observed in the historical GPM-IMERG data.

Double-beta processes involving $^{184}$Os and $^{192}$Os were investigated for a duration of 15,851 hours at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (LNGS) of the I.N.F.N., utilizing an 118 g ultra-pure osmium sample coupled to the endcap of an 112 cm$^3$ ultra-low-background broad-energy germanium detector. New constraints on double-electron capture and electron capture accompanied by positron emission in $^{184}$Os were established, reaching sensitivity levels of $\lim T_{1/2} \sim 10^{16}-10^{17}$ yr. Specifically, the $2\nu$2K and $2\nu$KL decay modes of $^{184}$Os transitioning to the ground state of $^{184}$W were limited to half-lives of $T_{1/2}\geq3.0\times 10^{16}$ yr and $T_{1/2}\geq2.0\times 10^{16}$ yr, respectively. Additionally, a lower bound on the half-life for the double-beta decay of $^{192}$Os to the first excited state of $^{192}$Pt was determined to be $\lim T_{1/2}=2.0\times 10^{20}$ yr at a 90\% confidence level.

This research investigates the asymptotic properties of the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant, defined using the square of an odd $n$-th root of unity, for Seifert fibered spaces resulting from integral Dehn surgery on torus knots. We demonstrate that this invariant can be expressed as the sum of Chern-Simons invariants and twisted Reidemeister torsions, both derived from representations of the fundamental group into the two-dimensional complex special linear group.

This paper establishes an upper bound for the first Robin eigenvalue of the $p$-Laplacian featuring a positive boundary parameter, and provides a quantitative reverse Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first Robin eigenvalue with a negative boundary parameter within convex sets of fixed perimeter. The demonstrations rely on a comparison method utilizing inner sets, as introduced by Payne, Weimberger, and Polya.

This paper introduces TF-Grasp, a transformer-based architecture designed for robotic grasp detection. The TF-Grasp framework incorporates two sophisticated designs tailored for visual grasping. First, it utilizes local window attention to extract detailed features and local context from graspable objects, while employing cross-window attention to model long-range dependencies between distant pixels. This aggregation of object knowledge, environmental configurations, and relationships among visual entities facilitates subsequent grasp detection. Second, the framework employs a hierarchical encoder-decoder structure with skip-connections, which transfers shallow features from the encoder to the decoder to enable multi-scale feature fusion. Thanks to this powerful attention mechanism, TF-Grasp can simultaneously capture local details, such as object contours, and model long-term connections, like relationships between distinct visual concepts in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments show that TF-Grasp outperforms state-of-the-art convolutional grasping models, achieving accuracy rates of 97.99% and 94.6% on the Cornell and Jacquard datasets, respectively. Furthermore, real-world tests using a 7DoF Franka Emika Panda robot confirm its ability to grasp unseen objects across various scenarios. The code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/WangShaoSUN/grasp-transformer.

We present RealTime QA, a dynamic question answering platform that poses and evaluates queries on a regular schedule (weekly in this iteration). Focused on the current state of the world, this system requires models to address novel events and fresh information, thereby challenging the static assumptions inherent in traditional open-domain QA datasets and targeting immediate, real-world applications. Our approach establishes robust baseline models using large pretrained architectures such as GPT-3 and T5. As an evolving benchmark, this preliminary report details real-time evaluation outcomes from the last month. Our findings indicate that GPT-3 frequently updates its responses appropriately using newly retrieved documents, underscoring the critical role of up-to-date information retrieval. However, we observed that GPT-3 often provides outdated answers when retrieved documents lack sufficient context to derive a solution. This highlights a key area for future investigation: whether open-domain QA systems can recognize unanswerable scenarios and interact with users or retrieval modules to adjust search results. We anticipate that RealTime QA will drive advancements in instantaneous question answering and related fields.

We demonstrate that if two equivariant vector bundles over an algebraic GKM manifold share identical equivariant Chern classes, then the genus zero equivariant Gromov--Witten theories of their respective projective bundles are naturally isomorphic.

Although one-dimensional models describing spin-polarized Fermi gases with tunable zero-range interactions have attracted significant theoretical attention, they remain unachieved in ultracold systems. This study investigates the two-body correlation strength of spin-polarized fermionic potassium ($^{40}$K) within a quasi-one-dimensional (q1D) regime, employing radio-frequency spectroscopy. We manipulate the interaction strength and spatial symmetry using a nearby p-wave Feshbach resonance and confinement anisotropy. Unexpectedly, we identify a scattering channel exhibiting even particle-exchange parity along the q1D axis. These emergent s-wave collisions arise from orbital singlet wave functions in the transverse directions, which simultaneously introduce high-momentum components to low-energy q1D collisions. For the first time, we measure both the q1D odd- and even-wave "contact" parameters and compare them against theoretical predictions for one-dimensional many-body models. Our results show that the even-wave contact approaches the theoretical unitary value, while the maximum observed odd-wave contact is two orders of magnitude below its unitary limit. This discovery of emergent s-wave interactions opens a new pathway for investigating strongly correlated ensembles of spin-polarized fermions with zero-range interactions.

This paper addresses the interpretation of the wave function by presenting the most recent iteration of the Växjö interpretation, which diverges significantly from the 2001 original. The core distinction of this updated Växjö interpretation lies in its synthesis of subquantum-level realism with the nonobjectivity of quantum observables, meaning their values cannot be assigned prior to measurement. Consequently, realism is effectively negated by detectors, which convert the continuous subquantum reality into discrete detection events. The Växjö interpretation-2012 is fundamentally contextual in the Bohrian sense, as the value of an observable relies on the specific measurement context. This form of contextuality is broader than Bell's contextuality, which is grounded in the joint measurement of compatible observables.

We introduce a self-consistently renormalized spin-wave theory, grounded in a mean-field approximation, to analyze the two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet with perpendicular easy-axis anisotropy on a honeycomb lattice, alongside its few-layer and bulk counterparts. Within this framework, temperature-dependent magnetization is determined by solving a self-consistency equation. By modeling distinct surface and bulk layers as separate sublattices, we capture their physical differences, allowing the approach to be easily extended to investigate diverse magnetic phenomena across various systems, particularly those with magnetically inequivalent sublattices. Applying our theory to two chromium-based layered van der Waals insulating magnets, Cr$_2$Ge$_2$Te$_6$ and CrI$_3$, we utilize multiple sets of Heisenberg exchange and single-ion anisotropy parameters drawn from existing literature. As anticipated, our results reveal a pronounced dimensionality effect: the ordering temperature decreases, and its sensitivity to anisotropy increases as the system's dimensionality is reduced.

Advancing state-of-the-art methods for specific tasks is a primary motivation within our research community, where achieving prestige in a task often yields significant visibility. Consequently, a critical question emerges regarding the reliability of evaluation methodologies used to compare these approaches. A standard practice involves partitioning data into training, development, and test sets; researchers train and tune their models using portions of the data, select the best-performing model based on the development set, and finally evaluate it on unseen test data. Subsequently, test scores from different methods are compared, and performance differences are assessed for statistical significance.

However, this publication demonstrates a high risk that statistical significance in such evaluations does not reflect a superior learning approach but rather stems from chance. For instance, using the CoNLL 2003 Named Entity Recognition dataset, we observed Type I errors (false positives) in up to 26% of cases with a p-value threshold of < 0.05, leading to the false conclusion of a significant difference between identical approaches. We establish that this evaluation framework is inadequate for comparing learning methods and formalize alternative setups grounded in score distributions.

Reinforcement learning (RL) agents are extensively applied to complex sequential decision-making tasks but often fail to generalize to unseen scenarios. Although previous online methods have shown that incorporating signals beyond the reward function, such as self-supervised learning (SSL), enhances generalization, these approaches struggle within offline RL contexts where learning occurs from static datasets. We demonstrate that online algorithms for RL generalization can underperform in offline settings due to inadequate estimation of observation similarity. To address this, we introduce a theoretically grounded framework termed Generalized Similarity Functions (GSF). GSF leverages contrastive learning to train offline RL agents to cluster observations based on the similarity of their anticipated future behaviors, quantified through \emph{generalized value functions}. Furthermore, we establish that GSF is versatile enough to recover existing SSL objectives while simultaneously boosting zero-shot generalization performance on the challenging offline RL benchmark, Offline Procgen.

It is a well-documented phenomenon that convolutional architectures, when used for image understanding, tend to learn oriented bandpass filters. The conventional explanation attributes this to the structure of natural images; since these images consist locally of oriented contours at various scales, the learned filters act as a match to this data. We propose an alternative explanation grounded in the mathematical structure of convolutional networks themselves. Specifically, because complex exponentials are the eigenfunctions of convolution, and because these functions are defined globally while networks operate locally, applying a windowing function to the eigenfunctions naturally yields oriented bandpass filters as the preferred operators for the network to learn. From a representational perspective, these filters provide a systematic local method for characterizing and manipulating images or signals. We provide empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that convolutional networks acquire such filters across all their convolutional layers. While prior research has identified these characteristics in early layers, our study appears to be the first to demonstrate their predominance throughout the entire network depth. Previous studies likely overlooked this because they focused on the cumulative compositional effects of filtering across layers, whereas we analyze the specific filter properties present at each individual layer.

The NICER telescope at NASA has recently quantified x-ray emissions from PSR J0740+6620, the most massive neutron star with a precisely determined mass of two solar masses. Based on data analysis by Miller et al. and Riley et al. (Astrophys. J. Lett. 918, L28/L27, 2021), the star's radius is estimated to be between $R_{2.0} \approx (11.4-16.1)$ km at the $68\%$ credibility level. This paper examines the consequences of these findings for sound speed within the high-density inner cores, utilizing recent next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order chiral effective field theory ($\chi$EFT) calculations to model the equation of state in lower-density outer regions. Our results indicate that the lower limit for the maximum sound speed in the inner core, $\textbf{min}\{c^2_{s, {\rm max}}\}$, rises sharply as the radius of massive neutron stars increases. Provided that $\chi$EFT remains a valid expansion for nuclear interactions up to approximately twice nuclear saturation density, a radius constraint of $R_{2.0}\geqslant 13$ km implies $\textbf{min}\{c^2_{s, {\rm max}}\} \geqslant 0.562$ and $0.442$ at the $68\%$ and $95\%$ credibility levels, respectively.

Although link prediction in dynamic networks has been widely researched and utilized across many fields, the related task of predicting temporal unlinks—crucial for understanding social network evolution—has received relatively little attention. Accurately forecasting both the formation and removal of future edges significantly aids network analysis by revealing hidden node relationships. This study introduces LULS, an effective algorithm for temporal link and unlink prediction, based on the assumption that node interactions consist of two distinct types: long-term and short-term relations. For every snapshot of a dynamic network, LULS first gathers higher-order structural information into two topological matrices via short random walks. It then employs non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to optimize a global matrix and a series of temporary matrices corresponding to each snapshot; the global matrix captures long-term relations, while the temporary matrices represent short-term relations specific to each snapshot. Subsequently, LULS computes the similarity matrix for a future snapshot to predict both links and unlinks. Furthermore, the method enhances prediction accuracy by incorporating graph regularization constraints to enrich the global matrix with comprehensive topological and temporal data. Experimental results on real-world networks demonstrate that LULS surpasses other baselines in both link and unlink prediction tasks.

We establish a formula for the index of a Dirac operator on a compact, even-dimensional incomplete edge space that meets a "geometric Witt condition." This result is achieved by truncating the space into a smooth manifold with boundary, utilizing the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index theorem, and subsequently taking a limit. From this derivation, we obtain corollaries concerning the existence of positive scalar curvature metrics on such incomplete edge spaces.

This work investigates nonperturbative aspects of QED where the gyromagnetic ratio $g$ deviates from the Dirac value $g_{\rm D}=2$. By employing the external field method, we analyze the effective action $V_{\mathrm{eff}}$ under conditions of an arbitrarily strong, constant, and homogeneous field. Our results reveal a cusp in the dependence on the gyromagnetic factor $g$ for: a) the QED $b_0$-renormalization group coefficient; and b) a subset of light-light scattering coefficients derived from the long-wavelength limit expansion. Furthermore, we identify the potential for asymptotic freedom within an Abelian theory across specific ranges of $g$.

This paper examines the impact of gauge freedom on the representation of quantum information processing devices and its consequences for device characterization. Using experimentally relevant examples, we show that multiple equally valid descriptions of the same experiment can exist, each distributing errors differently across the gate-set components, thereby resulting in varying error rates. Consequently, assigning specific operational significance to figures of merit for individual gate elements can be misleading. Instead, we propose an alternative operational metric for the gate-set known as the mean variation error, along with a corresponding measurement protocol.

In any simple graph $G$, a complete subgraph involving $k$ vertices is defined as a $k$-\emph{clique}. This paper introduces the concept of a $k$-clique's value (for $k>1$), extending the traditional notion of vertex degree. We subsequently derive a generalized form of the handshaking lemma, termed the clique handshaking lemma. While Mantel's theorem establishes that the maximum number of edges in triangle-free graphs with $n$ vertices is $\frac{n^{2}}{4}$, our primary objective is to extend this result to the class of $K_{\omega+1}$-free graphs by utilizing the concepts of clique values and the clique handshaking lemma.

Over the past ten years, object detection has advanced significantly. Nevertheless, identifying new classes with limited data remains difficult, as deep learning models often suffer from degraded feature representations when data is scarce. Current approaches typically utilize a holistic fine-tuning strategy: models are first pre-trained on base classes with ample data and then adapted to define feature spaces for novel classes. However, this method has limitations. During fine-tuning, novel classes may inadvertently draw upon knowledge from multiple base classes, resulting in a scattered feature space that compromises inter-class separability. To address these issues, we introduce FADI (Few-shot object detection via Association and DIscrimination), a two-step framework designed to create distinct, discriminative feature spaces for each novel class. First, in the association phase, rather than implicitly combining multiple base classes, we explicitly mimic the feature space of a single, semantically similar base class to build a compact representation for the novel class. Second, in the discrimination phase, we separate the classification branches for base and novel classes to ensure their separability. Additionally, we apply a set-specialized margin loss to enhance separability across all classes. Extensive evaluations on the Pascal VOC and MS-COCO datasets show that FADI achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving upon baselines by an average of +18.7 across various shot/split settings, with the most significant gains observed in extremely few-shot scenarios.

We examine non-linear differential equations defined on the punctured formal disc by analyzing the natural derived enhancements of their solution spaces. Specifically, by utilizing inverse theory from the calculus of variations, we demonstrate that a variational representation of a differential equation is \emph{equivalent} to the residue pairing, which generates a (-1)-symplectic form on the derived space of solutions, provided it carries a specific decoration of its tangent complex.

For strongly coupled systems possessing a gravity dual, we demonstrate that the standard holographic dictionary predicts a nonnegative susceptibility during thermodynamic equilibrium. In scenarios lacking spontaneous condensation or involving spontaneous $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry breaking, the "trace energy condition" is frequently violated. Furthermore, we identify a normalized grand potential density that decreases monotonically as lower scales are approached, serving as a candidate $c$-function to quantify the effective degrees of freedom. Additionally, we discover that several widely discussed holographic models in existing literature are inconsistent with the principles of holography.

Classifying hyperspectral remote sensing (HSRS) images using deep neural networks presents significant challenges due to the high dimensionality, numerous channels, and substantial inter-channel redundancy inherent in these images. Furthermore, training data for HSRS classification is scarce compared to other tasks, which complicates the training of parameter-heavy deep networks and often results in performance that lags behind conventional models. Additionally, standard convolutional neural networks tend to generate over-confident predictions, a critical flaw given the data limitations. To address these issues, this study employs Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) for HSRS image classification, marking the first known application of this approach in this domain. Since BNNs naturally quantify uncertainty, we conducted extensive experiments on the Pavia Centre, Salinas, and Botswana datasets. Our results demonstrate that BNNs surpass both standard convolutional neural networks and Random Forest models. Moreover, further analysis reveals that BNNs exhibit greater stability and robustness to model pruning, with higher uncertainty levels correlating to samples that are expected to have larger prediction errors.

Robotic systems often face uncertainties that can be explicitly modeled, such as parametric variations in mass and moments of inertia. Accurately quantifying these parametric uncertainties is crucial for predicting system behavior with greater precision, thereby ensuring safe and exact task execution. Complementing this, it is essential to establish robustness guarantees against prevailing uncertainties, including environmental disturbances and limitations in current model knowledge. To address these needs, the authors extend their previously introduced RATTLE algorithm—a framework for online, information-aware motion planning—to better suit real-world robotic applications. RATTLE balances the tradeoff between acquiring information and achieving traditional goals while supporting models that update online. Furthermore, this work introduces online-updateable low-level control robustness guarantees and a novel method for automatically adjusting information content to meet specified estimation precision. Extensive experiments conducted in microgravity using Astrobee robots on the International Space Station, along with practical implementation details, demonstrate RATTLE's effectiveness in enabling real-time, robust, online-updateable, and information-seeking motion planning under parametric uncertainty.

This paper examines a reducible degeneration of a hyperelliptic curve of genus $g$. By employing the Sato Grassmannian, we demonstrate that the limits of hyperelliptic solutions within the KP-hierarchy exist and evolve into soliton solutions of diverse types. We re-establish certain findings by Abenda, who investigated regular soliton solutions associated with a reducible rational curve resulting from the degeneration of a hyperelliptic curve. Furthermore, we analyze singular soliton solutions and elucidate the relationship between the singularity structure of these solutions and the matrices that define them.

This study investigates gravitational-wave transients linked to Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) identified by the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment Fast Radio Burst Project (CHIME/FRB) during the initial phase of the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo (1 April 2019 15:00 UTC to 1 October 2019 15:00 UTC). We analyzed triggers from 22 FRBs using a search targeting compact binary coalescences involving at least one neutron star, and conducted a targeted search for generic gravitational-wave transients across 40 FRBs. No significant evidence for a gravitational-wave association was found in either search. However, due to the substantial uncertainties in the distances of the FRBs in our sample, inferred from dispersion measures, this result does not definitively rule out progenitor models involving the emission of the searched-for gravitational waves from any of these events. Instead, we report $90\%$ confidence lower bounds on the distance to each FRB for various gravitational-wave progenitor models. By integrating the inferred maximum distance data for each FRB with the sensitivity of the gravitational-wave searches, we established upper limits on the energy emitted via gravitational waves across different emission scenarios. For a range of models with central gravitational wave frequencies between 70-3560 Hz, we derived values of approximately $10^{51}$-$10^{57}$ erg. Furthermore, we detected no significant coincidence of gravitational waves with the repeater FRB 20200120E, the nearest known extragalactic FRB.

In the framework of the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) effective field theory, accounting for the non-boost-invariant nature of the rapidity distribution, we adjust the normalization scheme for longitudinal rapidity ridge correlations. Following this correction, the large-rapidity ridge correlation recovers after reaching a minimum, aligning with observations from the CMS detector. Additionally, we observe that this correlation rebound occurs near the sum of the projectile and target saturation momenta and shifts toward higher rapidities as collision energies increase. These characteristics stem directly from gluon saturation and quantum evolution within the CGC framework.

Most spreading mechanisms necessitate physical proximity between agents. Consequently, the stationary state of spreading dynamics within a mobile population hinges on the interaction between the temporal and spatial scales of the epidemic process and the agents' movement. We examine the steady-state properties arising from this interplay using a simple model of Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible epidemic spreading on self-propelled particles undergoing Run-and-Tumble motion. Concentrating on the diffusive long-time regime, we observe that agent motion qualitatively alters the nature of the epidemic transition, defined by the emergence of a macroscopic fraction of infected individuals. Specifically, the transition adopts a mean-field character for agents diffusing in one, two, and three dimensions, whereas in the absence of motion, the outbreak depends on the dimensionality of the static network formed by fixed agent locations. These findings, derived from a continuum description, are corroborated by numerical simulations of an agent-based model. This work seeks to bridge the fields of soft active matter physics and theoretical epidemiology, offering potential relevance to researchers in both domains.

Over the past six decades, space exploration has revealed that the interplanetary medium is constantly disturbed by diverse solar winds and storms carrying solar material throughout the heliosphere. While the origin of the fast solar wind from coronal holes is generally accepted, the source of the slow solar wind (SSW) remains a subject of significant debate. Recent data from the Parker Solar Probe offers fresh insights into the solar wind's inception, yet a self-consistent explanation for the SSW's composition and bulk properties continues to be a major challenge. To address this, the thesis employs and refines models ranging from simple to highly complex. It begins by utilizing the first images from the Wide-Field Imager for Solar PRobe (WISPR), which captures the solar corona at unprecedented resolution, to test global models at smaller scales. These observations support the theory of transient plasma release from coronal loops, a phenomenon further explored using high-resolution magneto-hydrodynamics simulations. Furthermore, the thesis develops and applies a new multi-species coronal loop model, the Irap Solar Atmosphere Model (ISAM), to analyze plasma transport mechanisms between the chromosphere and corona. ISAM calculates the coupled transport of solar wind constituents and minor ions by comprehensively modeling collisions, partial ionization, and radiative cooling and heating near the chromosphere's upper layers. Using this model, the study investigates mechanisms that selectively extract ions based on their first ionization potential (FIP) as they move from the chromosphere to the corona.

Ultraviolet and X-ray photons emitted by active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are capable of ionizing hydrogen within the intergalactic medium (IGM). We model radiative transfer around AGNs at high redshifts to assess 21-cm line emission from neutral IGM hydrogen and determine the radial brightness temperature profile during the epoch of reionization. This ionization zone spans a comoving distance of approximately 10 Mpc, corresponding to an observable angular scale of roughly 10 arcminutes. By estimating radio galaxy number counts via high-sensitivity observations from the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), we evaluate the potential for constraining AGN luminosity function parameters using Fisher analysis across three evolutionary models throughout cosmic time. Our results indicate that when high-redshift AGNs are sufficiently luminous, parameter uncertainties can be limited to just a few percent. Furthermore, we explore the prospects for tightening these constraints with future observations extending beyond the SKA era.

Smart contracts serve as the foundation of the "code is law" philosophy, where their immutable code definitively dictates asset management. However, buggy smart contracts provide strong evidence against this paradigm's practicality, as documented flaws have led to the compromise of significant assets. To mitigate these risks, the Ethereum community has suggested (i) auditing and analysis tools, and (ii) design patterns enabling code mutability. Yet, neither approach alone fully resolves the challenges posed by "code is law." This paper presents a systematic framework that merges these two elements to transition from "code is law" to a new "specification is law" paradigm. Under this model, contracts can be deployed and upgraded only if they adhere to a specific formal specification. The framework relies on a \emph{trusted deployer}, an off-chain service that formally verifies and enforces this conformance. We have prototyped this system and tested its application against two prevalent Ethereum standards—ERC20 Tokens and ERC1155 Multi Tokens—yielding encouraging outcomes.

Identifying druggable binding sites on proteins is a crucial initial stage in the discovery of new medications. This computational prediction process can be significantly enhanced by leveraging recent breakthroughs in deep learning and utilizing the growing availability of relevant data. This paper introduces DeepSurf, a new computational approach designed to predict potential binding sites. DeepSurf integrates a surface-based representation, utilizing multiple 3D voxelized grids positioned on the protein surface, with advanced deep learning architectures. Trained on the extensive scPDB database, DeepSurf achieves superior performance across three diverse test datasets, outperforming all primary deep learning-based rivals while maintaining competitive results against traditional, non-data-driven methods.

General Relativity posits that matter or radiation emitted asymmetrically from a source induces a permanent alteration in the local space-time metric, a phenomenon known as the \emph{gravitational memory effect}. Although this effect remains unobserved, supernova neutrinos have long been regarded as a viable pathway for its future detection. The emergence of deci-Hertz gravitational wave interferometers now makes observing supernova neutrino memory feasible, offering significant advancements for multimessenger astronomy and gravitational tests. This study introduces a phenomenological, analytical toy model for this effect that aligns broadly with numerical simulation results, which is subsequently extended to various relevant case studies. Our findings indicate that for a galactic supernova, the dimensionless strain, $h(t)$, ranges between $\sim 10^{-22}$ and $10^{-21}$, evolving over a characteristic timescale of $\sim 0.1 - 10$ seconds, contingent upon the neutrino emission anisotropy's time evolution. The characteristic strain, $h_c(f)$, peaks at a frequency $f_{max} \sim {\mathcal O}(10^{-1}) - {\mathcal O}(1)$ Hz. The specific time- and frequency-domain features of this memory strain will elucidate the dynamics of matter near the collapsed core and enable the discrimination between different stellar collapse scenarios. Next-generation detectors such as DECIGO and BBO will be capable of detecting the neutrino memory effect from supernovae at typical galactic distances and further afield, with Ultimate DECIGO potentially reaching a detectability distance of 10 Mpc.

Recent angle-resolved measurements of the $c$-axis resistivity in stripe-ordered La$_{2-x}$Ba$_x$CuO$_4$ (LBCO) with $x=1/8$ uncovered an anomalous dependence on the orientation of the in-plane magnetic field. We contend that, alongside other existing data regarding $c$-axis transport, these findings indicate the presence of two distinct types of superconducting pairs in $x=1/8$ LBCO below the stripe ordering temperature. One type of pair possesses finite momentum and remains confined within the Cu-O planes, while the second type—likely conventional $d$-wave pairs with zero momentum—travels along narrow conducting channels extending through the sample along the $c$-axis. This hypothesis is supported by the observed exponential temperature dependence of the $c$-axis resistivity, $\rho_c(T)$, which we ascribe to thermally induced slips of the superconducting phase and flux flow. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward theoretical framework that successfully models the observed $\pi/2$-periodic variation of $\rho_c$ with respect to the in-plane magnetic field direction, as well as the remaining experimental data.

We establish a highly uniform variant of the prime number theorem for a specific family of $L$-functions. The interval for $x$ scales polynomially with the analytic conductor, and the error term is formulated as an optimization problem that explicitly relies on the known zero-free region. This family includes the Rankin-Selberg $L$-function $L(s,\pi \times \pi')$, which corresponds to cuspidal automorphic representations $\pi$ and $\pi'$ of $\mathrm{GL}_{m}$ and $\mathrm{GL}_{m'}$. Our primary finding yields the first uniformly valid prime number theorems for these $L$-functions (maintaining uniformity with respect to the analytic conductor) in complete generality.

Recently, artificial intelligence has expanded into numerous fields, including the legal sector. However, well-annotated public datasets for Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) documents remain scarce. Although SCOTUS rulings are public knowledge, conducting meaningful analysis is labor-intensive because researchers must manually collect and process the data from scratch. Consequently, our objective is to develop a high-quality SCOTUS dataset to facilitate natural language processing (NLP) research and other data-driven initiatives. Furthermore, recent NLP advancements enable the creation of predictive models capable of identifying patterns that shape judicial decisions. By applying sophisticated NLP algorithms to historical case records, these trained models can forecast and categorize court judgments based on textual facts provided by the plaintiff and defendant, effectively emulating a human jury to produce a final verdict.

In a secluded dark sector framework, a portal coupling facilitates the interaction between the visible and dark sectors, enabling non-adiabatic evolution within the latter. To investigate this phenomenon, we examine a $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau} \otimes U(1)_X$ extension of the Standard Model (SM), where the dark sector carries charge solely under $U(1)_X$, while SM fields remain neutral with respect to this symmetry. Tree-level kinetic mixing between the $U(1)_X$ and $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$ gauge bosons drives the non-adiabatic dynamics, with the portal coupling regulating thermal equilibrium between the two sectors. By analyzing the temperature evolution and various non-equilibrium phases across different values of the portal coupling ($\epsilon$), dark gauge coupling ($g_X$), dark matter mass ($m_\chi$), and dark vector boson mass ($m_{Z^\prime}$), we provide a detailed study of the dark sector's behavior. Additionally, we assess constraints on these parameters derived from laboratory and astrophysical observations. Our findings indicate that beam dump experiments and stellar cooling data significantly restrict the parameter space for non-adiabatic evolution when $m_{Z^\prime} \lesssim 100 \, {\rm MeV}$. The regions satisfying relic density requirements align with direct detection and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) bounds for a mass ratio $r \equiv m_{Z^\prime}/m_\chi = 10^{-3}$, with these limits becoming less stringent at higher $r$. Conversely, constraints arising from diffuse $\gamma$-ray background measurements and cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies are most severe at $r = 10^{-1}$, becoming negligible for smaller values of $r$.

Radio relics found at the edges of galaxy clusters suggest that electrons are accelerated via diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) at merger-induced shocks with Mach numbers ($M_s$) of approximately 3 to 4 within the intracluster medium (ICM). Recent research indicates that the necessary preacceleration and injection steps for DSA might happen at supercritical shocks ($M_s \gtrsim 2.3$) due to multiscale waves generated by microinstabilities like the Alfvén ion cyclotron (AIC), electron firehose (EFI), and whistler (WI) instabilities. Conversely, the observation of relics with subcritical shocks ($M_s \lesssim 2.3$) presents a significant challenge, as DSA at such weak shocks remains unresolved. One proposed solution is the reacceleration of preexisting nonthermal electrons. To investigate this, we conducted Particle-in-Cell (PIC) simulations of weak quasi-perpendicular shocks in high-$\beta$ ($\beta = P_{\rm gas}/P_B$) plasmas containing both Maxwellian thermal and power-law suprathermal electrons. Our findings show that while suprathermal electrons boost the excitation of electron-scale waves through the EFI and WI, they do not influence ion reflection or the subsequent creation of ion-scale waves via the AIC instability. Since ion-scale waves are essential for accelerating electrons to the momentum required for injection, the criticality condition for DSA remains unchanged. Consequently, we conclude that preexisting nonthermal electrons in the preshock region alone are insufficient to solve the problem of electron preacceleration at subcritical ICM shocks.

This study examines the dislocation content at grain boundary (GB) phase junctions, which are line defects where distinct GB phases coexist on a single plane. Although regular GB disconnections have been well-characterized across various interfaces, junctions arising from GBs with differing structures and excess atom counts remain unexplored. We utilize a generalized Burgers circuit analysis to determine the Burgers vectors ($b$) of junctions within two $\Sigma$5 Cu boundaries simulated via molecular dynamics. Our results indicate that these junctional Burgers vectors cannot be fully described by the displacement shift complete (DSC) lattice. We demonstrate that the normal component of $b$ generally does not equate to the difference in excess volumes; instead, it includes an additional contribution from the change in GB atom density per unit area ($\Delta N$) required to transition between phases. In the specific boundaries analyzed, this $\Delta N$-related component dominates, even reversing the sign of $b$. We derive formulas for both the normal and tangential components of $b$ expressed through DSC lattice vectors and non-DSC terms involving $\Delta N$ and other excess properties like volume and shear. These expressions establish a link between GB phase transformations driven by free energy differences and the motion of junctions under applied normal and shear stresses. Consequently, this analysis quantifies $b$, enabling the calculation of the elastic energy of these defects, assessment of their role in nucleation barriers during phase transformations, and evaluation of elastic interactions with other defects.

This paper examines orientation-preserving Morse-Smale diffeomorphisms on surfaces. By employing factorization techniques and the linearization of neighborhoods, we demonstrate that these diffeomorphisms possess only a finite count of orientable heteroclinic orbits.

Mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) is the predominant analytical method for clinical trials involving Alzheimer's disease and other progressive conditions with continuous longitudinal outcomes. This approach categorizes time, enabling unconstrained mean estimates for each study visit within randomized groups. However, treating time as categorical becomes problematic when assessments occur off-schedule; including these visits may introduce bias, while excluding them discards valuable data and compromises the intention-to-treat principle. This issue has been further intensified by pandemic-related delays in clinical trial visits. As an alternative, we propose a constrained longitudinal data analysis utilizing natural cubic splines, which treats time as a continuous variable and employs test version effects to model the mean trajectory. Both practical applications and simulation studies demonstrate that this spline-based model outperforms categorical-time models like MMRM as well as those assuming a proportional treatment effect.

A strongly deterministic physical theory allows for only a single possible trajectory of the universe. As Penrose (1989) stated, "it is not just a matter of the future being determined by the past; the entire history of the universe is fixed, according to some precise mathematical scheme, for all time." While such a remarkable characteristic might seem impossible to achieve within any realistic and straightforward physical framework, this paper offers a definition of strong determinism and distinguishes it from standard and super-determinism. I then examine its implications for explanation, causation, prediction, fundamental attributes, free will, and modality. Finally, I introduce the first example of a realistic, simple, and strongly deterministic physical theory: the Everettian Wentaculus. According to the laws of this theory, the history of the Everettian multiverse was necessarily unique. If the Everettian Wentaculus is empirically equivalent to other quantum theories, we will never be able to determine through observation whether our world is strongly deterministic. Even if strong determinism does not hold, it is closer to reality than previously thought, bearing significant consequences for key areas in philosophy and the foundations of physics.

We introduce a novel approach to scaling the automatic configuration of computer networks. The core concept involves transforming the computationally intensive search problem of identifying a configuration that meets a specific requirement into an approximate objective suitable for learning-based methods. Utilizing this strategy, we developed a neural algorithmic model trained to generate configurations that are likely to fully or partially adhere to a given specification within existing routing protocols. By loosening strict satisfaction guarantees, our method offers (i) enhanced flexibility through protocol-agnosticism, cross-protocol reasoning capabilities, and independence from hardcoded rules, and (ii) the ability to configure significantly larger networks than previously achievable. Our learned synthesizer achieves speeds up to 490 times faster than state-of-the-art SMT-based approaches, while generating configurations that satisfy over 93% of the specified requirements on average.

In type IIA string theory compactified on a Calabi-Yau threefold, the spectrum of BPS states undergoes dramatic jumps across codimension-one walls within the complexified Kähler moduli space, creating a complex chamber structure. The Split Attractor Flow Conjecture suggests that the BPS index $\Omega_z(\gamma)$, defined by a specific charge $\gamma$ and moduli $z$, can be derived from attractor indices $\Omega_*(\gamma_i)$—which count BPS states of charge $\gamma_i$ in their specific attractor chambers—by summing over a finite collection of decorated rooted flow trees. If valid, this framework classifies the BPS spectrum into various topologies of nested bound states, each possessing a simplified chamber arrangement. This work examines the conjecture using the simplest non-compact Calabi-Yau threefold, the canonical bundle over $P^2$. Given that the Kähler moduli space here has a complex dimension of one and attractor flow maintains the argument of the central charge, these flow trees correspond to scattering sequences of rays within a two-dimensional slice of the scattering diagram in the space of stability conditions on the derived category of compactly supported coherent sheaves on $K_{P^2}$. By integrating prior findings on the $K_{P^2}$ scattering diagram in the large volume limit with new data near the orbifold point $\mathbb{C}^3/\mathbb{Z}_3$, we argue that the Split Attractor Flow Conjecture holds for the physical slice of $\Pi$-stability conditions. Specifically, although an infinite set of initial rays exists, related by the auto-equivalence group $\Gamma_1(3)$, only a finite number of decompositions $\gamma=\sum_i\gamma_i$ contribute to the index $\Omega_z(\gamma)$ for any given $\gamma$ and $z$, where the constituent charges $\gamma_i$ are linked to fractional branes at the orbifold point via spectral flow.

This study derives a representation for the value process linked to solutions of FBSDEs within a jump-diffusion framework under multiple probability measures. Driven by specific financial applications, these representations are subsequently utilized to extend the change of numéraire technique, yielding recursive pricing formulas that account for multiple interest rates and collateralization.

Investigating outer halo globular cluster (GC) populations offers valuable insights into galaxy mergers, the accretion of clusters, and their origins. By combining archival Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) data with space-based observations from GALEX, IRAC, and Gaia EDR3, we identified candidate GCs in the M81 group's outer halo for further verification and analysis. We calibrated our selection criteria using a limited sample of previously known GCs, discovering that bright GCs in the M81 group are typically only marginally larger than the Subaru Point Spread Function (PSF). In optical bands, GC colors are barely distinguishable from stars; however, incorporating archival IRAC data significantly enhances color separation. The long-wavelength baseline helps distinguish GCs from stars and clearly separates them from many compact background galaxies. We demonstrate that several GCs previously identified spectroscopically in the M81 group are actually foreground stars or background galaxies. Furthermore, GCs near M82 exhibit radial velocities indicating they fell into the M81 group alongside M82. The overall GC luminosity function of M81 resembles those of the Milky Way and M31. While M81's outer halo GCs share metallicities and numbers with the Milky Way, they are far less numerous than M31's metal-rich outer halo population. These characteristics mirror the distinct merger histories of the three galaxies, underscoring the potential of using outer halo GCs to trace merger events in larger galaxy samples.

We introduce a succinct data structure for permutation graphs and their superclass, circular permutation graphs, which utilizes optimal space up to lower-order terms. In contrast to concurrent research on circle graphs (Acan et al. 2022), our approach additionally enables distance and shortest-path queries, as well as adjacency and neighborhood queries, all with optimal time complexity. Specifically, we offer the first succinct exact distance oracle for (circular) permutation graphs. Additionally, we provide a second succinct structure that supports degree queries in time independent of neighborhood size, incurring an $O(\log n/\log \log n)$ factor overhead across all operations. We also develop a succinct data structure for bipartite permutation graphs. We demonstrate the execution of various algorithms directly on our succinct representations for problems including Clique, Coloring, Independent Set, Hamiltonian Cycle, All-Pair Shortest Paths, and more. Finally, we initiate the study of semi-distributed graph representations, a concept bridging distributed (labeling schemes) and centralized (standard data structures) approaches. We illustrate how to convert certain data structures into semi-distributed forms by storing only $O(n)$ bits of extra global information, thereby bypassing the lower bounds applicable to distance labeling schemes for permutation graphs.

Traditionally, one-dimensional models relying on scaling laws have been employed to parameterize convective heat transfer in the interiors of terrestrial planets such as Earth, Mars, Mercury, and Venus, serving as a computational workaround for the high costs associated with 2D or 3D high-fidelity simulations. However, these approaches are constrained by their limited physical representation (for instance, they cannot account for depth-dependent material properties) and can only forecast mean values, such as the average mantle temperature. We previously demonstrated that feedforward neural networks (FNNs), trained on extensive datasets of 2D simulations, can overcome these constraints and reliably predict the temporal evolution of entire 1D laterally-averaged temperature profiles within complex models. This study extends that methodology to predict the complete 2D temperature field, thereby capturing richer information regarding convection structures like hot plumes and cold downwellings. Utilizing a dataset comprising 10,525 two-dimensional simulations of the thermal evolution of a Mars-like planet's mantle, we demonstrate that deep learning techniques can generate robust parameterized surrogates for the underlying partial differential equations. Specifically, we employ convolutional autoencoders to compress temperature fields by a factor of 142, followed by the use of FNNs and long-short term memory (LSTM) networks to predict these compressed representations. On average, FNN predictions achieve 99.30% accuracy and LSTM predictions reach 99.22% accuracy when compared against unseen simulations. Furthermore, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) analysis of the predictions reveals that, despite a slightly lower mean absolute relative accuracy, LSTMs better capture flow dynamics than FNNs. When aggregated, the POD coefficients derived from FNN and LSTM predictions account for 96.51% and 97.66%, respectively, of the coefficients found in the original simulations.

We introduce a theoretical framework to investigate the nonlinear optical properties of two-dimensional materials featuring a low-energy spectrum defined by strongly tilted, type-II Weyl cones, termed 2D Weyl materials. Our results demonstrate that the tilting of these Weyl cones drives the emergence of even harmonics in the nonlinear signal and induces a pronounced polarization dependence. Furthermore, we explore methods for manipulating this nonlinear response and propose potential applications of 2D Weyl materials in developing innovative photonic sensors.

Various innovative imaging and non-destructive testing methods rely on recovering a spatially varying coefficient within an elliptic partial differential equation using solution data. In practical scenarios, this unknown coefficient is typically modeled as piecewise constant over a specific pixel grid (defining the resolution), with only a limited number of measurements available. This scenario creates an inverse problem involving a finite-dimensional non-linear forward operator $\mathcal F:\ \mathcal D(\mathcal F)\subseteq \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^m$, where computing $\mathcal F$ necessitates solving one or more PDEs. Numerical inversion techniques demand the implementation of both this forward operator and its Jacobian. We demonstrate efficient implementation strategies using standard finite element method (FEM) software and establish the convergence of FEM approximations to their exact counterparts. Additionally, we provide basic example codes utilizing Comsol with the Matlab Livelink package to illustrate numerical challenges stemming from non-uniqueness, non-linearity, and instability. Finally, we examine the monotonicity and convexity characteristics of the forward operator under symmetric measurement configurations.

Modern electron microscopy and spectroscopy serve as pivotal tools for analyzing the structure and composition of quantum and biological materials across both fundamental and applied sciences. However, high-resolution spectroscopic methods and aberration-corrected microscopes are frequently constrained by the relatively broad energy distribution of existing beam sources. While monochromators can mitigate this issue, they typically incur a significant loss in beam current. This study investigates the field emission characteristics of a monocrystalline niobium tip emitter operating at 5.2 K, well beneath its superconducting transition temperature. The fabrication process yields two distinct tip geometries—those with and without an apex nano-protrusion—which profoundly affect the energy distribution of emitted electrons. The configuration lacking a nano-protrusion delivers high beam current and long-term stability with an energy width of approximately 100 meV, a current that can be enhanced by two orders of magnitude through xenon gas adsorption. Additionally, performance was evaluated up to 82 K, demonstrating that an apex nano-protrusion enables energy widths below 40 meV even at liquid nitrogen temperatures. The research further examines spatial and temporal electron-electron correlations under both normal and superconducting conditions and discusses the impact of Nottingham heating. Ultimately, this novel monochromatic source promises to deliver unprecedented accuracy and resolution for electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and high-coherence quantum applications.

Exploratory and discovery-based high-dimensional data analysis relies on three core tasks: dimensionality reduction, clustering, and visualization. When these tasks are executed independently, which is common practice, discrepancies often arise regarding data geometry, leading to potentially misleading or confusing interpretations. To address this, we introduce a novel neural network approach termed Consistent Representation Learning (CRL), designed to handle these three tasks end-to-end while enhancing consistency. The CRL architecture utilizes two nonlinear dimensionality reduction (NLDR) transformations: the first maps input data to a latent feature space optimized for clustering, and the second projects the clustering results into a final 2D or 3D visualization space. Crucially, both NLDR transformations are optimized to strictly adhere to local geometry preserving (LGP) constraints across the network layers, thereby improving data consistency throughout the processing pipeline. Additionally, we propose a new metric, clustering-visualization inconsistency (CVI), to assess these discrepancies. Extensive comparative experiments demonstrate that the proposed CRL method surpasses popular algorithms such as t-SNE and UMAP, as well as other contemporary clustering and visualization techniques, in terms of both evaluation metrics and visual quality.

Stochastic differential equations serve as fundamental models for dynamic environments, where a primary challenge involves designing decision-making policies for systems governed by unknown diffusion processes. The objectives include developing and analyzing efficient strategies to minimize quadratic costs associated with states and actions, as well as accurately estimating the underlying linear dynamics. Although recent progress has been made in statistical decision theory, the estimation and control of diffusion processes remain largely unexplored, which is the central focus of this study. A core difficulty lies in the continuous need to balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off: precise estimation is vital for optimal decisions, yet sub-optimal actions are necessary to gather accurate data.

This work introduces a straightforward reinforcement learning algorithm and provides theoretical performance guarantees demonstrating its ability to effectively resolve this dilemma. Specifically, the proposed method rapidly learns the true diffusion process and optimal actions, ensuring that the per-unit-time cost increase diminishes at a square-root rate as time progresses. Furthermore, we establish rigorous results regarding system stability and define the fundamental limits of sub-optimality arising from uncertainties. To achieve these findings, we develop several novel analytical techniques for matrix perturbations, comparative ratios of stochastic integrals, and the spectral properties of random matrices, alongside proposing a new framework for policy differentiation.

In contemporary multi-core Mixed-Criticality (MC) systems, parallel task execution at maximum frequencies often causes a surge in peak power consumption, particularly during overload conditions, which can trigger thermal problems and compromise both reliability and timeliness. Consequently, managing peak power has become essential for these systems. To address this, we introduce an online heuristic for peak power and thermal management tailored to multi-core MC environments. This approach minimizes peak power consumption during runtime by leveraging dynamic slack and per-cluster Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS). Specifically, the method evaluates multiple tasks in advance to identify the optimal candidate for slack allocation, prioritizing those that most significantly influence system power peaks and temperature. However, adjusting frequencies and selecting appropriate tasks for slack assignment or core re-mapping at runtime can be computationally expensive, potentially leading to deadline violations that are unacceptable for high-criticality tasks. Therefore, we analyze and optimize our runtime scheduler before evaluating it across various platforms. The approach is experimentally verified on the ODROID-XU3, a heterogeneous multi-core platform with DVFS capabilities, using diverse embedded real-time benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that our heuristic reduces system peak power by up to 5.25% and lowers maximum temperature by 20.33% compared to existing methods, while successfully adhering to deadline constraints across different criticality modes.

Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) represent a promising solution for improving coverage and spectral efficiency in both sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies. Current methods to harness IRS benefits typically rely on resource-heavy channel estimation and computationally intensive algorithms for optimizing reflection coefficients. This study focuses on the sub-6 GHz band, introducing and analyzing alternative strategies where IRS phase configurations are randomized and multi-user diversity is utilized to opportunistically select the optimal user for data transmission at any given moment. We demonstrate that the throughput of an IRS-assisted opportunistic communication (OC) system asymptotically approaches the optimal beamforming throughput under fair resource allocation as the user count increases. Additionally, we propose schemes to accelerate the convergence of OC rates to beamforming rates with respect to the number of users. For each proposed approach, we derive the scaling laws of throughput regarding system parameters in the limit of large user numbers. Subsequently, we extend this framework to wideband channels using orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), presenting two OC schemes within an IRS-assisted context that clearly illustrate the superior performance of IRS-aided OC systems compared to conventional ones, achieving these gains at minimal implementation cost and complexity.

We demonstrate that Stanley's Conjecture is valid for the intersection of four monomial prime ideals within a polynomial algebra $S$ over a field, as well as for any intersection of monomial prime ideals $(P_i)_{i\in [s]}$ in $S$, provided that $P_i\not\subset \Sigma_{1=j\not =i}^s P_j$ holds for all $i\in [s]$.

Determining robust indicators for Lyman continuum (LyC) photon escape from galaxies is crucial for estimating escape fractions during the reionisation epoch, where direct LyC flux measurements are unfeasible. This study examines whether prominent C IV $\lambda \lambda 1548,1550$ emission in rest-frame UV spectra signals environments conducive to significant LyC production and escape. We analyzed a sample of 19 star-forming galaxies ($z=3.1-4.6$) from the VANDELS survey with strong C IV emission, constructing a stacked spectrum that reveals all major rest-UV emission lines. Spectral energy distribution modeling, incorporating both stellar and nebular components, indicates requirements for low metallicity ($Z=0.1-0.2\,Z_\odot$), young stellar ages ($\log(\rm{age/yr}) = 6.1-6.5$), a high ionisation parameter ($\log U = -2$), and minimal dust attenuation ($E(B-V)=0.00-0.01$). Nevertheless, these models fail to fully account for the observed strengths of C IV and He II lines. Our results show that the Ly$\alpha$ line in the stacked spectrum is strong and peaks near the systemic velocity, suggesting substantial LyC leakage along the line of sight. Additionally, low covering fractions of low-ionisation interstellar absorption lines imply a LyC escape fraction between $\approx 0.05$ and $0.30$, accompanied by signs of outflowing gas. Furthermore, C IV/C III] ratios exceeding 0.75 in a subset of individual galaxies with reliable detections align with physical conditions favoring significant LyC leakage. In conclusion, we identify multiple spectroscopic indicators of LyC leakage within the stacked spectrum of strong C IV emitters, suggesting that C IV may serve as a vital tracer for LyC photon escape at $z>6$.

Individuals develop perceptions of their interlocutors, whether human or artificial, by interpreting signals within their communication style. Recent studies indicate that the disconnect between user expectations and the actual performance of Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) grows when these stylistic impressions fail to match the system's true capabilities. Consequently, some critics challenge the dominant focus on naturalness, advocating instead for communicative cues that are more representative and contextually appropriate. In fact, certain arguments propose abandoning naturalness as a primary objective in CUI design and interaction. We argue, however, that naturalness does not require abandonment if the goal shifts toward ecologically grounded design. Furthermore, we propose a method to achieve this and urge CUI designers to welcome "incompetence." By allowing systems to express uncertainty and embarrassment through cues that are ecologically valid and prevalent in human interaction, designers can foster more appropriate communication without completely rejecting naturalness.

This paper addresses the general equations $P(\lambda w) = p(w)f(P(w))$ for holomorphic functions $p$ and $f$ by employing infinite compositions. We outline the scenarios where these equations are applicable and evaluate their utility in characterizing the dynamical properties of the orbit $f^{\circ n}(z)$. Furthermore, through a change of variables, we investigate a generalized Abel equation of the form $F(s+1) = u(s)f(F(s))$. This work serves as an extended analysis of our previous research presented in "The Limits of a Family: Of Asymptotic Solutions to the Tetration Equation."

CeCd$_3$As$_3$ represents a rare-earth triangular-lattice antiferromagnet characterized by significant inter-layer spacing. By measuring heat capacity under varying magnetic fields at dilution refrigerator temperatures, we track the evolution of spin-excitation gaps across both antiferromagnetic and paramagnetic regimes. The unique pattern of gap development imposes stringent constraints on the microscopic pseudo-spin model, enabling a precise quantitative reproduction of the observed gap behavior. This analysis offers essential insights into the magnetic state of CeCd$_3$As$_3$, providing definitive confirmation of its stripe order and low-energy model parameters. These findings establish a robust framework for investigating and comprehending the expanding class of rare-earth-based triangular-lattice systems.

This paper investigates the existence and orbital stability of periodic standing wave solutions for the nonlinear fractional Schrödinger (fNLS) equation featuring cubic nonlinearity. Existence is established through a minimizing constrained problem within a complex framework, demonstrating that the associated real solution is invariably positive. Orbital stability is proven by integrating tools related to positive operators, the oscillation theorem for fractional Hill operators, and the Vakhitov-Kolokolov condition, which is well-established for standard Schrödinger equations. Furthermore, a numerical approach utilizing Petviashvili's iteration method is employed to generate these periodic standing wave solutions. Additionally, the Vakhitov-Kolokolov condition is examined numerically for specific values of the fractional derivative order where analytical derivation is not feasible.

We present the public release of data from the FIRE-2 cosmological zoom-in simulations of galaxy formation, accessible at http://flathub.flatironinstitute.org/fire, as part of the Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) project. These simulations feature parsec-scale resolution to explicitly model the multi-phase interstellar medium and incorporate direct models for stellar evolution and feedback mechanisms, including stellar winds, core-collapse and Ia supernovae, radiation pressure, photoionization, and photoelectric heating. We provide complete snapshots from three simulation suites. The first suite includes 20 simulations focusing on 14 Milky Way-mass galaxies, 5 Small/Large Magellanic Cloud-mass galaxies, and 4 lower-mass galaxies (one of which is ultra-faint), with snapshots available at redshifts z = 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. The second suite consists of four more massive galaxies simulated up to z = 1, offering snapshots at z = 1 through 6. The third suite comprises 22 high-redshift simulations at z = 5 and 6. Each simulation also contains numerous resolved lower-mass satellite galaxies within its zoom-in region. The released snapshots include all stored properties for dark matter, gas, and star particles, such as 11 elemental abundances for stars and gas, as well as the formation times (ages) of star particles.
