Additionally, we provide accompanying (sub)halo catalogs containing galaxy properties and member star particles. For simulations extending to z = 0, including all Milky Way-mass galaxies, we offer an "ex-situ" flag for star particles, pointers to track particles across snapshots, catalogs of stellar streams, and multipole basis expansions for halo mass distributions. Finally, we describe several publicly available Python packages designed for reading and analyzing these simulations.

We build a family of non-equivalent Calabi-Yau metrics on $\mathbf{C}^3$ that approach $\mathbf{C} \times A_2$ at infinity, meaning no two metrics in this set can be transformed into one another via scaling or a biholomorphism. This work presents the inaugural instance of such a family of Calabi-Yau metrics sharing a fixed tangent cone at infinity while maintaining a constant underlying complex structure. Furthermore, we suggest an improved version of Székelyhidi's conjecture concerning the classification of these metrics.

We report our recent computation of third-order corrections to semileptonic $b \to c$ decays and muon decay. The calculation was conducted using an expansion around the limit $m_c \sim m_b$, yet it demonstrates reasonable convergence even when $m_c=0$, allowing for the extraction of the muon decay contribution. For the semileptonic $b \to c$ process, we observe substantial perturbative corrections within the on-shell scheme; however, these are markedly diminished by adopting the kinetic scheme for the bottom quark mass. These findings provide essential inputs for the inclusive determination of the Fermi coupling constant $G_F$ and the CKM matrix element $|V_{cb}|$.

This study explores the relationship between inverse problems and final state observability within a broad category of parabolic systems. We extend a stability result concerning initial data, originally established by Garc\'ia and Takahashi [16] for self-adjoint dissipative operators, to systems governed by an analytic semigroup. Assuming final state observability, we derive a logarithmic stability estimate that relies on the semigroup's analyticity angle. This derivation utilizes a general principle of logarithmic convexity. To demonstrate the abstract findings, we apply them to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation.

Although biodegradable metals offer significant benefits for implant design, their uncontrolled degradation and subsequent release pose challenges for practical use. A validated computational model of the degradation process could enable the tuning of implant biodegradation rates through modifications to design properties. This study developed a physicochemical model by deriving a mathematical representation of magnesium biodegradation chemistry and integrating it into a 3D computational framework. Model parameters were calibrated using experimental hydrogen evolution data via a Bayesian optimization routine. Validation was achieved by comparing predicted pH changes in saline and buffered solutions against experimental corrosion test results, revealing a maximum discrepancy of 5%, which confirms the model's reliability for practical applications.

Silicon nanostructures functioning as optical Mie resonators enable the manipulation of light-matter interactions through sophisticated designs compatible with CMOS nanofabrication. By positioning optically active materials, such as monolayers of transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), within the near-field zone of these resonators, significant enhancements can be achieved. In this study, we experimentally confirm, supported by numerical simulations, the coupling between a MoSe2 monolayer and the near-field of dielectric nanoresonators. A comparative analysis of dark-field (DF) scattering spectroscopy and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) reveals that the nanoresonator's near-field amplifies MoSe2 absorption. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the absorption spectrum can be tuned by adjusting the geometry of individual Mie resonators. The presence of the optical near-field is verified by observing a spectral shift between the near-field resonances detected in PLE and the far-field resonances observed in DF scattering. Ultimately, our findings establish that MoSe2 serves as an effective probe for accessing the optical near-field above photonic nanostructures, eliminating the need for sophisticated near-field microscopy setups.

This research investigates the Cooperative Guarding problem within mobile multi-agent systems for polygons containing holes. Starting with a set of agents positioned at a single point inside a polygon defined by $n$ vertices and $h$ holes, the objective is to collaboratively explore the area and arrange themselves so that every location is visible to at least one agent, and the group remains visibly connected. We analyze this problem under two computational models: one where agents can calculate precise distances and angles within their visibility, and another where agents can only compare these values. In the stronger model, we present a deterministic algorithm that achieves a cooperative guard set in $O(n)$ rounds, utilizing no more than $\frac{n + h}{2}$ agents and $O(\log n)$ bits of persistent memory per agent. Conversely, for the weaker model, we offer an algorithm requiring $O(n^4)$ rounds that uses at most $\frac{n+2h}{2}$ agents.

Achieving real-time character animation in dynamic settings demands the creation of realistic upper-body motions, even when encountering non-rigid obstacles like vegetation. We introduce a versatile model for upper-body interactions that anticipates environmental conditions and utilizes antagonistic controllers to adjust muscular stiffness and response times for effective obstacle negotiation. Our approach employs a hybrid animation technique combining keyframe sequences with kinematic constraints and lightweight physics. The dynamic behavior of the character's arms is managed through antagonistic controllers, enabling precise tuning of tension and relaxation without deviating from the reference motion. Furthermore, a procedurally controlled sight model facilitates high-level authoring by allowing the character to adapt its interaction style through variable stiffness and reaction speeds. Results indicate that this real-time method provides explicit control over character behavior and style while seamlessly accommodating new scenarios, making it ideally suited for gaming applications.

We experimentally demonstrate the creation of one-dimensional cold gases of $^{87}$Rb atoms using diffuse laser cooling (DLC). The experiment utilizes a horizontal, slender vacuum glass tube measuring 105~cm in length and 2~cm in diameter. Inside this tube, diffuse laser light is produced through the multi-reflection of injected beams to cool the background vapor atoms. Using 250~mW of cooling light and 50~mW of repumping light, we achieve an evenly distributed atom cloud profile spanning one meter. For a typical cooling period of 170~ms, we observe a fourfold increase in atomic optical depth (OD) alongside a sub-Doppler temperature of 25~$\mu$k. Furthermore, the maximum count of detected cold atoms remains stable over a free-fall duration of 30~ms. These samples are well-suited for various quantum optical investigations, including those involving electromagnetically induced transparency, highly excited (Rydberg) atoms, and quantum precision measurements.

We introduce a novel machine learning approach to solve channel acquisition challenges at the base station within frequency division duplex systems. In this framework, the base station reconstructs complete downlink channel state information using only limited feedback from the mobile terminal. This recovery process relies on a convolutional neural network trained solely on uplink frequency domain channel samples, eliminating the need for any downlink training data collection. Following a comprehensive presentation and performance analysis of the method, we validate the central "transfer learning" assumption of the network through an analysis utilizing the maximum mean discrepancy metric.

End-to-end encrypted (E2EE) messaging serves as a crucial initial defense against increasingly invasive privacy laws, yet it remains susceptible to compelled key disclosure through coercion or device compromise. This paper presents Wink, the first plausibly-deniable messaging system that safeguards message confidentiality even when users are forced to surrender their keys or passwords. Wink achieves this by covertly embedding hidden messages within the standard random values (such as salts and IVs) utilized by current E2EE protocols. This process occurs as part of legitimate cryptographic operations executed within widely adopted trusted execution environments (TEEs) like TrustZone. Consequently, Wink enables powerful, untraceable hidden communication with virtually no changes to existing E2EE applications, while maintaining strong plausible deniability. Demonstrations with multiple established E2EE platforms, including Telegram and Signal, show that Wink operates with minimal external instrumentation, negligible performance overhead, and, most importantly, without altering on-wire message formats.

The kagome lattice metal AV$_3$Sb$_5$ family (where A = K, Rb, Cs) has garnered significant interest due to its superconductivity, charge density wave (CDW) behavior, and unique characteristics arising from a topologically nontrivial electronic structure. Using time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy, we demonstrate that the relaxation dynamics of excited quasiparticles align with the formation of an energy gap below the phase transition, resembling a conventional second-order CDW condensate. In contrast, the associated structural transformation is primarily a first-order phase transition. Additionally, no CDW amplitude mode was detected within the ordered phase. These findings indicate that the CDW order in this system differs substantially from traditional CDW condensates. Furthermore, we observe that a weak pump pulse can non-thermally melt the CDW order, driving the sample into its high-temperature phase, which suggests that the lattice potential differences between these phases are minimal.

This study re-examines the partial information optimal control problem introduced by Wang, Wu, and Xiong [Wang et al 2013], in which the system dynamics are governed by a controlled forward-backward stochastic differential equation featuring correlated noises between the system and the observation. Using a unified approach, we derive both a necessary condition and a sufficient condition (formulated as a verification theorem) for optimality in this specific type of partial information problem. Furthermore, we enhance the $L^p$-bounds on the control from $L^8$, as reported in [Wang et al 2013], to $L^4$ in this work.

We demonstrate the existence of five classes of planar curves whose arrangements of translates are combinatorially equivalent to line arrangements. These curves enable the definition of norms that facilitate constructions featuring numerous unit distances between points in the plane.

We introduce probabilistic task modelling, a generative probabilistic framework designed for collections of tasks within meta-learning contexts. This model integrates variational auto-encoding with latent Dirichlet allocation to represent each task as a Gaussian mixture distribution within an embedding space, thereby offering an explicit depiction of tasks via their task-theme mixtures. We develop an efficient inference approximation using variational methods for empirical Bayes parameter estimation. Empirical evaluations validate the generated task uncertainty and distances by analyzing correlation diagrams of prediction accuracy on test tasks. Furthermore, we conduct task selection experiments in meta-learning to illustrate how the inferred task relatedness enhances the performance of meta-learning algorithms.

Multivariate functional data can exhibit intrinsic multivariate characteristics, such as movement trajectories in two dimensions, or complementary relationships, like concurrent measurements of precipitation, temperature, and wind speed at a specific weather station. We introduce the multivariate functional additive mixed model (multiFAMM) and demonstrate its utility across both data types through case studies in sports science (snooker player movement paths) and phonetic science (acoustic signals and consonant articulation). This framework accommodates both linear and nonlinear covariate effects and utilizes multivariate functional principal component analysis to model dependencies among response dimensions. Multivariate functional random intercepts account for auto-correlation within individual functions and cross-correlations between multivariate dimensions, while also capturing between-function correlations arising from repeated measures or crossed study designs. By modeling these dimensional dependencies, the approach provides deeper insights into the multivariate functional process, enhances random effects estimation, and produces corrected confidence intervals for covariate effects. Extensive simulations reveal that this multivariate strategy is more parsimonious than fitting separate univariate models while sustaining or improving overall model fit.

Massive stars that lose their hydrogen envelopes via binary interactions or stellar winds manifest as either Wolf-Rayet stars, characterized by optically thick winds, or as transparent-wind stripped-envelope stars. We simulate their evolution using single helium star models, generating detailed grids for initial masses between 1.5 and 70 $M_{\odot}$ across metallicities of 0.01 to 0.04, spanning the period from core helium ignition to collapse. Throughout their lives, certain models reveal helium-burning byproducts. We suggest that models displaying nitrogen-rich envelopes represent candidate WN stars during core helium burning, whereas those with carbon-rich surfaces correspond to WC stars during this phase and WO stars thereafter. Our analysis quantifies the metallicity dependence of total lifetimes and the duration of specific evolutionary stages. We introduce an analytic method to estimate wind optical depth for distinguishing between Wolf-Rayet and transparent-wind stripped-envelope stars, revealing that the luminosity ranges for WN, WC, and WO stars are heavily dependent on metallicity. Our results indicate that all carbon-rich models in our grids possess optically thick winds and align with the observed luminosity distributions. By constructing population models, we predict the counts of both transparent-wind stripped-envelope stars and Wolf-Rayet stars and determine their ratios at various metallicities. We observe that increasing metallicity reduces the population of transparent-wind stripped-envelope stars while boosting the number of Wolf-Rayet stars, making WC and WO types more prevalent at high metallicities. When applying these population models to nearby galaxies, we find that stellar populations are more sensitive to the transition luminosity between Wolf-Rayet stars and transparent-wind helium stars than to metallicity-dependent mass loss rates.

Current weak lensing surveys derive constraints on cosmological parameters primarily from two-point statistics, which are statistically sub-optimal even for Gaussian fields. We evaluate a novel, rapid implementation of the Quadratic Maximum Likelihood (QML) estimator—known to be optimal for Gaussian fields—to assess Pseudo-Cl estimators and quantify the benefits of adopting a more optimal approach. Utilizing realistic survey geometries, noise profiles, and power spectra, we observe that the QML estimator reduces errors in recovered E-mode spectra by approximately 20% on the largest angular scales compared to the Pseudo-Cl estimator, while also yielding significant error reductions for B-modes. These findings enhance the potential for constraining new physics via improved B-mode sensitivity in upcoming surveys. Our QML method employs a new implementation featuring conjugate-gradient and finite-difference differentiation techniques, representing the most efficient full-sky QML estimator to date and enabling the processing of map resolutions that are currently computationally prohibitive. Additionally, we examine the impacts of apodization, B-mode purification, and non-Gaussian map usage on estimator statistical properties. The publicly available QML implementation can be accessed via GitHub.

Document images captured by cameras frequently exhibit geometric and perspective distortions, which not only compromise visual appeal but also degrade the performance of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems. While recent learning-based approaches prioritize accurate cropping, they often fall short in handling real-world scenarios, such as documents with extensive margins or those lacking margins entirely. The presence of large margins makes precise manual cropping difficult for users, while dewarping marginless images remains an unsolved challenge. Consequently, no existing pipeline fully and effectively rectifies wild-captured document images. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Marior (Margin Removal and Iterative Content Rectification), a novel method employing a progressive, coarse-to-fine strategy to enhance dewarping quality and readability. The approach consists of two key modules: a Margin Removal Module (MRM) and an Iterative Content Rectification Module (ICRM). Initially, the MRM predicts a segmentation mask to eliminate margins, yielding a preliminary output. Subsequently, the ICRM refines the image by generating dense displacement flows for content-aware rectification, with the number of refinement iterations determined adaptively. Experimental results on public benchmarks confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. The project resources are accessible at https://github.com/ZZZHANG-jx/Marior for further evaluation.

Drones are increasingly being deployed in safety-critical scenarios where they must operate near evolving human agents, necessitating robust collision avoidance through the fusion of multiple sensing modalities. While current drone-based people detection relies almost exclusively on standard cameras—with some recent efforts combining imaging and event-based cameras—radar systems offer superior resilience to environmental conditions. However, radars lack standalone completeness and have primarily been studied in automotive settings rather than for drones. To address this gap, we introduce KUL-UAVSAFE, the first dataset designed to study safety-critical people detection for drones by enabling the fusion of radars with both event-based and standard cameras. Furthermore, we propose a baseline CNN architecture featuring cross-fusion highways and a curriculum learning strategy named SAUL for multi-modal data. SAUL significantly boosts system robustness against difficult RGB failures, achieving a 15% improvement in peak F1 score over the previously proposed BlackIn cross-fusion network. We validate the approach's real-time performance and feasibility through implementation on an edge-computing unit and have made the dataset and supplementary materials available on our project website.

This paper extends the framework introduced by Gour and Tomamichel concerning the extension of monotones within resource theories. In such theories, a monotone assigns a real value to each resource, representing its utility or worth. While Gour and Tomamichel addressed extending monotones via set-theoretic methods when a resource theory fully and faithfully embeds into a larger one, we generalize this problem to scenarios involving functorial transformations between theories rather than simple inclusions. We demonstrate that (point-wise) Kan extensions offer a precise categorical structure for describing and calculating these monotone extensions. To establish this, we introduce partitioned categories (pCat) as a formalism for resource theories and pCat functors to capture relationships between them. We define monotones as pCat functors mapping into $([0,\infty], \leq)$ and utilize Kan extensions to extend them along any pCat functor. The utility of our approach is illustrated by applying it to extend entanglement monotones from bipartite pure states to mixed states, adapt classical divergences to the quantum domain, and transfer a non-uniformity monotone from classical probabilistic theory to quantum theory.

This study presents the highest spatial resolution measurement of magnetic fields in M17, achieved through thermal dust polarization data from SOFIA/HAWC+ at a 154 $\mu$m wavelength. Applying the Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi method, we detected strong magnetic fields of $980 \pm 230\;\mu$G in the lower-density M17-N region and $1665 \pm 885\;\mu$G in the higher-density M17-S region. In M17-N, the magnetic field morphology resembles that of gravitational collapse cores, whereas in M17-S, fields orient perpendicular to the matter structure, forming a pillar and an asymmetric hourglass shape. Calculated Alfv\'enic Mach numbers ($\mathcal{M_A}$) for both regions are sub-Alfv\'enic, indicating that magnetic fields dominate turbulence. The mass-to-flux ratios ($\lambda$) were determined to be 0.07 for M17-N and 0.28 for M17-S; these sub-critical values align with the observed absence of massive star formation in M17. Regarding dust physics, we examined the correlations between dust polarization fraction ($p$) and thermal emission intensity ($I$), gas column density ($N({\rm H_2})$), and dust temperature ($T_{\rm d}$). The polarization fraction declines with intensity following an $I^{-\alpha}$ relationship where $\alpha = 0.51$. It also decreases as $N(\rm H_{2})$ increases, likely due to reduced grain alignment via radiative torques (RATs) in denser, lower-radiation environments and/or magnetic field tangling. Furthermore, the polarization fraction initially rises with $T_{\rm d}$ before dropping when $T_{\rm d} > 50$ K. This trend, observed in M17-N where gas density varies slowly with temperature, supports the RAT disruption hypothesis.

SN 2017jgh, a type IIb supernova, was identified by Pan-STARRS during the Kepler/K2 C16/C17 observing campaigns. This study details both ground-based and Kepler/K2 data for SN 2017jgh, which recorded the shock breakout cooling phase with exceptional temporal resolution. This event offers a singular chance to examine the origins of stripped-envelope supernovae. Analytical modeling of the SN 2017jgh lightcurve indicates the progenitor was likely a yellow supergiant with an envelope radius of approximately 50–290 $R_{\odot}$ and a mass of 0–1.7 $M_{\odot}$, exhibiting a shock velocity of roughly 7,500–10,300 km s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we analyze how early observations of the lightcurve's rise inform progenitor constraints. When fitting only ground-based data, the derived envelope radius ranges from 50–330 $R_{\odot}$, mass from 0.3–1.7 $M_{\odot}$, and shock velocity from 9,000–15,000 km s$^{-1}$. However, without the rise phase, the explosion time remains poorly constrained, causing systematic shifts in velocity estimates and increased uncertainties in mass and radius. Consequently, progenitor property estimates derived from such models may harbor larger systematic errors than previously acknowledged.
We offer an explicit presentation for the automorphism group of an edge-separated CLTTF Artin group.

This study examines ${\cal N}=2\, SU(N_c)$ or $U(N_c)$ SQCD models containing $N_F<2N_c-1$ quark flavors of equal mass. The ${\cal N}=2$ supersymmetry is softly reduced to ${\cal N}=1$ via a mass term $\mu_{\rm x}{\rm Tr}\,(X^2)$ associated with the colored adjoint scalar partners of gluons, where $\mu_{\rm x}\ll\Lambda_2$ ($\Lambda_2$ denotes the $SU(N_c)$ gauge coupling scale). These theories exhibit a vast array of vacua, characterized by either unbroken or spontaneously broken global flavor symmetries, such as $U(N_F)\rightarrow U({\rm n}_1)\times U({\rm n}_2)$. This paper focuses on a significant subset of these vacua where a non-trivial discrete symmetry $Z_{2N_c-N_F\geq 2}$ remains unbroken, exploring various hierarchies among the Lagrangian parameters $m$ and $\mu_{\rm x}$ relative to $\Lambda_2$. The low-energy Lagrangian forms, charges of light particles, and mass spectra for these vacua are detailed in the main text.

Power corrections to the leading terms of low-energy quark and dyon condensates are calculated in two appendices. These results align with independent calculations of the same condensates derived from the roots of the Seiberg-Witten spectral curve, presented within those same appendices. This concordance non-trivially validates the internal self-consistency of the proposed approach.

Our findings differ substantially from recent related works by M. Shifman and A. Yung (e.g., arXiv:1304.0822, arXiv:1403.6086, arXiv:1704.06201) and their earlier publications on this topic; the reasons for these discrepancies are explained in the text. For further critique of certain results by these authors, see section 8 of arXiv:1308.5863.

We introduce the South Galactic Pole (SGP) data release from the GaLactic and Extragalactic All-sky Murchison Widefield Array (GLEAM) survey. This dataset integrates two years of MWA observations spanning 72–231 MHz, covering a 5,113 $\mathrm{deg}^2$ region centered on the SGP (defined by 20$^\mathrm{h}$40$^\mathrm{m}$ < RA < 05$^\mathrm{h}$04$^\mathrm{m}$ and $-48\deg$ < Dec < $-2\deg$). At a frequency of 216 MHz, the typical rms noise reaches approximately 5 mJy/beam with an angular resolution of roughly 2 arcmin. The resulting source catalogue lists 108,851 components exceeding the $5\sigma$ threshold, with 77% possessing measured spectral indices across the 72–231 MHz range. Enhancements in this release include utilizing the GLEAM Extragalactic catalogue as a sky model for calibration, implementing a more efficient and automated deconvolution algorithm for snapshot images, and applying a more precise primary beam model for flux scale correction. Consequently, this data release facilitates more sensitive large-scale investigations of extragalactic source populations and enables spectral variability studies over a one-year timescale.

Data analysis, particularly for frequently updated or real-time datasets, relies on three synchronized pillars: defining inference objectives, computing those objectives, and interpreting the results through drill-down or visualization. While research heavily emphasizes the first two steps, deriving actionable insights from the results remains challenging. Visualization bridges this gap, enabling both experts and non-experts to comprehend data and determine necessary actions. For instance, during the Covid-19 pandemic, identifying regions likely to experience case spikes allows for timely interventions regarding gatherings and business hours. This paper introduces an extensible architecture for visualizing both raw and analyzed data, proposing a modular dashboard that handles user interaction, visualization management, and complex base data analysis. Its key contributions are: (i) an extensible architecture that allows adding new analyses, visualizations, and interactions without disrupting the workflow; (ii) decoupled functional modules to accelerate and simplify development across different teams; and (iii) improved efficiency to reduce display response times. Utilizing Multilayer Networks (MLNs) for analysis, the paper demonstrates these concepts through the CoWiz++ (Covid Wizard) dashboard, detailing how web-based user interfaces and display components seamlessly connect with backend modules.

This paper introduces the putEMG dataset, designed for assessing sEMG-based hand gesture recognition techniques. Collected from 44 able-bodied participants, the dataset covers eight gestures (three full hand gestures, four pinches, and idle). It comprises continuous recordings of 24 sEMG channels from the forearm, alongside RGB video and depth camera images for hand motion tracking. Additionally, example processing scripts are provided. The putEMG dataset is accessible under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) license at https://www.biolab.put.poznan.pl/putemg-dataset/. Validation was conducted regarding sEMG amplitudes and gesture recognition performance, utilizing state-of-the-art classifiers and feature sets. An accuracy of 90% was attained with an SVM classifier using RMS features and an LDA classifier employing Hudgin's and Du's feature sets. Performance analysis revealed that the LDA/Du combination yields significantly higher accuracy for full hand gestures, whereas SVM/RMS performs better for pinch gestures. This dataset serves as a benchmark for various classification methods, the evaluation of electrode localization concepts, and the development of classification approaches invariant to user-specific characteristics or electrode displacement.

We present a timing analysis of coordinated three-day observations of Sagittarius A* using near-infrared (NIR), X-ray, and sub-millimeter (submm) data. Observations were conducted at 4.5 microns via Spitzer, 2-8 keV via Chandra, 3-70 keV via NuSTAR, 340 GHz via ALMA, and 2.2 microns via the GRAVITY instrument on the VLTI. Two dates exhibited moderate variability without significant submm-to-infrared lags at 99% confidence. On July 18, a moderately bright NIR flare (F_K ~ 15 mJy) coincided with an X-ray flare (F ~ 0.1 cts/s), which likely preceded a bright submm flux (F ~ 5.5 Jy) by approximately +34 (+14 -33) minutes at 99% confidence; this lag uncertainty is primarily due to missing the submm peak. A model involving a synchrotron source cooling via adiabatic expansion can explain the submm rise after the synchrotron-self-Compton NIR and X-ray peaks fade. This scenario predicts high GHz and THz fluxes during the NIR/X-ray peak and electron densities exceeding those expected from average Sgr A* accretion rates, though these higher densities align with the hypothesis that 2019 was an epoch of heightened accretion. However, since the NIR and X-ray peaks can also be modeled by a non-thermal synchrotron source with lower electron densities, we cannot exclude the possibility that the bright submm flare was an unrelated chance coincidence with the NIR/X-ray emission.

This study employs Gaussian mixture modeling to analyze the Milky Way's stellar halo within angular momentum space. By applying this method to a dataset of 5,389 stars near the Sagittarius (Sgr) stream plane, utilizing full 6D phase-space coordinates from Gaia EDR3 and SEGUE, four distinct dynamical components are identified. The largest and most numerous component represents the `smooth' Milky Way halo, while the smallest and faintest comprises 40 stars from the Orphan stream. A component characterized by minimal or zero angular momentum is likely linked to the GSE substructure. Additionally, the analysis identifies 925 stars and 7 globular clusters with greater than 90% probability of being Sgr stream members. Comparisons with $N$-body simulations indicate that some of these members trace the extensions of the leading and trailing tails in the Southern and Northern hemispheres, respectively. These new detections cover approximately 800° across the sky, effectively wrapping around the Galaxy twice.

Left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (LAAC) serves as a minimally invasive, implant-based strategy to mitigate stroke risk in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Accurate assessment of the LAA orifice via preoperative CT angiography is essential for selecting the correct implant size and optimizing C-arm angulation. However, precise orifice localization remains challenging due to significant anatomical variability and the difficulty of determining the orifice's position and orientation within standard CT views. Furthermore, existing deep localization models often struggle with high error rates because the minute size of the orifice contrasts sharply with the extensive scope of CT images. To address this, we introduce a centerline depth-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed for effective orifice localization within a constrained search space. In this approach, an RL agent utilizes centerline-to-surface distance metrics to navigate the LAA centerline toward the orifice, thereby substantially narrowing the search area and enhancing localization precision. Experimental results across 98 CT scans demonstrate that this formulation achieves high accuracy comparable to expert annotations. Additionally, the localization process requires approximately 8 seconds, representing an 18-fold improvement in efficiency over current methods. Consequently, this approach offers a valuable tool to assist physicians in preprocedural planning for LAAC.

We investigate lepton flavor universality violation (LFV) in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition within an R-parity violating supersymmetric (RPV-SUSY) framework. The recent LHCb update on $R_K$ indicates an approximate $3.1\sigma$ discrepancy from Standard Model expectations, thereby reinforcing the hypothesis of new physics driving LFV. Our study demonstrates that the $R_{K^{(*)}}$ anomaly can be resolved exclusively through sneutrino contributions under R-parity violating interactions, provided that the coupling constants remain within phenomenologically viable ranges.

This discussion examines two types of semantics pertinent to Computer Vision (CV) systems: Visual Semantics and Lexical Semantics. Visual semantics address how humans form concepts of a target reality through visual perception, whereas lexical semantics concern concept formation via language regarding the same reality. The discrepancy between these two forms of semantics significantly affects CV systems, manifesting as the Semantic Gap Problem (SGP). While the paper illustrates this misalignment with numerous examples, it also proposes a general, domain-independent methodology designed to align visual and lexical semantics.

For elliptic curves possessing complex multiplication over a number field, the $p^{\infty}$--Selmer rank is even for every prime $p$. While \v{C}esnavi\v{c}ius established this by utilizing the existence of a $p$-isogeny when $p$ splits in the complex multiplication field and relying on his prior proofs of the $p$-parity conjecture, we offer a distinct proof that bypasses the $p$-parity assumption. Furthermore, we extend this finding to principally polarised abelian varieties with complex multiplication.

Despite containing vast world knowledge, pretrained language models (PTLMs) often generate contradictory responses when queried, even following specialized training. This inconsistency obscures the model's actual "beliefs" and predisposes it to simple errors. To address this, we propose integrating a PTLM into a larger system featuring an evolving, symbolic BeliefBank that logs and potentially adjusts raw PTLM outputs. We introduce two mechanisms to enhance belief consistency: first, a reasoning module utilizing a weighted MaxSAT solver to revise beliefs that conflict significantly with existing ones; and second, a feedback component that directs future PTLM queries by incorporating known beliefs as context. In controlled experiments, these mechanisms demonstrated improved consistency within the system, boosting both answer accuracy and stability over time. This approach represents a foundational step toward PTLM architectures with a systematic understanding of belief, allowing them to build a more coherent worldview and self-improve without requiring model retraining.

We present Metatheory.jl, a lightweight and high-performance general-purpose framework for symbolics and metaprogramming designed to streamline the creation of complex Julia metaprograms. It significantly advances Julia by incorporating a native term rewriting system grounded in state-of-the-art equality saturation, alongside a dynamic, first-class AST pattern matching system that supports algebraic composition and fully leverages the language's robust reflection capabilities. This contribution enables general-purpose symbolic mathematics, including manipulation, optimization, synthesis, and analysis of syntactically valid Julia expressions through a clean and concise interface, functioning effectively during both compilation and execution.

This paper explores the application of artificial and computational intelligence within game research to facilitate physical therapy. We present an overview of preliminary research utilizing motion sensors and virtual reality equipment to rehabilitate motor impairments commonly associated with traumatic brain injury patients. Furthermore, we emphasize how advancements in procedural content generation and player modeling can drive progress in this field by enhancing the quality of rehabilitation programs and enabling precise measurement of patient performance.

This work investigates recent proposals utilizing a "wormhole paradigm" for black holes, which posit that semiclassical low-energy dynamics emerges at the horizon within certain effective variables. We establish the "effective small corrections theorem" to demonstrate that this horizon behavior is incompatible with the requirement that a black hole radiate thermally, akin to a piece of coal, when observed from the outside. Consequently, this theorem solidifies the necessity of nonlocality linking the black hole to its distant radiation within these proposals. To illustrate various nonlocality mechanisms, we construct simple bit models; in every instance, we encounter either nonunitary evolution in the black hole interior or a nonlocal Hamiltonian interaction between the hole and infinity—an interaction absent in the case of burning coal. Furthermore, we analyze recent arguments regarding the Page curve, noting that the quantity purported to follow the curve of a normal body is not entanglement entropy but a distinct measure. While some suggest this substitution stems from gravity's topology change generating replica wormholes, our examination of topology change in quantum gravity reveals no source of connections between different replica copies in the path integral for Rényi entropy. Finally, we contrast the wormhole paradigm with the fuzzball paradigm, where the fuzzball does radiate like coal. Similar to coal, the fuzzball lacks low-energy semiclassical dynamics at its surface at energies $E \sim T$; although effective dynamics at $E \gg T$ might exist under fuzzball complementarity, such high-energy modes are irrelevant to the Page curve or the information paradox.

Using recent STAR Collaboration data from $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV, we analyze the ratio of second-order cumulants for baryon number and electric charge. The baryon number cumulant is derived from the proton number distribution, with corrections applied for finite acceptance effects on transverse momentum under the assumption of independent particle emission. Our findings reveal that this ratio varies with the rapidity window. Comparing our results to hadron resonance gas models and lattice QCD simulations indicates that, should these fluctuations originate from a thermal medium, its temperature would be substantially below the chemical freezeout temperature.

The interaction of two-color femtosecond laser pulses with matter enables electron emission via multiple multiphoton excitation routes, where quantum interference among these pathways produces pronounced oscillations in the photoemitted current, quantified by visibility. This study presents two-color visibility spectroscopy for multiphoton photoemission originating from a solid-state nanoemitter. We examine the visibility of quantum pathway interference across an extensive wavelength range spanning nearly an octave, covering both the fundamental femtosecond pulses and their second-harmonic. The observed photoemission exhibits a remarkably stable high visibility of 90% ± 5%. Additionally, adjusting the relative intensity ratio between the two colors allows us to tune the visibility from 0 up to nearly 100%. A straightforward yet insightful theoretical model successfully explains all experimental findings with excellent quantitative agreement. We anticipate that these results will be universally applicable to diverse forms of photo-driven quantum interference, offering potential for quantum control in physics, chemistry, and quantum engineering.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art results across numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) benchmarks, driving the development of increasingly larger and complex architectures. However, constructing new models is often suboptimal due to associated costs, time constraints, and environmental consequences. As an alternative, we investigate whether reformulating data to align with model strengths can make questions easier to answer. Specifically, we examine if humans can break down complex queries into simpler components that models can solve more effectively. Our analysis of diverse reasoning datasets confirms that decomposition significantly enhances model performance—yielding a 24% improvement for GPT-3 and a 29% gain for RoBERTa-SQuAD combined with a symbolic calculator. This approach offers a meaningful way to integrate human expertise into NLP research. Our findings suggest that Human-in-the-loop Question Decomposition (HQD) provides a viable alternative pathway to advancing large language models. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/Pruthvi98/QuestionDecomposition.

This work introduces a novel Weighted Average model grounded in the Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework to enhance the resilience of Federated Learning (FL) against poisoned, corrupted, or outdated local models. Such threats, combined with the non-IID characteristics of data, can significantly degrade FL accuracy. The proposed MoE-FL architecture leverages trust between users and the server, where users contribute a subset of their public datasets to the server. The server then employs a robust aggregation technique—either by solving an optimization problem or using the Softmax method—to identify outliers and mitigate their negative impact on the FL process. Experimental results demonstrate that MoE-FL surpasses traditional aggregation methods when dealing with high rates of attacker-induced poisoned data.

On March 4, 2021, at 09:00 UTC, the 30-meter near-Earth asteroid 2021 DW1 flew past Earth at a distance of 570,000 km, peaking at a brightness of V=14.6 mag. Photometric observations were conducted from March 2 (V=16.5 mag) through March 7 (V=18.2 mag), during which the object traversed a 170-degree arc in the northern sky with solar phase angles ranging from 36 to 86 degrees. These conditions provided an ideal opportunity for physical characterization, specifically for determining the spin axis and shape. Convex inversion of the lightcurves yielded a sidereal rotation period of P=0.013760 ± 0.000001 hours and two possible solutions for the spin axis ecliptic coordinates: (A) λ₁=57 ± 10, β₁=29 ± 10, and (B) λ₂=67 ± 10, β₂=-40 ± 10. The magnitude-phase relationship was modeled using a standard H, G function with H=24.8 ± 0.5 mag (assuming G=0.24). Color indices were measured as g-i=0.79 ± 0.01 mag and i-z=0.01 ± 0.02 mag, indicating an S taxonomic class and a geometric albedo of p_V=0.23 ± 0.02. Based on H and p_V, the effective diameter is calculated as D=30 ± 10 m. Additionally, the spin axis inclination relative to the orbital plane (obliquity) was found to be non-perpendicular, with values of ε=54 ± 10 or ε=123 ± 10. Further determination of spin axes for Very Small Asteroids (VSAs) is necessary to ascertain whether 2021 DW1 represents an exception or a typical case.

Current state-of-the-art 3D models face limitations in understanding due to datasets characterized by scarce annotations and a fixed set of categories. While recent 2D advancements have mitigated similar issues by incorporating knowledge from other modalities, such as language, the potential of leveraging multimodal information for 3D understanding remains underexplored, particularly in data-scarce scenarios. To address this, we present ULIP, a framework that learns a unified representation of images, text, and 3D point clouds through pre-training on object triplets across these three modalities. To tackle the scarcity of available triplets, ULIP utilizes a pre-trained vision-language model that already operates within a shared visual-textual space derived from extensive image-text pairs. Subsequently, ULIP aligns a 3D representation space with this common image-text space using a limited set of automatically synthesized triplets. The method is backbone-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into any 3D architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that ULIP significantly enhances multiple recent 3D backbones by pre-training them on ShapeNet55, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both standard and zero-shot 3D classification tasks on ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN. Specifically, ULIP improves PointMLP's 3D classification accuracy on ScanObjectNN by approximately 3% and surpasses PointCLIP by 28.8% in top-1 accuracy for zero-shot classification on ModelNet40. Our code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available.

Bergman tau functions are utilized to investigate the Picard group of moduli spaces for quadratic differentials featuring at most $n$ simple poles on genus $g$ complex algebraic curves, thereby extending our earlier findings concerning moduli spaces of holomorphic quadratic differentials.

A crucial parameter in the theory of hot accretion flows around black holes is $\delta$, representing the portion of "viscously" dissipated energy that directly heats electrons. For a specific mass accretion rate, the radiative efficiency of such a flow is governed by $\delta$, yet determining its value from first principles remains difficult. Recent results from the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (EHTC) on M87* and Sgr A* offer an alternative approach to constrain $\delta$. By integrating the EHTC-estimated mass accretion rates for these two sources with their measured bolometric luminosities, we establish robust constraints on their respective radiative efficiencies. Simultaneously, we employ a theoretical model of hot magnetically arrested disks (MAD) to compute the expected radiative efficiency as a function of $\delta$ and accretion rate. Comparing the EHTC-derived efficiencies with predictions from MAD models indicates that Sgr A* requires $\delta \ga 0.3$, with $\delta \sim 0.5$ being the most probable value. Conversely, applying the same comparison to M87* yields inconclusive results due to significant uncertainties in the accretion rate for that source.

The first-order correction to the one-form sector in three-dimensional higher-spin theory is obtained from the generating nonlinear system using the shifted homotopy method. A set of solutions to this generating system is identified that separates the equations for dynamical and topological fields at the first order of perturbation theory. It is demonstrated that this set of solutions belongs to a distinct cohomology class compared to the solution previously obtained via direct methods. Furthermore, this cohomology is shown to correspond to the one underlying the mass deformation within the matter sector of three-dimensional higher-spin equations.

Let $\Omega$ be an $m$-hyperconvex domain within $\mathbb{C}^n$, and let $\beta$ denote the standard Kähler form on $\mathbb{C}^n$. We define finite energy classes of $m$-subharmonic functions of Cegrell type, specifically $\mathcal{E}_m^p$ for $p>0$ and $\mathcal{F}_m$. Employing a variational approach, we demonstrate that the degenerate complex Hessian equation $(dd^c\varphi)^m\wedge \beta^{n-m}=\mu$ admits a unique solution in $\mathcal{E}_m^1$ if and only if every function within $\mathcal{E}_m^1$ is integrable with respect to $\mu$. Furthermore, provided that $\mu$ possesses finite total mass and does not charge $m$-polar sets, the equation yields a unique solution in $\mathcal{F}_m$.

The two-pass information bottleneck (TPIB) speaker diarization system functions independently on each conversational recording, failing to utilize discriminative speaker information learned from prior tasks. Consequently, the system exhibits a high real-time factor (RTF) due to the extensive training time required by its artificial neural network (ANN). This paper proposes an incremental transfer learning strategy to enhance the TPIB system's RTF; instead of training the ANN from scratch for new conversations, it updates parameters previously learned from other conversations. This approach yields a significant reduction in RTF. Evaluated on standard NIST and AMI conversational meeting datasets, the proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness against baseline IB and TPIB systems. Although there is a slight performance drop, the system achieves substantial RTF improvements of 33.07% and 24.45% over the TPIB baseline on the NIST RT-04Eval and AMI-1 datasets, respectively.

Session types provide a type-driven approach to enforcing communication protocols in distributed programming. Building on our prior formalization of simple session types within a multi-threaded $\lambda$-calculus featuring linear types, this work introduces a variant of dependent session types inspired by DML. Our formulated type system ensures linearity and duality without requiring runtime checks or specialized encodings. This is the first formulation of its kind for dependent session types, making it highly suitable for practical implementation. As a demonstration, we present an implementation written in ATS that compiles to an Erlang/Elixir backend.

We introduce an algorithm designed to solve the "cocktail party problem"—separating multiple simultaneous speakers using a single microphone—by employing a deep recurrent neural network. This network performs regression into a vector space that captures the characteristics of independent speakers. The space is optimized by distinguishing between speaker masks and incorporates empirically derived speaker traits, a technique we term source-contrastive estimation. Drawing inspiration from negative sampling in natural language processing, our method learns embeddings by correlating and de-correlating input vectors with output weights. Although the output weight matrix relies on a known set of speakers, inference utilizes only input vectors, ensuring the separation process remains explicitly speaker-independent. While our approach shares similarities with recent deep neural network research on clustering and permutation-invariant training—specifically using weighted spectral features and masks to isolate individual speaker frequencies while filtering others—we avoid the heavy computational costs associated with other methods. Furthermore, by training a dedicated vector space rather than speaker combinations or differences, we circumvent the permutation problem typically encountered during training. Ultimately, our algorithm provides an intuitive and computationally efficient solution to the cocktail party problem, demonstrating superior empirical performance compared to existing techniques.

As part of the GRAVITY$^{+}$ initiative, the VLTI and its near-infrared beam combiner, GRAVITY, are currently undergoing major upgrades designed to enhance sky coverage and overall performance. These instrumental improvements are transformative, uniquely enabling GRAVITY to observe the broad line regions of hundreds of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) at redshifts of two or greater. Sky coverage is expanded by increasing the maximum angular separation between the target science object and the off-axis fringe tracking star from the current limit of 2 arcseconds to an unprecedented 30 arcseconds, constrained only by atmospheric conditions. This capability was successfully demonstrated at the VLTI for the first time.

This paper investigates the asymptotic properties of trajectories within a continuous dynamical system (CDS) linked to the discrete viscosity approximation method (DDS) for fixed point problems involving nonexpansive mappings, a framework originally proposed by Moudafi in 2000. We demonstrate that the trajectories $x(t)$ of the continuous system and the sequences $(x_{n})$ produced by the discrete process exhibit highly analogous asymptotic behaviors.

ASVspoof 2021 marks the fourth iteration of a bi-annual challenge series dedicated to advancing research on spoofing and developing countermeasures to safeguard automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems. While maintaining a focus on logical and physical access tasks—which have seen significant improvements over prior editions—this edition introduces a novel deepfake speech detection task. The paper details all three tasks, their respective new datasets, evaluation metrics, four baseline methods, the evaluation platform, and a summary of results. Although the inclusion of channel and compression variability increased the difficulty, performance on logical access and deepfake tasks remained comparable to previous editions. Conversely, outcomes for the physical access task highlight the challenges of detecting attacks in real, variable environments. Notably, ASVspoof 2021 was the first edition where participants lacked matched training or development data, mirroring real-world conditions where spoofed and deepfake speech characteristics cannot be confidently predicted. These results are highly encouraging, demonstrating substantial recent progress in the field.

Differentially private noise mechanisms typically rely on symmetric distributions, a choice favored for its alignment with differential privacy definitions and the resulting unbiased expectations of noisy outputs. However, certain scenarios require answers that are conservative—possessing known-signed error, termed "padded answers"—to remain useful. Although it appears paradoxical to satisfy differential privacy with one-sided error, we demonstrate that this contradiction can be resolved by incorporating it into the delta parameter of approximate differential privacy. We introduce several mechanisms for one-sided padding that consistently provide conservative results while maintaining approximate differential privacy. Furthermore, we illustrate applications of these mechanisms in specific domains, such as ensuring differential privacy for revealed cardinalities of set intersections and unions within Private Set Intersection protocols, and enabling multiparty computation on sparse data by making exact sizes differentially private, thereby avoiding the higher costs of fully oblivious computation.

We examine the stellar kinematics of the Galactic disc within the radial range of 7 to 13 kpc, utilizing a dataset of 118,945 red giant branch stars from LAMOST and Gaia. Our analysis characterizes the median, dispersion, and skewness of 3D stellar velocities, actions, and orbital parameters across the age-metallicity and disc $R$--$Z$ planes. The findings uncover numerous distinct kinematic patterns and structures in these planes. A primary feature is the significant variation in velocity, action, and orbital parameter distributions as one transitions from the young, metal-rich thin disc to the old, metal-poor thick disc. Additionally, smaller-scale structures, including velocity streams, north-south asymmetries, and spiral arm kinematic signatures, are clearly identified. Notably, the skewness of $V_{\phi}$ and $J_{\phi}$ highlights a new substructure at approximately $R\simeq12$ kpc and $Z\simeq0$ kpc, potentially linked to spiral arm dynamical effects in the outer disc. Furthermore, by analyzing orbital parameters and birth radii, we investigate stellar migration. Results indicate that thick disc stars near and beyond solar radii largely originated in the inner disc ($R\sim4-6$ kpc) due to highly eccentric orbits. Angular momentum transfer (churning) drives prominent stellar migration for both old, metal-rich stars moving outward and young, metal-poor stars moving inward. The spatial distribution of inward migrators born at Galactocentric radii greater than 12 kpc exhibits clear age stratifications, suggesting these populations result from past satellite galaxy merger events that triggered splashes over the last few gigayears.

We introduce a more precise secular version of the Redfield non-secular master equation that remains independent of basis selection, thereby fully resolving the ambiguity regarding the appropriate basis when applying the secular approximation to the Redfield master equation.

We investigate shape and topology optimization aimed at designing a structure that minimizes a weighted combination of material usage and linear elastic compliance under a fixed boundary load. This problem is generally ill-posed, as its solution typically demands infinitesimally fine microstructures. Consequently, we analyze the impact of singularly perturbing the problem by incorporating the structure's perimeter into the cost function. While energy scaling laws for uniaxial and shear loads in two dimensions have previously been established in the literature, this study derives the corresponding scaling law for a uniaxial load in three dimensions, representing the most fundamental three-dimensional scenario. Essentially, it is anticipated—and confirmed in this work—that under uniaxial loading, compliance behaves similarly to dissipation in a scalar flux problem, allowing lower bounds derived from superconductor pattern analysis to be applied directly. However, establishing upper bounds necessitates non-trivial modifications to constructions known from superconductivity, a requirement arising because elasticity imposes the additional constraint of torque balance.

Although Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents trained directly from visual inputs can tackle increasingly complex tasks, adapting these learned skills to new environments remains difficult. While extensive data augmentation offers a promising avenue for enhancing generalization, it frequently reduces sample efficiency and can cause algorithmic divergence. This paper examines the sources of instability when applying data augmentation to standard off-policy RL algorithms, identifying two issues both stemming from high-variance Q-targets. Leveraging these insights, we introduce a straightforward yet effective method to stabilize such algorithms during augmentation. We conduct comprehensive empirical evaluations on image-based RL using both ConvNets and Vision Transformers (ViT) across benchmarks derived from the DeepMind Control Suite and robotic manipulation scenarios. Our approach significantly boosts stability and sample efficiency for ConvNets under augmentation and delivers generalization performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in environments featuring unseen visuals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method scales to RL utilizing ViT-based architectures, suggesting that data augmentation may be particularly critical in this context.

Sound event localization and detection comprises two primary subtasks: sound event detection and direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation. While detection primarily depends on time-frequency patterns to differentiate sound classes, DoA estimation utilizes magnitude or phase disparities across microphones to determine source locations. Consequently, jointly training these tasks simultaneously is often challenging. We introduce a novel feature termed spatial cue-augmented log-spectrogram (SALSA), which establishes an exact mapping between signal power and source direction. This feature integrates multichannel log-spectrograms augmented with the estimated direct-to-reverberant ratio and a normalized principal eigenvector derived from the spatial covariance matrix at every time-frequency bin. Experiments on the DCASE 2021 dataset, specifically for sound event localization and detection with directional interference, demonstrated that deep learning models trained on SALSA significantly outperformed the DCASE baseline. Furthermore, we combined multiple models with slightly varied architectures trained on this new feature to enhance overall system performance for the DCASE challenge.

Mechanisms involving particle creation or annihilation, whether modeled through quantum field theory or the thermodynamics of irreversible processes, are pivotal to the early Universe's evolution, as seen in warm inflation. Adopting a comparable methodology rooted in open system thermodynamics, this study examines the effects of interaction, decay, and particle generation within a multi-component cosmos comprising dark energy, dark matter, radiation, and ordinary matter. In this framework, individual conservation equations for cosmological constituents are violated due to inter-component interactions and specific thermodynamic properties. We propose a thermodynamic description of the Universe that incorporates two new physical elements: particle number balance equations and creation pressures, thereby ensuring thermodynamic consistency in cosmological evolution. To restrict the model's free parameters, we utilize observational datasets including Planck results, Riess 2020 data, BAO, and the Pantheon sample. By applying a scaling ansatz for the dark matter-to-dark energy ratio and enforcing constraints from Planck+Riess 2020 data, the model yields an acceptable Hubble parameter value, offering a potential resolution to the recently debated Hubble tension.
We present an example of a monotone Boolean function on the hypercube defined by a low-depth decision tree that cannot be well approximated by any k-junta for small k.

While the dynamics of an initially uncorrelated system are described by a completely positive (CP) map, the presence of initial quantum correlations with an environment necessitates a not-completely positive (NCP) map for the system's evolution. A key inquiry concerns the relative measure of these two map types within the broader set of positive maps. After outlining the complexity of calculating the exact volume for generic maps acting on a qubit, this study focuses on Pauli channels within an abstract space where elements correspond to equivalence classes of maps identical up to a non-Pauli unitary. Within this framework, it is demonstrated that the volume occupied by NCP maps is exactly double that of CP maps.

We combine contrastive learning (CL) with adversarial learning to jointly optimize both the robustness and accuracy of code models. Unlike prior research, we demonstrate that code obfuscation—a standard transformation technique—offers a novel way to generate complementary "views" of code, facilitating the creation of models that are both robust and accurate. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic investigation into leveraging multi-view code obfuscations to enhance robustness and accuracy in code models. Specifically, during the self-supervised pre-training phase, we utilize adversarial codes as robustness-enhancing views within the CL framework, resulting in improved robustness and transferability for downstream applications. Subsequently, at the supervised fine-tuning stage, we show that adversarial training, guided by a carefully designed temporally staggered schedule for generating adversarial code, further boosts both robustness and accuracy of the pre-trained model. Building on these two components, we introduce CLAWSAT, a new self-supervised learning (SSL) framework for code that integrates $\underline{\textrm{CL}}$ with $\underline{\textrm{a}}$dversarial vie$\underline{\textrm{w}}$s (CLAW) and $\underline{\textrm{s}}$taggered $\underline{\textrm{a}}$dversarial $\underline{\textrm{t}}$raining (SAT). Evaluation across three downstream tasks in Python and Java reveals that CLAWSAT consistently achieves superior robustness and accuracy (e.g., an 11% improvement in robustness and a 6% improvement in accuracy on the Python code summarization task). Furthermore, we analyze the loss landscape and model interpretability to validate the efficacy of adversarial learning within the CLAW framework.

While parliamentary discourse is expected to be shaped by the ruling party and election cycles, the specific magnitude of these influences and their evolution over time remains under-researched. This study systematically examines how discussions in the Australian Federal Parliament shift in response to two distinct political events: elections and changes in prime ministers. Utilizing a novel dataset compiled from public records spanning 1901 to 2018, we extract and clean parliamentary transcripts to analyze spoken content. To track thematic shifts, we apply a correlated topic model to reduce data dimensionality, creating comparable topics across the timeline. These topics are then linked to the Comparative Agendas Project, and the impact of the identified events is assessed using a Bayesian hierarchical Dirichlet model. Our findings indicate that prime ministerial transitions often correlate with shifts in discussion topics, even when the governing party remains the same. Furthermore, the influence of elections on parliamentary discourse has grown since the 1980s, regardless of whether those elections result in a change of leadership.

Metric Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) is a well-established technique for creating meaningful low-dimensional, non-linear representations of high-dimensional data. It has been extensively utilized across statistics, machine learning, and graph visualization communities. Specifically, the widely adopted Kamada-Kawai force-directed graph drawing approach is mathematically equivalent to MDS and remains a primary method for embedding graphs into lower dimensions. However, despite its widespread use, theoretical insights into MDS are scarce due to the high non-convexity of its objective function. This paper demonstrates that minimizing the Kamada-Kawai objective is NP-hard and presents a provably correct approximation algorithm for its optimization, which functions as a Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for graphs with low diameter. Furthermore, experimental results are provided to explore potential links between the proposed greedy approximation strategy and gradient-based optimization techniques.

This study examines an oscillator system consisting of a seesaw linked to a simple pendulum, which is coupled to a mobile platform set at a specific incline. The system's response to potential displacements of the platform manifests as energy loss, observable through changes in angle, apparent weight, and height. Introduced variations prompt the system to adjust these parameters to maintain symmetry. The system's dynamics are modeled using a transformation matrix that characterizes the nature of the motion, allowing for the observation of rotational and translational effects. Consequently, this matrix provides a clear visualization of the system's values, highlighting the necessity of either supplying or removing energy.

This paper provides a resolution to the final unresolved instance of the directed Oberwolfach problem involving tables of equal length. Specifically, we examine the scenario with two tables of odd length. We demonstrate that the complete symmetric digraph $K^*_{2m}$ on $2m$ vertices can be decomposed into resolvable directed cycles of odd length $m$. This achievement fully resolves the directed Oberwolfach problem for tables of uniform length.

The program-over-monoid model of computation was introduced by Barrington's demonstration that it corresponds to the complexity class $\mathsf{NC^1}$. This work advances the understanding of the model's nuances. First, we define a novel tameness condition for a specific class of monoids, which provides a natural characterization of the regular languages recognizable by programs over monoids in that class. Second, we demonstrate that the class $\mathbf{DA}$ satisfies this tameness condition; consequently, the regular languages recognized by programs over monoids in $\mathbf{DA}$ are exactly those recognizable in the classical sense via morphisms from $\mathbf{QDA}$. Third, in contrast, we show that the well-known class of monoids $\mathbf{J}$ is not tame. Finally, we present a hierarchy based on program length within the set of languages recognized by programs over monoids from $\mathbf{DA}$.

Let $A=Q/(f)$, where $(Q,\mathfrak{n})$ is a complete regular local ring of dimension $d+1$, $f$ lies in $\mathfrak{n}^i\setminus\mathfrak{n}^{i+1}$ for some $i\geq 2$, and $M$ is a maximal Cohen-Macaulay $A$-module satisfying $e(M)=\mu(M)i(M)+1$. In this case, we establish that $\text{depth } G(M)\geq d-1$. Furthermore, if $(A,\mathfrak{m})$ is a complete hypersurface ring of dimension $d$ with an infinite residue field and $e(A)=3$, and $M$ is an MCM $A$-module with $\mu(M)=2$ or $3$, we prove that $\text{depth } G(M)\geq d-\mu(M)+1$. This paper represents the first systematic investigation into the depth of associated graded modules of MCM modules over hypersurface rings.

The practice of "backfilling," which involves enrolling extra patients into doses considered safe during phase I dose-escalation trials, is utilized to gather further data on a drug's safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy. These additional participants contribute to a more reliable estimation of the Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD) and provide critical insights for establishing the recommended phase II dose (RP2D). This paper investigates how backfilling impacts MTD estimation and trial length, examining scenarios with a single follow-up cycle for escalation as well as those involving delayed toxicity onset. Our findings indicate that across various scenarios, backfilling increases the rate of correct dose selections and significantly shortens trial duration, albeit at the expense of requiring a larger patient cohort.

We present an algorithm that enhances the edge connectivity of undirected graphs by leveraging the isolating cuts framework introduced by Li and Panigrahi (FOCS '20). By utilizing poly-logarithmic calls to any max-flow algorithm, our method achieves a running time of $\tilde O(m + n^{3/2})$, which represents an improvement over the prior best time of $\tilde O(n^2)$ established by Benczúr and Karger (SODA '98). Furthermore, we achieve the same performance gain for the closely related edge splitting off problem in undirected graphs.

Microwave transmission measurements were conducted on a three-dimensional (3D) layer-by-layer chiral photonic crystal (PhC) characterized by 3D singular points known as Weyl points in its photonic band structure. Near a Weyl point, the transmitted intensity was observed to be inversely proportional to the square of the propagation length for specific frequencies and wavevectors. Furthermore, the transmitted wave remained well-collimated within the plane parallel to the PhC layers, even under point-source incidence. Additionally, when a plane wave interacted with a PhC containing metal scatterers, the planar wavefront was restored post-transmission, demonstrating a cloaking effect.

We establish a set of transformation formulas for multivariate elliptic hypergeometric sums and integrals linked to the $A_n$ and $BC_n$ root systems, extending results originally derived by Rains. These expressions utilize the lens elliptic gamma function, which incorporates an extra integer variable alongside a complex variable and two elliptic nomes. Applying these findings, we demonstrate an equivalence between $S^1\times S^3/\mathbb{Z}_r$ supersymmetric indices for a pair of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theories connected by Seiberg duality, featuring $SU(n+1)$ and $Sp(2n)$ gauge groups. This result offers one of the most sophisticated validations of Seiberg duality to date. Additionally, we apply the $A_n$ integral to prove a star-star relation for a two-dimensional integrable lattice model in statistical mechanics, a relation previously established by the second author.

We introduce a configurable underwater drone model designed with components optimized for 3D printing. By utilizing printable adapters, this design enables various thruster and ballast arrangements, thereby expanding maneuverability options. Following an overview of the model and its potential configurations, we showcase a functional prototype built upon open-source hardware and software. This prototype has undergone successful testing during multiple dives in rivers and lakes near Berlin. However, the reliability of the printed models has only been verified in relatively shallow waters. We firmly believe that offering these models as freely downloadable resources will inspire the general public to construct and test their own underwater drones, accelerating the development of innovative solutions and applications. The models and accompanying documentation can be accessed at the following link: https://adapt.informatik.hu-berlin.de/schillaci/underwater.html.

While recent advancements in pre-trained language models have substantially boosted neural response generation, current approaches typically treat dialogue contexts as linear token sequences, relying on token-level self-attention to predict the next word. This granular encoding limits the ability to capture coherence at the discourse level across utterances. We introduce DialogBERT, an innovative conversational response generation model that builds upon existing PLM-based frameworks. DialogBERT utilizes a hierarchical Transformer architecture and introduces two training objectives—masked utterance regression and distributed utterance order ranking—to effectively model discourse-level coherence, mirroring the original BERT methodology. Evaluations across three multi-turn conversation datasets demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses baselines like BART and DialoGPT in quantitative metrics. Furthermore, human assessments indicate that DialogBERT produces responses that are notably more coherent, informative, and human-like compared to existing models.

Achieving precise control over the various degrees of freedom (DoFs) of structured light across both quantum and classical domains is critical in the field of optics. Traditionally, these DoFs are addressed individually during light shaping; however, recent attention has shifted toward the more comprehensive scenario of nonseparable states, where two or more DoFs are intrinsically coupled. Notably, classical nonseparable states share a mathematical equivalence with quantum entangled states, a similarity that has inspired significant research, such as studies on spin-orbit coupling in vector beams. Despite this, nonseparable classical states remain fragmented in their treatment, underutilizing their potential beyond vector beams. Examples include exotic space-time coupled pulses enabling novel shaping at ultrafast scales and ray-wave geometric beams that expand optical manipulation capabilities. This work offers a comprehensive overview of the rapidly expanding, yet currently disjointed, literature on general nonseparable states involving diverse light DoFs. Furthermore, we propose a unified framework for classifying and engineering these states, highlighting new avenues for both fundamental scientific inquiry and practical applications.

We calculate the static effective Lindbladian for a driven nonlinear oscillator interacting with a harmonic bath, extending beyond the rotating wave approximation (RWA). The resulting dissipative mechanisms account for significant discrepancies between standard RWA predictions and recent experimental outcomes from superconducting circuits regarding the Kerr-cat qubit. Furthermore, the higher-order dissipative terms identified in our analysis have substantial implications for quantum error-correction strategies and parametric processes.

Refining the traditional equivalence relation on Cauchy sequences produces a practical number system enriched with infinitesimals. This method effectively formalizes Cauchy's intuition that a null sequence "transforms into" an infinitesimal. Additionally, we highlight a previously overlooked construction of an infinitesimal system from Giuseppe Peano's 1910 work, which contradicts his earlier support for Cantor's dismissal of infinitesimals.

This paper introduces CRAWLING, a principled CRowdsourcing Algorithm on WheeLs designed for smart parking and in-car routing of connected vehicles. By leveraging data from third parties—such as other cars, pedestrians, smart sensors, and social media—CRAWLING enables vehicles to execute specific routing tasks through crowd-sourced information. Built upon a robust control-theoretical framework, the algorithm solves an optimal control problem where vehicles maximize a reward function that balances environmental conditions with desired behaviors. A distinctive capability of CRAWLING is its ability to handle stochastic behaviors while processing heterogeneous data streams. We present a standalone, general-purpose implementation of the system and demonstrate its efficacy across various scenarios that highlight its core features. Simulation results indicate that CRAWLING effectively orchestrates vehicles, allowing them to react online to changing road conditions and minimize their cost functions. Furthermore, the source code and data required to reproduce the numerical results are openly available.

This study proposes, develops, and evaluates an immersive Virtual Reality (VR) framework designed to enhance the comprehension of complex spatial arrangements in Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) compared to conventional 2D drawing methods. Focusing on construction details—a notoriously challenging subject for conveying geometric and semantic data to students—the research employs a mixed-methods approach. This includes analyzing test results from two groups regarding geometric and functional aspects, alongside surveys and interviews with lecturers, students, and laypeople about their VR experiences. Quantitative analysis indicates that participants with limited prior knowledge, such as novice students, achieved significantly higher learning scores in the test group. Furthermore, both groups found the VR experience enjoyable and engaging. Survey data confirms that students, academics, and professionals alike preferred the VR method over traditional learning. Qualitative interviews revealed improved understanding, heightened enthusiasm, and a desire for more VR-based content. Statistically significant improvements in exam results demonstrate that students grasped design concepts better after the VR session. These findings validate the core hypothesis that presenting contextual 3D models is a promising pedagogical strategy.

This study measures the time-integrated $CP$ asymmetry for the Cabibbo-suppressed decay $D^0\rightarrow K^-K^+$ using $3\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded by the LHCb detector at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. The initial flavor of the charm meson is identified via the charge of the pion in $D^{*+}\rightarrow D^0 \pi^+$ and $D^{*-}\rightarrow \bar{D^0} \pi^-$ decays. The calculation of $A_{CP}(K^-K^+)$ assumes minimal $CP$ violation in charm mixing and in the calibration channels $D^0\rightarrow K^-\pi^+$, $D^+\rightarrow K^-\pi^+\pi^+$, and $D^+\rightarrow \bar{K^0}\pi^+$. The measured asymmetry is $A_{CP}(K^-K^+)=(0.14\pm0.15(stat)\pm0.10(syst))\%$.
