Combining this finding with prior LHCb results produces $A_{CP}(K^-K^+)=(0.04\pm0.12(stat)\pm0.10(syst))\%$ and $A_{CP}(\pi^-\pi^+)=(0.07\pm0.14(stat)\pm0.11(syst))\%$. These represent the most precise single-experiment measurements to date, with the $K^-K^+$ result being the most accurate determination of a time-integrated $CP$ asymmetry in the charm sector; however, neither outcome indicates any evidence of $CP$ asymmetry.

Although machine learning holds significant promise across various medical disciplines, it has sparked concerns regarding potential biases and limited generalization across diverse factors such as gender, age, race, ethnicity, institutional settings, and data collection methods. This study addresses these issues by presenting experimental evidence from three neurological conditions, demonstrating that when adequately trained, machine learning models can effectively generalize across varied contexts without exhibiting bias. Specifically, utilizing multi-study magnetic resonance imaging consortia to diagnose Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder, we observed that well-trained models maintain consistent accuracy across different subgroups defined by gender, age, race, and clinical studies. Furthermore, models integrating multi-source data—including demographic, clinical, genetic, and cognitive factors—were also found to be unbiased. While these comprehensive models occasionally outperformed those trained solely on structural measures in terms of predictive accuracy across subgroups, there were instances where the inclusion of additional features offered no advantage.

This research investigates how the cosmological constant influences radial oscillations and gravitational wave echoes (GWEs) in non-rotating strange stars. Using two distinct equations of state—the MIT Bag model and the linear EoS—we modeled strange star configurations. By evaluating both positive and negative values of the cosmological constant, we derived the corresponding mass-radius relations. This involved first solving the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations with a non-zero cosmological constant, followed by solving the perturbation equations for pressure and radial oscillations. We then calculated the eigenfrequencies of the fundamental $f$-mode and the first 22 pressure $p$-modes for each equation of state. Treating the remnant of the GW170817 event as a strange star, we computed the echo frequencies generated by these stars in the presence of the cosmological constant. Our numerical analysis reveals relationships between the cosmological constant, mode frequencies, structural parameters, and GWE frequencies of strange stars. Specifically, our results indicate that for strange stars, the effective range of the cosmological constant lies between $10^{-15}\, \mbox{cm}^{-2}$ and $3\times 10^{-13}\, \mbox{cm}^{-2}$.

This work introduces the concept of coupling reduction in renormalizable theories and demonstrates its application within Particle Physics models. Reduced couplings emerge as functions of a fundamental coupling, adhering to the renormalization group equation and satisfying a specific system of ordinary differential equations. When these functions take the form of power series, the resulting theories mimic standard renormalizable ones, thereby significantly expanding the scope of constraints achievable through symmetries beyond previous limits. On a more abstract level, coupling reduction allows for the construction of theories where beta-functions vanish to all orders in perturbation theory. The method becomes physically significant and phenomenologically crucial when applied to the Standard Model and its extensions. Notably, within supersymmetric frameworks, it has become the most potent known tool, particularly after extending its application to couplings with mass dimensions and mass parameters themselves. This technical success rests on the fundamental property that coupling reduction is independent of the renormalization scheme. The accurate predictions of the top quark and Higgs boson masses prior to their experimental discovery underscore the profound physical importance of this concept.

This paper evaluates the closed-loop Whiplash gradient descent algorithm on L-smooth convex cost functions. Through numerical experiments, we examine its behavior across various condition numbers for convex costs. We analyze the momentum sequence's convergence via symplectic integration and define relaxation sequences to capture the method's non-classical characteristics. Assuming invexity, we derive a momentum-driven adaptive convergence rate. Additionally, we propose an energy method to forecast convergence rates for closed-loop inertial gradient dynamics with convex costs, utilizing an integral anchored energy function and a novel lower bound asymptotic notation that leverages the boundedness of solutions. Consequently, we demonstrate a polynomial convergence rate for the Whiplash inertial gradient system over a family of scalar quadratic cost functions and an exponential rate for a single quadratic scalar cost function.

Simulation-based testing has become a critical complement to physical road trials for ensuring the safety of autonomous vehicles (AVs), driving significant research efforts toward identifying failure scenarios within simulated environments. A pivotal, yet unresolved, question is whether these simulated failures translate to reality—specifically, if they are reproducible on actual systems. The "sim-to-real" gap, caused by differences between synthetic and real sensor data, means a scenario flagged in simulation could be either a spurious artifact of the data generation or a genuine failure that persists with real sensors. To validate simulated failures, we propose a method that searches for matching instances of a scenario within a corpus of real data to determine if the failure holds up. We introduce a formal definition for when a labeled data item corresponds to an abstract scenario, which is encoded as a scenario program using the SCENIC probabilistic programming language. Based on this definition, we developed a querying algorithm capable of extracting the subset of data from a labeled dataset that matches a given scenario program. Experimental results confirm that our algorithm is both accurate and efficient across diverse, realistic traffic scenarios and scales effectively to handle a reasonable number of agents.

In recent years, sharing short, personalized videos across social media platforms has gained significant traction, creating a demand for digital portrait retouching within video content. However, directly applying image editing techniques to individual video frames often results in unstable and uneven sequences. To address this, we propose a robust and user-friendly parametric approach designed to smoothly reshape portraits in videos. Our method operates in two primary stages: stabilized face reconstruction and continuous video reshaping. First, we estimate rigid pose transformations for faces across frames, jointly optimize multiple frames to preserve facial identity, and recover facial expressions throughout the video. Second, we reshape the reconstructed 3D face using a parametric model that reflects facial weight changes, then use this modified 3D structure to guide the warping of video frames. We introduce a novel signed distance function-based dense mapping technique to handle the warping between pre- and post-reshaped face contours, ensuring stable output with minimal distortion. Furthermore, we leverage the 3D facial structure to refine the dense mapping for temporal consistency. The final result is generated by minimizing background distortion through the optimization of a content-aware warping mesh. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces visually appealing results by adjusting a single reshaping parameter, thereby simplifying portrait video editing for social media and visual effects applications.

Estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) is crucial in contemporary medicine for guiding individualized treatment decisions. Recently, several metalearners have been introduced to estimate CATEs efficiently and flexibly by adapting predictive machine learning models for causal inference. This chapter reviews the existing literature on metalearners and offers practical guidance for applying them to estimate treatment heterogeneity using data from randomized controlled trials with survival endpoints. Our recommendations are backed by an extensive simulation study that manipulates factors such as the complexity of baseline risk and CATE functions, the degree of treatment effect heterogeneity, censoring mechanisms, and treatment assignment balance. To illustrate the practical utility of our findings, we reanalyze data from the Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRT) and the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) study. Although recent studies indicate heterogeneous effects of intensive blood pressure treatment with numerous modifiers, our analysis suggests that many of these modifiers may be false positives. Accompanying this chapter is the `survlearners` R package, which offers well-documented implementations of the CATE estimation strategies discussed, facilitating the adoption of our recommendations and the replication of our numerical experiments.

This paper addresses the challenge of exchanging sensitive or valuable files among users with partial reliance on an untrusted third party, such as a Cloud Storage Provider (CSP). While secure peer-to-peer (P2P) channels are an option for file sharing, they often introduce latency and require the sender to stay connected throughout the transfer. As an alternative, users can upload file metadata to a shared CSP and transmit only the critical data needed for the receiver to retrieve and reconstruct the original file. We introduce Bifrost, a novel file sharing system based on recent dual deduplication research. Bifrost fulfills the required functionality while ensuring that (1) the CSP can efficiently compress outsourced data; (2) the secure P2P channel is utilized solely for transmitting brief but vital information; (3) users can verify data integrity to detect any alterations by the CSP; and (4) access is restricted strictly to the sender and intended receiver, preventing the cloud or malicious actors from inferring details about the shared file. Through a proof-of-concept implementation, we evaluated compression and bandwidth performance. Our experiments demonstrate that secure file sharing can be achieved by transmitting only 650 bits over the P2P channel, regardless of file size, while allowing the assisting CSP to achieve an 86.9% compression rate.

Cortical surface registration serves as a cornerstone for neuroimaging analysis, offering superior alignment of functional areas compared to volumetric methods. Traditional registration relies on optimizing intricate similarity metrics, which results in prolonged processing times. Consequently, the standard practice of mapping all data to a global average template often fails to capture the inherent heterogeneity of the cortex. This study introduces a novel unsupervised learning framework that reformulates registration as a multi-label classification task, wherein points on a low-resolution control grid deform toward a fixed set of endpoints. Utilizing a spherical geometric deep learning architecture, the model learns this mapping in an end-to-end unsupervised manner, with regularization provided by a deep Conditional Random Field (CRF). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance in similarity and areal distortion metrics against leading classical algorithms while producing smoother deformations than other learning-based methods, even for subjects exhibiting atypical cortical structures.

By employing a modified pseudospin model for the ferroelectric NH$_3$CH$_2$COOH$\cdot$H$_2$PO$_3$, which incorporates piezoelectric coupling with strain components $\varepsilon_i$, $\varepsilon_4$, $\varepsilon_5$, and $\varepsilon_6$ using the Glauber method under a two-particle cluster approximation, we computed the dynamic dielectric permittivity tensor components and relaxation times. With an appropriate selection of theoretical parameters, we analyzed the frequency and temperature dependencies of the permittivity components, as well as the temperature dependencies of the relaxation times. The study yields satisfactory agreement between the theoretical predictions and experimental measurements for longitudinal permittivity.

This study identifies the minimum generating sets for three categories of one-generator $(1+u)$-quasi twisted (QT) codes defined over $F_2+uF_2$ where $u^2=0$. Additionally, it examines the generating sets and establishes lower bounds for the minimum Lee distance regarding a specific subclass of $A_2$ type one-generator $(1+u)$-QT codes. Through these code constructions, several high-quality (optimal or suboptimal) linear codes over $F_2$ are derived.

For unramified reductive groups, we identify the connected components of affine Deligne-Lusztig varieties within partial affine flag varieties. Leveraging the findings of Hamacher-Kim and Zhou, this outcome enables the verification of the He-Rapoport axioms, the "almost product structure" of Newton strata, and the exact characterization of mod $p$ isogeny classes anticipated by the Langlands-Rapoport conjecture, specifically regarding the Kisin-Pappas integral models of Hodge-type Shimura varieties equipped with parahoric level structure.

The magnetic properties of exchanged-biased CoO(20nm)/Co($d_F$) bilayers, where $d_F$ ranges from 5 to 20 nm, were investigated using polarized neutron reflectometry (PNR). By inserting a 20 nm Nb layer between the CoO/Co bilayer and the Al$_2$O$_3$ substrate, we constructed a waveguide structure that significantly amplified the intensity of spin-flip (SF) scattering at optical resonance positions. For the trained sample with the thinnest Co layer (5 nm), strong SF scattering was observed at resonance, reaching up to 30% of the incident intensity, which indicates high non-collinearity within the system. As $d_F$ increases, the SF scattering intensity decreases linearly. Simultaneously, asymmetry between up-down and down-up scattering channels was detected at resonance positions. We attribute this asymmetry to the Zeeman splitting of neutron energies with different initial polarizations occurring under a high external field. However, analysis reveals that the external field applied in the PNR experiment is insufficient to quantitatively explain the observed asymmetry for samples with $d_F > 5$ nm, necessitating the postulation of an additional magnetic field generated by the sample itself. We ascribe this additional field to stray fields produced by chiral Bloch domain walls, whose chirality arises from the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction at the CoO/Co interface. These findings are valuable for the design of spintronic devices utilizing the exchange bias effect.

We examine a one-shot query-guided object localization scenario where neither the target image nor the category name is provided as input. In this context, a hand-drawn sketch serves as a viable query option; however, crude sketches alone can lead to ambiguity, such as confusing a laptop with a sofa. Conversely, pairing a sketch with a linguistic description of the category, such as "a small portable computer small enough to use in your lap," offers superior visual and semantic cues for localization. This work introduces a multimodal query-guided object localization approach designed for the challenging open-set setting. Specifically, we utilize queries from two modalities—hand-drawn sketches and object descriptions (or glosses)—to achieve localization. This task is particularly difficult due to the significant domain gap between queries and natural images, as well as the difficulty of integrating the complementary yet minimal information contained within each query type. For instance, sketches provide abstract shape data, while text descriptions often capture only partial semantic details. To overcome these hurdles, we propose a novel cross-modal attention mechanism that directs the region proposal network to generate proposals aligned with the input queries, alongside a new orthogonal projection-based scoring technique that evaluates each proposal against the queries to produce the final localization results.

Accurate prognostic models hold significant value for both patients and clinicians. When individuals receive predictions, they may choose to take health-improving actions or find comfort in the information. However, when a clinical context defines a specific set of possible actions, a formal decision rule grounded in these predictions can yield a far wider impact. Even when not originally intended, informal decision rules often emerge in practice. To assess clinical utility, the use of prediction-based decision rules should be formalized and tested against standard care through randomized trials; yet, such trials require motivating evidence. This paper outlines how observational data can be leveraged to propose decision rules based on prognostic models. We subsequently introduce a framework for emulating prediction-driven trials within observational data to evaluate the utility of these rules. Furthermore, we argue that a split-sample design should be employed to develop the prognostic model, establish the decision rule, and assess its clinical effectiveness.

In Formal Concept Analysis, a base for a finite structure comprises a set of implications that fully characterize all valid implications of that structure. This concept extends to Description Logic, where the base consists of concept inclusions rather than implications; however, because concept expressions can be arbitrarily complex, the existence and size of a finite base remain uncertain. We first review existing literature on mining EL bases from finite interpretations, which primarily aims to identify a finite base or restrict role depth, often at the cost of omitting valid inclusions with deeper role structures. Subsequently, we introduce a novel strategy for mining EL bases that adapts to the local structure of an interpretation by bounding role depth dynamically. This approach ensures the capture of all EL concept inclusions valid within the interpretation, rather than limiting results to a fixed depth.

Machine translation, a key application of natural language processing, has recently seen increased research focus on resource-poor and closely related languages. A significant challenge for these systems is the divergence in orthographic conventions, which complicates traditional approaches; however, orthographic data can also serve to enhance translation performance. This survey examines the impact of orthography on machine translation for under-resourced languages, defining these languages in this context and explaining how orthographic insights can be leveraged for improvement. The article reviews prior research, analyzing underlying assumptions and demonstrating how orthographic knowledge boosts translation quality for these languages. It outlines various machine translation types and highlights a growing trend of integrating orthographic information with established methods. Particular emphasis is placed on current efforts regarding cognate information across different translation levels and the insights derived from them. Additionally, the survey focuses on multilingual neural machine translation for closely related languages. The piece concludes by outlining future directions in machine translation utilizing orthographic data, specifically within multilingual environments and bilingual lexicon induction.

With the web transitioning away from stateful tracking, browser fingerprinting is increasingly common. However, current detection methods often fail to consider evasion strategies like code obfuscation. To bridge this gap, we evaluated the resilience of a leading fingerprinting detection technique against various standard obfuscation tools. Our findings indicate that combining static and dynamic analysis effectively withstands different forms of obfuscation. Although certain obfuscators can cause false negatives in static analysis alone, dynamic analysis successfully identifies these instances. Furthermore, since obfuscation does not lead to significant false positives, the integrated approach remains capable of accurately detecting obfuscated fingerprinting scripts.

Heavy quarkonium remains a cornerstone for investigating nuclear matter under extreme temperature and density conditions in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. This talk presents recent advancements in the theoretical modeling of quarkonium's in-medium behavior via the open-quantum systems framework. Beyond offering a transparent interpretation of the imaginary component of the complex heavy-quark potential, this approach uncovers that the dissolution of heavy quarkonium states arises from a delicate balance between screening effects and wavefunction decoherence.

We theoretically examine injection and shift currents in zigzag graphene nanoribbons under a static electric field that breaks inversion symmetry, enabling nonzero second-order optical responses via dipole interactions. Injection currents can be selectively excited by circularly polarized light, whereas shift currents respond to linearly polarized light. Utilizing a tight-binding model based on carbon 2p$_z$ orbitals, we numerically determine the spectra of injection coefficients and shift conductivities, analyzing their dependence on static field strength and ribbon width. The resulting spectra display numerous peaks corresponding to optical transitions between various subbands, where the peak positions and amplitudes are effectively tuned by the static electric field. By developing a simple two-band model, we find that static electric fields modify edge states in a nonperturbative manner, causing their associated optical transitions to dominate current generation at low photon energies. For typical parameters—such as a static field of 10$^6$ V/m and light intensity of 0.1 GW/cm$^2$—injection and shift currents in a 5 nm wide ribbon can reach magnitudes on the order of 1 $\mu$A. These findings offer a physical foundation for developing passive optoelectronic devices utilizing graphene nanoribbons.

Recent research indicates that flat-minima optimizers, which aim to locate parameters within low-loss regions, enhance a neural network's generalization compared to stochastic and adaptive gradient-based methods. Among these, Stochastic Weight Averaging (SWA) and Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) have garnered significant attention due to their scalability. Despite this, their underlying properties remain underexplored, and there is a lack of systematic benchmarking across diverse domains. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the loss surfaces of models trained with each approach and conducting extensive evaluations across computer vision, natural language processing, and graph representation learning tasks. Our results reveal several unexpected insights, offering valuable guidance for researchers seeking to advance deep learning optimizers and practitioners aiming to select the most suitable optimizer for their specific problems.

We present an analytical framework for determining the superconducting volume fraction. Beyond this, our model forecasts the morphology of embedded superconducting regions. Applying this approach, we calculated the volume fractions and domain shapes in (TMTSF)$_2$PF$_6$, (TMTSF)$_2$ClO$_4$, YBa$_2$Cu$_4$O$_8$, $\beta$-(BEDT)TTF$_2$I$_3$, and FeSe. Typically, layered superconductors exhibit anisotropic resistivity decreases. Our analysis clarifies that this phenomenon arises from the flat or needle-like geometry of the superconducting samples.

The analysis examines divergences arising from specific sectors of gravitational fluctuations around a general background within quadratic gravity theories. These findings can be encapsulated in a distinct scalar model, the properties of which are subsequently investigated.

The bipartite Ramsey number $BR(H_1,H_2,\ldots,H_k)$ represents the minimal positive integer $b$ ensuring that every $k$-decomposition of the edge set of $K_{b,b}$ includes at least one $H_i$ within the $i$-th partition, for some $i$ between 1 and $k$. Alternatively, for two bipartite graphs $H_1$ and $H_2$ and a positive integer $m$, the $m$-bipartite Ramsey number $BR_m(H_1, H_2)$ is defined as the smallest integer $n$ such that any subgraph $H$ of $K_{m,n}$ necessarily contains either $H_1$ or the complement of $H$ contains $H_2$. Previous research has established the values of $BR_m(K_{2,2}, K_{3,3})$, $BR_m(K_{2,2}, K_{4,4})$ for various $m$, and $BR_m(K_{3,3}, K_{3,3})$ for specific $m$, alongside the finding that $BR(K_{2,2}, K_{5,5})=17$. This paper calculates the value of $BR_m(K_{2,2}, K_{5,5})$ for several integers $m \geq 2$.

In the classical $N$-body problem within $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d\ge2$, Maderna and Venturelli (Ann. Math. 2020) demonstrated the existence of hyperbolic motions for any positive energy, originating from any configuration and proceeding along any non-collision path. Their original argument depended on long-term solution behaviors identified by Chazy (1922) and Marchal-Saari (1976), Hölder estimates for Mané's potential established by Maderna (2012), and weak KAM theory. We present a distinct and entirely new proof for this existence result. Our core strategy involves constructing uniform estimates for the Euclidean length and angle of geodesics associated with Mané's potential—starting from a specified configuration and terminating along a given non-collision ray—based on geometric insights. Crucially, this approach does not rely on any of the prior studies utilized in the Maderna-Venturelli proof. Furthermore, our geometric method applies to Hamiltonians of the form $\frac12\|p\|^2-F(x)$, where $F(x)\ge 0$ is lower semicontinuous and decays very slowly toward zero at distances far from collisions. Consequently, we establish the existence of hyperbolic motions for such Hamiltonians with arbitrary positive energy, starting from any admissible configuration and moving along any non-collision configuration. This leads to similar existence results for hyperbolic motions in several important generalized $N$-body systems described by $\ddot{x} = \nabla_x F(x)$ where $F\in C^{2}(\Omega)$, thereby extending the findings of Maderna and Venturelli (Ann. Math. 2020).

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) offer promising approaches for reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from 2D image sets, making them ideal candidates for generating new facial expressions. However, two significant challenges limit their application. First, existing deformable NeRFs are object-agnostic and model global scene motion; while they can reproduce temporal movements, they lack the ability to manipulate them in a semantically interpretable manner. Second, controllable volumetric models usually depend on either labor-intensive manual labeling or 3D ground truth to assign semantic meaning to the scene. To address these issues, we introduce CoNFies, a controllable neural representation designed specifically for face self-portraits that operates within a unified framework using automated processing. Our method employs automated facial action recognition (AFAR) to define expressions as a synthesis of action units (AUs) and their intensities, where AUs simultaneously serve as semantic location markers and control labels. Consequently, CoNFies surpasses existing techniques in both novel view and expression synthesis, delivering superior visual and anatomical fidelity.

Existing methods for interpreting deep learning models in music typically generate explanations within low-level feature spaces, such as highlighting specific time-frequency bins in spectrograms or time-pitch bins in piano rolls. These outputs are often challenging for musicologists lacking technical expertise to comprehend. To overcome this barrier, our work prioritizes human-centric explanations grounded in high-level musical concepts. We investigate post-hoc explanations for trained systems through two distinct strategies: a supervised method allowing users to define and test specific musical concepts for relevance, and an unsupervised approach that automatically identifies and presents musical excerpts containing pertinent concepts for user interpretation. We validate both methodologies using an existing symbolic composer classification system, demonstrating their capabilities while also outlining their inherent constraints.

This work details an implementation of the Atiyah-Bott residue formula for $\overline{M}_{0,m}(\mathbb{P}^{n},d)$, which we utilize to calculate numerous genus $0$ Gromov-Witten invariants, such as intersection numbers of rational curves on general complete intersections. Additionally, we determine counts for rational contact curves that meet specific Schubert conditions. These calculations validate existing Mirror Symmetry predictions. The code created for these tasks is publicly accessible and applicable to various other computational problems.

This paper presents our submission to the WMT19 shared task on filtering low-resource parallel corpora. Our primary strategy leverages the LASER toolkit (Language-Agnostic SEntence Representations), which employs an encoder-decoder architecture trained on parallel data to generate multilingual sentence embeddings. We utilize these embeddings directly to score and filter noisy parallel sentences, bypassing the need to train a separate scoring function. By comparing our method with other promising approaches, we demonstrate that LASER delivers robust performance. Furthermore, we create an ensemble of various scoring techniques to achieve additional improvements. Our submission secured the top overall performance for both the Nepali-English and Sinhala-English 1M tasks, surpassing the second-best systems by margins of 1.3 and 1.4 BLEU scores, respectively. Additionally, our experiments indicate that this technique holds significant promise for low-resource and even zero-resource scenarios.

Contemporary software systems frequently rely on deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, making the security of these libraries a critical issue. Fuzzing these frameworks faces two primary obstacles: first, fuzzers must provide inputs from the valid domain of each API, which is often unknown; second, many generated inputs are redundant, meaning random invalid inputs rarely trigger new behaviors. Although existing methods partially tackle the first issue, they neglect the second. We introduce SkipFuzz, a fuzzing approach designed for deep learning libraries that utilizes active learning to learn the input constraints of each API function. SkipFuzz builds a model of these constraints using feedback from a test executor, enabling the generation of valid inputs. Specifically, an active learner iteratively queries the test executor, receiving feedback on whether inputs satisfy constraints (i.e., are accepted or rejected). By categorizing inputs—such as distinguishing tensors by shape—SkipFuzz eliminates candidates that do not fit specific constraint profiles, thereby refining its hypotheses. This active learning mechanism effectively addresses the problem of redundant inputs. Through the use of SkipFuzz, researchers discovered and reported 43 crashes, 28 of which were confirmed and assigned 13 unique CVEs.

For a set $P$ of $n$ red and blue points in the plane, a \emph{planar bichromatic spanning tree} is defined as a spanning tree where every edge links a red point to a blue point without any edge intersections. The bottleneck planar bichromatic spanning tree problem seeks to identify such a tree $T$ that minimizes the length of its longest edge. This paper demonstrates that the problem is NP-hard for points in general position. Additionally, we introduce a polynomial-time $(8\sqrt{2})$-approximation algorithm, based on the finding that any bichromatic spanning tree with a bottleneck of $\lambda$ can be transformed into a planar bichromatic spanning tree with a bottleneck no greater than $8\sqrt{2}\lambda$.

Transitioning from fossil fuels to low-carbon technologies is essential to mitigate anthropogenic climate change, a process that begins with decarbonizing the electricity grid but must also extend to sectors like transport and heating for comprehensive success. By reducing emissions from power generation and providing low-carbon alternatives for other sources, this approach effectively lowers overall carbon output. Carbon taxes have proven to be an effective mechanism for facilitating this shift. This study employs an agent-based electricity market model, ElecSim, combined with the NSGA-II genetic algorithm to identify optimal carbon tax policies. The objective is to simultaneously minimize the average electricity price and the relative carbon intensity of the energy mix. Our findings indicate that a range of carbon taxes can be determined to align with varying goals. Specifically, we successfully minimized electricity costs to below £10/MWh and reduced carbon intensity to zero across all scenarios. Regarding the optimal tax strategy, an increasing trajectory between 2020 and 2035 was found to be preferable. All Pareto-optimal tax strategies remained above £81/tCO2 for every year, with a mean carbon tax strategy of £240/tCO2.

Recent research in magnetic nanolithography demonstrates that diverse complex magnetic states arise depending on the aspect ratio of a solitary magnetic island. We introduce a model that not only aligns with experimental data but also forecasts magnetic configurations exhibiting continuous symmetry at specific aspect ratios, uncovering a duality between vortex and vertex states. Consequently, our model facilitates novel approaches to designing artificial spin systems, enabling their use in advanced magnetic textures for devices and computing applications.

A layered triangular lattice hosting spin-1/2 ions serves as an optimal system for investigating exotic, highly entangled states such as quantum spin liquids (QSL). This study details a systematic in-field neutron scattering investigation of CsYbSe$_2$, a perfect two-dimensional triangular-lattice antiferromagnet within the prominent rare-earth chalcogenide family of QSL candidates. Elastic neutron scattering data collected down to 70 mK reveal short-range 120$^{\circ}$ magnetic order in the absence of an external field. While heat capacity measurements suggest long-range magnetic order occurs at 3–5 T, the correlation lengths along the $c$ axis in field-induced ordered states remain relatively short. The inelastic neutron scattering spectra transition from highly damped, continuum-like excitations at zero field to distinct, sharp spin wave modes during the plateau phase. These experimental findings are well-reproduced by extensive large-cluster density-matrix renormalization group calculations using a Heisenberg triangular-lattice nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic model, which capture key features including zero-field continuum excitations, sharp magnons at the plateau, and high-energy two-magnon modes. This research offers a comprehensive experimental and theoretical synthesis of unconventional field-induced spin dynamics in triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnets, providing significant insight into quantum many-body phenomena.

In 2016, Google's CECPQ1 project incorporated the newhope1024 post-quantum key-exchange algorithm into TLS 1.2, followed by the 2019 Google-Cloudflare CECPQ2 experiment, which adopted the more efficient ntruhrss701 algorithm for TLS 1.3. This paper reevaluates the CECPQ2 decisions and demonstrates how to attain superior performance for post-quantum key exchange within TLS 1.3 by utilizing the sntrup761 algorithm, which offers higher security levels. Although prior research suggested that ntruhrss701 key generation was significantly faster than sntrup761, this study accelerates sntrup761 generation through batch key creation. While batch key generation remains transparent at the TLS protocol level, it introduces software engineering challenges related to integrating batch key exchange into current TLS libraries and applications. The authors prove that strategic software layering allows for the seamless integration of rapid post-quantum software, including batch key exchange, into TLS with minimal modifications to libraries and no changes to applications. To validate feasibility, the paper details the successful deployment of a high-speed sntrup761 library via a lightly patched OpenSSL into both an unmodified web browser and an unmodified TLS terminator. Additionally, TLS 1.3 handshake benchmarks reveal that this approach achieves a higher throughput of handshakes per second than any software currently included in OpenSSL.

This study introduces a new particle image velocimetry (PIV) method designed to create instantaneous two-dimensional velocity fields for sediment-laden fluids, utilizing the optical flow algorithm typically found in ultrasound imaging. The proposed ultrasonic PIV (UPIV) system combines a medical ultrasound device with a specialized ultrasonic PIV algorithm. Using a phased sensor array, the medical ultrasound instrument captures acoustic echo signals to produce two-dimensional underwater images. By applying the L-K local constraint to grayscale variations between consecutive images, the instantaneous particle velocities corresponding to pixels in the ultrasonic images are calculated, ultimately yielding a two-dimensional flow field. Multiple experimental trials validated the proposed algorithm, with results compared against traditional cross-correlation methods. These comparisons demonstrate that the L-K optical flow approach not only accurately measures underwater velocity fields but also offers superior smoothness and broader applicability, particularly for sediment-laden fluid flow measurements, compared to conventional algorithms.

This study derives a third-order linear differential equation describing the stationary distributions of run-and-tumble particles in a two-dimensional harmonic trap. By applying inference techniques and leveraging existing results under limiting conditions, we establish this equation based on the zero-flux condition ($j=0$). While the analogous equation for passive Brownian particles is of first order, the inclusion of second and third-order terms highlights the unique characteristics of active motion. Beyond formulating the problem as a third-order equation, we present solutions as a convolution of two distributions: a Gaussian distribution arising from thermal fluctuations and a beta distribution resulting from active motion at zero temperature. This convolution structure signifies the independence of the two random processes, with the total distribution representing their combined effect.

When cellular networks fail, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can function as aerial wireless base stations. While previous research on UAV-based coverage typically relies on Air-to-Ground path loss models—assuming outdoor users situated on a two-dimensional plane—this study proposes deploying a single UAV to serve indoor users within a high-rise building during disasters like earthquakes or floods. Assuming indoor user locations are uniformly distributed across each floor, we introduce a particle swarm optimization algorithm to determine an optimal three-dimensional placement for the UAV that minimizes the total transmit power needed to cover these users.

We derive multiple estimates concerning bilinear forms involving Kloosterman sums. These findings serve as a quantification of cancellations among parameters within short intervals. Specifically, for specific parameter ranges, we enhance several recent outcomes established by Blomer, Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel, and Milićević (2014) as well as by Fouvry, Kowalski, and Michel (2014).

Our recent study demonstrates that the flattening of galactic rotation curves can be attributed to retardation, provided that galactic mass evolves over time. While our prior research retained only second-order terms of the retardation time—ignoring higher-order contributions from the Taylor expansion—this paper presents an analysis encompassing all orders. We show that a second-order approximation is sufficient, as higher-order terms can be disregarded.

We briefly survey the life and work of P. L. Chebyshev and his enduring legacy. Our discussion covers his contributions to probability, number theory, and mechanics; his students and their mathematical lineage; and his pivotal role as the founding father of Russian mathematics, particularly the Russian school of probability.

This work investigates meta-learning within Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) featuring linear transition models in an undiscounted episodic framework. Utilizing a task sharedness metric grounded in model proximity, we examine task families defined by a distribution over models comprising both bias and variance elements. We introduce BUC-MatrixRL, an adaptation of the UC-Matrix RL algorithm, demonstrating its ability to efficiently solve test tasks drawn from the same distribution by learning an estimator for the task distribution's bias parameter, thereby leveraging sampled training tasks. Our analysis extends findings from learning to learn linear regression and linear bandits to the broader context of MDPs with linear transitions. Furthermore, we establish that, relative to learning tasks in isolation, BUC-Matrix RL yields substantial reductions in transfer regret, particularly for task distributions characterized by high bias and low variance.

We extend Milnor link invariants to encompass all codimension 2 embeddings, including every type of knotted surface in 4-space. This generalization relies on cut-diagrams, a higher-dimensional analogue of Gauss diagrams applicable to codimension 2 embeddings in Euclidean spaces. By defining a group associated with these cut-diagrams that extends the fundamental group of the complement, we derive Milnor-type invariants from the successive nilpotent quotients of this group. We demonstrate that these invariants remain unchanged under cut-concordance, an equivalence relation that includes the standard topological concept of concordance. Furthermore, we present multiple practical applications of these Milnor concordance invariants for knotted surfaces, evaluating their strength against existing invariants and establishing realization theorems. Our work also yields classification results for spun links up to link-homotopy, provides a criterion for determining when a knotted surface is ribbon, and advances the theory of cut-diagrams toward a combinatorial framework for analyzing surfaces in 4-space.

Star cluster formation and assembly are significantly influenced by feedback from massive stars, particularly depending on whether these stars emerge early or late in the process. To investigate the impact of early massive star formation, we conducted a controlled experiment using the $\texttt{Torch}$ software suite, which integrates self-gravitating magnetohydrodynamics, ray-tracing radiative transfer, $N$-body dynamics, and stellar feedback. We simulated four identical $10^4$ M$_\odot$ giant molecular clouds featuring a Gaussian density profile with a peak of $521.5 \mbox{ cm}^{-3}$. Through the $\texttt{AMUSE}$ framework, we adjusted three of these models to ensure the first-born star was extremely massive (50, 70, or 100 M$_\odot$). These early massive stars disrupted the natal gas structure, causing rapid gas evacuation from the star-forming region. Consequently, the star formation rate was suppressed, leading to a lower total stellar mass compared to the control model, which lacked an early massive star and exhibited a star formation rate and efficiency up to three times higher. Furthermore, while the control model produced a single massive cluster, the presence of early massive stars facilitated the creation of spatially distinct, gravitationally unbound subclusters.

We demonstrate that the implicit UCCA parser fails to consistently handle numeric fused-heads (NFHs), a shortcoming potentially stemming from inconsistent annotation, limited training data, or modeling constraints, and we identify the contributing factors. Given that NFHs are ubiquitous in text and vital for accurate inference, we regard this issue as significant. We argue that the careful design and fine-grained annotation of NFHs within meaning representation frameworks would enhance downstream applications—such as machine translation, natural language inference, and question answering—especially those involving numeric reasoning, by facilitating their recovery and categorization. Additionally, we are examining how other meaning representations, like AMR, address this phenomenon. We urge researchers in meaning representations and computational linguistics to investigate NFHs in their future work.

Coupling topological insulators (TIs) with magnetic insulators (MIs) has become a prevalent method for investigating the interplay between topological surface states and magnetism. Earlier transport experiments have typically identified the suppression of weak antilocalization or the emergence of the anomalous Hall effect as indicators of the magnetic proximity effect (MPE) within TIs. In this work, we demonstrate the presence of a nonlinear planar Hall effect (NPHE) in Bi₂Se₃ films epitaxially grown on MI substrates of thulium iron garnet (TmIG) and yttrium iron garnet (YIG). The NPHE observed in these systems is approximately ten times larger than that found in Bi₂Se₃ films grown on the nonmagnetic gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrate. Specifically, the nonlinear Hall resistance in the TmIG/Bi₂Se₃ system shows a linear dependence on the external magnetic field, whereas the YIG/Bi₂Se₃ system displays an additional hysteresis loop centered at zero field. Furthermore, the magnitude of the NPHE scales inversely with carrier density. We hypothesize that the observed NPHE arises from the exchange gap opening and out-of-plane spin textures induced by the MPE in the TI surface states, suggesting it could serve as an alternative transport signature for detecting MPE in MI/TI heterostructures.

We examine the recent hyperbolic space formulation of the Kuramoto model and connect it to information geometry. Specifically, the dynamical equation of the Kuramoto all-to-all model is characterized as the gradient flow of the Kullback-Leibler divergence over the statistical manifold. We calculate the Fisher information metric for both the Kuramoto and Kuramoto-Shakagichi models, arguing that its components diverge at the critical point, thereby establishing it as a viable alternative order parameter for the synchronization phase transition.

This study examines the impact of sterile neutrinos across various mass scales on cosmology within scenarios featuring MeV-scale reheating temperatures. Through calculations of sterile neutrino production driven by mixing and scattering in the early Universe, we determine that light sterile neutrinos, characterized by masses and mixing parameters derived from short-baseline oscillation experiments, align with both big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) and cosmic microwave background (CMB) constraints provided the reheating temperature is ${\cal O}(1)$ MeV and the parent particle decays radiatively into electromagnetic components. Conversely, if the parent particle predominantly undergoes hadronic decay, BBN limits become significantly tighter; under these conditions, light sterile neutrinos may be cosmologically ruled out, contingent upon the particle's mass and hadronic branching ratio.

This study details laboratory experiments designed to examine how Arctic warming influences the amplitude and drift speed of the mid-latitude jet stream. Our findings indicate that a gradual reduction in the meridional temperature difference leads to three outcomes: 1) a deceleration of the jet stream's eastward propagation, 2) a complication of its structural dynamics, and 3) a rise in the frequency of extreme events. Trends linking extreme events and temperature variability to Arctic warming are evident only in latitudes affected by the jet stream, whereas these trends invert in the equatorial region south of the subtropical jet. Although the laboratory model lacks land-sea contrasts, the observed patterns of temperature variability and extreme events align closely with NCEP reanalysis data. Furthermore, our results qualitatively support recent proxy-based proposals regarding a decrease in temperature variability as the meridional temperature gradient weakens. Finally, probability distributions demonstrate only weak sensitivity to changes in the temperature gradient, a finding consistent with recent quasigeostrophic model studies.

This paper investigates the unmixed property of the edge ideal $I(D)$ for a weighted oriented graph $D=(G,\mathcal{O},w)$ by characterizing it across several scenarios: when $G$ is an $SCQ$, chordal, simplicial, or perfect graph; when $G$ lacks 4- or 5-cycles; when $G$ contains no 3- or 5-cycles; and when the girth of $G$ is at least 5.

POLAR is a compact space-borne instrument engineered to accurately measure the polarization of transient phenomena, such as Gamma-Ray Bursts, within the 50-500 keV energy band. Operating on the Compton Scattering principle, it utilizes plastic scintillators as the primary detection medium, coupled with multi-anode photomultiplier tubes. Successfully deployed aboard the Chinese space laboratory TG-2 on September 15, 2016, the instrument requires a comprehensive understanding for both data analysis and Monte Carlo simulations to reliably reconstruct polarization data. Consequently, a thorough investigation of its in-orbit performance was conducted to derive essential calibration parameters, including electronic noise, pedestal, gain nonlinearity, thresholds, crosstalk, gain, and the influence of temperature on these metrics. Additionally, the correlation between the photomultiplier tube's gain and high voltage was analyzed, with all measurement uncertainties quantified. Finally, Monte Carlo simulations were employed to estimate the typical systematic errors in Gamma-Ray Burst polarization measurements arising from uncertainties in these calibration parameters.

During the broadcast of widely viewed televised events like presidential debates or TV programs, users often generate real-time commentary. This paper introduces a straightforward yet efficient method to merge social media discussions with video footage to produce multimedia summaries of these events. The proposed approach detects specific scenes by identifying spikes in mentions of key participants and automatically extracts relevant tweets and video frames that correspond to these spikes, ensuring they both depict and discuss the individuals involved.

Reinforcement learning (RL) agents deployed in human-computer interaction contexts typically need extensive user engagement to achieve optimal performance. To mitigate this "cold start" issue, we introduce a new strategy that utilizes cognitive models to pre-train RL agents prior to their deployment with actual users. Following a concise overview of pertinent cognitive models, we outline our general methodological framework and illustrate it through two case studies drawn from our past and current projects. Our aim with this position paper is to foster dialogue among researchers in RL, HCI, and cognitive science, thereby unlocking the complete potential of this approach.

This paper introduces a discrete model describing the deformation of a convex regular polygon as it deforms against a flat, rigid surface, initially touching it at a single point. First, the model is formulated as a set of variational inequalities defined over a non-empty, closed, and convex subset of a specific Euclidean space. Next, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the solution. The model serves as a simplified representation of processes in atomic force microscopy virus imaging, including surface adhesion, distributed strain, and relaxation into a shape that balances adhesion and elastic forces. Furthermore, analyzing numerical simulation results derived from this model offers a novel approach for estimating the contact area and elastic parameters in virus contact mechanics research.

Understanding outcomes is essential for grasping complex events, yet this knowledge is difficult to obtain. We demonstrate that by pre-selecting a participant within a complex event, crowd workers can (1) deduce the collective impact of significant constituent events, (2) label the volitional involvement of participants in generating the situation, and (3) link the situation's outcome to state changes experienced by those participants. Through the implementation of a multi-step interface and a rigorous quality control protocol, we assembled a high-quality annotated dataset comprising 8,000 short newswire narratives and ROCStories, achieving high inter-annotator agreement (0.74–0.96 weighted Fleiss Kappa). Our dataset, named POQue (Participant Outcome Questions), facilitates the investigation and creation of models capable of addressing various dimensions of semantic understanding. Empirically, we reveal that existing language models fall short of human performance in nuanced ways when tasked with abstract and specific comprehension of complex events, their outcomes, and a participant's influence on the event's resolution.

Beginning with a discrete $C^*$-dynamical system $(\mathfrak{A}, \theta, \omega_o)$, we examine and establish several primary ergodic characteristics of the associated crossed product system $(\mathfrak{A}\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb{Z}, \Phi_{\theta, u}, \om_o\circ E)$. In this context, $E$ denotes the canonical conditional expectation mapping $\mathfrak{A}\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb{Z}$ onto $\mathfrak{A}$, applicable under the condition that $\alpha \in \aut(\ga)$ commutes with the $*$-automorphism $\theta$ up to a unitary element $u \in \ga$. Furthermore, $\Phi_{\theta, u} \in \aut(\mathfrak{A}\rtimes_\alpha\mathbb{Z})$ serves as a fully noncommutative extension of the renowned skew-product introduced by H. Anzai for the product of two tori in classical settings.

We are presenting updates for version 0.2.0 of the Automated SpectroPhotometric REDuction (ASPIRED) pipeline, which is built for broad compatibility across various instruments. Its default configuration accommodates numerous standard long-slit spectrometer setups, while also providing a versatile suite of tools that allow users to customize the automated workflow to match specific instrument characteristics. This level of automation enables near real-time data reduction, facilitating adaptive observing strategies—a capability that is crucial for Time Domain Astronomy. Over the past year, the pipeline has seen substantial enhancements in internal data management, data input/output processes, as well as the accuracy and repeatability of wavelength calibration.

Benchmarking is essential for validating systems, particularly within real-time contexts where typical applications rely on predictable abstractions: periodic behavior, a defined working set, and stable response times free from unpredictable elements like page faults. Unfortunately, current benchmark suites do not adequately capture these critical characteristics. Consequently, practitioners and researchers are forced to either simulate real-time environments with significant approximations or manually re-engineer existing benchmarks to incorporate necessary features. Moreover, standard suites lack out-of-the-box measuring and logging capabilities suited for real-time systems, making adjustments to fundamental parameters, such as scheduling policies, a laborious and error-prone task.

This paper introduces RT-bench, an open-source framework that extends virtually any existing benchmark with standard real-time functionalities. RT-bench offers a user-friendly, unified command-line interface for customizing key aspects of real-time execution across multiple benchmarks. The framework is built upon four core principles: a cohesive interface, support for periodic behavior and deadline semantics, controllable memory footprints, and extensibility with portability. We have integrated applications from the popular SD-VBS and IsolBench suites into the framework and demonstrated a range of use cases that mirror typical real-time system evaluation scenarios, all of which can be efficiently executed using RT-bench.

Point-by-point strain scanning is frequently employed to map residual stress (strain) in engineering components, yet its spatial resolution and gauge volume are constrained by beam-defining apertures and can become anisotropic at extreme diffraction angles. In contrast, wavelength-resolved neutron transmission imaging offers the potential to retrieve tomographic data on residual strain by measuring Bragg edges in transmission; these crystallographic fingerprints vary in shape and position based on the material's microstructure and strain distribution. In this context, spatial resolution is governed by geometrical blurring and the detector's point spread function. Mathematically, reconstructing the strain tensor field involves the longitudinal ray transform, which possesses a non-trivial null-space that prevents direct inversion. Consequently, reconstructing strain fields in convex objects has required combining the longitudinal ray transform with physical constraints. To generalize reconstruction methods and relax these constraints, histogram tomography—a recently introduced concept—can be utilized. This approach depends on the ability to resolve strain distributions along the beam direction, as detailed in this paper. Specifically, Bragg edge strain tomography necessitates extracting the second moment (the variance about zero) of the strain distribution, a capability not yet demonstrated experimentally. This paper provides experimental verification that the second moment can be reliably measured using a well-characterized aluminium ring and plug sample. Furthermore, we compare our experimental measurements with numerical calculations and substantiate our findings through rigorous uncertainty quantification of the estimated mean and variance of the strain distribution.

Electro-optical management of on-chip photonic components is a fundamental requirement for achieving efficient integrated photonics. Lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) has emerged as a promising platform for on-chip applications, driven by its substantial electro-optic coefficient and high nonlinearity [1]. Embedding quantum emitters within LNOI would expand their utility from classical photonics to the realms of quantum computing and communication [2, 3]. In this work, we integrate single rare-earth ion (REI) quantum emitters into electro-optically tunable lithium niobate (LN) thin films, successfully demonstrating control over LN microcavities coupled to REIs across a 160 GHz frequency range with a 5 μs switching speed. The dynamic manipulation of these cavities allows for the modulation of the Purcell enhancement of the REIs using short time constants. Leveraging this Purcell enhancement, we provide evidence for the detection of single Yb3+ ions within LN cavities. Coupling quantum emitters to rapidly tunable photonic devices offers an efficient strategy to engineer emitter waveforms [4]. Furthermore, this approach creates a platform for encoding quantum information across the spectral, temporal, and spatial domains to realize high channel multiplexing, while also serving as a method for generating deterministic single-photon sources [5, 6].

Utilizing a dataset from Kaneko et al. (2006) and Kocevski et al. (2003), we analyzed 42 individual tracking pulses—defined as instances where spectral hardness mirrors the flux or count rate profile—drawn from 36 Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs) comprising 527 time-resolved spectra. Our investigation focused on the evolutionary characteristics of spectral hardness and $E_{peak}$ (the peak energy where $\nu F_{\nu}$ is maximized). The temporal evolution of these pulses consistently follows a soft-to-hard-to-soft pattern, with the soft-to-hard transition occurring during the rise phase and the hard-to-soft transition during the decay phase. Key findings regarding $E_{peak}$ include: 1) the rise phase invariably begins in a high-energy state, with $E_{peak}$ values exceeding 50 keV; 2) rise-phase spectra initiate at significantly higher energies (median $E_{peak} \approx 300$ keV) compared to decay-phase spectra, which conclude at lower energies (median $E_{peak} \approx 200$ keV); 3) rise-phase spectra are harder and the rise phase itself is shorter in duration than the decay phase. Consequently, for any complete pulse, the initial $E_{peak}$ exceeds the final $E_{peak}$, and the initial rise phase is much briefer than the subsequent decay phase. These results align well with the predictions of Lu et al. (2007) and prevailing theories on GRB production. We suggest that the spectral evolution of tracking pulses may involve both kinematic and dynamic processes, though current evidence is insufficient to determine which dominates. Furthermore, our statistical findings provide constraints that can help refine existing GRB models.

This study investigates the nebular phase of lanthanide-rich ejecta from a neutron star merger (NSM) using a one-zone model that represents atomic properties with a single species, neodymium (Nd). Assuming beta-decay of r-process nuclei serves as the source of heat and ionization, we calculate the ionization and thermal balance under non-local thermodynamic equilibrium conditions. Atomic data, including energy levels, radiative transition rates, collision strengths, and recombination coefficients, were derived using the GRASP2K and HULLAC structure codes. Our findings indicate that both permitted and forbidden lines contribute roughly equally to the cooling rates of Nd II and Nd III at nebular temperatures. We demonstrate that during the early nebular phase, both kinetic temperature and ionization degree rise over time; however, these quantities stabilize after the thermalization break of the heating rate. This stabilization occurs because, at later times, the ionization and thermalization balance relies primarily on two-body collisions between electrons and ions. Consequently, although luminosity drops rapidly, the emergent spectrum's shape remains largely unchanged after the break. Furthermore, the emission-line nebular spectrum of pure Nd ejecta spans a broad range from $0.5\,\mu m$ to $20\,\mu m$, featuring two distinct peaks near $1\,\mu m$ and $10\,\mu m$.

This study investigates high-order frequency mixing in graphene driven by a two-color radiation field, which combines the fundamental and second harmonic components of an ultrashort, linearly polarized laser pulse. Results indicate that harmonics arising from interband transitions are efficiently produced when the two-color field is orthogonally polarized. Under these conditions, the resulting high-harmonics exceed those from parallel polarization by over two orders of magnitude. This finding stands in stark contrast to atomic and semiconductor systems, where parallel polarization is typically preferred. The physical basis for this enhancement is analyzed using a three-step semi-classical electron-hole collision model, adapted for graphene's pseudo-relativistic energy dispersion. Furthermore, the impact of many-particle Coulomb interactions on the high-harmonic generation (HHG) process is examined within the dynamical Hartree-Fock approximation. The analysis demonstrates that, across all scenarios, the HHG signal is significantly enhanced compared to the free-charged carrier model due to the attractive interaction between electrons and holes.

A line field on a manifold is a smooth mapping that assigns a tangent line to every point on the manifold except for a finite set. In this sense, it serves as an extension of vector fields and is used to model various geometric and physical phenomena, such as the dynamics of principal curvature directions on surfaces or stress flux within elasticity. We introduce a discretization method for Morse-Smale line fields on surfaces, building upon Forman's construction for discrete vector fields. Furthermore, we define more general critical elements and their corresponding indices based on local matchings, ensuring that the Euler theorem and the characterization of homotopy type via critical cells remain valid.

Total Generalized Variation (TGV) is a widely used regularizer in imaging and inverse problems, effectively merging higher-order smoothing with the ability to handle discontinuous solutions. Empirical evidence indicates that its second-order variant particularly promotes piecewise affine functions. This manuscript formalizes that observation for the one-dimensional TGV functional by identifying the extremal points of its sublevel sets within an appropriate quotient space topology. Consequently, these findings demonstrate that linear inverse problems in one dimension, regularized by TGV with finite-dimensional observations, possess piecewise affine minimizers. Additionally, leveraging this characterization, we establish precise first-order necessary optimality conditions that do not require the fidelity term to be convex, along with a straightforward algorithm for solving TGV-regularized minimization tasks.

This paper establishes specific relationships between representation densities and offers a streamlined method for calculating them by leveraging these connections. As an application, we determine certain arithmetic intersection numbers of special cycles on unitary Shimura varieties and put forward a conjecture regarding these values.

Let $\mathbb P$ denote the polynomial algebra over the finite field $\mathbb Z_2$ in a single variable, and let $\mathbb P^{\otimes t} = \mathbb Z_2[x_1, \ldots, x_t]$ represent its $t$-fold tensor product, where each generator is assigned degree $1$. The objective is to identify a minimal set of generators for the ring of invariants $(\mathbb P^{\otimes t})^{G_t}$ as a module over the Steenrod algebra $\mathscr A_2$, with $G_t$ being a subgroup of $GL(t, \mathbb Z_2)$. This task is equivalent to determining a monomial basis for the space of "unhit" elements, $\mathbb Z_2\otimes_{\mathscr A_2} (\mathbb P^{\otimes t})^{G_t}$, across all $t$ and degrees $n \geq 0$. The structure of this tensor product proves remarkably complex and remains unresolved for $t \geq 5$, even when $G_t$ is the trivial subgroup $\{e\}$. In this paper, we focus on the case $G_t = \{e\}$ for $t \in \{5, 6\}$, deriving new findings regarding $\mathscr A_2$-generators of $(\mathbb P^{\otimes t})^{G_t}$ in specific degrees. We also outline potential applications and present a MAGMA algorithm to verify these results. This work extends our previous research detailed in [23, 25].

While language models trained on extensive prompted multitask datasets such as T0 (Sanh et al., 2021) and FLAN (Wei et al., 2021a) demonstrate generalization to unseen tasks, we demonstrate that training on a strategically selected subset of instances can surpass performance achieved using the entire dataset across various benchmarks. Our approach assumes access to a limited number (250–1,000) of unlabeled target task examples, from which we identify nearest neighbors within a pool of multitask data to train task-specific models. This method proves more data-efficient than training a single multitask model while still outperforming it significantly. We evaluate our approach on a diverse range of tasks outside the retrieval pool, including those used for T0 assessment and complex domains like legal and scientific document question answering. By retrieving small subsets from P3 (the source collection for T0) and fine-tuning T5 models, we achieve 3–30% higher performance than the T0-3B variant on 12 of 14 evaluation datasets while utilizing at most 2% of the data required for T0-3B. Furthermore, these models serve as superior initializations for few-shot fine-tuning, yielding 2–23% relative improvements over few-shot fine-tuned T0-3B models on 8 datasets. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/allenai/data-efficient-finetuning.

We present a computational approach to rational stable equivariant homotopy theory for a torus $G$, grounded in the homology of the Borel construction on fixed points. Specifically, we introduce an abelian torsion model, $A_t(G)$, which possesses finite injective dimension. This model supports a homology theory, $\pi A_t_*$, mapping into $A_t(G)$ via the Borel construction. Furthermore, we establish a finite Adams spectral sequence, $\text{Ext}_{A_t(G)}^{*,*}(\pi A_t_*(X), \pi A_t_*(Y)) \implies [X,Y]^G_*$, applicable to rational $G$-spectra $X$ and $Y$.

This study investigates the thermoelectric power in graphene nanoribbons, specifically focusing on the Nernst and Seebeck effects, using a non-equilibrium Green function approach combined with a tight-binding Hamiltonian. Due to electron-hole symmetry, the Nernst coefficient behaves as an even function of Fermi energy, whereas the Seebeck coefficient remains an odd function, independent of the magnetic field. Under strong magnetic fields, both coefficients become nearly independent of the nanoribbon's width and chirality, exhibiting peaks whenever the Fermi energy intersects Landau levels. For the $n$-th peak (where $n \neq 0$), the Nernst effect's height is $[\ln2/|n|]$ and the Seebeck effect's height is $\ln2/n$. The zeroth peak behaves anomalously: the Nernst effect reaches a height of $[2\ln2]$, while the Seebeck effect shows no peak. In the absence of a magnetic field, the Nernst effect vanishes, leaving only the Seebeck effect, which then strongly depends on chirality. While zigzag-edged nanoribbons display equidistant peaks, armchair-edged ones exhibit irregular distributions; notably, insulating armchair ribbons can generate a very large Seebeck coefficient near the Dirac point. As the magnetic field increases from zero to large values, the variations in Seebeck coefficients among different chiralities diminish, and a non-zero Nernst coefficient first emerges near the Dirac point before extending across the entire energy range.

The integration of emerging technologies—including Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), High Altitude Platform Stations (HAPS), Millimeter Wave (mmWave) frequencies, Massive MIMO, and beamforming—positions wireless backhaul as a cornerstone of 5G networks. Although not a novel concept, wireless backhaul historically lagged behind fiber in performance; however, advancements have diminished fiber's dominance. As networks become increasingly dense, wireless backhaul transitions from an option to a necessity. Despite this, significant challenges remain for efficient implementation, including resource allocation, deployment strategies, scheduling, power management, and energy efficiency. Beyond these hurdles, wireless backhaul serves as a critical enabler for innovations such as rural connectivity, satellite communications, and mobile edge computing, while also enhancing existing technologies. The proliferation of small cells utilizing wireless backhaul introduces distinct security concerns. Standardization efforts by governing bodies, particularly regarding Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB), are underway and will be addressed. Furthermore, wireless backhaul is poised to play a pivotal role in Beyond 5G architectures, supported by trends like cell-free networking, ultra-massive MIMO, and ultra-dense networks. This survey comprehensively examines the challenges, opportunities, and applications of wireless backhaul in 5G, while also touching upon related Beyond 5G concepts, security issues, and standardization initiatives.

This thesis investigates sequential decision-making scenarios in which the loss or reward resulting from an action cannot be deduced solely from observed feedback. A significant portion of the work addresses the unsupervised sequential selection problem, characterized by the inability to infer incurred losses from available feedback. Additionally, we propose a novel framework called Censored Semi Bandits, where action losses become observable under specific conditions. Furthermore, we examine the channel selection problem within communication networks, where an action's reward is revealed only if no other player chooses that channel in the same round. These issues have broad applications across domains such as healthcare, crowd-sourcing, security, and adaptive resource allocation. To tackle these sequential decision challenges, this thesis leverages the unique structural properties inherent to each setting. We design provably optimal algorithms tailored for these weak-feedback environments and empirically validate their performance using various problem instances derived from both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Dominant belief revision frameworks advocate adopting a new belief that remains as proximal as possible to the original one, a process that, even under standard conditions, involves minimizing surprise. In this work, we expand upon the current model by introducing a "relative surprise" metric; unlike traditional approaches that consider only the prior belief, this metric calculates surprise relative to both the prior belief and the wider context of the incoming information, utilizing distance measures between truth-value assignments. We then characterize the resulting surprise-minimizing revision operator through a collection of intuitive rationality postulates similar to those in the AGM framework. Furthermore, our analysis yields representation theorems for other established revision operators found in the literature, including the Dalal operator and a recently proposed distance-based min-max operator.

We introduce and demonstrate a novel formula for one-loop all-same-helicity Yang-Mills amplitudes, which are expressed as a sum of products of two tree-level Berends-Giele currents linked by an effective propagator. To define these propagators, one must incorporate the concept of regions, also known as dual momenta. The proof relies on the observation that the formula naturally satisfies the required collinear limit properties. The sole non-trivial aspect of the demonstration involves verifying that the amplitude remains invariant under shifts of the region momenta.

Although numerous theories exist regarding the Hall anomaly observed in the mixed-state Hall resistivity of type-II superconductors, a consensus on its origin remains elusive. This study presents a quantitative analysis of magnetotransport data from BSCCO thin films reported by Zhao et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 247001 (2019)], which supports a previously suggested vacancy mechanism [J. Phys. Condens. Matter. 10, L677 (1998)] enhanced by many-body vortex correlations. The model posits that the Hall anomaly arises from the movement of vacancies within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. Initial validation explores vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition within the vortex crystal. Subsequently, the measured activation energies are compared against the calculated creation energies for vortex-anti-vortex pairs and vacancies on the flux-line lattice without employing any adjustable parameters. This analysis clarifies the theoretical foundations and prerequisites of the vacancy model, notably revealing that vacancy activation energies are approximately one order of magnitude lower than those of an isolated vortex line. Ultimately, this proposed mechanism may offer a macro-theoretical framework applicable to other investigations.

Inferring the topology of network processes involving co-evolving and interacting time-series is essential for network research. While Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models are commonly used to infer directed graph structures, topology estimation becomes ill-posed in large networks with limited time-series data. This paper introduces a novel topology inference method for directed networks with co-evolving nodal processes that addresses this ill-posedness by preserving nonlinearity. The proposed approach, termed large-scale kernelized Granger causality (lsKGC), employs kernel functions to map data into a low-dimensional feature space where the autoregressive problem is solved; the method subsequently maps these solutions back to the input space to deduce the network topology. Extensive simulations on synthetic datasets featuring both linear and nonlinear dependencies with known ground truths show that lsKGC significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) for network recovery. Additionally, evaluations on real functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data achieved a 96.3% accuracy in diagnosing schizophrenia using only brain time-series information, marking the highest reported accuracy in the literature.

This review examines the "optimal fingerprinting" methodology, originally outlined by Allen and Tett (1999), through the lens of statistical inference, addressing recent critiques raised by McKitrick (2021). Our analysis concludes that the approach can withstand most of McKitrick's criticisms provided two conditions are met: (i) the null simulation generated by the climate model remains independent of physical observations, and (ii) this null simulation consistently estimates the residual covariance matrix of the physical data. Both conditions rely heavily on the conductivity and quality of the climate models used. If the second condition is not satisfied, the estimator retains its unbiasedness and consistency under standard circumstances, though it forfeits the "optimal" status of the method. Additionally, we confirm the validity of the residual consistency test proposed by Allen and Tett (1999) for verifying alignment between the residual covariances of the null simulation and physical observations. Finally, we detail the relationship between the "optimal fingerprinting" framework and Feasible Generalized Least Squares.

This work introduces and examines $C^0$-conforming hybrid high-order (HHO) methods designed for solving biharmonic problems subject to clamped or simply supported boundary conditions. These methods utilize cell unknowns, consisting of $C^0$-conforming polynomials of degree $k+2$ that approximate the solution within mesh cells, alongside face unknowns, which are polynomials of degree $k \ge 0$ approximating the normal derivative on the mesh skeleton. Consequently, the methods achieve $O(h^{k+1})$ $H^2$-error estimates for smooth solutions. A key innovation in the error analysis is the reduction of the minimal regularity requirements imposed on the exact solution. This technique is broadly applicable beyond $C^0$-conforming HHO methods; to demonstrate this versatility, the error analysis is also outlined for standard $C^0$-conforming interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin (IPDG) methods. Furthermore, the proposed approach avoids the need for bubble functions or $C^1$-smoothers when evaluating the right-hand side for rough loads.
