Transitioning to their derived or homotopy categories creates new frameworks for exploring homotopy theory. This paper outlines certain tools for analyzing these "brave new homotopy theories" and illustrates them by examining modules over the $K$-theory spectrum, which are closely tied to Mahowald's theory of $bo$-resolutions. A forthcoming sequel intends to apply these methods to the less well-known setting of modules over the $2$-local connective spectrum of topological modular forms.

This study introduces a novel integration of a continuum full-f gyrokinetic turbulence model with a 6D continuum kinetic neutral model, implemented via the Gkeyll code. The primary goal is to enhance the fundamental understanding of how neutrals influence plasma fueling, detachment, and their coupling with edge plasma profiles and turbulence statistics. The simulation framework accounts solely for atomic hydrogen, incorporating electron-impact ionization, charge exchange, and wall recycling processes. These capabilities have been validated against analytical predictions and benchmarked using the DEGAS2 Monte Carlo neutral code. Simulations were performed on a simplified scrape-off layer (SOL) geometry using NSTX parameters. When compared to a baseline case excluding neutrals, the results indicate that neutral interactions decrease normalized density fluctuation levels, skewness, and kurtosis, while extending auto-correlation times. Additionally, a flatter density profile emerges, mirroring the SOL density shoulder formation seen in experimental high-fueling scenarios.

We investigate certain characteristics of $\tau$-exceptional sequences associated with finite-dimensional algebras. Building on our previous work, which demonstrated a one-to-one correspondence between the collection of ordered support $\tau$-tilting modules and that of complete signed $\tau$-exceptional sequences, we detail how the symmetric group acts on the latter through its natural action on the former. Additionally, we explain the impact on a $\tau$-exceptional sequence resulting from the mutation of its corresponding ordered support $\tau$-tilting module, utilizing the framework developed by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten.

A polarized social network is represented as a system of interacting marked point processes featuring variable-length memory. Each process tracks the sequential moments a social actor voices either a "favorable" or "contrary" stance. Upon expressing an opinion, the social pressure on that actor resets to zero, awaiting the group's response. The frequency and direction of an actor's expressions are shaped by the social pressure they face, adjusted by a polarization coefficient. We demonstrate that as the polarization coefficient approaches infinity, the network achieves an instantaneous yet metastable consensus.

As part of the second phase of the Advanced Virgo upgrade program, instrumented baffles are being fabricated to surround the end mirrors in the main arms, extending the implementation previously achieved for the input mode cleaner end mirror during phase I. These baffles will incorporate photosensors to enable real-time monitoring of stray light near the mirrors. This paper presents optical simulations of light distribution within the detector's main cavities to evaluate the sensors' capability to effectively track mirror misalignments and surface defects, as well as to assist in the interferometer's pre-alignment process.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) offer the ability to extract and integrate features across all their architectural layers, the specific application of fusing intermediate features from these layers for Human Action Recognition (HAR) using depth and inertial sensors remains unexplored. To fully leverage the potential of all CNN layers, this paper introduces a novel Multistage Gated Average Fusion (MGAF) network. This architecture relies on a new, computationally efficient Gated Average Fusion (GAF) network to extract and combine features from every layer of the CNN. At the input stage, depth and inertial sensor data are converted into sequential front view images (SFI) and signal images (SI), respectively; the SFI are derived from the front-view information provided by the depth data. A CNN processes both modalities to generate feature maps, which are then effectively fused by the GAF network while maintaining the dimensionality of the resulting features. The proposed MGAF network is structurally extensible and capable of handling more than two modalities. Experiments conducted on three publicly available multimodal HAR datasets show that MGAF surpasses existing state-of-the-art fusion methods for depth-inertial HAR in terms of recognition accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, the proposed method achieves an average accuracy increase of 1.5% while reducing computational costs by approximately 50% compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper introduces a novel method for deriving market-directional signals, grounded in a non-stationary solution to the dynamic equation stating that "future prices gravitate toward the value that maximizes shares traded per unit time" [1]. Building on prior research [2] which demonstrated that share execution flow ($I=dV/dt$), rather than trading volume ($V$), drives the market and exerts a significantly stronger dynamic impact on asset prices, this study presents a key advancement. We define the "scalp-price" ${\cal P}$ as the aggregate of price movements exhibiting high execution flow $I$, thereby filtering out minor fluctuations ("little bounces") to capture only significant "follow the market" events. Consequently, shifts in this scalp-price signal genuine market trend reversals—distinguishing them from temporary bull rallies or bear sell-offs—and the methodology can be extrapolated to non-local price changes. Additionally, software that computes the scalp-price based on market observations (time, execution price, and shares traded) is available from the authors.

Practical recommendation systems typically operate in two stages. Initially, various predictive models estimate the likelihood of distinct immediate user actions. Subsequently, these predictions are combined based on specific "strategic parameters" designed to fulfill diverse business objectives, including increased user engagement, higher revenue, and enhanced community interactions. Beyond constructing precise predictive models, it is essential to optimize these strategic parameters to maximize primary goals without compromising secondary guardrails. In this multi-objective, constrained environment, the study finds that a probabilistic approach to strategic parameters yields superior value compared to the conventional method of selecting a single deterministic parameter. This probabilistic framework involves learning an optimal distribution over parameter choices and sampling a parameter from this distribution for each user session. To address this challenge, the problem is formulated as a stochastic compositional optimization task where unbiased stochastic gradients are inaccessible. The proposed method was deployed on a major social network with hundreds of millions of daily active users, resulting in a +0.22% increase in user engagement for a recommendation task and a +1.7% revenue boost in an advertising optimization scenario relative to the best deterministic strategy.

We suggest employing Church encodings within typed lambda-calculi to establish an automata-theoretic parallel to implicit computational complexity, mirroring how monadic second-order logic serves descriptive complexity. Our focus lies on transductions—specifically string-to-string or tree-to-tree functions exhibiting superlinear growth, including polyregular functions, HDT0L transductions, and S\'enizergues's "k-computable mappings." Initial findings demonstrate that certain transduction classes are contained within classes defined by lambda-calculi, thereby addressing a fundamental open question regarding the expressive power of the simply typed lambda-calculus. Furthermore, we successfully encode regular functions (and, via adjustments to program types, a broader subset of polyregular functions) into the elementary affine lambda-calculus, a linear logic variant originally conceived for implicit computational complexity.

The solar atmosphere is characterized by complex transients that signal the restructuring of magnetic fields and plasma. Solar jets, defined as collimated plasma ejections, are widespread phenomena crucial for understanding solar activities across various scales, including magnetic reconnection, particle acceleration, coronal heating, and solar wind acceleration. Advanced observations from ground-based and space-based telescopes, offering high spatiotemporal resolution, broad temperature coverage, spectroscopic data, and stereoscopic views, have provided significant insights to refine theoretical models. This review summarizes the primary observational features of solar jets, explores their physical interpretations and associated models, and highlights key unresolved questions for future research.

This paper introduces a preliminary investigation into various observation and action space representations for Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) applied to Real-time Strategy (RTS) games. The study contrasts two specific approaches: (1) a global representation, where the agent observes the entire game state and must select both target units and actions simultaneously; and (2) a local representation, where the input is filtered through the perspective of a single unit, allowing the agent to determine actions for each unit independently. Evaluation within the $\mu$RTS environment indicates that the local representation yields superior performance compared to the global representation for the specific task of resource harvesting.

Neural networks have proven effective in handling high-dimensional data across numerous real-world applications, a capability that has been extensively validated in recent literature regarding optimal control and dynamical systems. To uncover the fundamental reasons behind their success in solving such high-dimensional problems, we established an algebraic framework and approximation theory specifically for compositional functions and their neural network counterparts. This theoretical foundation is designed to facilitate error analysis for both input-output functional relations and numerical algorithms, a distinction that is crucial for analyzing approximation errors in problems lacking analytic solutions, such as differential equations and optimal control tasks. We have identified key characteristics of compositional functions and elucidated their relationship with neural network complexity. Beyond function approximation, we derive several error upper bound formulae for neural networks used to approximate solutions in differential equations, optimization, and optimal control.

This study investigates the impact of antishadowing effects on gluon distribution functions, $G(x,Q^2)$, utilizing the Gribov-Levin-Ryskin-Mueller-Qiu and Zhu-Ruan-Shen (GLR-MQ-ZRS) nonlinear equation within the small-$x$ regime. Here, $x$ represents the momentum fraction (Bjorken variable) and $Q^2$ denotes the squared four-momentum transfer or photon virtuality. We solved the GLR-MQ-ZRS equation for the kinematic domain $10^{-6} \leq x \leq 10^{-2}$ and $5\,GeV^2 \leq Q^2 \leq 100\, GeV^2$ by assuming Regge-like gluon behavior. The solutions for $G(x,Q^2)$ were derived under two specific scenarios: (a) a fixed strong coupling constant, $\alpha_s$, and (b) the leading-order QCD dependence of $\alpha_s$ on $Q^2$. A comparative analysis was conducted to contrast the gluon distribution with and without antishadowing effects. Our findings for $G(x,Q^2)$ were benchmarked against NNPDF3.0, CT14, and PDF4LHC datasets, as well as results from the IMParton C++ package. Furthermore, using these solutions, we predicted the $x$ and $Q^2$ evolution of the logarithmic derivative of the proton's $F_2$ structure function, $dF_2 (x,Q^2)/d\ln Q^2$, incorporating both leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD contributions from gluon-quark splitting kernels. Our predictions for this derivative show reasonable agreement with experimental data from HERA's H1 detector.

How do social-ecological systems evolve? In 2002, Holling and colleagues introduced the concept of Panarchy, framing these systems as interconnected adaptive cycles driven by the dynamic interplay between novelty and efficiency across various scales. Originally a conceptual framework utilizing metaphors, panarchy has since garnered significant scholarly attention across multiple disciplines, continuously inspiring new theoretical developments. Nearly two decades after its inception, this review examines how the concept has been applied, tested, expanded, and refined by integrating qualitative methods with machine learning. Through document analysis coding features in 42 scientific papers and complementing this with topic modeling of 2,177 documents, we identify the adaptive cycle as the most frequently cited element of panarchy. While challenges persist in empirically validating the underlying metaphor, recent theoretical and empirical advancements provide promising directions for future research.

We determine equilibrium emittances and damping times arising from synchrotron radiation in coupled storage ring lattices by projecting standard synchrotron radiation integrals onto the normal modes of the coupled motion. To account for orbit distortion, we compute off-axis contributions to these radiation integrals. We also present explicit formulas designed for rapid calculation, which have been integrated into the interactive lattice design software OPA.

Translating perceptual soundscape attributes between languages poses a significant challenge, demanding high fidelity in both psychoacoustic and psycholinguistic dimensions for the target audience. Given the inherently subjective nature of human perception, relying solely on small focus groups or expert panels for translation risks producing meanings that distort or deviate from the source language within non-expert contexts. This study introduces a quantitative evaluation method grounded in the circumplex model of soundscape perception to assess overall translation quality against a set of criteria. As a pilot application, we demonstrated this framework by evaluating the English-to-Thai translation of soundscape attributes.

Current methods for detecting personalized salience zones on web pages fail to account for the temporal dynamics of user gaze or changes in page content. To address this, the paper introduces "visit intention," a metric reflecting a user's visual attention across specific short time windows and distinct areas of interest. This indicator identifies regions a user is likely to focus on within a given timeframe without necessitating knowledge of the site's structure during each window. The proposed approach capitalizes on population-level general gaze patterns and individual visual kinetics. Experimental results demonstrate that multilabel classification models can effectively predict these areas using data from a small user cohort, achieving an average AUC of 84.3%, an accuracy of 79%, and an individual area-of-interest accuracy of 77%. Additionally, visual kinetics features were consistently selected across all cross-validation sets.

Small and medium-sized enterprises depend on comprehensive web analytics to understand their market landscape and competitive position. Focused crawlers address this need by systematically crawling and indexing specific web segments. Crucially, these crawlers must rapidly identify previously unindexed pages; since discovering new pages requires following new outbound links, accurately predicting such links is highly practical. While existing literature offers numerous feature designs for forecasting web changes, this study provides a structured analysis of the problem by treating new outbound links as the primary prediction target. We unify previous feature approaches into a taxonomy organized along two dimensions: static versus dynamic features, and page-specific features versus network-context features. Within this framework, supplemented by novel features (primarily dynamic network attributes), we identify the most effective predictors for new outbound links. Our primary finding is that the most informative features consist of the recent history of new outbound links on a page and its content-related neighbors. Consequently, we introduce a new "Look Back, Look Around" (LBLA) model that relies exclusively on these features. Using these predictions, we develop various scoring functions to guide focused crawlers toward pages with the highest potential for new outbound links and evaluate their performance. Notably, the LBLA approach demonstrated exceptional efficacy, surpassing models utilizing the most comprehensive feature sets. One of the learners employed is the recent NGBoost method, which assumes a Poisson distribution for new outbound link counts and learns its parameters. This bridges two previously distinct research areas: feature-based predictions and probabilistic modeling. All experiments were conducted on an original dataset provided by a commercial focused crawler.

Identifying reusable sub-routines streamlines decision-making and planning within complex reinforcement learning scenarios. While prior methods attempt to learn these temporal abstractions purely unsupervised by analyzing state-action trajectories generated from policy execution, they suffer from a key limitation: processing each trajectory strictly sequentially. This rigidity prevents the correction of earlier decisions regarding sub-routine boundaries when new data arrives. This paper introduces SloTTAr, a fully parallel framework that combines Sequence Processing Transformers with a Slot Attention module and adaptive computation to unsupervisedly determine the number of sub-routines. We show that SloTTAr surpasses robust baselines in discovering boundary points, even when sequences contain varying numbers of sub-routines, and achieves training speeds up to 7x faster on established benchmarks.

Let $E$ and $F$ denote complex Banach spaces, with $U$ as an open subset of $E$ and $1\leq p\leq\infty$. We define and examine the concept of a Cohen strongly $p$-summing holomorphic mapping from $U$ to $F$, which serves as a holomorphic analogue to strongly $p$-summing linear operators. For these mappings, we derive both Pietsch domination and factorization theorems, alongside an analysis of their linearizations from $\mathcal{G}^\infty(U)$ (the canonical predual of $\mathcal{H}^\infty(U)$) and their transpositions acting on $\mathcal{H}^\infty(U)$. Regarding the space $\mathcal{D}_p^{\mathcal{H}^\infty}(U,F)$, consisting of such mappings equipped with a natural norm $d_p^{\mathcal{H}^\infty}$, we demonstrate that it constitutes a regular Banach ideal of bounded holomorphic mappings, generated by composing with the ideal of strongly $p$-summing linear operators. Furthermore, we establish that the space $(\mathcal{D}_p^{\mathcal{H}^\infty}(U,F^*),d_p^{\mathcal{H}^\infty})$ is isomorphic to the dual of the completion of the tensor product space $\mathcal{G}^\infty(U)\otimes F$, where the latter is endowed with the Chevet--Saphar norm $g_p$.

Contemporary neural networks derive problem insights and compute outputs exclusively from input data. We contend that this approach is not always optimal and that network performance can be substantially enhanced by integrating a query mechanism. This mechanism enables the network to conduct multiple solution attempts during execution and receive feedback regarding the loss value for each trial. To illustrate the potential of this approach, we define an unsupervised loss function for the Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) and theoretically demonstrate that it facilitates the extraction of rich problem-specific information. Subsequently, we introduce QuerySAT, a neural SAT solver equipped with this query mechanism, and show that it surpasses standard neural baselines across a broad spectrum of SAT tasks.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is emerging as a pivotal force in the domain of adaptive interventions (AIs), garnering significant attention in both theoretical and methodological research and gaining widespread traction within health sciences. However, its practical deployment remains constrained by various operational and statistical hurdles, alongside ethical and financial concerns, many of which persist due to inadequate collaboration and communication between applied and methodological scientists. This study seeks to unify these distinct fields, proposing an integrated framework that converges RL, causal inference, and AIs. We present the inaugural comprehensive survey dedicated to RL methodologies for constructing AIs, covering both dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) and just-in-time adaptive interventions in mobile health (mHealth). By delineating the overlaps and distinctions between these two domains and analyzing their implications for RL application, we merge our methodological insights with illustrative case studies from both DTRs and mHealth. Ultimately, we highlight the vast potential for collaboration among researchers in statistics, RL, and healthcare within the adaptive interventions landscape.

Solving partial differential equations in two or more dimensions generates time-dependent fields that exceed the analytical processing limits of the human brain. While scalar reductions offer valuable insights into temporal dynamics, they sacrifice spatial detail. Dynamic Mode Decomposition addresses this trade-off as a data-driven technique that isolates oscillating spatial patterns and their associated frequencies. This paper outlines the algorithm and offers a physical interpretation of the findings by applying the method to progressively complex examples.

We introduce PMC-Patients, a dataset comprising 167,000 patient notes annotated with 3.1 million relevant articles and 293,000 similar patient cases. These notes are derived from specific sections of case reports in PubMed Central, re-distributed under CC BY-NC-SA licenses. Relevance between patients and articles, as well as similarity between patients, are determined by citation relationships within PubMed. To showcase the dataset's utility, we conducted four tasks: Patient Note Recognition (PNR), Patient-Patient Similarity (PPS), Patient-Patient Retrieval (PPR), and Patient-Article Retrieval (PAR). In summary, PMC-Patients offers the largest-scale collection of high-quality patient notes, featuring diverse conditions, easy accessibility, and extensive annotations.

Dynamic Adversarial Data Collection (DADC) involves human annotators identifying examples that models struggle to predict, resulting in systems that are more robust against adversarial and out-of-domain attacks and harder for humans to deceive. However, DADC is more time-consuming and expensive per example than traditional methods. This study investigates whether DADC's benefits can be retained without the associated costs. To address this, we propose Generative Annotation Assistants (GAAs)—generator-in-the-loop models that offer real-time suggestions for annotators to accept, edit, or reject. We evaluate this approach across twenty experimental settings for extractive question answering (QA), covering both standard and adversarial data collection. Our results show that GAAs deliver significant efficiency gains with a speed-up of over 30%, while simultaneously improving model fooling rates by more than 5x. Furthermore, models trained on GAA-assisted data demonstrate superior performance on various QA tasks compared to those trained using standard adversarial data collection.

By modeling the magnetic interaction of a neutron star binary as a dipole, we incorporate magnetic effects into the system's Newtonian and inspiral dynamics through an equivalent one-body framework. During the inspiral phase, we analyze the impact of magnetic interactions on the generated waveforms and derive explicit formulas for the reduction in stellar separation, the time required to reach a minimum radius, gravitational luminosity, and shifts in gravitational wave frequency, all within the quadrupole approximation. For the estimated magnetic field strength of these binaries ($\sim 10^{16} \, \text{G}$), we demonstrate that the influence on observable quantities is comparable to the 2PN correction, approaching the sensitivity limits of gravitational wave observatories. Additionally, we examine scenarios where the magnetic field might exert a more substantial effect.

This work investigates the geometric properties of noncommutative de Sitter space by calculating the Riemann and Ricci curvature tensors, energy, and Laplacian. Specifically, we establish that fuzzy de Sitter space constitutes an Einstein space, satisfying $R_{ab}=-3\zeta\,\eta_{ab}$. Within the noncommutative frame formalism, the Laplacian is found to be non-Hermitian, resulting in nonunitary evolution. However, when symmetrically ordered, it assumes the standard quadratic form $\Delta=\Pi_a\Pi^a$ (acting on functions $\Psi\in {\cal H}$ in representation space), allowing us to determine its eigenstates and analyze its spectrum. These findings serve as a foundational step for future research into the scalar field Laplacian, defined as $\Delta = [\Pi_a, [\Pi^a,\ ]]$, and its associated propagator.

We identify specific non-Markovian dynamics that inherently prevent information backflow. However, when the order of applying two such dynamical maps becomes indefinite, the resulting effective channel can exhibit information backflow, a phenomenon specifically activated by the quantum SWITCH. Unlike these cases, even using multiple copies of such channels in series or parallel configurations fails to trigger backflow. Our analysis of the underlying mechanisms reveals that the quantum SWITCH causes the breakdown of both complete positive (CP) divisibility and positive (P) divisibility after its action, thereby inducing information backflow. These findings provide new insights into the fundamental reasons behind the advantages offered by the quantum SWITCH.

Second-order optimization leverages curvature data from the objective function to accelerate convergence, but these methods are often impractical due to the costly computation of the Hessian matrix, which hinders scalability. Consequently, the most prevalent approaches rely on first-order approximations that omit curvature details because efficient computation methods were lacking. This paper introduces HesScale, a scalable technique for approximating the Hessian's diagonal to integrate second-order information efficiently. We demonstrate that HesScale matches the computational complexity of backpropagation. Experiments in supervised classification reveal that HesScale delivers high approximation accuracy, enabling scalable and efficient second-order optimization.

Line-of-sight obstructions pose a significant threat to the reliability and latency of millimeter wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) communication networks. This study introduces a method utilizing LiDAR sensory data to gain situational awareness of the communication environment and forecast dynamic link blockages proactively. This capability enables the network to make timely decisions regarding hand-offs and beam switching, thereby improving overall performance. We formalize the problem of LiDAR-aided blockage prediction and offer the inaugural real-world demonstration of this approach within mmWave systems. Specifically, we created a large-scale dataset, aligned with the DeepSense 6G architecture, featuring concurrent LiDAR and mmWave measurements in outdoor vehicular settings. Subsequently, we developed an efficient algorithm for denoising LiDAR data (via static cluster removal) and a machine learning model designed to predict dynamic link blockages ahead of time. Utilizing this real-world dataset, our LiDAR-aided method demonstrated 95% accuracy in predicting blockages occurring within 100ms and over 80% accuracy for those happening within one second. When applied to proactive hand-offs, the proposed solution could potentially reduce network latency by an order of magnitude, underscoring its potential as a viable strategy for overcoming blockage challenges in mmWave and sub-THz networks.

Shell-model computations are essential for understanding diverse nuclear properties, yet they typically demand extensive repeated calculations for parameter tuning and uncertainty assessment. To alleviate this computational load, we introduce a novel workflow leveraging Eigenvector Continuation (EC). This technique allows for the efficient approximation of eigenpairs under a specific Hamiltonian by utilizing previously sampled eigenvectors. We validate EC as an emulator for the valence shell-model, marking its first application to electromagnetic transition matrix elements. Additionally, we propose a new EC application for preprocessing, where Lanczos iterations are initiated using approximate eigenvectors to accelerate subsequent research cycles. With EC, eigenvectors generated during parameter optimization do not need to be discarded merely because their eigenvalues deviate significantly from experimental data; instead, they can be retained as accumulated knowledge.

Detecting lesions in digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) is a critical yet difficult task, primarily due to the extremely low prevalence of images containing tumors. Because of this scarcity of labeled data, large-scale deep learning models and computationally heavy algorithms often fail in this domain. This paper introduces a practical and lightweight backbone designed to enhance tumor detection accuracy. Specifically, we propose a novel modification to the visual transformer (ViT) that links feature patches of tumors with healthy breast tissue backgrounds, creating a more robust framework for detection. To our knowledge, this is the first application of a Transformer-based backbone for object detection in medical imaging. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly boosts lesion detection accuracy and reduces the need for labeled data compared to typical ViT architectures. Furthermore, with augmented tumor data, our approach substantially outperforms both the Faster R-CNN model and the state-of-the-art SWIN transformer.

This paper addresses the challenge of adaptive Kalman filtering for discrete linear time-varying systems with unknown noise covariance matrices. By employing the measurement difference autocovariance method, a linear least squares cost function is constructed using measurements, along with the process and noise covariance matrices. A Riemannian trust-region optimization technique is then developed to minimize this cost function while guaranteeing that the estimated noise covariance matrices remain symmetric and positive definite. Under conditions of sufficient system excitation, the estimated noise covariance matrices are proven to converge to their true unknown values. Notably, the study demonstrates that the proposed adaptive Kalman filter achieves exponential stability and convergence to the optimal Kalman filter (with known noise covariances) under the relatively mild assumptions of uniform observability and uniform controllability. Finally, numerical simulations on a linear time-varying system validate the effectiveness of the proposed adaptive filtering algorithm.

Decision diagrams are becoming an essential component of modern solvers for discrete optimization. However, as a relatively young field, the decision diagram community is still integrating the extensive technique libraries that conventional solvers have developed over decades. Drawing inspiration from warm-start methods used in traditional solvers, we addressed a key challenge facing decision diagram-based approaches: while wider diagrams offer greater utility, they are increasingly expensive to generate, particularly with many variables. We introduce a technique called "peel-and-bound," which extracts a sub-graph from previously constructed diagrams to serve as the initial structure for subsequent iterations. Applied to the sequence ordering problem, our results demonstrate that the peel-and-bound scheme produces stronger bounds than a branch-and-bound approach using identical propagators, while doing so at a significantly lower computational cost.

Social media has evolved into a primary channel for daily interaction and information exchange online, yet posts frequently turn aggressive and toxic, particularly regarding controversial or political subjects. Radicalization, extreme rhetoric, and specifically online misogyny directed at public women have emerged as disturbing characteristics of digital discourse. This study introduces a methodological framework to address how women, their experiences, and choices are assaulted within polarized social media responses. Drawing on existing theories and detection techniques for misogyny, we propose a classification system that accounts for eleven distinct explicit and implicit layers of online misogyny. We further apply these categories to a case study examining the aggression directed at Amber Heard concerning her domestic violence allegations against Johnny Depp. Finally, we assess the efficacy of Google's Perspective API—a standard tool for identifying toxic language—in detecting gender-based discrimination as toxicity. Our findings reveal that a significant portion of online misogyny, particularly when expressed implicitly rather than through explicit expletives, remains undetected by automated systems.

Compact binaries represent a vital category of gravitational-wave (GW) sources detectable by both existing and upcoming observatories, serving as a testing ground for general relativity (GR) under the extreme conditions of strong-field dynamics. This study utilizes GWs from inspiraling binary neutron stars and binary black holes to explore predictions made by alternative theories, such as scalar-tensor gravity, specifically regarding dipolar gravitational radiation (DGR) and a varying gravitational constant. Employing the parametrized post-Einsteinian framework, we incorporate parameters for both effects into the inspiral waveform of compact binaries and apply Fisher-information-matrix analysis to derive simultaneous constraints. Generally, space-based detectors yield tighter limits compared to ground-based ones. The most stringent constraints, achieved when the time to coalescence approaches the operational lifetime of space-based missions, are $\sigma_B < 3\times10^{-11}$ for the DGR parameter $B$ and $\sigma_{\dot{G}}/G < 7\times10^{-9} \, {\rm yr}^{-1}$ for the variation in $G$. Furthermore, we examine the correlation between these two phenomena and emphasize the necessity of accounting for both to obtain more realistic outcomes.

The primary mechanism limiting gradients in tokamak equilibria with negative triangularity ($\delta$) is instability in high toroidal mode number ($n$) ballooning modes, which blocks access to strong H-mode regimes when $\delta\ll0$. To assess how this mechanism applies to reactor scenarios, we modeled infinite-$n$ ballooning stability as a function of internal profiles and equilibrium shape using the CHEASE and BALOO codes. Although the critical $\delta$ needed to avoid $2^\mathrm{nd}$ stability to high-$n$ modes exhibits a complex dependence on shaping parameters such as aspect ratio, elongation, and squareness, negative triangularity configurations are consistently unable to reach the $2^\mathrm{nd}$ stability region. This suggests that negative triangularity reactors will likely sustain L-mode-like operation. Achieving high-$n$ $2^\mathrm{nd}$ stability requires the local shear across the entire bad curvature region to be sufficiently negative to counteract destabilization on the low-field side. Furthermore, scalings for the ballooning-limited pedestal height are provided as a function of plasma parameters to assist in future scenario development.

With noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors growing in size and complexity, their role as general-purpose quantum simulators will depend on algorithms utilizing the Trotter-Suzuki expansion. We conducted quantum simulations on a small, highly accurate quantum processor, demonstrating that simulation accuracy can be optimized by balancing algorithmic (Trotter) errors against the specific native errors inherent to the hardware. Additionally, we investigated the interplay among native errors, Trotter errors, and the onset of chaos, as observed through measurements of the time-averaged fidelity-out-of-time-ordered-correlator.

Utilizing sign-problem-free quantum Monte Carlo methods, we examine a continuum model of the graphene-vacuum interface within the quantum Hall regime, enabling the exploration of how topology and strong interactions interact in large-scale graphene quantum Hall edges. Our analysis centers on the topological phase transition from a symmetry-protected gapless helical edge state (spin-polarized) to a fully charge-gapped canted-antiferromagnet state characterized by spontaneous symmetry breaking, a process driven by Zeeman energy. Through extensive system size simulations, we characterize the behavior of experimentally accessible quantities across this transition, including spatially and energy-resolved local density of states and local compressibility. Our results reveal distinct kinks in edge dispersion branches and an unexpectedly high bulk charge susceptibility in the canted-antiferromagnet phase, which arises from its Goldstone mode.

TOI-849b is a rare inhabitant of the hot-Neptune desert and holds the distinction of being the densest Neptune-sized planet identified to date. Its extreme closeness to the host star, combined with the lack of a substantial H/He atmosphere above its $40.8 ~M_{\oplus}$ rocky core, challenges current understanding of stellar influence on system evolution. This study investigates how the host star's rotational history affects TOI-849b, specifically examining orbital migration driven by dynamical tides within the stellar convective envelope and high-energy emission. By coupling rotating stellar models of TOI-849 with an orbital evolution code, we analyzed the system's history. Additionally, the JADE code was employed to simulate atmospheric evolution using realistic XUV-fluxes derived from our rotating stellar models. Assuming the planet began at its current distance ($a=0.01598 \rm AU$) with a mass of $40.8~M_{\oplus}$ immediately after the protoplanetary disc dispersed, and testing a wide range of initial stellar rotation rates ($\Omega_{\rm in}$) from $3.2$ to $18~\Omega_{\odot}$, we determined that only initial rates of $\Omega_{\rm in} \leq 5 \Omega_{\odot}$ align with the planet's present position. Higher rotation rates ($> 5 \Omega_{\odot}$) cause the orbit to shift significantly due to efficient dynamical tides. Furthermore, varying the planet's initial mass up to $1~M_{\rm Jup}$ showed no change in tidal efficiency results. Finally, atmospheric evolution simulations using the JADE code across various initial masses (above the $40.8~M_{\oplus}$ core) reveal that the intense XUV-flux received by the planet can strip away the entire envelope within the first 50 Myr, even if the planet originally formed with a mass comparable to Jupiter.

Gene expression critically depends on RNA polymerase II (pol-II) transcription. The kinetics of pol-II traversing the transcribed region dictate both the speed and timing of this process. This study introduces a probabilistic framework for modeling transcription dynamics, calibrated against pol-II occupancy data derived from ChIP-Seq. This model facilitates the estimation of transcription velocity and the reconstruction of temporal pol-II activity profiles at gene promoters. Parameters can be derived through maximum likelihood estimation or Bayesian inference utilizing Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling; the latter offers confidence intervals for estimates and incorporates prior knowledge, such as expected transcription speed ranges from previous studies. Describing pol-II progression along the gene body, the model identifies induction times for transcriptionally active genes. By clustering inferred promoter activity profiles, we can distinguish genes with rapid responses to stimuli and group those sharing activity patterns, suggesting co-regulation. Applying this methodology to ChIP-Seq data from MCF-7 human breast cancer cells treated with estradiol (E2), we measured genome-wide pol-II occupancy. Our calculated transcription speeds align with prior findings for smaller gene sets but extend the analysis across the entire genome. We confirmed the biological relevance of pol-II promoter activity clusters by examining cluster-specific transcription factor binding and canonical pathway enrichment. Results indicate that rapidly induced genes are significantly enriched for estrogen receptor alpha (ER$\alpha$) and FOXA1 binding in their proximal promoter regions.

The repeating fast radio burst FRB 20190520B is situated in a galaxy at redshift $z=0.241$, a location much closer than anticipated given its high dispersion measure of $\rm DM=1205\pm4\ pc\ cm^{-3}$. This study evaluates the consequences of the substantial DM and scattering observed from FRB 20190520B regarding the plasma characteristics of its host galaxy. Analysis of 75 bursts detected by the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope reveals scattering across two scales: a mean temporal delay $\tau(1.41\ {\rm GHz})=10.9\pm1.5$ ms, attributed to the host, and a mean scintillation bandwidth $\nu_{\rm d}(1.41\ {\rm GHz})=0.21\pm0.01$ MHz, attributed to the Milky Way. Balmer line data for the host suggest an H$\alpha$ emission measure (in the galaxy frame) of $\rm EM_s=620$ pc cm$^{-6} \times (T/10^4 {\rm K})^{0.9}$, leading to an inferred $\rm DM_{\rm H\alpha}$ comparable to the FRB DM budget, with $\rm DM_h=1121^{+89}_{-138}$ pc cm$^{-3}$ for plasma temperatures exceeding the typical $10^4$ K. Combining $\tau$ and $\rm DM_h$ provides a nominal constraint on the host galaxy's scattering amplification, $\tilde{F} G=1.5^{+0.8}_{-0.3}$ (pc$^2$ km)$^{-1/3}$, where $\tilde{F}$ characterizes turbulent density fluctuations and $G$ denotes the geometric leverage dependent on the scattering material's location. Under a two-screen scattering model where $\tau$ originates in the host and $\Delta \nu_{\rm d}$ in the Milky Way, the distance between the FRB source and the primary scattering region is estimated to be $\lesssim100$ pc. The scattering and DM contributions from the host galaxy support a new method for estimating FRB redshifts via the $\tau-\rm DM$ relation and align with prior conclusions that scattering in localized FRBs is predominantly caused by plasma within host galaxies and the Milky Way.

Adversarial training has proven effective at enhancing the robustness of image classifiers against white-box attacks, yet its performance against black-box attacks is more complex. This study demonstrates that specific geometric changes to the decision boundaries of deep networks induced by adversarial training can actually benefit certain black-box attack strategies. Specifically, we introduce a metric termed "robustness gain" to illustrate that while adversarial training significantly bolsters defense in white-box settings, it may fail to deliver comparable gains against more realistic decision-based black-box attacks. Furthermore, we show that even minimal perturbation white-box attacks can converge more rapidly against adversarially trained networks than against standard ones.

Thermal X-ray observations of aged radio pulsars indicate that hot spot dimensions are significantly smaller than the polar cap size predicted by a purely dipolar magnetic field. A likely explanation for this discrepancy is that the stellar surface magnetic field deviates substantially from a simple dipole configuration. By applying the conservation of magnetic flux across the region bounded by open field lines, we estimate the surface field strength to be approximately $10^{14}$ G. Given that hot spot temperatures reach a few million Kelvins, the Partially Screened Gap (PSG) model was introduced, positing that the actual polar cap temperature matches a critical threshold. We analyze the relationship between temperature and the area of thermal X-ray emission across various pulsars. Our findings suggest that gap breakdown conditions in the polar cap region lead to either Curvature Radiation (CR) or Inverse Compton Scattering (ICS) as the dominant mechanism. When ICS dominates, the density of secondary plasma with Lorentz factors between $10^{2}$ and $10^{3}$ exceeds that of the CR scenario by at least an order of magnitude. We propose that these two distinct breakdown mechanisms account for mode-changing phenomena, including pulse nulling. Furthermore, measurements of the characteristic spacing between sub-pulses ($P_{2}$) and the interval at which pulse patterns traverse the window ($P_{3}$) have enabled us to establish stricter constraints on avalanche pair production within the PSG.

In hockey, executing passes during power plays is essential for advancing a team toward scoring. Utilizing tracking data and event records from women's ice hockey games in the 2022 Winter Olympics elimination round, we analyze passing dynamics and players' risk-reward strategies during these high-intensity situations. We created a probabilistic passing model that factors in the sequence of arrival at a target and the likelihood of interceptions. This model relies on individual player motion profiles and puck movement physics to calculate the distance each player can reach within the puck's travel time. Additionally, we simulate rink control for both teams and the offensive team's scoring probability. By integrating these elements, we developed new metrics to determine optimal pass locations that maximize either scoring chances or possession retention. Finally, we assessed actual passes made during power plays against these optimal benchmarks to reveal players' risk preferences. These insights can assist coaches in selecting the most appropriate players for power play units based on specific game conditions.

A vast array of significant resources exists online in English, often translated into native tongues to facilitate information exchange among locals with limited English proficiency. However, manual translation remains a laborious, expensive, and time-consuming endeavor. Consequently, machine translation offers a viable solution for converting text between languages without human intervention. Among existing systems, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) stands out as one of the most effective techniques. This study applies NMT to two of India's most morphologically complex languages: English-Tamil and English-Malayalam. We introduce a novel NMT model that integrates Multi-head self-attention with pre-trained Byte-Pair-Encoded (BPE) and MultiBPE embeddings. This approach creates an efficient translation system designed to mitigate the Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) issue, which is particularly challenging for low-resource, morphologically rich Indian languages lacking substantial existing data. Additionally, we gathered corpora from various sources, resolved associated data quality issues, and refined them for optimal use. System performance was assessed using the BLEU score. Experimental results and a comparative survey demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms Google Translate, achieving BLEU scores of 24.34 and 9.78 compared to Google's 9.40 and 5.94, respectively.

We introduce a classical approximation for the peaks of survival resonances that arise when matter waves diffract from absorption potentials. Generally, this simplified model accurately captures the absorption-diffraction process near the Talbot time, addressing a gap in existing classical treatments. For purely imaginary potentials, the classical approach yields results identical to quantum mechanical calculations. By enabling straightforward evolution of phase-space probability densities, the model facilitates a compact analytical expression for survival probability as the effective Planck's constant approaches zero. This work broadens the scope of processes that can be effectively described through classical analogues.

Object insertion stands as a fundamental yet demanding contact-intensive manipulation challenge, particularly when dealing with objects of unknown geometry, which hinders the comprehension of contact configurations between the object and its surroundings. This research investigates aligning objects and environments using a tactile-feedback-driven insertion policy. The insertion process is conceptualized as an episodic policy that cycles through insertion attempts and subsequent pose adjustments. We examine various mechanisms for learning such a policy via Reinforcement Learning. The primary contribution of this paper is demonstrating the feasibility of learning a tactile insertion policy that generalizes across diverse object geometries, alongside an ablation study of critical design choices for the learning agent: 1) learning scheme (supervised vs. reinforcement learning), 2) learning schedule (unguided vs. curriculum learning), 3) sensing modality (force/torque vs. tactile), and 4) tactile representation (tactile RGB vs. tactile flow). Results indicate that the optimal agent configuration (Reinforcement Learning combined with curriculum learning and tactile flow), trained on four objects, achieves an insertion success rate exceeding 85.0% for four novel objects within 3 to 4 attempts. Furthermore, comparing force/torque and tactile sensing reveals that while force/torque policies learn more efficiently, tactile-based policies offer superior generalization capabilities.

We re-examine the transport coefficients governing heavy quarkonia within high-temperature QCD plasmas. Specifically, the thermal width and mass shift of these quarkonia correspond directly to the momentum diffusion coefficient and its dispersive analogue for heavy quarks, respectively. For stationary quarkonium in a plasma, the longitudinal gluon component of the color-singlet self-energy diagram suffices to calculate the leading-order thermal width, while the momentum dependence arises from the transverse gluon channel. Leveraging an effective quarkonium-gluon vertex derived from the dipole interaction of color charges, we analyze the damping rate and the effective rest and kinetic mass shifts of slowly moving quarkonia, comparing these results with the analogous coefficients for heavy quarks.

This paper offers a concise, step-by-step guide to expressing parametric Feynman integrals within scalar perturbative quantum field theory as periods of motives. It reviews the application of motivic Galois theory to the algebro-geometric and categorical foundations of Feynman graphs, covering developments up to the present research frontier. Additionally, it provides a detailed examination of primitive log-divergent Feynman graphs in the context of scalar massless $\phi^4$ quantum field theory.

Unsupervised semantic segmentation seeks to derive high-level semantic representations from low-level visual features without relying on manual annotations. While most current methods follow a bottom-up strategy—grouping pixels into regions based on visual cues or predefined rules—they often struggle to achieve fine-grained segmentation in complex scenes containing multiple objects with similar appearances. In response, we introduce the first top-down framework for unsupervised semantic segmentation designed to handle extremely complicated scenarios. Our approach first extracts rich, high-level structured semantic concepts from large-scale vision data using self-supervised learning, which then serves as a prior to identify potential semantic categories within target datasets. Subsequently, these discovered high-level categories are mapped to low-level pixel features by computing Class Activation Maps (CAMs) relative to specific semantic representations. Finally, these CAMs function as pseudo-labels to train the segmentation module, yielding the ultimate semantic segmentation results. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our top-down method is robust to both object-centric and scene-centric datasets at various semantic granularities, surpassing all existing state-of-the-art bottom-up techniques. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/damo-cv/TransFGU}.

Producing indistinguishable single photons coherently is essential for numerous quantum communication and processing schemes. While solid-state implementations of two-level or three-level spin-$\Lambda$ systems provide notable benefits over atomic versions for this task, they face challenges from environmental-induced decoherence. A common strategy to counteract dephasing involves operating within the weak excitation regime, where excited-state populations remain negligible and coherent scattering outweighs incoherent emission. In this study, we investigate the coherence of photons generated by both two-level and spin-$\Lambda$ solid-state systems. Our findings reveal that the interaction between atomic-like transitions and the crystal lattice's vibronic modes remains constant regardless of driving strength or detuning. By utilizing a polaron master equation, we model the non-Markovian dynamics occurring within ground-state vibrational manifolds. These insights highlight fundamental constraints on photon coherence in solid-state quantum emitters, demonstrating that deterministic single-shot quantum protocols are unattainable and necessitating a shift toward inherently probabilistic methods.

A significant limitation of deploying deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in safety-critical domains stems from their opaque, black-box characteristics, which complicates the verification and monitoring of complex symbolic requirements on trained vision models. This study introduces a straightforward yet robust methodology to ensure that a CNN adheres to symbolic predicate logic rules connecting visual concepts. Notably, this approach is the first to (1) operate without modifying the CNN architecture, (2) incorporate visual concepts that are neither inputs nor outputs of the CNN features, and (3) utilize continuous confidence scores from the CNN. Our method integrates explainable artificial intelligence with logical reasoning in two steps: first, supervised concept embedding analysis is applied post-hoc to enrich CNN outputs with concept representations; second, prior knowledge rules are formulated as truth functions that accept CNN outputs and can be evaluated with minimal computational cost. We examine the application of fuzzy logic, employing continuous truth values, alongside proper output calibration, both of which demonstrate slight theoretical and practical advantages. The proposed framework's applicability is validated on state-of-the-art object detectors across three verification scenarios, illustrating how monitoring for rule violations can effectively uncover detection errors.

The CMS experiment at the LHC, utilizing proton-proton collision data from $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$, searched for the decay of the 125 GeV Higgs boson into a Z boson and either a $\rho^0$(770) or $\phi$(1020) meson. Event selection required the Z boson to decay into electron or muon pairs, while the $\rho$ and $\phi$ mesons decayed into pion and kaon pairs, respectively. No significant excess over the predicted background was observed. Because different polarization states for the Z boson and the $\rho$ or $\phi$ mesons influence signal acceptance, analyses accounted for both longitudinal and transverse polarization scenarios. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the branching fractions for Higgs decays into Z$\rho$ and Z$\phi$ were established at 1.04–1.31% and 0.31–0.40%, respectively. These ranges, reflecting the polarization assumptions, are 740–940 and 730–950 times higher than Standard Model predictions. These findings represent the first experimental constraints on these specific decay channels.

Although magnetic fields can distort neutron stars (NSs), gravitational-wave observations have not yet robustly verified this effect due to the lack of a rapidly rotating Galactic magnetar. However, gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) offer a promising avenue for investigation, as their progenitors may be millisecond magnetars capable of exhibiting magnetic distortions. This paper introduces a method to quantify such distortions within the GRB magnetar framework. Using GRB 070521 as a case study, we establish a relationship between the effective magnetic ellipticity, $\epsilon_{\rm B,eff}$, and the effective surface dipole magnetic field strength, $B_{\rm eff}$, expressed as $\epsilon_{\rm B,eff}\sim 10^{-3}(B_{\rm eff}/10^{15}\rm G)^{2}$. Additionally, we constrain the internal magnetic-field architecture of these magnetars to satisfy $B_{\rm eff}\sim 0.02 <B_{\rm t}>$ and $B_{\rm eff}\sim 0.1B_{\rm t}$, where $<B_{\rm t}>$ represents the volume-averaged internal toroidal field. These constraints can serve as initial conditions for modeling NS magnetospheres. Finally, we discuss the feasibility of validating this approach via gravitational-wave detections.

We introduce an exact and scalable algorithm for one-dimensional Gaussian process regression featuring Matérn correlations with a half-integer smoothness parameter $
u$. This method necessitates only $\mathcal{O}(
u^3 n)$ operations and $\mathcal{O}(
u n)$ storage, yielding a linear-cost solver because $
u$ is typically fixed and small in practical applications. The approach extends to multi-dimensional problems when utilizing either a full or sparse grid design. Grounded in a new theoretical framework for Matérn correlation functions, the method relies on rearranging these functions into compactly supported "kernel packets." Employing a collection of these kernel packets as basis functions generates a sparse covariance matrix representation, which drives the proposed algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that, where applicable, this algorithm significantly outperforms existing alternatives in both computational efficiency and predictive accuracy.

This paper presents findings from a climatological analysis of ionospheric disturbances, utilizing cosmic source observations from the Very Large Array (VLA) Low-frequency Sky Survey (VLSS). By applying ionospheric corrections to the 74 MHz interferometric data used in the VLSS imaging process, we derived fluctuation spectra for total electron content (TEC) gradients across spatial scales ranging from a few to hundreds of kilometers and temporal scales from under a minute to nearly an hour. The dataset covers nearly all times of day and seasons, spanning latitudes from 28°N to 40°N and longitudes from 95°W to 114°W. These fluctuation spectra were binned and averaged based on time of day, season, and levels of geomagnetic (Kp index) and solar (F10.7) activity. The resulting spectra offer a detailed, multi-scale depiction of seasonal and intraday ionospheric variations, revealing wavelike structures at wavelengths between approximately 35 and 250 km. In certain instances, correlations between spectral power and both the Kp index and F10.7 are evident. Furthermore, VLSS data enable measurements of the turbulent power spectrum down to periods of 40 seconds (corresponding to scales of roughly 0.4 km in the E-region). While turbulent activity shows no strong dependence on either the Kp index or F10.7, it appears more pronounced during winter daytime, summer nighttime, and near dusk in spring.

This study establishes an upper limit for the galactic diffuse gamma-ray flux using data from the GAMMA experiment at approximately 175 TeV. The analysis utilized extensive air showers with low muon content, recorded at an altitude of 700 g/cm² on Mt. Aragats in Armenia, applying a 5 GeV energy threshold for muons. At a 95% confidence level, the resulting upper limit for the differential flux at an energy of E=175±25 TeV is determined to be (5.8–7.0)×10⁻¹² [erg m⁻² s⁻¹ sr⁻¹].

A self-dual binary linear code is classified as a Type I code if it contains singly-even codewords, meaning it possesses codewords whose weights are divisible by 2. This paper examines various interesting properties of Type I codes across different lengths. Additionally, we develop a computer-based search program for these codes, leveraging our understanding of their characteristics, and present the computational results obtained through this program.

This article focuses on investigating the quantitative structure of projective symplectic groups $PSp_{4}(q)$ where $q$ is an even integer greater than 2. Specifically, we demonstrate that for these even $q>2$, the groups $PSp_{4}(q)$ are uniquely identified by their orders and the collection of counts for elements sharing the same order. This finding connects directly to the well-established problem posed by J. G. Thompson in 1987 regarding finite simple groups.

This paper tackles utterance-level emotion recognition in dialogues by leveraging commonsense knowledge. We introduce COSMIC, a novel framework that integrates various commonsense components—such as mental states, events, and causal relations—to model interactions between conversational participants. While existing state-of-the-art approaches often struggle with context propagation, detecting emotion shifts, and distinguishing between similar emotion categories, COSMIC overcomes these hurdles by learning distinct commonsense representations. Consequently, it achieves new state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark conversational datasets. The project's code can be accessed at https://github.com/declare-lab/conv-emotion.

This work investigates the acceleration of the recently introduced Local Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent (LPI-GD) method, which addresses empirical risk minimization (ERM) problems. Our analysis focuses on loss functions that are strongly convex, smooth, and possess a condition number $\sigma$, while also assuming $\eta$-Hölder continuity with respect to the data. We establish that the oracle complexity of LPI-GD is $\tilde{O}\left(\sigma m^d \log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$ to achieve an accuracy of $\varepsilon$, where $d$ represents the parameter space dimension and $m$ denotes the size of the approximation grid. Notably, the $m^d$ factor scales as $O((1/\varepsilon)^{d/2\eta})$. While LPI-GD already demonstrates superior oracle complexity compared to standard Gradient Descent (GD) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in specific regimes, we introduce two accelerated variants for ERM that achieve an oracle complexity of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\sigma} m^d \log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$. Furthermore, we present the first empirical evaluation of local polynomial interpolation-based gradient methods, confirming that LPI-GD outperforms both GD and SGD in certain scenarios and that our proposed acceleration techniques successfully enhance performance.

AI-Driven Development Environments (AIDEs) merge the capabilities of advanced artificial intelligence with integrated development environments such as Visual Studio Code and JetBrains IntelliJ. By utilizing large-scale language models and extensive repositories of open-source code, AIDEs aim to automate numerous routine programming tasks. However, their adoption introduces significant challenges, including concerns over bias, legal compliance, security risks, and the implications for learning to code.

This work focuses on synthesizing distributed control policies for homogeneous mobile sensor swarms to sustain a target spatial arrangement within a geophysical flow environment. Assuming the robots possess a map identifying Lagrangian coherent structure (LCS) boundaries, we develop agent-level hybrid control strategies that exploit local fluid dynamics and ambient environmental noise to preserve the desired formation. We rigorously analyze the stability of the resulting ensemble dynamics. To validate the approach, we employ a wind-driven multi-gyre flow model—motivated by realistic quasi-geostrophic ocean predictions of double-gyre patterns—to demonstrate feasibility and contrast our method against a baseline deterministic allocation strategy. Finally, the efficacy of the control strategy is confirmed using empirical flow data from our coherent structure experimental testbed.

Bayesian neural networks aim to merge the robust predictive capabilities of standard neural networks with formal uncertainty quantification within a Bayesian framework. Nevertheless, it is still ambiguous how to assign a meaningful prior distribution to network parameters when these are projected into the network's output space. To address this, we propose a solution that allows users to specify an appropriate Gaussian process covariance function for a given task. Our method constructs a "ridgelet prior" for the network parameters, which approximates the specified Gaussian process in the output space. Unlike previous research on the relationship between neural networks and Gaussian processes, our analysis is non-asymptotic, offering finite sample-size error bounds. This demonstrates the universality of Bayesian neural networks, proving they can approximate any Gaussian process with a sufficiently regular covariance function. Our experimental evaluation serves as a proof-of-concept, showing that the ridgelet prior can outperform unstructured priors on regression tasks where a suitable Gaussian process prior is available.

Amid the growing deployment of 5G and beyond networks, the surge in machine-type communications (MTC) devices presents significant challenges for network management, necessitating efficient support for massive connectivity within constrained resources. In response, Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has emerged as a promising solution for random access in MTC scenarios. This paper introduces a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework tailored for NOMA-based random access networks employing truncated channel inversion power control. Under this scheme, MTC devices probabilistically select from a set of predefined power levels for transmission, adhering to channel inversion principles while respecting maximum power limits. Due to stochastic channel fading and power constraints, devices are classified into distinct types based on their achievable power levels. To balance high throughput with inter-device fairness, the study formulates two optimization objectives: maximizing the minimum long-term expected throughput across all devices and maximizing the geometric mean of their long-term expected throughput. A policy-based deep reinforcement learning method is then utilized to dynamically adjust transmission probabilities, thereby solving these optimization problems. Comprehensive simulations are presented to validate the effectiveness and advantages of the proposed approach.

This work introduces a nonuniform quantized decoder for polar codes, designed with quantizers optimized to minimize quantization distortion. By employing dynamic programming to derive these quantizers, we establish their optimality. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed decoder, utilizing 5-bit nonuniform quantization, incurs less than 0.1 dB performance degradation compared to conventional floating-point decoders, significantly surpassing the capabilities of prior uniform quantized decoders for polar codes.

Partial PT symmetry has been investigated for non-Hermitian quadratic boson operators derived from a bi-orthogonal vector set in C². This symmetry behavior is analyzed within Fock space, modeled as a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). The study examines the reality of eigenvalues and their relationship to the existence or breaking of this symmetry, utilizing a deformation parameter that introduces non-Hermiticity.

Temporal grounding involves identifying specific video segments within unedited footage based on a textual query. This study is the first to examine superficial biases inherent to this task and introduces a new targeted solution. We find that current temporal grounding models excessively depend on visual biases, such as a preference for frequent concepts or specific time intervals. This reliance results in poor generalization performance when models are tested across different scenarios. To address this, we introduce the Debiased Temporal Language Localizer (DebiasTLL), a method designed to stop models from simply memorizing these biases and instead force them to ground queries based on genuine cross-modal relationships. DebiasTLL trains two models simultaneously; significant discrepancies in their predictions for a given sample indicate a higher likelihood of bias. Leveraging this informative discrepancy, we develop a data re-weighing strategy to mitigate these biases. We evaluated the proposed method in cross-scenario temporal grounding tasks using heterogeneous training and testing data. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art competitors.

In biomedical research, assessing treatment effect heterogeneity is crucial for advancing personalized medicine. The primary objectives of this analysis involve estimating treatment impacts within clinically meaningful subgroups and forecasting which patient populations would benefit from specific interventions. Traditional methods typically rely on parametric modeling to evaluate subgroup effects, making them vulnerable to model misspecification. This manuscript proposes a model-free semiparametric approach designed to efficiently assess heterogeneous treatment effects across multiple subgroups simultaneously using the one-step targeted maximum-likelihood estimation (TMLE) framework. Furthermore, when dealing with a large number of subgroups, we introduce a variation of one-step TMLE that remains robust against small estimated propensity scores in finite samples. Simulation results indicate that our method yields significant finite-sample improvements over conventional techniques. Additionally, a case study reveals the potential for treatment effect heterogeneity associated with the rs12916-T allele—a proxy for statin use—in reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease.

This research investigates tensor-on-tensor regression, aiming to link tensor responses with tensor covariates using a low-rank parameter tensor or matrix, even when the intrinsic rank is unknown. We introduce Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) and Riemannian Gauss-Newton (RGN) algorithms, addressing the unknown rank challenge by analyzing rank over-parameterization. We offer the first convergence guarantees for general tensor-on-tensor regression, demonstrating that RGD and RGN achieve linear and quadratic convergence, respectively, to a statistically optimal estimate in both correctly parameterized and over-parameterized regimes. Our theoretical findings highlight an interesting property: Riemannian optimization methods inherently adapt to over-parameterization without requiring implementation changes. Additionally, we establish the statistical-computational gap in scalar-on-tensor regression using a direct low-degree polynomial argument. Our theory uncovers a "blessing of the statistical-computational gap" in tensor-on-tensor regression for tensors of order three or higher, where the sample size needed for computation aligns with that required for moderate rank over-parameterization in feasible estimators, a benefit absent in matrix settings. This indicates that moderate rank over-parameterization is effectively "cost-free" regarding sample size for higher-order tensor regression. Finally, simulation studies are presented to validate the proposed methods' advantages and support our theoretical conclusions.

The enhanced memory and processing power of modern edge devices enable significant advancements in edge intelligence. Specifically within computer vision, adapting Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) structures and parameters to match input data distributions results in systems with reduced memory usage, latency, and power consumption. However, because edge devices face constraints on both compute resources and memory, it is essential for systems to forecast the training process's latency and memory requirements. This prediction allows for the identification of optimal network topologies and device pairings to ensure efficient adaptation. This paper introduces perf4sight, an automated approach for building precise models that estimate CNN training memory footprint and latency for a specific device and network architecture. This capability facilitates the swift selection of network topologies suitable for retraining on edge devices with minimal resource overhead. Utilizing PyTorch and targeting the NVIDIA Jetson TX2, the proposed models achieve 95% and 91% accuracy, respectively, in predicting training memory footprint and latency across a diverse range of networks, thereby paving the way for efficient network adaptation on edge GPUs.

This paper introduces and examines a wireless communication system supported by an aerial reconfigurable intelligent surface (aerial-RIS). Accounting for practical composite fading channels, the study models air-to-ground (A2G) links using Namkagami-m small-scale fading and inverse-Gamma large-scale shadowing. To assess the delay-limited performance, we derive a tight, closed-form approximation for the end-to-end outage probability (OP). Furthermore, addressing the analytical intractability of mobile environments, we employ machine learning-based prediction to evaluate the mobile aerial-RIS-aided system's performance. By incorporating the three-dimensional (3D) spatial mobility of the aerial-RIS, we construct a deep neural network (DNN) to precisely forecast the OP. Our findings demonstrate that: (i) fading and shadowing conditions significantly influence the OP, (ii) increasing the number of reflecting elements enhances the energy efficiency (EE) of the aerial-RIS, and (iii) the aerial-RIS-aided system surpasses conventional relaying systems in performance.

This white paper examines the path toward deploying broadband connectivity in upcoming 6G wireless networks. It evaluates diverse use cases, ranging from extreme capacity with peak data rates reaching 1 Tbps to significantly boosting typical speeds to support broadband access at railway velocities up to 1000 km/h. Achieving these objectives requires evolving terrestrial networks and integrating them with satellite systems to enable autonomous operations and interconnected structures. We posit that realizing these broadband goals necessitates several enablers across infrastructure, spectrum, and protocol/algorithmic domains. At the infrastructure level, we highlight ultra-massive MIMO (potentially via holographic radio), intelligent reflecting surfaces, scalable user-centric cell-free networking, integrated access and backhaul, and unified space-terrestrial networks. Regarding spectrum, networks must seamlessly leverage sub-6 GHz bands for coverage and device spatial multiplexing, while higher frequencies drive peak point-to-point rates. This trajectory involves terahertz communications, supplemented by visible light communications where appropriate. On the protocol and algorithmic front, enablers include enhanced coding, modulation, and waveforms to minimize latency, maximize reliability, and reduce complexity, with varied solutions tailored to specific use cases. Resource efficiency can be further optimized through combinations of full-duplex radios, rate-splitting-based interference management, machine-learning-driven optimization, coded caching, and broadcasting.

This paper introduces a method to align sentence representations from various languages into a shared embedding space, enabling semantic similarity calculations (both cross-lingual and monolingual) via a straightforward dot product. We fine-tune pre-trained language models using a translation ranking task. Unlike prior work by Feng et al. (2020), which relies on sentences within the same batch as negatives and risks encountering easy negatives, we adapt the MoCo framework (He et al., 2020) to enhance alignment quality. Our experimental results demonstrate that the sentence representations generated by our model achieve new state-of-the-art performance on multiple tasks, including Tatoeba en-zh similarity search (Artetxe and Schwenk, 2019b), BUCC en-zh bitext mining, and semantic textual similarity across seven datasets.

Sustained autonomy represents a highly sought-after capability for robots, particularly the ability to repeatedly execute tasks over extended periods with high reproducibility and robustness. This trait is vital for advancing robotics in precision agriculture, such as aiding humans in monitoring and harvesting crops across vast orchards. Focusing on this application, we detail an ongoing initiative deploying an autonomous mobile robot within a vineyard to gather data over several months. The primary objective is to collect information from identical locations at various times to analyze how environmental changes affect mapping and localization. This study presents a map-based localization analysis using four data sessions. We identify potential failures occurring when the pre-existing map diverges visually from the current environment and propose LTS-Net, a solution designed to extract stable temporal features to enhance long-term 4D localization outcomes.

Perceived as undesirable, inconsistency in pairwise comparison judgments has prompted researchers to develop various reduction and correction techniques. However, we argue that such inconsistency reveals distinct mindsets among decision-makers, which must be integrated into recommendation generation for decision support. To this end, we examine spanning tree analysis, an emerging method for pairwise comparisons that captures multiple mindsets through a plurality of vectors representing different spanning trees. Currently, these multiple vectors are typically merged into a single preference vector, thereby discarding information regarding the diversity of mindsets. To retain this information, we introduce a novel methodology inspired by Stochastic Multi-criteria Acceptability Analysis. By evaluating all alternative rankings associated with these varying mindsets, our approach calculates the probability of an alternative achieving a specific rank and the likelihood of one alternative being preferred over another. Given that the exponential number of spanning trees makes exhaustive enumeration impractical, we propose estimating these probabilities via statistical sampling of the trees. Furthermore, our method is advantageous because it accommodates incomplete sets of pairwise comparisons. We validate its utility through both a didactic example and a real-world application involving the selection of a Telecom backbone infrastructure for rural regions.

We examine scalar two-dimensional quantum field theories characterized by a factorizing S-matrix possessing poles within the physical strip.
