Building on prior research where we defined bound state operators and proposed candidate observables for wedges, this study demonstrates that, under specific S-matrix constraints, establishing the strong commutativity of these candidates reduces to proving the essential self-adjointness of the sum of the left and right bound state operators. We establish this essential self-adjointness up to the two-particle sector.

This study introduces recent Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) observations of the pulsar J1740+1000, confirming an unusual spectral turnover at 260 MHz that deviates from typical pulsar behavior. We demonstrate that interferometric imaging yields more precise flux estimates for this object compared to conventional methods like beamformed observations. Ultimately, we conclude that current calibration and imaging techniques are well-suited to facilitate a more thorough investigation of the interstellar medium's impact on point-like sources at very low frequencies in the near future.

The graph model is becoming an increasingly prevalent method for representing complex data. Unlike relational models, graphs excel at performing analytical tasks on such intricate datasets. Given that vast amounts of data remain stored in relational tables, understanding how to convert this data into graph structures is essential. This paper introduces a comprehensive mapping process capable of transforming any relational database—both its schema and instance—into a property graph database. Distinct from existing mapping approaches, our solution maintains the three core mapping attributes: information preservation, semantic preservation, and query preservation. Furthermore, we examine the translation of any SQL query into an equivalent Cypher query, ensuring the practicality of our approach. Since current solutions are either incomplete or rely on impractical query languages, this work stands as the first complete and practical method for mapping relations to graphs.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are increasingly recognized as a pivotal technology for enhancing spectral efficiency in 6G networks. While previous studies predominantly focused on reflective RIS, this paper introduces and experimentally validates a novel transmissive RIS design. The proposed 2-bit transmissive element employs a penetration structure that integrates a 1-bit current-reversible dipole with a 90° digital phase shifter derived from a quadrature hybrid coupler. A prototype consisting of a 16×16 element array was designed, fabricated, and tested to confirm the design's feasibility. Measurements of phase shift and insertion loss confirmed the element's 2-bit phase modulation capabilities. When illuminated by a horn antenna, the prototype achieved a peak broadside gain of 22.0 dBi at 27 GHz, with two-dimensional beamforming validated across scan angles up to ±60°. Experimental results from the RIS-aided communication system demonstrate that the transmissive RIS, by providing additional gain and beam steering, can increase data rates, lower transmit power, enhance signal penetration through obstacles, and dynamically adapt to varying propagation directions.

This paper introduces a field redefinition invariant Lagrange multiplier (LM) formalism that incorporates new ghost-like fields, similar to Lee-Yang ghosts. These ghost fields serve two purposes: they restore the field redefinition invariance inherent in the standard path integral of LM theory and simultaneously offset the extra contributions arising from the LM fields. We contend that the additional degrees of freedom introduced by the standard LM fields must be neutralized by those of the ghost fields. Consequently, within this invariant formalism, the doubling of degrees of freedom typically associated with LM fields does not occur.

This work generalizes the periodicity of birational rowmotion for rectangular posets to scenarios where the underlying field is substituted with a noncommutative ring, provided specific conditions are met. This achievement confirms a conjecture proposed in 2014. The proof employs a new methodology and stands independently.

We examine labelings of a finite poset $P$ using $|P| + 2$ elements from a ring $\mathbb{K}$: one label for each element of $P$ and two constant labels for the added top and bottom elements of $\hat{P}$. *Birational rowmotion* acts as a partial map on these labelings. Initially defined by Einstein and Propp for $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$, it serves as a lifting (through detropicalization) of *piecewise-linear rowmotion*, a map acting on the order polytope $\mathcal{O}(P) := \{\text{order-preserving } f: P \to[0,1]\}$. This polytope-based map, in turn, extends the established rowmotion map on the set of order ideals (or order filters) of $P$, which correspond to the vertices of $\mathcal{O}(P)$. While dynamical properties of these combinatorial maps do not always carry over to the birational level, any result established at the birational level necessarily implies the corresponding combinatorial result. By allowing $\mathbb{K}$ to be noncommutative, we further extend the birational framework, though some properties are consequently lost in this transition.

In 2014, the authors provided the initial proof of periodicity for birational rowmotion on rectangular posets (where $P$ is a product of two chains) for $\mathbb{K}$ as a field, hypothesizing that it persists (in a suitably twisted form) for noncommutative cases. In this paper, we establish this noncommutative periodicity alongside a related antipodal reciprocity formula. We conclude with conjectures regarding periodicity for other posets and address whether these findings can be extended to (noncommutative) semirings.

This study examines magnetic domain wall (DW) dynamics in uniaxial and biaxial nanowires subjected to a thermal gradient (TG). Results indicate that DWs move toward the hotter end in both types of nanowires, driven primarily by the transfer of magnonic angular momentum to the DW. While hard (shape) anisotropy in biaxial nanowires provides an extra torque that results in higher DW speeds compared to uniaxial ones, the relationship between damping and velocity behaves counterintuitively: DW speed increases with lower damping and decreases as damping rises, contrary to standard expectations. This anomaly is attributed to the potential formation of standing spin-waves alongside traveling ones when the propagation length of thermally generated spin-waves exceeds the nanowire's length. Conversely, at higher damping levels, DW speed drops because the magnon propagation length shortens. These insights hold promise for the development of spintronic devices, such as racetrack memory.

Enhancing the accuracy of machine learning models is insufficient; trustworthiness must also be improved to construct resilient AI for safety-critical domains like healthcare, finance, and automotive sectors. To address this, we introduce a multi-agent framework integrating human and machine agents. Within this system, a checker agent assigns and ranks trust scores for individual instances using an agreement-based approach that penalizes both overconfidence and overcautiousness. Subsequently, an improver agent identifies anomalous cases via a safe, human-defined rule-based filter, acquires human labels, applies geometric data augmentation, and retrains the model using transfer learning on the augmented data. Evaluations on corrupted MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets demonstrate that this approach yields gains in both accuracy and trust scores with only a minimal increase in labeled data compared to baseline methods.

The ATLAS detector analyzed the complete Run 2 dataset from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV to measure both inclusive and differential charge asymmetries in top-quark production. This analysis combined single-lepton and dilepton $t\bar{t}$ decay channels, applying fully Bayesian unfolding to correct for detector distortions. Within the dilepton channel, the leptonic charge asymmetry was specifically determined, and the findings were compared against Standard Model predictions. The results reveal a charge asymmetry excess relative to the zero hypothesis with a significance of 4.7 standard deviations.

Stock trend forecasting has emerged as a prominent research area drawing significant interest within the financial sector. Although deep learning techniques have yielded encouraging outcomes, they still face constraints, particularly in extracting clean features from raw stock data. This paper proposes an \emph{Augmented Disentanglement Distillation (ADD)} method designed to eliminate interfering features from noisy raw data. Specifically, we introduce: 1) a disentanglement architecture that isolates excess returns from market information to prevent mutual interference in predictions; 2) a dynamic self-distillation mechanism integrated within this framework to filter out other implicit interference factors; and 3) a novel sample augmentation strategy leveraging the decoder module to enhance training based on distinct excess and market features, thereby boosting performance. Experiments conducted on Chinese stock market data demonstrate that our method substantially enhances both stock trend forecasting accuracy and actual investment returns through backtesting, underscoring the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

We applied wavelet decomposition to calculate the Hurst exponent, a scaling metric reflecting long-range temporal behavior, for 46 long and 22 short Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed by the Fermi satellite's Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM). The analysis reveals that the mean Hurst exponent for short GRBs is substantially lower than that of long GRBs. This distinct difference could function as an unbiased criterion for classifying short versus long GRBs.

This paper outlines the rationale for structuring a third-semester BSc program. The initiative seeks to foster a feedback-driven atmosphere through assessment for learning and the gradual tracking of student advancement [Vleuten et al, 2012, "A model for programmatic assessment fit for purpose"]. Learning outcomes are designed to promote higher-order cognitive abilities, in line with [Biggs & Tang, 2011,"Teaching for quality learning at university: what the student does"]. Drawing on [Dochy et al. 2018, "Creating Impact Through Future Learning: The High Impact Learning that Lasts (HILL) Model"], various mechanisms are implemented to enhance focus and motivation.

This paper introduces SbF-Pruner, a novel sensitivity-based filter pruning algorithm designed to learn filter importance scores for every layer through an end-to-end process. By deriving these scores directly from filter weights, our approach captures correlations among filters within each layer. Furthermore, simultaneously training pruning scores across all layers allows the method to address layer interdependencies, which is crucial for identifying high-performance sparse sub-networks. SbF-Pruner can train and generate a pruned network from scratch using a simple, single-stage training procedure that does not rely on a pre-trained model. Additionally, the method eliminates the need for layer-specific hyperparameters or predefined layer budgets, as it implicitly determines the optimal number of channels per layer. Experimental results across various architectures demonstrate that SbF-Pruner surpasses advanced pruning techniques. Specifically, on CIFAR-10 without requiring a pre-trained baseline, we achieve accuracy improvements of 1.02% on ResNet56 and 1.19% on ResNet110 compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Simultaneously, SbF-Pruner reduces the parameter count by 52.3% for ResNet56 and 54% for ResNet101, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by significant margins of 9.5% and 6.6%, respectively.

Continuous technological progress has driven substantial advancements and enhancements in industrial processes, particularly in sectors requiring precise control and superior environmental air efficiency. Consequently, embedded systems enable the creation of products and services designed to address challenges or propose solutions within these industrial settings. This article details the development of an embedded system utilizing a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and Arduino for an industrial air dehumidifier. This system facilitates remote failure monitoring through a reliable wireless IEEE 802.11 network, communicating data to an Android mobile application. Ultimately, the study presents a test bench prototype for this embedded system, verifying key parameters such as temperature sensor readings and the dehumidifier's operational conditions.

Deep neural networks have recently achieved state-of-the-art results in visual and speech recognition due to their high expressiveness. However, this same capability allows them to learn uninterpretable solutions with counter-intuitive characteristics, two of which are reported here. First, various unit analysis methods reveal no meaningful difference between individual high-level units and random linear combinations thereof, suggesting that semantic information resides in the overall space rather than in specific units. Second, these networks learn input-output mappings that are significantly discontinuous. We can induce misclassification by applying imperceptible perturbations that maximize prediction error. Furthermore, these perturbations are not random artifacts; the same specific perturbation can cause a network trained on a different dataset subset to misclassify the identical input.

Rare charm decays provide a distinct avenue for investigating flavour-changing neutral currents in the up-quark sector, both within and beyond the Standard Model. Although their low-energy dynamics have historically been difficult to model reliably, casting doubt on their potential, this challenge does not preclude the discovery of New Physics; rather, it necessitates a revised research strategy. By leveraging exact or approximate Standard Model symmetries, physicists can establish clean null-test observables that offer a powerful path to uncovering New Physics, thereby complementing existing down-sector analyses. This review outlines the current theoretical and experimental landscape for rare charm $|\Delta c|=|\Delta u|=1$ transitions and highlights prospects for upcoming and ongoing experiments, including LHCb, Belle II, BES III, the FCC-ee, and proposed tau-charm factories. Furthermore, utilizing the latest experimental data, we present updated constraints on lepton-flavour conserving and lepton-flavour violating Wilson coefficients.

Platooning and other cooperative driving systems depend on information exchange to establish situational awareness for individual agents, meaning that control system performance is inextricably linked to communication capabilities. Consequently, the dynamics, stability, and scalability of a vehicle platoon are determined not only by the vehicle controllers but also by the Information Flow Topology (IFT). Cellular Vehicle-To-Everything (C-V2X) technology has become a primary enabler for connected and automated vehicles, yet wireless imperfections such as packet loss introduce random link interruptions and topology changes. To address this, we model communication links using a first-order Markov approach to capture temporal correlations, facilitating more accurate performance evaluation during system design. Our methodology involves collecting high-fidelity simulation data across various densities and communication rates to model Inter-Packet Gaps (IPG) via Markov chains and derive corresponding transition probability matrices. Finally, we leverage these IPG models to assess the mean-square stability of platoons under standard consensus protocols optimized for ideal conditions, quantifying performance degradation across different scenarios.

This work investigates the Dirichlet problem for least gradient functions within metric spaces characterized by a doubling measure and a (1,1)-Poincaré inequality, under the assumption that the domain's boundary exhibits positive mean curvature. Building on the existence results for continuous boundary data established by Malý, Lahti, Shanmugalingam, and Speight, we demonstrate that solutions also exist when the boundary data can be approximated from both above and below by continuous functions. Furthermore, we prove that for any $f\in L^1(\partial\Omega)$, a least gradient function exists in $\Omega$ whose trace matches $f$ at every point where $f$ is continuous, thereby guaranteeing solutions for boundary data continuous almost everywhere. These findings contrast with Spradlin and Tamasan's result, which identified an $L^1$-function on the unit circle lacking a least gradient solution in the unit disk of $\mathbb{R}^2$. By adapting their example, we reveal that the set of solvable $L^1$-functions on the unit circle is non-linear, despite the unit disk satisfying the positive mean curvature condition.

This paper establishes the theorem on freedom for relatively free groups with one relation, which parallels Magnus's well-known result, and similarly proves the theorem on freedom for relatively free Lie algebras with a single relation, corresponding to Shirshov's established finding.

Non-Hermitian topological effects manifest in mechanical systems governed by Newton's equations. Specifically, mechanical graphene structures, consisting of masses connected by springs, exhibit symmetry-protected exceptional rings (SPERs) when friction is introduced, though the resulting physical properties remain undefined. Our numerical investigation demonstrates that SPERs regulate dynamics within wavenumber space. Additionally, we outline a method to extract these wavenumber-space dynamics for bounded systems. Finally, we observe that SPER connectivity varies with friction levels, a behavior analogous to the Lifshitz transition observed in electronic systems.

In the MediaEval 2022 Predicting Video Memorability challenge, we investigate the connection between visual memorability, its visual representation, and the underlying concept depicted. Our model, trained and evaluated solely on surrogate dream images, achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting memorability. This success elevates concepts to a central role in memorability features and provides strong evidence that the intrinsic memorability of visual content can be distilled into its core meaning, regardless of its specific visual representation.

Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely utilized to model stochastic variability in astrophysical time series, particularly for addressing correlated stellar noise in planetary transit light curves. Recent methodological advances, such as the celerite approach, have enabled the efficient application of GPs to datasets comprising thousands to tens of thousands of points. This work introduces an extension of celerite to two input dimensions, typically involving a large primary dimension and a small secondary one. Under the condition that noise in the large dimension follows the same celerite kernel while only the amplitude of correlated noise varies in the second dimension, the method achieves linear scaling with the total number of datapoints. We apply this technique to deriving precise transit parameters from multiwavelength light curves, demonstrating its potential to enhance measurement accuracy by orders of magnitude. Furthermore, this approach is applicable to transit spectroscopy, exomoon detection, and a wide range of other astronomical challenges.

Jones et al. (2015) defined $u$-representable graphs, where $u$ is a word over $\{1, 2\}$ excluding the string of all 2s, as an extension of word-representable graphs. Kitaev (2016) demonstrated that for any word $u$ with a length of 3 or more, all graphs are $u$-representable. Consequently, the theory of $u$-representable graphs contains only two nontrivial categories: 11-representable graphs (equivalent to word-representable graphs) and 12-representable graphs. This work focuses on the latter. While Jones et al. (2015) characterized 12-representable trees via forbidden induced subgraphs, Chen and Kitaev (2022) provided such a characterization for a specific subclass of 12-representable grid graphs. The current study establishes that a bipartite graph is 12-representable if and only if it is an interval containment bigraph. Since the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for interval containment bigraphs are known, this equivalence yields a forbidden induced subgraph characterization for 12-representable bipartite graphs. Furthermore, this result resolves an open question posed by Chen and Kitaev (2022) by providing a similar characterization for grid graphs. The paper also proves that a graph is 12-representable if and only if it is the complement of a simple-triangle graph, confirming that a necessary condition identified by Jones et al. (2015) is also sufficient. Based on these equivalences, we determine that 12-representability can be decided in $O(n^2)$ time for bipartite graphs and in $O(n(\bar{m}+n))$ time for general graphs, where $n$ represents the number of vertices and $\bar{m}$ denotes the number of edges in the graph's complement.

This paper seeks to demystify black-box quantitative strategies by establishing a robust foundation that explains their mechanics and rationale. By deriving the underlying mathematics from basic intuitions, the manuscript clarifies both the formal and informal dimensions of these techniques. The goal is to equip readers with a profound understanding of the methods, covering when, how, and why to apply them. Strategies are demonstrated using S&P 500 and SH510300 datasets; however, the test results serve merely as illustrations of the methods' functionality, with no implication that they recommend actual market positions.

The control of light confinement has a long-standing history in optics and holds major significance for managing light-matter interactions. However, in inhomogeneous and disordered media, multiple scattering hinders the use of traditional methods for engineering light fields with specific characteristics. This limitation arises because local alterations to such media typically impact these fields in complex, non-local ways. In this work, we introduce a theoretical framework for designing inhomogeneous one-dimensional (1D) Hermitian dielectric index profiles that allow the intensity of an incoming light field to be manipulated purely locally, meaning the field outside a designated region of interest remains largely unaffected. Consequently, it becomes feasible to significantly increase or decrease light intensity at arbitrary points within the medium without altering the external reflectance or transmittance. These local adjustments can therefore remain undetectable via unidirectional far-field measurements. We demonstrate this approach by locally controlling light confinement within 1D materials featuring continuous inhomogeneous refractive indices, and we further extend the method to multilayer films and chains of coupled micro-resonators.

The ability of machine learning models to generalize to new regions is hindered by geographic variations in satellite imagery. This paper addresses geographic generalization in medium-resolution Landsat-8 data by framing it as a continuous domain adaptation problem, showing that models improve with suitable domain knowledge. We created a dataset spanning the entire continental United States to offer macroscopic insights into how geography influences crop classification within multi-spectral and temporally distributed satellite data. Our approach achieves enhanced generalizability by 1) integrating geographically correlated climate variables alongside satellite data into a Transformer model, and 2) reconstructing these domain variables by regressing on the model's features. Together, these contributions offer a new perspective on geographic generalization in satellite imagery and a straightforward yet effective method for leveraging domain knowledge. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/samar-khanna/cropmap}

We present the notion of $m$-shifted symplectic Lie $n$-groupoids alongside symplectic Morita equivalences connecting them. Subsequently, we develop several models for the 2-shifted symplectic structure on the classifying stack within this framework and establish explicit symplectic Morita equivalences among these models.

Most extensively researched explainable AI (XAI) methods are fundamentally unsound, a flaw that affects both popular model-agnostic techniques and those relying on saliency maps. While intrinsic interpretability offers a sound alternative, it often suffers from excessive redundancy. Formal explainability presents another option, exemplified by PI-explanations; however, these also face significant limitations, particularly regarding their large size. Recent findings suggest that the absolute rigor of PI-explanations can be balanced against a reduced explanation size by calculating "relevant sets." A feature set $S$ is defined as $\delta$-relevant if fixing the features in $S$ ensures the target class probability surpasses $\delta$. Despite this, computing these sets for circuit-based classifiers is theoretically prohibitive, classified as NPPP-complete. Contrary to these negative theoretical results, this paper explores practical methods for determining relevant sets across several common classifiers, including Decision Trees, Naive Bayes Classifiers, and various propositional language-based models. The study demonstrates that, in practice, computing relevant sets for these specific classifier families is efficient, and experimental results confirm that concise sets of relevant features can indeed be generated.

The half-life of the superallowed Fermi $\beta^+$ emitter $^{14}$O was measured with high precision using a direct $\beta$ counting experiment at TRIUMF's Isotope Separator and Accelerator (ISAC) facility. The resulting value, $T_{1/2}$($^{14}$O) = 70619.2(76) ms, aligns with but offers greater precision than the global average derived from 11 prior studies. Integrating the half-life determined in this study with the previous most accurate measurements reduces the overall uncertainty by nearly a factor of two. Consequently, the updated world average is $T_{1/2}$($^{14}$O) = 70619.6(63) ms, supported by a reduced $\chi^2$ of 0.87 across 8 degrees of freedom.

The Onsager algebra serves as a fundamental pillar in the study of exactly solvable models within statistical mechanics. By beginning with the generalised Clifford algebra, we establish its connections to both the graph Temperley-Lieb algebra and an extension of the Onsager algebra. We introduce several quantum lattice models that act as representations of the generalised Clifford algebra, characterized by a specific structure of the generalised Onsager algebra. The integrability of these models is demonstrated, drawing parallels to the free fermionic eight-vertex model. Furthermore, we discuss additional extensions of these models and their associated physical properties related to the generalised Onsager algebras, suggesting a broader framework that encompasses families of quantum lattice models exhibiting this generalised Onsager algebra structure.

This research investigates a parafermion Josephson junction formed by two counter-propagating edge modes from quantum Hall systems, coupled with an s-wave superconductor. We demonstrate that varying the lengths of these opposing chiral edges—adjustable via external gates—generates a spontaneous phase bias. For Laughlin filling fractions defined as $\nu = 1/m$ where $m$ is an odd integer, this mechanism enables electrical tuning of zero modes, specifically yielding Majorana modes when $m=1$ and parafermion modes for any other $m$.

The Super Tau-Charm Facility (STCF) represents a next-generation, high-luminosity electron-positron collider and stands as a primary option for future accelerator-based particle physics experiments in China. Within the STCF spectrometer, the undoped cesium iodide (CsI) crystal-based electromagnetic calorimeter (EMC) serves as a critical subsystem. To meet escalating physics demands for measurement precision and endure radiation exposure, enhancing the light yield detected by the EMC is a pivotal research objective. This paper investigates a "wavelength shifting in propagation" scheme utilizing nanostructured organosilicon luminophores (NOL) for the STCF EMC. The proposed approach was validated through both Monte Carlo simulations and experimental testing. Results from the experiments demonstrated a 1.59-fold improvement in light yield. Furthermore, radiation hardness assessments of the NOL confirmed its reliability; no significant performance degradation was observed even after accumulating a total ionization dose of 100 krad, a level far exceeding the projected radiation dose for the STCF over a ten-year operational period.

We provide numerical findings from 2D and 3D hydrodynamic simulations of an 11.2$M_\odot$ star undergoing core collapse. By systematically varying numerical resolution and seed perturbations, we investigate the differences in postbounce dynamics between 2D and 3D scenarios. These simulations utilize an energy-dependent neutrino transport method based on the isotropic diffusion source approximation, updated for high computational efficiency. All models examined, comprising fifteen 2D and nine 3D configurations, demonstrate the revival of the stalled shock wave, indicating a potential for explosion. This revival is driven by the neutrino-heating mechanism, enhanced by neutrino-driven convection and the standing-accretion-shock instability (SASI). While the stochastic nature of multi-dimensional neutrino-driven explosions causes variations in blast morphology across models, the ultimate fate regarding explosion success remains largely unaffected by this randomness. Consistent with prior research, higher resolutions result in a delayed onset of shock revival in both 2D and 3D. Based on these self-consistent models capable of explosion, our results systematically indicate that the revived shock expands with greater energy in 2D compared to 3D.

The Higgs boson mass was determined using 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (13 TeV center-of-mass energy) during 2015 and 2016, specifically through the $H\rightarrow ZZ^* \rightarrow 4\ell$ and $H\rightarrow \gamma\gamma$ decay channels. The individual measurements yielded $m_{H}^{ZZ^{*}} = 124.79 \pm 0.37$ GeV for the four-lepton channel and $m_{H}^{\gamma \gamma} = 124.93 \pm 0.40$ GeV for the diphoton channel. When these findings are combined with previous ATLAS results from 7 TeV and 8 TeV data, the resulting Higgs boson mass is $m_H=124.97 \pm 0.24$ GeV.

Accurate seismic phase picking and earthquake detection are vital for estimating body wave travel times (P and S waves) and pinpointing epicenters. While manual phase picking remains a reliable and optimal approach for determining arrival times, it is constrained by time and resource limitations. Furthermore, the presence of noise in seismic data significantly complicates the task of achieving fast and accurate picks. To address these challenges, this study introduces EPick, a deep learning model that combines a U-shaped neural network (UNet) with an attention mechanism, offering a robust alternative for seismic event detection and phase picking. The UNet architecture facilitates the extraction of features across various depths, while the attention mechanism guides the decoder to effectively utilize low-resolution features from the encoder, thereby enhancing picking precision. Comprehensive experiments indicate that EPick outperforms benchmark methods and demonstrates strong robustness when applied to different seismic datasets.

Contemporary weak-lensing surveys are gaining the sensitivity required to detect baryonic feedback processes, which remain poorly understood. Previous attempts to address this issue relied on applying scale-cuts to the data or utilizing simplified, single-parameter models. This study instead employs a more comprehensive, seven-parameter framework for baryonic feedback, derived primarily from observations and validated against numerous hydrodynamical simulations. By integrating weak-lensing data from the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS-1000) with measurements of intracluster gas—specifically X-ray gas fractions and kinematic Sunyaev-Zeldovich (kSZ) gas profiles—we constrain baryonic parameters and gain insights into feedback mechanisms and cosmology. Our analysis reveals evidence for baryonic feedback that is stronger than predicted by most hydrodynamical simulations. Regarding the matter power spectrum, we observe effects exceeding the percent level at scales $k\sim 0.1-0.45$ h/Mpc, with a maximum suppression of $12-33$ percent at $k\sim 7$ h/Mpc (68 percent confidence level). For the combined parameter $\Sigma_8=\sigma_8(\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.58}$, we find that including full baryonic effects reduces the known tension with Planck satellite data from $3.8$ to $2.9\sigma$. This tension further decreases to $2.6\sigma$ when weak-lensing data is combined with X-ray and kSZ observations. We conclude that although baryonic feedback is increasingly significant in modern weak-lensing surveys, it is unlikely to be the primary cause of the observed $\Sigma_8$ tension.

Logical functions can characterize properties of a Boolean network (BN) state, which represents an aggregation of states. To illustrate the dynamics of these functions regarding specific BN properties, an invariant subspace containing them is introduced and analyzed. Subsequently, an invariant subspace for Boolean control networks (BCN) is also proposed, with the property that its dynamics remain invariant. Finally, by treating outputs as a set of logical functions, a minimum realization of the BCN is suggested, offering a potential solution to address the computational complexity associated with large-scale BNs and BCNs.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has gained significant traction in semantic analysis recently. This paper presents a methodology for examining how context influences human perception of semantically similar words, addressing the third task of SemEval 2020. We employed multiple techniques to compute distances between embedding vectors produced by Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). Our team secured first place in the Finnish language track and second place in the English track for subtask 1.

Coronal holes represent the observable openings in the solar magnetic field that extend into the heliosphere, playing a critical role in understanding solar wind origins and acceleration. While missions like the Solar Dynamics Observatory now enable detailed studies of these features, instrumental limitations and other variables complicate their automated identification. Consequently, the scientific community employs various detection methods, yet there has been minimal effort to evaluate the discrepancies among them. This COSPAR ISWAT initiative compares nine widely used automated detection schemes, focusing specifically on a prominent coronal hole observed by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on May 30, 2018. Our findings demonstrate that the selected detection method significantly influences the determined boundary location of the coronal hole. Furthermore, key physical properties—such as area, mean intensity, and average magnetic field strength—vary by a factor of up to 4.5 between the highest and lowest estimates. We conclude that these results have significant implications for coronal hole research over the last decade and are of broad interest to the solar and space science communities.

Utilizing light to gauge an object's motion is fundamental to mechanical sensors designed to investigate forces and fields. Cavity optomechanical systems achieve this by placing mechanical resonators within optical cavities. While this configuration boosts measurement sensitivity, it requires the mechanical resonator to preserve the optical cavity's characteristics; otherwise, performance degrades. Consequently, detecting resonators composed of optically absorbing materials or those lacking appropriate geometric symmetry remains difficult. In this study, we present a solution that addresses the challenge of measuring high-frequency torsional motion in a nanodisk by translating such twisting movements into vibrations of a photonic crystal cavity. Subsequent optomechanical readout allows for the detection of the nanodisk's torsional resonances with a sensitivity ranging from $5.1\times 10^{-21}$ to $1.2\times 10^{-19}\,\text{Nm}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ across a mechanical frequency spectrum of 5 to 800 MHz. Furthermore, the nanodisk can incorporate magnetic nanostructures or metasurfaces without compromising the cavity's optical performance, rendering the system ideal for applications in torque magnetometry and structured light sensing.

This study derives the asymptotic behavior, as $t + |x| \rightarrow \infty$, of the fundamental solution to the heat equation featuring a compactly supported potential, under the condition that the associated stationary operator possesses at least one positive eigenvalue. The analysis identifies two distinct regions characterized by different asymptotic dynamics: within a specific conical surface in $(t,x)$ space, the asymptotics are governed by the principal eigenvalue and its corresponding eigenfunction; outside this cone, the leading term consists of a bounded function multiplied by the fundamental solution of the unperturbed operator, where the potential's influence becomes negligible as $|x|/t \rightarrow \infty$. A comprehensive formula for the global asymptotics over the entire half-space $t > 0$ is presented. In probabilistic terms, these findings characterize the asymptotic density of particles in a branching diffusion process subject to compactly supported branching and killing potentials.

To enhance the efficiency of ZUC primitives, we introduce two AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) modes: ZUC-GXM and ZUC-MUR. These modes are applicable to ZUC (ZUC-128) and two variants of ZUC-256. ZUC-GXM operates as a nonce-based AEAD scheme following the GCM framework, whereas ZUC-MUR is a nonce misuse-resistant mode based on the SIV variance framework, offering more robust applications for the ZUC family of stream ciphers.

This paper presents a representation result for the weak solutions of a specific class of evolutionary Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations defined on an infinite horizon, featuring Hamiltonians that are measurable in time and fiber convex. These Hamiltonians correspond to a faithful representation involving two functions that are measurable in time and locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to both state and control variables. Our findings address the recovery of convex Hamiltonian representations under a relaxed condition concerning the Fenchel transform of the Hamiltonian with respect to the fiber. We apply these results to examine the uniqueness of weak solutions that vanish at infinity for a class of time-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations. Under the assumption of a viability condition on the domain of the aforementioned Fenchel transform, these weak solutions are interpreted as the appropriate value function for an infinite horizon control problem subject to state constraints.

Emerging technologies in sensing and communication now enable the acquisition of high-frequency, real-time data from diverse physical systems, including power grids, climate models, and biological networks. Nevertheless, because this data originates from physical sensors, it inherently contains measurement noise. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for the online, real-time learning of dynamical systems from noisy time-series data, utilizing the Robust Koopman operator framework to counteract noise interference. The proposed method offers three primary benefits: a) it supports real-time online monitoring of dynamical systems; b) it generates a linear representation of the underlying system, allowing users to apply linear systems theory for analysis and control; and c) it is computationally efficient and less demanding than the widely used Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD) algorithm. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by applying it to identify the Van der Pol oscillator, the IEEE 68 bus system, and a ring network of Van der Pol oscillators.

Bayesian Optimisation (BO) aims to locate the global optimum of objective functions that are either black-box in nature or costly to evaluate. These approaches build a surrogate model of the objective function, using Bayesian inference to measure uncertainty within that model. At each iteration, the next evaluation point is chosen by maximizing an acquisition function. However, solving this secondary optimisation task can be challenging due to the non-convexity of the acquisition function, a difficulty that is amplified in batch Bayesian optimisation where multiple points are selected simultaneously. This work proposes reformulating batch BO as an optimisation problem defined over the space of probability measures. We introduce a novel acquisition function based on multipoint expected improvement that is convex within this probability measure space. Practical algorithms for resolving this inner optimisation problem emerge naturally as gradient flows of the proposed objective. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of this new approach on various benchmark functions and compare its performance against leading state-of-the-art batch BO techniques.

This study combines CDF and D0 results to search for Higgs bosons within the Standard Model (SM) and Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) frameworks, utilizing up to 6.7 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity from 1.96 TeV proton-antiproton collisions at the Tevatron. By merging specialized searches for Higgs production through gluon fusion, associated boson production, and vector boson fusion—covering decays into $b\bar{b}$, $W^{+}W^{-}$, $\tau^{+}\tau^{-}$, and $\gamma\gamma$—we establish 95\% confidence level upper limits on SM Higgs production rates as a function of mass. The analysis displays current Tevatron constraints, featuring a new exclusion region for SM Higgs masses ranging from 158 to 175 GeV$/c^2$, and outlines the prospects for future sensitivity improvements.

This paper addresses two open questions in fixed point theory concerning quasi metric spaces, originally raised by Berinde and Choban in their 2013 work on generalized distances. We provide a full resolution to the first issue and a partial solution to the second, further demonstrating the significance and intricacy of these problems through four detailed and engaging examples.

Most machine learning (ML) research on network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) relies on established datasets like KDD-CUP99, NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and CICIDS-2017. Current studies typically explore ML techniques to improve performance metrics against published baselines using a model-centric approach. However, these datasets suffer from aging limitations that hinder the practical application of ML-based NIDS in real-world scenarios. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes a systematic data-centric approach that addresses dataset constraints by generating NIDS datasets featuring the latest network traffic and attack patterns, with labeling inherently integrated into the creation process.

We incorporate both linear and nonlinear parameterizations of physics beyond the standard cosmological model into the halo model reaction framework, establishing a model-independent method for the nonlinear matter power spectrum. Specifically, we apply this to Horndeski theories, utilizing the Effective Field Theory of Dark Energy (EFTofDE) to describe linear and quasi-nonlinear perturbations. Within the nonlinear regime, we examine two strategies: a nonlinear parameterized-post-Friedmann (nPPF) approach and an approximate, physically motivated phenomenological model based on the error function (Erf). By comparing these parameterized predictions against exact solutions in two established modified gravity models, we achieve sub-percent agreement using the Erf model for $z\leq1$ and $k\leq 5~h/{\rm Mpc}$. This indicates that just three additional free constants, beyond those for background and linear theory, are adequate to model nonlinear, non-standard cosmology in the matter power spectrum with $2\%$ accuracy down to $k \leq 3h~/{\rm Mpc}$. Furthermore, we have integrated these parameterizations into version 2.0 of the ReACT code.

This work introduces a unified thermodynamic framework for characterizing learning efficiency. Initially, we establish an inequality that surpasses Clausius's inequality in strength, thereby defining a lower bound for the entropy production rate within a subsystem. Subsequently, this inequality is adapted to derive a general upper limit for learning efficiency. Specifically, we illustrate this efficiency bound in the context of nonequilibrium quantum-dot systems and cellular networks. Ultimately, the proposed framework elucidates a fundamental trade-off between energy and information inherent in stochastic thermodynamic processes.

Self-training based unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) holds significant promise for mitigating domain shift when deploying deep learning models trained on source data to unlabeled target environments. Although this approach has proven effective for discriminative tasks like classification and segmentation—leveraging reliable pseudo-label selection via softmax discrete histograms—its application to generative tasks, such as image synthesis, remains underexplored. To address this, we introduce a novel Generative Self-Training (GST) UDA framework designed for cross-domain image synthesis, utilizing continuous value prediction and a regression objective. Our method filters pseudo-labels using an uncertainty mask and assesses the confidence of generated images through practical variational Bayes learning. Additionally, we achieve rapid test-time adaptation via a round-based alternating optimization scheme. We evaluated this framework on the tagged-to-cine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) synthesis challenge, involving datasets from various scanners and centers. Extensive comparisons against leading adversarial training UDA methods confirm that our GST approach, even with tagged MRI data from new target domains, significantly enhances synthesis quality compared to adversarial alternatives.

Describing non-equilibrium states in superconductors at temperatures significantly below the critical point necessitates the Keldysh-Usadel technique (KUT). Yet, the non-stationary formulation of KUT has not yet been utilized in realistic circuit contexts, and the stationary version has been incorrectly applied to scenarios where time independence cannot be assured. To validate this approach, we employ a toy model based on the Ginzburg-Landau theory under conditions of extremely slow evolution. Our findings indicate that even in such regimes, ignoring the explicit effects of temporal variations results in inaccurate or qualitatively erroneous descriptions of phase slips.

This study examines the finite-size impacts on the structural characteristics and polarization of the rhombohedral phase of HfO$_2$ under biaxial compressive strain. We demonstrate that surface charges significantly diminish polarization compared to bulk values, a reduction attributed to two mechanisms: the interaction between compressive strain and the phase-transition order parameter, and alterations in the ferroelectric distortion. We offer two distinct interpretations of this phenomenon: an atomistic analysis tracking bond length evolution and a symmetry-based analysis evaluating changes in the amplitude of symmetry-allowed distortions within a slab configuration. These findings remain consistent across the considered slab thicknesses, indicating no critical thickness for ferroelectricity in HfO$_2$, which aligns with the theory of its improper ferroelectric nature.

The recent surge in ransomware has introduced significant new challenges for cybersecurity within large-scale networks. The high density of connections in these networks can accelerate the propagation of malware, thereby complicating containment and control efforts. This study proposes an impulse optimal control framework designed for epidemics on networks. The combination of discrete-time control policies applied to continuous-time epidemic dynamics, alongside the underlying network topology, creates a complex optimal control problem. To address this, we apply Pontryagin's minimum principle for impulsive systems to derive the optimal controller structure and validate our findings through numerical experiments.

Over the last decade, the study of two-dimensional (2D) materials has emerged as one of the most rapidly expanding areas within condensed matter physics and materials science. The unique combination of low dimensionality and strong interactions in these systems generates distinct electronic and structural characteristics—manifested as collective excitations—that are absent in conventional three-dimensional (3D) materials currently employed in technology. These 2D systems offer exceptional prospects for emerging applications, including flexible electronics. This review concentrates on plasmons, excitons, phonons, and magnons within 2D materials, examining the theoretical frameworks governing these collective modes and highlighting how they diverge from their 3D analogues.

For readers familiar with CVX (disciplined convex programming by M. Grant and S. Boyd), the aim of this research is to expand its capabilities beyond standard convex minimization to address convex-concave saddle point problems and variational inequalities involving monotone operators. To achieve this, we define the concepts of K-conic representations for these problem types, where K denotes a family of cones such as Lorentz, semidefinite, or geometric cones. We demonstrate that once a problem is expressed in this K-conic form, it can be directly transformed into a conic optimization problem over a cone in K, making it solvable by any solver capable of handling such conic problems (for instance, Mosek or SDPT3 for semidefinite cones). Furthermore, we establish a fully algorithmic calculus for K-representations of convex-concave functions and monotone vector fields, enabling the identification of cases where saddle point problems or variational inequalities can be converted into conic problems and the execution of such conversions.

The study of superconductors featuring pairing mechanisms beyond the conventional BCS s-wave has drawn significant attention. Superconductors with low-energy phonons may display unconventional superconductivity, as the interaction between electrons and these phonons can alter the superconducting ground state, potentially leading to strong coupling. This work presents a comprehensive investigation into the superconducting ground state of the strongly coupled material IrGe (T$_{C}$ = 4.7 K) using magnetization, AC transport, specific heat, and muon spin rotation/relaxation ($\mu$SR) techniques. Analysis of specific heat and transverse field $\mu$SR data aligns best with an isotropic s-wave model characterized by strong electron-phonon coupling, evidenced by $\Delta(0)/k_{B}T_{C}$ values of 2.3 and 2.1 (from SH and $\mu$SR, respectively) and $\Delta C_{el}/\gamma_{n}T_{C}$ = 2.7. Furthermore, zero-field $\mu$SR measurements verify the preservation of time-reversal symmetry within the superconducting state of IrGe.

This research investigates a decentralized online regularized linear regression algorithm operating on random time-varying graphs. At each time step, every node executes an online estimation procedure that integrates three components: an innovation term handling its own new measurement, a consensus term calculating a weighted sum of estimates from itself and its neighbors (incorporating both additive and multiplicative communication noises), and a regularization term to avoid over-fitting. The study does not impose restrictive statistical assumptions, such as mutual independence, spatio-temporal independence, or stationarity, on the regression matrices or graph structures. We establish a nonnegative supermartingale inequality regarding the estimation error and demonstrate that all nodes' estimates converge almost surely to the unknown true parameter vector, provided the algorithm gains, graphs, and regression matrices collectively satisfy the sample path spatio-temporal persistence of excitation condition. Specifically, this condition is met by selecting suitable algorithm gains when the graphs are uniformly conditionally jointly connected and balanced, and the regression models are uniformly conditionally spatio-temporally jointly observable; under these circumstances, the algorithm achieves convergence in both mean square and almost sure senses. Furthermore, we derive a regret upper bound of $\mathcal O(T^{1-\tau}\ln T)$, where $\tau\in (0.5,1)$ is a constant determined by the algorithm gains.

This note investigates the integral solutions to the equation $x^2+3y^2=12n+4$ for positive integers $n$, providing a parametrization of this set via 3-core partitions of $n$. Specifically, we define a crank by leveraging the action of a specific subgroup of the plane's isometry group, which corresponds to the unit group of the Eisenstein integers. We further demonstrate that this relationship is reversible: given the equation's solutions and the crank, one can characterize the 3-core partitions of $n$. Consequently, we establish an explicit bijection between 3-core partitions and ideals within the ring of Eisenstein integers, thereby offering a new perspective on a result previously derived by G. Han and K. Ono using modular forms.

Building upon our previous research regarding the three-dimensional effective velocity distribution of Galactic WIMPs (encompassing those striking detectors as well as those scattering off target nuclei), this study reveals both standard and "reverse" annual modulations in elastic WIMP-nucleus scattering signals, potentially detectable by direct Dark Matter experiments. Our simulations indicate that for light WIMPs with masses in the tens of GeV range, the number of events and total recoil energy from scattering off both light and heavy nuclei peak in summer and reach a minimum in winter. Conversely, for heavy WIMPs with masses in the hundreds of GeV range, the event count and accumulated recoil energy from interactions with heavy nuclei are minimal in summer. As expected, for intermediate WIMP masses, the event frequency and recoil energy from scattering off nuclei of intermediate mass exhibit an approximately uniform temporal variation.

Research on human-robot collaboration has predominantly concentrated on developing robot policies that enable smooth coordination during joint tasks, while the influence of the environment on these coordination behaviors has received comparatively less attention. To comprehensively investigate environments capable of eliciting a wide range of behaviors, we introduce a procedural generation framework that creates settings which are (1) stylistically consistent with those designed by humans, (2) guaranteed to be solvable by the human-robot team, and (3) diverse regarding coordination metrics. We evaluated these procedurally generated environments within the Overcooked benchmark domain using both simulations and an online user study. The findings indicate that these environments produce qualitatively distinct emergent behaviors and yield statistically significant variations in collaborative fluency scores, even when the robot employs an identical planning algorithm.

A prevalent method for estimating Hidden Markov Model (HMM) parameters involves calculating maximum likelihood (ML) estimates. Typically, users employ user-friendly implementations of these estimation routines through interpreted programming languages like R (R Core Team, 2021). However, this approach can demand substantial computation time, especially when processing longer observation sequences. Furthermore, determining appropriate methods for deriving confidence intervals for the estimated parameters is often unclear (see, e.g., Zucchini et al., 2016; Lystig and Hughes, 2002; Visser et al., 2000), frequently necessitating the use of computationally demanding bootstrap methods. This tutorial demonstrates how to significantly accelerate the calculation of ML estimates using the R package TMB, while also enabling the straightforward retrieval of standard errors. We evaluate the performance of our routines across various datasets: first, two smaller samples consisting of 87 and 240 data points from a mobile application for tinnitus patients and a well-known dataset of fetal lamb movements, respectively; second, larger simulated datasets with sizes of 2000 and 5000 for additional analysis. This tutorial is supported by a collection of scripts available on GitHub, allowing users with moderate programming experience to quickly leverage the computational benefits of TMB.

This study addresses channel allocation in uplink wireless systems with the objective of maximizing the total user rate under integer constraints. While a convex optimization algorithm yields an optimal closed-form solution at each step, its high computational cost necessitates the use of machine learning for efficiency. Specifically, data generated by the convex method are used to formulate a regression problem solved by integrating convolutional neural networks (CNNs), feed-forward neural networks (FNNs), random forests, and gated recurrent units (GRUs). Experimental results indicate that this machine learning approach significantly decreases computation time with only a minor reduction in prediction accuracy.

Each partial applicative structure induces an indexed binary relation, functioning as a contravariant functor from the category of sets to the category of sets equipped with binary relations and structure-preserving maps. This paper characterizes the partial applicative structures that yield indexed relations with specific elementary properties through their algebraic or computational attributes. Subsequently, we offer characterizations for those structures producing indexed preorders and posets, linking these to particular classes of unary partial endofunctions. We examine the interplay between various computational and algebraic properties within the posetal context. Finally, we investigate the existence of suprema for partial applicative structures generating indexed preorders by establishing necessary conditions for such structures to be complete.

This study investigates the flexible assignment of users to beams to align with non-uniform traffic demands in satellite networks, thereby transcending traditional cell boundaries and allowing non-dominant beams to serve users. This added flexibility in beam-user mapping establishes a user-centric framework implemented through a practical two-step optimization process. The proposed smart mapping is evaluated alongside adjustable per-beam bandwidth allocation against various flexible radio resource allocation techniques. Numerical results, derived from diverse non-uniform traffic distributions modeled by a conveniently parameterized Dirichlet distribution to ensure reproducible simulations, assess the performance of these solutions. Even under ideal power allocation conditions, both flexible beam-user mapping and adjustable power allocation significantly enhance average bandwidth assignment. The findings indicate that intelligently pairing users with beams yields substantial benefits in scenarios with highly asymmetric demand, achieving improvements of up to 10% in offered rates and 30% in minimum user rates during hot-spot cases, all without impacting user equipment.

Galaxy superclusters represent the most extensive structures within the cosmic web, originating from gravitational collapse despite often lacking gravitational binding. Investigating their geometric characteristics offers insights into structure formation across cosmological scales and the fundamental nature of gravity. This study analyzes the shape, topology, and morphology distributions of superclusters derived from the SDSS DR12 main galaxy sample, utilizing both fixed and adaptive density thresholds within the luminosity-density field. To evaluate the geometry and topology of individual superclusters, we apply Minkowski functionals and Shapefinders, computed precisely using the SURFGEN2 diagnostic tool. While both sampling methods yield comparable shape distributions, most superclusters exhibit spherical geometries with trivial topology. Conversely, large superclusters with volumes exceeding approximately $10^{4}$ Mpc$^{3}$ are statistically identified as filamentary, possessing non-zero genus values. The resulting shape distributions and catalogues are now publicly accessible.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), high-sensitivity observations of interstellar scintillation and polarization in PSR~B0656+14 across three epochs over a year reveal that scattering is primarily driven by two distinct compact regions. The region closer to the pulsar is identified with the shell of the Monogem Ring, confirming their link, while the other is likely connected to the Local Bubble. Our findings indicate that the angle between the pulsar's spin axis and its space velocity is significantly offset by $19\fdg3\pm$0\fdg8, contradicting earlier reports of near-perfect alignment ($1\degr\pm 2\degr$). Two robust forward parabolic arcs in the secondary spectra clearly delineate these independent scattering zones. Based on arc curvatures, the screens for the outer and inner arcs are situated roughly 185~pc from Earth and 28~pc from PSR B0656+14, respectively. Comparing observed Doppler profiles with electromagnetic simulations suggests both regions exhibit mild anisotropy. Specifically, for the outer arc, the anisotropy factor $A_R$ is estimated at approximately 1.3, with scattering irregularities oriented parallel to the pulsar's velocity. Additionally, comparing observed delay profiles against theoretical strong-scattering models implies that the spatial spectrum of irregularities in the Monogem Ring is flatter than the Kolmogorov spectrum, though further observations are needed to verify this conclusion.

Multi-modal named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE) seek to enhance task performance by utilizing pertinent visual data. While previous research primarily concentrates on directly extracting potentially useful image features—such as pixel-level details, detected objects, and captions—these methods often lack knowledge awareness, potentially yielding irrelevant information. To address this, we introduce MoRe, a novel Multi-modal Retrieval-based framework. MoRe employs a dual-retrieval system comprising a text module and an image module, which independently fetch relevant knowledge from a corpus corresponding to the input text and image. These retrieved results are then fed into separate textual and visual models for prediction. Ultimately, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) module aggregates the outputs from both models to determine the final result. Experimental results indicate that both the textual and visual components achieve state-of-the-art performance across four multi-modal NER datasets and one multi-modal RE dataset. Furthermore, the integration of the MoE mechanism boosts overall performance, with our analysis confirming the advantages of combining both textual and visual cues for these tasks.

Digital holography enables the volumetric reconstruction of coherent scattered light fields. By refocusing these fields onto sample planes, one can simultaneously deduce the 3D absorption and phase-shift profiles of sparsely distributed specimens. This capability is particularly advantageous for the spectroscopic imaging of cold atomic gases. However, unlike biological tissues or solid particles, quasi-thermal atomic gases cooled by lasers typically lack distinct features and sharp boundaries, rendering many standard numerical refocusing techniques ineffective. To address this, we extend a refocusing protocol based on the Gouy phase anomaly—originally designed for small phase objects—to free atomic samples. Leveraging prior knowledge of a coherent spectral phase angle relation for cold atoms that remains robust against variations in probe conditions, we can reliably identify an "out-of-phase" response. This response flips its sign during numerical back-propagation across the sample plane, serving as a precise refocusing criterion. Experimentally, we successfully determined the sample plane of laser-cooled $^{39}$K gas released from a microscopic dipole trap using a holographic microscope with a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.3 and a probe wavelength ($\lambda_p$) of 770 nm. This achieved an axial resolution of $\delta z \approx 1~{\rm \mu m}$, which satisfies the condition $\ll 2\lambda_p/{\rm NA}^2$.

Quantifying and managing entanglement within quantum materials is vital for advancing next-generation quantum technologies, yet establishing a measurable metric for such entanglement remains theoretically and experimentally difficult. While entanglement at equilibrium can be identified by deriving witnesses from spectroscopic data, applying this methodology to non-equilibrium states promises to reveal new dynamical behaviors. In this study, we introduce a systematic framework for measuring the time-dependent quantum Fisher information and entanglement depth of transient states in quantum materials using time-resolved resonant inelastic x-ray scattering, a recently developed solid-state pump-probe technique. By employing a quarter-filled extended Hubbard model as a test case, we evaluate the method's efficiency and forecast light-induced enhancement of quantum entanglement resulting from proximity to a phase boundary. This research paves the way for the experimental detection and regulation of entanglement in light-driven quantum materials through ultrafast spectroscopic measurements accessible in solid-state environments.

The discharge of granular material from a silo is investigated through both experimental and numerical approaches, tracking the temporal evolution of the discharge rate and the normal force (apparent weight) at the container's base. Our findings indicate that particle stiffness significantly influences the qualitative characteristics of silo discharge. For deformable grains with a Young's modulus of approximately $Y_m\approx 40$ kPa within a silo subjected to a basal pressure around 4 kPa, reducing the friction coefficient results in a gradual shift in the discharge profile: the flow rate becomes dependent on the filling height and diminishes as discharge progresses. In contrast, for hard grains with a Young's modulus near $Y_m\approx 500$ MPa, the flow rate exhibits minimal sensitivity to friction coefficient variations. By integrating DEM data with coarse-graining techniques, we calculate key macroscopic fields, including linear momentum, density, and stress tensors. The divergence in discharge behavior under low-friction conditions stems from a marked difference in the pressure field: while Janssen screening remains effective for hard grains, generating high vertical stress near the walls and low pressure above the orifice, deformable grains exhibit higher pressure above the orifice that gradually declines during discharge. Furthermore, we examined the momentum balance in the orifice region for soft particles with low friction and developed a phenomenological model predicting a linear reduction in flow rate as the filling height decreases.

This study presents a search for supersymmetry utilizing proton-proton collision data characterized by hadronically decaying top quarks, the absence of leptons, and significant transverse momentum imbalance ($p_\mathrm{T}^\text{miss}$). The dataset, acquired by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, totals an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Analysis regions are categorized based on the counts of bottom quark jets and top quark candidates, alongside variables including $p_\mathrm{T}^\text{miss}$, the scalar sum of jet transverse momenta, and the $m_{\mathrm{T2}}$ mass metric. No statistically significant deviation from Standard Model predictions was observed. Consequently, 95% confidence level lower limits on supersymmetric particle masses were established using simplified models involving top quark production. Specifically, in a scenario where top squarks pair-produce and decay into a top quark and a neutralino, masses up to 1020 GeV for top squarks and 430 GeV for neutralinos are ruled out. Similarly, for a model featuring pair-produced gluinos decaying into a top quark-antiquark pair and a neutralino, gluino masses up to 2040 GeV and neutralino masses up to 1150 GeV are excluded. These findings represent an extension of prior results.

This report introduces a new method for achieving broadband, high-precision mass measurements of short-lived exotic nuclides. Utilizing isochronous mass spectrometry (IMS), the technique enables the simultaneous determination of revolution time and velocity for stored ions at the Cooler Storage Ring (CSRe) in Lanzhou. Dubbed $B\rho$-defined IMS or $B\rho$-IMS, this approach enhances the efficiency, sensitivity, and accuracy of mass determinations, specifically applied here to neutron-deficient $fp$-shell nuclides. Within a single accelerator run, the masses of $^{46}$Cr, $^{50}$Fe, and $^{54}$Ni were measured with relative uncertainties of (5–6)$\times10^{-8}$, providing improved data to test the unitarity of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa quark mixing matrix. Consequently, $B\rho$-IMS is established as the optimal technique for future high-precision studies of the most rarely produced and shortest-lived nuclides.

Let $\mathfrak B_g$ represent the moduli space of primitively polarized $K3$ surfaces $(S,H)$ of genus $g$ over $\mathbb C$. It is established that $\mathfrak B_g$ is irreducible and that any such surface $(S,H)$ contains only a finite number of rational curves within the linear system $|H|$. This allows us to investigate the monodromy group of these curves. While the case for $g=2$ is essentially derived from Harris \cite{Ha}, showing it to be the full symmetric group $S_{324}$, this work addresses the cases for $g=3$ and $g=4$.

Uncertainty is fundamental to forecasting the future, which is inherently unpredictable. Consequently, numerous potential futures may exist, and a robust prediction method must account for all of them. In autonomous driving, the ability to model multiple modes within the prediction framework is essential for making safety-critical decisions. Despite significant recent advancements in computer vision, predicting future states remains a challenging task due to inherent future uncertainty, the need for comprehensive scene understanding, and the presence of noisy output spaces. This thesis addresses these obstacles by explicitly modeling motion through stochastic methods and learning temporal dynamics within a latent space.

Classifying malware presents a significant and difficult challenge within the realm of information security. Contemporary approaches to this task utilize machine learning models trained on diverse features, including API calls, byte $n$-grams, and opcode sequences. This study focuses specifically on opcode features. We develop a hybrid machine learning framework that constructs feature vectors by applying Word2Vec embeddings and a novel technique called HMM2Vec (which involves training hidden Markov models) to opcode sequences. These generated embeddings subsequently serve as input features for various classification algorithms, specifically support vector machines (SVM), $k$-nearest neighbors ($k$-NN), random forests (RF), and convolutional neural networks (CNN). We performed extensive experiments across a wide range of malware families, with our experimental scope surpassing all prior work in this domain.

We introduce analytic gradients and derivative couplings for CIS-1D, the most basic multireference configuration interaction method. This approach builds upon a Hartree-Fock reference by incorporating all single excitations along with a single specific double excitation. Our results demonstrate that the derived equations are numerically stable and demand an integral count comparable to standard CIS theory, allowing for the efficient differentiation of frontier orbitals ($\mathtt{h}$ and $\mathtt{l}$) at minimal computational cost. Implemented within the Q-Chem software suite, this algorithm offers immediate utility for investigating photochemical processes involving $S_{0}$-$S_{1}$ crossings.

Recent studies on Secure Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) have focused on the fundamental limits of the finite block length (FBL) regime. Analysis indicates that if eavesdroppers exceed the number of base station (BS) antennas or possess superior channel conditions relative to legitimate users, the BS must increase transmit power excessively to satisfy Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. Similarly, practical channel impairments like shadowing and blockage present significant challenges, severely restricting secure URLLC performance in the FBL context. To address these issues and enhance system resilience against stringent latency, availability, and reliability demands, Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) can be deployed. This work proposes a joint design for IRS platforms and secure URLLC networks. The objective is to minimize total BS transmit power by jointly optimizing BS beamformers and artificial noise alongside IRS phase-shifts, while ensuring the delivery of a required number of secure bits within specified constraints for packet error probability, information leakage, and maximum delay. Since the resulting optimization problem is non-convex, we employ block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation to iteratively solve a sequence of convex sub-problems. The proposed algorithm converges to a sub-optimal solution within a few iterations, achieving significant power savings and robustness compared to baseline methods.

Significant variations in face recognition performance can arise from aging and gender differences. Although existing research predominantly examines pose, illumination, and expression, it is crucial to account for gender effects and develop robust matching frameworks. This study investigates these issues using the extensive MORPH-II longitudinal database, which comprises 55,134 images of 13,617 individuals. We conduct four comprehensive experiments exploring various gender distributions and subset sizes: 1) balanced gender ratios; 2) highly skewed gender ratios; 3) specific gender configurations (male-only, female-only, or mixed); and 4) the impact of varying the number of individuals. Additionally, we evaluate eight nearest neighbor distance metrics alongside Support Vector Machines (SVM) to assess classifier efficacy. Finally, we explore diverse fusion techniques to enhance the overall matching framework and improve recognition accuracy.

First-order nonadiabatic coupling matrix elements (fo-NACMEs) serve as fundamental quantities for theoretically describing electronically nonadiabatic processes, which are pervasive in molecular physics and chemistry. Given the substantial size of chemically relevant systems, time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) is typically the preferred approach. Nevertheless, the absence of explicit wave functions in TDDFT makes the formulation of NAC-TDDFT for calculating fo-NACMEs conceptually challenging. This account critically and concisely examines the existing variants of NAC-TDDFT while identifying appropriate implementation strategies. Based on both theoretical and numerical analyses, it is concluded that the equation of motion-based variant of NAC-TDDFT is the optimal choice, with potential future developments for this approach also outlined.

Recent advances in quantum simulation have utilized divalent atoms confined in optical tweezer arrays, achieving notable performance. While the second valence electron offers potential via Isolated Core Excitation (ICE), autoionization remains a significant hurdle. This study introduces and validates a novel method to induce a substantial light shift on Rydberg states with near-resonant ICE without triggering autoionization. Specifically, we examined ICE in ytterbium atoms within $^1S_0$ Rydberg states. Multi-channel Quantum Defect Theory accurately describes both the induced autoionization spectroscopy and the resulting light shifts on the Rydberg states. This capability to manipulate the inner electron independently of the Rydberg electron provides a powerful new tool for the coherent, targeted control of Rydberg states in quantum simulations involving alkaline-earth atoms.

$(\mu;\nu)$-Hankel operators acting between separable Hilbert spaces were recently introduced and analyzed in *$\mu$-Hankel operators on Hilbert spaces*, Opuscula Math., **41** (2021), 881--899. The present work extends these operators to Hardy spaces defined over compact and connected Abelian groups, accommodating cases where the spaces are non-separable. Under specific natural assumptions, bounded $(\mu;\nu)$-Hankel operators are characterized in this context, and examples of integral operators are provided.

TV subtitles offer a diverse collection of speech transcriptions, spanning from read scripts in news broadcasts to casual, spontaneous dialogue found in talk shows and soap operas. Since subtitles are not exact verbatim records of spoken language, they cannot be directly utilized to enhance Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems. We introduce a multitask dual-decoder Transformer architecture that simultaneously executes ASR and automatic subtitling. In this setup, the shared encoder feeds into two decoders: the ASR decoder (which may be pre-trained) generates verbatim text, while the subtitle decoder produces subtitles. These decoders can operate either independently or with connections between them. By training the model to handle both tasks jointly, it effectively leverages subtitle data. Our results demonstrate enhanced performance on standard ASR tasks as well as spontaneous and conversational ASR scenarios by integrating the subtitle decoder. Furthermore, this approach eliminates the need for any subtitle preprocessing, such as alignment, filtering, or pseudo-labeling.

Two-dimensional regular atomic arrays represent a promising platform for quantum networks, offering long-lived storage through collective subradiant states and enabling natural coherent connections between arrays in free space via collimated emission. However, single-layer lattices are limited to symmetric light absorption and emission in both forward and backward directions. This study demonstrates that a bilayer lattice can absorb a single photon originating from a single direction or an arbitrary superposition of forward and backward propagating components.
