Beyond its significance for fundamental physics research, the realization of indefinite causal order (ICO)—where quantum superposition applies even to causal relationships between physical events—enables quantum information processing protocols that surpass those with definite causal structures. This paper posits that an observer existing in a quantum superposition of two distinct distances relative to a black hole's event horizon effectively inhabits an ICO spacetime generated by the black hole. Leveraging the fact that the near-horizon geometry of a Schwarzschild black hole mimics Rindler spacetime, we propose simulating an observer in ICO spacetime through a Rindler observer in a superposition of two different proper accelerations. Consequently, a pair of Rindler observers with entangled proper accelerations serves as a simulation for a pair of entangled ICO observers. Furthermore, these Rindler systems may have a feasible experimental implementation using optomechanical resonators.

This study examines a Dirichlet-type problem for an even-order equation featuring variable coefficients, establishing a criterion for solution uniqueness. The solution is constructed using a Fourier series, where the justification of convergence involves addressing the issue of small denominators; sufficient conditions ensuring these denominators remain non-zero are derived. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the problem's solvability depends not only on the rectangle's dimension but also on the orders of the derivatives prescribed at the lower boundary.

This report details the initial detection of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing proton-lead data from the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC, recorded at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 8.16$ TeV. The analysis focuses on events containing precisely one isolated electron or muon alongside a minimum of four jets, based on a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 174 inverse nanobarns. The observed $t\bar{t}$ signal exceeds the background-only hypothesis by more than five standard deviations. The resulting cross section of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 45 \pm 8$ nb aligns with predictions derived from perturbative quantum chromodynamics.

We investigate the properties of the $\chi_{c1}(3872)$, or $X(3872)$, within dense nuclear matter. Starting with a vacuum model where the $X(3872)$ is a purely molecular $(D \bar D^*-c.c.)$ state formed as a bound system via a leading-order heavy-quark symmetry interaction between charmed mesons, we analyze the $D \bar D^*$ scattering $T-$matrix ($T_{D \bar D^*}$) in the medium. Furthermore, we examine mixed-molecular scenarios; in all cases, we calculate the $X(3872)$ spectral function and the $D \bar D^*$ amplitude, accounting for mesons embedded in the dense environment. Our findings reveal significant nuclear corrections to both $T_{D \bar D^*}$ and the resonance's pole position, and we discuss how these outcomes depend on the molecular component of the $X(3872)$ wave function. These predictions may be tested in future finite-density regimes accessible via the CBM and PANDA experiments at FAIR.

Most machine learning algorithms operate under the assumption that training data is independent and identically distributed (iid); however, violations of this assumption degrade performance and trigger the well-known issue of catastrophic forgetting. This challenge defines the Continual Learning research domain. This paper investigates regularization-based methods for continual learning, demonstrating their inability to distinguish classes from different tasks within a fundamental continual benchmark: the class-incremental scenario. Through theoretical reasoning, supported by examples and experiments, we prove this limitation. Furthermore, we highlight significant implications for continual multi-task reinforcement learning and the application of pre-trained models in continual learning contexts. We argue that identifying and comprehending the deficiencies of regularization strategies is essential for their more effective utilization.

Hermann Weyl's classical invariant theory has proven essential for analyzing numerous geometric systems. Previously, Gover and Waldron utilized this framework to demonstrate that all (natural and local) invariants associated with hypersurfaces embedded in Riemannian manifolds can be formulated using the ambient curvature, the boundary conormal, the second fundamental form, and their derivatives. This paper extends the inquiry to hypersurfaces embedded within even-dimensional conformal manifolds. We establish a finite and minimal set of hypersurface tensors—comprising intrinsic curvatures and the "conformal fundamental forms"—which allows for the construction of every (natural, local) conformal hypersurface invariant that depends on a limited number of derivatives of the conformal metric.

The cocktail party problem, which seeks to isolate specific sources within complex acoustic environments, has long driven audio source separation research. While recent studies have primarily targeted separating speech from noise, speech from speech, musical instruments, or distinct sound events, the separation of mixed audio (such as movie soundtracks) into three broad categories—speech, music, and sound effects (encompassing ambient noise and natural sounds)—remains largely unexplored despite its significant potential applications. This paper defines this specific challenge as the "cocktail fork problem" and introduces the Divide and Remaster (DnR) dataset to advance research in this area. Constructed from three established datasets (LibriSpeech, FMA, and FSD50k), DnR is designed to emulate the source overlap and relative loudness found in professionally produced content and is provided in CD quality. We evaluate standard source separation algorithms on DnR and propose a new multi-resolution model to better handle the diverse acoustic characteristics of the three source types. Our top-performing model achieves Signal-to-Interference Ratio improvements of 11.0 dB for music, 11.2 dB for speech, and 10.8 dB for sound effects over the original mixture.

Although it is uncommon for texts or full-length books composed in a Controlled Natural Language (CNL) to gain significant popularity, Randall Munroe's book *Thing Explainer*, published last year, is a notable exception. This work explains complex subjects—including nuclear reactors, jet engines, the solar system, and dishwashers—by utilizing only the 1,000 most frequently used English words alongside illustrations. This constrained vocabulary represents a fascinating new case study for the CNL community. This paper examines the book's position within existing CNL methodologies and offers an initial scientific analysis that covers word production rules and word distribution patterns.

This paper proposes a novel geophysical theory, formulated as a single simple partial integro-differential equation, to account for the empirically observed oval shapes of stones smoothed solely by frictional abrasion on flat beaches. The theory rests on the intuitive premise that the rate of surface ablation at any given point is proportional to the product of the stone's local curvature at that point and the frequency of contact with the beach. Crucially, the new model relies on both the random nature of wave processes and the stone's global (non-local) geometry, meaning its overall shape influences wear even at points distant from immediate contact. The physical mechanism driving this process involves converting energy from the wave motion into the stone's potential energy. Although no closed-form or asymptotic solutions exist for this fundamental equation—even in two dimensions—the article presents basic numerical solutions in two contexts: a deterministic continuous-time framework using standard curve-shortening algorithms, and a stochastic discrete-time polyhedral-slicing approach utilizing Monte Carlo simulations.

Addressing the primary challenge of creating computationally efficient, accurate, and stable solvers for time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs), this work introduces a graph neural network methodology. By leveraging message-passing models, we learn efficient PDE solvers. First, we establish domain-invariant features for PDE-data, drawing inspiration from classical solvers to ensure an effective physical representation. Subsequently, we utilize graphs to depict PDE-data on unstructured meshes, demonstrating that message-passing graph neural networks (MPGNN) can parameterize governing equations. This capability enables the efficient learning of precise solver schemes for both linear and nonlinear PDEs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these solvers are geometry-independent; a solver trained on one configuration can accurately solve PDEs across various complex domains. Finally, we illustrate that a recurrent graph neural network approach can generate the temporal sequence of solutions for a PDE.

This study examines topological phase transitions within an effective model of a topological thin film subjected to high-frequency pumping. Specifically, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can break time-reversal symmetry to induce the quantum anomalous Hall insulator (QAHI) phase, while the bulk magnetic moment similarly breaks this symmetry. Consequently, varying the light intensity and film thickness yields a rich phase diagram. Utilizing parameters fitted to experimental data, we construct the topological phase diagram for Cr-doped Bi$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ thin films. Our findings reveal that modulating the strength of the polarized optical field within an experimentally accessible range generates four distinct phases: the normal insulator phase, the time-reversal-symmetry-broken quantum spin Hall insulator phase, and two distinct QAHI phases characterized by opposite Chern numbers. Unlike non-doped Bi$_{2}$Se$_{3}$, the interaction between light and the bulk magnetic moment distinguishes these two QAHI phases with opposing Chern numbers. Ultimately, these results indicate that an intrinsic magnetic topological insulator under high-frequency pumping serves as an ideal platform for investigating diverse topological phenomena involving spontaneously broken time-reversal symmetry.

We precisely determine the transverse velocity distribution of a thermal strontium (Sr) atomic beam using velocity-selective saturated fluorescence spectroscopy. The combination of an ultrastable laser system and Sr's narrow intercombination transition line enables a velocity resolution of 0.13 m/s, equivalent to 90 $\mu$K in energy units. Our experimental findings align very closely with theoretical predictions. Leveraging these spectroscopic methods, we also measured the absolute frequency of the intercombination transition in $^{88}$Sr using an optical-frequency comb referenced to the SI second via an H maser, yielding a value of 434 829 121 318(10) kHz.

Biofilm-templated gold nanonetworks offer a framework for investigating the shift from localized plasmons to surface plasmons. This transition from localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) to surface plasmon resonance (SPR) is triggered by the percolation of metal atoms connecting gold nano-islands. The resulting nanocomposites exhibited a change in their metal percolation status, shifting from non-percolating to percolating states, a phenomenon clearly indicated by alterations in their electrical properties. The optical analysis employed a previously validated method by our group, wherein biofilms induce photonic coherences. The resulting enhancement spectra displayed peaks corresponding to plasmonic resonances, with these peaks varying based on the concentration of the added gold precursor.

A port-Hamiltonian (pH) system formulation serves as a geometric approach for expressing conservation laws across diverse physical systems. Specifically, the distributed parameter pH formulation addresses infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian dynamical systems characterized by non-zero energy flow at their boundaries. This paper introduces a new framework for applying Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretizations to pH-systems. Integrating DG methods with pH-systems yields finite element discretizations that maintain structural compatibility while offering flexibility regarding geometry and the function spaces of the variables. Furthermore, the pH formulation explicitly defines boundary ports, thereby simplifying the selection of numerical fluxes that preserve structure and power. We establish the Discontinuous Finite Element Stokes-Dirac structure featuring power-preserving inter-element coupling, which serves as the mathematical foundation for a broad class of pH discontinuous Galerkin discretizations. Additionally, we present an a priori error analysis for the port-Hamiltonian discontinuous Galerkin Finite Element Method (pH-DGFEM). Finally, the pH-DGFEM is applied to the scalar wave equation, demonstrating optimal convergence rates.

Let $l \geq 6$ be an integer satisfying $l \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$. Assume $\mu(\tau)d\tau$ is a measure of bounded variation supported on a compact subset of the complex plane, with the constraints $\Im(\tau)$ and $\Im(-1/\tau)$ both exceeding $\sin(\pi/l)$. Define $f(x) = \int e^{i\pi \tau |x|^2} d\mu(\tau)$ for $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$, and let $\mathcal{F}(f)$ denote its Fourier transform. For any integer $k \geq 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^2$, we express $f(x)$ using the values of the $k$-th derivatives of $f$ and $\mathcal{F}(f)$ with respect to $u = |x|^2$ evaluated at $u = 2n/\lambda$, where $n$ is a non-negative integer and $\lambda = 2\cos(\pi/l)$. We demonstrate that the condition on the imaginary parts is optimal. Furthermore, we establish summation formulas relating these derivative values at $u = 2n/\lambda$ to the space of holomorphic modular forms of weight $2k+1$ for the Hecke triangle group $(2,l,\infty)$. By applying these formulas to the case $l=6$ alongside novel techniques, we prove Conjecture 7.5 of Cohn, Kumar, Miller, Radchenko, and Viazovska~\cite[Conjecture 7.5]{Maryna3}, a conjecture inspired by the universal optimality of the hexagonal lattice.

The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things has driven the growth of health monitoring applications. The recent COVID-19 pandemic has further heightened interest in permanent remote health monitoring solutions aimed at minimizing contact and conserving scarce medical resources. Among the technologies enabling efficient remote monitoring, federated learning (FL) has gained significant attention for its robustness in protecting data privacy. However, FL often incurs high communication costs due to frequent data exchanges between the server and clients. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a communication-efficient federated learning (CEFL) framework that integrates client clustering and transfer learning. Initially, clients are grouped based on calculated similarity factors derived from neural network characteristics. A representative client is then selected as the leader for each cluster. Unlike conventional FL, our method conducts training exclusively among these cluster leaders. Subsequently, transfer learning enables leaders to update their cluster members with the trained FL model, followed by fine-tuning of the received model using each member's local data. To further minimize communication overhead, we employ a partial-layer FL aggregation approach, which involves partially updating the neural network model rather than performing full updates. Experimental results demonstrate that CEFL can reduce communication costs by up to 98.45% compared to conventional FL while incurring an accuracy loss of less than 3%. Additionally, CEFL exhibits high accuracy even for clients with small or unbalanced datasets.

**Motivation:** Accurately predicting drug-target interactions is essential for both drug discovery and repurposing, making machine learning a prevalent tool for addressing drug-target affinity (DTA) challenges. However, these models often encounter a cold-start issue, where performance declines when evaluating interactions involving novel drugs or targets. While prior research has attempted to mitigate this by generating drug or target representations through unsupervised learning, such approaches often fail to capture critical interaction information inherent to drug-target systems. **Results:** To address this limitation, we propose leveraging transfer learning from chemical-chemical interaction (CCI) and protein-protein interaction (PPI) tasks to enhance the DTA task. Given the inherent similarities between these domains, representations derived from CCI and PPI tasks can be effectively transferred to DTA. Empirical results on drug-target affinity datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms other pretraining strategies in the DTA context.

Current extractive summarization models typically generate summaries by selecting salient sentences. However, a significant challenge in sentence-level extractive summarization is the discrepancy between human-written gold summaries and oracle sentence labels. To address this, we propose extracting fact-level semantic units to enhance extractive summarization. Furthermore, we introduce a hierarchical structure that integrates multi-level granularities of textual information into the model. Additionally, we combine our approach with BERT using a hierarchical graph mask, enabling the fusion of BERT's natural language understanding capabilities with structural information without increasing model size. Experiments on the CNN/DailyMail dataset demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance.

The global integration of the Integrated Circuit (IC) supply chain has shifted design, fabrication, and testing from a single trusted source to diverse, untrusted third parties worldwide. This shift introduces significant risks associated with untrusted third-party intellectual property (3PIP), specifically the potential for adversaries to embed malicious Hardware Trojans (HTs). Such trojans can undermine design integrity, degrade performance, disrupt services, or modify functionality. Although many literature-based methods exist for detecting HTs, the critical step of localizing them is often neglected. Furthermore, current localization techniques suffer from several limitations, including dependence on golden references, poor generalization across HT types, limited scalability, low resolution, and reliance on manual feature engineering. To address these gaps, we introduce a novel, golden-reference-free HT localization method for the pre-silicon stage utilizing Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN). Our approach transforms the circuit design into an intrinsic graph structure, extracting node attributes to enable automatic feature extraction and classification of nodes as either Trojan or benign. This automated solution eliminates the need for manual code reviews by designers, successfully identifying Trojan signals with 99.6% accuracy, a 93.1% F1-score, and a false-positive rate under 0.009%.

Recent years have seen substantial progress in deductive verification for C11, driven by operational semantics and corresponding logics that cover larger fragments of the language. However, these approaches have been confined to restricted environments to sidestep the thin-air-read issue. This paper introduces a novel operational semantics that utilizes an intra-thread partial order, termed semantic dependencies, derived from a recently created denotational event-structure-based semantics. We establish that our operational semantics is both sound and complete relative to the denotational counterpart. Furthermore, we develop a related logic that extends a recent Owicki-Gries framework for RC11 (repaired C11) and illustrate its application through multiple example proofs.

We develop a compartmental model to describe the spread of a respiratory disease within a fragmented landscape where patches are linked by human movement. This model assumes that both transmission and recovery can occur while individuals are traveling, with migration rates influenced by inter-patch distance and the perceived disease severity. We analyze the positivity and boundedness of the model's solutions and analytically demonstrate the existence and global asymptotic stability of the disease-free equilibrium. Through numerical investigations of three distinct network topologies, we identify that the underlying network structure plays a pivotal role in disease transmission. Additional simulations indicate that infections acquired during travel can shift the stability of the disease-free equilibrium from stable to unstable. Furthermore, coupling strength and transmission coefficients are critical factors in disease propagation. Evaluations of various exit screening strategies suggest that while the patch with the highest prevalence might suffer adverse effects, other patches could benefit from such measures. In the context of multi-strain dynamics, our observations show that two co-circulating strains cannot persist simultaneously in the long term; only one strain survives. The transmission coefficients for the second strain are particularly significant, exhibiting threshold-like behavior relative to the equilibrium density of that strain.

Kagome superconductors AV$_3$Sb$_5$ (where A represents K, Rb, or Cs) serve as an ideal platform for investigating fascinating phenomena including non-trivial band topology, superconductivity, a giant anomalous Hall effect, and charge density waves (CDW). Notably, the recent identification of a $C_2$ symmetric nematic phase preceding superconductivity in AV$_3$Sb$_5$ has garnered significant interest, suggesting that the peculiar superconductivity might adopt the symmetry of this nematic state. Despite extensive efforts employing real-space microscopy and transport measurements to clarify charge orders, direct evidence of rotation symmetry breaking within the electronic structure of the CDW state in reciprocal space remains scarce, leaving the underlying mechanism unclear. In this study, we utilize micron-scale spatially resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to detect band folding signatures in the CDW phase of KV$_3$Sb$_5$. These signatures exhibit unconventional unidirectionality and signal a symmetry reduction from $C_6$ to $C_2$. Furthermore, we identify that interlayer coupling between adjacent planes with a $\pi$-phase offset in the 2$\times$2$\times$2 CDW phase drives the formation of a preferred twofold symmetric electronic structure. Additionally, time-reversal symmetry breaking occurs below approximately 40 K, evidenced by a giant anomalous Hall effect induced by weak magnetic fields. These rarely seen unidirectional back-folded bands accompanied by time-reversal symmetry breaking in KV$_3$Sb$_5$ offer crucial insights into the material's unique charge order and superconducting properties.

This paper investigates the large population limit of a binary branching particle system featuring Moran-type interactions. We present a novel model in which particles evolve, reproduce, and die independently, yet the death of one particle can trigger the reproduction of another, and a branching event can induce the death of a different one, with these transition probabilities potentially depending on the system's configuration. We analyze the occupation measure of this new model by explicitly connecting it to the Feynman-Kac semigroup of the underlying Markov evolution and by quantifying the L2 distance between their respective normalizations. This framework extends the fixed-size Moran-type interacting particle systems explored in references [18, 19, 6, 7, 57], and we demonstrate that our model provides a superior approximation for birth and death processes compared to the latter. Furthermore, we explore additional applications of our model, such as the neutron transport equation [36, 15] and population size dynamics.

We determine the masses of the pseudoscalar mesons $\pi^+$, $K^0$, and $D^+$ at finite temperature and baryon chemical potential using a symmetry-preserving Dyson-Schwinger equation approach with a vector-vector four-quark contact interaction. Our findings regarding the temperature dependence of these meson masses align qualitatively with lattice QCD data and QCD sum rule calculations, whereas the dependence on chemical potential offers a new prediction from this study.

Hate speech classifiers suffer significant performance drops when tested on datasets distinct from their training sources. This issue arises because models learn spurious correlations between irrelevant words and hate speech labels within the training data. Previous attempts to address this have involved regularizing terms from fixed, pre-defined dictionaries. Although such methods enhance classifier generalizability, they suffer from limited coverage and necessitate frequent manual updates by human experts. This paper introduces a method to automatically detect and mitigate these spurious correlations using attribution techniques, featuring a dynamically refined list of terms requiring regularization during training. Our flexible approach improves cross-corpora performance compared to prior work, both when used independently and when combined with pre-defined dictionaries.

This study examines a generalized Hele-Shaw equation incorporating source and drift terms, subject to a space-time varying upper bound on density. Utilizing a generalized porous medium equation approximation, we construct a weak solution under mild conditions and subsequently prove its uniqueness. A primary contribution is a pointwise characterization of the density variable specifically within the congestion regime. To achieve this, we derive a novel uniform lower bound on the time derivative of the pressure for the generalized porous medium equation, employing a refined Aronson-Benilan estimate that ensures monotonicity in both density and pressure.

Although physically feasible, lanthanide polyhydrides known as samarium hydrides have not yet been experimentally confirmed at high pressures. This study integrates density functional theory (DFT) with dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to investigate the many-body interactions within samarium. By employing random structure searches across diverse pressures and stoichiometries, we identify a theoretically stable high-pressure phase for SmH$_2$, characterized by a layered hexagonal structure belonging to the $P6/mmm$ space group at approximately 200 GPa.

To prevent collisions, autonomous drones operating near obstacles must be capable of detecting and avoiding them. Previous approaches have relied on data from cameras, ultrasonic, or laser sensors mounted on the drone or within the environment; however, instrumenting the environment is often impractical, and adding sensors to the drone consumes limited power and payload capacity. This study investigates the use of data mining classification techniques to predict an obstacle's location relative to the drone by analyzing air-disturbance patterns alone. We physically modeled rotor airflow to derive higher-level features suitable for classification. Data was gathered from the drone's IMU during flights with walls positioned to the left, front, right, and in the absence of walls, yielding a total of 18 high-level features from the raw signals. Using an 80/20 train-test split, we evaluated Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), and Gradient Boosting (GB) classifiers. Our findings demonstrate that the Random Forest classifier achieved 90% accuracy in predicting the direction of a wall relative to the drone.

The United States is facing an unprecedented opioid crisis, where overdose has emerged as a primary cause of injury and mortality. Successful recovery from opioid addiction requires a dual approach combining medical treatments with behavioral interventions for affected individuals. This paper examines the communication and behavioral patterns of patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) found on social media, aiming to show how data from everyday online activities can enhance the prediction, assessment, and prevention of relapses. Adopting a multi-disciplinary and innovative analytical framework, we characterize OUD behaviors by analyzing Reddit groups dedicated to opioid issues. Our methodology includes modeling discussion topics, examining text co-occurrence and correlations, and detecting the emotional states of individuals with OUD. These quantitative analyses hold practical significance, illustrating novel methods to leverage social media information for developing technologies that aid in relapse prevention.

This paper proposes that for any nonconservative classical mechanical system and any given initial condition, there corresponds a conservative system sharing a unique common phase curve. The Hamiltonian of this conservative system equals the total energy of the nonconservative system along that specific phase curve plus a constant determined by the initial condition. Consequently, this method effectively replaces a single dissipative system with an infinite set of conservative systems tailored to various initial conditions. A primary demonstration relies on the Newton-Laplace principle, which allows the nonconservative force to be expressed as a function of a generalized coordinate component $q_i$ along the phase curve, thereby reformulating the nonconservative system into countless conservative equivalents. By applying this proposition, the methods of Hamiltonian or Lagrangian mechanics can be utilized for dissipative systems without altering the definition of canonical momentum or deviating from the original system's motion.

This paper investigates autonomous and AI-assisted control loops (ACLs) within the next generation of wireless networks, specifically through the perspective of multi-agent environments. We examine the varied interactions and conflict resolution strategies among these loops, proposing "interaction and conflict management" (ICM) modules to ensure coherence, consistency, and effective interaction between them. Furthermore, we define three categories of ACLs based on their scale, cooperative or competitive nature, and the extent to which they share datasets and models; these categories facilitate the development of conflict resolution and interaction management mechanisms for ICM. Finally, leveraging Kubernetes, we demonstrate an ICM implementation designed to eliminate conflicts during the scheduling and rescheduling of Pods for various ACLs within network infrastructures.

Recently, reconstructing 3D room layouts from multiple $360^{\circ}$ panoramas has gained significant interest, as deriving a complete layout for large, complex spaces from a single image remains challenging. The current leading approach, PSMNet, establishes the first learning-based framework to simultaneously estimate room layouts and registrations using a pair of panoramas; however, it depends on approximate ("noisy") registration inputs, which necessitates solving the difficult wide baseline registration problem. This work introduces a comprehensive multi-view framework that jointly learns panorama registration and layout estimation from a pair of images without requiring a pose prior. A key advancement is the novel Geometry-aware Panorama Registration Network (GPR-Net), which addresses wide baseline registration by leveraging layout geometry and calculating fine-grained correspondences on layout boundaries rather than in global pixel space. The proposed architecture comprises two main components: first, a vision transformer extracts 1D horizon features from two panoramas, encoding depth information for individual layout boundary samples along with correspondence and covisibility maps between them. Second, a non-linear registration module transforms these 1D features into corresponding 2D boundary points on the layout. The final relative camera pose is then determined using RANSAC, and the complete layout is generated by uniting the registered layouts. Experiments on the large-scale indoor dataset ZInD demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results in both panorama registration and layout estimation.

Domain adaptation is a theoretically established and widely applied field. Notable contributions include Ben-David et al.'s (2010) bound on target error and the Domain Adversarial Neural Network (DANN) algorithm introduced by Ganin and Lempitsky (2015), which leverages this theoretical foundation. While numerous DANN variants have recently been adapted for domain generalization, they often lack a thorough examination of the original motivating bound. This paper re-evaluates the applicability of DANN to domain generalization through that theoretical lens, analyzing the conditions under which it is effective and treating DANN as a dynamic training process. Our findings indicate that applying DANN to domain generalization is less straightforward than commonly assumed. Consequently, we propose an algorithmic extension of DANN specifically for this scenario, with experimental results confirming both our theoretical insights and the proposed method.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) enables computer vision systems to perceive connections between multiple objects within a scene, extending beyond simple object identification. Conventional VRD methods typically operate in two disjoint stages: first detecting objects and then separately inferring their relationships. This separation often leads to errors, such as generating redundant predicate tags with similar meanings or incorrect predictions that are semantically distinct from the ground truth despite superficial similarities. To address these limitations, we introduce a method that jointly trains a VRD model using both visual object features and semantic relationship features. Specifically, we propose VReBERT, a BERT-inspired transformer architecture designed for VRD that employs a multi-stage training strategy to simultaneously process these dual feature types. Our results demonstrate that this straightforward BERT-like model surpasses current state-of-the-art VRD approaches in predicate prediction. Additionally, leveraging our pre-trained VReBERT model significantly advances zero-shot predicate prediction performance, achieving substantial improvements of +8.49 R@50 and +8.99 R@100.

Measuring the charm production cross-section in proton-proton collisions at the LHC serves as a crucial benchmark for studying medium characteristics in heavy-ion collisions and acts as a vital test for perturbative QCD predictions within a novel energy regime. The ALICE collaboration has conducted measurements of D meson production in pp collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. This work details the analysis methodology for the $\rm D^{0}\to \rm K^{-}\rm \pi^{+}$ decay channel, including the determination of efficiency and acceptance corrections. Furthermore, preliminary findings on the $\rm D^0$ cross-section are presented for the transverse momentum range $2<p_{\rm t}<12$ GeV/$c$ at central rapidity $|y|<0.5$. These results are subsequently compared against perturbative QCD theoretical predictions.

We introduce a new Hamming distance-tolerant content-addressable memory (HD-CAM) optimized for energy-efficient approximate matching within memory systems. Unlike current state-of-the-art approaches that rely on the rise or fall times of matchlines, HD-CAM performs approximate search by utilizing matchline charge redistribution. Fabricated in 65 nm 1.2 V CMOS technology, the design underwent rigorous testing via extensive Monte Carlo simulations. Our results demonstrate that HD-CAM maintains robust functionality despite significant process variations and design parameter fluctuations, accommodating diverse pattern lengths and mismatch thresholds. Furthermore, functional evaluations for virus DNA classification confirm that HD-CAM is well-suited for hardware acceleration in genomic surveillance, including the monitoring of viral outbreaks like the Covid-19 pandemic.

Although Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are practically successful and possess universal function approximation capabilities, they suffer from catastrophic forgetting—the abrupt loss of previously learned tasks upon acquiring new ones. This phenomenon, which obstructs continual learning, is not predicted by existing universal approximation theorems for ANNs. This paper introduces a new universal approximation theorem for multi-variable functions constructed solely from single-variable and exponential functions. Building on this theorem, we propose ATLAS, a novel ANN architecture that serves as a universal function approximator with the ability to retain some memory and support continual learning. While ATLAS's memory is imperfect and may exhibit minor off-target effects during continual learning, its behavior remains predictable and well-controlled. An efficient implementation of ATLAS is provided, along with experiments evaluating both its function approximation and memory retention capabilities.

In 2008, Z.E. Musielak, in *J. Phys. A: Math. Theor.* {\bf 41} 055205, outlined techniques for deriving both standard and non-standard Lagrangians and for determining which classes of equations of motion possess a Lagrangian formulation. This commentary demonstrates a method to derive novel non-standard Lagrangians by utilizing those previously identified. Specifically, it is shown that for each existing non-standard Lagrangian, a corresponding new non-standard Lagrangian can be generated, which is linked to a distinct equation of motion.

This study demonstrates that the percolation cluster arising from the process on infinite perfect binary trees serves as a genuine encoding scheme for an infinite set of symbols. The average codeword length and entropy of this encoding scheme remain finite provided the percolation density $p$ satisfies $1/2 \leq p < \sqrt[3]{1/4}$.

This paper examines greedy strategies for the Hierarchical Aggregation (HAG) problem, a technique proposed by [Jia et al., KDD 2020] to accelerate Graph Neural Network (GNN) training by eliminating computational redundancies. While prior research presented a greedy method for HAG with an asserted 1-1/e approximation guarantee, we demonstrate through counterexamples that this claim is invalid and that no better than a 1/2 approximation factor is achievable. Instead, we establish that the original algorithm satisfies a weaker approximation guarantee by revealing a novel link between HAG and maximum matching in hypergraphs. Furthermore, we propose a second greedy algorithm that surpasses the first in performance and can be efficiently implemented under specific parameter settings. Finally, we present several rapid greedy heuristics that execute significantly faster than the previous methods while maintaining strong performance on real-world graph data.

We introduce SentiMATE, an innovative end-to-end Deep Learning framework for Chess that leverages Natural Language Processing (NLP) to develop a robust evaluation function for assessing move quality. This function undergoes pre-training on the sentiment of commentary linked to training moves, subsequently guiding and optimizing the agent's strategic decision-making. The study's contributions are threefold: first, we construct and deploy a classifier capable of extracting commentary describing move quality from extensive datasets; second, we train a Sentiment Analysis model on Chess commentary to accurately predict move quality, utilizing these predictions to determine the optimal next move for a Chess agent, with both classifiers achieving over 90% accuracy. Finally, we present the SentiMATE Chess engine, which evaluates moves based on this pre-trained sentiment-based evaluation function. Our findings strongly validate our initial hypothesis regarding the feasibility of using NLP to train a novel and sample-efficient evaluation function for Chess Engines. When integrated into modern Chess engines and pitted against agents utilizing traditional evaluation functions, SentiMATE successfully outperformed both random agents and a DeepChess implementation operating at a level-one search depth, which represents the number of moves a traditional agent using the alpha-beta search algorithm examines to evaluate a chess state.

This paper investigates the topological characteristics, structure, and classification of Morse flows featuring fixed points on the boundaries of three-dimensional manifolds. We develop a comprehensive topological invariant known as the Pr-diagram for these Morse flows, which parallels the Heegaard diagram used for closed 3-manifolds.

Beyond their intrinsic spin, electrons in numerous materials exhibit an extra pseudo-spin property termed "valley." In systems where spin and valley degrees of freedom are only weakly coupled, they can be manipulated and excited separately. This study investigates a model characterizing the interaction between spin and valley Hall effects in such two-dimensional materials. We show that an additional longitudinal neutral current emerges, which is simultaneously polarized in both spin and valley. This neutral current enables the regulation of spin density by adjusting the strength of the valley Hall effect. Furthermore, the interplay between these two effects can inhibit the Hanle effect—the oscillation of nonlocal resistance in a Hall bar device under an in-plane magnetic field. This finding offers a potential explanation for the missing Hanle effect observed in several recent experiments. Additionally, our work suggests new avenues for engineering the conversion between valley and spin degrees of freedom in two-dimensional materials.

We examine the eigenvalues of symplectic elliptic Ginibre matrices, which constitute a Pfaffian point process characterized by a correlation kernel defined via skew-orthogonal Hermite polynomials. We derive the scaling limits and convergence rates of these correlation functions at the real bulk and edge of the spectrum, thereby demonstrating local universality under strong non-Hermiticity. Additionally, we determine the subleading corrections to the edge correlation kernels, which vary with the non-Hermiticity parameter unlike the universal leading term. Our proofs rely on the asymptotic properties of the complex elliptic Ginibre ensemble established by Lee and Riser, alongside a specific version of the Christoffel-Darboux identity that corresponds to a differential equation satisfied by the skew-orthogonal polynomial kernel.

As datasets grow larger, the importance of change point detection increases, with unsupervised algorithms playing a key role in assisting users with data processing. Various unsupervised methods have been developed based on different principles, including an optimization approach that minimizes a cost function alongside a penalty function; in this framework, the selection of the cost function significantly influences the algorithm's predictions. Extending prior research, this study introduces a novel cost function utilizing Tikhonov regularization. Alternatively, a Bayesian approach calculates the posterior probability of a specific point being a change point by incorporating a priori knowledge of the distance between consecutive changes and a likelihood function derived from segment information. This research examines both optimization and Bayesian methods for offline change point detection, applying them to both simulated and real-world multi-phase datasets. While these approaches have been investigated separately before, the novelty of this work lies in comparing their predictive performance within a unified setting involving both simulated and real data. The findings indicate that the effectiveness of these change point detection algorithms is influenced by the specific features present in the data.

The reliability of a Boolean Conjunctive Query (CQ) on a tuple-independent probabilistic database represents the likelihood that the query evaluates to true when database tuples are sampled independently according to their specific probabilities. For CQs lacking self-joins, the data complexity of this reliability problem is defined by a established dichotomy: it is solvable in polynomial time for hierarchical queries but is #P-hard for those that are not. Motivated by this classification, we examine a core counting problem for self-join-free CQs: determining the number of fact subsets from the input database that satisfy the query. This corresponds to the uniform scenario of the reliability problem, where every tuple has a probability of 1/2. While uniform reliability is polynomial-time solvable for hierarchical queries, we demonstrate that hierarchy is a necessary condition for such tractability (assuming standard complexity constraints). Furthermore, we extend this dichotomy to encompass all restricted reliability instances where tuple probabilities are dictated by their relation.

Traditionally, high-throughput computational searches for materials begin with bulk compounds sourced from databases, which are then screened for specific applications. However, many functional materials, particularly semiconductors, are heavily engineered alloys or solid solutions rather than single bulk compounds. To enhance the design of functional materials, this study introduces a framework and open-source code that automatically generates potential "alloy pairs" and "alloy systems," and identifies "alloy members" from existing ordered compounds—whether experimental or calculated—using only their crystal structures, without needing extra metadata. The framework includes tools to assess stability across various alloys. As a demonstration, we applied this method to all inorganic materials in the Materials Project database, creating a new repository of over 600,000 unique "alloy pair" entries. These entries are now accessible via the Materials Project website, linked with material identifiers for user exploration, and can be utilized in discovery studies to find materials with tunable properties. Using p-type transparent conducting materials as an example, we show how this approach uncovers candidate systems that traditional screening methods might overlook. This work establishes a foundation for materials databases to move beyond simple stoichiometric compounds toward a more realistic representation of compositionally tunable materials.

Combining neural networks into ensembles is a proven strategy for boosting accuracy, sometimes rivaling the performance of larger individual models. This raises a key question: when choosing between a deep ensemble and a single model with comparable accuracy, which is superior? Although recent studies claim deep ensembles provide unique advantages in uncertainty estimation and robustness to data distribution shifts, this work challenges those claims. We demonstrate that a single, larger neural network can achieve the same qualities. Specifically, we find that ensemble diversity does not significantly enhance uncertainty quantification for out-of-distribution (OOD) data; rather, it correlates closely with the performance gains of a single larger model. Furthermore, an ensemble's OOD performance is primarily driven by its in-distribution (InD) results, suggesting it does not represent true robustness. While ensembles remain a practical method for improving predictive power, uncertainty, and robustness, our findings indicate that these benefits can be matched by scaling up a single model.

This study details the design and execution of a blockchain framework facilitating trustworthy transactive energy management for distributed energy resources (DERs). By framing interactions among DERs—such as energy trading and flexible appliance scheduling—as a cost minimization challenge, we propose a distributed algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to address the dispersed and multi-owned nature of these resources. Additionally, we construct a blockchain system integrating smart contracts to host this algorithm, ensuring transparency and accuracy in energy operations. A small-scale prototype was tested within a real-world data-driven network, with experimental outcomes confirming the viability and efficacy of the proposed design.

Simulating chemical reaction networks is frequently computationally intensive, primarily because of stiffness. We introduce a new simulation approach that avoids simulating long trajectories as single continuous runs; instead, these are constructed by assembling shorter, precomputed segments. This method accelerates the generation of multiple runs through segment reuse. While this raises concerns regarding the diversity and authenticity of the generated runs, we guarantee that the output closely matches the true distribution by employing an appropriate abstraction of the original system within the simulation framework. Notably, this process also yields a more efficient simulation scheme for the system's abstraction itself. These abstract runs offer a highly faithful approximation of concrete trajectories at a specific granularity with minimal cost. Our experiments confirm significant speedups while maintaining essential dynamical and quantitative properties.

This research introduces a novel family of correlation structures tailored for crossover designs with repeated measures, accommodating both Gaussian and non-Gaussian responses through generalized estimating equations (GEE). The approach utilizes two distinct matrices: one to capture between-period correlations and another for within-period correlations, with the resulting overall correlation matrix constructed via the Kronecker product of these two components. We propose a parameter estimation procedure for this matrix, analyze its statistical properties, and compare it against conventional models that rely on a single correlation matrix. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed structure outperforms standard models in terms of the quasi-likelihood criterion, efficiency, and ability to capture complex correlation patterns within longitudinal data from crossover designs.

In 2021, the BDF Working Group focused on investigating alternative sites and potential optimizations for reusing existing infrastructure to substantially lower facility costs. This report expands upon the BDF/SHiP Comprehensive Design Study (CDS), evaluating generic requirements and constraints necessary to maintain the facility's physics reach by utilizing the currently underutilized $4\times 10^{19}$ protons per year at 400\,GeV available at the SPS, a capability for which no existing site is suitable. The analysis examines underground options including TCC4, TNC, and ECN3, alongside recent enhancements to the current design (labeled 'TT90-TCC9-ECN4') and proposals for further improvements. By synthesizing existing data with conceptual studies conducted in 2021, the assessment compares these alternatives qualitatively, outlining the specific benefits and challenges of each to facilitate a recommendation on the preferred location. Furthermore, the document identifies the most critical site-specific studies needed to define implementation details and costs, ensuring that a thorough investigation of the selected option can be finalized by the end of 2022.

This paper examines four-top quark production at the LHC within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework. The investigation is conducted at the tree level, incorporating all terms from the mixed QCD-EW-coupling cross-section expansion alongside all pertinent dimension-six SMEFT operators. Our results identify scenarios where formally subleading terms yield significant contributions. Additionally, we derive constraints on SMEFT Wilson coefficients (WCs) across various collider configurations, including the FCC-hh and HL-LHC, utilizing a simplified chi-square fit. Through this approach, we also evaluated the necessity of incorporating differential information into the fitting procedure.

This study examines the state of the solar corona during the minimum and ascending phases of Solar Cycle (SC) 25, utilizing white-light data from the SOHO/LASCO-C2 coronagraph to analyze coronal mass ejection (CME) properties and coronal radiance temporal evolution. These findings are contrasted with data from the preceding two solar cycles. During the ascent of SC 25, the integrated K-corona radiance and CME occurrence rates closely mirrored solar activity indices—specifically total magnetic field strength for radiance and radio flux for CMEs—experiencing a sharp rise. This increase proved significantly steeper than expected based on predictions of quasi-similarity between SC 24 and 25, a trend corroborated by recent sunspot number developments. While coronal radiance returned to the same baseline levels at the minima of both SC 24 and 25, the latitudinal span of the streamer belt differed, appearing flatter during the latter minimum and resembling that of SC 23 more closely. When aligning the descending phases of SC 23 and 24, the duration of SC 24 was calculated at 11.0 years, consistent with sunspot records. Conversely, the CME occurrence rate baseline during the SC 25 minimum was notably higher than in the two prior minima. Activity was distinctly concentrated in the southern hemisphere, aligning with various predictions and current hemispheric sunspot trends. Throughout the early phase of SC 25, the mean apparent width of CMEs and the frequency of halo CMEs remained relatively large and stable, suggesting persistent weak total pressure within the heliosphere. These outcomes, coupled with the outlook of a more active corona than forecasted, offer promising prospects for upcoming observations by the Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe missions.

The widespread deployment of numerous small cells introduces significant energy efficiency challenges that have frequently been overlooked in fifth-generation (5G) cellular networks. Although massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology reduces transmission power, it increases computational costs, raising the question of which factor is more critical for energy efficiency in 5G small cell networks. Consequently, this paper aims to analyze computation power through the lens of the Landauer principle. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that computation power accounts for over 50% of energy consumption at 5G small cell base stations. Furthermore, when massive MIMO (such as configurations with 128 antennas) is utilized to handle high traffic volumes, the computation power of these base stations can reach approximately 800 watts. These findings clearly underscore that optimizing computation power is pivotal for enhancing the energy efficiency of small cell networks.

We analyze the ALMA CO(2-1) emission line and the associated 1.2 mm continuum of the local Seyfert 1.5 galaxy Mrk 509, achieving a spatial resolution of 270 pc. Although optically classified as a spheroid, this galaxy hosts an ionized disc, a starburst ring, and ionized gas winds on both galactic and nuclear scales. Based on CO(2-1) data, we derive a molecular gas mass of $M_{H_2}=1.7\times 10^9\, \rm M_{\odot}$ confined within a 5.2 kpc disc. The dynamical mass is estimated at $(2.0\pm1.1) \times 10^{10}\, \rm M_{\odot}$ for a disc inclined at $44\pm10$ degrees, yielding a gas fraction of $\mu_{gas}=5\%$. Kinematics within 700 pc of the nucleus indicate a warped nuclear disc. The coexistence of a molecular disc with active star formation in a starburst ring, alongside evidence of a minor merger, supports a scenario where mergers destabilize gas to fuel both AGN activity and star formation. The Toomre Q-parameter across the molecular disc ranges from $Q_{gas}=0.5$ to $10$, revealing marginal instability in the starburst ring while the nucleus and an inner lopsided ring-like structure remain stable. We observe complex molecular gas kinematics and significant perturbations at two sites—one within 300 pc of the nucleus and another 1.4 kpc away near a region of high $Q_{gas}$—which we interpret as molecular winds. The total molecular outflow rate falls between 6.4 and 17.0 $\rm M_\odot/yr$. The wind's total kinetic energy aligns with a multiphase, momentum-conserving AGN-driven wind, with a momentum ratio $\dot{P}_{of}/\dot{P}_{rad}$ ranging from 0.06 to 0.5. Finally, the spatial overlap and similar velocities between the inner molecular wind and the ionized wind suggest a cooling sequence within a multiphase AGN-driven outflow.

Honeypots represent a well-established defensive strategy within network security. This study introduces an efficient, low-cost honeypot designed for straightforward deployment and maintenance. Its unique approach involves processing commands non-standardly, either by blocking them or responding with insults to the attacker. To identify the optimal defense strategy, the interaction between defender and attacker is modeled as a Bayesian two-player game. For empirical evaluation, three honeypot instances with minor configuration differences were deployed, capturing over 200 distinct sessions to enable a qualitative assessment of post-exploitation behavior. Results indicate that attackers respond to insults and blocked commands in varied ways, including ignoring them or retaliating with insults. The primary contribution of this work is the proposed framework, which provides an affordable alternative to more complex and resource-heavy solutions.

The Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index is recognized as the eta invariant of Dirac operators featuring a domain wall mass, a concept central to the anomaly inflow in topological insulators with boundaries. This paper proposes a conjecture that, under valid adiabatic approximation, the reformulated Atiyah-Patodi-Singer index can be directly expressed via the Berry phase linked to domain wall Dirac operators. We explicitly verify this conjecture for a specific two-dimensional case where analytic calculations are feasible. In this context, the Berry phase decomposes into bulk and boundary components, corresponding respectively to the bulk integration of the Chern character and the eta-invariant.

A recent proposal offers a consistent description of the cross sections for $dd \rightarrow ^4\text{He}\eta$ and the decay chain $dd \rightarrow (^4\text{He}\eta)_{\text{bound}} \rightarrow X$, utilizing a wide range of real ($V_0$) and imaginary ($W_0$) optical potential parameters for the $\eta$-$^4$He system that align well with experimental data. This study compares the model's predictions below the $\eta$ production threshold with WASA-at-COSY excitation functions for $dd \rightarrow ^3\text{He}N\pi$ reactions to impose stricter constraints on $(V_0, W_0)$. The resulting allowed parameter space (estimated at 90% CL as $|V_0| \lesssim 60 \text{ MeV}$ and $|W_0| \lesssim 7 \text{ MeV}$) rules out most optical model predictions for $\eta$-$^4$He nuclei, retaining only those corresponding to loosely bound, narrow states.

Deep learning advancements in radiograph analysis are built upon pre-training, which establishes transferable image representations through extensive supervised or self-supervised learning on source domains. Yet, supervised pre-training demands a cumbersome, labor-intensive two-stage annotation process involving human assistance, whereas self-supervised methods struggle to match supervised performance. To address these challenges, we introduce REFERS (REviewing FreE-text Reports for Supervision), a cross-supervised approach that leverages free supervision signals from original radiology reports paired with radiographs. Utilizing a vision transformer, REFERS is engineered to capture joint representations across multiple views within each patient study. Under conditions of extremely limited supervision, REFERS surpasses both standard transfer learning and self-supervised baselines across four prominent X-ray datasets. Furthermore, it exceeds methods relying on source domains annotated with human-assisted structured labels, positioning REFERS as a potential successor to conventional pre-training strategies.

Kinser established a hierarchy of inequalities concerning specific spaces derived from a fixed collection of subspaces. These inequalities are applicable to the rank function of a matroid, a mathematical structure that models dependencies among subsets of a ground set. Any matroid that can be represented by a matrix over a finite field must adhere to all Kinser inequalities. This work presents findings regarding matroids that satisfy each individual inequality and explores the structural organization of the hierarchy formed by such matroids.

This work examines two-state discrimination within chaotic quantum systems. Given that one of two randomly selected $N$-qubit pure states is chosen, the probability of correctly identifying it via an optimal experiment on a subset of $N-N_B$ qubits equals the trace-distance of the states, where $N_B$ qubits are traced out. As $N$ approaches infinity, the average subsystem trace-distance for random pure states undergoes a sharp, first-order transition from 1 to 0 when the fraction $f=N_B/N$ of unmeasured qubits reaches $1/2$. We analytically derive the crossover behavior for finite $N$, investigate the impact of local conservation laws, and validate our findings through exact diagonalization of many-body chaotic models.

This note revisits the connections between barcodes in level and sub-level persistence and precisely defines their relationship with the Morse-Novikov complex associated with Morse real- or angle-valued maps. Although these findings are implicit in my prior work (with collaborators), they remain apparently obscure even among experts.

This study utilizes the star-Digital Gabor Transform for analyzing Compressed Sensing and speech denoising. Leveraging assumptions regarding ambient dimension, we construct a window vector that yields a Gabor frame deficient in spark, characterized by numerous linear dependencies among its elements. Through computational experiments on both synthetic and real-world signals, we benchmark our proposed method against three baseline Gabor transforms derived from state-of-the-art window vectors. The results demonstrate that the star-Gabor transform surpasses all other methods across every signal scenario tested.

This study presents a technique for estimating a pressure-dependent thermal conductivity coefficient within a heat diffusion framework, specifically for applications in food technology. To mitigate the smoothing effects inherent in the direct problem, we represent the uncertainty of the conductivity coefficient as a hierarchical Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF), constrained by uniqueness conditions for the inverse problem solution outlined by Fraguela et al. Additionally, we develop a Single Variable Exchange Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to sample the conditional probability distribution of this coefficient based on temperature observations. Sensitivity analysis of the direct problem indicates that substantial integration times are required to accurately identify the thermal conductivity coefficient. Numerical results demonstrate that a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 1000 is sufficient to reliably recover the coefficient.

This study introduces a robotic framework enabling unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) to autonomously perform the intricate task of object manipulation. The research centers on creating an autonomous robotic system designed to assemble elementary blocks into large 3D structures within GPS-denied settings. The system's primary contributions include: i) the development of a deep learning-driven, unified multi-task visual perception system covering object detection, part detection, instance segmentation, and tracking; ii) the design of an electromagnetic gripper to ensure robust grasping; and iii) the integration of various components into an optimized software stack. This work details the complete mechatronic and algorithmic architecture of the UGV for this specific application, with the overall system's performance and efficacy validated through extensive rigorous experiments.

The issue of meson exchange currents and nucleon-nucleon correlations has been a subject of intense debate regarding neutrino-nucleus cross sections. This study concentrates on nucleon-nucleon correlations by establishing a formal link between independent particle models and *ab initio* methods that utilize correlated wave functions. Employing a general technique involving unitary transformations, we map Fermion operators defined for bare nucleons to quasi-particle operators for dressed nucleons. Consequently, we derive versatile formulas applicable to any effective nucleon-nucleon interaction for calculating spectral functions, response functions, momentum distributions, and separation energies. We also clarify the connection between the non-energy-weighted sum rule and Fermi sea depopulation. Using these tools, we assess the compatibility of effective interaction approaches with the correlation magnitudes predicted by *ab initio* calculations, specifically by testing the Fermi sea depopulation and the kinetic energy per nucleon.

Detecting 3D objects in expansive environments presents significant challenges stemming not only from the sparse and irregular nature of 3D point clouds but also from severe foreground-background and class imbalances. While a prevalent strategy involves incorporating ground-truth objects from alternative scenes, our proposed method instead modifies scenes by removing specific voxels rather than adding them. We identify "meaningful" voxels in a way that simultaneously mitigates both forms of dataset imbalance. Although this general framework is compatible with any voxel-based detector, the determination of voxel meaningfulness depends on the specific network employed. Empirical results demonstrate that our voxel selection strategy enhances the performance of various leading 3D detection techniques.

Investigating the ambient solar wind—a continuous, pressure-driven plasma stream originating from the Sun—is a vital aspect of space weather studies. This flow within interplanetary space dictates how solar storms develop across the heliosphere prior to impacting Earth, and it acts as a primary driver of Earth's magnetic field activity, particularly during solar minimum periods. Consequently, accurately predicting ambient solar wind flow is essential for effective space weather monitoring. This study introduces a machine learning method that utilizes magnetic models of the solar corona to forecast solar wind conditions near Earth. Through a thorough validation analysis comparing results against observations and current models, the new approach demonstrates superior performance across nearly all metrics. Furthermore, this method provides a fresh perspective on the significance of various input data for ambient solar wind modeling and reveals insights into the underlying physical processes. Ultimately, the presented model constitutes an extremely rapid, rigorously validated, and open-source solution for forecasting ambient solar wind at Earth.

In recent times, research regarding how solar activity affects Earth's climate has gained significant prominence, largely because some researchers suggested that global warming stems from heightened solar output rather than human causes. While the anthropogenic denialist hypothesis has been disproven, substantial evidence confirms that solar variability does influence Earth's climate, particularly at regional levels. This review examines such evidence, specifically focusing on atmospheric moisture and related metrics like precipitation. We investigated the impact of solar activity on South American rainfall over several centuries. First, by analyzing streamflow data from the Paraná River and others in the region, we identified a robust correlation with the Sunspot Number across decadal timescales. Furthermore, correlations between the Sunspot Number and tree-ring chronologies enabled us to extend this analysis back over the last two centuries.

Gate Set Tomography (GST) serves as a protocol for the comprehensive and predictive characterization of logic operations on quantum processors. Emerging between 2012 and 2013, the method has since been refined and applied in numerous experiments. This paper provides a detailed exposition of GST's foundations. Its primary advantage over older state and process tomography techniques is its calibration-free nature; it does not depend on pre-calibrated state preparations or measurements. Instead, GST simultaneously and self-consistently characterizes all operations within a gate set relative to one another. Long-sequence GST enables the estimation of gates with exceptional precision and efficiency, reaching Heisenberg scaling in practically relevant regimes. The discussion covers the intellectual history of GST, the techniques and experiments employed to achieve its goals, data analysis methods, gauge freedom and fixing, error bars, and the interpretation of gauge-fixed gate set estimates. While the focus remains on the fundamental mathematical underpinnings rather than implementation specifics, the paper also addresses key algorithmic strategies utilized in the pyGSTi implementation.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) serves as a benchmark for evaluating Natural Language Understanding (NLU). This study introduces a scalable framework designed to systematically assess the diverse logical reasoning skills necessary for NLI and, by extension, NLU. Drawing inspiration from behavioral testing, we developed a semi-synthetic large-scale test suite comprising 363 templates and 363,000 examples, along with a framework that provides three key utilities: 1) the ability to independently evaluate and analyze reasoning across 17 distinct dimensions (including pragmatic reasoning); 2) tools to design experiments examining the interplay between different capabilities via "leave-one-out" or "bring-one-in" analyses; and 3) the capacity to control for artifacts and biases due to the synthetic nature of the data. Leveraging automated test case generation from free-form natural language templates (via CheckList) and a structured taxonomy of capabilities, we can extend to cognitively more challenging test cases while varying linguistic complexity. Our analysis of state-of-the-art NLI systems demonstrates that this benchmark is difficult and remains non-trivial even with additional training resources. Certain capabilities proved notably harder to master. Further fine-grained analysis and fine-tuning experiments offer deeper insights into these capabilities and model behaviors, supporting and expanding prior findings. Finally, we conducted a user study to explore whether behavioral information can facilitate superior generalization in certain models compared to others.

Core-envelope models described in {Ref1} and {Ref2}, characterized by compactness parameters $u \equiv M/a$ of 0.30 and 0.25 (representing the mass-to-size ratio in geometrized units), have been examined under slow rotation. These models successfully account for all observational estimates of the Vela pulsar's glitch healing parameter, $G_h = I_{\rm core}/I_{\rm total} < 0.55$ {Ref3}. Specifically, for the assigned surface density $E_a = 2\times 10^{14}\rm g{cm}^{-3}$ {Ref4}, the models produce maximum values for the Vela pulsar's mass ($M$), surface redshift ($z_a$), and moment of inertia ($I_{\rm Vela}$) within the ranges $M = 3.079M_\odot - 2.263M_\odot$, $z_a = 0.581 - 0.414$, and $I_{\rm Vela,45} = 6.9 - 3.5$ (where $I_{45}=I/10^{45}\rm g{cm}^2$) for $u = 0.30$ and $0.25$, respectively. Furthermore, realistic mass values ($M = 1.4\pm0.2 M_\odot$) can be derived for $u < 0.25$ within the same $G_h$ range; these fall below the previously cited unrealistic limit of $M \leq 0.5M_\odot$ found in literature using parametrized neutron star models based on dense nuclear matter equations of state {Ref3}. The models are confirmed to be causally consistent, gravitationally bound, and pulsationally stable. Notably, the upper mass bound for the Vela pulsar derived in this study aligns well with recent theoretical estimates {Ref7} and matches the mean of the classical upper bound {Ref5} and modern EOS-based predictions {Ref6}.

Individuals are typically described using attributes such as age, gender, height, clothing style, pattern, and color, collectively known as attributes and/or soft-biometrics. These descriptors bridge the semantic gap between human descriptions and their retrieval within video surveillance systems. While retrieving a specific individual based on a semantic query is a critical application in this field, the current research trend predominantly relies on image-based queries, which face significant practical limitations. Consequently, this paper investigates person retrieval in video surveillance using semantic descriptions rather than images. To address this, we propose PeR-ViS, a deep learning-based cascade filtering framework that integrates Mask R-CNN for person detection and instance segmentation with DenseNet-161 for soft-biometric classification. Evaluated on the SoftBioSearch standard dataset, our method achieves an Average IoU of 0.566 and a weighted IoU greater than 0.4 of 0.792%, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art solutions. We aim for this simple, reproducible, and effective approach to facilitate future advancements in video surveillance person retrieval. The source code and pretrained weights are accessible at https://parshwa1999.github.io/PeR-ViS/.

This paper addresses the question of whether a topological analysis can be performed on diverse classes of normal subgroups equipped with a hull-kernel-type topology. We introduce a novel category of normal subgroups termed "primitive subgroups" and investigate fundamental topological properties of the resulting spaces, including separation axioms, compactness, connectedness, and continuity. The study concludes by posing the open problem of identifying which of these spaces qualify as spectral spaces.

This paper investigates the uniqueness of a polynomial expression $ P(f) $ and its $ k $-th derivative, $ [P(f)]^{(k)} $, when a meromorphic function $ f $ shares a small function. Leveraging the concept of weakly weighted sharing proposed by \emph{Lin -Lin} [Kodai Math. J., 29(2006), 269-280], our main findings substantially advance the work of \emph{Liu - Gu} [Kodai Math. J., 27(3)(2004), 272-279]. We identify specific conditions under which $ P(f) $ simplifies to a non-zero monomial, thereby determining the explicit form of $ f $. Furthermore, constructive examples demonstrate that certain conditions in our primary results are essential and cannot be omitted, while confirming that some associated inequalities are sharp.

We observe that numerous 2-complexes constructed by Freedman-Krushkal-Teichner in their work on the incompleteness of the van Kampen embedding obstruction can be PL immersed in $\mathbb{R}^4$ such that the interiors of distinct cell images remain disjoint. In other words, these complexes PL almost-embed in $\mathbb{R}^4$, with singularities limited to self-intersections within certain 2-cells. This note is composed in (not necessarily modern) German.

To overcome the throughput limitations of single-chain Proof-of-Work blockchains, various proposals have replaced linear chains with Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). This study examines two prominent DAG-based architectures, specifically PHANTOM and its optimized variant, GHOSTDAG, which utilize a tailored transaction selection mechanism to enhance network throughput. However, existing research has not thoroughly analyzed corner cases where this selection strategy is deviated from. Consequently, we developed a custom simulator that extends open-source tools to support multi-chain environments, allowing us to investigate these edge cases. Our experimental results indicate that malicious actors who diverge from the prescribed selection strategy achieve higher profits than honest miners. Furthermore, such behavior degrades the processing throughput of PHANTOM and GHOSTDAG by causing duplicate transactions to be included across multiple blocks in different chains. Finally, we demonstrate that when multiple miners fail to adhere to the transaction selection strategy, they are incentivized to form a shared mining pool rather than mining independently, thereby negatively impacting decentralization.

We introduce a frame-based representation of k-mers designed to identify sequencing errors and rare variants in next-generation sequencing data derived from populations of closely related genomes. Frames, which are sets of non-orthogonal basis functions commonly utilized in signal processing for noise reduction, are defined here as discrete spatial signals representing every k-mer of a specific size within genomes and sequenced reads. We demonstrate that each k-mer in the sequencing data can be projected onto multiple frames, with these projections reaching maximum values for spatial signals corresponding to the k-mer's substrings. Our proposed classifier, MultiRes, utilizes these k-mer projections as features to distinguish between erroneous k-mers and genuine genomic variations. Evaluated on both simulated and real viral population datasets, MultiRes outperforms existing error correction methods by generating 4 to 500 times fewer false positive k-mer predictions, a critical advantage for accurately estimating viral population diversity and performing de-novo assembly. Furthermore, MultiRes achieves high recall for true k-mers comparable to other error correction techniques. In terms of variant detection, it exceeds 95% recall for identifying single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with fewer false positives and detects a higher quantity of rare variants than other methods used for viral populations. The software is freely accessible via the GitHub repository (https://github.com/raunaq-m/MultiRes).

Addressing link blockage is crucial for improving the reliability and latency of millimeter wave (mmWave) and sub-terahertz (sub-THz) networks. Prior methods primarily depended on either (i) multiple-connectivity, which inefficiently uses network resources, or (ii) out-of-band and non-RF sensors for blockage prediction, leading to higher costs and system complexity. This paper introduces a new solution that leverages exclusively in-band mmWave measurements to proactively forecast dynamic line-of-sight (LOS) blockages. Our approach employs deep neural networks to analyze specific received signal power patterns, termed "pre-blockage wireless signatures," to infer upcoming blockages. Specifically, the developed machine learning models aim to determine: (i) whether a blockage will occur, (ii) when it will happen, (iii) the type of blockage, and (iv) the direction of the moving obstruction. To validate this method, we constructed a large-scale real-world dataset containing nearly 0.5 million mmWave measurements covering both indoor and outdoor blockage scenarios. Results from this dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach can successfully predict future dynamic blockages with over 85% accuracy. Furthermore, in outdoor scenarios involving highly mobile vehicular blockages, the model predicts the exact timing of blockages occurring within the next 500ms with an error margin of less than 80ms.
