These findings underscore the significant potential of this proactive prediction solution to enhance the reliability and latency of future wireless networks.

We offer a unified graphical framework for addressing both SAT and #SAT. #SAT instances can be naturally modeled as tensor networks, which are then interpreted using ZH-calculus diagrams. This formal system allows reasoning about tensors over complex numbers via diagrams constructed from simple generators, where computation occurs through diagram transformations. Typically, ZH diagram nodes utilize parameters from the complex field to define tensor coefficients; however, standard #SAT representations restrict these coefficients to 0 or 1. By instead allowing coefficients to range over the Boolean semiring, we represent SAT instances. Consequently, interpreting a diagram over either the Boolean semiring or complex numbers instantiates the decision or counting variant of the problem, respectively. We observe that for problem classes within P, such as 2SAT and #XORSAT, specific rewrite rules enable efficient diagram simplification, yielding solutions in polynomial time. Conversely, for NP-complete classes like 3SAT or #P-complete classes like #2SAT, the applicable rewrite rules generate hyperedges whose quantities cannot be easily bounded by a polynomial. This diagrammatic methodology unifies the complexity analysis of CSPs and #CSPs and demonstrates potential for enhancing tensor network contraction algorithms.

Galactic archaeology has recently emerged as a dynamic area of astronomy, primarily focusing on the Galaxy's oldest stars, which are typically the most metal-poor. However, observational efforts to locate these ancient stellar fossils have introduced a significant bias, causing intermediate metal-poor stars (-2.5 < [Fe/H] < -1.5) to be frequently neglected. This gap in data hinders the precise analysis of the Galaxy's chemical enrichment, particularly regarding neutron-capture elements, and will only be partially addressed by upcoming multi-object spectroscopic surveys like WEAVE and 4MOST. The Measuring at Intermediate Metallicity Neutron Capture Elements (MINCE) project is currently collecting the first high-quality, high-resolution, and high signal-to-noise spectra for hundreds of bright, metal-poor stars, predominantly within the Galactic halo. Utilizing Gaia data for selection, the team characterized the stellar atmospheres and chemical abundances of their sample. This paper presents the initial set of 59 spectra from 46 stars, for which radial velocities were measured and Galactic orbits calculated. The analysis reveals that 8 stars belong to the thin disc, 15 to disrupted satellites, and the remainder are classified as halo stars due to their unaffiliated status. Abundance data up to zinc are provided for 33 of these stars, alongside chemical evolution results for eleven elements based on recent models. The strategy of employing multiple telescopes and spectrographs to obtain high-quality spectra proved highly efficient, as the entire sample was acquired in approximately one year. Furthermore, the target selection methodology demonstrated satisfactory effectiveness for the study's objectives.

The upgraded LHCb detector, scheduled to begin data collection in 2022, must handle a real-time data rate averaging 4~TB/s. Since LHCb's physics goals mandate that full detector information for every LHC bunch crossing be read out and processed in real time, this bandwidth demand matches the software read-out challenges faced by ATLAS and CMS at the HL-LHC, but must be achieved five years sooner. Over the last six years, the LHCb collaboration has executed a bottom-up overhaul of its software infrastructure, pattern recognition, and selection algorithms to optimize them for modern, highly parallel computing architectures. This review examines how this reoptimization affects the energy efficiency of both the hardware and real-time processing software for the detector upgrade. It also analyzes the consequences of adopting a hybrid computing architecture combining GPUs and CPUs for LHCb's future real-time data processing. Finally, we discuss how these findings influence the projected evolution of LHCb's real-time power requirements, especially in light of a planned second detector upgrade.

This study derives the crossing symmetry equations governing mixed correlators composed of two long and two BPS operators within 4D $\mathcal{N}=1$ SCFTs. The analysis demonstrates the application of our general group-theoretic framework for long superblocks and superconformal algebra tensor structures, yielding explicit, ready-to-use formulas. Specifically, we establish a system of four crossing symmetry equations for the pertinent OPE coefficients. While one of these equations matches the result previously derived and examined by Li, Meltzer, and Stergiou by focusing solely on the superprimary component of long multiplets, the remaining three are novel. These new equations impose significant additional constraints on the identical OPE data.

Heavy-ion collisions generate significant quantities of light and hyper-nuclei, yet the mechanisms driving their formation remain unclear. This report details the elliptic flow ($v_2$) as a function of transverse momentum and collision centrality for deuterons ($d$), tritons ($t$), and helium-3 ($^3\text{He}$) in Au+Au collisions at center-of-mass energies of 14.6, 19.6, 27, and 54.4 GeV. We demonstrate mass-number scaling of $v_2(p_T)$ for these light nuclei. Furthermore, we present the initial observation of directed flow ($v_1$) for hyper-nuclei $^{3}_{\Lambda}$H and $^{4}_{\Lambda}$H in mid-central (5–40%) Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 3 GeV conducted in fixed-target mode.

Comprehending the atomic-level mechanisms driving solid-phase transitions is vital for materials science. To examine displacive transitions at the atomic scale, we developed a numerical algorithm that automatically identifies symmetry relationships between any two candidate crystal structures. Leveraging this tool, we systematically evaluated all potential polar-nonpolar structure pairs within the Materials Project database, compiling a dataset of approximately 4500 pairs exhibiting close symmetry. These pairs are linked via continuous phase transitions involving minimal atomic shifts. From this collection, we have identified several novel ferroelectric materials previously unreported. Beyond ferroelectric discovery, this symmetry database holds utility for diverse applications, including material structure prediction and the discovery of new materials.

Equations governing the contour dynamics of dark solitons are derived for an arbitrary nonlinearity function. The self-similar solution, which characterizes the nonlinear phase of dark soliton bending instability, is analyzed in depth.

The balanced hypercube ($BH_{n}$), a new interconnection network designed for large-scale parallel systems, is known to retain Hamiltonicity even after the removal of up to $4n-5$ faulty edges, provided every vertex in the remaining graph has a degree of at least two for all $n \geq 2$. This paper demonstrates that a fault-free Hamiltonian cycle exists in $BH_{n}$ for $n \geq 2$ when the number of faulty edges $|F|$ is at most $5n-7$, under the conditions that every vertex in $BH_{n}-F$ maintains a degree of at least two and no $f_{4}$-cycles are present. These findings enhance several existing results.

In warped conformal field theories (WCFT), deriving the warped Cardy formula requires the zero mode spectrum to be bounded from below. While this condition generally fails for holographic WCFTs in the "canonical" ensemble, it holds in the "quadratic" ensemble, rendering the latter more suitable for holographic contexts. This study identifies a novel set of boundary conditions in three-dimensional Topologically Massive Gravity (TMG) such that the dual theory corresponds to a WCFT within the quadratic ensemble. Remarkably, solving the equations of motion yields a closed-form metric parameterized by two arbitrary chiral functions, mirroring the structure of Bañados metrics in Einstein gravity. Although surface charges associated with these boundary conditions are not inherently integrable, we explore two specific choices to ensure integrability. By applying the warped Cardy formula within its valid regime, we calculate the bulk thermodynamic entropy of warped BTZ black holes. Furthermore, we address the challenge of identifying the vacuum within our solution space; requiring the enhancement of global symmetries restricts the solutions to a specific family, from which the unique vacuum must be carefully distinguished.

This study addresses two pivotal aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing: schema linking and value filling. To enhance the model's encoding capabilities, we introduce an auxiliary column selection task that explicitly targets relevance matching to strengthen the encoder. Additionally, we develop two value filling strategies to bridge the gap between current zero-shot semantic parsers and practical applications, addressing the common oversight of value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments conducted on the Spider dataset demonstrate that our framework outperforms baseline methods in both execution accuracy and exact set match accuracy, particularly when database contents are missing, with detailed analysis offering insights for future research.

JT gravity admits a first-order description as a two-dimensional BF theory, interpretable as the dimensional reduction of the Chern-Simons formulation of $3d$ gravity. We examine $T\bar{T}$-type deformations of the $(0+1)$-dimensional dual associated with this $2d$ BF framework, characterizing the deformation as an alteration of the BF theory's boundary conditions. The core observables within this deformed BF theory and its $3d$ Chern-Simons extension are Wilson lines and loops. Focusing on the $3d$ Chern-Simons context, we analyze changes in correlators involving boundary-anchored Wilson lines triggered by a $T\bar{T}$ deformation on the $2d$ boundary, presenting findings at both the classical level (via modified boundary conditions) and the quantum-mechanical level (using conformal perturbation theory). Finally, we compute the corresponding deformed Wilson line correlators in $2d$ BF theory below the Hagedorn temperature, where the principal series prevails over the discrete series.

Extracting discriminative features from local regions is fundamental to fine-grained visual classification, with attention mechanisms becoming a popular approach for part-based feature extraction. However, current methods suffer from two primary drawbacks: they prioritize the most prominent parts while ignoring less obvious yet distinctive regions, and they analyze part features in isolation without considering their interrelationships. To address these issues, we propose a framework that explicitly identifies multiple distinct parts and models their relationships. We introduce two lightweight modules designed for easy integration into existing convolutional neural networks. First, a feature boosting and suppression module amplifies the most salient parts to generate part-specific representations while simultaneously suppressing them to encourage the network to discover other potential parts. Second, a feature diversification module learns semantically complementary information from these correlated part-specific representations. Our approach requires no bounding box or part annotations and supports end-to-end training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on various fine-grained benchmark datasets, with source code available at https://github.com/chaomaer/FBSD.

The Burkhardt-Cottingham (BC) sum rule links the twist-3 light-cone parton distribution function (PDF) $g_{T}(x)$ with the twist-2 helicity PDF $g_{1}(x)$, while its chiral-odd counterpart connects the twist-3 PDF $h_{L}(x)$ to the twist-2 transversity PDF $h_{1}(x)$. These BC-type relations are also applicable to the corresponding quasi-PDFs. We conducted a perturbative verification of these sum rules within the quark target and Yukawa models, extending beyond the ultra-violet (UV) divergent terms. Utilizing both dimensional regularization (DR) and cut-off schemes to manage UV divergences, we demonstrated that the BC-type sum rules remain valid under DR but are typically violated when a cut-off is applied. This violation stems from the breakdown of rotational invariance. Similar findings were obtained for the sum rule connecting the target mass to the twist-3 PDF $e(x)$. Additionally, our analytical findings were supported by numerical computations.

We re-examine the divide-and-conquer sequential Monte Carlo (DaC-SMC) algorithm, solidifying its theoretical foundation by demonstrating that it shares the core properties of standard sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods. Specifically, we derive key laws of large numbers, $L^p$ inequalities, and central limit theorems; we analyze the bias in normalized estimates while confirming the absence of bias in unnormalized ones. Additionally, we address practical implementation and various variants, derive formulas for globally and locally optimal intermediate targets, auxiliary measures, and proposal kernels, and demonstrate that under comparable conditions, DaC-SMC achieves greater statistical efficiency than its direct SMC counterpart. The paper concludes with a discussion of our findings, outstanding questions, and potential avenues for future research.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) represent a new method for generative modeling, which aims to learn the distribution of real data points. Training GANs has frequently proven challenging because, unlike many standard machine learning techniques, they function as a two-player game between a generator and a discriminator. This dynamic has resulted in training unreliability and a general lack of clarity regarding how and whether GANs converge. This dissertation aims to present a theory of GANs tailored for mathematicians, emphasizing both positive and negative findings. It examines the challenges inherent in training GANs and explains how recent advances in topological and game-theoretic perspectives have enhanced our understanding and refined these techniques.

Gaussian processes (GPs) represent a prominent nonparametric Bayesian inference method, yet they face scalability challenges with large datasets and performance declines when handling non-stationary or spatially heterogeneous data. To address these limitations, this study proposes two strategies: (i) combining variational free energy approximations of GPs with online expectation propagation, and (ii) implementing a local splitting mechanism that creates a new GP whenever the posterior distribution shifts significantly, as measured by the Wasserstein metric. Consequently, this approach generates an ensemble of sparse GPs capable of incremental updates, effectively adapting to local variations, heterogeneity, and non-stationarity within the training data.

Professor Tom Kibble was a globally acclaimed theoretical physicist whose research spanned elementary particle theory to contemporary early-universe cosmology. His work is unified by the study of non-abelian gauge theories, which extend electromagnetism through the Yang-Mills framework. A cornerstone of his contributions was investigating the symmetry-breaking mechanism that allows force-carrying vector particles to gain mass while simultaneously producing a massive scalar boson. Proposed independently in 1964 by Brout and Englert, by Higgs, and by Guralnik, Hagen, and Kibble—and later generalized by Kibble in 1967—this concept forms the foundation of the Standard Model and modern unified theories of fundamental particles. Its validity was confirmed in 2012 with the discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN. As Nobel Laureate Steven Weinberg noted, "Tom Kibble showed us why light is massless," a principle that underpins electromagnetism.

Building upon our earlier research (Cohn, Lam, Lu, Yang, Nonlinear Analysis (2011), doi: 10.1016/j.na.2011.09.053), we establish a class of Trudinger-Moser inequalities on the entire Heisenberg group that identify the optimal constants. While prior proofs for analogous inequalities on unbounded domains in Euclidean space or the Heisenberg group rely on rearrangement techniques, this note introduces a novel methodology. Specifically, we derive the global Trudinger-Moser inequality by combining local estimates using cut-off functions. This approach remains applicable to related problems whether the Heisenberg group is substituted with Euclidean space or complete noncompact Riemannian manifolds.

We analyze the system size and flavor dependence of the chemical freeze-out temperature ($T_\mathrm{ch}$) at zero baryo-chemical potential, derived from thermal fits to experimental yields across multiple multiplicity classes in pp, pPb, and PbPb collisions recorded by ALICE. Employing the Thermal-FIST Hadron Resonance Gas model, we evaluate the fit quality for various strangeness conservation treatments under different freeze-out conditions, parameterized by the charged particle multiplicity density $\big \langle dN_\mathrm{ch}/d\eta \big \rangle$. Furthermore, we investigate the evolution of anti-hadron to pion yield ratios for light and strange baryons, as well as the $\phi$ meson, within a flavor-dependent framework. By utilizing a distinctive two-temperature chemical freeze-out method, we demonstrate that the flavor dependence of $T_\mathrm{ch}$ in a Strangeness Canonical Ensemble naturally accounts for strangeness enhancement from small to large systems at LHC energies, eliminating the need for non-equilibrium particle production at low $\big \langle dN_\mathrm{ch}/d\eta \big \rangle$.

Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) have become a promising technology for dynamically reshaping radio propagation environments by manipulating the amplitude and/or phase of wireless signals through numerous reflecting elements. While extensive research exists on IRS performance in wireless communications, this paper explores a novel application: using IRS for target sensing and localization within wireless networks. We introduce a new self-sensing IRS architecture where the controller transmits probing signals that generate two types of echoes: those directly reflected by the target (the direct echo link) and those consecutively reflected by the IRS and then the target (the IRS-reflected echo link). Dedicated sensors at the IRS receive both echo types, enabling the system to determine the target's direction using a customized multiple signal classification (MUSIC) algorithm. Since calculating the mean square error (MSE) for angle estimation via the MUSIC algorithm is intractable, we propose optimizing the IRS's passive reflection to maximize the total power of average echo signals at the IRS sensors and derive the corresponding Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) for the angle estimation MSE. Finally, numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed IRS sensing architecture and algorithm compared to other benchmark systems.

Gallium nitride (GaN), a wide band-gap semiconductor, is widely utilized in power electronics owing to its high electron mobility and breakdown voltage. Its relatively high thermal conductivity further enhances its suitability for these applications, where effective heat dissipation is critical for maintaining device efficiency and long-term stability. However, the influence of electric fields on thermal transport properties in GaN-based transistors—devices capable of withstanding extremely strong electric fields in their active regions—has received limited attention. This study employs first-principles methods to examine the phonon properties of wurtzite GaN under near-breakdown electric fields applied along various crystallographic directions. We observe that while the electric field has minimal impact on phonon dispersions, it significantly alters thermal conductivity by modifying bond stiffness, ionicity, and crystal symmetry. Specifically, an out-of-plane electric field increases (decreases) thermal conductivity parallel (perpendicular) to the field direction, a phenomenon attributed to distinct variations in Ga-N bond stiffness and ionicity. Conversely, applying an in-plane electric field results in a substantial reduction of thermal conductivity across all directions, caused by crystal symmetry breaking that intensifies phonon-phonon scattering. These findings offer valuable insights into how extreme external electric fields affect phonon transport in wide-band-gap semiconductors.

This research examines the spatial distribution of highly variable plasma composition surrounding a prominent sunspot from solar cycle 24. By integrating observations of the photosphere, chromosphere, and corona with magnetic field modeling of the sunspot, we aim to understand the conditions governing plasma fractionation across loop populations with different connectivities. Our findings reveal that the coronal magnetic field above the sunspot umbra exhibits photospheric plasma composition. Conversely, coronal loops anchored in the penumbra display fractionated plasma, with the most significant levels found in loops connecting within the active region. Furthermore, tracing magnetic field lines from these fractionated coronal regions to Alfvenic fluctuations in the chromosphere demonstrates a magnetic linkage. These results suggest a direct connection between chromospheric activity in sunspots and observable variations in coronal plasma composition.

Graph clustering organizes entities (graph vertices) based on similarity, usually relying on a complex distance function across numerous features. The effectiveness of integrating clustering methods into automated decision-support systems depends heavily on how interpretable the resulting clusters are. This paper tackles the challenge of creating interpretable clusters by optimizing for specific user-defined features that signify interpretability, alongside standard clustering goals. We introduce a $\beta$-interpretable clustering algorithm that guarantees at least a $\beta$ fraction of nodes within each cluster share identical feature values, with $\beta$ being a user-defined parameter. Additionally, we offer a more efficient algorithm specifically for cases where $\beta\!=\!1$ and provide a theoretical analysis of both methods. Empirically, we validate the advantages of our approaches on four real-world datasets. Furthermore, we enhance cluster interpretability by generating straightforward explanations that identify the shared feature values of nodes within clusters, utilizing frequent pattern mining.

We investigate the univalency problem within the unit disc $\mathbb D$ for the function
$$g(z)=\frac{(z/f(z))-1}{-a_{2}},$$ where $f$ is a member of specific classes of univalent functions defined on ${\mathbb D}$ and $a_{2}=\frac{f''(0)}{2}\neq 0$.
We establish bounds for every derivative of the non-relativistic Coulombic one-particle density matrix $\gamma(x, y)$ in the vicinity of the diagonal where $x = y$.

Machine learning and big data analytics play significant roles in combating the COVID-19 pandemic through applications like diagnostics, prevention, risk management, and forecasting. This research specifically targets the prediction of patient shielding, which involves identifying and safeguarding those clinically most vulnerable to the virus. By employing multi-label classification techniques on medical text, the study utilizes de-identified ICU records alongside published data from the UK NHS and the World Health Organization. The labels are based on official shielding guidelines. We conducted an extensive evaluation of twelve multi-label classifiers, ranging from simple binary relevance methods to neural networks and state-of-the-art transformers. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive assessment of such a diverse array of classifiers applied to medical text for this specific task. The results underscore the advantages of different approaches, emphasizing that both high predictive accuracy and efficient processing time are critical for this application.

This work investigates a two-dimensional static spin-pseudospin model, which corresponds to a dilute frustrated antiferromagnetic Ising model containing charge impurities. Using classical Monte Carlo simulations on a square lattice with periodic boundaries under a strong exchange limit, we derived static critical exponents for specific heat ($\alpha$) and correlation length ($\nu$) across a broad spectrum of local density-density interaction parameters ($\Delta$) and charge densities ($n$) within the finite-size scaling framework. Our findings demonstrate that the system displays non-universal critical behavior contingent upon these specific parameters.
The Whitney partition holds significant importance in modern analysis. In this discussion, we explore a quasiconformal adaptation of the Whitney partition that proves useful for Sobolev spaces.

We examine density fluctuations in a liquid near a solvophobic substrate undergoing a surface critical drying transition. Employing classical density functional theory, we calculate three metrics for the spatial range and intensity of these fluctuations: the local compressibility $\chi_{\mu}(z)$, the recently introduced local thermal susceptibility $\chi_T(z)$, and the reduced density $\chi_*(z)$, where $z$ denotes the distance from the substrate. Although $\chi_{\mu}(z)$ is commonly utilized, the latter two were proposed only recently by Eckert et al. in Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 268004 (2020). Within the critical drying regime, all three measures, when normalized by their bulk values, display remarkably similar profiles, and the ratio of $\chi_T(z)$ to $\chi_{\mu}(z)$ remains constant for a fixed $z$ in the vapour-liquid transition region. Through a scaling analysis of surface thermodynamics, we demonstrate that this behavior is theoretically expected based on general principles.

This work details the application of the unitarity-based Dispersion Matrix method to semileptonic charged-current $B$ decays. This approach enables a non-perturbative and fully model-independent extraction of hadronic form factors. By utilizing lattice data from high momentum transfer, we determine the form factors' behavior across their entire kinematic range without imposing any explicit parameterization of their momentum dependence. Our analysis focuses on Lepton Flavour Universality by calculating the $	au/\mu$ ratios of branching fractions for $B 	o D^{(*)} \ell 
u$ and $B 	o \pi \ell 
u$ decays. The primary finding is that, for the first time, the tension between Standard Model predictions and experimental measurements of Lepton Flavour Universality ratios in $B 	o D^{(*)} \ell 
u$ decays is reduced to the 1.3$\sigma$ level for each channel individually.

Frictional sliding is an inherently complex process arising from the interaction of driving forces, elasto-frictional instabilities, interfacial nonlinearity, dissipation, material inertia, and bulk geometry. We demonstrate that homogeneous rate-and-state frictional systems, driven by a prescribed boundary velocity rather than stress within a rate-weakening regime, typically exhibit self-healing slip pulses—a sliding mode not yet fully grasped. These velocity-driven systems display coarsening dynamics that saturate at the system's length along the sliding direction, regardless of its height, resulting in steadily propagating pulse trains. These trains can be interpreted as a propagating phase-separated state, with slip and stick representing the respective phases. Although the periodicity of these pulse trains is limited by the system's length through coarsening, the single pulse width, characteristic slip velocity, and propagation speed display rich behaviors that are thoroughly elucidated by theory and extensive numerical simulations. Finally, we find that for sufficiently small system heights, pulse trains are accompanied by periodic elasto-frictional instabilities.

Negotiation represents a multifaceted social interaction that involves emotional exchanges within human decision-making processes. Virtual agents capable of negotiating with humans hold significant value for both educational applications and conversational AI. To further the development of these agents, this study investigates the prediction of two key subjective objectives in negotiation: outcome satisfaction and the perception of one's partner. Specifically, we examine how emotion attributes extracted from negotiations contribute to these predictions, surpassing the utility of individual difference variables. Our research utilizes a recent dataset from chat-based negotiations situated within a realistic camping context. We evaluate three levels of emotion dimensions—emoticons, lexical, and contextual—by employing affective lexicons and an advanced deep learning framework. The resulting insights will aid in creating adaptive negotiation agents that communicate through realistic interfaces.

This study treats the hierarchical structure of documents as graphs and employs geometric deep learning for classification. Although graph neural networks can effectively manage the variable structure of these documents through permutation-invariant message passing, we demonstrate that performance can be further enhanced by a proposed selective graph pooling operation, leveraging the observation that certain hierarchical components remain constant across documents. We applied this model to categorize clinical trial (CT) protocols as either completed or terminated. By utilizing both bag-of-words and pre-trained transformer-based embeddings to feature the graph nodes, we achieved F1-scores of approximately 0.85 on a large-scale public registry containing roughly 360,000 CT protocols. Additionally, we illustrate how selective pooling provides valuable insights into predicting CT termination status and have made the source code and dataset splits publicly available.

It is anticipated that local Hamiltonian evolutions over brief intervals will retain locality and remain constrained. This paper substantiates that intuition by demonstrating specific limitations on the short-time dynamics of local, time-dependent Hamiltonians. We demonstrate that measurement outcomes resulting from such short-duration (specifically, logarithmic or less) evolutions are \emph{concentrated} and adhere to an \emph{isoperimetric inequality}. To illustrate the practical implications of these findings, we analyze the \textsc{MaxCut} problem, concluding that quantum annealing requires a runtime scaling logarithmically with problem size to outperform classical methods. Furthermore, to support our main results, we establish a Lieb-Robinson bound applicable to time-dependent Hamiltonians, a contribution that may hold independent significance.

We compared local 1.4 GHz luminosity functions for star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and active galactic nuclei against 1.4 GHz differential source counts ranging from $0.25 \ \mu\mathrm{Jy}$ to 25 Jy, employing various combinations of luminosity and density evolution. We provide the most comprehensive and reliable local far-infrared (FIR)/radio luminosity correlation available to date, derived from a volume-limited sample of approximately $4.3 \times 10^3$ nearby SFGs. Our results reveal a relationship that is notably tight yet distinctly sub-linear, expressed as $L_\mathrm{FIR} \propto L_\mathrm{1.4\,GHz}^{0.85}$. Assuming the local FIR/radio correlation remains constant, the evolving 1.4 GHz luminosity function of SFGs allows us to derive the time-dependent star-formation rate density (SFRD), $\psi (M_\odot \ \mathrm{year}^{-1} \ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3})$, since the Big Bang. The SFRD derived from 1.4 GHz observations increases rapidly during the early universe, reaches a peak at "cosmic noon" when $t \approx 3 \ \mathrm{Gyr}$ and $z \approx 2$, and then declines with an $e$-folding timescale of $\tau = 3.2 \ \mathrm{Gyr}$. This evolutionary trend aligns closely with, though is slightly more pronounced than, SFRD estimates based on UV and FIR data.

This paper demonstrates that the density of integer pairs $(a, b)$ for which $a^4+b^3$ is squarefree, when ordered by $\max\{|a|^{1/3},|b|^{1/4}\}$, matches the conjectured product of local densities. We further establish that this result holds for polynomials of the form $\beta a^4 + \alpha b^3$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are fixed integers. Additionally, we provide an exact count of the number of integer pairs $(a,b)$ satisfying $\max\{|a|^{1/3},|b|^{1/4}\}<X$ such that $\beta a^4 + \alpha b^3$ is squarefree, including a power-saving error term.

Learning under noisy labels has become a major focus in robust deep learning. While recent empirical studies suggest that employing dual networks improves upon single-network performance, these findings lack theoretical justification. This paper introduces the Cooperative Learning (CooL) framework, which provides an analytical explanation for the benefits of using dual or multiple networks under noisy supervision. Specifically, CooL's simple yet efficient integration achieves more reliable risk minimization for unseen clean data. We conducted extensive experiments across various benchmarks, including both synthetic and real-world scenarios. The results demonstrate that CooL surpasses several state-of-the-art methods.

Commonsense knowledge-graphs (CKGs) serve as vital resources for developing machines capable of reasoning over textual or environmental data to make inferences that extend beyond mere perception. Although existing CKGs encode world knowledge for numerous concepts and have been successfully integrated into neural models to incorporate commonsense, they are limited by encoding primarily declarative or single-condition inferential knowledge while assuming all conceptual beliefs share equal likelihood. Furthermore, these graphs rely on a restricted set of shared relations and lack a coherent organizational structure, leading to redundancies and sparsity across the broader knowledge graph. Consequently, while current CKGs facilitate basic reasoning, they fail to adequately capture the nuanced, deeper human-level commonsense inferences that are often influenced by multiple contextual or situational factors. In response, this work investigates improved representations of commonsense knowledge by: (i) adopting a probabilistic logic scheme to model composite inferential knowledge and assign varying likelihoods to conceptual beliefs, and (ii) integrating a hierarchical conceptual ontology to identify salient, concept-specific relations and organize beliefs across different levels. The resulting framework can encode diverse world knowledge and flexibly represent beliefs using both grounded concepts and free-text phrases. This enables the framework to function as both a traditional free-text knowledge graph and a grounded logic-based inference system better suited for neuro-symbolic applications. We detail the extension of the PrimeNet knowledge base using this framework via crowd-sourcing and expert annotation, demonstrating its utility in enhancing interpretable passage-based semantic parsing and question answering.

Similar to fingerprints, cortical folding patterns are individually unique despite adhering to a general species-wide organization. While certain folding patterns have been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, the high degree of inter-individual variability makes identifying rare patterns that could serve as biomarkers a challenging task. This paper introduces a novel unsupervised deep learning framework designed to detect these rare folding patterns and evaluate the detectability of deviations. To achieve this, brain MR images are preprocessed to isolate folding morphology, and a beta-VAE is trained to model inter-individual variability in folding structures. We evaluate the detection capabilities of both the latent space and reconstruction errors using synthetic benchmarks and a specific rare configuration involving the central sulcus. Furthermore, we test the method's generalization on a developmental anomaly located in a different brain region. Our findings indicate that this approach successfully encodes relevant folding characteristics, which can be more clearly elucidated and interpreted through the generative capacity of the beta-VAE. Additionally, the latent space and reconstruction errors provide complementary insights, facilitating the identification of diverse rare patterns. The method demonstrates strong generalization across different regions and datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/neurospin-projects/2022_lguillon_rare_folding_detection.

This paper introduces a method for estimating camera pose from a single RGB image and a pre-existing map of objects modeled as ellipsoids. We demonstrate that, unlike point correspondences, defining a cost function for projecting a 3D object onto a 2D object detection is non-trivial. To address this, we develop an ellipse-ellipse cost function utilizing level set sampling, which exhibits robust properties for handling partially visible objects. We compare its performance against other standard metrics and show that incorporating predictive uncertainty into detected ellipses enables fair weighting of correspondences, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the computed pose. The source code is available at https://gitlab.inria.fr/tangram/level-set-based-camera-pose-estimation.

Although significant research and recent breakthroughs have advanced neural fake news detection, protecting against human-crafted disinformation remains largely unexplored. By examining existing methods for generating fake news alongside human-written articles, we identified a gap between them, which likely accounts for the poor performance of detectors trained on synthetic data when facing human-written fake news. To bridge this divide, we introduce a new framework designed to produce articles that more closely resemble human writing. Specifically, we utilize self-critical sequence training combined with natural language inference to guarantee the validity of the generated content. Furthermore, we explicitly integrate propaganda techniques into these articles to replicate the methods humans use when crafting fake news. This process resulted in the creation of PropaNews, a training dataset comprising 2,256 examples. Experimental findings indicate that detectors trained on PropaNews achieve 7.3% to 12.0% higher accuracy in identifying human-written disinformation compared to models trained using state-of-the-art synthetic data.

We investigate the parameter space of a two-temperature pseudo-Newtonian Keplerian accretion flow model to explain millimeter and shorter wavelength emissions from Sagittarius A*. Using a general relativistic ray-tracing code, we simulate the radiative transfer of polarized synchrotron emission, including contributions from synchrotron self-Comptonization and bremsstrahlung. Our results demonstrate that the model successfully reproduces millimeter to sub-millimeter emission features with an accretion rate of approximately 6x10^17 g.s^-1 and an inclination angle of roughly 40 degrees. However, the model's predicted near-infrared and X-ray fluxes fall more than an order of magnitude short of observed 'quiescent' state values. Although extended quiescent X-ray emission is attributed to thermal processes in the large-scale accretion flow, NIR emission and flares likely originate from regions inside the Schwarzschild black hole's last stable orbit or from outflows. Despite using a viscous parameter derived from numerical simulations, a degeneracy persists between the electron heating rate and the magnetic parameter. Incorporating black hole spin within a fully general relativistic framework is necessary to resolve these discrepancies.

The shift toward energy transitions integrates more volatile power sources into electrical grids, making High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) connections between synchronous regions increasingly vital. These links help stabilize fluctuating generation by facilitating long-distance transport and utilizing rapid control capabilities. This study examines the relationship between power imbalances—manifested as grid frequency shifts—and power flows on European HVDC corridors connecting synchronous areas. By applying explainable machine learning, we isolate key dependencies and clarify how critical features interact. Our findings indicate that market-driven HVDC flows cause deterministic frequency deviations, though these can be alleviated via stringent ramping constraints. Additionally, different HVDC operating modes significantly influence grid interactions; specifically, we demonstrate that load-frequency control through HVDC links can produce effects ranging from stabilizing (control-like) to destabilizing (disturbance-like) on overall frequency stability.

Can a website's visual design and aesthetic provide clues regarding the credibility of its content? This paper suggests utilizing this often-overlooked visual cue to detect misinformation. By capturing screenshots of articles from both reputable and unreliable domains, we employ a semi-supervised classification method based on tensor decomposition to analyze the overall appearance. Our proposed system, VizFake, demonstrates robustness against various image modifications, including grayscale conversion, vectorization, and partial data loss. Designed for practical application, VizFake operates effectively with a minimal set of labeled data, addressing the scarcity and rapid obsolescence of ground truth labels. On a dataset comprising 50,000 screenshots from over 500 domains, VizFake achieved an F1 score of approximately 85% using merely 5% of available ground truth. Additionally, the unsupervised tensor representations facilitate exploratory data analysis, offering valuable insights into the issue. When benchmarked against popular deep transfer learning models and text-based methods, VizFake matches their accuracy while operating two orders of magnitude faster and eliminating the need for extensive hyper-parameter tuning.

In recent years, there has been a surge in interest regarding the design and implementation of smart grid devices and their control algorithms. Each of these interconnected smart devices acts as a potential entry point for attackers, driving research into intrusion prevention and detection. Nevertheless, no security solution is entirely foolproof; intruders will inevitably compromise smart grid devices, forcing an interaction between the attacker and the system operator through the grid and its control mechanisms. The results of these machine-facilitated human interactions hinge on the architecture of the physical and control systems involved. If these outcomes can be forecasted through simulation, they can serve as essential tools for creating attack-resilient grids and control systems. However, achieving accurate predictions necessitates robust models of not only the physical and control infrastructure but also human decision-making processes. This manuscript introduces a methodology for developing such tools—specifically, models of the decisions made by both the cyber-physical intruder launching the attack and the system operator defending it—and demonstrates their utility in system design.

Distributed systems are growing increasingly vital to our daily lives, particularly in domains such as Smart Homes and the Internet of Things (IoT), where dependable, low-power sensor networks are becoming essential. To guarantee this reliability, numerous trust metrics have been developed. This paper evaluates a model of a distributed low-power sensor network featuring a single root node alongside the Simple Trust Metric against the requirements outlined in "Representation of Trust and Reputation in Self-Managed Computing Systems" [1]. Additionally, it compares these against the Weighted Trust Metric and the Weighted Simple Exponential Smoothing method.

In this study, we investigate the stability of protoneutron stars (PNS) by solving radial oscillation equations, utilizing numerical results from spherically symmetric, general-relativistic neutrino-radiation hydrodynamics simulations that track massive PNS evolution toward black hole formation. Our findings indicate that PNSs remain fundamentally stable against radial perturbations during their evolution until instability sets in just before the apparent horizon forms within the star. Furthermore, we analyze gravitational wave frequencies emitted by PNS under the relativistic Cowling approximation. We derive an empirical formula for the $f$-mode frequency, which exhibits only a weak dependence on specific PNS models. This universality implies that observing $f$-mode gravitational waves could reveal the intrinsic properties of PNS, specifically the combination of mass and radius defined in this work.

Spectropolarimetry of whole plant leaves offers a non-invasive, non-destructive method to investigate the molecular architecture of photosynthesis, providing extensive physiological data. Beyond signals from the photosynthetic machinery itself, cellular structure and arrangement within the leaf generate and alter polarization signatures. Employing Mueller matrix polarimetry with rotating retarder modulation, we mapped spatial variations in transmitted polarization across the chlorophyll a absorbance band (650–710 nm). We present linear and circular polarization data for maple and cultivated maize leaves, analyzing their corresponding Mueller matrices and decompositions, which reveal distinct characteristics in depolarization, retardance, polarizance, and diattenuation. Crucially, while standard leaf tissue exhibits a typical split signal with both positive and negative peaks in induced fractional circular polarization and circular dichroism, areas adjacent to veins display only a negative band. This observation aligns with previous reports of negative bands in single macrodomains. We hypothesize that chloroplast orientation around veins drives this effect. Systematic artifacts are excluded, as three independent measurements using different instruments yielded consistent results. These findings enhance understanding of circular polarization measurements on entire leaves and open new avenues for vegetation remote sensing utilizing circular polarization.

Accurately forecasting disasters using seismic data is critical for saving countless lives, particularly in seismically active zones and near volcanic craters. The recent exponential growth in seismic monitoring stations has generated vast datasets that now exceed the analytical capabilities of human seismologists. Given the intricate nature of this data, identifying subtle but significant patterns remains a significant challenge. Machine learning algorithms have proven highly effective for seismic classification and prediction tasks. It is well-established that certain animals can detect impending disasters by sensing specific seismic signals long before the event occurs. While Mel spectrograms are standard in speech recognition for scaling frequencies to match human hearing, this paper introduces a modified version tailored to scale raw seismic frequencies according to the hearing ranges of disaster-sensing animals. Furthermore, we employ a computer vision algorithm combined with clustering techniques to classify unlabeled seismic data.

We utilize a coarse-grained breakdown of ocean surface geostrophic flow, sourced from satellite observations and numerical models. In the extra-tropics, approximately $60\%$ of the global surface geostrophic kinetic energy resides at scales ranging from $100$ to $500$ km, with a maximum near $300$ km. Our analysis further identifies distinct seasonality in kinetic energy, characterized by a spring peak. We demonstrate that conventional mean-fluctuation (Reynolds) decomposition fails to reliably separate length-scales because the time-mean flow contains a substantial contribution ($>50\%$) from scales smaller than $500$ km. Through spatio-temporal coarse-graining, we observe that every length-scale evolves across a broad spectrum of time-scales. As a result, running time-averages of any duration diminish the energy of all length-scales, including those exceeding $1000$ km, and prove ineffective at eliminating scales smaller than $300$ km. By comparing our spatio-temporal analysis of numerical models and satellite data, we reveal that the AVISO gridded product suppresses temporal variations under 10 days across all length-scales, with a pronounced effect between $100$ and $500$ km.

This paper examines the planar Newtonian three-body problem, specifically focusing on configurations where the three bodies or their velocities align in a straight line. These arrangements, known as generalised syzygies, were previously explored by the author in [4] regarding bounded solutions. In this work, we extend those findings to systems with negative energy and offer a more straightforward proof. Additionally, we investigate periodic solutions that exhibit specific geometric rigidity, demonstrating that such solutions invariably encounter syzygies, meaning they pass through collinear positional states.

This expository article demonstrates two explicit techniques for computing special $L$-values associated with modular forms possessing complex multiplication (CM), drawing inspiration from the properties of $L$-functions derived from Calabi-Yau manifolds defined over $\mathbb Q$.

The incompressible Toner-Tu (ITT) partial differential equations (PDEs) serve as a significant example within the class of active-fluid PDEs. Although they exhibit shared characteristics with the Navier-Stokes equations (NSEs), such as identical scaling invariance, they possess distinct features. Unlike NSEs, which are typically analyzed under decaying or additively forced conditions, the ITT equations lack additive forcing. Instead, they incorporate a linear activity term, $\alpha \bu$ (where $\bu$ represents the velocity field), that injects energy into the system, alongside a negative $\bu|\bu|^{2}$ term that facilitates both frozen and statistically steady states. Collectively, these distinctions render the ITT equations a compelling subject for investigation through combined PDE analysis and pseudo-spectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs). In two dimensions ($d=2$), global regularity of solutions has been proven, and the existence of bounded hierarchies of weighted, time-averaged norms for both higher derivatives and higher moments of the velocity field has been demonstrated. Similar bounded hierarchies for Leray-type weak solutions have also been established in three dimensions ($d=3$). This work presents findings on these norms from DNSs in both $d=2$ and $d=3$, contrasting them with their Navier-Stokes equivalents.

This paper establishes a class of second-order Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg inequalities that includes the sharp second-order uncertainty principle recently derived by Cazacu, Flynn, and Lam \cite{CFL2020} as a particular instance. We further demonstrate the sharpness of these inequalities across multiple parameter regimes. Additionally, we prove two stability versions of the sharp second-order uncertainty principle attributed to Cazacu, Flynn, and Lam by establishing that the discrepancy between the left and right sides of the inequality governs the distance to the set of extremal functions, measured in the $L^2$ norm of the gradient.

This work examines Dyson equations within perturbative QFT in AdS space and explores their implications for large-N CFT. We demonstrate that the dressed one-particle AdS propagator exhibits wavefunction renormalization and operator mixing, which lead to finite adjustments in OPE data. Furthermore, we illustrate how the resummation of 1/N effects in CFT arises from the dressing mechanism in AdS. When a boundary-to-bulk propagator is dressed by propagators whose combined conformal dimensions fall below the primary dimension, it fails to correspond to a standard CFT source; we connect this phenomenon to an AdS/CFT analogue of particle instability. Additionally, we analyze the dressing of the two-particle propagator, deriving a conformal Bethe-Salpeter equation for the partial wave of a "bound state" operator. In the case of a ladder kernel, we briefly show that a bound state emerges with a conformal dimension equal to the sum of its constituents plus a 1/N-suppressed "binding energy." Finally, we emphasize that the resummation of Dyson equations is crucial for obtaining these findings.

Dark energy is the leading candidate capable of generating effective negative pressure, driving galaxies and galaxy clusters apart in an accelerating manner. Cosmic structures have developed from initial primordial fluctuations, with their evolution contingent upon the background dynamics of various components, including dark matter, dark energy, and others. This thesis aims to explore how specific dark energy models influence the formation of these universal structures.

It is widely recognized that classical PID control dominates numerous industrial control loops. Nevertheless, a theoretical framework explaining why linear PID effectively manages ubiquitous uncertain nonlinear dynamical systems, alongside a method yielding explicit design formulas for PID parameters, remains absent. This paper continues the authors' recent efforts to establish a theoretical foundation for PID control. We investigate the underlying rationale of PID control for a broad class of high-dimensional, second-order, non-affine, and uncertain systems. We demonstrate that an explicit three-dimensional parameter set can be constructed; selecting PID parameters from this set ensures global closed-loop stability and exponential convergence of the regulation error to zero, provided certain conditions on system uncertainties are met. Additionally, we show that PD (or PI) control can globally stabilize several specific classes of high-dimensional uncertain nonlinear systems. Furthermore, we apply the Markus-Yamabe theorem from differential equations to derive a necessary and sufficient condition for choosing PI parameters for a class of one-dimensional non-affine uncertain systems. These theoretical findings explicitly indicate that controller parameters do not necessarily require high gain values, confirming that PID control possesses strong robustness regarding both system structural uncertainties and controller parameter selection.

This study revisits a 2014 NeurIPS investigation into inconsistencies within conference peer review, revealing that half of the variance in reviewer scores stemmed from subjectivity. Seven years later, our analysis shows no correlation between quality scores and citation-based impact for accepted papers. However, by tracking the eventual publication venues of rejected papers, we discovered a significant correlation between their scores and impact. We conclude that the 2014 review process was effective at filtering out low-quality submissions but failed to identify high-quality ones. While offering recommendations for process improvement, we caution against eliminating subjective judgment. Ultimately, we argue that the community should rely less on "top-tier conference publications" as a primary metric for researcher quality. For NeurIPS 2021, Program Committees are repeating this experiment alongside launching new studies.

In multi-component scalar dark matter frameworks, a single discrete $Z_N$ symmetry with $N \geq 4$ can ensure the stability of various dark matter constituents. This study examines the specific case where $N$ is even ($N=2n$), involving two species—a complex scalar and a real scalar—that together constitute the observed dark matter density. We conduct a phenomenological investigation of three distinct scenarios grounded in $Z_4$ and $Z_6$ symmetries, mapping their viable parameter spaces and evaluating their detectability. Our findings indicate that the novel interactions permitted by $Z_{2n}$ symmetries allow current experimental limits to be met across a broader spectrum of dark matter masses, potentially yielding observable signatures in direct detection experiments. Furthermore, we propose that these three scenarios function as archetypes for other two-component $Z_{2n}$ models comprising one complex and one real dark matter particle.

By employing $p$-adic families of generalized Gross-Kudla-Schoen diagonal cycles, we build an anticyclotomic Euler system associated with the Rankin-Selberg convolution of two modular forms. This construction yields new instances of the Bloch-Kato conjecture for analytic rank zero, advances toward results for analytic rank one, and establishes a divisibility result relevant to an Iwasawa main conjecture.

Effective loop closure detection is critical for real-time, large-scale Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). This paper introduces a novel, compact, and reliable unsupervised deep neural network architecture designed for visual loop closure through feature embedding. Built on an autoencoder framework specifically adapted for this task, the model employs a unique training strategy: rather than using random dropout, it applies randomized projective transformations to input images to simulate natural viewpoint shifts caused by robot movement. Furthermore, the system leverages the illumination invariance and geometric details offered by Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG), compelling the encoder to reconstruct HOG descriptors instead of raw pixel data. Consequently, the trained model extracts features that remain robust against extreme appearance variations directly from raw images, eliminating the need for labeled data or environment-specific training. Extensive experiments on diverse, challenging datasets demonstrate that this proposed deep loop-closure model consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both efficiency and effectiveness. The model operates rapidly and reliably enough to close loops in real-time without dimensionality reduction, making it a viable replacement for generic off-the-shelf networks within ConvNet-based loop closure systems.

Many individuals attempting to learn a foreign language struggle to understand or converse with native speakers due to their accents, a challenge that native speakers face equally when encountering unfamiliar ones. An accent conversion system capable of altering a speaker's accent while maintaining their unique voice identity—specifically timbre and pitch—holds significant potential for applications in communication, education, and entertainment. However, current accent conversion models often inadvertently alter the speaker's identity alongside the accent. This study employs adversarial learning to separate accent-dependent features while preserving other acoustic traits. The primary distinction of our approach is its ability to transform an unseen speaker's utterance into multiple accents without compromising the original voice identity. Subjective evaluations confirm that our model produces audio that more closely resembles the target accent while sounding like the original speaker.

This paper outlines the mathematical basis for assembly code designed to handle finite element approximations of nonlocal models featuring compactly supported, weakly singular kernels. The code's capabilities are illustrated through a nonlocal diffusion model across multiple configurations and a two-dimensional bond-based peridynamics model. The nlfem code is released under the MIT License and is available for free download.

This paper investigates a multi-agent system originating from the dynamics of a single nonlinear affine control agent. It examines the system's behavior as the number of agents approaches infinity through two distinct methodologies: a granular mean-field approach, which controls a finite subset while the remainder grows indefinitely, and a kinetic approach, where the proportion of controlled agents remains constant in the limit. In each scenario, an optimal control problem is formulated based on the solution derived from the finite-dimensional case.

Identifying and analyzing network patterns are fundamental to scientific research. This study introduces and assesses a novel method that learns graph components capable of both interpreting and creating realistic new graphs. Our primary insight is that a graph's clique tree contains robust and precise data. We demonstrate that a Hyperedge Replacement Grammar (HRG) can be derived from this clique tree and present a fixed-size algorithm for generating new graphs of a specific dimension. Experimental results on large real-world networks indicate that graphs produced via the HRG approach display a diverse array of properties mirroring those of the original networks. Beyond global metrics such as degree or eigenvector centrality, a graph's appearance relies heavily on subtle details within local substructures, which are challenging to characterize at a global scale. We further show that the HRG model successfully preserves these local substructures during graph generation.

This study examines the influence of polarization effects on the orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes of an optical fiber. Specifically, it revisits the lifting of degeneracy between $HE$ and $EH$ vector modes, which merge into a single spatial (scalar) OAM mode characterized by a common topological charge and associated with left or right circular polarization under the weakly guiding approximation (WGA). While the polarization term in the vector wave equation, acting as a Hermitian perturbation, successfully explains the splitting of these $HE$ and $EH$ modes, extending this framework to account for the resulting polarization-induced field correction presents significant challenges; this correction is distinguished by a topological charge magnitude differing by two. The study critically analyzes these issues, proposing a potential solution and discussing its implications.

This study presents a predictive control approach designed to identify unstable periodic orbits within the generalized tent map. Because the invariant set housing these orbits forms a repelling structure with a complex, Cantor-like geometry, simple local stabilization techniques often fail to locate the orbits due to the minimal size of their basin of attraction. The analysis demonstrates that for specific control parameter values, both local and global solution behaviors shift in the controlled system; notably, the invariant set expands into an interval or covers the entire real axis. The paper addresses the computational aspects of this control strategy and establishes necessary conditions for periodicity. Furthermore, it thoroughly examines the local asymptotic stability of subcycles within the stable cycles of the controlled system and outlines statistical characteristics of the specific subset of the classical Cantor middle-thirds set defined by the map's periodic points.

Graph property testing aims to determine if a graph satisfies a specific property or is significantly distant from doing so, ideally using sublinear query and time complexities. This paper introduces the study of property testing for signed graphs, where each edge carries either a positive or negative sign. We demonstrate that sublinear algorithms exist for testing three fundamental properties of signed graphs: balance (also known as 2-clusterability), clusterability, and the absence of signed triangles. The research covers both the dense graph model, which allows querying the signed adjacency matrix, and the bounded-degree model, which permits querying node neighbors and edge signs. Our methods employ various techniques from graph property testing, including reductions between these two models. A primary technical achievement is a sublinear algorithm for testing clusterability in the bounded-degree model, distinguishing it from k-clusterability, which cannot be tested with sublinear queries. This tester extends the foundational work by Goldreich and Ron on bipartiteness testing.

We present NuSTAR observations of the solar microflare SOL2015-09-01T04. Although too dim for the GOES X-ray Sensor, we classify the event as an A0.1 class flare. Detected by RHESSI at a mere 5 counts per second per detector, this microflare represents the faintest hard X-ray (HXR) event recorded in current literature. Occurring during a solar observation window, the highly sensitive NuSTAR observatory utilized its direct focusing optics to generate detailed HXR spectral and imaging data for this microflare. The event displays HXR characteristics typical of larger flares, such as a rapid rise followed by a slower decay, an earlier peak at higher energies, spatial dimensions comparable to RHESSI microflares, and a high-energy excess beyond an isothermal component during the impulsive phase. While the microflare exhibits low emission measure, temperature, and energy, its physical size remains significant, with observations suggesting an origin from the interaction of at least two magnetic loops. We estimate the thermal energy increase at the time of the flare to be 2.4x10^27 ergs. These findings indicate that flares can scale down to extremely low energies while retaining the properties traditionally associated with "flarelike" phenomena.

We examine the natural time-reversal symmetry of the first-order Langevin equation governing the overdamped dynamics of interacting systems, a property that yields unexpected results for correlation functions. This symmetry establishes the correlation of interactions as a strictly restraining component within the system's time-dependent diffusion tensor, thereby deriving the relationship initially proposed by Fixman. When applied to the time-dependent diffusion of dilute polymer coils, this approach enables the quantitative calibration of Kirkwood's approximation for their hydrodynamic radius. Furthermore, we derive a generalized "Fixman Law" for dissipation featuring a memory kernel with a revealing causal structure and also address the scenario described by the second-order Langevin equation.

Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterized by spectra featuring intense, broad emission lines linked to significant mass loss. In the context of massive stars, approximately 90% of identified WR stars are believed to have evolved past the main sequence. Known as classical WR (cWR) stars, these hydrogen-poor objects mark a vital stage before collapsing into black holes, providing a unique perspective on hot-star wind dynamics. Their origins are attributed to either intrinsic mass loss or interactions within binary systems. Despite using modern atmospheric models, current analyses struggle to align WR star properties with stellar evolution predictions. Notably, standard stellar evolution models fail to account for the majority of cWR stars, an issue that intensifies at subsolar metallicities. Future progress may come from advanced atmospheric models and upcoming observational efforts aimed at detecting previously unseen companions.

This paper applies the $\bar{\partial}$ steepest descent method to analyze the initial value problem for the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger (fNLS) equation, specifically addressing non-generic weighted Sobolev initial data that permits high-order discrete spectrum. We precisely characterize the eigenfunctions and scattering coefficients when high-order poles are present, formulate an appropriately enlarged Riemann-Hilbert (RH) problem, and transform it into a solvable model through a sequence of deformations. Consequently, we derive the asymptotic expansion of the fNLS solution within any fixed space-time cone defined by $\mathcal{S}(x_1,x_2,v_1,v_2):=\left\lbrace (x,t)\in \mathbb{R}^2: x=x_0+vt, \ x_0\in[x_1,x_2]\text{, }v\in[v_1,v_2]\right\rbrace$. These findings indicate that the solution satisfies the soliton resolution conjecture. The leading-order term comprises a high-order pole-soliton, with parameters influenced by both soliton-soliton interactions within the cone and soliton-radiation interactions on the continuous spectrum. The error term is of order $\mathcal{O}(t^{-3/4})$, originating from the associated $\bar{\partial}$ equation.

We investigate an interior solution featuring a physically symmetric vierbein with two unknown functions within the framework of conformal teleparallel gravity. For specific metric potentials and an appropriate anisotropic function, the field equations form a closed system, yielding a new set of configurations compatible with observed pulsars. Specifically, boundary conditions for the interior spacetime are applied to the Schwarzschild solution to constrain the conformal field, ensuring it maintains a unit value across the surface of a compact object. Additionally, the model is applied to pulsar $4U1608-52$, utilizing an approximate radius of $R= 9.52 \pm 0.15$ km and a mass of $M= 1.74 \pm 0.14\, M_{\circledcirc}$. To assess stability, we examine causality conditions and the adiabatic index under the assumptions of the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov equation, a static state, and the adiabatic index. Finally, we evaluate the model's consistency with other pulsars.

We investigate the holographic field theory dual of a probe SU(2) Yang-Mills field situated within a $(4+1)$-dimensional asymptotically Anti-de Sitter background. Our analysis reveals a novel ground state emerging when the gauge field's magnetic component exceeds a specific critical threshold. In this state, a triangular Abrikosov lattice forms in the spatial dimensions orthogonal to the magnetic field, consisting of superconducting vortices generated by the condensation of a charged vector operator. We execute this computation under both finite and zero temperature conditions, employing a hard wall cutoff to model a confining gauge theory. This research holds significance for holographic condensed matter frameworks and heavy ion physics alike. Furthermore, our findings lend credence to the hypothesis that such a ground state exists within the QCD vacuum in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

Although productivity convergence is a cornerstone of empirical growth research, current analysis faces three unresolved issues: (1) a lack of investigation into the hierarchical structure of industry-level data; (2) the neglect of heterogeneity in industry-level technology; and (3) the infrequent consideration of cross-sectional dependence. This study tackles these challenges using a hierarchical panel data framework, proposing a new estimation method and establishing its associated asymptotic theory. The framework is subsequently applied to data covering 23 manufacturing sectors across various countries from 1963 to 2018. The findings indicate that both the manufacturing sector as a whole and individual two-digit ISIC industries demonstrate strong conditional convergence in labor productivity, yet fail to show unconditional convergence. Furthermore, the results highlight that both global and industry-specific shocks play significant roles in explaining the convergence patterns of these manufacturing industries.

The MICROSCOPE mission was designed to verify the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) with a precision of $10^{-15}$. This principle asserts that objects of varying mass and composition accelerate identically within a gravitational field. In this experiment, test masses composed of titanium and platinum alloys travel along a quasi-circular path around Earth as part of a dual-accelerometer system. By measuring the differential accelerations of these masses, the mission seeks to detect any potential WEP violations occurring at frequencies determined by the satellite's orbital dynamics and orientation. This document outlines the primary mission drivers that informed the specifications for key subsystems, including the satellite, ground infrastructure, instruments, and orbit. Utilizing the measurement equation, the study establishes the statistical and systematic error allocation required to achieve the test objectives and presents the projected error budget for the mission.

Despite the promise of efficiency, objectivity, and accuracy, algorithms can inadvertently introduce or exacerbate biases. This study examines two prominent algorithms, PageRank and Who-to-Follow (WTF), to assess how their ranking outputs generate inequality and inequity within directed social networks. We introduce a directed network model incorporating preferential attachment and homophily (DPAH) to analyze how network structure impacts the distribution of these algorithmic ranks. Our primary results indicate that (i) inequality correlates positively with inequity; (ii) inequality stems from the interaction of preferential attachment, homophily, node activity, and edge density; and (iii) inequity arises from the interplay between homophily and the size of minority groups. Specifically, when majorities exhibit homophily, neutrality, or heterophily, these algorithms respectively reduce, replicate, or amplify the representation of minorities in top rankings. Furthermore, minorities can enhance their visibility by forming strategic connections, such as increasing their out-degree or homophily, particularly when majorities are homophilic. These insights reveal the social and algorithmic mechanisms that obstruct equality and equity in network-based ranking and recommendation systems.

This paper introduces an analytical solution for the eigenmodes and associated electric fields of a composite system comprising a nanorod near a plasmonic, semi-infinite metallic surface. Specifically, silver is selected as the material for both the nanorod and the planar metal. The system consists of two subsystems with distinct symmetries: the rod possesses cylindrical symmetry, whereas the interface exhibits rectangular symmetry. By employing a boundary integral method originally proposed by Eyges, we analytically calculate the integrals that couple the two subsystems. Ultimately, the problem is simplified into a linear algebra framework where all system terms are defined analytically. For configurations where the nanorod is far from the planar surface, only a limited number of these integrals are required to achieve a complete analytical solution. Our findings serve as a benchmark for other numerical methods and provide a foundational reference for discussing systems involving nanorods and two-dimensional materials.

The Dark Matter In CCDs (DAMIC) project utilizes silicon Charge-Coupled Devices (CCDs) as detectors to search for low-mass dark matter. Each CCD features a 675-micrometer thick silicon target, with its top surface segmented into over 16 million pixels, each measuring 15 micrometers by 15 micrometers. Currently, the DAMIC collaboration has deployed several of these devices at SNOLAB. By 2019, the SNOLAB setup achieved operational status with five CCDs exhibiting a leakage current below 8.2e-22 amperes per square centimeter and a readout noise of 1.6 electrons. A future upgrade, DAMIC-M, will be installed at the Laboratoire Souterrain de Modane using enhanced CCDs from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory equipped with skipper amplifiers. These amplifiers employ non-destructive, multi-sample readout techniques, reducing readout noise to 0.068 electrons. This ultra-low noise, combined with minimal leakage current, will enable DAMIC-M to detect physics processes involving collision energies as low as 1 electronvolt. The DAMIC-M array will comprise 50 large-area skipper CCDs, each containing more than 36 million pixels. This proceeding outlines the DAMIC apparatus and its results at SNOLAB, alongside the capabilities and current status of the upcoming DAMIC-M experiment.

We conducted Monte Carlo simulations investigating the colloidal epitaxy of hard spheres on a square lattice, extending earlier work. Our results revealed an intrinsic stacking fault that shrinks and runs obliquely due to the glide of a Shockley partial dislocation, with its lower end anchored in fcc (001) stacking; this finding addresses the question of why gravity reduces defects in colloidal crystals. We addressed a limitation in prior simulations by replacing the artificial stress from a small periodic boundary box with realistic stress generated by a bottom pattern. Under these physically realizable conditions, we observed the elimination of stacking faults. Furthermore, the center of gravity settled smoothly via a single relaxation mode when gravitational energy (mgd) was slightly lower than thermal energy (kT). Frequent appearances of tetrahedral structures in the snapshots indicate the formation of stacking fault tetrahedra.

Stem cell heterogeneity plays a critical role in maintaining homeostasis during tissue development. This study introduces a comprehensive framework for analyzing stem cell regeneration dynamics, accounting for cellular heterogeneity and stochastic shifts in epigenetic states. By extending the classical G0 cell cycle model, the approach integrates stem cell epigenetic profiles as a continuous multidimensional variable, alongside kinetic rates for proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis that vary according to these epigenetic conditions. Furthermore, random transitions between epigenetic states are modeled through an inheritance probability defined by a conditional beta distribution. This generalized formula not only facilitates the investigation of tumor development driven by gene mutations but also provides a versatile tool for understanding diverse dynamic processes in stem cell regeneration, such as tissue maturation, degeneration, and aberrant growth.

We investigate the task of aligning two sets of 3D geometric primitives when correspondences are known. Our primary contribution demonstrates that this primitive alignment framework unifies five distinct perception challenges: point cloud registration, primitive (mesh) registration, category-level 3D registration, absolute pose estimation (APE), and category-level APE. Second, we introduce DynAMical Pose estimation (DAMP), the first general and practical algorithm for solving primitive alignment by simulating rigid body dynamics generated by virtual springs and damping forces that span the shortest distances between corresponding primitives. We evaluate DAMP on both simulated and real datasets across all five problems, showing that (i) it consistently converges to the globally optimal solution for the first three problems involving 3D-3D correspondences; and (ii) while it may occasionally converge to suboptimal solutions for the last two problems involving 2D-3D correspondences, a local minima escaping scheme ensures DAMP always succeeds. Finally, we demystify DAMP's surprising empirical performance by formally proving a global convergence result for point cloud registration, achieved by characterizing the local stability of equilibrium points within the underlying dynamical system.

We propose a novel direction for turbulence research centered on multi-mode correlations, which expose the previously obscured characteristics of turbulent states. By applying this framework to models of fundamental vortex and strong wave turbulence, we investigate regimes near thermal equilibrium, occurring when interaction times exhibit weak dependence on mode numbers.
