As the mode count rises, one-mode statistics converge toward a Gaussian distribution (as seen in weak turbulence) and occupation numbers increase, yet the three-mode cumulant governing energy flux remains invariant. Conversely, we observe that higher-order multi-mode cumulants increase with their order, a growth scaling law derived analytically and validated numerically. We demonstrate that the sum of squared dimensionless cumulants corresponds to the relative entropy between the complete multi-mode distribution and the Gaussian approximation of independent modes. We posit that this relative entropy may scale logarithmically with the number of modes, mirroring entanglement entropy in critical phenomena. Consequently, multi-mode correlations offer a new method for characterizing turbulence states and potentially categorizing them into distinct universality classes.

Ensuring safe navigation in multi-robot systems remains a core challenge, primarily because of the uncertainty regarding the future paths of robots that serve as obstacles to one another. This study introduces a principled, data-driven method in which every robot iteratively solves a finite-horizon optimization problem. This problem includes collision avoidance constraints, specifically formulated as the distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of the distance between an agent and a polyhedral obstacle. These CVaR constraints must remain valid for all probability distributions that are sufficiently close to the empirical distribution derived from observed prediction error samples gathered during operation. The flexibility of this framework enables robustness against prediction errors common in both distributed and decentralized scenarios. By utilizing convexity and min-max duality principles from Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, we derive tractable, finite-dimensional approximations of these constraints. The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated through a multi-drone navigation simulation executed on the Gazebo platform.

This study reports a measurement of the electroweak production of a W boson, a photon ($\gamma$), and two jets (j) during proton-proton collisions. The analysis selects events where the W boson decays leptonically by identifying one electron or muon and observing significant missing transverse momentum. Additionally, the two jets must exhibit a large invariant dijet mass and substantial pseudorapidity separation. Using data from the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$, the measured cross section for electroweak W$\gamma$jj production is 23.5$^{+4.9}_{-4.7}$ fb, compared to a total W$\gamma$jj production cross section of 113 $\pm$ 13 fb. Differential cross sections were also determined, with distributions unfolded to the particle level. All findings align with standard model predictions. The analysis imposes constraints on anomalous quartic gauge couplings (aQGCs) using dimension-8 effective field theory operators, establishing the most restrictive limits to date on the parameters $f_\mathrm{M,2-5}/\Lambda^4$ and $f_\mathrm{T,6-7}/\Lambda^4$.

Let $G$ be a simple graph, where $n$, $\Delta(G)$, and $\chi'(G)$ represent the order, maximum degree, and chromatic index, respectively. A graph $G$ is defined as \emph{overfull} when $|E(G)|/\lfloor n/2\rfloor > \Delta(G)$, and as {\it critical} if $\chi'(H) < \chi'(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H$. It is evident that if $G$ is overfull, then $\chi'(G) = \Delta(G)+1$. The \emph{core} of $G$, denoted by $G_{\Delta}$, refers to the subgraph induced by all vertices of maximum degree. We propose that examining the core degree condition offers a viable strategy for addressing the overfull conjecture. In this paper, we demonstrate that for any integer $k\geq 2$, if $G$ is critical with $\Delta(G)\geq \frac{2}{3}n+\frac{3k}{2}$ and $\delta(G_\Delta)\leq k$, then $G$ must be overfull.

Andromeda (And) XXV was previously identified as a dwarf spheroidal galaxy (dSph) lacking significant dark matter, though earlier findings suffered from substantial uncertainties. This study addresses those limitations by doubling the sample of member stars to re-evaluate the system's kinematics and mass. We determine a systemic radial velocity of $\nu_\mathrm{r}=-107.7\pm1.0 \mathrm{~km s}^{-1}$ and a velocity dispersion of $\sigma_\nu=4.5\pm1.0\mathrm{~km s}^{-1}$. These refined measurements yield a mass within the half-light radius of $M(r< r_\mathrm{h})=6.9^{+3.2}_{-2.8}\times10^6\mathrm{~M}_\odot$, corresponding to a mass-to-light ratio of $\mathrm{[M/L]}_\mathrm{r_\mathrm{h}}=37^{+17}_{-15}\mathrm{~M}_\odot/\mathrm{L}_\odot$. This result provides the first unambiguous evidence of a dark matter component in And XXV. Additionally, we confirm the metallicity as $\mathrm{[Fe/H]}=-1.9\pm0.1$ dex, consistent with prior studies. Extending our analysis with GravSphere mass modeling, we identify a low central dark matter density of $\rho_\mathrm{DM}(150\mathrm{pc})= 2.7^{+1.8}_{-1.6}\times10^7\mathrm{~M}_\odot\mathrm{kpc}^{-3}$, distinguishing And XXV as a clear outlier among Local Group dSphs of comparable stellar mass. A companion paper will investigate whether dark matter cusp-core transformations and/or tidal effects can account for this low density.

Frustration-induced quantum fluctuations generate numerous exotic ground-state phases, making the investigation of these quantum phase transitions a formidable challenge in condensed matter physics. This study examines a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg $J_1-J_2$ chain, characterized by nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) exchange interactions, utilizing Principal Component Analysis (PCA), an unsupervised machine learning approach. In this framework, the most probable spin configurations (MPSC) for both the ground state (GS) and the first excited state (FES) across various $J_2/J_1$ ratios serve as inputs to build a covariance matrix. The "quantified principal component," defined as $p_1(J_2/J_1)$ derived from the largest eigenvalue of this matrix, is computed. Results indicate that the behavior and fluctuations of $p_1(J_2/J_1)$ reliably forecast phase transitions and degeneracies within the GS. Specifically, $p_1(J_2/J_1)$ derived from GS MPSC reveals only GS degeneracies, while the version calculated from FES MPSC captures the gapless spin liquid (GSL)-to-dimer phase transition alongside all system degeneracies. A jump in the FES-derived $p_1(J_2/J_1)$ at $J_2/J_1 \approx 0.241$ signals the GSL-dimer transition, whereas kinks in the same metric correspond to GS degeneracies. Furthermore, scatter plots of the first two principal components of the FES display distinct band structures that differentiate the various phases.

Inflation is frequently modeled as a scalar field slowly rolling down an appropriate potential, which ultimately must be identified as the expectation value of a quantum field evolving within a quantum effective potential. This potential's form arises from the underlying tree-level potential, modified by quantum corrections originating from both the scalar field and metric perturbations. Following reference [1], we derive the effective scalar field equations and corrected Friedmann equations up to quadratic order in scalar fields, scalar metric perturbations, and tensor perturbations. We isolate the leading-order quantum corrections from various sources within benchmark inflation models and estimate their magnitudes, while also discussing the implications of non-minimal coupling to gravity in this framework.

This paper introduces a hybrid position/force controller designed for joint robots, targeting two primary objectives: motion tracking and force regulation. When these goals do not conflict, they can be decoupled; this work achieves that by utilizing a smooth, invertible mapping between joint and task spaces to design independent controllers for each objective. A traditional task-space motion controller handles movement, while the force controller indirectly regulates force by manipulating the desired trajectory. The effectiveness of this hybrid approach is demonstrated through two case studies—contour tracking and surface polishing, as well as dual-arm box manipulation—and further validated via simulations using physics engines.

Unpaired image-to-image translation involves learning mappings between image domains in an unsupervised fashion. Current approaches typically rely on deterministic mappings that fail to explicitly account for predictive uncertainty or robustness against outliers, resulting in performance drops when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) patterns during testing. To overcome this, we introduce a new probabilistic framework named Uncertainty-aware Generalized Adaptive Cycle Consistency (UGAC). This method models per-pixel residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution, enabling it to capture heavy-tailed distributions. We evaluated our approach against various state-of-the-art techniques on two demanding tasks: unpaired image denoising for natural images and unpaired modality propagation in medical imaging. Experimental outcomes show that our model achieves superior image generation quality compared to recent methods, as measured by quantitative metrics like signal-to-noise ratio and structural similarity. Additionally, the model demonstrates enhanced robustness when handling OOD test data.

This study addresses monotone inclusions in Hilbert spaces where the operator comprises the sum of a maximal monotone operator $T$ and a single-valued, monotone, Lipschitz continuous, and expectation-valued operator $V$. Inspired by Attouch and Cabot's foundational work on relaxed inertial methods, we introduce a stochastic variant of the relaxed inertial forward-backward-forward (RISFB) algorithm. By leveraging an online variance reduction technique through mini-batching, we establish that the RISFB sequence weakly converges to the solution set. Furthermore, we provide an estimate for the decay rate of the discrete velocity in the stochastic process. Under conditions of strong monotonicity, we prove strong convergence and offer a comprehensive analysis of the scheme's iteration and oracle complexities. If the mini-batch size increases at a geometric (polynomial) rate, the convergence rate improves to linear (or a suitable polynomial rate), and the oracle complexity for finding an $\epsilon$-solution becomes $O(1/\epsilon)$. This latter result is significant because it accommodates potentially biased oracles, representing a major theoretical advance that expands the method's applicability. Additionally, utilizing a restricted gap function derived from the Fitzpatrick function, we demonstrate that the expected gap of an averaged sequence decreases at a sublinear rate of $O(1/k)$, with an oracle complexity of $O(1/\epsilon^{1+a})$ for a suitably defined $\epsilon$-solution where $a>1$. Numerical experiments on two-stage games and an overlapping group Lasso problem highlight the superiority of our approach over stochastic forward-backward-forward (SFBF) and stochastic approximation (SA) schemes.

Energy squeezing has garnered significant interest for its potential in electromagnetic (EM) energy harvesting and optical communication. Nevertheless, Fabry-Perot resonance restricts this phenomenon to discrete frequencies, and prior energy-squeezing devices have relied on stringent material or geometric constraints. While structures utilizing epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) media have demonstrated the ability to squeeze and tunnel EM waves at specific frequencies like the plasma frequency, the associated group velocity is typically negligible, severely limiting information transmission. This paper demonstrates low-loss energy squeezing and tunneling (EST) via unidirectional modes in yttrium iron garnet (YIG)-based one-way waveguides operating at microwave frequencies. Theoretical analysis and finite element method simulations confirm the achievement of broadband EST, even within highly bent structures. Furthermore, comparable EST was realized in a practical three-dimensional remanence-based one-way waveguide. These unidirectional mode-based EST mechanisms open avenues for ultra-subwavelength EM focusing, enhanced nonlinear optics, and the design of diverse functional devices within integrated optical circuits, such as phase modulators.

While citation counts are a conventional metric for assessing a research paper's impact, they offer limited insight into how deeply a paper influences the content of later works due to the varied reasons behind citations. To address this, we introduce a new approach for quantifying linguistic influence within timestamped document sets. This method involves two primary stages: first, detecting lexical and semantic shifts via contextual embeddings and word frequencies; second, compiling these changes into per-document influence scores by fitting a high-dimensional Hawkes process with a low-rank parameter matrix. We demonstrate that this linguistic influence metric predicts future citations, as the estimated influence derived from the two years following a paper's release correlates with and forecasts its citation count over the subsequent three years. This finding is validated through an online evaluation using incremental temporal training and test splits, outperforming a robust baseline that accounts for initial citation counts, topics, and lexical characteristics.

Federated Learning (FL) addresses contemporary issues related to data privacy and computational constraints by training models locally, ensuring raw data remains at its source. Despite these benefits, FL faces specific hurdles, particularly the substantial network bandwidth demands associated with transmitting model weight updates in distributed settings. To mitigate this, we introduce a mechanism that compresses weight updates using Autoencoders (AE), which extract features from the updates to facilitate compression. In this architecture, the encoder operates on the training nodes, while the decoder resides on the aggregation node, enabling compression at the source and reconstruction of weights after each communication round. This study demonstrates that a dynamic, orthogonal AE-based compression technique offers a highly advantageous solution for large-scale FL. It achieves compression ratios between 500x and 1720x (or higher) and allows for customization based on specific accuracy needs, computational resources, and other system requirements.

We present the derivation of the heat transport equation for nonmetals based on a quantum Markovian master equation formulated in Lindblad form. Initially, we derive the equations of motion governing the temporal evolution of on-site atomic energies within a one-dimensional periodic chain interacting with a thermal reservoir. In the continuum limit, Fourier's law of heat conduction emerges naturally, allowing for an explicit determination of thermal conductivity. Our results indicate that the influence of the heat reservoir on the lattice manifests as a heat source density determined by the atoms' diffusion coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Markovian dynamics corresponds to the long-wavelength approximation for phonons, a characteristic feature of elastic solids. Finally, we show that the high-temperature limit recovers the classical heat conduction equation.

This paper investigates fully connected neural networks featuring Gaussian random weights and biases, comprising $L$ hidden layers where each layer's width scales with a large parameter $n$. For non-linearities bounded by polynomials, we provide precise estimates in powers of $1/n$ regarding the joint correlation functions of the network's output and its derivatives. Additionally, we derive exact layer-wise recursions for these functions and resolve specific cases for various non-linearities, including $\mathrm{ReLU}$ and $\tanh$. Our findings indicate that in both scenarios, the ratio of depth to width ($L/n$) acts as an effective measure of network depth, governing both the magnitude of fluctuations at individual neurons and the extent of inter-neuron correlations. Leveraging this insight, we analyze a simplified version of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem, demonstrating that this specific variant arises if and only if $L/n$ is large. Several fundamental concepts presented here were initially formulated with a physics-based level of rigor in a recent monograph co-authored with Roberts and Yaida.

Generating dialogue is a critical yet challenging NLP task, with these difficulties intensifying for low-resource African languages. To facilitate the development of dialogue agents for these languages, we introduce the first high-quality datasets for six African languages: Swahili, Wolof, Hausa, Nigerian Pidgin English, Kinyarwanda, and Yorùbá. Each dataset contains 1,500 turns translated from a subset of the English MultiWOZ dataset. We then evaluate the efficacy of transfer learning by employing state-of-the-art deep monolingual models, DialoGPT and BlenderBot, comparing them against a simple seq2seq baseline using perplexity metrics. Additionally, we perform human evaluation on single-turn conversations via majority voting and assess inter-annotator agreement. Our findings support the hypothesis that deep monolingual models learn cross-lingual abstractions, as we observed human-like dialogue generation in five of the six languages. Nigerian Pidgin English demonstrated the highest transferability with a 78.1% human-likeness score (34.4% unanimous). We openly release the datasets and host model checkpoints and demos on the HuggingFace hub for public use.

The interaction between static and dynamic disorder and the collective optical response within molecular ensembles represents a defining feature of nanophotonic and nanoplasmonic systems. This study examines the cooperative superradiant behavior of a quantum emitter ensemble subject to environmental disorder, specifically inhomogeneous broadening caused by the static random distribution of transition frequencies and motional narrowing resulting from the stochastic modulation of excitation energies. While inhomogeneous broadening disrupts the coherence of collective excitations and inhibits superradiant emission, rapid stochastic modulation of molecular excitation energies can effectively restore quantum emitter coherence and revive superradiant output, demonstrating an unexpected aspect of motional narrowing. Furthermore, in light scattering processes triggered by an off-resonant incident pulse, this stochastic modulation results in inelastic fluorescence at the average excitation energy over long durations, indicating that dynamic disorder can indeed facilitate collective excitation within the molecular ensemble.

This study explores how asteroid lightcurves vary with phase angle by applying numerical scattering models to basic geometric shapes. To simplify the analysis, Kaasalainen scattering parameters are derived from Hapke scattering laws for C-type, S-type, and V-type asteroids. Although these spectral types exhibit significant differences in multiple scattering effects—primarily driven by their geometric albedos—the resulting variations in light curve versus phase angle relationships are relatively minor. Using a Kaasalainen scattering law and a biaxial ellipsoid shape model, we plot amplitudes and axis ratios across phase angles ranging from $0^\circ$ to $140^\circ$ for these asteroid types. Furthermore, we analyze the correlation between amplitude and axis ratio for a contact binary modeled as identical biaxial ellipsoids, accounting for shadowing between components. When comparing our models to published high-phase-angle observations and the interstellar object 1I/'Oumuamua (which showed a $\Delta m = 2.5$ magnitude change at $\alpha = 23^\circ$), we derive an axis ratio of $5.2:1$ for a single ellipsoid representation versus $3.5:1$ for each component in a nose-to-nose contact binary model. Although a detailed fit was not pursued, the comparison indicates that the single ellipsoid model provides a better match.

The rapid expansion of online meal delivery is driven by its surging popularity, yet platforms face significant challenges in balancing service quality for both customers and restaurants. On the Meituan platform alone, hundreds of thousands of orders are canceled daily due to crowdsourcing drivers refusing them, a trend that severely harms customer retention and the platform's reputation. To counter this, Meituan management allocates specific funds to incentivize drivers to accept more orders. To optimize these resources, we propose a framework designed to address the multi-stage bonus allocation problem, with the goal of maximizing accepted orders within a fixed budget. This framework integrates three key components: a semi-black-box model to predict how allocated bonuses influence order acceptance probabilities, a Lagrangian dual-based dynamic programming algorithm to determine empirical multipliers offline using historical data, and an online allocation algorithm that applies these offline results to calculate precise bonuses for individual orders. The framework's effectiveness and efficiency were validated through offline experiments on real-world data and online A/B tests on the Meituan platform. Results indicate that implementing this approach reduced total order cancellations by over 25% in practice.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) possess the capacity to fully memorize noisy labels given enough training time, a trait that unfortunately results in degraded performance. Recently, virtual adversarial training (VAT) has gained attention for enhancing the generalization of DNNs in semi-supervised learning scenarios. VAT operates by preventing overfitting through the enforcement of consistency between original inputs and their perturbed counterparts. This approach could effectively mitigate the impact of noisy labels by stopping models from learning from erroneous samples while promoting generalization for clean data. In this paper, we introduce Context-based Virtual Adversarial Training (ConVAT) to stop text classifiers from overfitting to noisy labels. Distinct from prior methods, our approach applies adversarial training at the context level instead of the input level. This enables the classifier to learn not only the labels but also the surrounding contextual information, thereby reducing the influence of noisy labels by maintaining contextual semantics for each data point. Extensive experiments on four text classification datasets involving two types of label noise demonstrate that the proposed method performs robustly, even under extremely noisy conditions.

Although quantum entanglement boosts various technologies like computing, sensing, and cryptography, its broad application is restricted by susceptibility to noise and loss. Notably, certain tasks retain a quantum advantage, denoted as $Q$ (representing a $Q$-time speedup), even after entanglement is lost, surpassing all classical methods. A key example is quantum radar, which improves target detection amidst noise. To outperform classical strategies, Lloyd suggested a probe initially entangled with an idler, which is later recombined and measured alongside the reflected probe. Achieving any quantum advantage necessitates exploiting these correlations via a joint measurement of the probe and idler. While optical-frequency quantum illumination protocols have been successfully demonstrated, microwave radar proposals, which align more closely with conventional systems, have attracted significant attention. However, existing microwave implementations have yet to show a quantum advantage because the probe and idler were always measured separately. In this study, we implement such a joint measurement using a superconducting circuit and demonstrate a quantum advantage ($Q>1$) for microwave radar. We find that storing the idler reduces the negative effects of microwave loss on the quantum advantage, with the purity of the initial entangled state becoming the subsequent limiting factor. Although this experiment serves as a proof-of-conduct within a dilution refrigerator, it highlights inherent challenges in building quantum radars, including the narrow parameter range where advantages occur and the need for extremely low temperatures for both the probe and idler.

This paper investigates a specific class of contracting flows for closed, star-shaped hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ by employing novel auxiliary functions. The flow evolves with a speed defined as $r^{\frac{\alpha}{\beta}}\sigma_k^{\frac{1}{\beta}}$, where $\sigma_k$ denotes the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial of the principal curvatures, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive constants, and $r$ represents the distance from the origin. Under certain conditions on $k$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$, we establish convergence results. Specifically, when $k\geq2$, $0<\beta\leq 1$, and $\alpha\geq \beta+k$, we demonstrate that the $k$-convex solution exists globally and converges smoothly to a sphere following normalization; this extends Li-Sheng-Wang's findings from the uniformly convex case to the $k$-convex setting. Furthermore, for the case where $k \geq 2$, $\beta=k$, and $\alpha \geq 2k$, we prove global existence and smooth convergence to a sphere after normalization, thereby generalizing Ling Xiao's result from $k=2$ to all $k \geq 2$.

Recent interest has surged regarding Nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond for quantum sensing, offering enhanced sensitivity for applications from geophysics to biomedicine. Traditional methods rely on detecting red fluorescence shifts in NV centers under green laser and microwave excitation; however, strong background fluorescence from the NV triplet state and low output contrast limit sensitivity due to high optical shot noise. This study proposes a solution by leveraging changes in green pump absorption through the diamond within a semiconductor external cavity laser operating near its lasing threshold. Theoretical analysis indicates that magnetic field sensitivity at the pT/sqrt(Hz) level is achievable with an optimal NV center density. Furthermore, we examine the physical constraints and limitations of this approach, specifically the impact of amplified spontaneous emission near the threshold, and investigate feasible implementations using existing technology.

The wave functions for half-integer magnetic flux derived in [Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm, Phys. Rev. 115, 485 (1959)] are missing an angle-dependent prefactor necessary to ensure single-valuedness; however, this omission does not impact the paper's physical conclusions.

The growing intricacy of IT infrastructures necessitates robust solutions for handling operational failures, driving a surge in research and industry focus on Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations (AIOps). A primary obstacle in this domain is the scarcity of properly labeled data, largely stemming from legal restrictions and industrial confidentiality concerns. While federated learning offers a mitigation strategy by eliminating the need for direct access to raw training data, existing centralized approaches face significant limitations. These traditional methods rely on a central server to synchronize models through periodic aggregation of parameters, which poses risks: trained models may inadvertently leak confidential knowledge or allow the reconstruction of sensitive data, and the central server itself becomes a trusted single point of failure. To address these issues, we introduce a fully decentralized framework that facilitates knowledge sharing between models without transmitting either the original training data or model parameters. This approach employs a teacher-student paradigm where student models are trained on teacher outputs using synthetically generated inputs. We validate this method through a case study on log anomaly detection, demonstrating that untrained student models achieve F1-scores comparable to their teachers. Additionally, our results confirm that this technique effectively synchronizes multiple models trained on distinct data subsets.

The global surge of COVID-19 has resulted in millions of viral genomic sequences being stored in public repositories like GISAID. This vast Big Data offers a unique chance to research effective vaccines for current pandemics and strategies to prevent or mitigate future ones. Each viral sequence includes its collection location, making the relationship between viral variants and geography a critical component of this analysis. However, researchers struggle to process such massive, high-dimensional data quickly. Most existing methods lack the scalability required for this data magnitude. This paper introduces an approach that first converts the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein sequence into a numerical representation using $k$-mers (substrings) and then employs various machine learning models to classify sequences by geographical origin. Our model significantly outperforms baseline methods. Additionally, we demonstrate the significance of specific amino acids in spike sequences by calculating information gain relative to the true class labels.

This study reports the first observation of the suppressed semileptonic decay $B_s^0 	o K^-\mu^+
u_\mu$. Based on a data sample from 2012 {\it pp} collisions recorded by the LHCb detector, with an integrated luminosity of 2 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$, the branching fraction \mbox{$\mathcal{B}(B_s^0 	o K^-\mu^+
u_\mu)$} is determined to be $(1.06\pm0.05~(\mathrm{stat})\pm0.08~(\mathrm{syst}))	imes 10^{-4}$. In this measurement, the first uncertainty arises from statistics, while the second encompasses combined systematic errors. To reduce experimental systematic uncertainties, the decay $B_s^0 	o D_s^-\mu^+
u_\mu$ serves as a normalization channel, with the $D_s^-$ reconstructed via the $K^+K^-\pi^-$ final state. Furthermore, theoretical form factor calculations for the $B_s^0 	o K^-$ and $B_s^0 	o D_s^-$ transitions are utilized to derive the ratio of CKM matrix elements ${|V_{ub}|}/{|V_{cb}|}$ across both low and high momentum transfer regimes of the $B_s^0 	o K^-$ transition.

The concept of effective dimension has demonstrated significant utility in geometric measure theory, particularly via the point-to-set principle \cite{LuLu18}, which defines Hausdorff dimension using relativized effective dimension. Within this framework, finite-state dimension represents the most minimal form of effective dimension \cite{FSD}, a property that, among other applications, allows for the characterization of Borel normality \cite{BoHiVi05}. This paper establishes a characterization of finite-state dimension based on the information content of a real number at specific precision levels. Subsequently, we leverage this characterization to prove a point-to-set principle specifically for finite-state dimension.

This framework integrates partial least squares (PLS) with deep learning to offer high-dimensional data reduction, presenting a nonlinear extension of PLS alongside a structured approach to feature selection and architectural design in deep neural networks. This integration facilitates a statistical interpretation of deep learning specifically tailored for predictive tasks. By leveraging PLS diagnostic tools such as scree plots and bi-plots, we can effectively analyze model performance. Furthermore, posterior predictive uncertainty is quantified using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods at the final layer, combining the scalability and rapid rule construction of deep learning with rigorous uncertainty estimation. The core mechanism involves applying deep learning within the PLS structure, where a deep learner predicts output scores based on input scores. Similar to traditional PLS, our X-scores are derived via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), enabling efficient and scalable solutions for both regression and classification. Adhering to the Bayesian shrinkage interpretation proposed by Frank and Friedman (1993), we define a nonlinear predictor. We introduce several novel models, including PLS-ReLU, PLS-Autoencoder, PLS-Trees, and PLS-GP. The methodology is demonstrated through simulated data and real-world applications, such as analyzing orange juice preferences and predicting wine quality based on input features. Additionally, we apply Brillinger's estimation procedure for feature selection and dimension reduction, concluding with suggestions for future research directions.

Over the past few years, steganography has garnered growing interest from numerous researchers as its applications extend beyond information security into broader domains. While the most conventional techniques rely on digital signal processing methods like least significant bit encoding, recent advancements have introduced deep learning approaches to tackle steganographic challenges. However, existing solutions predominantly focus on embedding images within images. This paper proposes a novel application of deep learning to conceal secret audio within digital images. We utilize a joint deep neural network architecture comprising two sub-models: one network embeds the secret audio into an image, while the second decodes the image to recover the original audio. Extensive experiments were conducted using a dataset of 24K images and the VIVOS Corpus audio collection. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional approaches, effectively preserving the integrity of both the image and audio while significantly increasing the maximum length of the hidden audio.

The decay $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to n\pi^{+}$, which is singly Cabibbo-suppressed, has been observed for the first time with a statistical significance of $7.3\sigma$. This result is based on $3.9\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^{+}e^{-}$ collision data gathered at center-of-mass energies ranging from 4.612 to 4.699 GeV using the BESIII detector at BEPCII. The measured branching fraction for this process is $(6.6\pm1.2_{\rm stat}\pm0.4_{\rm syst})\times 10^{-4}$. By utilizing the upper limit on the branching fraction of $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to p\pi^0$ from the Belle experiment, the ratio of branching fractions between $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to n\pi^{+}$ and $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to p\pi^0$ is determined to exceed 7.2 at the 90% confidence level, a finding that contradicts existing phenomenological model predictions. Furthermore, the branching fractions for the Cabibbo-favored decays $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to \Lambda\pi^{+}$ and $\Lambda_{c}^{+} \to \Sigma^{0}\pi^{+}$ are measured as $(1.31\pm0.08_{\rm stat}\pm0.05_{\rm syst})\times 10^{-2}$ and $(1.22\pm0.08_{\rm stat}\pm0.07_{\rm syst})\times 10^{-2}$, respectively, showing consistency with prior results.

The variation in atom populations between a Bose-Einstein condensate and the ambient thermal gas has long been a contentious theoretical issue, focusing on the choice of thermodynamic ensemble and the influence of interactions on these fluctuations. We present the Fock state sampling method to address this enduring challenge, which is highly relevant to current experiments on weakly interacting gases. Our results show that utilizing a microcanonical ensemble, as opposed to a canonical one, leads to a reduction in the predicted peak fluctuations. Additionally, interactions cause the temperature at which peak fluctuations occur to shift in harmonically trapped systems. The magnitude of these fluctuations also relies on the total atom count and the aspect ratio of the trapping potential. Consequently, due to the combined impact of these factors, fluctuations are not universally suppressed or enhanced.

We introduce a continuous-variable (CV) SWAP test that operates without an ancilla register, effectively extending the ancilla-free approach previously developed for qubits. In this framework, standard computational basis measurements are substituted with photon number-resolving detection, and we derive an upper limit for the error in overlap estimation arising from a finite Fock cutoff in the detector. As a demonstration, we show that estimating the overlap of pure, centered, single-mode Gaussian states with energy $E$ and squeezed in opposite quadratures to an error $\epsilon$ requires photon statistics below a Fock basis cutoff of $O(E\ln \epsilon^{-1})$. This requirement is significantly lowered to $E + O(\sqrt{E}\ln \epsilon^{-1})$ when the states exhibit rapidly decaying Fock tails, such as coherent states. Furthermore, we illustrate how the ancilla-free CV SWAP test can be scaled to multiple modes and utilized in CV quantum algorithms like variational compiling and entanglement spectroscopy; for the latter, we present a novel algorithm without a qubit counterpart. Finally, we demonstrate the implementation of this ancilla-free CV SWAP test on Xanadu's 8-mode photonic processor to estimate the vacuum probability of a two-mode squeezed state.

The MICROSCOPE mission seeks to verify the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) in orbit with a groundbreaking precision of 10$^{-15}$ for the E\"otv\"os parameter, utilizing electrostatic accelerometers aboard a drag-free micro-satellite. This level of precision is governed by both statistical errors, arising from environmental and instrumental noise, and systematic errors, which are the primary focus of this paper. These systematic error sources are categorized into three groups: external perturbations like residual atmospheric drag and gravity gradients at the satellite's altitude; design-related perturbations including thermal and magnetic effects; and internal instrument perturbations. Each systematic error is assessed or bounded to establish a trustworthy upper limit on the uncertainty of the WEP parameter estimation.

This paper examines a general parameterization of order-3 magic squares originally derived by Lucas and extends it to generate parameterized order-9 magic squares, while also addressing sequential compounding for higher orders. We derive expressions for the matrices within the Jordan canonical form and singular value decomposition of compound Lucas magic square matrices. Furthermore, we establish a procedure to determine whether an order-n magic square can be natural, facilitating the calculation of specific parameter values for natural compound Lucas magic squares. Additionally, we identify commuting pairs of compound Lucas matrices and provide formulas for the matrix powers of order-3 and order-9 Lucas matrices. Finally, we relate a parameterization by Frierson to Lucas' approach, showing that our results specialize to the former and complement existing findings.

Using the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we examined the properties of a quiescent polar prominence. Initially, small-scale barb-like structures appeared on the solar disk, first expanding vertically before shifting toward the south-west limb. Subsequently, a spine linked these barbs, and we detected apparent rotating motions in the prominence's upper section. These rotations likely contribute to the filament's evolution and growth by transporting cool plasma and magnetic twist. A large-scale vortex motion, characterized by a swirl-like structure, is visible in the upper prominence. Magnetic shear from the slow twisting of the footpoints deforms the prominence legs, triggering two distinct types of magnetic reconnection. Internal reconnection begins via a resistive tearing-mode instability, creating multiple plasmoids within an elongated current sheet, with an estimated growth rate of 0.02--0.05. Although magnetic reconnection briefly heats the current sheet, the majority of the released energy is absorbed by the surrounding cool, dense plasma to drive plasmoid ejections. These multiple ejections dismantle the current sheet, causing nearby magnetic arcades to collapse around the X-point. Conversely, oppositely directed arcades may reconnect with the prominence's southern segment, forming an elongated thin current sheet; this external reconnection ultimately drives the prominence eruption.

This article presents a proof of the multiplicativity of $\gamma$-factors and establishes the equality between parabolically induced and inducing factors within the Braverman-Kazhdan/Ngo framework, contingent upon the commutativity of associated Fourier transforms and a specific generalized Harish-Chandra transform. Additionally, we examine the resolution of singularities and their rationality concerning reductive monoids, which serve as fundamental components of this program.

We present a precise measurement of the top-quark mass calculated to next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD within specific renormalization schemes, utilizing Large Hadron Collider data from single-top and top-pair production processes. Additionally, we examine the calibration of the Monte Carlo top-quark mass parameter derived from events featuring top-quark decay products. The consequences of this measured mass for the stability of the electroweak vacuum are explored. For future lepton colliders, we introduce, for the first time, matched exclusive calculations applicable both at the top threshold and in the continuum, with full differential capabilities. Furthermore, we compute fully off-shell top-pair production (including associated Higgs boson production) at next-to-leading order in QCD, enabling the extraction of the top-Yukawa coupling with exceptional precision.

Most multi-view 3D reconstruction techniques, particularly those relying on shape-from-shading, rely on the assumption that object surfaces are primarily diffuse. To overcome this limitation, we present S2Dnet, a generative adversarial network designed to convert multi-view images featuring specular reflections into their diffuse equivalents, thereby enhancing the efficacy of reconstruction algorithms. Our approach expands unsupervised image-to-image translation to handle "specular-to-diffuse" transformations across multiple views. To maintain object consistency across these views, we introduce a Multi-View Coherence loss (MVC), which assesses the similarity and fidelity of local patches following view transformation. This loss function ensures that local correspondences remain consistent throughout the translation process. Consequently, our network outperforms several single-view baseline methods. Furthermore, we constructed a large synthetic training dataset using physically-based rendering. During inference, the network accepts only raw glossy images as input, eliminating the need for auxiliary data like segmentation masks or lighting estimates. Experimental results indicate that multi-view reconstruction is significantly improved by filtering images through our network, and we also demonstrate promising performance on real-world training and testing datasets.

A persistent gap exists between Standard Model predictions and experimental results for the anomalous magnetic moments of the electron and muon. This issue is especially critical regarding the muon $g-2$, which has drawn significant attention following the Muon $g-2$ collaboration's announcement at Fermilab. This new data aligns with earlier findings from the E821 experiment at Brookhaven and increases the statistical significance of the discrepancy to $4.2 \sigma$. This paper examines an extension of the inverse type-III seesaw model incorporating a pair of vector-like leptons that generate neutrino masses at the electroweak scale. We demonstrate that this framework can simultaneously account for the electron and muon anomalous magnetic moments while remaining consistent with all pertinent experimental constraints.

Strange metals display diverse anomalous magnetotransport characteristics, most notably a resistivity that rises linearly with magnetic field $B$ across extensive temperature and field ranges. This phenomenon is ubiquitous among various correlated metals—whether single- or multi-band, dominated by spin or charge fluctuations, varying in disorder, or situated near quantum critical points—necessitating the discovery of a fundamental principle independent of specific material details. Although strongly anisotropic (momentum-dependent) scattering can produce linear magnetoresistance, it is limited to intermediate field strengths, as magnetoresistance must eventually saturate at high fields. This work examines the extreme limit of such anisotropy: regions on the Fermi surface that completely block orbital (cyclotron) motion, yet can be modeled via a modified Boltzmann approach. Applying this proposed theorem indicates that transitioning from quadratic to linear magnetoresistance requires a bounded sector on the Fermi surface, potentially separating two distinct carrier types. Regardless of the sector's specific origin or form, its existence is expected to explain the anomalous magnetotransport observed in a broad spectrum of correlated materials.

Quantum simulators capable of leveraging the dynamics of intricate quantum systems have emerged as a promising tool for investigating exotic topological phases. The adaptability of controllable quantum systems has facilitated deeper insights into simulating such complex problems, demonstrating the feasibility of analog quantum simulators for exploring these phases. Nevertheless, digital quantum simulation and the detection of topological phases remain challenging. In this work, we develop and experimentally demonstrate the digital quantum simulation of topological phases using a solid-state quantum simulator operating at room temperature. Unlike previous studies focused on static topological phases, the phases emulated here are Floquet topological phases. Additionally, we outline the procedure for digitally simulating a quantum quench and observing the nonequilibrium dynamics of these Floquet phases. Through the quantum quench, 0- and π-energy topological invariants are clearly identified by measuring time-averaged spin polarizations. Our experiment establishes a new pathway for digitally simulating and detecting Floquet topological phases using rapidly advancing programmable quantum simulators.

Point process data are increasingly prevalent across modern domains like finance, healthcare, and social networks. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are powerful for modeling such data, their recurrent architectures often fail to capture complex non-stationary dependencies. In contrast, another prominent deep learning approach models the influence kernel directly rather than the intensity function. Adopting this latter strategy, we introduce a new deep non-stationary influence kernel designed for spatio-temporal point processes. Our core innovation involves approximating the influence kernel using a novel, general low-rank decomposition, which facilitates efficient representation via deep neural networks and enhances both computational speed and performance. Additionally, we enforce the non-negativity constraint on the conditional intensity through a log-barrier penalty. Experimental results on both real and simulated datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The potential of magnetism in two-dimensional atomic layers has garnered significant attention due to its promise for advancing electronic and spintronic technologies. However, mere magnetism is inadequate for functional devices; instead, magnetic states must be controllable and tunable via external stimuli. We demonstrate that defects within hexagonal boron nitride exhibit a pronounced coupling between the N-N separation at the defect edge and the associated magnetic moments. By inducing geometric changes through stress, we successfully alter the ground-state magnetic moment of these defects. This tunability arises from the triangular configuration of the defects combined with the robust spin localization inherent to their magnetic state.

For an extended period, detector design has been primarily dictated by constraints on transverse momentum, impact parameter, jet energy resolution, and hermeticity. Only recently has it become apparent that distinguishing between various charged hadrons—specifically kaons and protons—offers significant potential for Higgs factories such as the International Linear Collider (ILC). These capabilities could enhance tracking, vertexing, and flavor tagging, as well as enable measurements dependent on strangeness identification. While gaseous tracking systems, such as Time Projection Chambers (TPCs), can utilize specific energy loss for identification, all-silicon detectors must depend on fast timing layers positioned before or within the initial stages of their electromagnetic calorimeters (ECals). This paper reviews the available options for achieving particle identification (PID) for pions, kaons, and protons, introduces newly developed reconstruction algorithms, and outlines full detector simulation scenarios for physics applications, using the International Large Detector (ILD) concept as a case study.

This manuscript offers a comprehensive proof of the undecidability regarding the equivalence of finite substitutions on the regular language $b\{0,1\}^*c$, relying on the research of Leonid P. Lisovik.

This paper explores the application of nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) for multi-body dynamics using physics-informed machine learning. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a promising approach to approximating partial and differential equations; however, their original architecture is ill-suited for control tasks because they do not natively accommodate variable control inputs or initial conditions. To address this, we propose enhancing PINNs by incorporating control actions and initial states as additional network inputs. To manage the resulting high-dimensional input space, we employ a sampling strategy combined with a zero-hold assumption. This framework facilitates controller design by treating the PINN as an approximation of the system's underlying dynamics. A further advantage is that sensitivities can be efficiently calculated through automatic differentiation, enabling robust gradient-based optimization algorithms. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our PINN-based MPC by solving a tracking task for a complex mechanical system, specifically a multi-link manipulator.

We demonstrate cases involving high-dimensional unimodal posterior distributions within non-linear regression models utilizing Gaussian process priors, where MCMC methods may require exponential time to reach the regions of highest posterior concentration. These findings concern worst-case initialized ("cold start") algorithms that are local, meaning their average step sizes cannot be excessively large. The counter-examples are valid for general MCMC schemes employing either gradient-based or random walk steps, with the theoretical framework illustrated using Metropolis-Hastings adjusted techniques such as pCN and MALA.

This work initiates an investigation into the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP) within the quantum realm. MCSP concerns computing the circuit complexity of Boolean functions and remains a captivating topic in complexity theory due to the enigmatic nature of its hardness, which could yield significant insights across various computer science disciplines. We begin by defining and analyzing the fundamental complexity-theoretic characteristics of minimum quantum circuit size problems for three key entities: Boolean functions, unitaries, and quantum states. Our findings indicate that these problems are not trivially contained in NP but reside within QCMA (possessing QCMA protocols). Subsequently, we examine the interrelationships among the three quantum MCSPs and their variants, revealing reductions—such as search-to-decision and self-reduction—that exist for quantum unitaries and states but remain unestablished for classical MCSP. Finally, we systematically extend classical MCSP results to the quantum domain, covering areas like quantum cryptography, learning theory, circuit lower bounds, and fine-grained complexity, while also uncovering novel links to tomography and quantum gravity. Given the inherent distinctions between classical and quantum circuits, our results necessitate additional scrutiny and expose phenomena unique to the quantum setting. These findings offer valuable directions for future research, for which we outline several open problems.

This paper introduces an effective approach to fusing visual and language representations for various question-answering tasks, such as visual question answering and visual entailment. Unlike previous methods that rely on concatenating unimodal features or exclusively utilizing cross-attention, our technique composes multimodal representations through channel fusion. This channel-level fusion allows the model to align tokens more effectively than standard approaches. We refer to these resulting multimodal representations as "compound tokens," which are generated using cross-attention transformer layers. Specifically, vision tokens act as queries to retrieve compatible text tokens via cross-attention, which are then chained with the vision tokens along the channel dimension to form compound tokens. A second set of compound tokens is created using a similar process where text tokens serve as queries to the cross-attention layer. All generated compound tokens are concatenated and fed into a multimodal encoder. We validate the efficacy of compound tokens using an encoder-decoder vision-language model trained end-to-end in an open-vocabulary setting. Our results demonstrate that compound tokens achieve highly competitive performance across multiple question-answering benchmarks, including GQA, VQA2.0, and SNLI-VE.

It is established that electric spin and orbital angular momentum remain conserved during the paraxial propagation of traveling waves in free space. In this study, we examine electric and magnetic angular momentum within counter-propagating waves, demonstrating both theoretically and experimentally that neither component is conserved individually, except under specific conditions. We attribute this lack of conservation to spin-spin and orbit-orbit interactions between the electric and magnetic fields. This research extends earlier results derived from traveling waves, clarifies the observed spin-orbit coupling in counter-propagating paraxial light, and enhances our comprehension of angular momentum conservation across arbitrary structured light waves.

The LHCb experiment analyzed 0.37 fb-1 of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV to measure the ratio of branching fractions for the radiative decays B0 -> K*0 gamma and Bs0 -> phi gamma. The resulting value is BR(B0 -> K*0 gamma)/BR(Bs0 -> phi gamma) = 1.12 +/- 0.08 ^{+0.06}_{-0.04} ^{+0.09}_{-0.08}, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical, systematic, and the fs/fd fragmentation fraction ratio, respectively. By applying the world average for BR(B0 -> K*0 gamma) = (4.33 +/- 0.15) x 10^{-5}, the study determines the branching fraction BR(Bs0 -> phi gamma) to be (3.9 +/- 0.5) x 10^{-5}, representing the most precise measurement available to date.

This research addresses the classical challenge of establishing minimax rates for density estimation within convex density classes. Drawing on foundational contributions by Le Cam (1973), Birge (1983, 1986), Wong and Shen (1995), and Yang and Barron (1999), we establish the precise minimax rate (up to constant factors) for any such convex density class. By showing that the local metric entropy of the density class consistently determines the minimax optimal rates in these settings, this work generalizes existing findings. Furthermore, our bounds offer a unified framework for both parametric and nonparametric convex density classes under less restrictive assumptions regarding class richness than prior studies. We introduce a `multistage sieve' MLE applicable to any convex density class and utilize our risk bounds to recover established minimax rates for bounded total variation and Hölder density classes. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical value of these results by deriving upper bounds for underexplored classes, such as convex mixtures of densities.

Explicit Semantic Analysis (ESA) functions by mapping text into a vector space defined by concepts, such as Wikipedia articles. We introduce a methodology that enhances these ESA-derived vectors by integrating knowledge of inter-article relationships through a technique known as Retrofitting, thereby boosting the performance of downstream tasks reliant on these embeddings. Specifically, we model this relational knowledge using an undirected graph where nodes represent articles and edges signify connections between them. Furthermore, we highlight the contrast between the ESA process as a bottom-up approach generating representations from a corpus, and the subsequent integration of top-down knowledge via article relations to refine these vectors. Our hypothesis was validated across various subsets of the Wikipedia corpus, demonstrating that our proposed approach yields significant performance gains, particularly in improving Spearman's Rank correlation coefficients.

This paper computes the next-to-leading order (NLO) quantum chromodynamics (QCD) corrections for the exclusive decays $B_c^+\to \chi_{cJ}(h_c)\pi^+$ within the nonrelativistic QCD (NRQCD) factorization framework. The findings indicate that NLO QCD corrections significantly increase the branching ratios, yielding $K$ factors of approximately 2.5. When combined with an analysis of $B_c^+\to J/\psi\pi^+$, the NLO NRQCD prediction for the ratio of branching fractions $\frac{\mathcal{B}(B_c^+\to \chi_{c0}\pi^+)}{\mathcal{B}(B_c^+\to J/\psi \pi^+)}$ aligns with experimental data.

In 2010, Silva, Kschischang, and K\"otter introduced the Additive-Multiplicative Matrix Channel (AMMC) to describe data transmission via random linear network coding, where the input and output are $n\times m$ matrices over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. Given an input matrix $X$, the channel produces an output $Y=A(X+W)$, with $A$ being a uniformly selected invertible $n\times n$ matrix and $W$ a uniformly chosen $n\times m$ matrix of rank $t$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. Silva \emph{et al.} previously analyzed the scenario where $2n\leq m$, establishing the asymptotic capacity for fixed $t$, $n$, and $m$ as $q\rightarrow\infty$, as well as the leading term of the capacity when $q$ is fixed and $t$, $n$, and $m$ grow linearly. This work extends those findings by eliminating the requirement that $2n\leq m$. Our derived capacity formula comprises two cases, one of which encompasses the $2n\leq m$ scenario. Additionally, we refine the error term for the case where $q$ remains fixed.

We introduce a novel second-order oracle bound for the expected risk of a weighted majority vote. This bound relies on a new parametric representation of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality (also known as one-sided Chebyshev's), which allows for efficient minimization. This approach overcomes the optimization difficulties encountered in previous oracle bounds based on the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality, such as the C-bounds proposed by Germain et al. [2015], and simultaneously surpasses the second-order Markov's inequality-based oracle bound introduced by Masegosa et al. [2020]. Furthermore, we derive the PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality to facilitate empirical estimation of the oracle bound; this improves upon the PAC-Bayes-Bernstein inequality by Seldin et al. [2012]. Our empirical evaluation confirms that the new bounds can outperform the results of Masegosa et al. [2020]. Both the parametric form of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality and the PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality hold independent interest for studying concentration of measure in other fields.

Coherent structures play a significant role in atmospheric and oceanic transport, making Lagrangian methods increasingly valuable for their identification and analysis. Among these, Finite-Size Lyapunov Exponents (FSLEs) are gaining prominence in oceanography, yet substantial questions remain regarding their reliability for analyzing ocean dynamics, particularly concerning their robustness against real-world data. This study examines the impact of two critical factors inherent to real data—noise and unresolved-scale dynamics—on this Lagrangian technique. Using data from a primitive numerical model of the Mediterranean Sea as a benchmark, our findings indicate that FSLEs continue to provide an accurate representation of oceanic transport properties, even when certain dynamic processes are omitted.

This study introduces a machine learning methodology for static code analysis and fingerprinting aimed at identifying security, software engineering, and other weaknesses. The approach utilizes the open-source MARF framework and the derived MARFCAT application, which were demonstrated at the NIST SATE2010 static analysis tool exposition workshop (http://samate.nist.gov/SATE2010Workshop.html).

This paper establishes the monotonicity of the period map with respect to energy levels for specific periodic solutions of the equation $-\varphi''+\varphi-\varphi^{k}=0$, where $k>1$ is a real number. We demonstrate this property using an alternative approach that leverages spectral data from the linearized operator associated with the periodic solution, alongside tools from Floquet theory.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are capable of producing images that appear visually identical to real ones; however, recent research indicates substantial discrepancies between generated and real images in the frequency domain. This paper investigates the impact of high-frequency components during GAN training. Our observations suggest that in most GANs, pronounced high-frequency differences cause the discriminator to overemphasize these components, thereby preventing the generator from adequately learning low-frequency elements crucial for image content. To mitigate these adverse effects, we introduce two straightforward yet effective frequency-based operations: High-Frequency Confusion (HFC) and High-Frequency Filter (HFF). These methods are versatile, applicable to the majority of existing GAN architectures with minimal computational overhead. Their efficacy is validated across various loss functions, network structures, and datasets. Notably, the proposed HFF yields marked improvements, achieving a $42.5\%$ reduction in FID for unconditional CelebA (128*128) generation using SNGAN, a $30.2\%$ reduction using SSGAN, and a $69.3\%$ reduction using InfoMAXGAN.

Although the empirical effectiveness of self-supervised learning (SSL) depends heavily on deep nonlinear models, current theoretical analyses of SSL predominantly address linear models. This paper investigates the function of nonlinearity within the training dynamics of contrastive learning (CL) applied to one and two-layer networks featuring homogeneous activations defined as $h(x) = h'(x)x$. We present two primary theoretical insights. First, nonlinearity can generate numerous local optima even in a single-layer architecture, where each optimum corresponds to specific data distribution patterns; conversely, linear activation restricts learning to a single dominant pattern. This implies that models with extensive parameters serve as a \emph{brute-force} approach to identifying these nonlinearity-induced local optima. Second, in two-layer settings, linear activation is shown to be insufficient for learning specialized weights that capture diverse patterns, thereby highlighting the necessity of nonlinearity. Furthermore, for the two-layer case, we identify \emph{global modulation}: local patterns that are discriminative at a global level are prioritized during learning, offering a deeper characterization of the learning process. Simulations confirm these theoretical results.

We present an $r-$adaptive framework for solving Partial Differential Equations via Deep Neural Networks. This approach is restricted to tensor product meshes, where boundary node positions in one dimension are optimized to construct two- or three-dimensional grids. The method supports the creation of conforming meshes with fixed interfaces and allows for topological changes, such as nodes crossing these interfaces. Simultaneously optimizing both node locations and PDE solution values over the generated mesh, we demonstrate the $r-$adaptive method's efficacy using collocation, Least Squares, and Deep Ritz approaches. We concentrate on the Deep Ritz Method to address one- and two-dimensional problems featuring smooth solutions, singularities, and/or strong gradients.

Few-Shot Remote Sensing Scene Classification (FSRSSC) is a critical task focused on identifying new scene categories using limited examples. Although recent approaches adapting few-shot natural image classification techniques have achieved significant progress, they fail to account for two distinct traits of remote sensing imagery: (i) object co-occurrence, where multiple objects frequently appear together in a scene, and (ii) object spatial correlation, where these co-occurring objects follow specific spatial patterns. Leveraging these traits is highly advantageous for FSRSSC, as they offer more detailed scene descriptions that help mitigate the scarcity of labeled data. To capitalize on these features, we introduce SGMNet, a novel meta-learning framework based on scene graph matching. This framework employs a scene graph construction module to represent both test images and scene classes as graphs, where nodes denote co-occurring objects and edges capture their spatial relationships. Subsequently, a scene graph matching module calculates similarity scores between test images and scene classes. Finally, a nearest neighbor classifier predicts the scene class based on these scores. Extensive experiments on the UCMerced LandUse, WHU19, AID, and NWPU-RESISC45 datasets demonstrate that SGMNet outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

The combination of high-resolution integral field unit spectroscopy and robust full-spectral fitting codes now enables the analysis of spatially resolved kinematics, chemical composition, and star-formation histories in nearby galaxies. Utilizing new MUSE data from the Snapshot Optical Spectroscopic Imaging of Mergers and Pairs for Legacy Exploration (SOSIMPLE) survey, we investigate NGC 7135. Despite being obscured by an ongoing merger characterized by counter-rotating gas, disrupted kinematics, and an asymmetric chemical distribution, we identify stellar populations from a previous merger event that occurred 6–10 Gyr ago. Additionally, we observe a radial gradient in ex-situ material, where the fraction of accreted matter increases from 0% at the galaxy's center to approximately 7% within 0.6 effective radii.

Accurate, autonomous forecasting of traffic demand is becoming a critical capability for next-generation cellular networks. Historically, researchers relied on statistical approaches like Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA); however, these methods struggle to deliver precise forecasts for highly dynamic inputs such as cellular traffic. Recently, the field has shifted toward deep learning architectures, specifically Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, for autonomous traffic prediction. This study introduces an LSTM-based model designed for cellular traffic forecasting. We evaluated this model against baseline ARIMA and a standard feed-forward neural network (FFNN). The findings indicate that both LSTM and FFNN achieved accurate predictions; however, the LSTM model demonstrated significantly faster training times compared to the FFNN. Consequently, we conclude that LSTM models are highly effective, particularly when trained on limited datasets, enabling timely predictions of future cellular traffic.

AI systems are increasingly employed to offer guidance that supports human decision-making. Although extensive research has focused on optimizing these systems for accuracy and fairness, as well as on how to present algorithmic recommendations, this study addresses a fundamental question: When should algorithms intervene? Driven by the drawbacks of continuously providing automated advice, we propose designing AI systems that engage users in a two-sided interaction, offering recommendations only when they are likely to benefit the decision-making process. Our systems learn advising strategies based on historical human decisions; for new scenarios, these learned policies analyze human input to determine whether algorithmic advice is necessary or if the human is better suited to decide independently. We evaluated this approach through a large-scale experiment utilizing US criminal justice data regarding pretrial-release risk assessments. Participants assessed the likelihood of defendants violating release terms under various advising conditions. The findings demonstrate that our interactive-advising method successfully delivers guidance when needed and significantly enhances human decision-making compared to static, non-interactive approaches. Furthermore, our approach offers additional benefits by promoting human learning, maintaining the complementary strengths of human judgment, and fostering more positive receptiveness to the advice.

This research investigates the spatio-temporal correlations of photons generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, specifically examining how the waists of the pump and detection beams influence the photons' spectral bandwidth. Our findings reveal that this parameter is significantly sensitive to the spatial characteristics of the detection beam, but far less so to those of the pump beam. Consequently, the bandwidth of biphoton spectra can be easily controlled through a straightforward experimental setup that merely adjusts the optical configuration for photon collection. Additionally, we conducted Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry measurements to determine both the phase and temporal profile of the biphoton wavefunction. These results are explained using a simplified toy model based on specific approximations, which successfully reproduces the majority of the key experimental observations.

Current state-of-the-art face completion techniques predominantly rely on autoencoders or their derivatives to reconstruct missing facial regions. While encoders are typically employed to learn robust representations essential for tackling complex learning tasks, they struggle to capture such powerful features when faced with the intricate mask patterns prevalent in real-world images, a challenge exacerbated by the widespread adoption of face masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a self-supervised Siamese inference network designed to enhance encoder generalization and robustness. This framework enables the encoding of contextual semantics from full-resolution images, yielding more discriminative representations. Furthermore, to address geometric variations, a dense correspondence field is incorporated into the architecture. We also propose a multi-scale decoder equipped with a novel dual attention fusion module (DAF), which adaptively merges restored and known image regions. This multi-scale design facilitates the effective utilization of encoder-derived discriminative features for image reconstruction. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach not only outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods but also significantly boosts the performance of masked face recognition.

This study examines a topological stabilizer code defined on a honeycomb lattice, termed the "XYZ$^2$" code. Drawing inspiration from the Kitaev honeycomb model, this system represents a concrete instantiation of the "matching code" proposed by Wootton [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 48, 215302 (2015)], featuring a specific boundary configuration. The architecture employs weight-six ($XYZXYZ$) plaquette stabilizers and weight-two ($XX$) link stabilizers across a planar hexagonal grid of $2d^2$ qubits, achieving a code distance of $d$. Additionally, weight-three stabilizers at the boundary protect a single logical qubit. Using maximum-likelihood decoding under the assumption of ideal stabilizer measurements, we analytically determine the logical failure rate for pure $X$, $Y$, or $Z$ noise, yielding a threshold of 50%. Unlike the rotated surface code and XZZX code, which achieve a code distance of $d^2$ solely under pure $Y$ noise, this code maintains a distance of $2d^2$ for both pure $Z$ and pure $Y$ noise. While thresholds for noise with finite $Z$ bias resemble those of the XZZX code, the sub-threshold logical failure rates are significantly lower. Furthermore, the code exhibits unique syndrome characteristics, characterized by unidirectional pairs of plaquette defects along the three axes of the triangular lattice for isolated errors, a feature that could facilitate efficient matching-based or other approximate decoding strategies.

We introduce a new image retouching approach that models the process as a series of novel, trainable neural color operators. These operators replicate the functionality of traditional ones by learning pixel-level color transformations, with their intensity regulated by a scalar value. To capture the homomorphism inherent in color operators, we utilize equivariant mapping within an encoder-decoder framework, converting complex non-linear transformations into simpler translations within a high-dimensional space. The scalar strength for each operator is determined by CNN-based predictors that analyze global image statistics. In summary, our method is computationally efficient and provides flexible control. Experimental results and user studies on public datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual quality. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/amberwangyili/neurop.

The proliferation of dozens of new tools and technologies is causing consternation among developers who struggle to select the most suitable option. For instance, the availability of at least ten web application frameworks creates a dilemma in choosing the one that best fits specific needs. Consequently, developers constantly evaluate the pros and cons of various APIs, frameworks, and tools. A common method involves reviewing official documentation and community discussions, but this process is time-consuming and often makes it difficult to identify which features are most critical to an individual developer versus the broader community. This paper utilizes the Opiner dataset, a benchmark of software aspects derived from StackOverflow posts, to analyze how Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, and XLNet) perform in detecting software aspects within textual discussions compared to a baseline Support Vector Machine (SVM) model. Extensive experimentation reveals that Transformer models generally outperform the SVM baseline across most aspects, including `Performance`, `Security`, `Usability`, `Documentation`, `Bug`, `Legal`, `OnlySentiment`, and `Others`. However, these models struggle to grasp certain aspects such as `Community` and `Potability`, with performance varying by category. Furthermore, larger architectures like XLNet proved less effective at interpreting software aspects than smaller architectures like DistilBERT.

This focus letter aims to provide a thorough classification of the primary entropic forms developed over the past half-century within statistical physics and information theory. The majority of these can be categorized into three families, each defined by two deformation parameters: the Sharma, Taneja, and Mittal entropies of degree $(\alpha, \beta)$; the Sharma and Mittal entropies of order $(\alpha, \beta)$; and the Hanel and Thurner entropies of class $(c, d)$. Various entropic forms will be systematically analyzed using key concepts, including their Shannon-Khinchin axiomatic foundations and the resulting composability rule for statistically independent systems. Additionally, general discussions will address critical issues such as Lesche stability and consistency with the Shore-Johnson axioms.

This study introduces a framework of nonlinear equations that respect Lorentz invariance. The dynamics of their localized solutions mirror the formation of azimuthal-anisotropic elliptical flows within quark-gluon plasma and hadron jets. Unlike hydrodynamic models of ideal fluids, the elliptic flow in this model exhibits substantial negative acceleration. This characteristic negative acceleration supports a hypothesis regarding the direct elliptic flow of photons as braking radiation from the QGP.

This study examines pattern formation within a two-dimensional thin film situated on a planar substrate, characterized by Derjaguin disjoining pressure and periodic wettability stripes. We rigorously validate and contextualize the numerical findings of Honisch et al. within the broader framework of thin-film equations. Under conditions of constant wettability, we analyze how the global structure of steady-state solution branches evolves with variations in average film thickness and surface tension. Employing local bifurcation theory and the AUTO continuation software, we identify both nucleation and metastable regimes. Furthermore, we evaluate permissible forms of spatially non-homogeneous disjoining pressure, advocating for a formulation distinct from that used by Honisch et al., and investigate how steady-state solutions respond to changes in wettability contrast under this revised model.

We introduce novel serial and parallel approximation algorithms to determine a maximum weight $b$-matching in an edge-weighted graph featuring a submodular objective function. Since this problem is NP-hard, our proposed methods achieve a $1/3$ approximation ratio. These algorithms function as relaxations of the Greedy approach, utilizing only local graph data to enable parallel execution. We have developed and deployed Local Lazy Greedy algorithms for both serial and parallel environments. Specifically, we applied the approximate submodular $b$-matching technique to distribute tasks for Fock matrix calculations in quantum chemistry across parallel systems. This task assignment strategy aims to minimize runtime by balancing computational loads and limiting the message volume per processor. Our results demonstrate that this new assignment method delivers a four-fold speedup compared to the existing approach in NWChemEx software when executed on 8,000 processors of the Summit supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Lab.

Process mining relies on event logs that record business process executions, but these logs often contain sensitive data in customer-facing scenarios, limiting their use under data protection laws. To bypass these restrictions, logs can be anonymized so that no individual can be uniquely identified. This article tackles the challenge of anonymizing event logs to ensure that the probability of an attacker re-identifying any individual does not exceed a specific threshold after publication. The proposed solution employs a differentially private mechanism that involves sampling log cases and adding noise to timestamps to meet privacy requirements.
