Furthermore, the study presents an empirical evaluation comparing this approach with state-of-the-art methods across 14 real-world event logs, focusing on data utility loss and computational efficiency.

This study presents a clustering method for histogram data that utilizes Self-Organizing Map (SOM) learning. The approach integrates dimensionality reduction via SOM with clustering performed in the resulting reduced space. To address the specific nature of the data, a distribution dissimilarity measure, specifically the $L_2$ Wasserstein distance, is introduced. Unlike traditional methods, the number of clusters is not predetermined; instead, it is automatically determined through local density estimation in the original data space. The proposed strategy is validated through applications on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become prevalent in numerous computer vision tasks, including object detection for autonomous driving. Despite their widespread application, the internal mechanisms of these networks remain largely unexplained. This study aims to analyze how the intrinsic dimension—the minimum number of parameters needed to represent data—in various network layers impacts the accuracy of object detection models when trained on augmented datasets. Our findings reveal distinct differences in how normal and augmented data are represented during the feature extraction phase.

A potentiostat serves as a critical instrument for analyzing electrochemical reactions and devices. As device designs advance, systems incorporating multiple working electrodes are increasingly prevalent, creating a demand for affordable, multi-channel potentiostats. We have engineered a portable, scalable system featuring a modular architecture capable of supporting 8 to 64 channels at a cost as low as \$8 per channel. This solution offers functionality comparable to commercial potentiostats, which can exceed \$10,000 for specific uses. Each channel includes an independent, adjustable voltage source along with a built-in ammeter and switch, ensuring flexibility for diverse configurations. Although optimized for low-current applications in the nanoampere range, the system's purpose can be adapted by adjusting the shunt resistor value. The device operates either as a standalone unit or under remote control. We have demonstrated its capability to manage a 24-channel bioelectronic ion pump, enabling both open- and closed-loop pH regulation.

We introduce techniques for executing arbitrary qubit permutations within interaction constraints. Leveraging prior methods for quickly reversing qubit order along a path, our protocols demonstrate that, given nearest-neighbor interactions on a path of length $n$, there exists a constant $\epsilon \approx 0.034$ such that quantum routing time is bounded by $(1-\epsilon)n$. In contrast, any swap-based protocol requires at least $n-1$ time units, marking the first known quantum advantage over swap-based routing and offering improved times for practical architectures like grids. Moreover, we show that our algorithm achieves an expected quantum routing time of $2n/3$ for uniformly random permutations, compared to the asymptotic $n$ time required by swap-based methods. Finally, we address sparse permutations routing $k \le n$ qubits, presenting algorithms with quantum routing times of at most $n/3 + O(k^2)$ on paths and $2r/3 + O(k^2)$ on general graphs with radius $r$.

We present a new technique designed to remove background-induced systematic shifts that compromise the precision of saturation absorption signal measurements. Utilizing this approach, we determined the absolute frequency of the $6s^2~^1\text{S}_0 \to 6s6p~^3\text{P}_1$ transition in $^{201a}\text{Hg}$ (specifically the $F=3/2\to F'=5/2$ transition) to be $1181541111051(83)$~kHz. This measurement was calibrated against an optical frequency comb synchronized with the local representation of UTC. The selected atomic line lies on the steep slope of the Doppler background present at room temperature, leading to frequency systematic shifts. We established how this shift depends on the characteristics of both the spectral line and the measured signal's background.

We introduce a lensing model for the cluster SPT-CLJ0615$-$5746, the highest-redshift ($z=0.972$) system within the Reionization of Lensing Clusters Survey (RELICS), marking it as the first cluster at this redshift to have a fully published strong lensing model. Our analysis identifies three multiply-imaged galaxy systems, two of which are spectroscopically confirmed at redshifts $z=1.358$ and $z=4.013$, serving as key constraints for the model. While we detect a foreground structure at $z\sim0.4$ and test a model incorporating it as a second cluster-sized halo, two distinct statistical tests indicate that the optimal fit comprises a single cluster-sized halo alongside three individually optimized galaxy-sized halos, along with contributions from the cluster galaxies themselves. We determine the total projected mass density within $r=26.7"$ (the area constrained by strong lensing) to be $M=2.51^{+0.15}_{-0.09}\times 10^{14}$~M$_{\odot}$. When extrapolated to $r_{500}$, this projected mass aligns with estimates derived from weak lensing and the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect ($M\sim10^{15}$~M$_{\odot}$). Furthermore, this cluster magnifies a previously identified galaxy at $z\sim10$; if its redshift is spectroscopically confirmed, it will represent the highest-redshift strongly lensed galaxy ever discovered.

As parallel computing capabilities expand, there is a heightened emphasis on parallelizing algorithms for critical automated reasoning tasks, particularly Boolean satisfiability (SAT). Divide-and-Conquer (D&C) represents a prominent parallel SAT solving approach that splits SAT instances into independent sub-problems to be solved concurrently. While state-of-the-art D&C solvers produce DRAT refutations for each sub-problem when instances are unsatisfiable, they fail to generate a unified refutation for the original instance. To address this limitation, we introduce Proof-Stitch, a method for merging refutations from various sub-problems into a single refutation for the entire instance. We establish the correctness of this procedure and suggest optimizations to minimize the size and verification time of the combined refutations by leveraging existing trimming tools during the proof-combination phase. Additionally, we offer an extensible implementation of the proposed technique. Experimental results using instances from the previous year's SAT competition demonstrate that the optimized refutations can be verified up to seven times faster than their unoptimized counterparts.

Periodic modulation patterns frequently appear in natural systems where multiple competing states coexist. In strongly correlated electron systems, such behavior is usually attributed to the competition between short- and long-range interactions, such as the rivalry between exchange and dipole-dipole forces in ferromagnetic thin films. This study demonstrates, however, that spin-stripe textures can emerge even in antiferromagnets, where long-range dipole-dipole interactions are negligible. An extensive investigation of magnetic susceptibility, high-field magnetization, specific heat, and neutron diffraction data identifies $\beta$-TeVO$_4$ as an almost ideal example of a frustrated (zigzag) ferromagnetic spin-1/2 chain. Remarkably, a narrow spin stripe phase arises at high magnetic fields, driven by weak frustrated short-range interchain exchange interactions, potentially aided by symmetry-allowed electric polarization. This mechanism offers an alternative pathway for stripe formation in strongly correlated electron systems and may aid in elucidating other common but previously unexplained stripe-related phenomena.

This paper introduces a new parsing algorithm capable of handling all context-free languages, which operates by analyzing the relationship between configurations and transitions within a recursive transition network. Its parsing complexity aligns with current best practices: worst-case cubic time, quadratic for unambiguous grammars, and linear for LR-regular grammars. The algorithm's primary distinction lies in its elegant mathematical formulation, where parsing is defined as a composition of straightforward operations on languages and relations, enabling implementation via immutable data structures alone. By selecting these structures appropriately, the majority of operations typical in parsing programming languages can be memoized. Consequently, our proof-of-concept implementation surpasses standard generalized parsing algorithms, achieving speedups of orders of magnitude in certain scenarios.

Combining galaxy-galaxy lensing (GGL) with galaxy clustering provides a potent method for investigating matter clustering at low redshifts, particularly when applied to the non-linear regime. Building on the N-body and halo occupation distribution (HOD) emulator framework from arxiv:1907.06293, we have adapted the tool to model the colour-selected passive redMaGiC sample within the Dark Energy Survey (DES). This extension incorporates parameters for central galaxy incompleteness, assembly bias, and a scale-independent multiplicative lensing bias, $A_{lens}$. Utilizing this emulator, we project cosmological constraints derived from the GGL surface density profile $\Delta\Sigma(r_p)$ and the projected galaxy correlation function $w_{p,gg}(r_p)$ for the final Year 6 DES dataset, covering scales of $r_p=0.3-30h^{-1}$ Mpc. Assuming a $3\%$ prior on $A_{lens}$, we anticipate precisions of $1.9\%$, $2.0\%$, and $1.9\%$ for $\Omega_m$, $\sigma_8$, and $S_8 \equiv \sigma_8\Omega_m^{0.5}$, respectively, after marginalizing over all HOD parameters, $A_{lens}$, and a point-mass contribution to $\Delta\Sigma$. Expanding the scale range to include $r_p=0.3-3h^{-1}$ Mpc enhances $S_8$ precision by approximately $1.6$ times compared to a large-scale-only analysis ($3.0-30.0h^{-1}$ Mpc), an improvement equivalent to doubling the survey area. Tightening the $A_{lens}$ prior to $1\%$ further boosts $S_8$ precision by a factor of $1.7$ (reaching $1.1\%$) and significantly amplifies the benefits of incorporating non-linear scales. The emulator demonstrates percent-level accuracy, matching the projected DES statistical uncertainties and validating the viability of fully non-linear analyses. Furthermore, utilizing diverse galaxy types and measurements across both linear and non-linear clustering regimes enables extensive internal cross-checks to identify systematics and confirm the robustness of cosmological findings.

Bibliometrics serves as a valuable tool for assessing research quality by analyzing research impact. Various bibliographic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, are utilized to track publication and citation trends over time, though these resources vary between free access and subscription models. Since the superiority of any single database remains a subject of debate, we have developed a unified, authentic database called "conflate" designed to retrieve an author's publication and citation trends. To enhance the reliability of this database and ensure transparency for all stakeholders, we propose a consensus mechanism known as "proof of reference" (PoR). Given that the PoR incorporates three consent-based verification checks, we believe it establishes an authentic and trustworthy source for citation data, facilitating the calculation of a unified informetrics profile for any author.

Simulating quantum dynamics on digital quantum computers using parameterized circuits holds significant promise for both fundamental and applied research in physics and chemistry. In this domain, hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that integrate classical optimizers with quantum hardware represent a competitive approach for tackling specific challenges. This study proposes applying such methods to optimal quantum control by simulating the wave-packet expansion of a trapped particle on a device with a finite qubit count. Utilizing gradient descent-based circuit learning, we investigate the inherent relationship between control phase transitions and the quantum speed limit dictated by unitary dynamics. Furthermore, we analyze the method's resilience against errors and confirm the absence of barren plateaus within the circuit. Ultimately, the synergy between digital quantum simulation and hybrid circuit learning establishes new avenues for advancing quantum optimal control.

Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) serves as a probabilistic framework for identifying hidden topics within document collections, typically utilizing variational Bayes (VB) algorithms to approximate the posterior distribution via a lower bound. While variational message passing (VMP) has been developed as a "black-box" mechanism to streamline the derivation of variational update equations for novel models, practical application remains fraught with subtleties. Current literature lacks the specific steps required to implement VMP for the standard smoothed LDA, and existing black-box probabilistic graphical modeling tools fail to execute the necessary word-topic updates. Consequently, this paper provides a comprehensive derivation of the VMP update equations for LDA, aiming to facilitate the calculation of similar updates for other graphical models by the broader research community.

This paper demonstrates the existence of a sharp threshold for the emergence of a giant component following percolation on Cartesian products of graphs, provided certain conditions regarding maximum degrees and isoperimetric constants are met. Specifically, this work extends the findings of Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi from 1982, which addressed percolation on the high-dimensional hypercube.

**Background:** Continuous Experimentation (CE) has emerged as a data-driven methodology for software product development. While challenges in large organizations have been documented, its implementation in smaller firms with early-stage products remains under-researched. **Aims:** This study aims to identify factors influencing CE adoption within early-stage software startups. **Method:** We conducted a descriptive multiple-case study involving five Finnish startups with varying levels of experimentation usage. **Results:** Our findings reveal that while foundational practices like iterative development and continuous integration/delivery are common, CE itself is rarely recognized or applied as described in existing literature; only one company systematically utilized experiments and experimental data. **Conclusions:** Small companies are unlikely to adopt CE unless specific conditions are met: at least some staff possess prior experience with the practice, resource constraints are not overwhelmed by the adoption, and the practice addresses an immediate company problem or offers near-term benefits. We discuss implications for advancing CE in startups and suggest directions for future research.

Weakly U-abundant semigroups are defined through specific generalized Green's relations. This paper explores various forms of weakly U-abundant semigroups, demonstrating that their idempotent variants retain this property. Additionally, the study examines the natural partial order applicable to these semigroup variants.

Regularization techniques enhance the stability of ill-posed inverse problems by incorporating prior knowledge about the solution, such as its smoothness or sharpness. This study introduces a multidimensional, scale-dependent wavelet-based L1-regularization term designed to address the ill-posed nature of airborne (time-domain) electromagnetic induction inversion. This regularization approach offers flexibility, capable of recovering blocky, smooth, or tunable intermediate models depending on the selected wavelet basis function. By allowing distinct wavelet bases for each orientation, the method introduces an additional relative regularization parameter. To streamline the process, we propose a calibration method to establish an informed initial estimate for this parameter, thereby minimizing the need for extensive optimization and keeping computational time manageable. We demonstrate the efficacy of this novel scheme on a time-domain airborne electromagnetic dataset concerning saltwater intrusion in Belgium, noting that the approach is equally applicable to other two-dimensional or three-dimensional geophysical inverse problems.

The quaternionic offset linear canonical transform (QOLCT) serves as an extension of the quaternionic linear canonical transform (QLCT). This paper introduces the QOLCT, establishes its connection to the quaternion Fourier transform (QFT), and utilizes this relationship to demonstrate the Plancherel formula alongside several QOLCT-related properties. Furthermore, various uncertainty principles—specifically Heisenberg-Weyl, Hardy, Beurling, and logarithmic principles—are generalized to the QOLCT domain under a broader framework.

While expression levels are recognized as a major driver of a protein's evolutionary rate, the reverse relationship also holds true: evolutionary processes can influence expression levels. This bidirectional connection suggests the existence of a feedback loop, wherein highly expressed systems are more likely to optimize and further increase their expression, whereas lowly expressed ones may eventually be eliminated by genetic drift. By employing a minimal model to examine this dynamic within a shifting environment, we show that an unexpected outcome of this feedback mechanism is that a gradual transition to a new environment can enable genotypes to achieve superior fitness more rapidly than immediate exposure would.

Let $ \mathbb{Q}\mathcal{E}_{\mathbb{Z}} $ denote the collection of power sums $ G: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q} $ where the characteristic roots are integers and the coefficients are rational, specifically taking the form $ G(n) = \sum_{i=1}^h b_i c_i^n $ with $ c_i \in \mathbb{Z} $ and $ b_i \in \mathbb{Q} $. Given an absolutely irreducible polynomial $ f \in \mathbb{Q}[x,y] $ and a solution $ \alpha: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \overline{\mathbb{Q}} $ satisfying $ f(G_n, \alpha(n)) = 0 $ identically, we establish, under appropriate conditions, a lower bound for the approximation error of $ \alpha(n) $ by rationals with bounded denominators, valid for all but finitely many $ n $. We subsequently extend this analysis to the scenario where $ \alpha $ solves $ f(G_n^{(0)}, \ldots, G_n^{(d)}, y) = 0 $, involving multiple power sums, provided $ f $ meets suitable criteria. This work generalizes findings by Bugeaud, Corvaja, Luca, Scremin, and Zannier.

Collimated beam ultrasound technology enables imaging within complex, multi-layered environments like geothermal wells. This approach utilizes a narrow-band, collimated transmitter capable of penetrating various layers of heterogeneous materials, allowing for measurements across multiple transmit frequencies. However, standard reconstruction methods, such as the Synthetic Aperture Focusing Technique (SAFT), often yield subpar results because they fail to account for collimated beam dynamics and do not simultaneously process multiple frequencies.

This paper introduces a model-based iterative reconstruction (UMBIR) algorithm specifically tailored for multi-frequency collimated beam ultrasound systems aimed at imaging reflective features in heterogeneous, layered structures. For every frequency band transmitted, we implement a physics-based forward model to precisely simulate the propagation of the narrow-band ultrasonic beam through the media. Furthermore, we demonstrate the computation of joint multi-frequency UMBIR reconstruction by integrating direct arrival signals, detector noise, and a spatially varying image prior. Experimental and simulated data confirm that this multi-frequency UMBIR approach significantly outperforms both single-frequency UMBIR and SAFT in terms of reconstruction quality.

This paper addresses the zero-one composite optimization problem (0/1-COP), which involves minimizing the sum of a smooth function and the composition of a zero-one loss function with a linear operator. This framework serves as a versatile model encompassing support vector machines (SVM), multi-label classification (MLC), and maximum rank correlation (MRC). Despite its utility, the 0/1-COP is generally intractable due to its nonconvexity, discontinuity, and NP-hard nature, making globally convergent algorithms rare. To address this, we introduce and characterize proximal stationarity to establish the minimum and strongly exact penalization of a Lyapunov function—a variant of the augmented Lagrangian tailored for 0/1-COP. Leveraging these findings, we propose an inexact augmented Lagrangian method (IALM), where subproblems are efficiently solved using the zero-one Bregman alternating linearized minimization (0/1-BALM) algorithm. Under appropriate assumptions, we demonstrate that the IALM sequence converges to a local minimizer. Furthermore, assuming the data matrix has full row rank, we prove the global convergence of IALM for solving SVM, MLC, and MRC.

Central nodes play a pivotal role in maintaining the structural connectivity of complex networks; targeting these nodes can severely disrupt the entire system. We introduce attack strategies grounded in four distinct centrality measures: betweenness, degree, median, and center. Our study evaluates the vulnerability of both synthetic and real-world networks against these center-based attacks, which function by identifying and removing a specific set of central nodes. Our findings indicate that attacks utilizing recalculated network metrics are more effective than those relying on initial data. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that the median-based attack, a novel strategy proposed herein, proves to be highly destructive across both synthetic and real-world network structures.

This short paper introduces a baseline, off-the-shelf framework for Continual Learning in Computer Vision by harnessing pretrained models. Our method delivers robust performance across most standard benchmarks with a straightforward approach that is both rapid and memory-efficient, requiring only kilobytes of storage since it involves no parameter updates. Specifically, the "training" stage organizes data to generate class prototypes using pretrained models and populate a memory bank; during inference, predictions are made by matching inputs to the nearest prototype via a k-nearest neighbor strategy. We demonstrate how this seemingly naive solution functions as a practical off-the-shelf continual learning system. To validate our findings, we benchmark this pipeline against standard CNNs, highlighting the superiority of Vision Transformers due to their capacity to generate higher-quality features. Furthermore, this simple pipeline brings to light the same critical questions posed by prior work \cite{gdumb} regarding the community's actual progress in continual learning, particularly concerning dataset usage and pretrained models. The code is available at https://github.com/francesco-p/off-the-shelf-cl.

Bosonic dark matter may form halos around the Sun or Earth. We explore the potential of using atomic clocks to investigate these structures. By examining interactions through either a Higgs portal or a photon portal between dark matter and the Standard Model, we identify parameter ranges where frequency discrepancies would be detectable between a terrestrial clock and one in space. Specifically, current optical atomic clocks have the capability to probe bosonic dark matter halos surrounding Earth.

This study introduces the correlation between stellar surface mass density and gas metallicity ($\Sigma_*-Z$) based on data from over 500,000 spatially resolved star-forming spaxels within 653 disk galaxies from the SDSS IV MaNGA survey. We observe a strong link between these local characteristics, where metallicity rises with increasing surface density. This relationship spans three orders of magnitude in surface mass density and a four-fold range in metallicity. We demonstrate that this local connection can simultaneously account for two established disk galaxy properties: the global mass-metallicity relation and radial metallicity gradients. Furthermore, the $\Sigma_* - Z$ relation appears largely independent of a galaxy's total stellar mass and specific star-formation rate (sSFR), with exceptions only at low stellar masses and high sSFR. These findings indicate that in the current universe, local properties are a primary factor in determining gas-phase metallicity in typical disk galaxies.

We introduce PowerGridworld, an open-source, lightweight, modular, and customizable framework designed to build multi-agent Gym environments focused on power systems that seamlessly integrate with existing reinforcement learning (RL) training tools. While numerous frameworks support multi-agent RL (MARL) policy training, few enable the rapid prototyping of environments, particularly for heterogeneous (composite, multi-device) power systems where grid-level variables and costs depend on power flow solutions. PowerGridworld addresses this specific gap. To showcase its capabilities, we present two case studies demonstrating the learning of MARL policies using OpenAI's multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) and RLLib's proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithms. In both scenarios, a subset of agents incorporates power flow solution elements into their reward (negative cost) structures at each time step.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a crucial method for analyzing the chemical micro-environment within cells and tissues, offering enhanced contrast over standard fluorescence imaging. However, exciting two fluorophores within the diffraction limit induces non-linear spatial distortions and localization artifacts in both intensity (magnitude) and lifetime (phase) signals. To resolve this, we develop a theoretical convolution model for FLIM that characterizes these behaviors differently from conventional fluorescence microscopy. Furthermore, we introduce a Richardson-Lucy (RL) deconvolution algorithm incorporating total variation (TV) regularization to correct optical convolution distortions in FLIM data. Finally, we validate this FLIM deconvolution approach experimentally using multi-photon microscopy (MPM)-FLIM images of fluorescently labeled fixed bovine pulmonary arterial endothelial (BPAE) cells.

Blockchain functions as a decentralized, immutable, and transparent distributed ledger that continuously appends transaction records organized into blocks. At the heart of blockchain technology, the consensus algorithm serves as the mechanism for validating transaction accuracy. In public blockchains like Bitcoin, every node employs the Proof of Work (PoW) algorithm to achieve consensus by competing to solve cryptographic puzzles. In contrast, consortium blockchains are designed for enterprise use and avoid the resource-intensive challenges of establishing a global consensus protocol. This paper examines advanced consensus solutions for enterprise blockchains, such as the Linux Foundation's HyperLedger, which utilizes Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT). PBFT can handle malicious nodes but operates with quadratic complexity. Additionally, Facebook's Libra project implements the HotStuff algorithm, which achieves linear complexity for authentication. The study details the operational mechanics of these protocols and provides an analysis and comparison of their respective strengths and weaknesses.

The source of dark energy, responsible for the universe's accelerated expansion, remains unknown. We investigate the hypothesis that dark energy undergoes fluctuations, generating spatial correlations and causing the Hubble rate to vary. We examine how these variations impact measurements of Type Ia supernovae, which are critical for determining luminosity distance. Our analysis reveals that spatial correlations influence luminosity distance in multiple ways: first, the distance becomes modified by these fluctuations, deviating from standard $\Lambda$CDM predictions; second, angular correlations emerge within the luminosity distance's two-point correlation function. To study this, we calculate the angular power spectrum of luminosity distance fluctuations. We then forecast results for two surveys—the current Dark Energy Survey (DES) and the future Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST)—and contrast these findings with relativistic lensing effects in perturbed $\Lambda$CDM. Our results indicate that the signal can exceed lensing effects, suggesting LSST could probe this phenomenon across a significant portion of the parameter space. As a specific case, we consider a scenario where quantum fluctuations of an early-universe field imprint predictable spatial correlations on today's dark energy density, causing the Hubble rate to fluctuate due to the field's intrinsic quantum properties. While we determine that testing this specific model with LSST would be difficult, we conclude that the model becomes observable if the dark energy fluid possesses a sound speed $c_s<1$.

This study examines the validity of the generalized second law of thermodynamics for an $(n-1)$-dimensional brane situated within an $(n+1)$-dimensional bulk. We analyze the evolution of apparent horizon entropy, derived from the relationship between the gravitational field equations and the first law of thermodynamics, alongside the entropy of matter fields contained within the horizon. Our findings indicate that this thermodynamically derived apparent horizon entropy adheres to the generalized second law. This conclusion remains robust whether the brane possesses an intrinsic curvature term or the bulk includes a cosmological constant. The observed compliance with the generalized second law further reinforces the thermodynamic interpretation of gravity, underscoring the deep link between gravitational dynamics and thermodynamic principles.

This study investigates the dynamics of multimode polariton lasing within organic microcavities using a second-order cumulant equation method. By analyzing the temporal evolution of photon mode occupations, we demonstrate that the observation of multiple lasing peaks in time-integrated data can stem from either bi-modal lasing or temporal switching among several modes; the former is confined to a narrow parameter range, whereas the latter is more prevalent. We discover that the mechanisms driving temporal switching differ between weak- and strong-coupling regimes: in weak coupling, slope efficiency is the critical factor, while in strong coupling, it involves alterations in eigenmodes and the gain spectrum induced by pumping. These distinctions are elucidated through an examination of photoluminescence and momentum-resolved gain spectra. Our findings highlight the necessity of analyzing population time evolution to characterize lasing behavior in multimode polariton systems and illustrate how these dynamics vary across weak and strong coupling conditions.

We introduce the inaugural full (3+1)D dynamical simulations of ultra-peripheral Pb+Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Building on insights from p+Pb collisions, we investigate if a quasi-real photon ($\gamma^*$) interacting with a lead nucleus in such an event can generate a many-body system displaying fluid-like properties. Under the assumption of strong final-state interactions, our model yields predictions for charged hadron multiplicity, identified particle mean transverse momenta, and charged hadron anisotropic flow coefficients, which are then compared against experimental results from the ALICE and ATLAS collaborations. We find that the elliptic flow hierarchy between p+Pb and $\gamma^*$+Pb collisions is primarily driven by differences in longitudinal flow decorrelations, achieving a good reproduction of the observed data. Furthermore, we have established that this theoretical framework serves as a quantitative instrument for examining particle production and collectivity across all system sizes, spanning from central heavy-ion collisions to small asymmetric systems at the Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collider and the Large Hadron Collider, and extending to the future Electron-Ion Collider.

Document Layout Analysis (DLA) presents significant challenges due to the intricate physical structures often found in documents, yet it serves as a crucial pre-processing step for content extraction, particularly for capturing rich information in historical or scientific materials at scale. While deep-learning approaches from computer vision have successfully detected *Figure* elements, they remain inadequate for identifying *List*, *Table*, *Text*, and *Title* blocks. To address this, we introduce the VTLayout model, which integrates deep visual, shallow visual, and textual features to localize and classify various document blocks. The framework operates in two stages: the first employs Cascade Mask R-CNN for direct localization of all block categories, while the second constructs three feature extractors to fuse deep visual, shallow visual, and text features for precise identification. By enhancing the classification capabilities of existing localization techniques, VTLayout demonstrates superior performance on the PubLayNet dataset, achieving an F1 score of 0.9599, outperforming the most advanced current DLA methods.

MTRESS is a utility designed to streamline the modeling of residential energy supply systems by offering templates equipped with intuitive presets, which subsequently enable the linear optimization of system operations. Version 3.0 introduces the capability to define multiple locations within a single energy system and incorporates hydrogen as an energy carrier, allowing for power-to-gas conversion via electrolysis and gas storage at various pressure levels. Moreover, the Python API has been refactored to provide users with enhanced flexibility.

Since the LHC resumed operations for its second data-taking run in 2015, the LHCb experiment has implemented a specialized computing framework designed to select and analyze calibration samples, enabling the measurement of particle identification (PID) detector and algorithm performance. This innovative approach was developed within the context of LHCb's advanced trigger model, which prioritizes online event reconstruction for the majority of datasets while reserving offline reconstruction for specific physics scenarios. The paper discusses the strategy for choosing and processing these calibration samples, detailing a dedicated data-processing scheme that integrates both online and offline reconstruction. Furthermore, it describes how these samples are utilized to assess detector PID performance and the efficiency of PID requirements across a wide variety of decay channels, as well as their application in data-quality monitoring and validation procedures.

This work presents a formulation and proof of the reverse hypercontractive inequality within the sum-of-squares (SOS) proof system. As a direct result, we demonstrate that for any constant $0 < \gamma \leq 1/4$, the SOS/Lasserre SDP hierarchy at degree $4\lceil \frac{1}{4\gamma}\rceil$ proves that the maximum independent set in the Frankl--R\"odl graph $\mathrm{FR}^{n}_{\gamma}$ has a fractional size of $o(1)$. In this context, $\mathrm{FR}^{n}_{\gamma} = (V,E)$ denotes a graph where $V = \{0,1\}^n$ and edges connect vertices $x$ and $y$ if their Hamming distance $\Delta(x,y)$ equals $(1-\gamma)n$ (an even integer). Specifically, we establish that the degree-$4$ SOS algorithm certifies the lower bound "$\chi(\mathrm{FR}^{n}_{1/4}) = \omega(1)$", despite the fact that $\mathrm{FR}^{n}_{1/4}$ serves as the standard integrality gap example where conventional SDP relaxations fail to even certify "$\chi(\mathrm{FR}^{n}_{1/4}) > 3$". Furthermore, we provide an SOS proof for a generalization of the sharp $(2,q)$-hypercontractive inequality, applicable to any even integer $q$.

This study examines the gauge transformation characteristics of Skyrme–Chern–Simons (SCS) densities, identifying two distinct classes of SCS actions. Type$_{\text{I}}$ actions utilize a gauge group smaller than the maximum possible, incorporating only a single power of the gauge connection without curvature, whereas Type$_{\text{II}}$ actions employ the largest permissible gauge group and include both the gauge connection and curvature. Abelian Type$_{\text{I}}$ SCS actions are explicitly gauge invariant; in contrast, non-Abelian Type$_{\text{I}}$ and all Type$_{\text{II}}$ actions are invariant only up to a total divergence, resulting in gauge covariant equations of motion. Functioning as gauged analogues of standard Chern–Simons (CS) actions, SCS actions extend the domain of CS theory beyond odd dimensions to include even dimensions. The text also highlights various applications of these actions in soliton construction.

This study examines the nonwandering set of a monotone map $f$ on a regular curve $X$ and analyzes the structure of special $\alpha$-limit sets. We establish that the sets of almost periodic points, recurrent points, and nonwandering points are identical, i.e., AP$(f) = \textrm{R}(f) = \Omega(f)$. This finding generalizes previous results by Naghmouchi for homeomorphisms on regular curves and by Abdelli, Abdelli, Abouda, and Marzougui for monotone maps on local dendrites. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any point $x \notin \textrm{P}(f)$, the special $\alpha$-limit set $s\alpha_{f}(x)$ constitutes a minimal set and remains closed for all $x \in X$. Additionally, we prove that the union of all special $\alpha$-limit sets, denoted $\textrm{SA}(f)$, coincides with the set of recurrent points, $\textrm{R}(f)$; this extends recent work on interval and graph maps by Hantáková, Roth, Forys-Krawiec, and Oprocha to the monotone case. Finally, we derive results regarding the continuity of limit maps, showing that the maps $\omega_{f}$, $\alpha_{f}$, and $s\alpha_{f}$ are continuous on $X\setminus \textrm{P}(f)$, $X_{\infty}\setminus \textrm{P}(f)$, and $X\setminus \textrm{P}(f)$, respectively. Specifically, these maps are continuous on the entire spaces $X$ or $X_{\infty}$ if the set of periodic points $\textrm{P}(f)$ is empty.

Consider two $k$-uniform hypergraphs, $F$ and $H$. The hypergraph $H$ is defined as $F$-saturated if it contains no subgraph isomorphic to $F$, yet adding any missing hyperedge $e$ results in a graph that does contain $F$. The saturation number of $F$, denoted by $\mathrm{sat}_k(n,F)$, represents the minimum edge count of an $F$-saturated $k$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices. Let $C_3^{(3)}$ represent the $3$-uniform loose cycle consisting of 3 edges. In this study, we establish the bounds:
\[
\left(\frac{4}3+o(1)\right)n\leq \mathrm{sat}_3(n,C_3^{(3)})\leq
\frac{3}2n+O(1).
\]
This finding marks the first non-trivial result concerning the saturation number for a fixed short hypergraph cycle.

Micro and nanodroplets are vital for applications ranging from drug delivery and liquid-liquid extraction to nanomaterial synthesis and cosmetics. A prevalent technique for producing these droplets efficiently is solvent exchange, or nanoprecipitation, where displacing a good solvent with a poor one creates an oversaturation pulse that triggers nucleation. However, the subsequent droplet growth within this ternary system remains poorly understood. This study investigates this growth experimentally and theoretically using Hele-Shaw-like channels, specifically measuring the total volume of nucleated oil droplets. To retain the oversaturated oil within the system, certain channels were modified with a central porous region. By varying solution compositions, flow rates, and channel geometries, we observed that droplet volume increases with the Péclet number ($Pe$), following an approximate power law of $V \propto Pe^{0.50}$. We developed a theoretical model to explain this observation, successfully accounting for the $V \propto Pe^{1/2}$ scaling and its prefactor. This model allows data from various "porous" channel configurations and mixture compositions to collapse onto a single universal curve. Ultimately, our work offers a macroscopic perspective on this bottom-up droplet generation method and may inform future research into oversaturation and nucleation in ternary systems.

The scattering-adapted flexible inner region ensemble separator (SAFIRES) is a partitioning method designed to split a simulation cell into two zones for distinct computational treatments. It prevents particle crossing between these zones and manages boundary events via energy- and momentum-conserving elastic collisions mediated by the separator. The method introduces a multiple-time-step propagation scheme where the time step scales automatically to detect collision moments. When the time step remains constant, the new propagator simplifies to a standard Langevin dynamics algorithm or a velocity Verlet algorithm for classical dynamics (with zero friction). SAFIRES represents the exact limit of the premise underlying boundary-based approaches like FIRES, BEST, and BCC, which leverage the indistinguishability of molecules across the separator. It ensures correct average ensemble statistics despite the presence of the separator. Tested on Lennard-Jones liquids, Lennard-Jones liquids near a surface, and TIP4P force field simulations, SAFIRES reproduces unconstrained reference results without significant deviations.

This study introduces a novel framework for identifying community structures within a graph by analyzing signals observed at its nodes. We treat these observed signals as noisy realizations of an underlying network process, modeled as a graph filter driven by a set of unknown, low-rank excitations. This model applies to various scenarios, including diffusion dynamics, pricing experiments, and opinion formation. Instead of estimating the exact parameters of the graph, our objective is to directly recover the community structure. We demonstrate that communities can be identified using a spectral method applied to the covariance matrix of the graph signals. Our theoretical analysis reveals that detection performance relies on a "low-pass" characteristic of the graph filter. Furthermore, we show that performance can be enhanced through low-rank matrix plus sparse decomposition when the latent parameter vectors are known. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

We demonstrate that eliminating the sigmoid transformation within the skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) framework preserves word vector quality substantially. This approach corresponds to factorizing a squashed and shifted Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) matrix, which can be interpreted as the connection probability matrix of a random graph. Empirical analysis reveals that this graph constitutes a complex network characterized by robust clustering and a scale-free degree distribution, exhibiting a strong relationship with hyperbolic spaces. In summary, we establish a link between static word embeddings and hyperbolic geometry via the squashed shifted PMI matrix, utilizing both analytical and empirical methodologies.

Current observations reveal a $4.9\sigma$ discrepancy between the CMB and quasar dipoles, which poses a challenge to the cosmological principle. We suggest that this tension can be resolved if our location is within a gigaparsec-scale void, as our position is unlikely to be at its center. A 15% offset from the void's center would affect the dipolar anisotropies of quasars and the CMB differently, thereby reconciling the two. Furthermore, considering a large and thick void allows this framework to also alleviate the Hubble tension.

Gravitational microlensing, which involves the bending of light from Milky Way stars by intervening stars, has been employed to investigate compact dark matter candidates, exoplanets, and black holes. The Einstein crossing time, representing the duration of these events, depends on the distance, mass, and velocity of the lensing object. Because lenses with varying ages and masses may exhibit different characteristic velocities within the galaxy, this variability can lead to the misinterpretation of microlensing observations. In this study, we utilize archived \gaia data to establish a relationship between stellar velocity dispersion, mass, and age. While this mass-velocity dispersion relation corroborates the established age-velocity correlation for early-type and massive stars, it also uncovers a significant dependence of velocity dispersion on mass for low-mass and late-type stars at a $2$-$3$ sigma confidence level. Incorporating this correlation, we simulate brief microlensing events caused by brown dwarfs. Our results indicate that when modeling short-duration and degenerate microlensing events using Bayesian analysis, lens masses are systematically underestimated by approximately $2.5$-$5.5\%$.

We demonstrate that oscillations in germanium (Ge) concentration within the quantum well of a Si/SiGe heterostructure can substantially boost the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) of the low-energy conduction-band valleys. Specifically, at a Ge oscillation wavelength of approximately $\lambda = 1.57~\text{nm}$, we observe a Dresselhaus SOC that exceeds that of conventional Si/SiGe heterostructures lacking such oscillations by more than an order of magnitude. We offer a detailed mechanistic explanation for this resonance effect: the Ge concentration modulations generate wavefunction satellite peaks in momentum space, positioned at a distance of $2 \pi/\lambda$ from each valley, which subsequently couple to the opposing valley via Dresselhaus SOC. Our findings suggest that this enhanced SOC facilitates rapid spin manipulation in Si quantum dots using electric dipole spin resonance without requiring micromagnets. Furthermore, our calculations predict a Rabi frequency satisfying $\Omega_{\text{Rabi}}/B > 500~\text{MHz/T}$ near the optimal wavelength of $\lambda = 1.57~\text{nm}$.

Research indicates that Casimir-Polder interaction energies between an anisotropically polarizable point atom and an annular dielectric can generate localized repulsive long-range forces under specific conditions. When the atom resides at the annulus's center, energy minimization favors alignment between the atom's and dielectric's polarizabilities. Moving along the symmetry axis away from the center, the atom reaches a height where torque vanishes and energy becomes orientation-independent; at this precise level, the preferred orientation abruptly shifts to perpendicular. At greater distances, a second torque-free point may exist, beyond which parallel alignment is once again favored. If the atom is sufficiently close and oriented near an energy maximum, repulsion can occur, potentially below or above the initial torque-free height depending on the annular polarization. Qualitative differences arise between interactions with a ring versus an infinite plate with a hole; notably, at large distances, the atom may prefer a perpendicular orientation relative to the plate, contrary to the expected parallel alignment. To clarify this discrepancy, we examine an annular disc, which bridges the limiting cases of both geometries. Although these energies are currently too weak for direct application, we propose a conceptual Casimir machine utilizing these configurations.

A primary objective in modeling complex networks is to create accurate embeddings that facilitate structure detection and the prediction of node and link attributes. Latent Space Models (LSMs) have emerged as key frameworks for this task, with Latent Distance Models (LDMs) and Eigenmodels (LEMs) being the most prevalent specifications. In the context of latent community detection, LDMs typically incorporate a clustering model within their embedding space, while LEMs rely on part-based non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) inspired representations to foster community discovery. This work unifies LSMs with latent community detection by constraining the LDM representation to the D-simplex, resulting in the Hybrid-Membership Latent Distance Model (HM-LDM). We demonstrate that for sufficiently large simplex volumes, this constraint incurs no loss in expressive power; conversely, extending the model to squared Euclidean distances recovers the LEM formulation with constraints that promote part-based representations similar to NMF. Crucially, by systematically decreasing the simplex volume, the model becomes unique and eventually yields hard assignments of nodes to simplex corners. Experimental results show that HM-LDM provides accurate node representations in regimes that ensure identifiability and valid community extraction. Furthermore, HM-LDM naturally bridges soft and hard community detection with network embeddings through a simple continuous optimization procedure on a volume-constrained simplex, enabling the systematic exploration of trade-offs between hard and mixed-membership community detection.

We examine the transcendental entire function $f(z) = z + e^{-z}$, which possesses a doubly parabolic Baker domain $U$ of degree two. This domain is an invariant stable component where all iterates converge locally uniformly to infinity, and the hyperbolic distance between successive iterates approaches zero. While general theory establishes that dynamics on the boundary are ergodic and recurrent, and that the set of boundary points with orbits escaping to infinity has zero harmonic measure, our analysis of this specific model yields stronger conclusions. Specifically, we demonstrate that this escaping set is non-empty, structured into curves governed by symbolic dynamics, and its closure coincides exactly with $\partial U$. Furthermore, we prove that despite these properties, no escaping points in $\partial U$ are accessible from $U$, contrasting with boundary points having bounded orbits, which are all accessible. Additionally, we show that repelling periodic points are dense in $\partial U$, resolving a question posed by Baranski, Fagella, Jarque, and Karpinska. None of these characteristics are currently known to exist in general doubly parabolic Baker domains.

This study examines the complexity of determining reachability in (deep) neural networks—specifically, whether a valid input yields a valid output. While recent work asserted that this problem is NP-complete for general networks with conjunctive input/output specifications, we identify and correct flaws in both the original upper and lower bound proofs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NP-hardness applies even to restricted classes of simple specifications and single-layer neural networks, as well as networks with minimal constraints on their parameters.

We have re-evaluated the calculations for flavor-violating leptonic decays of $\tau$ and $\mu$ leptons into three lighter charged leptons within the Standard Model, assuming non-zero neutrino masses. This work was motivated by a previously claimed, unnaturally large branching ratio for $\tau^-\to \mu^- \ell^+ \ell^-$ ($\ell=\mu, e$) decays \cite{Pham:1998fq}, which conflicted with predictions for the corresponding $\mu^-\to e^- e^-e^+$ processes \cite{Petcov:1976ff}. Unlike the prediction in \cite{Pham:1998fq}, our findings show strong suppression and align well with the approximation in ref.~\cite{Petcov:1976ff}, where external particle masses and momenta were neglected to simplify loop integrals. However, by retaining these external momenta and masses in the calculation of the dominant penguin and box diagrams, we obtained branching fractions that are even slightly lower. Consequently, we confirm that the observation of any such processes in the future would unequivocally indicate new physics beyond the Standard Model.

This study examines how noise intensity influences the solution $u(t,x)$ of a stochastic heat equation subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions on the interval $[0,1]$. We demonstrate that while the $p$-th moment of $\sup_{x \in [0,1]} |u(t,x)|$ exhibits exponential stability under small noise intensity, it grows at least exponentially when the intensity is large. Furthermore, we establish that the $p$-th energy of $u(t,x)$ excited by the noise converges to $4$ as the noise intensity approaches infinity. Additionally, we develop a unified approach to derive lower bounds for these distinct behaviors under large noise intensity, addressing challenging aspects previously encountered in \cite{FoJo-14}, \cite{FoNu}, and \cite{KhKi-15}.

Creating adversarial methods to challenge NLP systems offers a promising path for enhancing both model performance and interpretability. This paper outlines the strategy employed by the "longhorns" team in Task 1 of the First Workshop on Dynamic Adversarial Data Collection (DADC), which required teams to manually deceive a model on an Extractive Question Answering task. Our team secured first place, achieving a model error rate of 62%. We advocate for a systematic, linguistically informed methodology in crafting adversarial questions and present the outcomes of our pilot experiments alongside our official submission.

Predicting future 3D human poses from a given sequence is a critical and challenging task within computer vision and machine intelligence, offering machines the ability to comprehend human behavior. Driven by the rapid advancement of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) and the proliferation of large-scale motion datasets, the field of 3D human motion prediction has seen remarkable progress, sparking significant interest in both academic and industrial sectors. Consequently, this survey provides a comprehensive retrospective and analysis of existing literature on the topic. To organize these approaches, a specific taxonomy is established, classifying methods into three main categories: human pose representation, network structure design, and prediction targets. This review systematically examines journal and conference papers published since 2015, detailing them according to the proposed classifications. Additionally, the paper outlines public benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance comparisons. Finally, the limitations of current state-of-the-art methods are discussed to guide future research directions.

Superfluid $^4$He represents a promising medium for the direct detection of light dark matter (mass $<$ 1 GeV), offering several readout channels such as prompt photons, triplet excimers, and roton or phonon quasiparticles. The sensitivity and discrimination capabilities of such detectors depend on the relative yields of these signals. In this study, we utilized a 16~cm$^3$ volume of superfluid $^4$He at 1.75~K, read out by six immersed photomultiplier tubes, to measure scintillation from electronic recoils (36.3–185 keV$_\mathrm{ee}$) and nuclear recoils (53.2–1090 keV$_\mathrm{nr}$). The mean signal size for electronic recoils was determined to be $1.25^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$~phe/keV$_\mathrm{ee}$. We compared these relative scintillation yield measurements against an existing semiempirical model grounded in helium-helium and electron-helium interaction cross sections. Additionally, we investigated the behavior of delayed scintillation components as a function of recoil type and energy, exploring this aspect as another method for signal discrimination in superfluid $^4$He detectors.

Simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) is a widely adopted method for delivering both data and radio frequency energy to receivers. This paper examines a two-way relay architecture involving multiple users and a multi-antenna relay that utilizes SWIPT, where signal splitting creates a trade-off between transmission rate and harvested energy. While previous research on transceiver design often relies on computationally demanding and suboptimal convex relaxation techniques, this study investigates a balanced precoder design based on chordal distance (CD) decomposition. This approach offers significantly reduced complexity and adaptability to fluctuating energy needs. Analysis demonstrates that for any non-negative CD value, the proposed balanced precoder achieves greater harvested energy compared to perfect interference alignment (IA) precoders, with the associated sum rate loss quantified via an upper bound. Furthermore, simulation results indicate that IA schemes utilizing mean-squared error are more effective for maximizing SWIPT performance than those relying on subspace alignment.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as the dominant learning frameworks for graph-structured data, finding applications across diverse fields such as quantum chemistry, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, and natural language processing. However, arbitrary graphs often lack canonical positional information for nodes, which limits a GNN's ability to differentiate between isomorphic nodes and other symmetries. One solution is to incorporate node Positional Encodings (PE) into the input layer, similar to the approach used in Transformers, with Laplacian eigenvectors serving as a viable option for graph-based PE. This work proposes decoupling structural and positional representations to facilitate the network's learning of these two critical properties. We introduce a novel, generic architecture termed LSPE (Learnable Structural and Positional Encodings). By evaluating various sparse and fully-connected (Transformer-like) GNNs, we observed a significant performance boost on molecular datasets, with improvements ranging from 1.79% to 64.14% when utilizing learnable PE across both GNN architectures.

Stellar bars are fundamental catalysts for the secular evolution of galaxies, and they are best analyzed using rest-frame near-infrared (NIR) imagery. These images map the underlying stellar mass and are less susceptible to obscuration from dust and star formation compared to rest-frame UV or optical data. By utilizing the high-resolution (~1.3 kpc at z ~ 1-3) {\it{JWST}} CEERS NIRCam images in the F444W filter, this study delivers the first quantitative detection and characterization of stellar bars at redshifts greater than 1. Using ellipse fitting criteria, we identify six robust bar examples at $z>1$ with confirmed spectroscopic redshifts. This pilot study notably includes the two highest-redshift bars identified to date, at approximately $z=2.136$ and $z=2.312$. The bars observed at $z \sim 1.1-2.3$ exhibit projected semi-major axes ranging from ~2.9 to 4.3 kpc and ellipticities of ~0.41-0.53 in the rest-frame NIR. Their host galaxies possess stellar masses between ~$1 \times 10^{10}$ and $2 \times 10^{11} M_{\odot}$, star formation rates from ~21 to 295 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, and several have nearby companions. These findings indicate an early emergence of such instabilities, aligning with simulations that predict bars form early in massive, dynamically cold disks. Furthermore, if these bars at lookback times of 8-10 Gyr persist to the present day, bar-driven secular mechanisms could operate over extended periods, significantly influencing some galaxies by $z \sim 0$.

We present a novel class of Hodge cycles featuring non-reduced associated Hodge loci, termed "fake linear cycles." For all Fermat varieties, we characterize these cycles and demonstrate that they occur exclusively at degrees $d=3,4,6$, where an infinite number exist within the space of Hodge cycles. These cycles are considered pathological because the Zariski tangent space of their associated Hodge locus achieves maximal dimension, contradicting Movasati's conjecture. Furthermore, they serve as examples of algebraic cycles that are not generated by their periods, according to the Movasati-Sert\öz framework. Our investigation involves computing their Galois action in cohomology and their second-order IVHS invariant. We conclude that for any degree $d\ge 2+\frac{6}{n}$, the minimal codimension component of the Hodge locus passing through the Fermat variety corresponds to the parametrization of hypersurfaces containing linear subvarieties of dimension $\frac{n}{2}$, thereby extending previous results by Green, Voisin, Otwinowska, and the second author.

To achieve a record-breaking single-mode fiber transmission capacity of 120.0 Tbit/s over 9x70 km spans, hybrid distributed Raman-EDFA amplifiers with a continuous 91 nm gain bandwidth were employed, supporting 312x35 GBd DP-256QAM modulation.

We present a computationally efficient technique grounded in path integral formalism for modeling defect-modified graphene. By encompassing the full Brillouin zone, our approach maintains lattice symmetry and enables the study of both short-range and long-range phenomena. The method's primary benefit is that its computational cost scales with the number of defects rather than the system size. To illustrate this approach, we examine the graphene-mediated RKKY interaction among multiple magnetic impurities. Our findings align with previous studies, confirming that interaction strength and sign are influenced by impurity spacing, sublattice configuration, and system doping. Furthermore, we show that frustration between impurity spins can be induced by adjusting their relative positions and toggled on or off through modulation of the chemical potential.

We present a concise theoretical framework applicable to diverse time-varying dispersive media. In this approach, traditional continuous wave reflection and transmission coefficients are substituted with equivalent operator formulations. When compared to established numerical and analytical methods, our analysis reveals that the eigenfunctions of these operators correspond to pulses whose spectra remain invariant after interacting with the time-varying, dispersive material. Furthermore, the poles of these operators signify the system's non-time-harmonic bound states.

Interferometry stands as a cornerstone method for contemporary precision measurements. Because atoms interact significantly with electric, magnetic, and gravitational fields—unlike light—they offer unique versatility in interferometric applications. In this work, we utilize atom interferometry to map optical and magnetic potential landscapes across a region larger than $240 \mu m \times 600 \mu m$. Differential potentials used in our setup create phase shifts within an atom laser, which are revealed via a Ramsey pulse sequence. Additionally, we illustrate how sophisticated pulse sequences can improve specific imaging capabilities, such as resolving steep potential gradients. The study concludes with a theoretical examination featuring a semiclassical analysis supported by corresponding numerical simulations.

This work establishes new connections among algebraic geometry, information theory, and Topological Field Theory (TFT). We examine noisy database models, defined as probability distributions on finite sets associated with exponential families. It is explicitly demonstrated that these manifolds possess the structure of a pre-Frobenius manifold, a concept central to the axiomatization of TFT. This finding bridges the gap to algebraic geometry by proving that a statistical pre-Frobenius manifold constitutes an algebraic variety over $\mathbb{Q}$ (specifically, a $\mathbb{Q}$-toric variety). Simultaneously, it advances recent findings regarding the hidden symmetries of such objects, which have been identified via classical web theory as Commutative Moufang Loops. Our results deepen this algebraic understanding in two dimensions: algebraically, statistical pre-Frobenius manifolds are shown to be equipped with algebraizable webs; differentially, these webs are proven to be hexagonal and isoclinic. This characterization is significant as it directly influences the geometric properties of statistical data, which are intrinsically linked to the web structures. Consequently, this fosters stronger ties to algebraic statistics, a field employing tools from algebraic and commutative geometry to solve statistical problems and their applications. The paper includes examples and discussions to illustrate these concepts.

This study investigates the joint analysis of multiple functionally connected structures within classification contexts. Specifically, our proposed approach leverages the coordinated variation of functionally correlated brain regions between individuals with autism and control subjects. To achieve this, we developed a methodology combining (1) non-Euclidean statistics capable of accurately mapping non-Euclidean data into Euclidean spaces and (2) a non-parametric integrative technique that decomposes multi-block Euclidean data into joint, individual, and residual components. Our results demonstrate that the derived joint structure is effective, robust, and interpretable for identifying patterns of joint variation in multi-block non-Euclidean datasets. We validated this method by classifying structural shape data from cases that either progressed to or did not develop into Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD).

We examine spin and planar squeezing within generalized superpositions of atomic or spin coherent states (ACS). Spin squeezing has proven valuable for detecting entanglement in multipartite systems, such as ensembles of two-level atoms, and signals reduced projection noise and sub-shot-noise phase uncertainty in Ramsey spectroscopy, particularly for phases $\phi \sim 0$. Conversely, planar-squeezed states exhibit reduced projection noise in two directions at once, enabling enhanced metrological precision for phase measurements without requiring prior knowledge of the phase value. This paper demonstrates that the generalized superposition state can be parametrized to exhibit both spin squeezing along all orthogonal axes and planar squeezing along all orthogonal planes for all $J > 1/2$. We conclude by applying these maximally spin- and planar-squeezed states to the field of quantum metrology.

This study re-examines biases in cosmic shear power spectra arising from multiplicative bias terms scaling up to quadratic powers of the shear. By expanding the multiplicative bias field into a series of independent spin-$s$ fields, we identify coefficients $m_s$ that couple with both integer and half-integer powers of the shear. We trace how these biases influence shape measurement statistics and the cosmic shear power spectrum, concluding that regression analysis on calibration data can detect them. Our results indicate that for integer shear powers, quadratic-order terms introduce an additional bispectrum dependency; neglecting these terms may bias cosmological parameters by up to $2(m_2+m_{-2}-m_6)0.4\sigma$ in Stage-IV dark energy experiments, though this sensitivity can be mitigated by reducing small-scale dependencies. Furthermore, for half-integer shear powers, Stage-IV experiments must constrain bias terms to a precision better than $\sigma[m_0+15(m_1+m_3)+0.1(m_{-1}+m_5)]\leq 0.01$. Consequently, future Stage-IV dark energy surveys should aim to measure and minimize all such bias contributions.

The abundances of thermally sensitive elements, such as lithium, the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio ([C/N]), and the 12C/13C ratio, are known to vary near the red giant branch bump. The prevailing explanation for these changes is double diffusive thermohaline mixing within the star. In this study, we examine whether thermohaline mixing can account for the observed timing of these chemical depletions. Recent observations indicate that lithium abundance declines prior to the drop in [C/N], whereas MESA-based numerical simulations of thermohaline mixing predict that synthetic abundances decrease simultaneously. Consequently, we conclude that thermohaline mixing alone cannot explain the distinct, separate depletion events of lithium and [C/N], as the predicted simultaneity contradicts the observed sequential drops. We therefore call for more advanced theoretical models to address this temporal separation and broader observational studies spanning various stellar masses and metallicities.

Graph comparison represents a specific condition within a metric space defined by a finite graph. We demonstrate that any nontrivial graph comparison necessarily leads to one of two Alexandrov comparisons. Furthermore, the proof provides a comprehensive characterization of graphs that exhibit trivial graph comparisons.

Driven largely by the information technology revolution, deep learning has seen significant advancement due to the vast availability of data in diverse digital formats. Nevertheless, in specific contexts, individuals may wish to prevent their data from being utilized to train commercial models, prompting research into attacks targeting the learnability of deep learning systems. Prior research on learnability attacks focused solely on blocking unauthorized exploitation of particular datasets, neglecting the mechanism to restore learnability for authorized scenarios. To address this gap, this paper introduces and explores the concept of "learnability lock," which controls a model's ability to learn from a specific dataset using a unique key. Specifically, we propose an adversarial invertible transformation—a mapping between images—that subtly modifies data samples to render them "unlearnable" by machine learning models while preserving visual features with minimal loss. Conversely, the corresponding key allows for the restoration of learnability, enabling normal model training. This proposed learnability lock utilizes class-wise perturbation, applying a universal transformation function to data samples sharing the same label. This approach ensures that learnability can be easily recovered via a simple inverse transformation while remaining difficult to detect or reverse-engineer. We empirically validate the effectiveness and practicality of our method on visual classification tasks.

We introduce a state redistribution technique designed for high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods applied to curvilinear embedded boundary grids. This method alleviates the excessively restrictive CFL constraints caused by explicit time stepping in the presence of arbitrarily small cut cells, allowing time steps to scale with the background grid cell sizes. Stability is achieved by post-processing the numerical solution after each stage of an explicit time-stepping scheme. This process involves temporarily merging small cells into larger, potentially overlapping neighborhoods via a specialized weighted inner product, followed by a conservative return of the solution to the base grid. The primary benefit of this strategy is its reliance on fundamental mesh data already present in many cut cell codes, eliminating the need for intricate geometric operations. We present several test cases that highlight the method's promising potential for curvilinear embedded geometries. Numerical results indicate that the scheme achieves $p+1$ order convergence in $L_1$ and between $p$ and $p+1$ in $L_\infty$ for smooth solutions, while also demonstrating the capability to accurately capture shocks.

The Vision Transformer (ViT) has become a powerful competitor to convolutional neural networks for diverse computer vision tasks. By utilizing multi-head attention layers, ViT enables global information embedding across entire images. However, the computation and storage of these attention matrices require a quadratic cost relative to the number of patches, which restricts efficiency, scalability, and deployment on resource-limited devices. While sparse attention has proven effective for accelerating NLP models, a systematic equivalent approach for ViT remains absent. To address this gap, we introduce ViTALiTy, a novel algorithm-hardware codesigned framework designed to enhance ViT inference efficiency. Distinct from sparsity-based accelerators used in NLP, ViTALiTy integrates both low-rank and sparse components within ViT attention mechanisms. On the algorithmic side, we approximate the dot-product softmax operation using first-order Taylor attention with row-mean centering as the low-rank component to linearize attention block costs, while further improving accuracy through sparsity-based regularization. On the hardware side, we design a dedicated accelerator that optimizes for the specific workload generated by ViTALiTy's linear Taylor attention, which executes only the low-rank component, thereby maximizing hardware efficiency. Comprehensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that ViTALiTy achieves significantly improved end-to-end efficiency—such as being $3\times$ faster and $3\times$ more energy-efficient—while maintaining comparable accuracy against state-of-the-art solutions.

Brownian dynamics simulations have been employed to investigate the self-assembly of two-dimensional dodecagonal quasicrystals (DDQCs) from patchy particles featuring a five-fold rotational symmetry pattern defined by spherical harmonics $Y_{55}$. Analysis of the DDQC formation via an annealing process reveals a specific mechanism: the early dynamics are dominated by hexagonal structures, followed by the nucleation of dodecagonal motifs through particle rearrangement, which subsequently expand across the entire system. This transition from hexagonal to dodecagonal ordering occurs via the collective rational motion of the particles. The resulting DDQCs comprise clusters of dodecagonal motifs that fall into various packing categories. Under fixed temperature conditions, fluctuations in the DDQC are characterized by alterations in the network of these motifs. Finally, a comparison between DDQCs assembled from patchy particles and isotropic particles shows that both systems exhibit similar mechanisms for formation and fluctuation.

A notable characteristic of closed light rings in Kerr black holes was recently identified (Int.Journ.Mod.Phys. D27 (2018), 1847025). We elucidate the underlying cause of this property and establish a somewhat broader theorem.

We are submitting our approach for the 2021 3C Shared Task on Citation Context Classification based on Purpose. The objective of this competition is to categorize citations within scientific papers according to their specific function. This task holds significant potential for developing more thorough methods to summarize the roles and applications of scientific articles; however, it presents considerable challenges, primarily stemming from the scarcity of hand-labeled training data and the inherent subjectivity of these labels. Our solution employs a multi-task model integrating several modules that address the problem from diverse angles, utilizing hand-crafted linguistic features, TF-IDF vectors, and an LSTM model enhanced with attention mechanisms. Additionally, we present an ablation study and feature analysis, offering insights that may guide future research.

This paper addresses several erroneous claims found in textbooks covering data analysis, machine learning, and computational methods, as well as in broader research literature. The central issue highlighted is the proper application and relevance of statistics to scientific and engineering data. Unlike critiques targeting specific authors, this work focuses on widespread mistakes prevalent in introductory materials. Following an overview of frequentist and Bayesian linear regression, the article examines six representative cases. For each, it provides a specific example of the textbook error, directs readers to authoritative specialist literature, and offers a summary correction. These insights are broadly applicable to any technical context where statistical methods are used to derive practical conclusions, spanning from elementary courses on experimental measurements to advanced regression techniques.

A generalized Langevin equation with fluctuating diffusivity (GLEFD) is introduced, demonstrating that it adheres to a generalized fluctuation-dissipation relation. When the memory kernel follows a power law, the GLEFD displays anomalous subdiffusion, non-Gaussian behavior, and stretched-exponential relaxation. Additionally, the system is examined under a single-exponential memory kernel as an analytically manageable case, where the mean-square displacement and self-intermediate-scattering function reveal plateau structures. Finally, a numerical integration scheme for the GLEFD is provided.

We present a superconducting artificial atom featuring robust unidirectional coupling to a microwave photonic waveguide. This artificial atom is constructed by linking a transmon qubit to the waveguide at two distinct spatial locations using time-modulated interactions. Direction-sensitive interference generated by these parametric couplings yields a non-reciprocal response, with our measurements showing a spontaneous emission forward-to-backward ratio greater than 100. We confirm the quantum nonlinear characteristics of this artificial chiral atom by analyzing the resonance fluorescence spectrum under strong resonant excitation, where distinct Mollow triplets are observed. Additionally, we demonstrate chirality for the atom's second transition energy and manipulate it via pulse sequences to achieve a qubit-state-dependent non-reciprocal phase for traveling photons. This work establishes a superconducting hardware platform capable of scaling key functionalities in chiral quantum optics, such as all-to-all connected quantum networks, driven-dissipative stabilization of many-body entanglement, and the creation of complex non-classical light states.

Time-dependent data serves as a critical information source in the modern data-driven landscape, yet generating it presents significant challenges, making it a compelling area for generative machine learning research. Smith et al. previously introduced the Time Series Generative Adversarial Network (TSGAN), which demonstrated strong capabilities in producing time-dependent data and few-shot generation, despite exhibiting certain training and learning flaws. This paper aims to refine TSGAN's performance by unifying the training of its independent networks to establish dependencies throughout both training and learning processes. The resulting model, termed unified TSGAN (uTSGAN), was rigorously evaluated against its predecessor using 70 benchmark time series datasets. Results indicate that uTSGAN surpassed TSGAN in 80% of these datasets over the same number of epochs and achieved superior performance in 60% of the datasets using three-quarters or less of the training time, all while maintaining few-shot generation capabilities and delivering improved FID scores.

Measurement errors in observed variable values can significantly alter the results of various causal discovery techniques. While this issue has been widely studied across multiple disciplines, the extent to which a causal model for error-free variables can be identified when measurement error with unknown variance is present remains unclear. This paper investigates precise sufficient conditions for identifying the underlying causal model free of measurement error and demonstrates what aspects of the causal structure can be recovered from observed data.
