We investigate how varying $\alpha$ impacts prediction outcomes. Experiments were performed on two datasets comprising 580 patients in total: 434 with head-neck cancer and 146 with lung cancer. The findings indicate that Tsallis-Havrda-Charvat entropy yields superior prediction accuracy for certain values of $\alpha$.

Symplectic integrators, which maintain the geometric properties of Hamiltonian flows and avoid secular energy drift, are ideal for the long-term simulation of N-body systems within the solar system. However, constructing explicit symplectic integrators in general relativity is often challenging because variables are inseparable. Furthermore, even when a relativistic Hamiltonian can be split into two analytically integrable components, their solutions are not always explicit functions of proper time. In such cases, implicit symplectic methods, like the midpoint rule, are viable, though they are generally more computationally expensive than explicit algorithms of the same order. To overcome this limitation, we decomposed the Hamiltonian of Schwarzschild spacetime into four integrable parts with analytical solutions explicitly dependent on proper time. This approach enables the straightforward development of second- and fourth-order explicit symplectic integrators. These new algorithms are also effective for modeling the chaotic dynamics of charged particles around a black hole under an external magnetic field. When appropriate proper time steps are used, they exhibit superior long-term stability in keeping Hamiltonian errors bounded while reducing computational costs.

We investigate the phenomenology of a two-fluid cosmological framework, in which general relativity (GR) field equations are driven by both baryonic matter and cold dark matter. Our findings indicate that this model offers a unified account of late-time cosmological dynamics across both small and large scales. In the static limit, we demonstrate that demanding a matter density profile scaling as $1/r^2$ successfully reproduces the flattening of galactic rotation curves. This same scaling governs the distribution of matter inhomogeneities at small cosmological scales, thereby linking galactic dynamics directly to structure formation. At large scales, we examine how spacetime geometry back-reacts to matter inhomogeneities. We observe that averaging this back-reaction term over spatial scales of approximately 100 Mpc yields a cosmological constant of the observed magnitude, naturally tied to the matter distribution. This approach resolves both the cosmological constant and coincidence problems, revealing a compelling connection between small-scale and large-scale cosmic behaviors.

Turbulence within the interstellar medium (ISM) plays a pivotal role in star formation, driven primarily by shocks from supernovae, stellar jets, radiation from massive stars, and galactic spiral-arm dynamics. Despite this, the specific mechanism by which shocks generate turbulence remains unclear, particularly regarding whether the driving force is predominantly solenoidal (rotational and divergence-free) or compressive (potential and curl-free). This distinction is critical, as compressive driving yields density dispersions three times greater and star formation rates an order of magnitude higher than solenoidal driving. In this study, we employ hydrodynamical simulations to examine shock-induced turbulence within a structured, multi-phase medium, modeling a laser-driven shock propagating through a foam material in preparation for an experiment at the National Ignition Facility (NIF). We analyze the resulting density and velocity distributions to calculate the turbulence driving parameter $b$, defined by density dispersion, turbulent Mach number, and the polytropic exponent $\Gamma$. While purely solenoidal and compressive driving correspond to $b \approx 1/3$ and $b \approx 1$ respectively, our simulations of shocks entering a multi-phase medium with varying structures and $\Gamma < 1$ consistently yield $b \approx 1$. These findings indicate that shock-driven turbulence aligns with strongly compressive driving.

This article revisits the mass spectrum of ground-state triply-heavy baryons using QCD sum rules, implementing a consistent operator product expansion that extends to dimension-6 vacuum condensates through a new analysis. Notably, this work marks the first instance where three-gluon condensates are incorporated into QCD sum rules for these baryon states.

This work investigates gravity surface waves within the ideal fluid framework in (2+1) dimensions. We employ a systematic method to derive Boussinesq equations based on specific relationships among the expansion orders for four parameters: the amplitude ($\alpha$), long-wavelength ($\beta$), transverse wavelength ($\gamma$), and bottom variation ($\delta$) parameters, while also incorporating surface tension when applicable. For all examined scenarios, these (2+1)-dimensional Boussinesq equations cannot be simplified into a single nonlinear wave equation for the surface elevation. Instead, they can be reduced to a single, highly nonlinear partial differential equation governing an auxiliary function $f(x,y,t)$, which defines the velocity potential rather than the directly observable surface elevation; however, solving for $f$ allows one to determine the surface elevation. Furthermore, restricting the derived equations to (1+1) dimensions recovers established models, including the KdV, extended KdV, fifth-order KdV, and Gardner equations.

We analyzed radio-loud (RL) and radio-quiet (RQ) quasars within the SDSS DR7 parent sample, focusing on MgII broad emission line sources with i-band magnitudes $\leq 19.1$ and redshifts $z \leq 1.9$. Among sources exhibiting full-width half maxima (FWHM) exceeding 15,000 km s$^{-1}$ (the very broad line or VBL sample), we determined the radio loud fraction (RLF) to be approximately 40\%. To explore this finding further, we compared the bolometric and optical continuum luminosities, black hole (BH) masses, and Eddington ratios of RL and RQ quasars in the VBL sample. Our results indicate that RL quasars possess higher luminosities and BH masses compared to their RQ counterparts. However, the similar distributions of covering fraction (CF) suggest no difference in dust distribution between VBL RL and RQ quasars, implying that dust does not influence our findings. Additionally, we found no correlation between RL quasar properties and either optical continuum luminosity or BH mass.

Modeling user preferences is both crucial and difficult for personalized product search. Although recent latent space-based approaches have reached state-of-the-art results by simultaneously learning semantic embeddings for users, products, and text tokens, they struggle to effectively capture user preferences. These methods typically rely on attentive models that only consider products viewed within a brief timeframe, failing to leverage relational data such as user-product interactions or item co-occurrences. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce a method that analyzes both local and global user behavior patterns on a user successive behavior graph, built from the short-term actions of all users. By employing an efficient jumping graph convolution, our approach uncovers high-order relations to capture implicit preference signals and collaborative trends, thereby enriching product representations. This method integrates smoothly with existing latent space techniques and can be applied to various product retrieval systems that utilize purchase history. Extensive experiments across eight Amazon benchmarks validate the efficacy and promise of our approach, with the source code available at \url{https://github.com/floatSDSDS/SBG}.

Learning unsupervised representations for attributed graphs is difficult because the latent space must capture both structural and feature data. Current approaches rely on reconstruction tasks to derive latent representations; however, they fail to optimize representations directly and suffer from oversmoothing, which restricts their effectiveness in downstream applications. To address these limitations, we introduce Deep Manifold Attributed Graph Embedding (DMAGE), a new graph embedding framework. This method calculates inter-node similarity between the data and latent spaces using node-to-node geodesic similarity and employs Bergman divergence as the loss function to minimize the gap between them. Furthermore, we develop a novel network architecture with reduced aggregation layers to mitigate oversmoothing and integrate graph structure augmentation to enhance representation stability. Experimental results on four standard datasets demonstrate that DMAGE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across three downstream tasks: unsupervised visualization, node clustering, and link prediction.

As urban populations expand worldwide, air pollution is escalating at a disturbing pace, severely compromising public health. A key strategy to mitigate this harm involves regulating polluters through effective policy and enforcement. CleanAirNowKC (CAN-KC), an environmental justice group based in Kansas City, Kansas, has deployed nine PurpleAir sensors in community-identified areas to advance its mission. This paper presents an interactive map enabling residents to efficiently monitor air quality. Additionally, the system facilitates the reporting and tracking of industrial emissions and toxic releases, aiding in the identification of primary pollution sources. These tools provide crucial evidence to support community-led advocacy for just policies aimed at enhancing air quality regulation in Kansas City.

This study introduces and experimentally validates a microwave kinetic inductance traveling-wave amplifier (KIT) that achieves noise performance near the quantum limit when measured via a shot-noise tunnel junction (SNTJ). By utilizing a three-wave mixing mechanism under DC bias, this KIT significantly lowers the microwave pump power and related parasitic heating by orders of magnitude compared to traditional four-wave mixing designs. The device features a 50 Ohm artificial transmission line engineered with specific dispersion properties to enable controlled amplification bandwidth. Experimental results show a gain of $16.5^{+1}_{-1.3}$ dB over a 2 GHz bandwidth, with an input 1 dB compression point of -63 dBm, aligning well with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, employing a theoretical model that incorporates SNTJ-generated noise at both the signal and idler ports, we characterized the system-added noise of an amplification chain where the KIT serves as the initial stage. The measured noise, $3.1\pm0.6$ quanta (or $0.66\pm0.15$ K) within the 3.5 to 5.5 GHz range, represents the noise floor experienced by a subsequent device replacing the SNTJ. Consequently, this KIT is well-suited for reading large arrays of microwave kinetic inductance detectors and holds promise for multiplexed superconducting qubit readout.

Graph-based Semi-Supervised Learning (GSSL) offers a practical approach to leveraging limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. However, because these algorithms depend on known labels to predict unknown ones, they are highly susceptible to data quality issues, particularly label poisoning. This paper introduces a novel data poisoning technique that efficiently approximates label inference outcomes to pinpoint inputs that, when poisoned, maximize the number of incorrect label predictions. We rigorously tested our approach across three classification tasks under 24 distinct experimental configurations. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, our influence-driven attack achieves an average error rate increase of 50% while operating multiple orders of magnitude faster. Additionally, our method assists engineers in identifying high-priority inputs for investigation and relabeling prior to model training. We demonstrate that relabeling just one-third of the poisoned inputs—selected based on their influence—reduces the overall poisoning impact by 50%.

This study presents various strengths and yields of 2-particle direct photon-hadron correlations in both $p+p$ and $Au+Au$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. The per-trigger yield of direct photon-hadron pairs, derived from direct-photon-jet correlations, is determined by statistically subtracting decay photon pairs from the inclusive photon-hadron sample. Estimates for decay photon per-trigger yields are generated using a Monte Carlo calculation based on measured $\pi^0$-hadron data, accounting for decay kinematics and detector response. Assuming near $p_T$-independent suppression with a specific averaging method, we calculate an average ratio ($I_{AA}$) of $Au+Au$ to $p+p$ per-trigger photon yields that aligns with the single particle suppression level ($R_{AA}$), offering qualitative support for the basic geometrical model of jet suppression at RHIC. Applying event-by-event photon isolation cuts to $p+p$ results yields our most precise measurement to date, enabling detailed studies of the baseline fragmentation function $D(z)$ and a variable $\langle p_{out} \rangle$, which scales with the apparent intrinsic $k_T$ or non-zero transverse momentum of the initial collision partons. Using a model-dependent extraction technique, the average $\sqrt{\langle k_T^2 \rangle}$ in $p+p$ at this center-of-mass energy is found to be approximately 3 GeV, consistent with di-hadron (di-jet) correlation analyses. These findings, alongside the enhanced precision in isolated yields, justify further comparisons with baseline perturbative QCD (pQCD) calculations employed in various jet energy loss models. Finally, we report a unique direct measurement of single prompt photons originating from jet fragmentation.

Most multichannel speech enhancement techniques follow a two-stage process, pairing a linear spatial filter (beamformer) with a single-channel postprocessor. However, this serial arrangement is rarely optimal under the minimum mean square error (MMSE) criterion when noise deviates from a Gaussian distribution; instead, the ideal MMSE filter functions as a joint, nonlinear spatial and spectral operator. Although traditional parameter estimation for such filters is difficult, modern neural networks offer a promising avenue to learn these nonlinear mappings directly from data. This study investigates the viability of replacing standard two-step methods with joint nonlinear filters by assessing performance gains across three non-Gaussian scenarios: high-kurtosis super-Gaussian noise, inhomogeneous noise fields generated by five sources using a two-microphone setup, and real-world data from the CHiME3 database. Results indicate significant improvements in all cases. Notably, the analysis reveals that nonlinear spatial filters leverage spatial information more effectively than linear counterparts, capable of suppressing more than $D-1$ directional interferers with a $D$-dimensional array without requiring spatial adaptation.

Three-dimensional Lorentzian quantum gravity, conceptualized as the continuum limit of a nonperturbative sum over spacetimes, appears nearly accessible to analytical techniques, with certain characteristics already described using effective matrix and related models. To deepen our comprehension of this framework, we conducted a numerical study of spatial hypersurfaces within three-dimensional Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDT). This investigation involved measuring and analyzing various quantum observables, including the entropy exponent, both local and global Hausdorff dimensions, and the quantum Ricci curvature of spatial slices, aiming to correlate them with established continuum properties of two-dimensional quantum geometry systems. Above the first-order phase transition in CDT quantum gravity, our results provide compelling evidence that the spatial dynamics belong to the same universality class as two-dimensional Euclidean (Liouville) quantum gravity. Conversely, below the transition, the behavior of spatial slices fails to align with any recognized quantum gravity model. This discrepancy may suggest the emergence of a novel class of two-dimensional quantum systems, driven by the intricate nature of the underlying three-dimensional quantum geometry embedding.

In reinforcement learning (RL) research, the standard practice is *tabula rasa* learning, which begins with no prior knowledge. However, in large-scale applications, RL systems rarely follow this approach. Instead, they undergo numerous design or algorithmic modifications during development, relying on ad hoc methods to integrate these changes without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. Furthermore, the high computational inefficiency of deep RL often prevents researchers lacking industrial-scale resources from addressing complex problems. To overcome these challenges, we introduce "reincarnating RL," an alternative workflow where prior computational efforts, such as learned policies, are reused or transferred between design iterations of an agent or across different agents. As an initial step toward universal policy transfer, we focus on efficiently adapting an existing sub-optimal policy to a standalone value-based RL agent. We identify that current methods fail in this context and propose a straightforward algorithm to resolve these limitations. Using this algorithm, we demonstrate the advantages of reincarnating RL over *tabula rasa* approaches on Atari 2600 games, a challenging locomotion task, and the real-world navigation of stratospheric balloons. Ultimately, this work advocates for a shift in RL research methodology that we believe will significantly enhance real-world adoption and further democratize the field. Open-sourced code and trained agents are available at https://agarwl.github.io/reincarnating_rl.

We firmly assert that the actual dynamical and gauge structure of the QCD ground state is far more intricate than what the exact gauge symmetry of its Lagrangian suggests. This complexity originates from the tadpole/seagull term, whose renormalized form is known as the mass gap. Although the mass gap's true dynamical function is concealed within the QCD ground state, it is explicitly manifested in the complete gluon self-energy. To reveal this, we derived the discrepancy between the transverse constraints applicable to the full gluon self-energy and its subtracted counterpart. Furthermore, an equation of motion for the full gluon propagator, incorporating the mass gap, was established, enabling the determination of dynamical and gauge structures through a newly introduced generalized gauge. We developed a novel non-perturbative analytical framework, termed the mass gap approach, for QCD and its ground state. This method yielded a general, non-perturbative singular solution for the full gluon propagator that remains valid across the entire gluon momentum spectrum and dominates at large distances compared to other solutions. This solution encompasses all significant infrared singularities that may arise in the QCD ground state due to the self-interaction of massless gluon modes. Additionally, a corresponding non-perturbative multiplicative infrared renormalization scheme was formulated. The resulting full gluon propagator ensures that gluons do not exist as physical states at large distances, thereby enforcing the confinement of color gluons. Our approach further elucidates scale violation within the asymptotic freedom regime and accounts for the strictly linear nature of the potential between heavy quarks.

State machines are widely used to model and visualize discrete systems, including software, and to represent regular grammars. Most algorithms that passively learn these machines from data assume full data availability upfront, loading everything into memory. This approach hinders their application to continuous data streams and leads to high memory consumption when handling large datasets. This paper proposes a method for learning state machines from data streams using the count-min-sketch data structure to minimize memory usage. Additionally, we employ state merging based on the established red-blue-framework to shrink the search space. Our approach was implemented within a recognized state machine learning framework and evaluated on a well-known dataset. The resulting experimental data demonstrates the method's effectiveness regarding both result quality and runtime performance.

We introduce BASIC, a combined scaling approach that reaches 85.7% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet ILSVRC-2012 validation set without utilizing any labeled ImageNet data. This performance exceeds the best comparable published models, CLIP and ALIGN, by 9.3%. Furthermore, the BASIC model demonstrates notable enhancements in robustness; across five test sets featuring natural distribution shifts—including ImageNet-{A,R,V2,Sketch} and ObjectNet—it maintains an 84.3% top-1 average accuracy, representing only a minor decline from its baseline ImageNet performance.

To attain these outcomes, we expanded the contrastive learning frameworks of CLIP and ALIGN across three key dimensions: data volume, model capacity, and batch size. Our dataset comprises 6.6 billion noisy image-text pairs, making it four times larger than ALIGN and sixteen times larger than CLIP. Our largest model contains 3 billion weights, which is 3.75 times more parameters and eight times more FLOPs than ALIGN and CLIP. Additionally, we employed a batch size of 65,536, doubling that of CLIP and quadrupling that of ALIGN.

Our implementation of the BASIC scaling rules addressed two primary challenges. First, limited accelerator memory on GPUs and TPUs hindered the application of our combined scaling strategy; we overcame this by introducing two straightforward techniques utilizing gradient checkpointing and model parallelism. Second, while increasing dataset and model sizes are standard practices for boosting deep learning performance, the impact of large contrastive batch sizes on image-text models remains poorly understood. To clarify the advantages of large batch sizes, we developed a theoretical framework demonstrating that larger contrastive batch sizes reduce generalization gaps in models like BASIC.

We examine a degenerate wave equation featuring drift, where the leading operator does not adhere to divergence form. We establish specific conditions required for the boundary controllability of the corresponding Cauchy problem.

This study introduces a new fault detection and isolation (FDI) framework tailored for distributed parameter systems described by parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) featuring nonlinear uncertainties. A central advantage of this FDI method is its ability to handle system uncertainties effectively to ensure precise fault detection. The approach begins by deriving an approximate ordinary differential equation (ODE) system that captures the primary dynamics of the original PDE model. Building on this, an adaptive dynamics identification strategy utilizing a radial basis function neural network is developed to locally and accurately identify uncertain system dynamics across both normal and faulty operating conditions. Finally, a set of FDI estimators equipped with adaptive thresholds is constructed for real-time fault decision-making. The paper provides a rigorous analysis of FDI performance regarding fault detectability and isolatability, and a simulation of a representative transport-reaction process is presented to validate the approach's effectiveness and benefits.

Accurate modeling of physics in structural and fluid engineering simulations depends on understanding how contacts occur between various 3-D geometric surfaces. While machine learning typically represents 3-D surfaces as point clouds or meshes, deriving representations of interacting geometries from point-based data remains difficult. This work introduces ActivationNet, a machine learning algorithm designed to learn from point clouds or meshes of interacting 3-D surfaces and predict their contact quality. ActivationNet generates activation states from point-based surface representations using a multi-dimensional binning technique, which are then processed by deep neural networks to determine contact quality. The model's performance is validated through multiple experiments, including tests on interacting surfaces derived from engineering geometries. Across all presented experiments, ActivationNet's contact quality predictions align well with expected outcomes.

This study primarily employs the nonnegative continuous function sequence $\{\zeta_n(r)\}_{n=0}^{\infty}$ to redefine the Bohr radius for two specific categories of analytic functions within the unit disk $|z|<1$. The first category consists of functions where $\real f(z)<1$, while the second involves alternating series $A_f(r)$ derived from analytic functions of the form $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{pn+m}z^{pn+m}$. In the latter scenario, insights regarding the Bohr radius for both even and odd analytic functions are also obtained. Additionally, the paper establishes connections between the majorant series $M_f(r)$ and the odd and even components of $f(z)$. Finally, the authors demonstrate that the majority of the derived results are sharp.

Fine-grained visual classification involves identifying images that fall into multiple sub-categories within a single broader class. This task is difficult because of the subtle distinctions between highly similar categories. Many current approaches process images individually, which can restrict the model's capacity to leverage comparative clues across different images. To address this, we introduce the Progressive Co-Attention Network (PCA-Net). Our method first computes channel-wise similarity by fostering interaction between feature channels within pairs of images from the same category to isolate common discriminative traits. Furthermore, recognizing the importance of complementary data, we mask the salient regions highlighted by this channel interaction, compelling the network to attend to other informative areas. The PCA-Net model has demonstrated competitive performance on three benchmark datasets: CUB-200-2011, Stanford Cars, and FGVC Aircraft.

Determining whether an optimal solution is local or global has historically been a challenging issue in complex optimization scenarios. In this study, we demonstrate that for rapid and weak driving processes, a unique global optimal protocol exists for entropy production. We establish this by proving the functional's convexity with respect to the control parameter. This convexity also confirms monotonicity in this context, contrasting with our earlier findings where the entropy production rate was not necessarily positive at all times. Finally, we illustrate that the analytical approach employed in our prior work [Journal of Physics Communications 6, 083001 (2022)] yields the global optimal protocol by comparing it against results from genetic programming, a global optimization method.

This study investigates the stable recovery of four spatially varying coefficients within a coupled semilinear parabolic system featuring variable diffusion matrices and dynamic boundary conditions that link internal and boundary dynamics. We establish a Lipschitz stability theorem for both interior and boundary potentials using a single observation component, restricted to any arbitrary open subset of the physical domain. The demonstration primarily utilizes novel Carleman estimates tailored for dynamic boundary conditions of surface diffusion type.

Grant-free access serves as a fundamental enabler for massive machine-type communications (mMTC), facilitating connections for a vast number of users to a base station with minimal signaling overhead and latency. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm (GA) to generate a novel set of user-specific, non-orthogonal, unimodular sequences tailored for uplink grant-free access. The initial stage of the GA identifies a subsampling index set for a partial unitary matrix that approximates an equiangular tight frame. Subsequently, the second-stage GA determines a masking sequence for each column of this matrix to lower the peak-to-average power ratio, which is critical for multicarrier transmission. These masked columns are then proposed as the new non-orthogonal sequences for uplink grant-free access. Simulation outcomes indicate that the sequences developed via this two-stage GA demonstrate superior performance in compressed sensing-based joint activity detection and channel estimation within uplink grant-free scenarios. Unlike algebraic designs, this GA-based approach yields high-quality non-orthogonal sequences of arbitrary lengths, offering greater flexibility for uplink grant-free access in mMTC environments.

It is established that certain equational theories, such as groups and Boolean algebras, can often be defined using fewer axioms than originally required, yet determining whether a specific set of axioms is minimal remains challenging. Malbos and Mimram proposed a general approach to establish a lower bound for the number of equational axioms or rewrite rules equivalent to a given theory or term rewriting system by employing homological algebra; their method serves as an analog to Squier's homology theory for string rewriting systems. This paper extends the homology theory for term rewriting systems and derives a superior lower bound under a stricter equivalence criterion. Furthermore, the author implemented a computational program to calculate these bounds and tested it on 64 complete term rewriting systems.

Electoral forecasting remains a significant scientific challenge with profound societal implications, particularly as existing data-driven approaches strive to integrate statistics, economic indicators, and machine learning. Recent research in network science, however, highlights the critical role of temporal dynamics in opinion diffusion. Consequently, we synthesize micro-scale opinion dynamics with temporal epidemic models to create a novel macro-scale Temporal Attenuation (TA) model designed to enhance forecasting precision using pre-election polling data. Our hypothesis posits that the timing of poll releases substantially influences opinion oscillations, especially in the immediate lead-up to elections. To this end, we conceptualize opinion momentum as a temporal function that surges when opinions are introduced into a multi-opinion voter system and decays during relaxation phases. Validated against survey data from US Presidential Elections spanning 1968 to 2016, the TA model surpassed both statistical methods and the leading pollsters of the era in 10 out of 13 elections. We demonstrate two TA implementations that achieved an average cumulative forecasting error of 2.8 to 3.28 points over the 48-year period. In contrast, statistical methods accumulated an error of 7.48 points, while top pollsters recorded 3.64 points. Overall, the TA model delivers a 23% to 37% improvement in forecasting performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we show that TA maintains effectiveness even with limited poll availability; indeed, as pre-election survey data becomes more abundant, we anticipate the TA model will serve as a key reference alongside other modern election forecasting tools.

Fundamentally, compressed sensing focuses on creating decoding algorithms to reconstruct a sufficiently sparse vector or code from a lower-dimensional linear measurement, typically assuming the decoder possesses knowledge of the encoder matrix, which is often binary and sparse in combinatorial settings. This paper addresses the challenge of designing a decoder to recover sparse codes from linear measurements alone, without access to the encoder matrix. To achieve this, we investigate the matrix factorization problem of simultaneously recovering both the encoder and sparse coding matrices from the corresponding linear measurement matrix. Our contribution is a computationally efficient decoding algorithm, termed Decoder-Expander Based Factorisation, which offers robust performance guarantees. Specifically, under mild assumptions regarding the sparse coding matrix and utilizing a novel random encoder matrix, we demonstrate that Decoder-Expander Based Factorisation recovers both matrices at the optimal measurement rate with high probability using a near-optimal number of measurement vectors. Furthermore, experimental results confirm the algorithm's practical efficacy and computational efficiency. Beyond the scope of compressed sensing, these findings hold relevance for researchers in fields such as linear sketching, coding theory, and matrix compression.

This study aims to correlate muscle effort distributions with the trajectory and resistance parameters of a robotic device used for exercise and rehabilitation. Muscle effort distribution, which quantifies the contribution of each muscle to the training activity, was measured using electromyography (EMG) sensors and calculated as the ratio of individual muscle activation to the total activation of the muscle group. The research utilizes a four degrees-of-freedom robot equipped with an impedance control system to generate sophisticated exercise protocols. In these protocols, users are instructed to trace an elliptical path against the machine's neutral path and adjustable resistance, while the robot enforces a zero-effort circular path. The control system modulates the stiffness between the neutral path and the subject's applied torque based on user-defined settings. Specifically, experiments varied the ellipse's orientation and a stiffness parameter to assess their impact on muscle effort distribution. An artificial neural network (ANN) was trained on a subset of this data, with the remaining data used to evaluate the model's accuracy. Results indicate that model precision degrades over time, highlighting the complexity of long-term muscle dynamics and suggesting the presence of time-varying factors, such as fatigue.

Inhomogeneous broadening is recognized for obscuring the specific traits of individual emitters, replacing distinct single-particle characteristics with a wider probability distribution. This study offers an analysis of emission spectra from mesoscopic ensembles of inhomogeneously distributed emitters, specifically within the range of 10 to 10^4 particles (below the thermodynamic limit). Utilizing both a straightforward analytical model and comprehensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the count of emitters and their individual linewidths can be directly derived from the ensemble autocorrelation function, even when the emission is inhomogeneously broadened. As a practical application, we examine the photoluminescence of colloidal nanocrystal aggregates encased in a gold shell. This generalizable method is applicable to various mesoscopic many-body systems and may offer novel insights into their first-order coherence properties.

Maintaining species biodiversity within ecological communities remains a difficult challenge given Darwinian selection pressures. This article moves beyond traditional pairwise competition to offer a new perspective on how higher-order interactions drive the evolution of social traits. A proposed simple model illustrates how perturbations affect intransitive competitive higher-order interactions, providing a promising framework. By employing a specific mathematical approach, we demonstrate that a perturbed interaction network alone can rapidly establish coexistence equilibria for competing species, eliminating the need to solve extensive systems of ordinary differential equations. Depending on the number of perturbations, the system can be divided into multiple feasible cluster states. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the ratio between perturbed and unperturbed species is inversely related to the magnitude of the perturbation applied. Our findings suggest that combining nonlinear dynamical systems with interaction topologies offers valuable insights into species coexistence under stressful conditions. Notably, our results imply that reduced competition between two species leads to increased abundance, allowing them to outperform others.

While the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) is designed for nonlinear systems, it fails to reduce to the classical Kalman filter when applied to linear systems. This discrepancy suggests that modifying the UKF to recover the classical filter for linear cases would be beneficial. Consequently, the primary objective is to develop UKF variants that specialize to the Kalman filter for linear systems while offering enhanced accuracy for nonlinear scenarios. To achieve this, the paper introduces two such modifications: EUKF-A, which relies on the Jacobian of the dynamics map, and EUKF-C, which depends on the Jacobian of the measurement map. The performance of both EUKF-A and EUKF-C is then evaluated against standard UKF using various nonlinear examples.

Driven by profit motives, organizations often engage fraud rings to fabricate reviews that boost their own standing or undermine competitors. These groups are particularly effective at deceiving consumers because individuals are more susceptible to the consensus of a large collective. To identify such rings, conventional methods typically analyze the static network structures of fraud groups, thereby neglecting the longitudinal behavior of individual reviewers and the dynamic nature of their collaborative interactions. Consequently, these static models fail to filter out "outlier" reviewers—specifically, fraudsters who intentionally blend into the group or legitimate reviewers who coincidentally co-review within a fraudulent cluster. To overcome this limitation, this study leverages the HIN-RNN model's ability to learn reviewer representations and capture collaboration dynamics. First, we apply HIN-RNN to model co-review relationships within a 28-day window, a process termed "spatial relation learning" to highlight the method's adaptability to various networked contexts. Next, an RNN processes these spatial relations to forecast spatio-temporal dynamics among group members. Subsequently, a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) refines the reviewer vector representations based on these predicted relations. These enhanced representations are then utilized to eliminate outlier reviewers. Finally, the average representation of the remaining reviewers is passed through a fully connected layer to classify the group as either fraudulent or legitimate. Extensive experiments on the Yelp and Amazon datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms three recent state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 5% and 4% in precision, 12% and 5% in recall, and 12% and 5% in F1-score, respectively.

Satoh established a correspondence between virtual knots and ribbon surfaces within $S^4$. In this work, we extend this correspondence to virtual $m$-links, leveraging it to develop higher-dimensional analogues of welded and extended welded knots. Furthermore, this approach enables the creation of two novel geometric representations for virtual $m$-links, encompassing the case of 1-links.

This study examines the cosmological consequences of Maxwell theory augmented by a non-local $U(1)$-symmetric term. While this framework reduces to Proca theory in flat spacetime, we demonstrate that in curved spacetime, it diverges from the coupled Einstein-Proca system. We further analyze cosmological perturbations within de Sitter spacetime, detailing the dynamics of individual modes, and investigate the model's anisotropic cosmology. Our findings indicate that the universe's late-time behavior aligns with observational data, ultimately predicting an isotropic cosmos.

We introduce a framework for compressive sensing tailored to images containing local, distinguishable objects, such as stars, specifically addressing challenges in celestial navigation. Let $x$ represent an $N$-pixel real-valued image composed of a few distinct local objects and noise; our objective is to design an $m \times N$ measurement matrix $A$, where $m \ll N$, enabling the recovery of an approximation of $x$ from the measurements $Ax$.

We have developed a matrix $A$ and a corresponding recovery algorithm characterized by three key properties: (i) when there are $k$ objects, the required number of measurements $m$ scales as $O((k \log N)/\log k)$, which improves upon the current best-known bound of $O(k \log(N/k))$; (ii) the matrix $A$ is highly sparse, a feature crucial for the hardware implementation of compressive sensing systems; and (iii) the recovery algorithm is empirically efficient, executing in time polynomial with respect to $k$ and $\log(N)$.

Furthermore, we provide an extensive analysis of applying this algorithm to attitude determination, or determining spatial orientation. Spacecraft typically capture images of the sky to identify stars and calculate their orientation; however, imaging is power-intensive for small spacecraft. Our approach optically compresses the image prior to it reaching the camera's pixel array, thereby reducing the number of sensors required.

This paper presents a QCD-inspired model designed to describe both hard and soft interactions at high energies. Within this framework, the long-distance behavior of the scattering amplitude is derived from an approximate solution to the non-linear evolution equation governing the parton system in the saturation regime. All phenomenological parameters regarding dipole-proton interactions were extracted from deep inelastic scattering data, while soft processes are characterized by a single new parameter linked to the hadron's wave function. Notably, the model eliminates the need for the traditional soft Pomeron, which has been a staple in high-energy phenomenology for forty years. It successfully accounts for all data on soft interactions, including total, elastic, and diffractive cross sections, as well as their dependence on $s$ and $t$. Furthermore, the calculated survival probability for diffractive Higgs production is found to be less than 1% within the LHC energy range.

Data augmentation is extensively utilized to enhance the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks during training. Recent studies indicate that employing worst-case transformations or adversarial augmentation strategies can substantially boost both accuracy and robustness. Nevertheless, because image transformations are non-differentiable, optimization techniques like reinforcement learning or evolution strategies are required, making them computationally infeasible for large-scale tasks. In this study, we demonstrate that achieving state-of-the-art performance on domain adaptation (DA) and generalization (DG) tasks is possible through simple consistency training with random data augmentation. Furthermore, to enhance accuracy and robustness against adversarial examples, we introduce a differentiable adversarial data augmentation approach leveraging spatial transformer networks (STN). This combined method, utilizing both adversarial and random transformations, surpasses current state-of-the-art results across multiple DA and DG benchmarks. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits strong robustness against data corruption, a capability validated on widely used datasets.

This paper presents a method for automatically generating difficult road networks designed to test automated lane-keeping systems in virtual environments. Utilizing a set of control points, we create a parametric curve that models the road network and establishes the dynamic driving task for the vehicle. Adjusting these control points globally alters the resulting road geometry. Our approach employs search algorithms to identify an optimal set of control points that produce a challenging geometry, compelling the vehicle to deviate from its intended path. We assessed this method across three distinct search configurations, evaluating their test efficiency and practical suitability for the automatic virtual testing of automated lane-keeping systems.

The High Energy Photon Source (HEPS), a 6 GeV synchrotron light source currently under construction in Beijing, aims to deliver ultralow emittance and requires superconducting cavities featuring low RF frequencies and effective damping of higher-order modes (HOM). A compact 166.6 MHz cavity utilizing a quarter-wave beta=1 geometry was proposed, followed by the design of a HOM-damped version after a successful proof-of-principle cavity was developed. To suppress HOM impedance below the critical threshold for coupled-bunch instabilities, a ferrite damper was mounted on the beam pipe. Due to the cavity's compact size, heating from the RF field on the vacuum seal was meticulously analyzed to prevent quenching of the NbTi flange. The cavity was subsequently equipped with a helium vessel and a tuning mechanism, ultimately demonstrating excellent RF and mechanical performance. Furthermore, a two-cavity string configuration was engineered to facilitate smooth transitions between components and provide appropriate shielding for synchrotron light. This paper details the comprehensive design of a fully dressed, HOM-damped, low-frequency beta=1 superconducting cavity tailored for HEPS.

A recent breakthrough by Chi et al. (STOC'22) introduced an $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{3 + \omega}{2}})$-time algorithm for computing the Monotone Min-Plus Product of two $n \times n$ matrices with entries bounded by $O(n)$, significantly surpassing the prior $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{12 + \omega}{5}})$ approach and enhancing related application bounds. Although Chi et al.'s method appears applicable to rectangular matrices, the generalization is not direct. This paper extends Chi et al.'s algorithm to efficiently solve the Monotone Min-Plus Product for rectangular matrices with polynomially bounded values. Leveraging this improved algorithm, we accelerate several applications involving rectangular Monotone Min-Plus Product, including $M$-bounded Single Source Replacement Path, Batch Range Mode, $k$-Dyck Edit Distance, and a 2-approximation for All Pairs Shortest Path. Additionally, we improve the running time for Unweighted Tree Edit Distance by applying Chi et al.'s original algorithm.

Since the Klein-Gordon and Proca equations incorporate $\hbar$, they govern quantum fields; however, their solutions can be approximated as classical when the typical action satisfies $S^{\rm typical}\gg \hbar$. This approximation is feasible due to the bosonic character of these fields, which permits the existence of multi-particle states. Through general reasoning, we demonstrate that for bosonic stars, the ratio ${\mathcal{S}^{\rm typical}}/{\hbar}$ exceeds $\left({M^{\rm max}}/{M_{\rm Pl}}\right)^2\sim 10^{76}\left({M^{\rm max}}/{M_\odot}\right)^2$, where $M^{\rm max}$ denotes the maximum mass of the specific bosonic star model and $M_{\rm Pl}$ represents the Planck mass. Consequently, for models where $M^{\rm max}\gg M_{\rm Pl}$ and solutions near this maximal mass, the classical description is valid, encompassing the astrophysically relevant range of masses greater than or equal to $M_\odot$.

We introduce PACMAN, an end-to-end framework designed to reduce and analyze data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 (HST/WFC3). This pipeline integrates spectral extraction with light curve fitting and forms the foundation of numerous highly cited publications (e.g., Kreidberg et al., 2014; Kreidberg et al., 2018). As the primary facility for characterizing exoplanets, HST relies heavily on two powerful instruments: the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) for ultraviolet observations and WFC3 for near-infrared observations. The advent of WFC3's spatial scan mode, where the target moves perpendicular to the dispersion direction during exposure, has significantly increased efficiency by minimizing overhead and enabling longer exposures without saturation. In exoplanet studies, WFC3 facilitates transit and secondary eclipse spectroscopy as well as phase curve measurements. Equipped with two grisms—G102 (800–1150 nm) and G141 (1075–1700 nm)—the instrument covers critical spectral ranges. The G141 grism is particularly sensitive to water molecular absorption around 1.4 microns, enabling the detection of atmospheric water in over a dozen exoplanets. Additionally, the G102 grism is sensitive to water and was instrumental in the first detection of a helium exosphere.

The permute-and-flip mechanism is a newly introduced differentially private selection algorithm that has been demonstrated to surpass the exponential mechanism. In this paper, we demonstrate that permute-and-flip is equivalent to the well-known report noisy max algorithm when utilizing exponential noise.
By employing an iterative tree construction, we demonstrate that for simple computable subsets of the Cantor space, Hausdorff, constructive, and computable dimensions can be incomputable.

We introduce a scaling law governing the transition to turbulence in pipe flows containing neutrally buoyant suspensions. Derived from extensive experimental data, this law correlates the amplitude of particle-induced disturbances ($\epsilon$) with the critical suspension Reynolds number, $Re_{s,c}$. The disturbance amplitude is defined by the particle-to-pipe diameter ratio and the suspended particles' volume fraction as $\epsilon = (d/D)^{1/2} \phi^{1/6}$. Analysis reveals that $Re_{s,c}$ scales inversely with $\epsilon$ ($\epsilon^{-1}$). Additionally, the magnitude of these perturbations enables the differentiation among classical, intermediate, and particle-induced transition regimes.

We present and examine the concept of soficity for Lie algebras, drawing inspiration from linear soficity in associative algebras. We establish two equivalent characterizations of this property: one based on metric ultraproducts and another on almost representations. We demonstrate that all Lie algebras with subexponential growth are sofic. Furthermore, we show that for a Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0, soficity holds if and only if its universal enveloping algebra is linearly sofic. Finally, we provide explicit families of almost representations for both the Witt and Virasoro algebras.

This paper investigates the non-commuting graph associated with the group $U_{6n}$, where vertices represent non-central elements and edges connect pairs of non-commuting elements. We examine key properties of this graph, including its clique number, chromatic number, and independence number. Additionally, we derive a general formula for the resolving polynomial and calculate the detour index, eccentric connectivity, total eccentricity, and independent polynomial.

This study tackles the trajectory tracking challenge for an autonomous tractor-trailer system by employing a rapid distributed nonlinear model predictive control algorithm paired with nonlinear moving horizon estimation for state and parameter estimation, allowing for the inclusion of constraints on both inputs and states. The suggested control method effectively guides the tractor-trailer along any desired path, guaranteeing superior control precision and resilience against environmental disturbances.

This work investigates how an environment influences a molecule's electromagnetic response within a dielectric medium. By utilizing dipole-dipole coupling between the molecule and its surroundings, we decompose the complex system to predict the excitation lifetimes of single and few molecules on dielectric surfaces, relying solely on the molecules' full quantum-mechanical properties, such as transition energies and dipole moments. The resulting theory enables the description of superradiance between two molecules as a function of their geometric configuration, specifically their separation and mutual orientation. Furthermore, we examine superradiance in a system of two molecules bound to a dielectric sphere, identifying a shift in the relevant length scale: the typical free-space wavelength is replaced by the binding distance, which significantly reduces the scales at which collective effects occur.

We provide a concise overview of our efforts to introduce a "product picture" formulation to quantum electrodynamics (QED), designed to complement and enhance the accessibility of a more extensive treatment recently published in *Foundations of Physics*. This product picture offers a formulation equivalent to standard Coulomb gauge QED, where the Hilbert space is constructed as a product of a subspace for the electromagnetic field and one for charged matter (the Dirac field), and the Hamiltonian decomposes into distinct electromagnetic, matter, and interaction components. Notably, this differs from the Coulomb gauge approach, which constructs the longitudinal electromagnetic field using charged matter operators. We also revisit the "Contradictory Commutator Theorem" in QED, which highlights issues in prior temporal gauge quantization attempts, and demonstrate how our product picture potentially resolves these problems. Furthermore, we examine the theorem's applicability to Yang-Mills fields. We extend this framework to nonrelativistic charged particles interacting with electromagnetic fields, revealing a new perspective on the theory of many nonrelativistic particles with Coulomb interactions. Additionally, we suggest that establishing a product picture for QED offers hope for achieving similar formulations for Yang-Mills theory and quantum gravity, the latter being essential for validating the author's "matter-gravity entanglement hypothesis." Finally, in an afterword, we briefly compare this hypothesis and its predictions with Roger Penrose's ideas regarding gravity's role in quantum state reduction and cosmological entropy.

Charge distribution patterns within liquid electrolytes are vital for technologies ranging from batteries and fuel cells to supercapacitors and the organization of particles in biological or colloidal environments. Typically, generating localized (screened) charge distributions in the bulk of these electrolytes necessitates physical surfaces, such as those from colloidal particles or material boundaries, which imposes significant limitations on material engineering. In this study, we demonstrate that topological defects in nematic electrolytes can serve as sites for local charge separation, creating charged defect cores and, in specific configurations, electric multilayers, unlike the electric double layers characteristic of isotropic electrolytes. Employing a Landau-de Gennes-Poisson-Boltzmann framework, we reveal that ions couple efficiently with topological defect cores through ion solvability and interact with local director-field distortions via flexoelectricity. We illustrate defect charging across various defect types—including lines, points, and walls—using scenarios involving ionically screened flat isotropic-nematic interfaces, radial hedgehog point defects, and half-integer wedge disclinations within the bulk or stabilized by charged colloidal particles. Broadly, these results hold relevance for applications where topological defects function as diffuse ionic capacitors or as carriers of ionic charge.

Semantic textual similarity (STS) within the clinical field enhances diagnostic efficiency and generates concise outputs for subsequent data mining. Nevertheless, the substantial domain expertise inherent in clinical texts makes it difficult for standard language models to deduce implicit medical relationships and determine accurate similarities. This paper introduces a graph-augmented cyclic learning framework designed for clinical similarity estimation. This approach can be easily integrated into state-of-the-art backbone language models, boosting performance by co-training with an auxiliary graph convolution network (GCN) that leverages domain knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating domain knowledge via the GCN and co-training strategy, achieving improvements of 16.3% and 27.9% over the Bio-clinical BERT baseline, respectively.

Over the past twenty years, leveraging knowledge sharing and transfer across multiple related tasks has gained significant importance. To effectively transfer information between tasks, it is essential to comprehend both the commonalities and distinctions among the respective domains. This paper introduces the concept of the \emph{performance gap}, a fresh and intuitive metric for quantifying the distance between learning tasks. Contrary to traditional measures like $\mathcal{H}$-divergence or discrepancy distance, which serve primarily to bound differences in expected risks, we demonstrate theoretically that the performance gap functions as a regularizer dependent on both data and algorithms. This approach controls model complexity and yields more refined theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, the performance gap offers new perspectives and inspires a novel strategy for knowledge transfer and sharing: gap minimization. We implement this principle through two algorithms: 1. \textbf{gapBoost}, a principled boosting method that explicitly reduces the performance gap between source and target domains for transfer learning; and 2. \textbf{gapMTNN}, a representation learning algorithm that recasts gap minimization as semantic conditional matching for multitask learning. Comprehensive evaluations on benchmark datasets for both transfer and multitask learning demonstrate that our proposed methods surpass existing baselines.

By applying the probability formulas of quantum trajectories directly, we establish an auxiliary open quantum system for a periodically driven system governed by the Floquet quantum master equation. This auxiliary framework produces a quantum trajectory ensemble consistent with the canonical one. Our findings indicate that, in the long-time limit, despite modifications to the Lindblad operators, the coherent dynamics of the auxiliary system mirror those of the original system. A periodically driven two-level system serves as an illustration of this construction.

The equilibrium bunch lengths, typically on the order of tens of picoseconds in contemporary light sources, constrain the spectral capabilities of superradiant methods for investigating materials and biological specimens. Specifically, producing terahertz radiation holds promise for pump-probe experiments. By leveraging self-wakes created within precisely designed structures, one can manipulate both the bunch length and profile, thereby substantially enhancing high-frequency spectral components. Numerical simulations reveal the existence of self-consistent steady states achievable through passive corrugated or dielectric structures. This methodology offers promising applications for generating superradiant terahertz radiation and pulse shaping within circular accelerators.

Although neural conditional language generation models have reached state-of-the-art performance in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), they remain heavily reliant on the quality of parallel training data. When exposed to low-quality datasets, these models frequently generate various errors, most notably hallucinations—outputs that appear fluent yet bear no relation to the source text. Such errors are especially hazardous because they can be mistaken for correct translations, particularly by readers unfamiliar with the source language. This study presents a case investigation into model understanding and regularization techniques aimed at mitigating hallucinations in NMT. Initially, we employ feature attribution methods to analyze the behavior of an NMT model prone to hallucinations. Subsequently, we utilize these insights to develop a novel loss function that significantly reduces hallucinations without necessitating retraining the model from the ground up.

The significance of utilizing unmanned vehicles for victim search and localization in disaster zones, such as earthquake-affected areas, is increasing. Navigating autonomously in these environments presents distinct challenges, primarily the detection of irregular obstacles like street debris, road cracks, and water puddles. This study evaluates several state-of-the-art Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) models on mobile embedded platforms specifically designed for self-navigation in terrains with highly irregular obstacles. We assess these models based on accuracy, performance, and energy efficiency, while also proposing optimizations for our custom vision system. Furthermore, we analyze the trade-offs among these models across various mobile platforms capable of autonomous navigation. To facilitate safe navigation, we have compiled a novel annotated image database of diverse earthquake-impacted regions, distinguishing it from traditional road damage datasets. Using this database, we trained multiple state-of-the-art semantic segmentation models to identify obstacles unique to earthquake zones. Based on statistical analysis and trade-off evaluations, we selected an optimal Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model for mobile vehicular platforms, applying it to both low-power and ultra-low-power configurations. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to address the unique challenges of edge-based self-navigation for mobile vehicles in earthquake-struck areas, detailing impacts on accuracy, performance, and energy consumption. Our proposed database and trained models are now publicly accessible.

We present the inaugural quasioptical simulations of wave beams propagating through hot plasma, utilizing the specialized code PARADE (PAraxial RAy DEscription) [Phys. Plasmas 26, 072112 (2019)]. This software stands alone for its ability to concurrently address the inhomogeneity of the dissipation rate across the beam and mode conversion. Our findings demonstrate that variations in the dissipation rate cause beams to deviate from their trajectories predicted by cold plasma models, while simultaneously coupling the two electromagnetic modes—a phenomenon previously overlooked. Furthermore, we introduce a streamlined method for handling dissipation-rate inhomogeneity, offering a computationally efficient solution that facilitates the analysis of real-world experiments.

Current methods for modeling moist air thermodynamics often rely on approximations that compromise thermodynamic consistency, causing violations of the first and second laws or introducing other irregularities. Recently, a solution to this inconsistency has been proposed: utilizing thermodynamic potentials defined by their natural variables to derive all thermodynamic quantities and relations. This study extends that approach to unapproximated moist air thermodynamics as well as two prevalent approximations: the constant $\kappa$ method and the dry heat capacities method. The consistent constant $\kappa$ approximation is notably advantageous because, when employing virtual potential temperature ($\theta_v$) as the thermodynamic variable, it yields adiabatic dynamics reliant solely on total mass, regardless of how water exists in different forms. Furthermore, this paper synthesizes a broad range of existing literature on thermodynamics in atmospheric modeling. We aim to provide a comprehensive reference for applying thermodynamic potentials in atmospheric modeling, specifically focusing on the three systems examined herein.

Machine Learning (ML) workflows depend on supplying input data for model consumption. Historically, this data preprocessing occurs on the same machine as the ML computation. However, when resources are inadequate to process data rapidly, this step becomes a bottleneck, slowing down the overall computation and wasting scarce ML hardware like GPUs and TPUs.

This paper introduces tf.data service, a disaggregated input processing service built upon tf.data. Beyond detailing the design and implementation of a system that separates preprocessing from ML computation, our work provides: (1) empirical evidence from production workloads demonstrating the necessity of disaggregation, along with a quantitative assessment of its impact on performance and costs; (2) advantages of disaggregation extending beyond horizontal scaling; and (3) an analysis of tf.data service's deployment at Google, including lessons learned and future research directions.

We demonstrate that horizontally scaling data processing with tf.data service eliminates input bottlenecks, delivering speedups of up to 110x and reducing job costs by as much as 89x. Additionally, we show that the service supports computation reuse via data sharing across ML jobs sharing identical pipelines (such as hyperparameter tuning tasks), achieving this without performance penalties while lowering total resource costs. Finally, we illustrate that advanced features of tf.data service can enhance non-input-bound jobs; specifically, coordinated data reads through the service can provide up to 2x speedups and cost savings for NLP workloads.

Email fraud, a significant driver of cybercrime, inflicts considerable annual economic damage. To combat these criminals, "scam-baiters" volunteer to act as victims, engaging scammers in lengthy, futile dialogues to divert their focus. In an effort to enhance scam-baiting efficiency and mitigate email fraud, we created and deployed a scalable mailserver capable of executing these interactions autonomously. By implementing three distinct reply strategies powered by different models, we conducted a one-month experiment that successfully elicited 150 messages from 130 unique scammers. Our analysis compares how each strategy attracts and retains scammer attention, highlighting the tradeoffs between human-crafted and automatically generated responses. Furthermore, we have released both our platform and a dataset comprising conversations between our automated baiters and real scammers to facilitate future research in online fraud prevention.

We calculate the existential completion for a primary doctrine, demonstrating that the resulting 2-monad is lax-idempotent and that the 2-category of existential doctrines is isomorphic to the 2-category of algebras for this monad. Furthermore, we establish that the existential completion of an elementary doctrine remains elementary. Lastly, we generalize the concept of exact completion, originally defined for elementary existential doctrines, to apply to any elementary doctrine.

This study provides an analytical examination of pattern formation within higher-order lumps of the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I equation at asymptotically large times. For a wide range of these higher-order lumps, two distinct solution patterns emerge as time progresses toward infinity. The first pattern consists of fundamental lumps organized into triangular configurations, which are analytically characterized by the root structures of Yablonskii-Vorob'ev polynomials; this arrangement undergoes a reversal along the x-axis as time transitions from large negative to large positive values. The second pattern features fundamental lumps arranged in non-triangular shapes within the outer region, described by nonzero-root structures of Wronskian-Hermit polynomials, potentially accompanied by fundamental lumps in triangular formations inside the inner region, governed by Yablonskii-Vorob'ev polynomial roots. As time evolves from large negative to large positive, the outer non-triangular pattern exchanges its x and y directions, whereas the inner triangular pattern, if present, reverses its orientation along the x-axis. Comparisons between these predicted large-time patterns and actual solutions reveal excellent agreement.

We introduce Winoground, a new dataset and task designed to assess the visio-linguistic compositional reasoning capabilities of vision and language models. The task requires matching two images to two captions, where the captions contain the exact same set of words but in different orders. This dataset was meticulously curated by expert annotators and annotated with a comprehensive set of fine-grained tags to facilitate performance analysis. Our evaluation of a diverse array of state-of-the-art models reveals that, unexpectedly, none perform significantly better than random chance. This indicates that current models lack the anticipated proficiency in visio-linguistic compositional reasoning. We conducted an in-depth analysis to derive insights for addressing these limitations in future work. Our goal is for Winoground to become a valuable benchmark for advancing the field. The dataset can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/winoground.

This technical report details the proceedings and discussions of the Second Workshop on Sustainable Software for Science: Practice and Experiences (WSSSPE2). The document outlines an alternative submission and review methodology, covers two keynote addresses, a series of lightning talks, and thematic discussions on sustainability, including software development experiences, credit and incentives, reproducibility and reuse, and code testing and review. For each theme, the report catalogs proposed tangible actions aimed at driving change. The workshop acknowledged the ubiquitous reliance on scientific software in top-tier global research and examined various perspectives on sustainability, identifying key enablers and barriers based on participant experiences. Furthermore, the report outlines recommendations for new requirements, such as software credit files and prize frameworks, to enhance sustainable software engineering practices. A significant consensus emerged that formal software development or engineering training is uncommon among practitioners. Consequently, substantial efforts are needed to foster community through software and technical training, expand its scope, and integrate it more effectively into graduate education. Additionally, journals should establish policies to enhance reproducibility, while reviewers must demand sufficient data and software access from authors to verify results. To facilitate this, the report compiles a set of criteria for journals to provide reviewers, streamlining the evaluation of software submitted as "Software Papers."

This report details the most recent findings from ATLAS and CMS regarding Higgs boson couplings to fermions. The discussion covers decays into tau lepton pairs and bottom quark pairs, along with observations on ttH production. Additionally, the report includes tests of CP invariance and searches for lepton flavor-violating decays, concluding with an overview of future Higgs analyses planned for the High Luminosity LHC. The primary results rely on 2016 LHC data acquired at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{\mathrm{s}}=13~\mathrm{TeV}$, with an integrated luminosity of approximately 36$~\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$.

The rapid expansion of multimedia publishing within our interconnected world has heightened the danger of sensitive data leakage and misuse, thereby intensifying the necessity to safeguard information from unauthorized exposure. Data sanitization, which involves obfuscating or eliminating sensitive elements, serves as a critical strategy to reduce the severe consequences of potential security and privacy threats. This paper offers a comprehensive review of mechanisms intended to protect digital visual media, such as images and videos, including the attacks targeting these methods and viable countermeasures. The systematic organization presented, combined with an analysis of current challenges and future research avenues, is poised to facilitate further scholarly investigation.

This study computes the contributions to the branching ratio of $B_s \to \gamma\gamma$ arising from charged Pseudo-Goldstone bosons within a one-generation Technicolor framework. We observe that the theoretical branching ratio, $BR(B_s\to\gamma\gamma)$, incorporating the effects of the PGBs $P^\pm$ and $P^{\pm}_8$, deviates significantly from Standard Model predictions. These new physics contributions can amplify the Standard Model result by two to three orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the decay $B_s\to \gamma\gamma$ serves as a viable probe to detect new physics signals originating from the Technicolor model.

This study presents an analysis of theoretical uncertainties in four-boson processes at the one-loop level, incorporating transverse polarization. The calculations employ a helicity amplitudes approach for Standard Model 4-boson interactions mediated by fermion and boson loops, explicitly accounting for the non-zero masses of the loop particles. The resulting predictions are applicable across a broad energy spectrum and cover arbitrary regions of the phase space, including extreme limits. Uncertainty estimates were derived using the novel Monte-Carlo tool SANCphot, which simulates $\gamma\gamma$ collisions with final states $\gamma\gamma$, $\gamma Z$, and $ZZ$ specifically adapted for polarized photon beams.

Since Bitcoin's emergence in 2009, more than 6,000 cryptocurrency projects have emerged. The crypto landscape is unique in that numerous competitors provide similar services while asserting distinct advantages, such as enhanced scalability, rapid transactions, and improved security. However, the question remains whether these projects genuinely deliver unique features and meaningful improvements. To address this, we performed a large-scale empirical study examining code maintenance, originality, and security across 592 crypto projects. Our findings indicate that approximately half of these projects have not seen updates in the past six months, and over a two-year period, about three-quarters either vanished or were identified as scams or inactive. Additionally, we analyzed whether security vulnerabilities patched in Bitcoin were similarly addressed in other projects. We discovered that roughly 80% of the 510 C-language-based cryptocurrency projects contain at least one unpatched vulnerability, with an average remediation time of 237.8 days. Among these 510 altcoins, at least 157 appear to be forks of Bitcoin, with about one-third containing only minor modifications from the original. As case studies, we conducted an in-depth analysis of 20 altcoins (such as Litecoin, FujiCoin, and Feathercoin) similar to the Bitcoin version used for forking. Approximately half of these failed to implement any technically significant changes, thereby failing to adhere to the promises outlined in their whitepapers, such as the adoption of Proof of Stake.

X-ray observations of galaxy clusters offer valuable insights into gaseous turbulent motions, their physical scales, and the underlying processes involved. High-resolution, spatially-resolved spectral measurements of X-ray emission lines serve as diagnostic tools for understanding turbulence within emitting atmospheres. Because these processes operate on scales comparable to the objects themselves, uncertainties in these physical parameters are constrained by sample variance, which depends on the number of observational measurements. We propose a complementary approach to estimating sample variance by combining repeated numerical simulations (specifically Monte-Carlo sampling) with new analytical developments for line diagnostics. Our model assumes a "turbulent gas cloud" characterized by isotropic, uniform turbulence described by a universal Kolmogorov power spectrum with random amplitudes and phases within an optically thin medium. By following a straightforward prescription for the four-term correlation of Fourier coefficients, we derive general expressions for the sample mean and variance of line centroid shifts, line broadening, and projected velocity structure functions. We validate these results numerically using Monte-Carlo simulations based on two popular gas emissivity models derived from the beta-model. The resulting generic expressions for sample variance in line centroid shifts and broadening across arbitrary apertures align with simulations within their applicable ranges. Furthermore, we provide and verify generic expressions for the mean and variance of the structure function. Finally, we apply these findings to forecast the capabilities of future Athena/X-IFU and XRISM/Resolve instruments in using sensitive, spatially-resolved spectroscopy to probe the inertial range of turbulent velocity cascades in Coma-like galaxy clusters.

With the rising frequency of cyber-attacks, cybersecurity has become a critical priority for businesses worldwide. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), particularly Deep Learning (DL), serve as essential technologies for cyber-defense by enhancing threat detection and offering actionable recommendations to analysts. To accelerate the integration of AI/ML into cybersecurity and develop robust defense systems, a global collaboration among industry, academia, and government is imperative. This paper examines various deep learning methods used for network intrusion detection and presents a new DL framework designed for cybersecurity applications.

This study calculates the transcendental lattices for singular K3 surfaces within three specific pencils: the Apéry-Fermi pencil, characterized by a transcendental lattice of $U\oplus \langle 12 \rangle$; Verrill's pencil, with a lattice of $U \oplus \langle 6 \rangle$; and a third pencil associated with Verrill's, featuring a lattice of $U \oplus \langle 24 \rangle$. The analysis yields several corollaries, including instances where singular K3 surfaces appear in multiple pencils or function as Kummer surfaces derived from K3 surfaces belonging to a different pencil.

Descriptions are frequently included with recommendations to facilitate user discovery. However, automatically generating music playlists (such as personalized ones) creates the challenge of creating corresponding descriptions. This paper introduces a method termed music captioning for generating these playlist descriptions. The proposed approach leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to extract and utilize information from each individual track.

Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches.

To investigate non-Euclidean extensions of higher-order topological phenomena, we develop a model for higher-order topological insulators within hyperbolic lattices by disrupting the time-reversal symmetry (TRS) inherent in quantum spin Hall insulators.
