The five-band framework enables the estimation of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) strength in $\rm Mg_2X$, revealing its dependence on the atomic number of $\rm X$ and strain levels. Additionally, band structure calculations highlight significant strain-induced band gap tuning and splitting. For instance, a $-10\%$ compressive strain opens a band gap at the $\Gamma$ point in the metallic $\rm Mg_2Pb$, while a $+10\%$ tensile strain closes the semiconducting band gap in $\rm Mg_2Si$. Furthermore, a $+5\%$ tensile strain eliminates the three-fold degeneracy of valence bands at the $\Gamma$ point in semiconducting $\rm Mg_2Ge$.

Within the stable category of bounded below $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules, each module arises as an extension involving a component with trivial $Q_0$-Margolis homology and another with trivial $Q_1$-Margolis homology. We demonstrate that bounded below $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules of finite type possessing trivial $Q_1$-Margolis homology are stably equivalent to direct sums of suspensions drawn from a specific family of $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules. Every module in this family consists of multiple copies of $\mathcal{A}(1) /\!/ \mathcal{A}(0)$ connected via the action of $Sq^1 \in \mathcal{A}(1)$. This classification theorem facilitates the simplification of computations for $h_0^{-1}\mathrm{Ext}_{\mathcal{A}(1)}^{\bullet, \bullet}\big(-, \mathbb{F}_2\big)$ and establishes necessary criteria for lifting $\mathcal{A}(1)$-modules to $\mathcal{A}$-modules. Furthermore, we examine a Davis--Mahowald spectral sequence that converges to $h_0^{-1}\mathrm{Ext}_{\mathcal{A}(1)}^{\bullet, \bullet}(M, \mathbb{F}_2)$ for any bounded below $\mathcal{A}(1)$-module $M$, where the differentials identify obstructions to such liftings. Additionally, we present a formula for the second differential.

The International Olympiad in Cryptography, NSUCRYPTO, is a unique event featuring scientific mathematical challenges for professionals, as well as university and high school students from around the world. Its primary goal is to engage young researchers in tackling intriguing and demanding modern cryptographic issues. In 2020, marking its seventh iteration, the competition awarded prizes and diplomas to 84 individuals in the initial round and 49 teams in the final round, representing 32 nations. This paper presents the problems and their solutions from NSUCRYPTO 2020, covering topics such as cipher and hash function attacks, protocols, permutations, and primality testing. Additionally, we discuss several open problems concerning JPEG encoding, the Miller–Rabin primality test, special bases in vector spaces, and AES-GCM. During the Olympiad, a modified Miller–Rabin primality test problem was fully solved, while the challenge regarding the identification of special bases was partially resolved.

Rapidly ejected matter from binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers, occurring within less than 10 milliseconds, produces unique electromagnetic signatures alongside gravitational waves, offering a definitive method to differentiate BNS events from neutron-star–black-hole mergers. This study introduces new first-principles models of kilonova precursors and afterglows, derived from three-dimensional general-relativistic magneto-hydrodynamic simulations of BNS mergers. These simulations incorporate tabulated, temperature-dependent equations of state (EOSs) that vary by composition, account for weak interactions, and utilize approximate neutrino transport. We examined dynamical mass ejection in 1.35–1.35 solar mass binaries, representative of Galactic double-neutron star systems and aligned with the characteristics of GW170817, utilizing three nuclear EOSs covering the full range of permitted compactness. Calculations involving nuclear reaction networks confirm a robust second-to-third peak in the r-process. Our results indicate the production of approximately $1 \times 10^{-6}$ solar masses of fast ejecta ($v > 0.6c$), which generate broad-band synchrotron emission over roughly a year, aligning with recent tentative observations of excess X-ray and radio emission post-GW170817. Additionally, we identified $2 \times 10^{-5}$ solar masses of free neutrons capable of driving a kilonova precursor within an hour of the merger. Relativistic effects, previously overlooked, are predicted to enhance early UV/optical brightness by a factor of a few, with significant increases persisting up to 10 hours post-merger, suggesting viable prospects for detection by UV/optical telescopes like Swift or ULTRASAT out to 250 Mpc. Furthermore, a recently proposed opacity boost from highly ionized lanthanides at ~70,000 K is unlikely to impact the early kilonova lightcurve given the derived ejecta structures. Finally, azimuthal compositional inhomogeneities in the dynamical ejecta for soft EOSs—specifically "lanthanide/actinide pockets"—could have observable implications for both early kilonova and late-time nebular emission.

Investigating the dynamic behavior of bubbles within the interstellar medium is crucial for comprehending feedback mechanisms driven by star formation in galaxies. Current integral field spectroscopy of nearby star-forming galaxies has identified numerous expanding bubbles and superbubbles, characterized by localized increases in gas velocity dispersion. However, limited angular resolution frequently hinders the accurate measurement of expansion velocities in galaxies beyond the Local Group, even when spectroscopic resolution is adequate. This paper introduces a technique capable of determining the expansion velocities of bubbles surrounding massive stars and clusters by analyzing local variations in gas velocity dispersion. The method is adapted for Fabry-Perot interferometers utilized with the 6-meter telescope at the Special Astrophysical Observatory of the Russian Academy of Sciences, as well as for any integral field spectrograph featuring a Gaussian line spread function. We apply this approach to examine the kinematics of ionized superbubbles and the sole known supernova remnant in the IC 1613 galaxy. The resulting kinematic age estimate for the supernova remnant (approximately 3,100 years) aligns closely with independent prior estimates derived from X-ray data.

We examine model-independent collider bounds on the effective couplings of leptophilic dark matter (LDM), focusing on its production at a prospective electron-positron linear collider using both polarized and unpolarized beams within mono-photon and mono-$Z$ channels. Our results demonstrate that these future collider constraints largely complement existing direct and indirect detection limits on LDM, potentially achieving the highest sensitivity to date for LDM in the low-mass regime (below $\sim$ 10 GeV).

This paper investigates the computation of the majority function $\mathrm{MAJ}_n$ on $n$ bits using depth-two formulas, where each gate computes a majority function on at most $k$ inputs. We introduce a formula that establishes the first nontrivial upper bound for this problem, specifically with $k = \frac{2}{3} n + 4$, thereby resolving an open question from [Kulikov, Podolskii, 2017]. Furthermore, we analyze the problem in an adaptive setting, where the goal is to minimize the number of queries to $\mathrm{MAJ}_k$ on any subset. We provide a simple lower bound of $\lceil n/k \rceil$ queries for this scenario and propose two algorithms: the first requires approximately $2\frac{n}{k} \log k$ queries when restricted to standard majority functions, while the second achieves $\frac{n}{k} \log k$ queries by allowing adjustments to the majority function's threshold.

The Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) provides a robust framework for physics beyond the Standard Model, offering consistent explanations for the Higgs signals observed at the LHC. This study examines the decays of neutral Higgs bosons into Standard Model fermions and gauge bosons, utilizing full one-loop calculations of decay widths that incorporate leading higher-order QCD corrections. We begin by outlining the technical methodology, comparing our predictions with existing public tools, conducting a numerical analysis, and evaluating remaining theoretical uncertainties. Specifically, we demonstrate that radiative corrections dominate the decay widths of doublet-heavy Higgs bosons into electroweak gauge bosons, rendering common tree-level approximations in phenomenological studies inadequate. Furthermore, we analyze the phenomenological implications of a mostly singlet-like state with a mass below $125\,$GeV, a frequent scenario in the NMSSM. The potential existence of a singlet-dominated state near or just below $100\,$GeV carries significant implications, potentially explaining the $2.3\sigma$ local excess from LEP's $e^+e^-\to Z(H\to b\bar{b})$ searches at $\sim 98\,$GeV and the recent CMS diphoton excess in the same mass range, while simultaneously alleviating the "Little Hierarchy" problem.

Range-aggregate queries, which seek structural insights about points within a specified region $B$ using an aggregate function $F(\cdot)$, are crucial in various applications. This paper addresses range-aggregate queries in high-dimensional spaces for two specific functions: (1) identifying the farthest point in $P \cap B$ relative to a query point $q$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and (2) computing the minimum enclosing ball (MEB) of $P \cap B$. For the first problem, termed the In-Range Farthest Point (IFP) Query, we introduce a bi-criteria approximation scheme. Given any $\epsilon > 0$ for the distance approximation and $\gamma > 0$ for the range expansion tolerance, we preprocess the point set $P$ into a data structure of size $\tilde{O}_{\epsilon,\gamma}(dn^{1+\rho})$ in $\tilde{O}_{\epsilon,\gamma}(dn^{1+\rho})$ time. Upon receiving a query ball $B$ and point $q$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the structure returns a point $p$ in $\tilde{O}_{\epsilon,\gamma}(dn^{\rho})$ time that is a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximation of the farthest point in $q$ among all points in the $(1+\gamma)$-expanded ball $B(1+\gamma)$. Here, $0 < \rho < 1$ is a constant dependent on $\epsilon$ and $\gamma$, with hidden big-O constants relying solely on $\epsilon$, $\gamma$, and $\text{Polylog}(nd)$. Regarding the second problem, we demonstrate that the IFP approach can be adapted to achieve a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for the MEB with comparable time and space complexities.

This study examines how an additional longitudinal degree of freedom influences perturbation evolution within mimetic gravity. Using a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) background, we analyze linear perturbations via the spherically symmetric collapse formalism. By selecting an appropriate mimetic field potential, we solve the linear perturbed field equations to express the matter density contrast ($\delta_m$) as a function of redshift ($z$). Our results show that $\delta_m$ begins growing early and accelerates more rapidly than in standard cosmology as the universe expands, a behavior attributed to the extra gravitational degree of freedom. However, at small redshifts, the growth rate function remains lower than that of the $\Lambda$CDM model. We further investigate the potential's impact on density abundance, the deceleration parameter, and the jerk parameter, concluding that the mimetic potential can act as dark energy (DE) while modifying matter perturbation dynamics and cosmological parameters. Additionally, we explore the mass function and number counts of collapsed objects in this scenario. We find that models with a potential exhibit a smaller mass function compared to those without. As the DE contribution diminishes, the mass function begins to rise at earlier redshifts, indicating later halo formation. Consistent with hierarchical structure formation, we observe that more massive structures are less abundant and form at later times.

This manuscript presents a definite integral expressed through the Lerch function, incorporating logarithmic terms, powers, and polynomials. The findings are compiled into a table of definite integrals to facilitate easy reference for readers.

This study presents direct numerical simulations of quasi-one-dimensional bidirectional capillary-wave turbulence. Despite the absence of nontrivial three- and four-wave resonant interactions in this specific geometry, we demonstrate that energy transfer between scales persists, centered around the linear dispersion relation and broadened by nonlinear effects. The resulting wave spectrum exhibits a distinct power-law scaling with respect to wave number, aligning well with dimensional predictions for capillary-wave turbulence involving four-wave interactions. High-order correlation analyses, including bicoherence and tricoherence, quantitatively confirm the predominance of four-wave quasi-resonant interactions. Additionally, the Kolmogorov-Zakharov spectrum constant is estimated numerically. We conclude that these findings represent the first numerical observation of anisotropic capillary-wave turbulence where four-wave interactions are the dominant mechanism.

Entanglement plays a pivotal role in numerous quantum applications, such as quantum information processing, simulating quantum many-body systems, and achieving enhanced sensing capabilities. Molecules are considered a promising platform for quantum science due to their complex internal structures and interactions; however, achieving deterministic entanglement of individually controlled molecules has remained a significant experimental hurdle. In this work, we present the first demonstration of on-demand entanglement for individually prepared molecules. By leveraging the electric dipolar interaction between molecule pairs generated via a reconfigurable optical tweezer array, we implement an entangling two-qubit gate to deterministically produce Bell pairs. These findings establish essential components required for quantum information processing, quantum spin model simulations, and quantum-enhanced sensing. Furthermore, these results pave the way for new opportunities, including utilizing trapped molecules for fundamental physics tests and investigating collisions and chemical reactions involving entangled matter.

The rise of machine learning has increased the prevalence of data-driven decision-making, yet training data often reflects human biases, leading to unfair model outcomes. This paper addresses this issue for decision trees and random forests by proposing a method that transforms these models into fair versions relative to a specific dataset, fairness metric, and sensitive attributes. We introduce \emph{FairRepair}, a tool grounded in automated program repair principles, which leverages an SMT solver to identify paths within decision trees where flipping outcomes enhances fairness. Experiments using the UCI Adult dataset confirm that FairRepair effectively scales to realistic models. Additionally, the tool offers formal guarantees regarding the soundness and completeness of its repair process. By repairing trees and forests derived from biased datasets, this fairness-guided technique assists organizations in detecting and correcting decision-making biases.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), resulting from the collapse of massive stars or the mergers of compact objects, represent the most luminous phenomena in the universe. Despite their brightness, the characteristics of the relativistic jets emitted by their central engines remain poorly understood. This study investigates how variations in jet structure—specifically the angular distribution of energy and velocity—influence observed GRB afterglow light curves. Utilizing the afterglowpy package, we simulate light curves for a range of jet configurations and provide a suite of models capable of explaining the coincident electromagnetic data from GW190814 (likely a background active galactic nucleus). Our findings highlight the critical need for broadband spectral and timing observations to differentiate between jet structure models, as well as the importance of high-resolution radio follow-up to distinguish genuine GRB afterglows from background sources that may produce similar signals.

Charm and beauty quarks, characterized by masses of 1.28 GeV/$\textit{c}^2$ and 4.18 GeV/$\textit{c}^2$ respectively, are generated during initial hard scattering events. Given their brief formation time ($\Delta t \sim0.1 fm/\textit{c}$) relative to the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) formation time ($\Delta t \sim0.3 fm/\textit{c}$) at the LHC, they traverse all phases of the hot, dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions. Consequently, measuring open charm and beauty production provides insights into QGP characteristics and explores the mass and color charge dependencies of parton energy loss within the medium. Additionally, because their masses ($m_c , m_b$) significantly exceed $\Lambda_{QCD}$, their production cross-sections in proton-proton collisions can be calculated using perturbative QCD, offering a robust validation of pQCD models. This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms behind charm quark production via the creation of $D^+$, $D^0$, $D^+_s$, and $\Lambda_c^+$ hadrons. Furthermore, to investigate charm quark hadronization, ratios such as $\Lambda_c^+$/$D^+$, $D_s^+$/$D^+$, $\Lambda_c^+$/$D^0$, and $D_s^+$/$D^0$ are analyzed. For this analysis, events were simulated using PYTHIA 8 for proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV, a tool that has demonstrated significant success in describing heavy-flavor particle production at LHC energies.

For complex dimensions of 3 or greater, we establish the geometric existence of generalized ALG complete non-compact Ricci-flat Kähler manifolds exhibiting Schwartz decay. This decay condition implies that the metric approaches an ALG model $\mathbb{C} \times Y$ (modulo a finite cyclic group action) at any polynomial rate, where $Y$ is a Calabi-Yau manifold. Consequently, for any $K3$ surface admitting a purely non-symplectic automorphism $\sigma$ of finite order, the Kähler crepant resolution of the orbifold $(\mathbb{C} \times K3) / \langle \sigma \rangle$ supports ALG Ricci-flat Kähler metrics with Schwartz decay, given that such resolutions exist in this context. Specifically, there are 39 integers where dividing $2\pi$ by each yields the asymptotic angle of an ALG Ricci-flat Kähler 3-fold with Schwartz decay. Additionally, we present a 1638-parameter family of ALG Ricci-flat Kähler 3-folds with an asymptotic angle of $\pi$ that realize 64 distinct triples of Betti numbers; these are isotrivially fibred by $K3$ surfaces equipped with a non-symplectic Nikulin involution. A simplified version of the local Kunneth formula for $H^{1,1}$, alongside the local $\partial\overline{\partial}$-lemma, underpins both the Schwartz decay and the construction of an isotrivial ansatz, which matches a Ricci-flat ALG model outside a compact set. Finally, the proof of Schwartz decay depends on the non-concentration of the Newtonian potential and cannot be directly extended to fibrations with higher-dimensional bases due to the presence of concentrating sequences of $L^2$-normalized eigenfunctions on unit round spheres of real dimension $\geq 2$.

Prescriptive process monitoring aims to optimize business operations by suggesting runtime interventions to avert negative outcomes or underperforming cases. While numerous methods have emerged recently, this paper conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to examine the current landscape. To organize the domain, the study introduces a framework for classifying these methods based on their performance objectives, metrics, intervention types, modeling techniques, data inputs, and policies. The review identifies key challenges and future research directions to improve the utility and applicability of such methods. Furthermore, the paper emphasizes the necessity of validating both established and novel approaches in real-world environments, expanding interventions beyond temporal and cost considerations, and designing policies that account for causality and second-order effects.

This study investigates unique gapped topological phases that exhibit $\mathbb{Z}_N$ fractional excitations similar to topologically ordered systems, but whose ground state degeneracy is contingent upon the system's local geometry. When these phases are mapped onto a 2D lattice formed by an arbitrary connected graph and a 1D line, we demonstrate that quasiparticle fusion rules correspond to the graph's Laplacian, with the count of superselection sectors determined by the Laplacian's kernel. Building on this, we derive that the ground state degeneracy equals $\bigl[N\times \prod_{i}\text{gcd}(N, p_i)\bigr]^2$, where $p_i$ represents the Laplacian's invariant factors exceeding one and gcd denotes the greatest common divisor. Additionally, we examine the braiding statistics of these quasiparticle excitations.

Dust attenuation exhibits significant variation across galaxies and remains elusive to theoretical models based on first principles. In Nagaraj et al. (2022), we introduced the first Bayesian population model for dust attenuation, utilizing spectral energy distribution (SED) fits of approximately 30,000 galaxies from the 3D-HST grism survey and incorporating stellar population properties and projected galaxy shape, with broadband photometry spanning from the rest-frame UV to the IR. This study applies that model to galaxies within the large-volume cosmological simulation TNG100. We generate a UVJ diagram and contrast it with a prior result derived from approximate radiative transfer applied to the same simulated galaxies. Our findings indicate that the UVJ diagram produced by our empirical model aligns more closely with observations than the previous approach, particularly regarding the number density of dusty star-forming galaxies. Furthermore, we construct intrinsic dust-free UVJ diagrams for both TNG and 3D-HST galaxies at z ~ 1, observing qualitative agreement alongside residual discrepancies at the 10-20% level. These discrepancies are primarily attributable to TNG galaxies having, on average, stellar populations that are 29% younger and metallicities 0.28 dex higher than those observed in real galaxies.

This study presents the initial search for supersymmetry targeting events characterized by a single soft, hadronically decaying $\tau$ lepton, one high-energy jet from initial-state radiation, and significant transverse momentum imbalance. Such signatures align with the direct or indirect production of scalar $\tau$ leptons ($\tilde{\tau}$) in supersymmetric frameworks featuring coannihilation between the $\tilde{\tau}$ and the lightest neutralino ($\tilde{\chi}^0_1$), a process capable of accounting for the observed dark matter relic density. The analysis utilizes an integrated luminosity of 77.2 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC during 2016 and 2017. Results are interpreted within a supersymmetric scenario where a small mass difference ($\Delta m$) exists between the chargino ($\tilde{\chi}^\pm_1$) or next-to-lightest neutralino ($\tilde{\chi}^0_2$) and the $\tilde{\chi}^0_1$, assuming the $\tilde{\tau}$ mass is the average of the $\tilde{\chi}^\pm_1$ and $\tilde{\chi}^0_1$ masses. The observed data agree with standard model background predictions. Consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits are established on the combined production cross sections of the $\tilde{\chi}^\pm_1$, $\tilde{\chi}^0_2$, and $\tilde{\tau}$ for $\Delta m(\tilde{\chi}^\pm_1, \tilde{\chi}^0_1) =$ 50 GeV. This yields a lower mass limit of 290 GeV for the $\tilde{\chi}^\pm_1$, representing the tightest constraint to date and exceeding previous bounds from LEP experiments.

We calculate the degree $0$ relative symplectic cohomology sheaf over the bases of nodal Lagrangian torus fibrations situated on four-dimensional symplectic cluster manifolds. Our results demonstrate that this sheaf corresponds to the pushforward of the structure sheaf of a specific rigid analytic manifold via a non-archimedean torus fibration. This rigid analytic manifold, termed the \emph{closed string mirror}, is derived canonically from the relative SH sheaf. Our approach avoids ad hoc analysis of holomorphic curves by instead leveraging general axiomatic properties to compute relative SH for local models. These axioms encompass previously known principles, such as the Mayer-Vietoris property and locality for complete embeddings, alongside novel findings like the Hartogs property and the holomorphic volume form preservation property associated with wall crossing in relative $SH$.

Deep learning serves as a robust method for retrieving missing data and solving complex inverse function challenges. Within natural language processing, this technique leverages contextual cues to infer information by maximizing likelihood. The recent "Tieq Viet" linguistic study, which sparked debate among researchers and the public, offers an ideal case study to showcase the capacity of deep learning to restore lost information. In this proposed system, standard Vietnamese consonants are substituted, causing a single written sentence to map onto multiple distinct standard Vietnamese sentences with varying meanings. Our objective is to evaluate whether a deep learning model can successfully reconstruct the original information when translating text from Vietnamese into the Tieq Viet format.

Nonlinear responses within condensed matter systems are extensively investigated due to their ability to reveal deep material insights and their potential for applications in diodes and high-frequency optical technologies. Although nonlinear behavior in noninteracting models has been thoroughly examined, the impact of strong correlations remains largely obscure, despite hypotheses suggesting these correlations amplify nonlinear effects. This study begins with an analytical derivation of nonlinear responses via Green's function techniques at finite temperatures. It subsequently highlights the challenges associated with incorporating dissipation through traditional approaches like the reduced density matrix method, specifically showing that the relaxation time approximation imposes significant constraints on optical response modeling. Ultimately, the work demonstrates that correlation phenomena—such as band structure renormalization and varying orbital or sublattice lifetimes—can substantially boost nonlinear responses and even invert the sign of nonlinear conductivity.

Segmenting the fetal cortical plate is critical for quantifying brain maturation and cortical folding. While manual segmentation or refining automatic results is labor-intensive and slow, automatic segmentation faces significant hurdles due to the low resolution of reconstructed fetal MRI scans relative to the thinness of the cortical plate, partial volume effects, and the substantial morphological variations that occur as the brain develops during gestation. To alleviate the need for manual refinement, we propose a novel and robust deep learning segmentation approach. This method integrates new deep attentive modules featuring mixed-kernel convolutions into a fully convolutional neural network architecture that incorporates deep supervision and residual connections. We assessed the method quantitatively using various performance metrics and expert reviews. The results demonstrate that our approach surpasses several state-of-the-art deep learning models as well as advanced multi-atlas segmentation techniques. On reconstructed fetal brain MRI scans covering a gestational age range of 16 to 39 weeks, we achieved an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.87, an average Hausdorff distance of 0.96 mm, and an average symmetric surface difference of 0.28 mm. With a processing time of under one minute per brain, this method can significantly expedite large-scale investigations into normal and altered fetal cortical maturation and folding.

For a manifold with corners $X$, we associate a simplicial complex $\Sigma_X$ representing its corner structure. The reduced K-homology of this complex corresponds to the K-theory of the $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{K}_b(X)$ of b-compact operators on $X$, and the homology of $\Sigma_X$ is equivalent to the conormal homology of $X$. This note constructs a manifold with corners $X$ for any given finite abstract simplicial complex $\Sigma$ such that $\Sigma_X$ is isomorphic to $\Sigma$. Consequently, the homology and K-homology groups found in finite simplicial complexes also arise as the conormal homology of manifolds with corners and the K-theory of their associated b-compact operator algebras. Notably, these groups may include torsion.

We develop a generalized interacting framework for Barrow Holographic Dark Energy (BHDE), utilizing the Hubble horizon as the infrared cutoff. This study examines the cosmological evolution of a flat Friedmann-Lema\^itre-Robertson-Walker universe containing pressureless dark matter, BHDE, and a radiation fluid. The interaction between dark sectors is assumed to be non-gravitational, adhering to both the second law of thermodynamics and the Le Chatelier-Braun principle. We investigate key model parameters, including the BHDE density parameter, equation of state, deceleration parameter, jerk parameter, and the square of the sound speed. Our results demonstrate that the model effectively reconstructs the thermal history of the universe and aligns with current observational data for specific parameter values, presenting a viable candidate for dark energy. Finally, we analyze the thermodynamics of this framework, with particular emphasis on the validity of the generalized second law.

This research investigates Hamiltonicity within graphs formed by combining a deterministic $n$-vertex graph $H$ featuring linear degrees and a $d$-dimensional random geometric graph $G^d(n,r)$, where $d\geq1$. We establish an asymptotically optimal threshold for the minimum value of $r$ ensuring that $H\cup G^d(n,r)$ is Hamiltonian almost surely. Furthermore, our proof yields a linear-time algorithm capable of identifying a Hamilton cycle in these graphs.

Leveraging the distinct advantages of network coding and compressed sensing, their integration promises significant advancements for future 5G networks. This study evaluates the efficacy of combining these techniques within cluster-based wireless sensor networks, specifically accounting for temporal and spatial correlations. The primary objective is to enhance compression efficiency by minimizing payload size through temporal compression and decreasing transmission counts via practical network coding. To further limit transmissions, cluster heads employ a low-complexity spatial pre-coding strategy that transmits packets with a specific probability. Benchmark comparisons were conducted, and simulations using the NS3 environment confirm that the proposed method drastically reduces the number of transmitted packets within the cluster topology while maintaining a very high reconstruction SNR.

The Rubik's Cube stands as the world's most renowned puzzle, with two key areas of study being God's Number—the fewest moves required to solve any configuration—and the first law of cubology, which determines solvability. This work revises prior formulations of the first law to apply to $n \times n \times n$ Rubik's Cubes, establishing both necessary and sufficient conditions for solvability. Additionally, we calculate the order of the Rubik's Cube group and the total number of unique configurations for the $n \times n \times n$ variant. Finally, by combining group theory with a counting argument, we derive a lower bound for God's Number.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered the most significant technological revolution in history. Within the financial sector, it offers substantial opportunities to enhance customer experiences, democratize access to financial services, strengthen consumer protection, and markedly improve risk management. Although deploying cutting-edge machine learning models has never been easier, creating and implementing systems that effectively support real-world financial applications remains difficult. This challenge stems largely from a lack of transparency and explainability, which are critical for establishing trustworthy technology, particularly in research focused on credit risk management applications. This paper implements two advanced, post-hoc, model-agnostic explainability techniques—Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)—to evaluate machine learning-based credit scoring models using an open-access dataset from the US-based P2P lending platform, Lending Club. Specifically, we utilize LIME to provide local explanations and SHAP to generate both local and global interpretations. We analyze the results in depth, presenting multiple comparison scenarios by employing various kernels for explaining graphs derived from SHAP values. Furthermore, we address the practical challenges involved in deploying these state-of-the-art Explainable AI (XAI) methods and document them for future use. We have strived to meticulously document every technical aspect of this research while simultaneously offering a general summary of the conclusions.

Based on a dataset of roughly 2 million phenomenological equations of state that align with observational data, we develop novel universal relations that are insensitive to the equation of state, linking the multipolar tidal deformability parameters ($\Lambda_l$) of neutron stars for higher-order multipoles ($l = 5,6,7,8$). We validate a universal connection between the radius of a $1.4 M_\odot$ neutron star ($R_{1.4}$), the binary's reduced tidal parameter ($\tilde{\Lambda}$), and the chirp mass. This relationship is generalized to encompass a wide range of chirp masses and the radii of isolated neutron stars across various masses ($R_M$). Our findings reveal an optimal mass $M$ for each chirp mass $\mathcal{M}$ that minimizes the uncertainty in estimating $R_M$ via these relations. Finally, we examine the practical applications and implications of these findings for the upcoming LIGO O4 observations and future third-generation detectors.

The representation theory of the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$ possesses a notably combinatorial character, where both conjugacy classes and irreducible characters correspond to integer partitions $\lambda \vdash n$. We define class functions on $\mathfrak{S}_n$ that enumerate specific tilings of Young diagrams. This counting perspective yields a uniform expression for these functions within the ring of character polynomials, as established in \cite{murnaghanfirst}, with contemporary treatments available in \cite{orellana-zabrocki}. We establish a relationship among these combinatorial class functions in the (virtual) character ring. Leveraging this relation, we prove Goupil's generating function identity \cite{goupil}, which subsequently enables the derivation of Rosas' formula \cite{rosas} for Kronecker coefficients associated with hook shape and two-row partitions.

This study examines the overcharging issue and thermodynamic properties of five-dimensional spherically symmetric topological black holes within an extended phase space, utilizing the absorption of scalar and fermionic particles. By treating the cosmological constant as a variable pressure, its conjugate is identified as thermodynamic volume, thereby recovering the first law of thermodynamics. However, the second law is found to be violated in the extended phase space for both extremal and near-extremal black holes. The feasibility of overcharging is assessed through the persistence of event horizons, which are defined by the metric component $f(r)$. Analysis of the minimal values of this metric component at the final stage demonstrates that neither extremal nor near-extremal black holes can be overcharged.

This paper addresses the challenge of learning a named entity recognition (NER) tagger using noisy labels derived from multiple weak supervision sources. While these sources are cost-effective, their labels often suffer from incompleteness, inaccuracies, and contradictions, hindering the development of precise NER models. To overcome this, we introduce a Conditional Hidden Markov Model (CHMM), an unsupervised method capable of inferring true labels from multi-source noisy data. CHMM extends the traditional Hidden Markov Model by integrating the contextual capabilities of pre-trained language models. Specifically, it learns token-level transition and emission probabilities based on BERT embeddings to deduce latent true labels from noisy inputs. We further enhance CHMM through an alternate-training strategy (CHMM-ALT), which fine-tunes a BERT-NER model using CHMM-inferred labels and subsequently utilizes this BERT-NER output as an additional weak source to retrain CHMM. Experiments across four NER benchmarks from diverse domains demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art weakly supervised NER models.

Radiology reports are essential for guiding patient care in clinical settings, yet composing them places a significant burden on radiologists. To address this, we introduce an automatic, multi-modal system for generating reports from chest x-rays. Inspired by the strong correlation between report descriptions and specific visual details, our method employs two key components: (i) a Learned knowledge base that automatically distills and reconstructs medical knowledge from textual embeddings without requiring manual intervention, and (ii) Multi-modal alignment, which explicitly uses textual embeddings to optimize the visual feature space and ensure semantic consistency among images, disease labels, and reports. We assessed the model's performance using both natural language generation and clinical efficacy metrics on the public IU-Xray and MIMIC-CXR datasets. Our ablation study confirms that each module enhances report quality, and the combined approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods across nearly all metrics.

First-order gradient methods, such as SGD, suffer from slow convergence and pathological curvature, prompting the development of faster second-order optimization techniques that maintain generalization performance. However, despite their batch-size-independent convergence rates, these second-order algorithms are often impractical due to the high computational cost per iteration required to invert the loss function's Hessian. Recent advances by [ZMG19,CGH+19] addressed this overhead by creating an $O(mn^2)$-time second-order algorithm for two-layer overparametrized networks with polynomial width $m$. We further accelerate the [CGH+19] approach to achieve an $\tilde{O}(mn)$-time backpropagation algorithm for mildly overparametrized ReLU networks, which scales near-linearly with the dimension of the full gradient (Jacobian) matrix. Our method reformulates the Gauss-Newton iteration as an $\ell_2$-regression problem and employs Fast-JL type dimension reduction to precondition the underlying Gram matrix in time independent of $M$, enabling the discovery of a sufficiently accurate solution via first-order conjugate gradient. This work demonstrates that advanced randomized linear algebra techniques, previously instrumental in breakthroughs for convex optimization (including ERM, LPs, and Regression), can also be effectively applied to deep learning.

This study examines the United Kingdom's Northern Powerhouse strategy (NPS), a decentralization initiative launched in 2010 aimed at enhancing connectivity among English Northern cities. The research specifically investigates economic interactions within this region, characterized by ownership ties between firms, from the strategy's inception to the present. Findings indicate a modest rise in the intensity of regional economic patterns in the North, despite a transition away from the area's traditional manufacturing foundation. These outcomes offer policy-makers insights for the future execution of the NPS.

We establish a general finiteness result concerning the ordered abelian group of tropical functions defined on the skeleta within Berkovich analytifications of algebraic varieties. Our methodology relies on the framework of stable completions of algebraic varieties, which represent a model-theoretic analogue of Berkovich analytifications; we first demonstrate a comparable result for this latter framework, from which the primary finiteness statement follows.

The rainbow connection number, denoted as rc(G), for a connected graph G represents the minimum number of colors required to color its edges such that every pair of vertices is linked by at least one path containing no two edges of the same color. In this note, we establish that for every bridgeless graph G with radius r, rc(G) is at most r(r + 2). We prove that this bound is optimal for rc(G) as a function of r, applicable not only to bridgeless graphs but also to graphs with any higher level of connectivity. It is worth noting that for general 1-connected graphs, rc(G) can exceed the radius by an arbitrary amount, as illustrated by the star graph. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for every bridgeless graph G with radius r and chordality k (defined as the size of the largest induced cycle), rc(G) does not exceed rk. It is established that determining rc(G) is an NP-Hard problem [Chakraborty et al., 2009]. In this work, we introduce an approximation algorithm with a factor of (r+3) that operates in O(nm) time, and another with a factor of (d+3) running in O(dm) time, both capable of assigning rainbow colors to any connected graph G comprising n vertices and m edges, characterized by diameter d and radius r.

This study investigates the impact of initial perturbations on Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI), Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI), and their coupled form (RTKHI) using a multiple-relaxation-time discrete Boltzmann model. To analyze these effects, six distinct perturbation interfaces were designed. The detailed examination of the coupled RTKHI system relies on the mean heat flux strength ($D_{3,1}$). The research concentrates on two primary areas: (i) the dominant mechanism during the early phase of RTKHI, and (ii) the transition point from KHI-like to RTI-like behavior in scenarios where KHI prevails initially but RTI dominates later. Findings indicate that the early-stage mechanism is closely tied to the initial interface's shape, characterized by the bilateral contact angle ($\theta_{1}$) and the middle contact angle ($\theta_{2}$). Furthermore, inverted parabolic and inverted ellipse perturbations ($\theta_{1}<90$) exert a stronger influence on the RTKHI transition point compared to other interface types.

We introduce an atrous convolutional encoder-decoder network designed to denoise 512$\times$512 patches extracted from electron micrographs. This architecture features a modified Xception backbone, an atrous convolutional spatial pyramid pooling module, and a multi-stage decoder. The model was trained end-to-end to eliminate Poisson noise in low-dose ($\ll$ 300 counts ppx) micrographs, which were generated from a novel dataset of 17,267 high-dose ($>$ 2500 counts ppx) 2048$\times$2048 images, before being fine-tuned for ordinary doses (200-2500 counts ppx). We evaluated its performance against standard restoration techniques—including bilateral, non-local means, total variation, wavelet, and Wiener filters—using their default settings. Our network surpassed the best mean squared error and structural similarity index results by 24.6% and 9.6% for low doses, and by 43.7% and 5.5% for ordinary doses, respectively. Furthermore, our approach achieved the lowest variance in mean squared error across both scenarios. The source code, along with links to the new high-quality dataset and the trained model, are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Jeffrey-Ede/Electron-Micrograph-Denoiser.

TimeML is an XML schema designed for annotating temporal data within discourse. While the standard has been widely adopted for annotating various resources and has inspired numerous tools developed through extensive research, many existing implementations are flawed, produce invalid outputs, or include ambiguous and custom modifications. These inconsistencies were underscored during the TempEval-3 exercise, which introduced additional stipulations beyond the conventional TimeML standard. To unify the current landscape of resources and facilitate the adoption of the ISO-TimeML standard, this paper presents TimeML-strict: a valid, unambiguous, and easily processable subset of TimeML. Additionally, three resources are introduced: a schema for TimeML-strict, a validator to ensure document compliance, and a repair tool that corrects common invalidating errors and adds disambiguating markup to convert documents from the looser TimeML standard to TimeML-strict.

This study originates from a machine learning initiative at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology during the fall of 2020, beginning with a review of recent advancements in time-series forecasting methods over the last five years. The paper encapsulates the core findings of this research, introducing the architecture of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) cells and detailing how their components interact to manage memory and generate predictions. It further outlines the foundational formulas required to perform a forward pass through an LSTM network. Additionally, the work examines practical applications and studies that highlight the strengths and limitations of LSTMs within both time-series analysis and natural language processing (NLP). The text also discusses alternative statistical approaches for time-series forecasting, specifically ARIMA and exponential smoothing. However, given the complexity of LSTM architectures, the paper presupposes that readers possess a foundational understanding of machine learning concepts, including multi-layer perceptrons, activation functions, overfitting, backpropagation, bias, and related topics.

This article presents the appendix for "Lifelong Generative Modelling Using Dynamic Expansion Graph Model," which features supplementary visual outcomes and numerical evaluations on demanding datasets. Furthermore, it contains comprehensive proofs supporting the proposed theoretical analysis framework. The source code is available at https://github.com/dtuzi123/Expansion-Graph-Model.

We establish potential automorphy for a single Galois representation $G_F \rightarrow GL_n(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_l)$ over a CM number field $F$. Our approach utilizes the $p,q$ switch technique, adapting the Dwork motives from \cite{HSBT} to disrupt self-duality without altering the Hodge-Tate weights. Additionally, we demonstrate the ordinarity of specific $p$-adic representations using log geometry methods, relying on the automorphy lifting theorem found in \cite{tap} as a key input.

Mathematical research into addiction epidemiology has gained significant momentum recently, yet distinguishing the social and psychological mechanisms of substance use disorders from those of infectious diseases has complicated the development of epidemiological theories for substance abuse. This challenge is particularly evident in the opioid crisis, where both prescription patterns and social contagion are pivotal. To investigate these dynamics, this study employs an agent-based modeling framework on social networks. By applying parameter estimation techniques, we benchmark our findings against the Phillips et al. SPAHR model, which was previously calibrated using data from Tennessee. Our analysis reveals that the average path length of a social network is strongly correlated with social contagion driving drug use initiation; however, other routes to substance use disorder should not be limited to social network interactions that occurred prior to an individual's initial drug use.

We have transformed Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs)—chips specifically engineered for machine learning—into massive supercomputers designed for dense linear algebra. The TPUs' high-bandwidth memory (HBM), fast inter-core interconnects (ICIs) with a physically two-dimensional topology, and rapid data movement allow distributed matrix multiplication algorithms to quickly become computation-bound. In this scenario, the matrix-multiply units (MXUs) dominate execution time, resulting in exceptional scaling, performance, and scale. When operating in float32 precision, a full pod of 2048 third-generation TPU cores can multiply two matrices of linear size $N = 2^{20} = 1,048,576$ in approximately two minutes. By utilizing optimized algorithms that prioritize large, single-core matrix multiplications, other dense linear algebra tasks can achieve similar scalability. As illustrations, we demonstrate (i) QR decomposition, (ii) solving linear systems, and (iii) computing matrix functions through polynomial iteration, specifically using matrix polar factorization.

Edge Computing offers a transformative technology for domains demanding real-time data processing. Researchers in machine and deep learning heavily rely on both edge and cloud computing due to the substantial computational and storage resources they supply. Robotics is now aiming to leverage these capabilities, with the advent of 5G networks helping to resolve current sector limitations. Consequently, it is crucial to understand how to deploy emerging edge architectures, identify the available types and platforms, and determine which solutions best fit specific robotic applications. Generally, edge platforms can be implemented in various ways, as multiple providers offer similar service sets with distinct nuances. Therefore, this study examines these considerations for developers of next-generation robotic systems, providing insights into the pros and cons of each architecture to facilitate informed selection for every application.

We provide an explicit rational parameterization over $\mathbb{Q}$ for the surface $\mathcal{H}_3$, which corresponds to genus 2 curves $C$ possessing a full 3-level structure on their Jacobians $J$. Utilizing this model, we construct abelian surfaces $A$ where the Tate-Shafarevich group of the quadratic twist $A_d$ exhibits non-trivial 3-torsion for a positive proportion of twists $d$. Specifically, for every rational point $x \in \mathcal{H}_3(\mathbb{Q})$, this property holds for the surface $A = \mathrm{Jac}(C_x)/\langle P \rangle$, with $P$ denoting the marked point of order 3. Furthermore, our approach yields an explicit upper bound on the average rank of $J_d(\mathbb{Q})$ and provides statistical insights into the cardinality of $C_d(\mathbb{Q})$ as $d$ ranges over squarefree integers.

Recognizing emotions in speech has been a persistent challenge. Although early approaches depended on manually engineered features and basic classifiers, the domain has since transitioned to end-to-end learning and classification powered by deep neural networks. Concurrently, researchers have introduced various data augmentation methods to expand the scale and diversity of labeled datasets. Despite these significant advancements, there remains a limited understanding of how network architecture interacts with specific data augmentation choices. Furthermore, only a few studies have validated a model's generalizability across multiple datasets, a necessity for reliable real-world application. This paper presents a thorough assessment of prominent deep learning methods for emotion recognition. To mitigate bias, we standardize model architectures and optimization hyperparameters using the VESUS dataset, subsequently evaluating performance via repeated 5-fold cross-validation on the IEMOCAP and CREMA-D datasets. Our findings indicate that capturing long-range dependencies in speech is vital for emotion recognition, and that speed or rate augmentation yields the most consistent performance improvements across different models.

We demonstrate that specific homological regularity conditions for graded connected algebras, including AS-Gorenstein and AS-Cohen-Macaulay properties, can be verified by examining their associated graded rings. Drawing from noncommutative algebraic geometry, this finding mirrors the classical theorem regarding flat families over the affine line, where regularity in an exceptional fiber extends to every fiber. Furthermore, we establish that quantized coordinate rings for flag and Schubert varieties admit filtrations yielding twisted semigroup rings as associated graded structures. This result serves as a noncommutative counterpart to Caldero's finding that flag and Schubert varieties degenerate into toric varieties, thereby confirming that the quantized coordinate rings of these varieties are AS-Cohen-Macaulay.

This paper examines the density of rational points on the "stacky" curve $\mathcal{X}(\mathbb{P}^1;0,2;1,2;\infty,2)$, which consists of $\mathbb{P}^1$ augmented by three half points, relative to the Ellenberg-Satriano-Zuerick-Brown height. Specifically, we establish a conjecture proposed by Ellenberg.

This study investigates a subgrid multiscale stabilized formulation featuring dynamic subscales, applied to a non-Newtonian Casson fluid flow model tightly coupled with the variable-coefficient Advection-Dispersion-Reaction (VADR) equation. In this framework, the Casson viscosity coefficient is modeled as a function of solute mass concentration. The paper provides stability and convergence analyses for the stabilized finite element solution, demonstrating that the proposed stabilization parameter expressions yield optimal convergence orders. Furthermore, suitable numerical experiments are presented to support these findings.

Silver, particularly when structured at the nanoscale, is extensively utilized as an antimicrobial component in numerous commercial applications. Over recent decades, the mechanism behind its biocidal activity has been clarified, primarily involving the release of silver cations via oxidative dissolution, which are then absorbed by cells, severely disrupting bacterial metabolism and resulting in their elimination. Although extensive research has examined how the shape and size of nanosilver influence antibacterial efficacy and the associated physicochemical pathways, comparatively little attention has been paid to investigating the plasmonic response of silver nanoparticles during their interaction with bacteria. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of alterations in plasmonic spectral and dynamic characteristics induced by bacterial exposure, specifically using *Escherichia coli* as a model organism. Ultrafast pump-probe measurements reveal that significant changes in particle size, shape, and crystallinity—driven by bacteria-induced oxidative dissolution—directly correspond to distinct modifications in plasmonic features. These findings could pave the way for innovative developments in the biophysics of bio-responsive materials, establishing new and reliable biophysical signatures for how such materials interact with complex biological systems.

Cyber-physical human systems (CPHS) rely on real-time human decisions as a fundamental component for effective system operation. Addressing these decision-making challenges often requires accurate models of human behavior. While Utility Theory has proven effective in transportation contexts for resource allocation and balancing supply and demand \citep{ben1985discrete}, Prospect Theory has recently emerged as a powerful alternative in behavioral economics and cognitive psychology. Prospect Theory enables the development of behavioral models that capture subjective decision-making under stochastic uncertainty and risk \citep{kahneman_prospect_2012}. This article will detail these models, explore the theoretical implications of Prospect Theory, and illustrate the distinctions between Utility Theory and Prospect Theory using transportation applications, such as shared mobility.

This research advances neural forecasting models by introducing novel learning techniques based on randomization. Compared to standard approaches, these methods enhance the model's fitting capabilities by generating network parameters aligned with specific data and target function characteristics. By employing a pattern-based representation of time series, the proposed approach proves particularly effective for forecasting scenarios involving multiple seasonalities. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed models achieve forecasting accuracy comparable to fully trained networks. The model is highly attractive for diverse complex time series forecasting tasks due to its extremely rapid and straightforward training process, simple architecture, ease of implementation, high accuracy, and ability to handle both nonstationarity and multiple seasonality.

Gauge invariance, a mathematical principle with significant implications for physics as it underpins fundamental interactions, has recently been adapted to the Cellular Automaton (CA) framework under restricted conditions. This paper extends that approach to non-abelian gauge invariance, incorporating concepts such as gauge-equivalent theories and gauge-invariant configurations.

A weak asynchronous system is defined as a trace monoid equipped with a partial action on a set. A polygonal morphism between such systems maintains commutativity with the actions and preserves event independence. We demonstrate that the category comprising weak asynchronous systems and polygonal morphisms possesses both limits and colimits.

This study examines $\Sigma$-composition of terms, a mechanism that expands the derivation rules used in formally deducing identities. A crucial component in streamlining formal deduction is the notion of essential variables and positions within terms relative to a specific set of identities. $\Sigma$-composition is defined as the replacement of terms that are $\Sigma$-equal, a process that generates $\Sigma$-deductively closed sets of identities. Drawing an analogy to balanced identities, we define and analyze $\Sigma$-balanced identities for a given set of identities $\Sigma$.

Although large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language tasks, their performance in medical and clinical settings must meet stringent standards. Current assessments of clinical knowledge often depend on restricted automated benchmarks, lacking a unified standard for evaluating model reasoning and predictions across diverse tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MultiMedQA, a comprehensive benchmark aggregating six open-source question-answering datasets covering professional exams, research, and consumer queries, alongside HealthSearchQA, a novel dataset of online medical search questions. We also propose a human evaluation framework assessing model outputs based on factuality, precision, potential harm, and bias. Our evaluation of the 540-billion parameter PaLM and its instruction-tuned variant, Flan-PaLM, on MultiMedQA reveals that Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on all multiple-choice datasets—including MedQA (US Medical License Exam), where it reaches 67.6%, improving upon previous records by over 17%. Despite these metrics, human review highlights significant deficiencies in Flan-PaLM's responses. To mitigate this, we develop instruction prompt tuning, a parameter-efficient method for adapting LLMs to specific domains using few-shot examples. The resulting Med-PaLM model shows promising results, though it still falls short of clinical expertise. Our findings demonstrate that model scale and instruction tuning enhance comprehension, knowledge recall, and medical reasoning, indicating potential utility for medicine. However, human evaluations also underscore current model limitations, emphasizing the critical need for robust evaluation frameworks and continued methodological development to ensure safe and effective LLMs in clinical practice.

We trained Transformer-based neural machine translation models for the Hungarian-English and English-Hungarian language pairs using the Hunglish2 corpus. Our top-performing models reached a BLEU score of 40.0 for Hungarian-to-English translation and 33.4 for English-to-Hungarian translation. Additionally, we share findings from our ongoing research into syntax-based augmentation for neural machine translation. Both our code and models are open to the public.

By applying the methodology from the companion study, we derived effective continuum theories for two distinct microscopic tight-binding models of twisted bilayer graphene at a twist angle of $1.05^\circ$: one grounded in Slater-Koster parameters and the other in ab-initio Wannier functions. Our results show that energy spectra generated by these continuum theories—whether assuming a rigid twist or incorporating lattice relaxation—align almost perfectly with those from the tight-binding models when the gradient expansion is performed to second order, thereby validating the approach. Furthermore, an examination of the Bloch states within the resulting narrow bands uncovered a non-negligible breaking of particle-hole symmetry near the $\Gamma$ point in the continuum model based on the ab-initio data. This discrepancy arises from a specific term in the continuum theory that had previously been neglected, highlighting a key distinction from all existing continuum models, which exhibit nearly perfect particle-hole symmetry within the narrow band Hilbert space.

Although the software community has established specific meanings for concepts like "open source software," "free software," and "permissive license," scientists submitting proposals to NASA often lack familiarity with these distinctions. Such misunderstandings can create fairness issues in solicitations, as researchers may misinterpret NASA's intent, leading them to either unnecessarily restrict their proposed work or inadvertently submit proposals that fail to meet software licensing requirements. Consequently, it is recommended that NASA adopt definitions aligned with standard software community usage, include these definitions in solicitations to foster a shared understanding, and require proposers to specify the software licenses they intend to utilize.

Current adversarial attacks in reinforcement learning (RL) typically presume the adversary has extensive access to the victim's data, environment, or internal parameters. In contrast, this paper introduces a new adversarial framework known as a "Cheap Talk" Markov Decision Process (MDP). In this setting, the adversary is restricted to appending deterministic messages to the victim's observations, granting them minimal influence. Specifically, the adversary is barred from hiding ground truth, altering environment dynamics or reward functions, introducing non-stationarity or stochasticity, observing the victim's actions, or accessing their model parameters. We also introduce Adversarial Cheap Talk (ACT), a straightforward meta-learning algorithm designed to train adversaries within these strict constraints. Our results demonstrate that even under such severe limitations, an ACT-trained adversary can substantially degrade both the training and testing performance of the victim. This ability to compromise training performance uncovers a novel attack vector and sheds light on why existing RL algorithms succeed or fail. More specifically, we find that an ACT adversary can either impair performance by disrupting the learner's function approximation or enhance it by providing useful features. Furthermore, we show that the adversary can manipulate messages during training to achieve arbitrary and direct control over the victim at test time.

We analyzed a double torsion pendulum setup, quantifying the torque generated by photon spin. Our approach mirrored Beth's 1936 experiment, which utilized forced oscillations via polarization modulation of incident light to measure this same torque on a suspended mass. By employing straightforward passive isolation to shield the suspended object from external vibrations, we achieved a torque sensitivity of $2 \times 10^{-17} \text{ N m}$ over a measurement duration of $10^4 \text{ s}$. This sensitivity approaches the thermal noise limit and is approximately one order of magnitude lower than the minimum torque recorded in Beth's original study. Furthermore, the measured spin-induced torque acting on the light-absorbing optics aligns with the theoretical angular momentum transfer of $\hbar$ per photon.

A Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) is a system designed to record central nervous system activity and convert this data into a format that computers can process as input. Typically, a BCI comprises three components: signal acquisition, signal processing, and feedback or stimulus presentation. This paper introduces Wyrm, a Python-based signal processing toolbox for BCIs. Wyrm is versatile enough to address a wide spectrum of neuroscientific challenges, supporting both real-time online experimentation and offline data analysis with visualization capabilities.

This report outlines the creation and application of an online educational resource that provides students with exercises in logical modelling, also referred to in older texts as \emph{formalisation}. The initial iteration, titled `Logic for Fun', was launched in 2001 but saw minimal adoption, being utilized primarily by small cohorts at the Australian National University. It is currently undergoing replacement by a new version, which will be freely accessible to all internet users and designed for broad promotion as a valuable supplement to both conventional and digital logic curricula.

Electronic devices are increasingly incorporating materials with diverse properties, driven by the dual goals of enhancing device performance and advancing materials science. A key example is the Josephson junction, which leverages the proximity effect between superconductors and quantum materials for both fundamental research and technological applications. When both contacts reside on a single surface, such as a two-dimensional material, the structure is termed "planar." However, a significant challenge exists because many materials are incompatible with standard planar fabrication, meaning device quality often limits observed results rather than intrinsic material properties. To address this, we present a novel technique where nanowires placed on the surface serve as a shadow mask for the superconductor. This approach offers distinct benefits: the minimum feature size is defined by the nanowire diameter, eliminating the need for lithography, and the junction remains free from chemical exposure, such as etchants. We validated this method using an InAs quantum well paired with superconductors (Al and Sn) and semiconductor nanowires (InAs and InSb). The resulting junctions displayed critical currents indicative of transparent interfaces and uniform widths. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the template nanowire functions as a self-aligned electrostatic gate. Extending beyond single junctions, we fabricated SQUIDs comprising two gate-tunable junctions. Finally, we propose that this methodology is applicable to a wide range of quantum materials, including van der Waals layers, topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, and emerging materials where proximity effect devices hold great promise.

We employ a semiclassical framework to optimize a microwave single-photon detector utilizing switching events in a current-biased Josephson junction coupled to a resonator. To capture extremely rare occurrences, the average interval between dark counts ($\tau_{\rm dark}$) must be maximized while ensuring the switching time ($\tau_{\rm sw}$) remains sufficiently brief. We show that these timescales can be broadly tuned by adjusting junction parameters, achieving ratios of $\tau_{\rm dark}/\tau_{\rm sw} \sim 10^9$. Consequently, this junction-resonator configuration is suitable for detecting ultra-low photon fluxes, such as in the search for galactic axions.

We offer a mathematical examination of a hybrid ODE-PDE framework that captures the spatial patterns and temporal dynamics of both tumor and healthy cells in tissue, accounting for the impact of chemotherapy. The model posits that drug delivery is confined to a specific tissue region, simulating a blood vessel traversing perpendicularly. Furthermore, we establish findings regarding the existence and uniqueness of the solution, complemented by numerical simulations that demonstrate various model behaviors.

Recent astrophysical observations suggest the potential presence of strange quark matter alongside baryonic resonances like $\Lambda^0, \Sigma^0, \Xi,$ and $\Omega$ within neutron star cores. This study investigates the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein (MSW) effect within quark matter. We determine that achieving complete conversion of down-quarks to strange quarks necessitates an extremely high matter density ($\rho_u \simeq 10^{5}\,\mbox{fm}^{-3}$). However, neutron stars offer optimal conditions for statistically significant conversion, a scenario consistent with charge neutrality constraints. These findings may help resolve the hyperon puzzle and clarify the equation of state for dense baryonic matter.

We introduce a version of the classical exponential map for Lie groups, adapted for Hopf $*$-algebras equipped with differential calculus. The primary distinction from the classical scenario lies in the interpretation of the map's output; whereas classically it yields an element of the Lie group, here it is interpreted as a state on the Hopf algebra, an element of a Hilbert $C^{*}$-bimodule of $\frac{1}{2}$ densities, or an element of the dual Hopf algebra. We provide examples involving complex-valued functions on the groups $S_{3}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$, Woronowicz's matrix quantum group $\mathbb{C}_{q}[SU_2]$, and the Sweedler-Taft algebra.

Electron-positron collisions represent a highly promising setting for searching for new physics, specifically targeting dark sector observables. However, the primary experimental challenge in detecting dark sector candidates is the overwhelming Standard Model background. Consequently, it is crucial to identify observables that are minimally suppressed in the dark sector while being highly suppressed in the Standard Model. A prime example is the $e^+ e^-\to 3(e^+e^-)$ process, which can proceed either through the production and decay of a dark Higgs boson ($h'$) via $e^+e^-\to A'h'\to 6e$ or through a Standard Model interaction. This letter investigates the relative contributions of the $h'$-mediated channel versus the Standard Model process to the total observed cross section for $e^+ e^-\to 3(e^+e^-)$ within the context of fixed-target and low-energy collider experiments, with a specific focus on the PADME experiment at the INFN Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati.

This work addresses the challenges of optimal power allocation within maximum power limits to achieve two objectives: (i) maximizing the minimum Shannon capacity and (ii) minimizing weighted latency. For the first objective, the global optimum is attainable in polynomial time by solving a series of linear programs (LPs). Regarding the second objective, the original non-convex problem is transformed into a convex surrogate known as a geometric program through functional approximation. Given the minimal approximation error, the surrogate's optimum closely approximates the global optimum of the original problem. Crucially, neither approach relies on assumptions regarding the SINR range. The application of LPs and geometric programming ensures that the proposed algorithms are numerically efficient, with computational results provided to validate these findings.

We introduce an implicit neural representation designed to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of kinematic movements. Departing from prior approaches that rely on discrete sequential samples, we define the extensive motion space as a continuous function of time, termed Neural Motion Fields (NeMF). Specifically, a neural network learns this function across diverse motion sets, acting as a generative model conditioned on a temporal coordinate $t$ and a random vector $z$ to regulate stylistic variations. The model is trained as a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) incorporating motion encoders to explore the latent space. We validate the model's versatility using both human and quadruped motion datasets, subsequently deploying it as a universal motion prior to address task-agnostic challenges. Our results demonstrate its superiority in various motion generation and editing tasks, including interpolation, in-betweening, and re-navigating. Additional information is available at our project page: https://cs.yale.edu/homes/che/projects/nemf/.

We introduce a compact and stable configuration for detecting optical second harmonics, characterized by an incident plane that rotates relative to the sample. This system utilizes rotating Fresnel-rhomb optics and a femtosecond ytterbium-doped fiber laser operating at 10 MHz. Covering an area of 1 m² including the laser source, the setup maintains sufficient stability to keep laser harmonic intensity fluctuations below 0.2% over a four-hour period. We demonstrate the system's integrity and sensitivity by presenting the isotropic harmonic signal from a 0.5 pW gold mirror. Additionally, we illustrate the polarization-dependent six-fold pattern of harmonics generated by few-layer WSe₂ to infer the extent of local-field effects. Finally, we outline the setup's adaptability for investigating samples under diverse conditions, including cryogenic temperatures, strain, ultrafast non-equilibrium states, and high magnetic fields.

Correlation clustering is a prevalent method in unsupervised machine learning. Driven by applications where individual privacy is paramount, we begin an investigation into differentially private correlation clustering. We introduce an algorithm that attains subquadratic additive error relative to the optimal cost, whereas simple modifications of current non-private algorithms result in a trivial quadratic error. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound demonstrating that any pure differentially private algorithm for correlation clustering must incur an additive error of $\Omega(n)$.

Extracting concepts is vital for numerous downstream tasks, yet surprisingly, simple methods like dictionary lookups or single-token alignment (e.g., DBpedia Spotlight) remain dominant. We introduce a generic, open-domain extractive model designed for out-of-vocabulary terms, which utilizes distant supervision to train a pointer-generator network enhanced with bidirectional LSTMs and a copy mechanism. Trained on a large, custom-annotated corpus derived from 250,000 Wikipedia pages, the model was evaluated on standard pages, treating hyperlinks to other pages as ground-truth concepts. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses conventional techniques and further boosts performance when integrated with DBpedia Spotlight. Additionally, the model proves adaptable to other datasets, consistently achieving state-of-the-art results.

Galaxy redshift surveys aim to map three-dimensional cosmic structures for large-scale structure research, yet unavoidable limitations in sampling and survey windows degrade cosmological constraints. This study analyzes the VIMOS Public Extragalactic Redshift Survey (VIPERS) within the redshift range $0.6 < z < 1$, optimizing the extraction of cosmological parameters while rigorously accounting for the survey's complex geometry. Using the Gibbs sampling algorithm, we iteratively generate samples for the galaxy density field in redshift space, galaxy bias, matter density, baryon fraction, and the growth-rate parameter $f\sigma_8$, based on a multivariate Gaussian likelihood and prior for the density field. Despite the high number of degrees of freedom, the samples successfully converge to the joint posterior distribution, yielding self-consistent constraints on model parameters. We validate this method using VIPERS mock galaxy catalogues. Although the Gaussian likelihood underestimates uncertainty by 50% on the scales considered, the dispersion of results from the mocks provides a robust error estimate. Our findings indicate that result precision matches that of traditional VIPERS analyses using more constrained models. By relaxing model assumptions, we confirm that the data yield consistent constraints on the $\Lambda$CDM model. This work serves as a case study for applying maximum-likelihood analyses to future generations of galaxy redshift surveys.

We examined the anti-Jaynes-Cummings (AJC) dynamics of a two-level atom initially in its ground state interacting with a field mode prepared in a squeezed coherent state, considering arbitrary squeeze parameters ($r$), and compared these results with the standard Jaynes-Cummings (JC) interaction. Our analysis focused on the degree of entanglement (DEM), quantified via von Neumann entropy, and the field's nature, assessed by the Mandel $Q$ parameter, alongside atomic population inversion during both AJC and JC evolutions. Our findings indicate that for $r > 1.4$, photon statistics transition from sub-Poissonian to super-Poissonian during the respective interactions. Furthermore, at elevated $r$ values, the atomic population inversion exhibits enhanced ringing revivals within the collapse region compared to scenarios with an initial coherent state. Additionally, higher $r$ values lead to faster oscillations in DEM and higher peak values, accompanied by an increased degree of mixedness.

We introduce Sparrow, an information-seeking dialogue agent trained to surpass prompted language model baselines in helpfulness, accuracy, and harmlessness. Our approach utilizes reinforcement learning from human feedback, enhanced by two novel methods to facilitate human evaluation of agent behavior. First, to improve helpfulness and harmlessness, we decompose dialogue requirements into specific natural language rules and query raters about each individually; this strategy yields more targeted judgments and enables efficient rule-conditional reward models. Second, when gathering preference data, Sparrow supplies source evidence for its factual claims, which supports the sampled response 78% of the time. Compared to baselines, Sparrow is preferred more frequently and demonstrates greater resilience to adversarial probing, adhering to our rules in 92% of probed instances. Finally, extensive analyses reveal that while the model successfully learns to follow these rules, it may still exhibit distributional biases.

This study introduces an a posteriori error control framework for a generalized Boussinesq model featuring temperature-dependent thermal conductivity and viscosity. The approach couples stationary Navier-Stokes equations with a stationary heat equation, solving the resulting system monolithically. We focus on multigoal-oriented error estimation using the dual-weighted residual method, which leverages an adjoint problem to derive sensitivity measures for multiple goal functionals. Error localization is accomplished via a partition-of-unity within a weak formulation, a strategy particularly suited for the coupled nature of this problem. These error indicators drive adaptive algorithms, whose robustness and efficiency are validated through several numerical experiments, including one benchmark and two case studies inspired by laser material processing.
