HoughCL demonstrates robustness against background noise and outliers. Moreover, compared to baseline methods, our dense positive pairing strategy introduces no additional learnable parameters and incurs minimal computational overhead. Our approach yields superior or comparable performance on dense prediction fine-tuning tasks relative to prior works.

This study investigates multiphonon quantum dynamics within laser-driven cavity optomechanical systems featuring a vibrating mirror, with a specific focus on dispersive interaction regimes. In these regimes, the frequency detuning of the externally applied coherent field from the optical resonator frequency differs from both the mirror's oscillation frequency and its harmonics. Consequently, under moderately strong coupling conditions among the subsystems, the quantum evolution of this complex system is characterized by multiphonon absorption or emission processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate effective methods for tracking phonon quantum dynamics through photon detection and discuss the feasibility of extracting key sample parameters, such as the coupling strength between the mechanical mirror and the electromagnetic field.

This study tackles the visibility-based pursuit-evasion challenge, in which a team of robots in a 2D polygonal environment aims to maintain sight of a highly agile evader. While this task is computationally intensive—with the most efficient complete algorithm requiring doubly exponential time relative to the number of robots—recent sampling-based techniques have made strides in finding viable solutions. However, a critical gap remains regarding how to handle catastrophic failures that render one or more robots unable to contribute. To bridge this gap, we introduce an algorithm designed for rapid recovery from such incidents. Upon failure, the system triggers a replanning process that utilizes retained data and partial progress from the prior search to formulate a new strategy for the remaining robots. We present an implementation of this method and provide quantitative evidence demonstrating that it recovers from robot failures significantly faster than a baseline approach that must plan from the beginning.

Dual active galactic nuclei (AGN) represent the phenomenon of two supermassive black holes (SMBHs) actively feeding within merging galaxies, offering a critical environment to investigate SMBH accretion and feedback during a vital phase of galactic evolution. This study reports NOEMA CO(2-1) observations of seven kpc-scale dual-AGN candidates identified in a recent Chandra survey of low-redshift, optically classified AGN pairs. These systems were chosen due to their anomalously low 2-10 keV X-ray luminosities relative to their small physical separations, indicating an intermediate-to-late merger stage. Circumnuclear molecular gas, traced by CO(2-1) emission, was significantly detected in six of the seven pairs and ten of the fourteen nuclei, with estimated masses ranging from $(0.2 - 21) \times 10^9\rm~M_{\odot}$. Primary nuclei, characterized by higher stellar velocity dispersions, generally possess greater molecular gas masses than their secondary counterparts. Most CO-detected nuclei exhibit compact morphologies with velocity fields consistent with kpc-scale rotation. Inferred hydrogen column densities fall between $5\times10^{21} - 2\times10^{23}\rm~cm^{-2}$, predominantly around a few times $10^{22}\rm~cm^{-2}$, aligning well with X-ray spectral analysis. Combined with relatively weak mid-infrared emission, these moderate column densities suggest that heavily obscured, intrinsically luminous AGN are not prevalent in these seven systems. Instead, the data support a feedback scenario where AGN activity, triggered by a recent pericentric passage of the galaxy pair, has expelled circumnuclear gas and suppressed further SMBH accretion.

This study investigates the existence and uniqueness of periodic mild solutions for the Boussinesq system on the real hyperbolic manifold $\mathbb{H}^d(\mathbb{R})$ where $d \geqslant 2$. The analysis utilizes Ebin-Marsden's Laplace operator corresponding to the linear system. Our approach relies on the dispersive and smoothing properties of the semigroup generated by this operator. Initially, we establish the existence and uniqueness of bounded periodic mild solutions for the linear system. Subsequently, employing fixed-point arguments, we extend these results from the linear to the semilinear system to confirm the existence of periodic mild solutions. Finally, within the framework of hyperbolic spaces, we demonstrate the unconditional uniqueness of large periodic mild solutions for the Boussinesq system.

Microstructure evolution in metal additive manufacturing (AM) constitutes a complex, multi-physics, and multi-scale challenge. Investigating how AM process parameters influence microstructural development and the subsequent mechanical properties of printed components remains a vibrant field of study. While thermo-fluidic governing equations have been widely modeled at the melt pool scale to characterize thermal gradients and local conditions, dimensional analysis offers profound insights into the dynamics of phenomena described by partial differential equations. This work introduces a novel approach combining dimensional analysis with linear least squares regression to numerically examine the thermo-fluidic equations governing Laser Powder Bed Fusion. The study first solves these equations via the Finite Element Method, validating the results against experimentally derived cooling rates and existing numerical data. Subsequently, dimensional analysis identifies a critical dimensionless parameter representing heat absorption by the powder and melt pool, which, alongside classical numbers like Peclet, Marangoni, and Stefan, is employed to analyze advective transport across various alloys. Furthermore, this framework assesses variations in thermal gradients and solidification cooling rates. The primary contribution of this research lies in establishing key correlations between melt pool morphology, microstructure evolution variables, and classical dimensionless numbers.

This study examines the thermodynamics of Einstein-Power-Yang-Mills AdS black holes within the gauge-gravity duality framework, specifically varying the Newtonian gravitational constant and the cosmological constant. We reformulate the first law of thermodynamics into an extended version that incorporates both pressure and the central charge of the dual conformal field theory, resulting in a restricted phase transition formula. A new phenomenon emerges where the dual counterpart to pressure is identified as the effective volume rather than the geometric volume. This discovery leads to a novel Van der Waals-like phase transition behavior characterized by a supercritical phase transition at a fixed central charge. Additionally, we analyze the second-order phase transition of the EPYM AdS black hole using the Ehrenfest scheme and investigate the impact of the non-linear Yang-Mills parameter on these thermodynamic properties.

We examine the equilibrium states of one-dimensional proton conductors featuring hydrogen bonds. Our study utilizes an extended hard-core boson lattice model that accounts for short-range interactions among hydrogen ions, their transfer along bonds via a two-minima local anharmonic potential, inter-bond hopping, and the influence of a modulating field. Employing the exact diagonalization method on finite one-dimensional systems with periodic boundary conditions, we analyze the frequency dependence of the one-particle spectral density to identify various system phases at $T = 0$ based on short-range interaction strengths and modulating field intensity, ultimately constructing the corresponding phase diagrams.

For the last ten years, attention regarding the security and privacy of implantable medical devices (IMDs) has grown significantly, spurred by numerous cybersecurity flaws discovered in current systems. However, standard security protocols cannot be directly applied to IMDs because of their rigid limitations in computation, energy, and physical resources. While custom solutions have been suggested, they do not fully address the broad range of security capabilities essential for modern IMDs and their ecosystems. This paper introduces IMDfence, a security protocol designed for IMD ecosystems that offers a comprehensive yet practical security suite encompassing availability, non-repudiation, access control, entity authentication, remote monitoring, and system scalability. Furthermore, the protocol supports emergency access that ensures graceful service degradation without endangering security or patient safety. We extensively evaluate the protocol's performance, feasibility, and impact on contemporary IMDs, finding that IMDfence meets all stated security requirements with an energy consumption increase of under 7%, alongside system delays and memory footprint increases of less than 14 ms and 9 kB, respectively.

Graphene oxide (GO) reduction was conducted via Joule heating within an in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) setup. This method enables the concurrent monitoring of GO's electrical conductivity through measurements and its compositional and structural evolution using TEM, electron diffraction, and electron energy-loss spectroscopy during reduction. Minor property changes at low electric currents are linked to enhanced diffusion processes. The genuine reduction phase initiates at a power density of approximately 2 × 10¹⁴ Wm⁻³, proceeding in a highly localized and uniform fashion. Conductivity rises by over four orders of magnitude to reach 3 × 10³ Sm⁻¹, with the final oxygen content dropping below 1%. The study also contrasts Joule heating with thermal annealing for GO reduction.

This study focuses on identifying the most critical weak-interaction nuclei during the presupernova evolution of massive stars. To this end, an ensemble of 728 nuclei spanning the mass range A = 1–100 was analyzed. Mass fractions were derived using the Saha equation for fixed values of temperature ($T$), density ($\rho$), and electron fraction ($Y_e$), under the assumption of nuclear statistical equilibrium. A novel approach was employed to calculate nuclear partition functions, treating excited states up to 10 MeV as discrete entities. Weak interaction rates, specifically electron capture (ec) and $\beta$-decay (bd), were computed entirely microscopically via the proton-neutron quasiparticle random phase approximation (pn-QRPA) model, explicitly avoiding the Brink-Axel hypothesis. These rates were integrated with the calculated mass fractions to determine the temporal evolution of the lepton-to-baryon fraction. When compared to existing literature, our findings reveal significant discrepancies, sometimes differing by orders of magnitude, which could substantially alter the late-stage presupernova evolution of stars. We provide a list of the top 50 nuclei whose ec and bd processes most significantly impact $Y_e$ following silicon core burning. Furthermore, an analysis of the competition between ec and bd rates in the stellar core indicates that $\beta$-decay rates exceed electron capture rates within the $Y_e$ interval of 0.424–0.455.

Duvall and Hanasoge (2013) recently demonstrated that large center-to-annulus travel-time differences ($\Delta$) correspond to an average supergranular cell model featuring a peak upflow of $240\rm{ms^{-1}}$ at $2.3\rm{Mm}$ depth and a peak outward horizontal flow of $700\rm{ms^{-1}}$ at $1.6\rm{Mm}$. This study extends that investigation by analyzing center-to-quadrant travel-time differences ($\delta t_{\rm{qu}}$), which align reasonably well with the aforementioned model. Simulations confirm that such a flow structure produces the anticipated travel-time variations. To rule out systematic errors, the center-to-annulus differences ($\delta t_{\rm{oi}}$) were observed to remain independent of the heliocentric angle. Furthermore, a consistency check revealed that $\delta t_{\rm{oi}}$ increases by a factor of two with temporal frequency ($\nu$), a trend not predicted by ray theory.

The potential for a Casimir electromotive force (EMF) to exist in principle is demonstrated for nonparallel, nanoscale metal plates configured in a periodic arrangement. Results indicate that EMF does not occur in strictly periodic structures composed of parallel plates. Conversely, when strict periodicity is disrupted in nonparallel plates, an EMF is produced, with its magnitude corresponding to the number of plate pairs within the setup. Additionally, specific configuration parameters—including interplate angles, plate lengths, and length ratios—exist where the EMF generated per unit length of the periodic structure reaches its maximum.

We have determined all feasible parameters for Plotkin-optimal projective codes with two Lee weights over $\mathbb{Z}_4$, along with their corresponding weight distributions. By establishing an infinite family of two-weight codes, we demonstrate the existence of these codes and their weight distributions. Notably, the codes previously identified by Shi et al. (\emph{Des Codes Cryptogr.} {\bf 88}(3):1-13, 2020) emerge as a specific instance of our findings. Furthermore, we establish that the Gray image of any such Plotkin-optimal two-Lee weight projective code over $\mathbb{Z}_4$ shares identical parameters and weight distribution with certain two-weight binary projective codes classified as type SU1 according to Calderbank and Kantor (\emph{Bull. Lond. Math. Soc.} {\bf 18}:97-122, 1986).

This study introduces a novel method for building Calabi-Yau orbifold models essential for superstring theory compactification. Leveraging the relationship between CY orbifolds and exactly solvable N=2 superconformal field theories (SCFTs), we explicitly derive a full set of fields for these models by applying spectral flow twisting and enforcing mutual locality conditions.

We will establish a vanishing theorem of the Kodaira-Nakano type for the logarithmic de Rham complex of a unitary local system. Subsequently, we will examine the weight filtration on this complex and demonstrate a more robust result regarding its associated graded complex.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a recent advancement in distributed machine learning, enabling collaborative model training without transferring data from client devices, thereby ensuring data privacy. However, in practical FL scenarios, training data across clients is often highly non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID), which negatively impacts both convergence speed and final model performance. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel, generalized method for integrating adaptive optimization into FL via the Federated Global Biased Optimiser (FedGBO) algorithm. FedGBO enhances FL efficiency by utilizing a set of global biased optimizer values throughout training, which mitigates "client-drift" caused by non-IID data while leveraging the benefits of adaptive optimization. We demonstrate that global model updates within FedGBO can be reformulated as centralized training using biased gradients and optimizer updates, allowing us to apply this framework to prove convergence on nonconvex objectives when employing the momentum-SGD (SGDm) optimizer. Furthermore, we performed extensive experiments across four FL benchmark datasets (CIFAR100, Sent140, FEMNIST, Shakespeare) and three widely used optimizers (SGDm, RMSProp, Adam) to evaluate FedGBO against six state-of-the-art FL algorithms. The findings indicate that FedGBO achieves superior or competitive performance across all datasets with minimal data-upload and computational overhead, offering valuable insights into the trade-offs involved in selecting different adaptive FL algorithms and optimizers.

We examine a game set in the Euclidean plane involving a countable number of unit-speed lions and a single man capable of running at speed $1+\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon > 0$. We demonstrate that the man can indeed survive for any such positive value of $\varepsilon$.

In modern cosmology, dark matter and inflation are fundamental to explaining the origin of cosmic structures, yet their precise physical descriptions remain elusive. The Weyl scaling invariant theory of gravity offers a promising framework to address both mysteries simultaneously by introducing a massive gauge boson as a dark matter candidate and utilizing the quadratic scalar curvature term ($R^2$) to achieve an inflationary mechanism consistent with observational data. This study investigates dark matter production within the Weyl $R^2$ model, accounting for both non-perturbative generation via quantum fluctuations during inflation and perturbative production through scattering. We identify three viable parameter regimes for dark matter generation: (1) If the reheating temperature exceeds $10^3~\mathrm{GeV}$, the Weyl gauge boson can be abundantly produced with masses surpassing the inflation scale of $\sim 10^{13}~\mathrm{GeV}$. (2) A small mass region exists at $3\times10^{-13}~\mathrm{GeV}$, applicable to higher reheating temperatures. (3) At elevated reheating temperatures, annihilation channels become significant, allowing the freeze-in mechanism to produce Weyl gauge bosons with masses up to $4\times10^{16}~\mathrm{GeV}$.

While network science has historically concentrated on pairwise connections, often overlooking many-body interactions, hypergraphs offer a promising mathematical framework for modeling these complex relationships. This work introduces null models for analyzing hypergraphs that extend the classical Erdős-Rényi and Configuration Models by randomizing incidence matrices under specific constraints. Following a discussion of these models, we generalize several network metrics to apply to hypergraphs, calculate their expected values, and contrast them with empirical data to identify significant departures from random behavior.

As Artificial Intelligence advances, interactions with autonomous agents are becoming increasingly common. For effective collaboration, users must comprehend agent behavior; otherwise, productivity may decline, leading to misuse or frustration. Current agent strategy summarization methods aim to enhance user understanding of an agent's capabilities by demonstrating its actions across specific scenarios. However, these existing approaches are limited when comparing multiple agents because each summary is created independently. This paper introduces a novel method for generating dependent and contrastive summaries that highlight differences in agent policies by pinpointing states where agents disagree on optimal actions. User studies evaluating these disagreement-based summaries for identifying superior agents and clarifying distinctions between them demonstrate that they improve user performance compared to summaries generated by HIGHLIGHTS, an algorithm that produces independent summaries for each agent.

The paper establishes the existence of a positive entire weak solution to a singular quasi-linear elliptic system featuring convection terms, primarily utilizing perturbation methods, fixed point arguments, and a priori estimates. Subsequently, regularity results are applied to demonstrate that the derived solution is, in fact, strong.

We conducted an extensive constant-temperature Molecular Dynamics simulation of two-dimensional systems comprising Janus dumbbells and spherical particles. In this model, Janus dumbbells consist of two spheres, designated as 1 and 2, connected by harmonic bonds. Sphere 1 of a given dumbbell attracts spheres of the same type on other dumbbells, whereas interactions between pairs 1-1 and 1-2 are repulsive. Conversely, spherical particles are attracted to centers 2 and repelled by centers 1 of the Janus particles. Our findings indicate that the structure of the resulting oriented phases relies on the bond length of the Janus dumbbells and the ratio of spherical particles to Janus dumbbells. Furthermore, the presence of spherical particles is essential for the development of oriented phases, with phase formation depending on their concentration. Specifically, an equal number of Janus and spherical particles creates optimal conditions for the emergence of lamellar phases.

We employ exceptional field theory to determine Kaluza-Klein mass spectra for ${\rm AdS_{3}}$ vacua within half-maximal three-dimensional gauged supergravity. This framework is applicable to any vacuum resulting from a consistent truncation of higher-dimensional supergravity, regardless of the preserved symmetries. To demonstrate its efficiency, we calculate the spectra of ${\cal N}=(2,0)$ and ${\cal N}=(1,1)$ six-dimensional supergravities on ${\rm AdS_{3}}\times S^{3}$, as well as type II supergravity on ${\rm AdS_{3}}\times S^{3}\times S^{3}\times S^{1}$.

Hair-thin optical fibres offer the potential for transformative applications ranging from industrial inspection to biomedical imaging; however, their practical use has been hindered by the fact that minor mechanical shifts or temperature fluctuations can severely distort optical data and ruin images. Because these disturbances occur dynamically, accurate correction demands the immediate in-situ measurement of the fibre's transmission matrix (TM) prior to imaging. Standard TM calibration usually necessitates simultaneous access to both the distal and proximal fibre ends, a requirement that is often impractical in real-world scenarios due to the bulky optics needed, which compromise the fibres' slim profile. This study introduces a novel method for determining the TM of multi-mode (MMF) or multi-core (MCF) fibres in a reflection-only setup, eliminating the need for distal facet access. By employing a thin stack of structured metasurface reflectors at the distal end, we create spatially heterogeneous, wavelength-dependent reflectance profiles. We developed a first-order fibre model that accounts for these wavelength-specific TM variations, enabling the unambiguous reconstruction of the full TM using reflected data from just three wavelengths via an iterative optimisation algorithm. Following this reconstruction, we outline a technique for sample illumination and imaging. Distinct from prior methods, our approach does not assume the TM is unitary, thereby accommodating physically realistic fibre systems. We validated the method by demonstrating TM reconstruction and imaging using simulated non-unitary fibres with noisy reflection matrices, followed by experiments on large-scale TMs from a densely packed MCF, and finally on multi-wavelength TM data recorded from an MMF. These results establish a foundation for online, in-situ transmission matrix calibration in hair-thin optical fibres.

We determined the electron-positron pair production rate at the base of the Cyg X-1 jet by analyzing collisions between photons from its hot accretion flow, utilizing soft gamma-ray spectral data from the Compton Gamma Ray Observatory and INTEGRAL satellites. Our results indicate that this rate closely matches the flow rate of leptons responsible for the jet's observed synchrotron emission across the radio-to-IR spectrum, as derived from an extended jet model based on Blandford & Koenigl. This alignment suggests the jet is likely dominated by pairs. Similar coincidences were previously identified in the microquasar MAXI J1820+070 and the radio galaxy 3C 120, implying that this mechanism may be universal for certain classes of relativistic jets. Additionally, we recalculated the jet power of Cyg X-1; the presence of pairs significantly diminishes the power available for the bulk motion of ions, thereby constraining the parameter space within which the jet can energize the nearby $\sim$5-pc nebular structure.

The $N$-body problem holds historical importance as the initial application of Newtonian dynamics to model our Solar System. Driven by this legacy, the project aims to re-examine the problem for small $N$, deriving solutions for trajectories in specific two-body and three-body systems, as well as planetary orbits, by employing a fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta iterative method. Our findings demonstrate satisfactory agreement with existing online data regarding planetary trajectories.

This study examines the inherent line profile asymmetry in photon scattering within quantum electrodynamics (QED), specifically targeting the two-photon $1s-2s$ transition in hydrogen atoms through high-precision spectroscopy. Given its status as one of the most accurately measured transition frequencies, this process serves as a cornerstone for optical frequency standards and is essential for determining fundamental constants, verifying physical laws, and probing constraints on new interactions. The findings of this work demonstrate that precision spectroscopic experiments must account for this natural line profile asymmetry.

Recent refinements to the standard model predictions for the hadronic decays of $B$-mesons, specifically $\bar{B}^0 \to D^{(\ast)+}K^-$ and $\bar{B}^0_s \to D^{(\ast)+}_s \pi^-$, utilizing the QCD factorization approach, have revealed a new puzzle. These updates highlight mild yet universal discrepancies between experimental data and the predicted branching ratios. Under the assumption that higher-order QCD corrections are insufficient to resolve these tensions, we investigate various new physics scenarios. Our analysis indicates that a left-handed $W^\prime$ model can partially account for this discrepancy while remaining consistent with other flavor observables and collider constraints.

We introduce a new multi-task pre-training framework for Speech Emotion Recognition (SER). By concurrently pre-training a SER model on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and sentiment classification tasks, we enhance the acoustic ASR model's sensitivity to emotional cues. Sentiment labels are generated using a text-to-sentiment model trained on publicly accessible datasets. Subsequently, the acoustic ASR model is fine-tuned on speech data annotated with emotion labels. Evaluated on the MSP-Podcast dataset, this approach yielded the highest reported concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) of 0.41 for valence prediction.

Effective communication among agents serves as a potent solution for decision-making challenges that individual agents cannot resolve alone. Nevertheless, achieving continuous coordination and communication learning among machine agents or in human-machine collaborations remains a significant open challenge. Addressing this, we present a comprehensive study on "Pavlovian signalling," defined as a mechanism where an agent's learned, temporally extended predictions guide the decisions of another agent with limited perceptual access to their shared environment. Our goal is to determine how various temporal processes and representational choices influence this signalling between learning agents. To achieve this, we introduce the "Frost Hollow," a partially observable decision-making domain where a prediction learning agent and a reinforcement learning agent function as a coupled two-part system designed to obtain sparse rewards while evading time-dependent hazards. We assess two variations of this domain: 1) machine-based prediction and control learning within a linear walk, and 2) an interaction between a prediction learning machine and a human participant in a virtual reality setting. Our findings highlight the rapid learning capabilities of Pavlovian signalling, demonstrate the effects (and limitations) of different temporal representations on agent coordination, and reveal how temporal aliasing affects machine-machine versus human-machine interactions differently. As a primary contribution, we position Pavlovian signalling as a natural bridge connecting static signalling paradigms with fully adaptive communication learning. Consequently, our results outline a practical, constructivist approach toward continual communication learning among reinforcement learning agents, with promising applications across diverse real-world scenarios.

To address anomalies in charged-current semi-leptonic $B$ meson decays and the muon anomalous magnetic moment, alongside charged fermion masses and quark mixing, we propose an extension of the Standard Model incorporating a scalar leptoquark $\phi\sim (3,1,-\tfrac13)$ and the discrete flavour symmetry $G_f=D_{17}\times Z_{17}$. Within this framework, the $Z_{17}^{\rm diag}$ subgroup, part of $G_f$, is preserved by leptoquark couplings at leading order, effectively suppressing interactions with first-generation quarks and/or electrons to evade strict experimental limits. The most significant constraints on the model's parameters arise from radiative charged lepton flavour violating processes, specifically $\tau\to\mu\gamma$ and $\mu\to e\gamma$. Comprehensive analytical and numerical investigations confirm that the model can simultaneously account for the lepton flavour universality ratios $R(D)$ and $R(D^\star)$ and the muon anomalous magnetic moment without violating bounds from other relevant flavour observables.
This document serves as an introduction to intuitionistic mathematics.

Multiplicative and additive matrix compounds are fundamental in various mathematical domains, such as geometry, multilinear algebra, combinatorics, and the study of nonlinear time-varying dynamical systems. Their applications, along with related generalizations, are increasingly significant within systems and control theory. This tutorial aims to offer a comprehensive and accessible introduction to these subjects, prioritizing the geometric perspective of matrix compounds. Additionally, it outlines recent applications, featuring non-trivial extensions of concepts like positive systems, cooperative systems, and contracting systems.

Let $S$ denote a finitely generated free or surface group. We prove a Tits alternative for groups residing in the finite, soluble, and $p$-genus of $S$, which extends and offers a novel proof for Baumslag's analogous finding regarding parafree groups. Subsequently, we explore implications for profinite rigidity. Addressing Remeslennikov's longstanding query—whether a finitely generated residually finite group $G$ with a profinite completion $\widehat G$ isomorphic to $\widehat S$ must satisfy $G \cong S$—we provide an affirmative answer for groups within the class $\mathcal{H}_{ab}$, characterized by a finite abelian hierarchy originating from finitely generated residually free groups. This result improves upon earlier work by Bridson, Corner, Reid, and Wilton. Furthermore, we demonstrate that one-relator groups in the genus of $S$ are both hyperbolic and virtually special. Finally, we establish that $S \times \mathbb{Z}^n$ exhibits profinite rigidity among finitely generated residually free groups.

This study investigates the quantum characteristics of light emitted by exciton polaritons within a pillar semiconductor microcavity containing an embedded quantum well. By modeling bare excitons and photon modes as coupled quantum oscillators, the analysis accurately captures nonlinear and dissipative effects. Specifically, employing a quantum phase space representation through quasiprobability functions (the $P$-function and Wigner function), we examine how laser parameters and exciton-photon detuning influence the second-order correlation function of emitted photons. We identify the conditions governing photon bunching, giant bunching, and antibunching. Notably, we predict giant bunching under conditions of a high exciton-to-photon population ratio and demonstrate bunching effects within the parameter range supporting a bistability regime.

By leveraging the coroot lattice of $D(2,1;a)$, we derive an explicit expression for the mock theta function $\Phi^{[m,s]}$ whenever $m$ or $s$ represents half an odd integer. This result, combined with the recurrence relation for $\Phi^{[m,s]}$, allows us to determine the function for all values of $m$ and $s$. As a practical application, we establish explicit formulas for the character and supercharacter of N=3 modules arising from the quantum Hamiltonian reduction of $\hat{osp}(3|2)$-modules.

Discrete Morse theory, serving as a cell complex counterpart to smooth Morse theory, has evolved over the last few decades following Robin Forman's initial formulation in 1998. Specifically, discrete gradient vector fields defined on simplicial complexes are essential for capturing the key properties of discrete Morse functions. This work demonstrates that the characteristic polynomials of the Laplacian matrices for a simplicial complex act as generating functions for the discrete gradient vector fields associated with discrete Morse functions, provided the complex is either a graph or a triangulation of an orientable manifold. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive characterization of the relationship between rooted forests in higher dimensions and discrete gradient vector fields.

This work describes paraxial light propagation from a modal viewpoint. By decomposing the initial transverse field into a spatial basis with well-defined analytical propagation properties, we can analytically advance any target field efficiently. Choosing a basis distinct from plane waves resolves the numerical artifacts inherent in the angular spectrum method while simultaneously providing intuitive insight into the propagation behavior of specific field classes. We present the theory, contrast it with the numerical angular spectrum technique, and validate its accuracy through various instructive experimental examples. We contend that this modal approach for propagating light constitutes a valuable addition to the toolkit for optical field propagation.

Estimating multiple parameters in quantum systems is a significant challenge with both theoretical and practical implications. This study addresses the simultaneous estimation of two parameters linked to the length and direction of the Bloch vector for identically prepared qubit states confined to a plane. Achieving optimal precision for both parameters necessitates collective measurements across multiple qubits. By modeling $N$ qubits as an ensemble of spin-1/2 systems, we demonstrate that asymptotic simultaneous optimality is achievable through a straightforward collective strategy: first estimating the length parameter via measurements of populations in subspaces corresponding to distinct total angular momentum values $j$, followed by estimating the direction parameter through spin projections onto an optimal basis. Additionally, for nearly pure states and sufficiently large but finite $N$, we show that the majority of information resides within the largest three $j$-subspaces. We further investigate the realization of total angular-momentum measurements by analyzing output signatures from a Bell multiport setup, achieving exact results for $N=2,3$ and approximate results for other $N$ when the state is nearly pure. Finally, numerical analysis indicates that a Bell multiport setup can distinguish between projections onto the $j=N/2$ and $j=N/2-1$ subspaces based on their respective interference patterns at the output.

We introduce an updated version of ReLoC, a relational separation logic designed for verifying refinements in programs featuring higher-order state, fine-grained concurrency, polymorphism, and recursive types. At its core, ReLoC utilizes a refinement judgment, $e \precsim e' : \tau$, indicating that program $e$ refines program $e'$ at type $\tau$. Unlike previous approaches that required unfolding judgments into model definitions for languages with higher-order state and concurrency, ReLoC employs type-directed structural and symbolic execution rules within a separation-logic framework to manipulate this judgment. These abstract proof rules simplify refinement verification and extend the concept of logically atomic specifications to a relational context, termed "logically atomic relational specifications."

Built upon the Iris framework for separation logic in Coq, ReLoC leverages Iris capabilities to prove soundness and execute refinement proofs. We have implemented tactics for interactive reasoning, enabling the mechanization of multiple case studies in Coq to demonstrate ReLoC's practicality. ReLoC Reloaded, an extension of the LICS'18 version, incorporates various technical enhancements, a new Coq formalization, and support for Iris's prophecy variables, which facilitate reasoning about a program's future during refinement proofs. Additionally, we expand the concept of logically atomic relational specifications by introducing a new variant based on the HOCAP pattern proposed by Svendsen et al.

This study revisits the classical digital sequence design challenge, specifically the search for binary sequences with optimal peak sidelobe levels (PSL). By integrating prior research with new mathematical insights, we developed several hybrid heuristic algorithms. Experimental results using these algorithms successfully identified PSL-optimal binary sequences for all lengths previously determined through exhaustive searches in existing literature. Furthermore, leveraging a general-purpose computer, we demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed methods by generating binary sequences with lengths ranging from 106 to 300, many of which achieve record-breaking PSL values. Finally, by applying established algebraic constructions, we outlined strategies to efficiently optimize PSL for highly competitive binary sequences using the suggested algorithms.

This technical report provides a comprehensive, formal account of the features presented in the paper by Adrien Ycart, Lele Liu, Emmanouil Benetos, and Marcus T. Pearce, titled "Investigating the Perceptual Validity of Evaluation Metrics for Automatic Piano Music Transcription," which was accepted for publication in Transactions of the International Society for Music Information Retrieval (TISMIR) in 2020.

This study focuses on detecting mu-suppression within electroencephalographic (EEG) signals for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. To achieve this, a novel algorithm is introduced that combines a statistical model with a linear classifier. Specifically, the generalized extreme value distribution (GEV) is employed to model the power spectral density of EEG signals originating from the central motor cortex. The three parameters of this distribution are estimated via the maximum likelihood method. Utilizing these parameters, a straightforward and efficient linear classifier is constructed to differentiate between three distinct events: imagery, movement, and resting states. Initial findings indicate that the proposed statistical framework enables precise detection of mu-suppression and accurate discrimination among various EEG events, yielding high classification performance.

This study addresses the engineering challenge of positioning traffic sensors on long highways featuring ramps. Given that installing large sensors on every segment is practically unfeasible, the primary objective is to identify placements that maximize network-wide traffic observability, thereby enabling accurate density estimates even in sensor-free areas. The paper's main contribution lies in combining control-theoretic observability analysis with integer programming to determine optimal sensor locations based on the nonlinear dynamics and parameters of traffic networks. Specifically, the asymmetric cell transmission model guides the placement strategy, integrated with observability analysis of nonlinear dynamic systems using Gramians. Comprehensive numerical case studies validate the proposed theoretical methods and address various computational research questions. Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to other traffic dynamics models.

This study presents commissioning observations of the transiting exoplanet HAT-P-14 b using the NIRSpec instrument's Bright Object Time Series (BOTS) mode with the G395H/F290LP grating/filter setup ($3-5\mu$m). Although the primary goal was to validate the NIRSpec BOTS mode for routine scientific applications, the resulting data provide a precise transmission spectrum that appears featureless within the instrument's precision limits. This lack of features aligns with theoretical expectations for HAT-P-14 b, given its small atmospheric scale height. The exceptional stability and quality of the \emph{JWST/NIRSpec} transit spectrum, which show minimal systematic effects, enabled median uncertainties of 50–60 ppm across the wavelength range at a resolution of $R=100$ in a single exposure. These results match pre-flight predictions and approach the photon-noise limit for an F-type star with $J = 9.094$ like HAT-P-14. Furthermore, these observations demonstrate NIRSpec/BOTS's capability to advance transiting exoplanet atmospheric science, paving the way for future discoveries in Cycle 1 and subsequent cycles.

A partition polynomial serves as a refinement of the partition number $p(n)$, where its coefficients enumerate specific partition statistics. Much like partition numbers possess practical asymptotic properties, so too do partition polynomials; indeed, their asymptotics govern the limiting behavior of their zeros, which arrange themselves into a network of curves within the unit disk. A crucial development in this field necessitates a thorough examination of the "root dilogarithm," defined as the real component of the square root of the standard dilogarithm.

Contemporary laboratory methods, including ultrafast laser excitation and shock compression, can induce matter into highly nonequilibrium states characterized by intricate structural transformations, metallization, and dissociation dynamics. Conventional approaches struggle to model the profound changes in electronic structures and ion dynamics occurring during these rapid processes. In this work, we demonstrate that deep neural networks (DNNs) can effectively capture the dependence of the electronic density of states (DOS) on local atomic environments. This capability is validated for both multicomponent systems under exoplanetary thermodynamic conditions and nonequilibrium systems undergoing super-heated melting. The DNN model achieves large-scale, time-resolved DOS diagnostics with accuracy comparable to *ab initio* methods. Furthermore, the atomic contributions to the DOS provided by the DNN accurately reflect the local neighborhood of specific atoms, serving as robust order parameters to identify various phases and intermediate local structures, thereby underscoring the model's efficacy in investigating dynamic phenomena.

Growing attention is directed toward flexible joint modeling for diverse data measurement scales, including complex formats like images, documents, and functions. This study proposes a general nonparametric Bayesian framework utilizing mixture models that capture dependencies across data types via a joint mixing measure. This measure employs a novel infinite tensor factorization (ITF) prior, constructed as a tensor product of stick-breaking processes, to enable flexible cluster allocation. We establish foundational theory and asymptotic properties for a specific Parafac factorization case. Furthermore, we introduce a Gibbs sampling algorithm for ITF mixtures of product kernels, utilizing slice sampling for efficient implementation. Finally, the proposed methods are evaluated against alternative joint mixture models based on Dirichlet processes through both simulation studies and real-world data applications.

This paper addresses several open problems regarding gamma subordinators. Specifically, we derive a representation for the moments of the inverse gamma subordinator. Furthermore, we examine $\lambda$-potentials and investigate the governing equations linked to gamma subordinators and their inverse processes. These representations are expressed using higher transcendental functions, also referred to as Volterra functions.

When an i.i.d. sequence of letters is segmented into words based on i.i.d. renewal times, the resulting sequence of words is also i.i.d. In the context of the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of these words, the rate function corresponds to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of words. Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander \cite{BGdH10} established the quenched LDP (conditional on a typical letter sequence) for scenarios where renewal times exhibit an algebraic tail; their derived rate function consists of two components: the annealed rate function and a second term proportional to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of letters, where the reference law is generated by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This proportionality constant matches the tail exponent of the renewal process. The current paper aims to generalize both LDPs to cases where the underlying letter sequences are not i.i.d. It demonstrates that both principles remain valid when the letter sequence satisfies a mixing condition known as \emph{summable variation}. The resulting rate functions are still expressed as specific relative entropies with respect to the reference laws of words and letters, respectively. However, because neither reference law is i.i.d., the extension requires several approximation arguments.

This study investigates how anisotropic wind driving influences accretion characteristics onto black holes within close binary systems, with a specific emphasis on the line-driven winds prevalent in high-mass X-ray binaries. In such close configurations, the companion star's tidal forces alter the wind structure through two primary mechanisms: a decrease in terminal velocity caused by reduced effective surface gravity, and a drop in mass flux resulting from gravity darkening. We integrate these factors into the CAK theory in a simplified manner to examine wind dynamics around the accreting object across the orbital scale. Our findings indicate that a focused accretion stream forms naturally when the Roche lobe filling factor exceeds approximately 0.8 to 0.9, a phenomenon similar to wind Roche lobe overflow, but contingent upon accounting for velocity reduction. The presence of this stream is essential for delivering the requisite angular momentum to establish an accretion disc around the black hole. While gravity darkening diminishes the angular momentum available for accretion, it does not preclude disc formation. Consequently, we anticipate a distinct shift in the observability of high-mass X-ray binaries, determined by whether the donor star's Roche lobe filling factor falls below or surpasses the $\sim$0.8-0.9 threshold.

This research examines the fine-grained complexity of connectivity problems in unweighted undirected graphs. Recent advancements have established that all edge connectivity variants—such as single-source-single-sink, global, Steiner, single-source, and all-pairs—are solvable within $m^{1+o(1)}$ time, effectively collapsing their complexity into the almost-linear-time regime. Historically, vertex connectivity was considered significantly more difficult; however, recent findings demonstrated that both single-source-single-sink and global vertex connectivity can also be solved in $m^{1+o(1)}$ time, sparking optimism that all vertex connectivity variants might similarly fall into the almost-linear-time category. We prove this optimism is unfounded, assuming conjectures regarding the identification of 4-cliques. Furthermore, we delineate the complete complexity landscape by providing tight bounds for combinatorial algorithms in dense graphs. Three distinct regimes emerge: (1) all-pairs and Steiner vertex connectivity exhibit a complexity of $\hat{\Theta}(n^{4})$, (2) single-source vertex connectivity has a complexity of $\hat{\Theta}(n^{3})$, and (3) single-source-single-sink and global vertex connectivity operate at $\hat{\Theta}(n^{2})$. For graphs with general density, assuming Gomory-Hu trees for element connectivity can be computed in almost-linear time, we derive tight bounds of $\hat{\Theta}(m^{2})$, $\hat{\Theta}(m^{1.5})$, and $\hat{\Theta}(m)$, respectively.

Solar PV yield nowcasting aids grid integration by predicting fluctuations in demand. This study evaluates several low-resource methods for forecasting solar output using a UK dataset comprising satellite imagery and energy readings spanning 1 to 4 hours. Additionally, the research calculates the carbon emissions produced versus avoided by these models, revealing that even compact models suitable for resource-constrained environments can offer benefits exceeding their carbon footprint by several orders of magnitude. The analysis further investigates prediction errors and the activation patterns within a CNN.

We demonstrate that every left-invariant metric with harmonic curvature on a solvable Lie group possesses Ricci-parallel properties. We establish the same conclusion for any Lie group with a dimension of 6 or less.

Musical gestures bridge the gap between a score's symbolic representation and the physical reality of sound. This paper concentrates on the mathematical framework of musical gestures, suggesting an extension that incorporates braids and knots. Such an expansion allows the formalism to address additional case studies, particularly those concerning conducting techniques. Furthermore, recent findings regarding the parallels and distinctions between gestures performed by orchestral musicians can be situated within the context of braided monoidal categories. Given that both knots and braids are applicable to fields ranging from music to biology (such as the study of knotted proteins), the article concludes with a novel musical composition based on the structure of DNA.

The performance of Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS) systems has stalled despite the rapid advancement of deep neural networks, particularly the adoption of large pre-trained models. This paper reviews current achievements and re-evaluates the remaining challenges in the CWS task. Methodologically, we introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework for existing CWS systems. This approach not only diagnoses the strengths and weaknesses of current models under in-dataset conditions but also quantifies discrepancies between different evaluation criteria, thereby mitigating negative transfer in multi-criteria learning. Strategically, although we do not propose a new model, our comprehensive experiments across eight models and seven datasets, along with detailed analysis, identify promising directions for future research. We have made all code publicly available and released an interface for quickly evaluating and diagnosing user models: https://github.com/neulab/InterpretEval.

This paper explicitly investigates non-integrable mass within Einstein-scalar gravity frameworks featuring weakened boundary conditions. By applying both the Hamiltonian and Wald formulas, we demonstrate that the resulting masses are non-integrable. While imposing boundary conditions offers a potential resolution, it introduces additional complications. These findings suggest that the macroscopic thermodynamic properties of scalar hairy black holes require a description involving an additional charge alongside mass, which we term the scalar charge. Indeed, mass non-integrability consistently emerges when matter fields possess charges unrelated to spacetime diffeomorphisms. We identify that the non-integrability arises specifically from the misapplication of Wald's formula. Leveraging Wald's formula alongside the existence of the scalar charge, we propose a revised definition of mass: we stipulate that the variation of the Hamiltonian must not contribute from the variation of other charges. This new definition remains applicable to a broader class of gravities coupled to matter fields with various charges.

This study examines the existence, uniqueness, and stability of periodic traveling waves in the fractional Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation. Our methodology establishes sufficient conditions to demonstrate the uniqueness of single-lobe solutions derived from a constrained minimization problem. Spectral stability is subsequently proven by showing that the linearized operator, restricted to the orthogonal complement of the tangent space associated with the wave's mass and momentum, possesses no negative eigenvalues. Additionally, we employ Petviashvili's method to numerically analyze the spectral stability of these periodic waves. Finally, several remarks regarding the orbital stability of periodic traveling waves are included.

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has recently garnered significant attention within wireless communications research. Composed of passive reflective elements, an IRS can adjust the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incident waveforms. These advantageous properties enable the control and optimization of wireless channel characteristics to meet specific signal design and processing requirements, thereby offering substantial potential for radar applications. This paper establishes the theoretical basis for integrating IRS into radar systems and examines the potential for enhancing target parameter estimation. Specifically, we analyze IRS deployment in scenarios where line-of-sight (LOS) links are weak or obstructed. We demonstrate that IRS can create a virtual or non-line-of-sight (NLOS) connection between the radar and the target, resulting in improved radar performance. The efficacy of this IRS-enabled virtual link in estimating moving target parameters is illustrated under both optimized and non-optimized conditions. Numerical simulations reveal that IRS enhances target parameter estimation when the LOS link's relative strength is weaker than approximately $10^{-1}$ compared to the NLOS link.

We present ALPACA, a Lorentz-invariant parton cascade that implements the AMY effective kinetic theory for QCD at elevated temperatures. By explicitly simulating the evolution of parton ensembles within single events, ALPACA solves the Boltzmann equation. We outline methods for estimating effective masses and temperature from individual events to determine rates for elastic collisions and splitting/merging processes. Furthermore, we extensively validate the framework by demonstrating its ability to reproduce expected thermal equilibrium behavior.

This article introduces a Shell Language Preprocessing (SLP) library designed for tokenization and encoding of Unix and Linux shell commands. We outline the justification for this novel approach, illustrating scenarios where traditional Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipelines are ineffective. Additionally, we assess our methodology on a security classification task, comparing it against established information and communications technology (ICT) tokenization methods, and demonstrate a substantial improvement in F1 score, rising from 0.392 to 0.874.

This study investigates the impact of counter-rotating oscillators within an ensemble comprising both co- and counter-rotating types by incrementing their relative proportion. An aging transition was identified at a specific critical ratio of these counter-rotating oscillators, a phenomenon previously attainable only by introducing a significant number of inactive oscillators. Additionally, the influence of mean-field feedback strength under symmetry-preserving coupling was analyzed. Notably, even a slight reduction in feedback strength caused an abrupt expansion of the aging transition parameter space, eventually allowing the aging transition to occur at a critical feedback value without any counter-rotating oscillators present. The research was further extended to symmetry-breaking coupling using conjugate variables, revealing that such coupling can also induce the aging transition in the absence of counter-rotating oscillators and at a feedback strength of unity. Generally, increasing either the oscillator frequency or the proportion of counter-rotating oscillators broadens the parameter space for the aging transition across both coupling types. The transition from oscillatory behavior to the aging state occurs via a Hopf bifurcation, whereas the shift from the aging state to an oscillation death state is driven by a Pitchfork bifurcation. Finally, analytical expressions were derived to determine the critical ratio of counter-rotating oscillators, thereby defining the stable boundaries of the aging transition.

Wave propagation within artificial crystals, such as phononic and sonic structures, is fundamentally anisotropic. Drawing on the principles of periodic composites, this anisotropy stems directly from the unit cell's space group and the rank of the elastic tensor. This study investigates effective velocities in the long-wavelength limit of periodic acoustic and elastic composites relative to propagation direction. By employing second-order perturbation theory, we develop explicit and efficient formulas to estimate effective velocity surfaces, extending the Christoffel equation for elastic waves in solids. Our analysis reveals strongly anisotropic sonic crystals governing scalar acoustic waves and similarly anisotropic phononic crystals for vector elastic waves. Additionally, we demonstrate that under particular conditions, quasi-longitudinal waves can propagate significantly slower than shear waves in the same direction.

**Purpose:** To enhance target coverage and lower radiation doses to surrounding organs-at-risk (OARs), we created an image-guided therapy approach utilizing a precomputed library of treatment plans that are controlled and executed in real-time.

**Methods:** This library is built by optimizing a treatment plan for every breathing phase identified in a 4DCT scan. Therapy delivery is simulated using a continuous series of synthetic CTs derived from actual MRI sequences. During the procedure, spots are delivered using plans corresponding to the phase where the tumor is closest to its current position. The study evaluated this method on five liver cases.

**Results:** Under conditions simulating a 2 mm error in tumor position knowledge, our approach averaged a 5% increase in dose homogeneity within the target (calculated as 1-(D_5-D_95)/prescription) compared to a standard 4D robustly optimized plan, alongside a 23% reduction in mean liver dose. Although treatment duration approximately doubled, it remained under 4 minutes on average.

**Conclusions:** This image-guided framework surpasses current state-of-the-art 4D-robust plans for all patients in the study regarding both target coverage and OAR sparing, achieving these results with a manageable increase in treatment time given existing tumor tracking accuracy.

This study examines the intertwined dynamics of opinion formation and social balance. We introduce a model in which agents develop opinions based on bounded confidence, interacting solely with their friends. Meanwhile, the nature of social connections—friendships and enmities—evolves to achieve social balance, influenced by the similarity of agents' views. The analysis covers both one-dimensional and two-dimensional opinion spaces. Our findings reveal that the dynamics lead to agent segregation into two distinct cliques, characterized by differing opinions between them. The level of bounded confidence determines whether each clique reaches a unified consensus or sustains multiple internal opinion clusters. In the one-dimensional scenario, opinions in one clique are consistently lower than those in the other, creating a "left" and a "right" group. For the two-dimensional case, numerical evidence indicates that the cliques are separated by a hyperplane within the opinion space. Additionally, we demonstrate that the partial extension of the unidimensional opinion phenomenon described by DeMarzo, Vayanos, and Zwiebel (Q J Econ 2003) holds true within our framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for political science, specifically regarding ideological fragmentation and the rise of new political parties.

Disorder-free localization is a recently identified form of nonergodicity occurring in quantum many-body systems with gauge symmetries, provided the initial state is a superposition of gauge superselection sectors. This phenomenon halts thermalization indefinitely, even in nonintegrable, translation-invariant models. Previous research [Halimeh, Zhao, Hauke, and Knolle, arXiv:2111.02427] demonstrated that terms linear in the gauge-symmetry generator can stabilize disorder-free localization in $\mathrm{U}(1)$ gauge theories against errors coupling distinct superselection sectors. In this work, we examine $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theories, revealing that disorder-free localization can not only be stabilized but also **enhanced** by incorporating translation-invariant terms linear in a local $\mathbb{Z}_2$ **pseudogenerator**. This pseudogenerator mimics the full generator within a single superselection sector but may differ outside it. Through analytical and numerical analysis, we show that this mechanism induces the quantum Zeno effect, leading to the dynamical emergence of a renormalized gauge theory featuring an enhanced local symmetry. This new symmetry, linked to the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ pseudogenerator, generates a proliferation of superselection sectors that creates effective disorder exceeding that of the original model, thus strengthening disorder-free localization. Finally, we outline the experimental viability of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ pseudogenerator by presenting a detailed, readily implementable proposal to observe disorder-free localization using a Rydberg system.

This study demonstrates that spacetime's quantum characteristics, represented by noncommutativity at the Planck scale, result in a generalized time evolution where quantum pure states can transition into mixed states. Specifically, a decoherence mechanism emerges as a Lindblad-like evolution for the density operator when the generator of time translations is modified by spacetime noncommutative effects. Furthermore, analyzing the decoherence time for a free particle's evolution indicates that the Planck mass represents the upper limit for the mass of elementary quantum systems.

This paper introduces a novel deep framework that predicts facial attributes and utilizes them as a soft modality to enhance face recognition accuracy. The proposed end-to-end system comprises a convolutional neural network (CNN) whose output diverges into two distinct branches: one dedicated to predicting facial attributes and the other to identifying face images. Unlike traditional multi-task approaches that rely solely on a shared CNN feature space for joint training, our method fuses the predicted attributes with features from the face modality to boost identification performance. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our model improves both face identification and facial attribute prediction, particularly for identity-related attributes like gender. Evaluated on two standard datasets annotated with identities and attributes, the results indicate that the proposed model surpasses most existing methods in both tasks.

Recent studies have utilized comparisons of spectral linewidths between ions and neutral molecules to estimate magnetic field strengths in turbulent star-forming regions. However, the specific ion (HCO+) and neutral (HCN) species employed in these investigations may not evolve together across all scales and densities, potentially failing to trace identical regions. This work employs coupled chemical and dynamical models of evolving prestellar molecular cloud cores, incorporating non-equilibrium chemistry with and without magnetic fields, to analyze the spatial distributions of HCO+ and HCN, which have historically been used to assess linewidth differences. Furthermore, we search for new ion-neutral pairs that serve as superior candidates for such observational studies, characterized by similar evolutionary paths and approximate co-spatiality within our models. We identify three promising candidate pairs: HCO+/NO, HCO+/CO, and NO+/NO.

Diffuse low-grade gliomas are slowly proliferating tumors that invariably recur following treatment. This study revisits the mathematical modeling of tumor radius evolution both prior to and subsequent to radiotherapy, introducing a novel framework that is both biologically grounded and computationally simple, addressing limitations found in earlier models. We validated this approach against clinical data comprising time-series tumor radius measurements from 43 patients, employing stochastic optimization to achieve excellent model fits across all cases. Because the model accounts for tumor evolution starting from the initial glioma cell, it enables the estimation of tumor age. By applying profile-likelihood analysis to extract maximum information from the data, we constructed confidence intervals for the birth age of the tumor, confirming that low-grade gliomas typically emerge during late adolescence. Furthermore, an approximate analytical expression for the temporal changes in tumor radius allows us to elucidate the correlations observed in the dataset.

Highly saturated models are a fundamental component of the model-theoretic machinery used in nonstandard analysis. Between the two methods for constructing them, ultrapowers utilizing $\kappa^+$-good ultrafilters appear significantly less popular. Driven by the hypothesis that this relative unpopularity stems partly from the standard exposition being overly dense, this paper presents an alternative account designed to be more accessible.

Measurements from the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) detail the production of K$^{*}(892)^{0}$ and $\phi(1020)$ mesons in both proton-proton (pp) and lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. Transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) spectra were recorded at midrapidity ($|y|<0.5$), extending up to 20 GeV$/c$ for inelastic pp events and across various centralities for Pb-Pb collisions. The observed dependencies of average transverse momentum on collision centrality and energy align with the radial flow model established for stable hadrons, indicating that this effect intensifies with greater centrality and higher energies. A suppression of the $\mathrm{K^{*0}/K}$ ratio relative to pp collisions in Pb-Pb environments suggests signal loss due to rescattering of decay products within the hadronic phase; however, no such suppression is seen for the longer-lived $\phi(1020)$ mesons. Nuclear modification factors ($R_{\rm AA}$) were derived using pp reference spectra at the same energy. In central Pb-Pb collisions with $p_{\rm T} > 8$ GeV$/c$, $R_{\rm AA}$ values for both meson types fall below unity and resemble those of pions, kaons, and (anti)protons. Furthermore, high-$p_{\mathrm T}$ $R_{\rm AA}$ values for K$^{*}(892)^{0}$ and $\phi(1020)$ remain consistent within uncertainties across $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}}$ energies of 5.02 and 2.76 TeV.

Intermediate-level nuclear waste requires storage until it is safe for permanent disposal, making temperature monitoring of waste packages a critical task for the nuclear decommissioning sector to facilitate effective management. At the Sellafield Ltd site, phosphor thermometry and thermal imaging have been employed to track the temperatures of intermediate-level waste containers under anticipated environmental storage conditions, specifically within a range of 10°C to 25°C and relative humidities between 60% and 90%. These studies have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of inferring internal temperatures from external surface measurements within these specified environmental parameters.

Godsil introduced the concept of $t$-designs within the symmetric group on $n$ elements in 1988, noting that $t$-transitive permutation sets inherently constitute such designs. We establish upper bounds for the covering radius of these designs as a function of $n$ and $t$, expressed in relation to the largest zeros of Charlier polynomials.

This paper re-examines the Pseudo-Bayesian method for estimating density matrices in quantum state tomography. While Pseudo-Bayesian inference has proven to be a powerful paradigm with compelling theoretical and empirical outcomes, calculating these estimators remains challenging due to the need to sample from complex, high-dimensional distributions, which limits their practical application. To address this limitation, we introduce an efficient adaptive MCMC sampling technique tailored for the Pseudo-Bayesian estimator. Simulation results demonstrate that our method is at least two orders of magnitude faster than prior implementations, a significant improvement for practical quantum tomography.

In the era of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, efficiently compiling quantum algorithms is crucial. Although several open-source frameworks for quantum compilation and circuit optimization exist—including IBM Qiskit, CQC Tket, Google Cirq, Rigetti Quilc, and PyZX—quantum programmers often lack clarity regarding their comparative performance. The increasing complexity and diversity of compilation algorithms necessitate a specialized tool for cross-benchmarking and profiling the internal workflows of the quantum compilation stack. We introduce Arline Benchmarks, an open-source package designed to automate the benchmarking of quantum compilers with a specific focus on NISQ applications. The name "Arline" honors Arline Greenbaum Feynman, the first wife of Richard Feynman, a pioneer in quantum computing. We evaluated multiple quantum compilation frameworks using key metrics such as post-optimization gate counts, circuit depth, hardware-dependent cost functions, and compiler execution times, accompanied by a detailed analysis of metrics at each compilation stage. Our testing covered various compilers applied to random circuits and structured quantum algorithms (including VQE, Trotter decomposition, Grover search, and Option Pricing via Amplitude Estimation) across several popular quantum hardware architectures. Utilizing Arline's cross-platform capabilities, we propose a composite compilation pipeline concept that integrates compiler-specific optimization subroutines into a unified stack to determine the optimal sequence of compilation passes. By offering granular insights into the compilation flow, Arline Benchmarks serves as a valuable toolkit for quantum computing researchers and developers to better understand compiler characteristics.

This study examines the two-dimensional gas-phase oxygen abundance distributions of 100 nearby galaxies from the Calar Alto Legacy Integral Field Area survey. Following the removal of large-scale radial metallicity gradients, we calculated the two-point correlation functions for the resulting metallicity fluctuation maps. We identified correlations in most targets, demonstrating that they significantly exceed expectations based on beam-smearing alone and remain robust regardless of the metallicity diagnostic used. These correlation functions are generally well-described by a simple model combining stochastic metal injection with diffusion. After accounting for beam-smearing and noise effects derived from this model, the sample galaxies exhibit characteristic correlation lengths of approximately 1 kpc. These lengths increase with both stellar mass and star formation rate but show no significant dependence on Hubble type, barredness, or merging status. Furthermore, we found no evidence for a theoretically predicted link between gas velocity dispersion and correlation length, though this may stem from the limited dynamic range in velocity dispersion within our sample. Ultimately, our findings indicate that measuring 2D metallicity correlation functions offers a potent method for investigating galaxy evolution.

Deep neural networks have achieved significant advancements in medical image analysis; however, their reliance on large datasets often limits their effectiveness given the typically small sample sizes in medical imaging. Generating synthetic data offers a viable solution to augment training sets and facilitate large-scale research. Recently, diffusion models have gained prominence in computer vision for their ability to create photorealistic synthetic images. This study investigates the application of Latent Diffusion Models to generate synthetic images derived from high-resolution 3D brain scans. Utilizing T1w MRI data from the UK Biobank (N=31,740), we trained our models to capture the probabilistic distribution of brain images, conditioning the generation on covariates such as age, sex, and brain structure volumes. Our results demonstrate that the models produce realistic data, with effective control over generation through the conditioning variables. Furthermore, we compiled a synthetic dataset comprising 100,000 brain images and released it openly for the scientific community to utilize.

We present a deterministic counterpart to Markov chains, termed the hunger game. Similar to rotor-routing, this game deterministically replicates the dynamics of both recurrent and absorbing Markov chains. For recurrent Markov chains with a finite state space, the hunger game simulation converges toward the stationary distribution, with the discrepancy decreasing at a rate of $N^{-1}$ (where $N$ represents the number of steps). Likewise, for absorbing Markov chains with a finite state space, the simulation demonstrates concentration regarding hitting measures and expected hitting times, also achieving a discrepancy decay of $N^{-1}$ instead of the typical $N^{-1/2}$. When the transition probabilities of a finite Markov chain are rational, the game becomes eventually periodic; the period appears consistent across all initial configurations, and the basin of attraction seems to partition the configuration space (the set of hunger vectors) via translation, though this remains unproven.

The scotogenic framework produces Majorana neutrino masses through radiative loops involving dark matter particles. We investigate the parameter space where fermionic dark matter abundance arises from a conversion-driven freeze-out. Small Yukawa couplings are required to trigger chemical decoupling for these conversions, which naturally yields minimal neutrino masses provided active neutrinos exhibit a hierarchical spectrum. Furthermore, this model addresses the recent $W$-boson mass anomaly while remaining consistent with limits from direct detection, charged lepton flavor violation, and collider experiments. Specific regions of the parameter space predict long-lived particle signatures detectable at the LHC.

The continuous-time framework serves as the cornerstone of contemporary finance. Since real-world trading does not occur at every instant, it is intuitive to assume that the continuous model should represent the limit of discrete-time models where transactions happen at specific intervals. However, this paper shows that when terminal wealth and self-financing constraints are applied rigorously in the discrete setting as they are in the continuous one, the continuous model is not necessarily the limit of discrete models. This finding casts significant doubt on the foundational validity of the continuous-time approach.

This study investigates the Penrose process involving an extremal braneworld black hole, specifically analyzing the interaction of two massive spinning particles near the event horizon. Upon calculating the maximum energy extraction efficiency for this mechanism, the results indicate that efficiency rises as the braneworld black hole's charge parameter $d$ diminishes. Notably, when $d$ takes a negative value, the achievable efficiency surpasses that of the Kerr case.

As the distance from the training data increases, predictive uncertainty should rise because limited information allows for numerous plausible explanations. To address the overconfidence of Bayesian deep learning models in out-of-distribution scenarios, we propose Distance-Aware Prior (DAP) calibration. This method defines prior distributions over model parameters that vary based on the input's distance from the training set. Being independent of the posterior inference technique, DAP calibration functions as a post-processing step. We validate its superiority over various baselines across multiple classification and regression tasks, including benchmarks specifically designed to evaluate predictive distribution quality outside the training domain.

Video analysis tasks, particularly action recognition, have gained significant research attention and found expanding applications in areas like smart healthcare, driven by the availability of large-scale datasets and deep learning representations. However, video models trained on existing datasets often experience substantial performance drops when applied to real-world scenarios due to domain shifts between public training sources and actual target videos. Additionally, given the high expenses associated with video annotation, utilizing unlabeled videos for training is more practical. To simultaneously address performance degradation and the challenge of annotation costs, Video Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (VUDA) has been proposed. This approach adapts models from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains by mitigating domain shifts, thereby enhancing model generalizability and portability. This paper reviews recent advancements in deep learning-based VUDA. It starts with the motivation behind VUDA, proceeds to its definition, examines recent methods for both closed-set VUDA and various scenarios, outlines current benchmark datasets, and concludes by suggesting future research directions to advance the field.

Design automation for analog circuits remains a persistent challenge within the integrated circuit industry. This study introduces a deep reinforcement learning approach to accelerate the pre-layout design phase, specifically targeting the identification of device parameters that meet desired circuit specifications. Drawing inspiration from seasoned human designers who leverage domain expertise regarding circuit topology and specification interdependencies, our method uniquely integrates these critical insights into policy learning via a graph-based network. This architecture effectively models the relationships between circuit parameters and design objectives, distinguishing it from all previous methods. Experimental evaluations on representative circuits demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves human-level accuracy (approximately 99%) while offering 1.5 times the efficiency of current top-performing techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits superior generalization to unseen specifications and enhanced optimality in performance tuning. Notably, it is applicable to a wide variety of analog circuits across different semiconductor technologies, overcoming the constraints of prior ad-hoc solutions that were limited to specific circuit types and conventional processes.

The triumph of deep learning sparked inquiry into whether the brain employs gradient-based mechanisms to acquire hierarchical representations. Yet, existing biologically plausible gradient-based credit assignment methods rely on infinitesimally small feedback signals, creating conflicts with noisy biological realities and contradicting neuroscience data that indicates top-down feedback substantially shapes neural activity.
