Our conclusion is that the specific atomic data employed in electron density calculations entirely dictate the derived density structures. We demonstrate this by presenting three sets of atomic data combinations that yield observational results consistent with each of the three modeled density structures.

To safeguard Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) systems against spoofing attacks and mitigate personal information leakage, a Countermeasure (CM) model has been developed. Given the constraints of practicality and security, this model is typically deployed on edge devices, which possess fewer computing resources and storage capacity than cloud-based systems, thereby necessitating strict limits on model size. To optimize the balance between model size and performance, we introduced an adversarial speaker distillation approach. This method enhances standard knowledge distillation by integrating generalized end-to-end (GE2E) pre-training with adversarial fine-tuning. During the evaluation phase of the ASVspoof 2021 Logical Access task, our proposed ASD-ResNetSE model achieved a min t-DCF of 0.2695 and an EER of 3.54%. Notably, the ASD-ResNetSE model utilized only 22.5% of the parameters and 19.4% of the multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations required by the original ResNetSE model.

Exact solutions detailing the collapse of a particle toward a singular potential in both classical and quantum frameworks have been derived, analyzed, and contrasted. These solutions reveal remarkable parallels between the quantum and classical regimes. Specifically, at zero energy, both systems display self-similarity with characteristic spatial scales following identical temporal evolution. Beyond collapse, exact solutions describing particle escape from the singularity also exist for both scenarios. Crucially, collapse and escape are independent processes, not connected via the singularity. In the quantum context, the norms of the exact solution wave functions vary with time, necessitating a revision and generalization of continuity equations and mean value rules, which has been accomplished. This analysis provides fresh insights into the foundations of quantum mechanics.

To date, the specific source of relativistic solar protons during major flare and coronal mass ejection (CME) events has remained ambiguous. This study conducts a comprehensive comparative analysis of the temporal profiles of relativistic protons observed globally by neutron monitors at Earth alongside electromagnetic indicators of coronal particle acceleration during the significant particle event of January 20, 2005. The neutron monitor-derived intensity-time profile of these protons reveals two distinct successive peaks. We demonstrate that microwave, hard X-ray, and gamma-ray emissions exhibit multiple episodes of particle acceleration confined to the impulsive phase of the flare. The initial relativistic protons detected at Earth are accelerated simultaneously with relativistic electrons and protons responsible for pion-decay gamma-rays during the second acceleration episode. The second peak in the Earth-bound relativistic proton profile coincides with new signatures of coronal acceleration occurring roughly one solar radius above the photosphere. These signatures are indicated by low-intensity hard X-ray and microwave emissions, as well as renewed radio emissions from electron beams and a coronal shock wave. Finally, we evaluate these observations within the context of various coronal particle acceleration scenarios.

Natural language processing models derive word representations from the distributional hypothesis, which posits that word context (such as co-occurrence) reflects meaning. We introduce "garble"—$n$-grams formed from random character sequences—as a new context for investigating word meaning both inside and outside existing language. Unlike real words, these randomly generated character $n$-grams lack semantic meaning but retain primitive information derived from their character composition. By analyzing embeddings of a large dataset comprising garble, standard language, and pseudowords using CharacterBERT, we discovered a specific axis within the model's high-dimensional embedding space that distinguishes between these $n$-gram classes. Moreover, we demonstrate that this axis corresponds to structural features of existing language, including part-of-speech, morphology, and concept concreteness. Consequently, while prior research has largely focused on extant language, our findings reveal that meaning and primitive information are fundamentally connected.

While solitonic symmetry is traditionally understood through the homotopy-group classification of topological solitons, we identify a more complex algebraic framework when solitons of varying dimensions coexist within the spectrum. This insight is revealed in a specific quantum field theory, the four-dimensional $\mathbb{C}P^1$ model, which supports two distinct solitonic excitations: vortices and hopfions. Although homotopy groups suggest these should obey two separate $U(1)$ solitonic symmetries, we demonstrate that the hopfion $U(1)$ symmetry does not exist by calculating the hopfion charge of vortex operators. Instead, we show that hopfion numbers are conserved by a non-invertible symmetry arising from three-dimensional spin topological quantum field theories (TQFTs). The invertible subgroup of this symmetry is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, identified as a spin bordism invariant. Compared to the three-dimensional $\mathbb{C}P^1$ model, our findings propose a unified approach to describing solitonic symmetries and their interactions with topological phases.

We investigate the embedding of continuous dynamical systems into higher-dimensional spaces using projector operators, a method we term Projective Embedding of Dynamical Systems (PEDS). This approach recovers the stable fixed points of the dynamics by projecting them from the expanded space. In this paper, we establish a general definition and demonstrate that for a specific class of rank-1 projector operators, namely the uniform mean field projector, the equations of motion reduce to a mean field approximation of the system. Unlike general embeddings, which rely on a specific variable ordering, the uniform mean field projector does not share this dependency. Furthermore, we prove that while stable fixed points remain stable and saddle points remain saddles in the embedded dynamics, unstable fixed points transform into saddles.

We present sublinear-time algorithms for Max Cut and Max E2Lin$(q)$ on expander graphs within the adjacency list model, capable of distinguishing instances with an optimal value exceeding $1-\varepsilon$ from those below $1-\rho$ where $\rho \gg \varepsilon$. Specifically, the time complexities for Max Cut and Max 2Lin$(q)$ are $\widetilde{O}(\frac{1}{\phi^2\rho} \cdot m^{1/2+O(\varepsilon/(\phi^2\rho))})$ and $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(\frac{q}{\phi\rho})\cdot {(mq)}^{1/2+O(q^6\varepsilon/\phi^2\rho^2)})$, respectively, with $m$ representing the edge count and $\phi$ the conductance of the graph. Furthermore, we introduce a sublinear-time algorithm for Unique Label Cover on expanders where $\phi \gg \epsilon$ in the bounded-degree model. Its time complexity is $\widetilde{O}_d(2^{q^{O(1)}\cdot\phi^{1/q}\cdot \varepsilon^{-1/2}}\cdot n^{1/2+q^{O(q)}\cdot \varepsilon^{4^{1.5-q}}\cdot \phi^{-2}})$, where $n$ denotes the number of variables. Complementing these algorithmic achievements, we demonstrate that testing 3-colorability necessitates $\Omega(n)$ queries, even when restricted to expander graphs.

Understanding how electromagnetic transitions evolve across isotope chains is crucial for nuclear structure, dynamics, and r-process nucleosynthesis. Recent measurements of inelastic proton scattering on even-even $^{112-124}$Sn isotopes offer new insights into the isotopic dependence of E1 and M1 strength distributions. From a theoretical standpoint, we examine M1 transitions in even-even $^{100-140}$Sn isotopes using relativistic nuclear energy density functionals. The resulting M1 strength distribution features an interplay between single and double peaks, explained by the evolution of single-particle states, their occupation dictated by pairing correlations, and two-quasiparticle transitions. Our findings indicate that the discrepancy between model predictions and experimental B(M1) data is significantly reduced compared to previous results. To match experimental M1 data, the quenching of free nucleon g-factors required is $g_{eff}/g_{free}$=0.80-0.93. However, since some B(M1) strength above the neutron threshold might be absent in the proton scattering data, additional experimental work is necessary to verify whether only minor adjustments to bare g-factors are sufficient for finite nuclei.

This study examines how defect geometry influences the critical buckling sensitivity of spherical shells subjected to external pressure. Specifically, we conduct a comparative analysis between shells featuring inward-dimpled and outward-bumpy Gaussian defects. While dimpled defects have become the conventional shape in recent buckling research, bumpy defects have largely been overlooked. Using validated finite-element simulations, we calculate knockdown factors for both scenarios while systematically varying defect geometric parameters. For identical defect amplitudes and angular widths, shells with bumpy defects consistently demonstrate significantly higher knockdown factors compared to those with traditional dimpled defects. Moreover, the functional relationship between knockdown and defect amplitude and width differs qualitatively between the two cases, accompanied by distinct post-buckling behaviors. We offer a speculative interpretation of these findings based on the qualitative disparities in the mean-curvature profiles of the respective defect types.

Publicly accessible astronomical archives offer fresh opportunities to investigate Solar System objects, yet they necessitate sophisticated methods to manage the resulting data volumes. These unbiased surveys help constrain the size distribution of minor bodies, providing crucial insights into Solar System formation theories. Our objective was to detect asteroids within archival images from the ESA Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Science Archive using data mining. To achieve this, we launched a citizen science initiative, Hubble Asteroid Hunter, hosted on the Zooniverse platform, inviting the public to spot asteroid trails in HST imagery. We utilized the volunteers' annotations to train an automated deep learning model via Google Cloud AutoML Vision, enabling a comprehensive search of the HST archive for asteroids crossing the field-of-view. Our efforts yielded the discovery of 1,701 new asteroid trails in archival HST data. These asteroids were detected down to a magnitude of 24.5, making them statistically fainter than those typically found by ground-based surveys. As anticipated, the majority are clustered near the ecliptic plane, with an estimated density of 80 asteroids per square degree. We cross-referenced 670 trails (39% of the total) with the Minor Planet Center database, identifying 454 known Solar System objects, while 1,031 trails (61%) remained unmatched. These unidentified asteroids are significantly fainter, averaging 1.6 magnitudes dimmer than the matched ones, suggesting they are likely previously unknown objects. This study confirms that combining citizen science with machine learning is an effective approach for systematically searching existing astronomy archives for Solar System objects.

Despite their success in medical image segmentation, deep convolutional neural networks typically demand extensive manually annotated datasets and struggle to generalize to unseen classes. Few-shot learning offers a promising solution by enabling the learning of new classes from minimal labeled examples. This paper introduces a novel few-shot medical image segmentation framework built upon prototypical networks, featuring two primary innovations: 1) a context relation encoder (CRE) that leverages correlations to capture local relationships between foreground and background areas, and 2) a recurrent mask refinement module that iteratively employs the CRE and prototypical network to update context relationships and refine segmentation masks. Experimental results across two abdominal CT datasets and one abdominal MRI dataset demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving average improvements of 16.32%, 8.45%, and 6.24% in Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The source code is publicly accessible.

We investigate three distinct experiments involving dry friction and periodic driving, utilizing both single-particle and many-particle systems. Beyond serving as a platform to explore frictional phenomena, these setups hold significance across various scientific and engineering domains. In each case, we track the behavior of objects on a horizontally moving substrate; the driving mechanism couples with the substrate's degrees of freedom, thereby affecting the objects' motion. Our results indicate the emergence of stationary states characterized by non-trivial properties. To account for these findings, we propose a minimalistic phenomenological model. In this framework, energy injection is contingent upon the system's dynamical state, occurring only when the system resides in a specific frictional configuration. This model relies on the principle that such state-dependent driving generates a force that periodically switches frictional states over time, successfully explaining our experimental observations.

Space-based gravitational wave (GW) detectors will detect signals from sources that are nearly inaccessible to current ground-based systems. Consequently, the standard matched filtering technique will necessitate a complex template bank, resulting in computational costs that are impractical. In this study, we propose a high-accuracy method for detecting and extracting GW signals from all space-based sources. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that a science-driven, uniform multi-stage deep neural network can identify synthetic signals buried within Gaussian noise. Our approach achieves over 99% detection accuracy across various sources while maintaining at least 95% similarity to target signals. Additionally, we validate the method's interpretability and robust generalization capabilities across several extended scenarios.

Although optimizers such as Adam and AdaGrad excel at training large-scale neural networks, their efficacy relies heavily on meticulously tuned learning rate schedules. This paper demonstrates that significantly enhancing performance in many large-scale scenarios is possible by integrating an adaptive step-size tuning mechanism into existing optimizers. Specifically, we employ a global step-size scale alongside a per-coordinate gain factor. The global scale is adjusted by analyzing the alignment between average and current gradient vectors, while a comparable strategy updates the local gain factors. While step-size scaling has previously been applied to gradient descent, our approach utilizes exponentiated gradient updates to modify both the step-size scale and gain variables. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves competitive accuracy on standard models without requiring any specially tuned learning rate schedules. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's capability to rapidly adapt to data distribution shifts during training.

This study theoretically examines hot electron injection in carbon nanotubes (CNTs) under the simultaneous influence of a direct current (dc) electric field ($\mathbf{E}$) and a quasi-static alternating current (ac) electric field, defined by the condition where the ac frequency $\omega$ is significantly lower than the scattering frequency $v$ (i.e., $\omega\tau\ll 1$, with $v=\tau^{-1}$ and $\tau$ representing relaxation time). The analysis involves solving the semiclassical Boltzmann transport equation, both with and without a hot electron source, to determine current densities. Graphical representations of normalized current density against the applied axial dc field ($\mathbf{E}$) demonstrate an initial ohmic conductivity that transitions into negative differential conductivity (NDC) when $\omega\tau\ll 1$. However, sufficiently strong axial injection of hot electrons induces a switch from NDC to positive differential conductivity (PDC) at electric fields of approximately $\mathbf{E} \geq 75 \text{ kV/cm}$ for zigzag CNTs and $\mathbf{E} \geq 140 \text{ kV/cm}$ for armchair CNTs. Consequently, the introduction of hot electrons can suppress space charge instabilities, a critical issue within the NDC regime, by shifting the behavior to PDC. This transition suggests the potential for generating terahertz radiation, which holds significant relevance for modern technology, industry, and research.

This study offers a systematic approach to deriving calculable approximation errors for mean-field models under heavy-traffic conditions, specifically targeting the widely recognized power-of-two-choices (Po2) load balancing algorithm. The methodology integrates Stein's method applied to linearized mean-field models with State Space Concentration (SSC), which relies on geometric tail bounds. Specifically, the state space is partitioned into a region surrounding the mean-field equilibrium and its complement. First, a tail bound demonstrates that the steady-state probability of residing outside this neighborhood is negligible. Subsequently, a linearized mean-field model combined with Stein's method is employed to characterize the generator difference, yielding the dominant component of the approximation error. Leveraging this dominant term, the authors derive both an asymptotically tight bound and a nonasymptotic upper bound; unlike many existing studies that provide only order-wise scaling results, these are fully calculable bounds. Finally, the theoretical bounds are validated against numerical evaluations, demonstrating their effectiveness. Notably, simulations indicate that both bounds remain accurate even in small-scale systems, such as those comprising just ten servers.

This research examines the Taylor expansions of Jacobi forms with lattice indices. Our primary finding establishes an embedding that maps specific spaces of these forms—encompassing both scalar and vector-valued cases, as well as integral and half-integral weights, across all levels and characters—into a product of finitely many modular form spaces. Applying this result, we explore linear dependencies among Jacobi theta series of lattice index. Specifically, we derive numerous linear relations involving the squares of theta series for the $D_4$ and $A_3$ lattices, alongside relations for the cubes of series related to the $A_2$ lattice. Additionally, we provide the complete SageMath implementation for the $D_4$ lattice.

Since Dyson introduced Brownian motion in the early 1960s, the study of stochastic processes on the space of Hermitian matrices has advanced significantly, with particular focus on their eigenvalue properties. This research includes detailed analyses of limiting behaviors as the matrix dimension approaches infinity, a field closely linked to random matrix theory. This survey examines key findings regarding the eigenvalues of stochastic processes over the last thirty years, extending to recent variations such as matrix-valued processes driven by fractional Brownian motion or the Brownian sheet. The review concludes by proposing several open problems within this domain.

We outline the current status of our investigation into the order of the finite temperature transition in QCD featuring two flavors of degenerate fermions. Recent simulations conducted on extensive lattices bolster the hypothesis that this transition is first-order, evidenced by a preliminary two-state signal. We will address the resulting implications and outline forthcoming steps in our analysis.

Although genes exhibiting comparable transcriptional activation kinetics may exhibit markedly distinct temporal mRNA profiles, these differences stem from variations in transcription duration, RNA degradation rates, and processing speeds. Recent research highlights that delays in RNA production associated with splicing can be substantial. We present a unified model integrating transcriptional activation and mRNA accumulation, designed to infer transcription rates, RNA production delays, and degradation rates using genome-wide data from high-throughput sequencing time courses. By merging a mechanistic differential equation framework with a non-parametric statistical approach, we accommodate diverse activation kinetics and employ Bayesian parameter estimation to quantify uncertainty in kinetic parameters. We apply this model to estrogen receptor (ER-α) activation data within the MCF-7 breast cancer cell line, utilizing RNA polymerase II (pol-II) ChIP-Seq time courses to profile transcriptional activation and mRNA-Seq time courses to measure mature transcripts. Our analysis reveals that 11% of genes with robust data signals exhibit a delay exceeding 20 minutes between transcription completion and mature mRNA production. Furthermore, genes with such prolonged delays are significantly more likely to be short. We also observe a statistical correlation between high delays and late intron retention in pre-mRNA data, underscoring significant splicing-associated production delays across many genes.

A novel approach termed "clean numerical simulation" (CNS), introduced in *J. Computational Physics* (2020), enables the generation of reliable, converged simulations of spatiotemporal chaotic systems over extended periods by minimizing numerical noise, thereby establishing benchmark solutions. This study demonstrates that machine learning (ML) can produce adequate fitting predictions for such chaos using two distinct training sets: a "clean database" derived from CNS with negligible noise, and a "polluted database" generated by conventional single/double-precision algorithms containing significant numerical noise. Despite the similarities, statistical analyses reveal that ML predictions based on the "polluted database" differ substantially from those based on the "clean database." This indicates that database noise exerts a profound influence on ML predictions for certain spatiotemporal chaotic systems, even at the statistical level. Consequently, a "clean" database is essential for machine learning applications involving specific spatiotemporal chaos. This unexpected finding may offer new avenues for future research in machine learning.

Interactions between galactic dark matter (DM) particles and the constituents of celestial bodies can lead to DM accumulation within those objects. However, the medium's finite temperature imposes a lower mass limit, known as the evaporation mass, required for DM particles to remain trapped. Particles lighter than this threshold are likely to scatter to velocities exceeding the escape velocity, causing them to be ejected from the object. This study calculates the DM evaporation mass for all spherical bodies in hydrostatic equilibrium across a mass range of $[10^{-10} - 10^2]~M_\odot$, assuming constant scattering cross sections and $s$-wave annihilations. We highlight the critical role of the exponential tail in the evaporation rate, a factor often overlooked in recent literature, and derive a robust finding: for geometric scattering cross sections and nucleon interactions at the local galactic position, the DM evaporation mass for these bodies is approximately $E_c/T_\chi \sim 30$, where $E_c$ represents the escape energy at the object's core and $T_\chi$ is the particle temperature. Under these conditions, the minimum evaporation mass occurs for super-Jupiters and brown dwarfs, with $m_{\rm evap} \simeq 0.7$ GeV. For other scattering cross section values, the evaporation mass varies by less than a factor of three within the range $10^{-41}~\textrm{cm}^2 \leq \sigma_p \leq 10^{-31}~\textrm{cm}^2$ (where $\sigma_p$ is the spin-independent DM-nucleon cross section). Furthermore, dependencies on galactic DM density, velocity, and scattering or annihilation cross sections are only logarithmic, and variations in celestial body density and temperature profiles have minimal impact.

This paper examines the constraint equations for a specific class of scalar-tensor effective field theories of gravity, encompassing operators with up to four derivatives in the action ($4\partial$ST). By adapting the conformal transverse traceless and conformal thin sandwich techniques from General Relativity, we reformulate the scalar-tensor constraint equations as a system of elliptic partial differential equations. We demonstrate that, in the weak coupling regime, unique solutions exist for the associated elliptic boundary value problems on asymptotically Euclidean initial slices, provided conditions analogous to those in General Relativity are met. Additionally, we derive a generalization of the Bowen-York solution applicable to $4\partial$ST theories. These findings indicate that standard procedures for constructing initial data in General Relativity can be extended to weakly coupled $4\partial$ST theories with only minor adjustments.

The study of Riemann problems in chemical flooding models employs vanishing viscosity as a criterion for admissibility. We demonstrate that when the flow function exhibits non-monotonic dependence on chemical concentration, non-classical undercompressive shocks emerge. Furthermore, we prove that the shock velocity's monotonicity depends on the ratio of dissipative coefficients. To achieve this, we classify the phase portraits of the associated travelling wave dynamical systems and examine saddle-saddle connections.

Automatic defect detection in 3D printing, a task closely related to change detection, is essential for ensuring product quality. Nevertheless, current practical applications face significant hurdles. First, existing computer vision methods for process monitoring often function effectively only under fixed camera angles and lighting conditions, necessitating costly pre-processing, alignment, and specific camera configurations. Second, many detection techniques are limited to predefined defect patterns or print schematics. This study addresses the problem differently by introducing a novel Semi-Siamese deep learning model that directly compares a reference schematic of the intended print with a camera capture of the actual result. The model performs image segmentation to pinpoint defect locations relative to the reference frame. Unlike typical change detection approaches, this model is specifically engineered to handle images from disparate domains and remains robust against imaging perturbations, such as variations in camera angle and illumination. Defect localization was achieved in 2.75 seconds per layer on a standard MacBookPro—a speed comparable to the tens of seconds required to print a single layer on an inkjet-based 3D printer—while maintaining an F1-score exceeding 0.9.

This paper establishes various identities and recurrence relations for degenerate Stirling numbers of both the first and second kinds, which serve as degenerate analogs of their ordinary counterparts. These results are derived from the normal orderings of degenerate integral powers of the number operator and their inverses, alongside specific boson operator relations and the intrinsic recurrence relations of Stirling numbers. Notably, whereas the normal ordering of an integral power of the number operator relies on standard Stirling numbers of the second kind, the normal ordering of a degenerate integral power is expressed using degenerate Stirling numbers of the second kind.

This study demonstrates how the phase relationship between tandem bioinspired fins flapping at high stroke amplitudes influences rear fin thrust and wake dynamics. Load cell data indicates that when the rear fin lags the front fin by a quarter cycle, it produces 25% more thrust, whereas leading the front fin by the same interval results in an 8% performance decrease. To analyze the underlying flow interactions, the research combines two-dimensional particle image velocimetry with three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations. Velocity distributions clarify how phase offsets alter the effective flow experienced by the rear fin, while vortex structure interactions and particle rakes highlight the roles of the front fin's leading- and trailing-edge vortices in modulating suction at the rear fin's leading edge. Additionally, the wake structure far downstream exhibits changes in coherence, as well as axial and radial dimensions, depending on the phase offset. These insights offer valuable guidance for optimizing the design and performance of unmanned underwater vehicles employing tandem fin configurations.

This supplementary material summarizes, for the reader's convenience, the general framework of the proposed multiscale model (Section 1) and the fundamental information regarding the pilot study approaches. Specifically, it provides a detailed account of the interaction model (Section 2) and the dynamical methods employed for the dark dynamics step (Section 3), which were previously reported in two earlier studies [1, 2]. Furthermore, a comprehensive description of the treatment of radiative processes is also included (Section 4).

Recent advancements in representation learning have significantly enhanced various language-related tasks involving text and speech. However, current methodologies face two key constraints: (a) they rely exclusively on a single input modality, despite the need for a unified representation combining both speech and text for applications like end-to-end speech translation; and (b) they fail to leverage extensive large-scale text and speech datasets, leading to performance bottlenecks caused by the scarcity of parallel speech translation data. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Fused Acoustic and Text Masked Language Model (FAT-MLM), which jointly learns a unified representation from diverse corpora, including parallel data for speech recognition and machine translation, as well as pure speech and text resources. Building on this cross-modal framework, we also develop an end-to-end model for Fused Acoustic and Text Speech Translation (FAT-ST). Experiments across three translation directions demonstrate that fine-tuning our speech translation models using FAT-MLM substantially boosts translation quality, achieving gains of up to +5.9 BLEU.

This study examines binary configurations consisting of unequal Kerr-Newman black holes situated on an axis and separated by a massless strut. By employing a specific fitting parametrization, the authors exactly solve the axis conditions and the constraint eliminating individual magnetic charges to construct a 7-parameter, asymptotically flat exact solution. Explicit analytical expressions are derived for the half-length of each horizon ($\sigma_i$, where $i=1,2$) using arbitrary physical Komar parameters: mass ($M_i$), electric charge ($Q_i$), angular momentum ($J_i$), and coordinate distance ($R$). The paper concisely presents the thermodynamic properties of the black holes along with the interaction force associated with the strut. Furthermore, the analysis details the physical limits of the solution and proposes scenarios in which the strut vanishes during the merger process.

This study reports the initial X-ray detections of ultracool dwarfs (UCDs) derived from the first all-sky survey conducted by eROSITA, an instrument aboard the Russian Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) mission. We utilized three public catalogs containing nearly 20,000 spectroscopically confirmed UCDs and Gaia-selected candidates to identify X-ray counterparts. Specifically, we extracted X-ray sources from the first eROSITA survey (eRASS1) that lie within three times their positional uncertainty of a UCD or candidate. By analyzing 96 such X-ray sources and evaluating nearby Gaia objects based on spatial proximity and multiwavelength characteristics, we identified 40 UCDs with secure X-ray associations and 18 plausible candidates. Among these, 21 have spectroscopic confirmation, while the remainder were selected via Gaia photometry with spectral types estimated from G-J colors. The detected UCDs span spectral types M5 to M9 and distances from 3.5 to 190 parsecs. Most exhibit X-ray to bolometric luminosity ratios exceeding the canonical saturation limit of log(Lx/Lbol) ~ -3. For the two most extreme outliers, analysis of eRASS1 light curves indicates that elevated ratios result from flaring activity. Additionally, the X-ray spectra of the two brightest objects show an emission-measure weighted plasma temperature of approximately kT ~ 0.75 keV. These findings highlight eROSITA's potential to advance our understanding of faint coronal X-ray emission from UCDs by enabling the construction of statistical samples to derive average X-ray brightness, flare frequencies, and coronal temperatures.

This study presents the first demonstration that a biologically plausible spiking neural network (SNN) utilizing Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) can continuously learn to detect moving pedestrians in real time using event-based, retina-inspired cameras. The proposed pipeline operates by first feeding a brief sequence of event data (under two minutes), captured by a drone tracking a walking human, into a convolutional SNN with STDP. This system simultaneously receives teacher spiking signals from a readout, establishing a semi-supervised framework. Subsequently, STDP adaptation is halted, and the trained model is evaluated on independent test sequences. Through various experiments, we analyze the impact of critical system parameters and benchmark our approach against conventionally trained CNNs. Our results indicate that the system achieves a significantly higher peak $F_1$ score (an improvement of 19%) compared to CNNs processing event-based camera frames, while also supporting online adaptation.

Currently, the prevailing hypothesis posits that fast radio bursts (FRBs) originate from coherent emission driven by magnetic energy release in magnetars. Despite this consensus, the precise emission mechanism remains unidentified. Two primary theoretical frameworks currently exist: magnetospheric emission and radiation generated by external relativistic shocks. This concise review outlines the fundamentals of both models and examines how contemporary observations test these theories.

Global traffic congestion has emerged as a paramount challenge. Annually, gridlock costs the United States approximately $160 billion, the United Kingdom more than £13 billion, and the world over one trillion dollars. As metropolitan regions face increasingly severe traffic conditions, the capacity to analyze, comprehend, and enhance traffic dynamics becomes essential. This dissertation aims to develop such capabilities by proposing various techniques that integrate simulation and machine learning to address traffic challenges from two angles: city-scale traffic reconstruction and autonomous driving.

The growing prevalence of multicore systems, data processing platforms, and in-memory databases has heightened the demand for scalable concurrent ordered sets that support linearizable range queries. This paper introduces a novel concurrent ordered set featuring such linearizable range query capabilities. Built upon a contention-adapting search tree and an immutable data structure, the proposed solution demonstrates performance up to three times faster than related structures in experimental evaluations. Its strong scalability stems from the ability to dynamically adjust the sizes of its immutable components based on contention levels and the specific demands of range queries.

Tupper's formula, expressed as $\frac{1}{2}<\bigg\lfloor \bmod \bigg(\lfloor \frac{y}{17}\rfloor 2^{-17\lfloor x \rfloor -\bmod (\lfloor y \rfloor,17)},2\bigg)\bigg\rfloor$, possesses a unique characteristic: for any monochrome image definable within a $106\times 17$ pixel grid, there is a specific integer $k$ such that plotting the equation for $0\leq x <106$ and $k\leq y<k+17$ reproduces that image. This paper extends that concept to $m$ colors and $n$ dimensions. We introduce a set of $m$ equations involving $n$ independent variables, where each equation corresponds to one of the color levels $C_1, \cdots, C_m$. The property holds that for any $n$-dimensional object composed of $m$ colors and representable as hypervoxels (the multidimensional equivalent of pixels) in an $A_1\times \cdots \times A_n$ array, there exists a natural number $k$ such that graphing the first formula with color $C_1$, the second with $C_2$, and so on up to the $m$th formula with $C_m$—within the bounds $0\leq x_i<A_i$ for $i=1,\dots,n-1$ and $k\leq x_n <k+A_n$—results in the union of these graphs forming the complete $n$-dimensional object.

Local graph neighborhood sampling serves as a core computational challenge essential for node representation learning algorithms. Numerous studies have developed methods for learning discrete node embeddings, representing graph nodes via discrete features like neighborhood attributes. These discrete embeddings provide significant benefits over continuous, word2vec-style embeddings, including computational ease, scalability, and interpretability. We introduce LoNe Sampler, a collection of algorithms for generating discrete node embeddings through Local Neighborhood Sampling, which resolves two key limitations in prior research. First, our methods are backed by rigorously understood theoretical properties. Second, we demonstrate techniques for creating approximate explicit vector maps that eliminate the costly computation of a Gram matrix required for kernel model training. Experimental results on benchmark datasets validate our theoretical insights and highlight the superior performance of the proposed approaches.

The risk of ice accumulation on rotor blades compromises the safety of rotorcraft in cold conditions. Ultimately, high centrifugal forces can cause this ice to detach, potentially striking other rotorcraft components or creating rotor imbalance. To determine when and where shedding occurs, this study introduces a robust and efficient multi-step numerical simulation tool designed to predict such phenomena. A volume-mesh approach facilitates the representation of ice geometry, while an implemented interpolation procedure enhances method robustness by predicting shedding events and narrowing the search domain. Ice shapes along the blades are generated using two-dimensional accretion simulations, which are subsequently interpolated across the blade span. Numerical results align closely with experimental data from the AERTS test facility regarding both shedding timing and location, validating the reliability of this approach.

Cloud services are integral to societal functions including healthcare, commerce, entertainment, and education. While they offer valuable features like enhanced collaboration and cost-effective computing, their immense scale and complexity make failures inevitable, leading to reduced reliability and efficiency. For instance, bugs in the infrastructure of major providers have caused numerous high-severity outages lasting hours and resulting in irrecoverable data loss. Existing research on cloud failures is often limited and relies on secondary sources like news articles; therefore, a comprehensive study analyzing failure data gathered directly from vendors is necessary. Additionally, cloud failures during the Covid-19 pandemic warrant specific attention, as cloud services were critical for activities such as remote work. Developing a program to address this task will enable a deeper understanding of these failures and facilitate mitigation strategies to minimize their impact.

Android remains the leading smartphone operating system, celebrated for its flexibility and security. Despite its robust reputation, occasional vulnerabilities allow attackers to bypass security controls and access sensitive user data, with side-channel flaws emerging as a particularly pressing concern. While various side-channel issues exist, those targeting APIs offer a significant exploration area; historically analyzed manually, recent years have seen the publication of automatic scanning solutions driven by the expanding Android codebase, though these tools still face limitations. This paper presents a novel method for detecting side-channel leaks in the Android NDK, an area never before investigated using automatic or semi-automatic techniques. The proposed approach successfully identified over eight new leaks across multiple Android NDK functions, enabling highly accurate inference of application and website launches on victim devices. These findings constitute the first discovered side-channel vulnerabilities within Android NDK functions and were responsibly disclosed to Google's Android Security Team.

Stochastic gradient MCMC (SGMCMC) provides a scalable alternative to conventional MCMC methods by generating an unbiased estimate of the log-posterior gradient using a small, uniformly weighted subset of data. Although computationally efficient, this approach often yields high-variance gradient estimators that can degrade sampler performance. Traditionally, variance reduction has been tackled by refining the stochastic gradient estimator, typically through the use of control variates. In contrast, we introduce a discrete, non-uniform probability distribution that preferentially selects data points with a higher impact on the stochastic gradient. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive mechanism to adjust the subsample size at every iteration, expanding the sample in regions where the gradient is difficult to estimate. Our results demonstrate that this strategy preserves accuracy while significantly decreasing the average subsample size required.

This study examines position-dependent mass (PDM) Lagrangians and Hamiltonians in their conventional textbook format, maintaining the established \emph{gain-loss balance} between kinetic and potential energies to ensure total energy conservation (specifically, $L=T-V$, $H=T+V$, and $dH/dt=dE/dt=0$). Within this standard framework, we analyze and present findings on $n$-dimensional PDM damped harmonic oscillators (DHOs). By employing specific $n$-dimensional point canonical transformations, we demonstrate that the dynamical equations of $n$-PDM systems can be linearized into those of $n$-linear DHOs with constant mass. As a result, the well-known exact solutions for linear DHOs are readily mapped onto the exact solutions for PDM DHOs. We provide illustrative examples for both one-dimensional and $n$-dimensional PDM-DHO systems, accompanied by their respective phase-space trajectories.

We anticipate robust Ising ferromagnetism, driven by Coulomb interactions, within the metallic regime of twisted transition metal dichalcogenide homobilayers across various small twist angles. Enabled by spin-valley locking and Chern bands, the fully spin-polarized state—characterized as a half metal—possesses a spin gap and demonstrates the anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, near the magic angle where the Chern band is theoretically predicted to be exceptionally flat, the anomalous Hall metal at $1/3$ filling may become unstable at low temperatures, potentially transitioning into a $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ charge density wave or a fractional Chern insulator.

This study establishes the local nonlinear Lyapunov stability for a class of $(n+1)$-dimensional cosmological models within general relativity that are locally isometric to Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetimes and incorporate a positive cosmological constant. Specifically, we demonstrate that solutions to the Einstein-Euler equations, perturbed from a set of spatially compact FLRW metrics (where spatial slices are generally compact negative Einstein spaces, with hyperbolic geometry being the physically relevant case for $n=3$), remain uniformly bounded under regular Cauchy data and decay toward a family of metrics characterized by constant negative spatial scalar curvature. To achieve this, we apply an energy method tailored to the coupled Einstein-Euler system within the constant mean extrinsic curvature spatial harmonic (CMCSH) gauge. To address Euler's equations, we construct an energy functional based on a current analogous to Christodoulou's (which matches his current in Minkowski space), proving that this energy effectively controls the fluid degrees of freedom. Combining this fluid energy current with the CMCSH gauge condition reformulates the Einstein-Euler equations as a coupled elliptic-hyperbolic system. By leveraging estimates from the elliptic components, we first establish that the gravity-fluid energy functional stays uniformly bounded in the expanding direction. Building on this uniform boundedness, we derive sharp decay estimates when a positive cosmological constant $\Lambda$ is present, indicating that the accelerated expansion driven by $\Lambda$ is capable of managing nonlinearities for small data. Finally, several physical implications of this stability finding are examined.

Grasping the continuum limit of discrete random geometry theories presents a formidable yet captivating challenge. Through this lens, we examine the insights gained from applying the Landau framework of critical phenomena to Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDT). Specifically, focusing on two and three dimensions, we argue that the volume configuration of spatial slices functions effectively as an order parameter, thereby illuminating CDT's phase structure. Furthermore, alignment with numerical CDT simulations suggests that the model's effective field theory resides within the space of theories invariant under foliation-preserving diffeomorphisms. Within this class, Horava-Lifshitz gravity holds a unique position as a perturbatively renormalizable theory, whereas General Relativity occupies a subspace characterized by enhanced symmetry. Achieving either of these limits likely requires fine-tuning specific parameters within the CDT action or extending it further.

Breaking reciprocity is a significant area of study in fundamental physics and optical information processing. We have demonstrated non-reciprocal light transport within a quantum system of hot atoms by tailoring the dissipative atomic reservoir. Our approach relies on phase-sensitive light transport in a multi-channel photon-atom interaction setup, where the phase of collective atomic excitations can be adjusted via external driving fields. Notably, we detected inter-channel quantum correlations stemming from interactions with the carefully engineered reservoir. This non-reciprocal transport in a quantum optical atomic system establishes a new paradigm for atom-based non-reciprocal optics and provides prospects for quantum simulations involving coupled optical channels.

Electroencephalograms (EEGs) offer a promising avenue for developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). However, one-dimensional (1-D) EEG signals are highly susceptible to artifacts due to their high temporal resolution, making noise removal essential. While recent deep learning-based denoising methods have outperformed traditional techniques, existing approaches often overlook specific data self-similarity characteristics. Typically, both local and non-local self-similarity are leveraged for denoising in various data types, yet current deep learning models for EEG either ignore non-local patterns (e.g., using 1-D CNNs) or local ones (e.g., using fully connected or recurrent networks). To resolve this limitation, we introduce EEGDnet, a novel 1-D EEG denoising network utilizing a 2-D transformer. This architecture comprehensively integrates both local and non-local self-similarity by embedding non-local features within self-attention blocks and local features within feed-forward blocks, thereby significantly mitigating the effects of noise and outliers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EEGDnet surpasses state-of-the-art models in both quantitative and qualitative performance metrics.

To address nonlocality within a suitable ontological framework, we introduce a "cosmological solution." Our premise is that since the universe's inception, every spatial point has hosted a scalar field representing zero-point vacuum energy, which vibrates nonlocally at diverse frequencies throughout the cosmos. Consequently, a quantum particle is defined as a nonequilibrium steady state—a "bouncer"—that resonates with a specific frequency dependent on its particle type, drawing a remote parallel to Couder's experiments with bouncing oil drops on an oscillating bath. A key distinction from this analogy lies in the nonlocal character of the vacuum oscillations. Using double- and $n$-slit interference as examples, we demonstrate that the nonlocality of the distribution functions alone is sufficient to derive the de Broglie-Bohm guiding equation for $N$ particles using purely classical methods. In this model, no configuration space influences are necessary, as all phenomena can be described within three-dimensional space. Furthermore, the configuration of an experimental setup is characterized as "vacuum landscaping," which constrains and shapes both the forward and osmotic contributions.

Convection is a pervasive phenomenon in stars, manifesting under a wide range of conditions. This study examines convection within main-sequence stars using two perspectives: dimensionless parameters derived from stellar structure and those resulting from mixing length theory. We begin by defining these quantities in terms accessible to both the 1D stellar evolution and hydrodynamics communities. Subsequently, we analyze how these parameters vary across diverse convection zones, stellar masses, and evolutionary stages of the main sequence. Our findings reveal remarkable diversity in stellar convection zones, which can range from thin shells to deep envelopes and nearly spherical cores. Convection processes may be efficient or inefficient, rotationally constrained or unconstrained, and transsonic or deeply subsonic. This atlas acts as a resource for future theoretical and observational research by identifying active convection regimes in specific stars and outlining suitable modeling assumptions for numerical simulations.

This work addresses data clustering with $\ell_p$-norm objectives, such as $k$-Median and $k$-Means, under the framework of individual fairness. Given a dataset of $n$ points, the goal is to identify $k$ centers that minimize the objective function while satisfying a fairness constraint: every point $v$ must be assigned to a center within distance $r(v)$, where $r(v)$ corresponds to the distance to the $(n/k)$th nearest neighbor. Jung, Kannan, and Lutz [FORC 2020] originally proposed this concept, developing an algorithm with provable approximate fairness and objective guarantees for the $\ell_\infty$ or $k$-Center problem. Subsequently, Mahabadi and Vakilian [ICML 2020] extended the approach to all $\ell_p$-norms using local search. While their methods significantly outperform Jung et al. in terms of cost for $k$-Median and $k$-Means, they result in a notable reduction in fairness. In this paper, we leverage Linear Programming (LP) techniques to develop superior algorithms both theoretically and empirically. By adapting established LP rounding methods, we achieve a worst-case objective guarantee that substantially improves upon the results of MV20, with empirical performance nearly matching the optimum. Additionally, our theoretical fairness bounds are on par with those of MV20, yet our solutions are empirically significantly fairer. Although exact LP resolution can be computationally expensive, we show that a straightforward sparsification technique effectively reduces the algorithm's runtime in practical applications.

Over recent decades, the presence of both amorphous and crystalline water ice in the outer solar system and interstellar medium has been widely confirmed. To derive water ice grain sizes from near-infrared data, radiative transfer models (RTMs) are employed. However, significant inconsistencies in grain size estimates for water ice on Saturnian moons, as well as nitrogen and methane ices on Kuiper Belt objects, have been documented, largely due to the use of different scattering models (Emran and Chevrier, 2022; Hansen, 2009). This study evaluates these discrepancies for water ice at temperatures relevant to the outer solar system and beyond: 15, 40, 60, and 80 K for amorphous phases, and 20, 40, 60, and 80 K for crystalline phases. By comparing single scattering albedos derived from optical constants between 1 and 5 $\mu$m, we contrast the Mie theory (Mie, 1908) with Hapke approximation models (Hapke, 1993). Our findings indicate that while Hapke models generally predict crystalline grain sizes more accurately than amorphous ones across the 15–80 K range, the Hapke slab model yields estimates closer to those of the Mie model, whereas the internal scattering model (ISM) demonstrates greater uncertainty. Consequently, we recommend the Mie model for estimating water ice grain sizes from unknown spectra of outer solar system bodies. When selecting an approximation model for RTMs, the Hapke slab model is preferred over the ISM.

Two semigroups are said to be lattice isomorphic when their respective lattices of subsemigroups are isomorphic, and a class of semigroups is termed lattice closed if it includes every semigroup that is lattice isomorphic to a member of that class. An orthodox semigroup is defined as a regular semigroup where the set of idempotents constitutes a subsemigroup. We demonstrate that the class of all orthodox semigroups, where every nonidempotent element possesses infinite order, is lattice closed.

The ideal morphologies adopted by contractile cells on adhesive surfaces result from the balance between internal contractile forces and their attachment to the extracellular matrix. In our model, the cell is represented as a contractile sheet enclosed by an elastic cortex and linked to the substrate through elastic connections. When adhesion sites are spread continuously, the optimal cell shape is limited by the geometry of adhesion, causing the spread area to vary sensitively with substrate stiffness and contractile tension. Conversely, with discrete adhesion points, the equilibrium cell shape remains convex under low contractility but develops local concavities at intermediate levels. Once contractility surpasses a critical threshold—dictated by the mechanical and geometric attributes of adhesion—the cell boundary abruptly transitions into a star-like configuration featuring cusps and protrusions, a process accompanied by bistability and hysteresis.

We examine how effectively end-users can deduce the degree of data protection when the obfuscation mechanism remains unknown to them, a scenario known as "black-box." Specifically, we investigate various forms of differential privacy, including epsilon-DP, local DP, and R\'enyi DP. On one hand, we demonstrate that without any assumptions regarding the underlying data distributions, no algorithm can infer the protection level with provable guarantees. Conversely, under reasonable assumptions—specifically, that the involved densities are Lipschitz continuous on a closed interval—we show that such guarantees are attainable through a straightforward histogram-based estimator. Practically, by employing the well-known Laplacian DP mechanism, we observe that the theoretical sample count required to validate our bounds significantly exceeds the actual number of samples needed for satisfactory performance. Additionally, our results indicate that the estimated epsilon value is empirically much closer to the true value than what our theoretical bounds predict.

Determining the radii of massive stars across their life cycles is crucial for addressing many questions in stellar physics, ranging from binary interactions on the main sequence to pre-supernova dimensions. A key factor influencing a star's radius is its metallicity ($Z$), defined as the mass fraction of elements heavier than helium. However, metallicity affects stellar evolution through various distinct microphysical processes, and the dominant mechanism can shift depending on the evolutionary stage and the overall magnitude of $Z$. To isolate the impact of each process, we conducted numerical experiments using 15M$_{\odot}$ MESA models, varying the metallicity input separately for radiative opacity, the equation of state, and the nuclear reaction network. We analyzed models centered on two metallicity regimes: one near solar ($Z=0.02$) and another sub-solar ($Z\sim10^{-3}$), examining key epochs from the end of the main sequence through core carbon depletion. Our results indicate that for solar metallicity models, the metallicity entering the opacity dominates at most epochs, accounting for an average of 60–90% of the total radius change. In contrast, nuclear reactions exert a larger influence (50–70%) during most epochs in sub-solar $Z$ models. This methodology can be broadly applied to propagate uncertainties from known microphysics errors into macrophysical observables, such as stellar radii.

Randomized smoothing currently stands as the leading approach for providing provable defenses against adversarial examples, yet it has recently been shown to face significant information-theoretic constraints. We contend that these constraints are not inherent flaws in the method itself, but rather artifacts of existing certification techniques. Specifically, current certificates rely on insufficient information regarding the classifier and fail to account for the local curvature of the decision boundary, resulting in increasingly suboptimal robustness guarantees as problem dimensions grow. We demonstrate, however, that this limitation can be circumvented by gathering richer information about the classifier. By probing the decision boundary with multiple noise distributions, it is possible to approximate the optimal certificate to any desired degree of precision. Because this enhanced certification occurs at the certification stage rather than during inference, natural accuracy remains unaffected while the quality of the robustness guarantees improves. This finding encourages further exploration of classifier-specific certification, proving that randomized smoothing remains a promising avenue. Although such tailored approaches may increase computational demands, we also offer theoretical perspectives on strategies to alleviate this overhead.

Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning approach that facilitates collaborative model training without requiring direct data exchange, making its privacy-preserving nature particularly valuable in healthcare. However, standard FL methods struggle with stability and demand extensive hyperparameter tuning when faced with heterogeneous client data distributions. Traditional optimization techniques are often unfeasible for practical FL applications due to their reliance on numerous training trials that exceed available computational budgets. To address this, we introduce Auto-FedRL, an efficient reinforcement learning (RL)-based algorithm for federated hyperparameter optimization. This method employs an online RL agent to dynamically adjust client-specific hyperparameters according to real-time training progress. We evaluated various search strategies and RL agents through extensive experiments, validating the proposed approach on a heterogeneous CIFAR-10 dataset split and two real-world medical image segmentation tasks: COVID-19 lesion detection in chest CT scans and pancreas segmentation in abdominal CT scans.

Recently, two-dimensional (2D) array codes have emerged as valuable tools in wireless communication. This paper introduces a direct method for constructing 2D complete complementary codes (2D-CCCs) with adjustable array dimensions and flexible set sizes by employing multivariable functions (MVF). We analyze the Peak-to-mean envelope power ratio (PMEPR) characteristics of the row and column sequences within these constructed 2D-CCC arrays. The proposed construction extends numerous existing state-of-the-art techniques, including Golay complementary pairs (GCP), one-dimensional (1D)-CCC, 2D Golay complementary array sets (2D-GCAS), and 2D-CCC, offering superior parameters compared to prior work.

We introduce a flexible approach to generating state-dependent optical lattices through the application of a temporally modulated magnetic field gradient. This technique enables precise control over both the magnitude and sign of tunneling rates for various internal states. Our experiments reveal markedly distinct momentum distributions for fermionic 40K atoms based on their spin states. By analyzing dipole oscillations, we map the spin-dependent band structure, which aligns well with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, in-situ expansion dynamics confirm that one state can be fully localized while others remain itinerant. A systematic investigation indicates negligible heating and lifetimes extending into several seconds within the Hubbard regime.

Reach-avoid optimal control problems, essential for guaranteeing safety and liveness in autonomous robotics by requiring systems to hit specific goals while avoiding failure states, are notoriously difficult to solve exactly for complex dynamics. Although reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown promise in approximately solving optimal control tasks with performance goals, its standard Lagrangian objectives cannot effectively encode temporal logic constraints. Recent advances have adapted RL machinery for safety-focused problems that rely on minimizing or maximizing values over time rather than summing them. This work extends the RL formulation to encompass all reach-avoid optimal control scenarios. We derive a time-discounted reach-avoid Bellman backup exhibiting contraction mapping properties, proving that the resulting Q-learning algorithm converges under conditions similar to traditional Lagrangian problems, producing an arbitrarily tight conservative approximation of the reach-avoid set. Furthermore, we apply this framework to deep reinforcement learning, maintaining zero-violation guarantees by treating approximate solutions as untrusted oracles within a model-predictive supervisory control architecture. We validate the proposed framework across various nonlinear systems, comparing results against analytic and numerical benchmarks and demonstrating success in previously intractable problems via Monte Carlo simulations. These findings pave the way for diverse learning-based approaches to safe and live autonomous behaviors in robotics and automation. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/SafeRoboticsLab/safety_rl.

Smart contracts are compact yet notoriously error-susceptible programs that enforce agreements among multiple entities. We introduce a reactive synthesis method designed to automatically generate state machines that handle the temporal control flow inherent in smart contracts. To address typical contract specifications, our approach leverages temporal stream logic (TSL) enhanced with a specialized parameterization mechanism. We demonstrate the capability to fully define the control flow for diverse common contract types, such as ERC20 token systems, election mechanisms, and asset transfer protocols. We propose a synthesis algorithm grounded in the past-time fragment of parameterized TSL and illustrate an efficient method for translating the resulting infinite-state machine into Solidity code. Our tool, SCSynt, executes this approach and incorporates a feedback loop to alert developers of potential specification flaws. Experimental results indicate that SCSynt can generate correct-by-construction Solidity code from formal smart contract specifications in mere seconds.

Radio galaxies carve out enormous voids within the intergalactic medium. These voids manifest in X-ray observations as regions where the surrounding medium has been displaced, creating a hot, low-density bubble encasing the radio lobes. This study investigates the predicted thermal X-ray output using an extensive collection of high-resolution, three-dimensional simulations of radio galaxies powered by supersonic jets. The models employ adiabatic, non-relativistic hydrodynamics, featuring straight and precessing jets of supersonic gas expelled from nozzles. Simulated X-ray Bremsstrahlung images typically produce oval cavities in soft keV bands and arcuate features in hard X-rays. However, the cavity morphology depends on the contrast between jet and ambient density; it shifts from concave at a density ratio ($\eta$) of 0.1 to convex at $\eta = 0.0001$. In specific scenarios, we identify lateral ribs in soft X-rays and suggest these account for similar structures observed near Cygnus A. For bi-lobed, X-shaped, or curved jets, the peak X-ray emission originates from relic lobes or deflection sites rather than hotspots, as regions of high pressure and high compression do not align. When viewed head-on, the cavity resembles a deep, circular hole bordered by concentric ripples. Furthermore, brief radio-mode outbursts with a 10% duty cycle cause the intracluster medium to simmer with low Mach number shocks, which widely dissipate jet energy during inactive periods.

Ethereum has emerged as the second-largest blockchain platform following Bitcoin, largely driven by the extensive adoption of smart contracts. This ecosystem hosts a diverse range of active accounts—including those involved in ICOs, mining, and gambling—making the analysis of their transaction records crucial for deciphering specific behavioral traits and labeling pseudonymous identities. While conventional research often relies on static, global transaction networks that overlook dynamic shifts, this study focuses on six key account categories by constructing ego networks for each. We prioritize a temporal analysis of interactions between target nodes and their neighbors. Experimental results reveal significant disparities in various network features across account types, offering deeper insights into their transaction patterns. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural effort to examine the dynamic characteristics of labeled Ethereum accounts through the lens of transaction ego networks.

When a viscous fluid exits a long, horizontal circular pipe, it forms a complex structure featuring a primary upper jet, a smaller secondary lower jet, and a thin connecting fluid curtain. This study, integrating experimental, theoretical, and numerical approaches, investigates the "Torricelli's curtain" phenomenon with a focus on the factors governing its morphology. We introduce a theoretical model for the curtain where particle paths arise from combining two movements: a horizontal element reflecting the evolving axial velocity profile of an axisymmetric viscous jet, and a vertical element caused by gravitational free fall. While the model accurately predicts the trajectory of the primary jet, its performance for the secondary jet is less precise. We attribute this discrepancy to surface tension-induced (Taylor-Culick) retraction of the secondary jet. Furthermore, direct numerical simulations uncover recirculating 'Dean' vortices within vertical sections of the primary jet, thereby situating Torricelli's curtain firmly within the broader context of curved pipe flow dynamics.

Blockchain systems utilizing reusable resources, such as Proof-of-Stake (PoS), offer weaker security compared to Proof-of-Work mechanisms. Specifically, they are susceptible to long-range attacks, enabling adversaries to compromise past participants and rewrite the entire chain history. To mitigate this threat on PoS chains, we introduce a decentralized protocol that anchors the PoS state to a Proof-of-Work blockchain like Bitcoin. By employing Schnorr signatures and leveraging Bitcoin's recent Taproot upgrade, our approach generates constant-sized checkpointing transactions without relying on any central authority. We provide a security analysis of the protocol and present an open-source implementation validated on the Bitcoin testnet.

We present an investigation into the enveloping norms associated with regularly P-operators, where P denotes an "almost" variant of limited, Grothendieck, and Dunford–Pettis operators within Banach lattices, alongside several related subjects.

Understanding how light irradiation affects the electronic and transport characteristics of bilayer heterostructures is crucial for advancing optoelectronic device performance. This work presents a theoretical investigation into how time-periodic external light fields alter the transport behavior of bilayer graphene and various bilayer heterostructures. We analyze bulk electronic and transport properties within a Landauer-type framework utilizing the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism. To demonstrate the impact of light on the differential conductance of bilayer contacts, we employ tight-binding models for both bilayer graphene and graphene/hexagonal boron-nitride heterostructures. The non-adiabatic driving force generates sidebands in the original band structure and creates gaps within the quasienergy spectrum. In terms of transport, these gap openings result in a reduction of differential conductance. Furthermore, while conductance is typically suppressed, an external light field can enhance differential conductance when photoexcited electrons tunnel through Van Hove singularities.

Recent theoretical developments in Deep Learning have revealed specific geometric patterns emerging after the Interpolation Threshold, the point where training error vanishes. This study investigates the phenomenon of Neural Collapse within intermediate network layers, focusing on the mechanics of Nearest Class-Center Mismatch. We demonstrate that these dynamics manifest across both vision and language model architectures. Furthermore, we introduce a Stochastic Variability-Simplification Loss (SVSL) designed to foster superior geometric characteristics in intermediate layers, thereby enhancing both training performance and generalization capabilities.

We tackle the challenge of calculating a textural loss function by analyzing statistics derived from feature activations within a convolutional neural network trained for object recognition, such as VGG-19. The core mathematical task involves measuring the distance between two distributions in feature space. While the Gram-matrix loss is a common approximation for this issue, it suffers from multiple limitations. Our objective is to advocate for the Sliced Wasserstein Distance as a superior alternative. This method is theoretically sound, practical, easy to implement, and delivers visually superior outcomes for texture synthesis through optimization or the training of generative neural networks.

This paper addresses the initial boundary value problem for the heat flow of surfaces with constant mean curvature, building upon the work of Huang et al. in *Manuscripta Mathematica* (2011), where they established global well-posedness and finite-time blow-up for regular solutions. The current study extends these findings by introducing new conditions on the initial data that ensure the development of finite-time singularities in the solutions.

We demonstrate that spin-independent scattering between two initially separated qubits—located in different traps or distant lattice sites—can facilitate the creation of an entangling quantum gate. This process occurs under one-dimensional confinement, examined through two distinct scenarios: a 1D waveguide and a tight-binding lattice. We analyze models involving contact-like interactions between pairs of fermions or bosons, with each qubit encoded in separate spin or internal states of the particles. Our proposed scheme allows for gate implementation between qubits that are too distant to interact directly, offering a photonic-mediator-free alternative for scaling quantum computers. A fundamental requirement for the gate's operation is the combination of identical particles (such as atoms of the same species) and 1D confinement. Furthermore, we assess the scheme's feasibility, the control precision needed to initialize wave-packet momenta, and how gate fidelity is influenced by momentum distributions and initial separation. In lattice systems, the control of quasi-momenta is naturally achieved through a small number of local edge impurities in the lattice potential.

This study investigates a three-dimensional version of the polynomial affine model of gravity, a framework that generalizes general relativity by omitting the metric from fundamental fields to relax the equivalence principle. Specifically, to better understand the roles of torsion and nonmetricity within gravitational theories, we analyze homogeneous and isotropic cosmological models, classifying their solutions using a \emph{decision tree}. Furthermore, we present several explicit solutions that enable the construction of alternative or emergent metrics derived from the connection.

This paper proposes a framework utilizing a class of abelian gauge symmetries where only the third generation of quarks and leptons acquire mass at the tree level. In contrast, fermions belonging to the first and second families obtain their masses via radiative corrections driven by new gauge bosons within loop diagrams. The analysis demonstrates that abelian symmetries capable of effectively implementing this mechanism are inherently flavour non-universal. By extending the well-known leptonic $L_\mu-L_\tau$ and $L_e-L_\mu$ symmetries to include all fermions, we construct an explicit renormalizable model based on two $U(1)$ groups. This model successfully reproduces the observed fermion mass spectrum of the Standard Model, where first and second generation masses are suppressed by loop factors. Furthermore, the mass hierarchy between these two generations emerges from a disparity in the masses of the two vector bosons associated with the extended gauge symmetries. Finally, various phenomenological implications of this flavour-sensitive new physics are explored, along with the derivation of lower bounds for the vector boson masses.

We present lrsarith, a compact C library designed for hybrid and fixed-precision arithmetic operations on integers and rationals, developed to support the lrslib library for polyhedral computations. By utilizing a generic set of operations, programs can be compiled to run with either 64-bit or 128-bit (where available) fixed precision, alongside extended precision options like GMP or built-in MP routines. A straightforward mechanism detects overflows, either halting execution or switching to higher-precision arithmetic in hybrid mode. Integrating these arithmetic methods into lrslib required only minor modifications to the original codebase. We report computational results from lrs and mplrs, which are vertex/facet enumeration tools in lrslib, tested across various configurations including 64/128-bit fixed integer arithmetic (with and without overflow checks), GMP arithmetic, lrsarith hybrid modes using GMP or MP, and FLINT hybrid arithmetic. Additionally, we provide a concise, self-contained C example demonstrating the lrsarith package in both fixed precision and hybrid modes.

I have identified that multiple information-sharing models within social networks can be understood as age-dependent multi-type branching processes, constructed independently in accordance with Sewastjanow's framework. This approach enables the characterization of criticality across both real and random social networks. For random networks, I devised a moment-closure technique to manage the models' high dimensionality: by adjusting the timing of information dissemination among followers, all users can be aggregated into a single representative without altering the total progeny. Consequently, I calculated the precise popularity distribution, which exposes the viral nature of critical models through fat tails of order -3/2.

This study introduces a resistance-based threshold logic family designed to emulate brain-like, large-scale variable logic functions within VLSI systems. We present a universal Boolean logic cell constructed from an analog resistive divider and a threshold logic circuit. The resistive divider, realized using memristors, generates an output voltage representing the weighted sum of input voltages. A threshold operation, executed via a CMOS inverter and/or operational amplifier, converts this voltage into a binary value. To reduce overall implementation complexity and component count, a universal cell architecture is proposed. As the number of input variables increases, this proposed cell demonstrates superior advantages in terms of reduced area and design simplicity compared to traditional CMOS-based logic circuits.

Non-invertible symmetries have recently emerged as a powerful tool for constraining renormalization group (RG) flows in quantum field theories (QFTs). In this study, we demonstrate that these symmetries can also generate entirely new RG flows through a mechanism known as "non-invertible twisted compactification." We apply this concept to the twisted compactification of 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills (SYM) down to three dimensions. Following a catalog of non-invertible symmetries derived from Montonen-Olive duality transformations in 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, we show that compactifying via these non-invertible symmetries yields 3d $\mathcal{N}=6$ theories that remain inaccessible when restricting the process to invertible symmetries.

This study addresses the effective deployment of smart inverters for Volt/Var (VVC) control within distribution networks. Although modern smart inverters provide reactive power (Var) support, their optimal utilization requires coordination with existing VVC strategies. To achieve this, a novel VVC framework is introduced that operates on a two-level structure. The first level manages voltage levels across the circuit by coordinating Load Tap Changers (LTCs) and Voltage Regulators (VRs) with smart inverters to maintain voltages within target limits. The second level calculates the necessary Var support from smart inverters to minimize total system power losses. Supervisory commands are transmitted to device local controllers to execute these adjustments. To prevent excessive dispatching, the scheme shifts the Volt/Var characteristics of smart inverters as required, enabling near-optimal operation while adhering to the communication constraints typical of distribution systems. A case study based on the IEEE 34-bus system demonstrates that this supervisory approach outperforms traditional VVC methods.

This study details Google's contribution to the BioASQ 7 biomedical question answering competition (specifically Task 7b, Phase B), utilizing BERT QA models based on the architecture described in \cite{alberti2019bert}. Our work addresses two primary research inquiries: first, we examine the domain portability of QA systems pre-trained and fine-tuned on general corpora like Wikipedia.
