This is evaluated through two submissions: a non-adapted model fine-tuned on the Natural Questions dataset \cite{kwiatkowski2019natural}, and a second system that further fine-tunes the former using BioASQ training data. Second, we investigate error propagation within end-to-end retrieval and QA pipelines. We test this by comparing a submission using human-annotated documents and snippets against one using predicted documents and snippets. Our key findings indicate that domain-specific fine-tuning enhances biomedical QA performance. However, the most significant quality bottleneck lies in the retrieval stage, where using non-gold inputs causes substantial metric drops exceeding 10 percentage points.

Discovering skills without rewards or supervision offers a compelling solution to the challenge of manually designing rewards, particularly in settings where task supervision is limited or costly. However, existing skill pre-training approaches, similar to many reinforcement learning methods, rely on the fundamental assumption that the environment remains stationary during training. Because traditional methods attempt to learn all skills simultaneously, they struggle to rapidly adapt to environmental changes without forgetting previously acquired abilities. Conversely, in dynamic or expanding environments, effective skill learning requires both quick adaptation to new situations and the retention of prior knowledge. These conflicting demands hinder the performance of classic skill discovery in evolving contexts. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that learns skills incrementally, one after another. This approach enables newly acquired skills to adapt to changes in the environment or agent dynamics, while previously learned skills remain fixed to prevent forgetting. Experimental results demonstrate that, in both evolving and static environments, this incremental method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques regarding skill quality and downstream task success. Videos of the learned skills and the associated code are publicly available at https://notmahi.github.io/disk.

Dividing large graphs into balanced components with minimal inter-block edges is fundamental to efficient distributed processing. While streaming algorithms are currently favored for partitioning massive graphs due to their low computational overhead, this paper introduces a shared-memory, streaming, multi-recursive partitioning scheme. This approach performs recursive multi-sections dynamically without requiring prior knowledge of the entire input graph. Compared to state-of-the-art non-buffered one-pass algorithms, our method achieves significantly lower time complexity. Furthermore, if the distributed system's topology is known, communication costs can be further optimized by mapping partitions to specific processing elements. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms competing tools in both speed and the quality of process mappings. Specifically, for graph partitioning tasks, our framework is up to two orders of magnitude faster than Fennel, accepting only a 5% increase in cut edges.

What do generic networks with specific attributes resemble? We define Relative Canonical Network ensembles as collections that exhibit a particular property $R$ while remaining as indistinguishable as possible from a generic network ensemble. This framework enables the investigation of the most fundamental characteristics of networks that produce the property in question. To validate this method, we initially apply it to the network metric "small-world-ness," which is believed to define small-world networks. Our results reveal multiple phase transitions as we move toward less generic networks, where cliques and hubs begin to appear. Since these features are absent in typical small-world networks, this suggests that high "small-world-ness" does not accurately capture the common understanding of small-world networks. Conversely, for embedded networks, the average shortest path length and total Euclidean link length serve as superior characterizers of small-world networks, with hubs emerging as a defining trait at low levels of genericity. We anticipate that this overall approach will have broad applicability in elucidating network properties of real-world significance.

This work examines the (algebraic-)functional technique introduced by Galleas and subsequently refined by Galleas and the author. We begin by illustrating the method with the most straightforward case: calculating the partition function for the six-vertex model under domain-wall boundary conditions. Central to this approach is a linear functional equation governing the partition function. Following the derivation of this equation, we sketch its analysis, which yields a closed-form solution expressed as a symmetrized sum or, alternatively, a multiple-integral formula capable of reproducing Izergin's determinant. We also highlight connections to other methodologies, demonstrating that the Korepin--Izergin approach emerges naturally within the functional framework. We discuss the method's scope and apply it to the more complex elliptic solid-on-solid model with domain walls and a reflecting boundary. For this model, we derive a novel partition function formula, previously presented by Tsuchiya--Filali--Kitanine as a determinant. Our result appears as a 'crossing-symmetrized' sum containing $2^L$ terms involving the elliptic domain-wall partition function, a form that seems new even for the rational six-vertex limit. Finally, by taking the rational limit, we recover Frassek's expression, which was originally obtained via the boundary perimeter Bethe ansatz.

Designing cranial implants is a critical and complex endeavor, where precision is paramount for successful cranioplasty. Traditionally, this process is carried out manually by specialists using computer-aided design tools. In this study, we introduce and assess novel automatic deep learning models capable of reconstructing cranial implants directly from CT scans. Utilizing the dataset from the AutoImplant challenge and benchmarking against the organizers' baseline, we trained our models on complete skull data via simulated virtual craniectomies. We evaluated two distinct strategies: a direct estimation approach grounded in the UNet architecture and a second method that integrates shape priors to enhance robustness against out-of-distribution implant geometries. Our direct estimation technique surpassed the organizers' baselines, whereas the model leveraging shape priors demonstrated superior performance in handling out-of-distribution scenarios. Collectively, these methods yield promising outcomes for the arduous task of cranial implant design.

The effectiveness of machine learning in predicting material properties relies critically on the representation of those materials. Two primary descriptor categories exist: one encoding crystal structures and another relying solely on stoichiometry to facilitate the discovery of new materials. While graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated exceptional accuracy in property prediction, they are currently restricted to a single approach due to the lack of overlap between these representation types. This work introduces a novel "formula graph" concept that unifies stoichiometry-based and structure-based descriptors. We further develop a self-attention-enhanced GNN incorporating this formula graph, demonstrating that the resulting architecture generates embeddings transferable across both domains. Our model surpasses existing structure-agnostic and structure-based models in performance while achieving superior sample efficiency and faster convergence. Finally, we apply the model to a challenging task: predicting complex dielectric functions to identify candidate materials with potential epsilon-near-zero characteristics.

This work presents refined estimates for the fat-shattering dimension associated with the $k$-fold maximum of real-valued function classes, which are formed by taking the pointwise maximum of $k$ selected functions, one from each of $k$ distinct classes. The derived bounds are expressed using the fat-shattering dimensions of the individual component classes. Specifically for linear and affine function classes, we establish a significantly tighter upper bound alongside a corresponding lower bound, thereby achieving an optimal dependency on $k$. Additionally, the study identifies and rectifies several incorrect assertions found in existing literature.

Entropy-related concepts span various disciplines, from statistical mechanics in physics to evolutionary biology. While Shannon entropy quantifies the information content within a system and is typically estimated using frequentist methods, this paper presents a fully objective Bayesian framework to derive its posterior distribution. We specifically employ the Gamma distribution, which models numerous natural phenomena across physics, engineering, and biology, and reparameterize the model directly in terms of entropy. We derive several objective priors, including Jeffreys, reference, and matching priors. Although these priors are improper, we demonstrate that the resulting posterior distributions are proper and possess finite posterior means. An extensive simulation study evaluates these priors based on bias, mean square error, and coverage probabilities to identify the most effective option. Finally, the proposed methodology is applied to two datasets: one concerning the reign period of the Achaemenid dynasty and another detailing the time to failure of an electronic component in a sugarcane harvesting machine.

This paper presents a novel method for computing the quantum mechanical propagator under geometrically complex Dirichlet boundary conditions. The approach extends an integral transform of the propagator previously identified as the "hit function," utilizing a convergent sequence of Padé approximants. We define the generalized hit function as a many-point propagator and elucidate its connection to the trajectory summation within the Feynman path integral, demonstrating its utility in calculating the Feynman propagator. Analytically, we derive all such hit functions for $D=1$ and $D=3$ dimensions, establishing recursion relations between them across varying dimensions. These results are applied to propagation scenarios involving perfectly conducting planar and spherical plates. Based on these findings, we propose a general analytical formula for the propagator in the presence of Dirichlet boundary conditions within specific geometries, alongside an explanation of its extension to more general, non-localized potentials. Our findings resonate with prior work by Grosche concerning path integrals involving delta potentials. Finally, we outline the potential application of this technique in a relativistic framework to determine Casimir energies.

This paper presents VGGFace2, a novel large-scale face dataset comprising 3.31 million images from 9,131 individuals, with an average of 362.6 images per person. Sourced from Google Image Search, the dataset exhibits significant diversity in pose, age, illumination, ethnicity, and profession (including actors, athletes, and politicians). Its collection was driven by three objectives: maximizing both the number of identities and images per identity; ensuring broad coverage of pose, age, and ethnicity; and reducing label noise. We detail the collection process, specifically the automated and manual filtering steps taken to guarantee high image accuracy for each identity. To evaluate face recognition capabilities, we trained ResNet-50 models (with and without Squeeze-and-Excitation blocks) on VGGFace2, MS-Celeb-1M, and their combined set. Results demonstrate that training on VGGFace2 improves recognition performance regarding pose and age. Furthermore, models trained on these datasets achieve state-of-the-art results on all IARPA Janus benchmarks (IJB-A, IJB-B, and IJB-C), surpassing previous records by a substantial margin. The datasets and models are publicly accessible.

The Internet of Things (IoT) plays a significant role in our everyday lives, particularly in reshaping the educational sector as we transition into the "Smart Educational" era. This article examines the profound transformation IoT brings to education, influencing everything from classroom dynamics and assessments to cultural attitudes. Smart Education serves as a critical instrument for addressing future educational challenges. As IoT tools become increasingly prevalent in learning environments, they aim to boost student engagement, satisfaction, and overall learning quality, fundamentally altering student habits and culture. However, Smart Education extends beyond mere technology adoption; it encompasses a comprehensive spectrum of factors, including educational management, pedagogical strategies, and their effectiveness. Educators in the 21st century now leverage gamification, smart devices, data analytics, and immersive technologies to gather diverse insights into student performance. These tools enable the monitoring of engagement levels and the adaptation of learning strategies to enhance effectiveness. Through Smart Education, instructors can better identify individual student needs and adjust their workload accordingly, fostering an optimal environment that supports learning and prevents failure. A primary challenge for educators is leveraging new technologies to tackle persistent issues regarding engagement and achievement, especially given the unprecedented scale and speed of change in the technological IoT era. Since the jobs students train for today may not exist tomorrow, education must focus not only on knowledge acquisition but also on cultivating digital skills, adaptability, and creativity—qualities essential for thriving in the future world.

This study provides a comprehensive examination of an anomalous absorption line system associated with the quasar SDSS J122826.79+100532.2. The system exhibits absorption features sharing a common redshifted velocity profile, ranging from approximately $v\sim0$ to $\sim1,000\ \mathrm{km~s}^{-1}$. These lines are distinctly observed in hydrogen Balmer series transitions up to H$\iota$, metastable neutral helium triplets, and optical transitions from excited states of singly ionized iron. Our estimates place the absorber's density at $n_{\mathrm{H}}\approx10^{8.4}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ and its ionization parameter at $U\approx10^{-1.2}$, positioning it roughly $1.5$ pc from the central supermassive black hole. This distance closely matches the calculated evaporation radius for dust grains ($r_{\mathrm{evap}}\approx1$ pc) within the quasar environment, suggesting the absorber could serve as a tracer for an inflow originating from the dusty torus and supplying the accretion disk. While the featureless continuum and broad emission lines show significant reddening with $E(B-V)\approx0.66$, the narrow emission lines exhibit negligible reddening. This disparity implies the dusty medium resides between the broad and narrow emission line regions, potentially linking to a 'cold' narrow absorption line system identified in \ion{Ca}{2} and \ion{Na}{1} doublets that is nearly unshifted from the quasar's systemic velocity. Consequently, SDSS J122826.79+100532.2 may constitute a rare instance where both inflow dynamics and the torus structure are observable through absorption lines.

Ultraperipheral collisions at the LHC and RHIC provide the highest currently accessible energies for interactions involving photons and nucleons or nuclei, making them an essential instrument for investigating the gluonic structure of hadrons and nuclei at small $x$. This discussion reviews recent theoretical developments aimed at understanding these exclusive processes at next-to-leading order (NLO) within QCD perturbation theory. Such theoretical progress is directly applicable to elucidating the physics of deep inelastic scattering at small $x$. Furthermore, we examine experimental findings from ultraperipheral collisions, with a primary focus on exclusive vector meson production.

Effective policy responses to the COVID-19 pandemic depend on a thorough understanding of events, their origins, and their consequences, yet the sheer volume and velocity of reported information can be overwhelming. This paper introduces ExcavatorCovid, a machine reading system that processes open-source documents—such as news articles and scientific journals—to identify pandemic-related events and their interconnections, constructing a Temporal and Causal Analysis Graph (TCAG). By addressing information overload, Excavator enables government agencies to anticipate the downstream effects of political and economic decisions and respond promptly to mitigate the pandemic's impact. Beyond the crisis itself, the system's utility is expected to endure, empowering analysts and decision-makers to tackle complex future challenges. An interactive TCAG visualization can be accessed at http://afrl402.bbn.com:5050/index.html, and a demonstration video is available at https://vimeo.com/528619007.

The advent of the information age has generated an overwhelming volume of data, much of which exists in textual form that is too vast for humans to manage and too unstructured for computers to comprehend. Text mining has emerged as a growing research area aimed at extracting value from massive document collections. However, traditional machine learning-based data mining techniques struggle with the sheer scale of text, creating a demand for more scalable approaches.

This thesis introduces a solution to scalable text mining by integrating generative models with sparse computation. A unified formalization for generative text models is established, merging distinct research traditions that previously utilized formally equivalent models without acknowledging their parallel evolution. This framework enables the application of methods developed for various processing tasks, such as retrieval and classification, to produce effective outcomes across diverse text mining applications. Furthermore, sparse computation utilizing inverted indices is proposed for probabilistic model inference. This approach reduces computational complexity based on data sparsity, resulting in probabilistic models that possess the scalability of contemporary search engines.

The resulting combination yields sparse generative models, offering a text mining solution that is general, efficient, and scalable. Comprehensive experiments on text classification and ranked retrieval datasets demonstrate that this approach matches or exceeds the performance of leading task-specific methods. Notably, it achieves a tenfold reduction in classification time for categorizing Wikipedia articles with one million classes. Additionally, these methods were successfully applied in two 2014 Kaggle data mining competitions, where over a hundred teams participated, securing first and second place honors.

Deep learning techniques have emerged as the leading methodology for addressing complex challenges across diverse fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and others. Driven by its rapid advancement and impressive performance benchmarks, researchers have begun applying these techniques to intrusion detection tasks. As a natural evolution and subset of classical machine learning, deep learning represents an advanced form of neural networks. This paper examines and discusses the state-of-the-art deep learning and neural network models specifically tailored for Intrusion Detection Systems.

This paper concludes our investigation into bounded solutions $u$ of the semilinear parabolic equation $u_t=u_{xx}+f(u)$ defined on the real line, where the initial data $u_0=u(\cdot,0)$ possesses finite limits $\theta^\pm$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. We assume $f$ is a locally Lipschitz function on $\mathbb{R}$ subject to mild nondegeneracy constraints. The objective is to characterize the asymptotic behavior of $u(x,t)$ as $t\to\infty$. Previous sections primarily addressed scenarios where $\theta^-\neq\theta^+$, or where $\theta^\pm=\theta_0$ with $f(\theta_0)\neq 0$, or where $\theta^\pm=\theta_0$, $f(\theta_0)=0$, and $\theta_0$ constitutes a stable equilibrium for $\dot \xi=f(\xi)$. In these instances, we demonstrated that bounded solutions are quasiconvergent, meaning their limit profiles as $t\to\infty$ (convergence in $L^\infty_{loc}(\mathbb{R})$) are steady states. This current work examines the remaining case: $\theta^\pm=\theta_0$, $f(\theta_0)=0$, with $\theta_0$ being an unstable equilibrium. While our prior quasiconvergence result for unstable equilibria required restrictive technical assumptions on the solution, those conditions are now eliminated. The only requirement imposed on $u(\cdot,t)$ is that it is nonoscillatory (possessing finitely many critical points) at some $t\geq 0$. Given that oscillatory bounded solutions are not invariably quasiconvergent, this finding is nearly optimal.

Sampling from constrained continuous distributions is a common challenge in various machine learning and statistical models. To address this, numerous Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) techniques have been modified to accommodate different variable constraints, with Hamilton Monte Carlo (HMC) and its derivatives demonstrating superior computational efficiency over alternatives. This article begins by reviewing HMC and its extensions, followed by a detailed explanation of three specific constrained HMC approaches: reflection, reformulation, and spherical HMC. To illustrate these methods, we apply them to three classic constrained sampling tasks: truncated multivariate normal distributions, Bayesian regularized regression, and nonparametric density estimation. Furthermore, this review links constrained sampling to the related problem of constrained design space within statistical experimental design.

It is commonly believed that visual media, such as photographs and drawings, cannot represent negation (e.g., "the train is not coming"). This assumption is empirically refuted through an analysis of real-world comic (manga) illustrations. In an experiment involving image captioning, participants were asked to interpret comic panels. The results indicated that certain comics convey negation independently of sequential panels or conventional symbolic devices. These specific illustrations were further tested in classification tasks to distinguish between images with and without negation. While humans found this task straightforward, deep learning models (CNNs) struggled to match their performance. Consequently, we argue that these particular comic illustrations leverage background knowledge to depict negation using purely visual elements.

We introduce Loc-NeRF, a real-time, vision-driven robot localization framework that integrates Monte Carlo localization with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Our system leverages a pre-trained NeRF model as an environmental map, enabling the robot to localize itself in real-time using solely an onboard RGB camera as an exteroceptive sensor. Although NeRFs have been widely adopted for visual rendering in computer vision and graphics, their application in robotics remains limited. Current NeRF-based localization methods often demand a precise initial pose estimate and substantial computational resources, rendering them unsuitable for real-time robotic tasks. By employing Monte Carlo localization to infer poses directly from a NeRF map, Loc-NeRF surpasses state-of-the-art performance in speed and eliminates the need for an initial pose guess. Beyond evaluations on synthetic data, we validated the system using real-world data from a Clearpath Jackal UGV, demonstrating, for the first time, the capability of real-time global localization with NeRFs. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/MIT-SPARK/Loc-NeRF.

This research analyzes the volatility of daily Bitcoin returns and the market's multifractal characteristics using a rolling window approach, focusing on the connection between volatility asymmetry and market efficiency. Although we observe an inverted asymmetry in Bitcoin volatility, its intensity fluctuates and has recently diminished; this asymmetric pattern persists across higher-frequency returns as well. Other metrics, including kurtosis, skewness, mean, serial correlation, and multifractal degree, also exhibit temporal variations, leading us to conclude that Bitcoin market properties are predominantly time-dependent. Regarding efficiency indicators such as the Hurst exponent, multifractal degree, and kurtosis, our findings suggest that as these measures indicate increased efficiency, volatility asymmetry decreases. Consequently, current data on both efficiency-related metrics and volatility asymmetry demonstrate that the Bitcoin market is becoming more efficient.

This work examines singular real analytic Levi-flat subsets that remain invariant under singular holomorphic foliations within complex projective spaces. We establish sufficient conditions under which a real analytic Levi-flat subset arises as the pull-back of a semianalytic Levi-flat hypersurface in a complex projective surface via a rational map, or as the pull-back of a real algebraic curve through a meromorphic function. Specifically, we apply these findings to singular real analytic Levi-flat hypersurfaces. Our findings refine and extend earlier results by Lebl, Bretas--Fernández-Pérez--Mol.

Lift forces are a common phenomenon in hydrodynamics, typically appearing in large, fast-moving objects where they arise from the interplay between fluid inertia (characterized by high Reynolds numbers) and specific symmetry-breaking mechanisms. Conversely, low-Reynolds-number flows are generally overdamped and lack these distinctive characteristics. However, the introduction of boundary effects fundamentally alters this understanding. Recent research in soft and biological matter has uncovered the generation of new lift forces driven by boundary softness, flow gradients, and/or surface charges. This review aims to consolidate and analyze this body of literature to unify key questions within the relevant scientific communities and to establish a foundation for future investigations into lift effects at low Reynolds numbers.

Recently, weighted triangulation algebras linked to triangulation quivers and their socle deformations have been introduced and analyzed in references [15]–[20] and [2]. Derived from surface triangulations and rooted in cluster algebra theory, these algebras (excluding minor exceptions) are established as finite-dimensional, tame, symmetric, and periodic algebras with a period of 4. This paper presents a novel concept of a generalized triangulation quiver, which expands the traditional definition. Specifically, it demonstrates that such generalized quivers can be derived from triangulations of orientable surfaces featuring marked self-folded triangles. Furthermore, inspired by recent findings in [28], we define and examine weighted generalized triangulation algebras associated with these generalized quivers, which emerge naturally from the mutations of weighted triangulation algebras.

This paper introduces our system for the RSNA Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection challenge. The architecture is a lightweight deep neural network combining a convolutional neural network (CNN) that processes individual CT slices and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that utilizes feature embeddings from the CNN. To enhance efficiency, we employed various feature selection techniques to identify a subset of valuable CNN features for the LSTM and reduced the number of CT slices by a factor of 2x to accelerate training. Despite prioritizing both speed and accuracy, our model achieved a weighted mean log loss of 0.04989 on the final test set, securing a top 30 ranking (2%) among 1345 participants. While our hardware constraints prevented processing slices at their original resolution, which could potentially boost performance, we made our code open source at https://github.com/warchildmd/ihd to facilitate reproducibility. Post-challenge, a subjective assessment by radiologists confirmed that our deep learning model's performance matches that of CT-specialized doctors. Additionally, we integrated Grad-CAM visualizations to offer interpretable explanations for our predictions. Consequently, we view this system as a practical solution for rapid diagnosis or providing a second opinion on intracranial hemorrhage detection.

Resting-state functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) serves as a potent tool for investigating fetal brain development; however, its clinical utility is hindered by unpredictable and excessive fetal motion, which induces significant signal fluctuations and systematically distorts functional connectivity patterns. While prior research has addressed large fetal head movements by estimating motion parameters and applying a 3D single-step interpolation method at each timepoint to restore motion-free images, this approach does not ensure that the resulting images represent the minimum error solution for the fMRI time series given the acquired data. In this study, we introduce a novel technique utilizing four-dimensional iterative reconstruction of the scattered slices obtained during fetal fMRI. Quantitative evaluation on a cohort of real clinical fetal fMRI data demonstrates that the proposed method yields superior reconstruction quality compared to conventional 3D interpolation strategies.

This research examines the q-analogue of the Euler-Maclaurin formula, deriving this result through the introduction of a novel q-operator. Furthermore, the approximation characteristics of q-Bernoulli polynomials are analyzed. We identify appropriate functions by combining truncated series of q-Bernoulli polynomials and compute the associated error. This study offers utility in two distinct areas: solving differential equations via function estimation and applying these methods within operator theory.

A Geant4-based simulation framework was created to realistically model the RIBRAS facility, incorporating a second-order expansion of the finite solenoid magnetic field to ensure high precision in beam optics calculations. A systematic investigation into coil currents across various magnetic rigidities and focal points was conducted, yielding parameterizations for both single and dual operational modes. Specialized routines were also implemented to simulate direct reactions involving two- and three-particle final states. These simulations were utilized to assess the feasibility of implementing a Solenoidal Spectrometer within the RIBRAS system. Initial findings suggest that this concept is viable under specific conditions, and further research through both simulations and experiments is currently underway.

This study reinterprets existing searches for exotic decays of Standard Model-like Higgs bosons, specifically $H \to aa (hh)$, within the context of the Type-I Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM). Furthermore, we examine a novel search for these light Higgs candidates ($a$ and $h$) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) during Run 3, utilizing an integrated luminosity of 300 $\text{fb}^{-1}$. Following a comprehensive scan of model parameters, the inverted Type-I scenario emerges as a promising avenue, characterized by the cascade decay chain $H \to Z^{*}a \to Z^{*}Z^{*}h \to b\overline{b} \mu^- \mu^+ jj$. Finally, we assess the statistical significance of this signal through a full Monte Carlo simulation extending down to the detector level.

The IFOSMONDI iterative algorithm, first presented by the authors at the Simultech conference in July 2019 (pp. 176–186), facilitates implicit co-simulation of coupled physical systems by solving nonlinear coupling functions while maintaining interface smoothness without inducing delays. Furthermore, the algorithm dynamically adjusts the step size between data exchanges based on the complexity of the coupling constraint solution. While the original implementation relied on a fixed-point algorithm, this paper introduces the JFM (Jacobian-Free Methods) variant. Most Newton-like methods typically require a Jacobian matrix, which is often difficult to compute in co-simulation contexts unless interfaces utilize Zero-Order-Hold (ZOH) representations. Since the IFOSMONDI coupling algorithm employs Hermite interpolation to enhance smoothness up to the Third-Order-Hold level, we propose a new formulation of the nonlinear coupling function that incorporates both values and time derivatives of the coupling variables. This formulation is specifically optimized for solving coupling problems using Jacobian-free Newton-type methods. Consequently, successive function evaluations involve running multiple system simulations within a co-simulation time step using rollback techniques. The algorithm's orchestrator-workers architecture allows for the integration of the PETSc framework on the orchestrator side for nonlinear Newton-type solvers, combined with parallel system integrations on the worker side via MPI processes. Finally, various nonlinear methods are compared against each other and the original fixed-point implementation using a newly proposed two-system academic test case (mass-spring-damper type) featuring direct feedthrough on both sides.

This study addresses top-k subset selection within Dueling Bandit frameworks that incorporate score data. Since real-world pairwise ranking tasks frequently display significant transitivity, previous research has utilized parametric preference models, such as Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) and Thurstone models, to leverage this property via sampling methods. However, existing approaches have primarily dealt with binary win/loss outcomes. We broaden this scope to selection scenarios involving quantitative sampling results by introducing a Thurstonian-style model and modifying the Pairwise Optimal Computing Budget Allocation for subset selection (POCBAm) to efficiently exploit this model. Finally, we evaluate the empirical performance of our approach against standard POCBAm and other competing algorithms.

Current indoor localization approaches typically combine inertial odometry with map data using manually designed techniques to mitigate drift; however, these methods are prone to noise and lack generalizability across different odometry sources. To enhance the robustness of map integration, we introduce a data-driven prior for feasible user locations by merging learned spatial map embeddings with temporal odometry embeddings. This prior more accurately identifies viable map regions compared to previous hand-crafted methods. When integrated into a particle filter, this prior boosts inertial-only localization accuracy by 49%, a significant achievement that demonstrates our relative positioning technique can rival the performance of absolute positioning via Bluetooth beacons. Furthermore, we validate the method's generalizability by demonstrating comparable gains when applied to wheel encoder odometry.

This study examines how illumination influences the magnetotransport characteristics of a two-dimensional electron system at the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface. Upon illumination, the zero-field sheet resistance decreases substantially, the Kondo effect vanishes at low temperatures, and the magnetoresistance transitions from negative to positive. A significant rise in high-mobility carrier density following illumination triggers quantum oscillations in magnetoresistance due to Landau quantization. Analysis of these oscillations yields a carrier density of approximately $2 \times 10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$ and an effective mass of about $1.7 ~m_e$, indicating that the high-mobility electrons reside in the d$_{xz/yz}$ subbands of the Ti:t$_{2g}$ orbital, extending deep into the SrTiO$_3$ conducting layer. These findings illustrate that illumination-induced carrier injection at the interface offers a mechanism to manipulate Kondo-like scattering and investigate quantum transport within complex oxide heterostructures.

The mechanical and electrochemical performance of high-strength Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys is significantly governed by grain boundary (GB) microchemistry and precipitation behavior. Accurately simulating solute distribution, precipitation, and GB segregation in these multi-component systems demands a precise description of their thermodynamic and kinetic properties. While CALPHAD databases have long supported equilibrium thermodynamic calculations in complex systems and have recently been integrated with diffusion simulations, this study directly embeds a CALPHAD database within a phase-field framework. This approach enables high-fidelity simulation of the complex non-equilibrium GB microstructures that evolve during heat treatment in these commercial alloys. Specifically, the study systematically examined how GB solute segregation, GB diffusion, precipitate number density, and far-field matrix composition affect the growth of GB precipitate populations in a model Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloy with a composition near AA7050. The simulation outcomes demonstrated good agreement with experimental characterization data obtained via scanning transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography on alloys of similar composition.

A sequence $\bfx=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)$ with elements from $\Z_n$ is termed an \textit{$A$-weighted Davenport Z-sequence} if there exists a non-zero vector $\bfa:=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in (A\cup\{0\})^m$ such that $\sum_i a_ix_i=0$, where $\bfzero_m=(0,\ldots,0)\in\Z_n^m$. Likewise, $\bfx$ is defined as an \textit{$A$-weighted Erd\H{o}s Z-sequence} if there exists a non-zero vector $\bfa:=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in (A\cup\{0\})^m$ with $|Supp(\bfa)|=n$ satisfying $\sum_i a_ix_i=0$, given that $Supp(\bfa):=\{i: a_i\ne 0\}$. A $\Z_n$-sequence $\bfx$ is said to be $k$-restricted when no element of $\Z_n$ occurs more than $k$ times within it. This paper investigates finding the minimum length $m$ required for a $k$-restricted $\Z_n$-sequence to become an $A$-weighted Davenport Z-sequence (or an $A$-weighted Erd\H{o}s Z-sequence). Furthermore, we examine this problem for random $\Z_n$ sequences, assuming specific natural selections for the set $A$.

This work offers a critical evaluation of recent advancements in molecular biology, arguing that they fail to provide a conceptual grasp of life and biological systems. The text outlines Maturana and Varela's concept of autopoiesis, proposing that logical circularity is resolved by positing underlying living processes. These processes entail amplification from the microscopic to the macroscopic scale, characterized by increasing complexity across levels. Based on this perspective, the prevailing model of condensed matter, which relies on electrostatics and short-ranged forces, is challenged. Instead, it is suggested that interpreting quantum dispersion forces (such as van der Waals forces and hydrogen bonding) as quantum coherence effects indicates the need to incorporate long-ranged forces or mechanisms into biological condensed matter theories. The review highlights various quantum effects in biology, asserting that quantum mechanics is conceptually indispensable because, without it, most biological structures and signaling processes would not exist. Furthermore, the text proposes that long-range quantum coherent dynamics, including electron polarization, could explain signal amplification in biological systems.

Automatic Program Repair (APR) has garnered increasing attention recently, leading to the proposal of many techniques. A prominent category within APR involves search-based methods that utilize syntactic analysis to create repair candidates and explore a generated search space for valid fixes. In this study, we investigate an alternative strategy inspired by the adversarial concepts of bugs and repairs. By employing the deep learning Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) architecture, our method aims to propose repairs that closely mimic those generated by humans. Preliminary evaluations show promising outcomes, with our approach producing repairs identical to human fixes for 21.2% of 500 tested bugs.

The LHCb experiment analyzed 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 7 and 8 TeV to search for the lepton-flavour violating decay $D^0 \to e^\pm \mu^\mp$. Candidate $D^0$ mesons were identified via the decay $D^{*+} \to D^0 \pi^+$, while the branching fraction for $D^0 \to e^\pm \mu^\mp$ was determined relative to the normalisation channel $D^0 \to K^-\pi^+$. No significant excess of signal candidates over the predicted background was observed, leading to an upper limit on the branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}(D^0 \to e^\pm \mu^\mp) < 1.3 \times 10^{-8}$ at 90 % confidence level. This result represents an improvement of one order of magnitude over the previous constraint and imposes tighter restrictions on parameter spaces within leptoquark models and supersymmetric models featuring R-parity violation.

Current dynamical mass estimates for simple systems like globular clusters (GCs) remain uncertain by up to a factor of two, largely because standard models oversimplify long-term evolutionary effects. We present a novel method for determining GC dynamical properties that combines deep learning with extensive data from direct $N$-body simulations. Our algorithm, $\texttt{$\pi$-DOC}$ ($\textit{Predicting Images for the Dynamics Of stellar Clusters}$), utilizes two convolutional networks to map observed luminosity profiles to corresponding mass distributions, ages, and distances. Trained on mock $N$-body simulation data, the algorithm achieves a mean pixel-wise mass prediction error of 27%, with age and distance accuracies of 1.5 Gyr and 6 kpc, respectively. Furthermore, the method recovers the mass-to-light profile shape and global value with a 12% mean error, effectively tracing mass segregation. Preliminary comparisons with real observations suggest the algorithm performs well within the scope of its training data. These promising results indicate that this forward-modelling deep-learning framework offers a rapid, adaptable alternative that competes effectively with traditional dynamical models.

Strongly correlated quantum particles within lattice potentials serve as fundamental components for diverse quantum insulators, including Mott phases and symmetry-breaking density waves, which can exist in both fermionic and bosonic systems. To broaden the range of accessible quantum matter phases, theoretical models suggest mixing these species is promising because density order competes with phase separation. In this study, we manipulate such a Bose-Fermi mixture by trapping neutral, boson-like and charged, fermion-like dipolar excitons within an artificial square lattice formed by a GaAs bilayer. At unitary lattice filling, robust inter- and intra-species interactions stabilize insulating phases when the proportion of charged excitons is approximately 1/3, 1/2, or 2/3. We demonstrate the realization of dual Bose-Fermi density waves, characterized by species ordered in alternating stripes. These findings underscore that dipolar excitons facilitate the controlled implementation of Bose-Fermi Hubbard models augmented by off-site interactions.

Building upon Schultz's (Calc.Var.PDE 2018) extension of Rajala and Sturm's (Calc.Var.PDE 2014) work regarding weak non-branching conditions in very strict CD spaces, this article addresses the lack of stability of the very strict CD condition under measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence, a known issue similar to that of the strong CD condition. By imposing specific metric constraints on both the converging sequence and the limit space, I establish a stability result for the very strict CD condition. The proof utilizes the concepts of \textit{consistent geodesic flow} and \textit{consistent plan selection} to separately address the static and dynamic components of a Wasserstein geodesic. As a practical application, it is demonstrated that $\mathbb R^N$ endowed with a crystalline norm and Lebesgue measure satisfies the very strict $CD(0,\infty)$ condition.

Helicity-orbital coupling represents a fascinating characteristic of magnetic skyrmions within frustrated magnets. This study investigates skyrmion dynamics in such a system using the $J_{1}$-$J_{2}$-$J_{3}$ classical Heisenberg model, with a specific focus on incorporating dipole-dipole interactions. This interaction induces a helicity-dependent energy shift, leading to current-driven translational motion that maintains a fixed helicity. The ground states consist of degenerate Bloch-type configurations, which hold potential for binary memory applications. As the driving current increases, a transition from helicity locking to unlocking occurs, shifting the motion from translational to rotational. Additionally, we demonstrate that two skyrmions can spontaneously form a bound state and analyze the separation of this state under current influence. We also observe the annihilation of a skyrmion-antiskyrmion pair. These findings suggest that frustrated skyrmions possess unique properties that could facilitate practical applications in topological magnetism.

Device density in cellular networks is anticipated to rise significantly in the near future. To meet this growth, access points (APs) will adopt massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) antennas, leveraging collimated millimeter-wave (mmW) and sub-THz communications to expand bandwidth for higher data rates. In this environment, interference becomes a pivotal factor; without proper characterization and mitigation, it could severely constrain network performance. This study derives the statistical properties of aggregated interference power for a cellular network utilizing a cylindrical mMIMO array. The proposed statistical model accounts for link blockage alongside other critical parameters, including antenna configuration and device density. Results indicate that the characteristic function (CF) of the aggregated interference power can be modeled as a weighted mixture of two alpha-stable distributions. Additionally, service probability analysis reveals an optimal array configuration dependent on AP height and device density. Ultimately, this statistical model offers valuable insights for designing dense networks and optimizing their deployment.

In recent years, numerous open-source machine learning fairness toolkits have emerged to assist practitioners in evaluating and mitigating bias within their systems. Despite this growth, research into how practitioners actually utilize these tools in real-world scenarios remains scarce. This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study examining the ways industry professionals engage with existing fairness toolkits. Specifically, we employed think-aloud interviews to uncover how participants learn about and apply these tools, and we validated the broader applicability of our insights through an anonymous online survey. Our analysis revealed several key opportunities for improving fairness toolkits to better meet practitioner needs and guide them toward effective, responsible usage. Drawing from these findings, we outline implications for the design of future open-source fairness toolkits, emphasizing their potential to help practitioners better contextualize, communicate, and collaborate on machine learning fairness initiatives.

Deep learning significantly accelerates the parameter estimation process for coalescing compact binary systems, such as black holes and neutron stars, identified via gravitational waves (GWs). As an initial step, we introduce two neural network architectures designed to quickly derive the posterior distributions of chirp mass and mass ratio for detected binary black holes using strain data from LIGO's Hanford and Livingston observatories. These parameters enable the prediction of component masses, which is crucial for estimating the probability that a merger involves a neutron star. When benchmarked against LALInference, the "gold standard" employed by the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration (LVC), our models produce posterior distributions consistent with LALInference while achieving processing speeds orders of magnitude faster after training. Furthermore, the median predictions for all tested parameters fall within the 90% credible intervals of LALInference when evaluated on real binary black hole events from the LVC's first and second observing runs. We conclude that deep learning holds substantial promise for enabling low-latency, high-accuracy parameter estimation tailored for real-time GW search pipelines.

The effectiveness of machine learning in healthcare hinges on the trust clinicians place in model predictions. This paper introduces a method to equip clinical experts with domain-specific evidence explaining why a prediction should be trusted. We begin by designing a probabilistic model that links meaningful latent concepts to prediction targets and observed data. In this framework, inferring latent variables serves a dual purpose: generating the prediction itself and supplying the supporting rationale. To achieve efficient inference, we propose a two-step process: first, estimating model parameters via variational learning, and second, approximating the maximum a posteriori estimation of latent variables using a neural network trained on an objective function derived from the probabilistic model. We validate this approach on predicting mortality risk for patients with cardiovascular disease. By utilizing electrocardiogram and tabular data as inputs, we demonstrate that our method successfully generates relevant, domain-specific evidence to support accurate predictions.

Current video polyp segmentation (VPS) architectures predominantly utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for feature extraction; however, their restricted receptive fields prevent the comprehensive capture of global spatial and temporal data across consecutive frames, often leading to inaccurate segmentation. To address this, we introduce PNS-Net (Progressively Normalized Self-attention Network), a model capable of efficiently learning representations from polyp videos at real-time speeds (approximately 140 frames per second) on a single RTX 2080 GPU without requiring any post-processing. Built exclusively from a fundamental normalized self-attention block alongside CNNs and recurrence mechanisms, PNS-Net demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across challenging VPS benchmarks. Furthermore, extensive experiments evaluating the efficacy of channel splitting, soft-attention, and progressive learning strategies reveal that PNS-Net remains robust under various configurations, positioning it as a highly promising approach for VPS tasks.

The coinvariant algebra arises as a quotient of the polynomial ring $\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with its algebraic characteristics determined by the combinatorics of permutations of length $n$. A word $w = w_1 \dots w_n$ over the positive integers is defined as packed if the presence of any letter $i > 2$ implies that $i-1$ also appears in $w$. We define a new quotient $S_n$ of $\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ that is governed by the combinatorics of these packed words. Furthermore, we establish connections between this quotient $S_n$ and the generalized coinvariant rings developed by Haglund, Rhoades, and Shimozono, as well as the superspace coinvariant ring.

Although reinforcement learning (RL) has advanced recently, applying it to safety-critical areas such as autonomous driving remains difficult. While penalizing risky actions helps RL agents learn safe behaviors, it often results in overly conservative strategies. This paper introduces a distributional RL framework designed to learn adaptive policies that dynamically adjust their level of conservativity at runtime based on desired comfort and utility levels. By employing proactive safety verification, the framework ensures that RL-generated actions are fail-safe under worst-case assumptions while simultaneously minimizing safety interference to promote comfort. We trained and evaluated our proposed approach against baseline policies using a high-level simulator across diverse randomized scenarios, including rare but critical corner cases. Experimental results demonstrate that policies learned via distributional RL are robust to environmental uncertainties and can adapt their behavior in real-time. Quantitatively, the distributional RL agent achieves an average speed increase of 8 seconds compared to a standard DQN policy and reduces safety interference by 83% relative to a rule-based policy, with only a marginal rise in average crossing time. Furthermore, our analysis of sensitivity in high-perception-noise environments reveals that the algorithm produces reliable driving policies for automated merging and crossing at occluded intersections, even when noise levels are double those present during training.

Recent advancements in lattice investigations of heavy quarks and quarkonium at finite temperatures are reviewed. By modeling the spectral function tail as a transport coefficient, researchers have determined the momentum diffusion coefficient ($\kappa$) for charm quarks in the heavy mass limit and calculated the chemical equilibration rate for heavy quark-antiquark pairs within NRQCD. A large-volume quenched lattice simulation reaching the continuum limit yields $\kappa/T^3 = 1.8 \cdots 3.4$. Additionally, studies utilizing $N_f = 2+1$ configurations estimate the charmonium chemical equilibration rate $\Gamma_{\rm chem}$; at $T = 400$ MeV and $M \sim 1.5$ GeV, this rate corresponds to a timescale of approximately 150 fm/c. Previous findings from two distinct lattice approaches—employing different setups and Bayesian priors to analyze bottomonium correlators via NRQCD—indicate that the $\Upsilon (1S)$ state persists until $T \sim 1.9 T_c$, while excited $\Upsilon$ states are sequentially suppressed. However, results for the $\chi_{b1}$ spectral function exhibit sensitivity to the chosen Bayesian prior: using the Maximum Entropy Method (MEM) prior suggests melting above $T_c$, whereas a newer prior implies survival up to $\sim 1.6 T_c$. Preliminary insights into the discrepancies driving these differing $\chi_{b1}$ behaviors are also presented.

The notion of statistically unbounded $p$-convergence serves as an abstraction encompassing statistical order, unbounded order, and $p$-convergence. This study examines statistically unbounded convergence within lattice-normed Riesz spaces, specifically regarding statistical $p$-decreasing sequences. Furthermore, we establish connections between this concept and other forms of statistical convergence in Riesz spaces.

Catalysis, defined as the acceleration of chemical reactions by non-consumed molecules, is fundamental to life but currently missing in artificial physical systems attempting to mimic biological functions. In this study, we present a method for designing catalysts composed of spherical building blocks that interact through programmable potentials. We demonstrate that a minimal catalyst design—a rigid dimer—can speed up a common elementary reaction, specifically bond cleavage. By integrating coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with theoretical analysis and comparing reaction times with and without the catalyst, we establish the necessary geometric and physical constraints for catalyst design and identify the conditions required for catalytic emergence. The resulting framework and design principles are broadly applicable, extending from micron-scale DNA-coated colloids to centimeter-scale magnetic handshake materials, thereby paving the way for the development of self-regulated artificial systems with bio-inspired capabilities.

Recent discourse highlights significant challenges in science communication, including the overwhelming volume of published articles that obscures a clear view of the state-of-the-art, and the limited reproducibility caused by fixed-length documents that often omit crucial research details. While recent initiatives have suggested knowledge graphs (KGs) as a remedy, their scope typically remains confined to narrow use cases. This paper seeks to broaden that perspective by delivering a thorough analysis of the requirements for an Open Research Knowledge Graph (ORKG). We achieve this by (a) gathering and reviewing a scientist's daily essential tasks, (b) deriving the resulting needs for a KG-based system, and (c) examining overlaps, unique characteristics, and the extent to which current solutions address them. Consequently, we identify both necessary and desirable requirements for effective KG-driven science communication, draw relevant implications, and propose potential solutions.

Both Pomset logic and BV extend multiplicative linear logic (including Mix) by introducing a third connective that is self-dual and non-commutative. Pomset logic stems from research on coherence spaces and proof nets, whereas BV arises from the study of series-parallel orders, cographs, and proof systems. Although both logics admit cut-admissibility, this property cannot be established within a sequent calculus framework. Instead, provability in Pomset logic is verified using a proof net correctness criterion, while BV relies on a deep inference proof system. Despite a long-standing conjecture suggesting these two logics are identical, this paper demonstrates that the conjecture is incorrect. Furthermore, the study reveals a significant complexity gap between them: while provability in BV is NP-complete, it is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete for Pomset logic. The paper also offers observations regarding potential sequent systems for both logics.

Optical-field emission from nanostructured solids, including subwavelength nanoantennas, offers a pathway to developing petahertz-scale electronics capable of sub-femtosecond operation for optical-field detection. A key application in this domain is the measurement of the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) of incident optical pulses. Achieving CEP detection necessitates broadband, few-cycle optical excitation, during which the antenna's resonant characteristics significantly modulate the temporal evolution of the near field. However, there has been limited quantitative research into optimizing antenna geometry and resonant properties to maximize CEP sensitivity and signal-to-noise ratio. This study investigates the engineering of planar plasmonic nanoantennas' geometry and resonance frequency to boost the emitted CEP-sensitive photocurrent under few-cycle optical driving. We demonstrate that incorporating curved sidewalls toward the apex and precisely tuning the resonance wavelength can enhance the net CEP-sensitive current per antenna by $5$-$10\times$ and the signal-to-noise ratio by $50$-$100\times$ compared to simple triangular antennas operating at resonance. These results will guide the design of future nanoantennas for advanced ultrafast photoelectron metrology and petahertz electronics.

We present a new methodology and a corresponding high-resolution dataset designed for the accurate assessment of indoor positioning algorithms based on wireless signals. This approach utilizes an augmented reality (AR) positioning system to tag wireless signal parameter samples with highly precise location information. Specifically, we track the movement of a practical, low-cost setup comprising cameras and a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacon within an environment marked by AR features. To optimize the performance of AR-based localization, we employ a redundant array of markers. The video feeds from the cameras undergo a sequence of marker recognition, subset selection, and filtering processes to generate highly accurate pose estimations. Our findings indicate that the positional error of the AR localization system can be reduced to below 0.05 meters. Subsequently, this high-precision position data is used to annotate BLE signals captured simultaneously by sensors deployed in the area, thereby creating a ground-truthed wireless signal dataset that enables the rigorous evaluation of wireless signal-based localization systems.

In recent years, automation has driven significant innovation within the industrial sector, fundamentally incorporating sensor networks for status monitoring and data aggregation. A primary challenge in these data-intensive settings is extracting and leveraging vast amounts of information to identify anomalies, uncover patterns that minimize downtime and manufacturing errors, lower energy consumption, forecast failures, and optimize maintenance schedules. To tackle these problems, we created TSML, a technology built on a pipeline of lightweight filters designed to process massive volumes of industrial time-series data in parallel.

The Penrose strong cosmic censorship conjecture posits that Cauchy horizons within dynamically created black holes are unstable due to remnant matter fields falling into them. This conjecture is physically significant because it establishes a necessary condition for general relativity to function as a genuinely deterministic theory of gravity. Recently, determining the validity of this conjecture in non-asymptotically flat black-hole spacetimes has been a major focus of research. In this essay, we offer a remarkably concise proof, grounded in Bekenstein's generalized second law of thermodynamics, confirming the conjecture's validity for physically realistic (dynamically formed) curved black-hole spacetimes.

We re-examine how axial-vector mesons influence the hyperfine splitting in muonic hydrogen. Our analysis centers on the doubly-virtual asymptotic behavior of these mesons' relevant form factors, alongside their nucleon couplings derived from resonance saturation and short-distance constraints. Notably, our results diverge significantly from earlier studies, revealing an opposite sign and an approximately 50% magnitude difference attributable to the doubly-virtual high-energy behavior.

Beyond standard parameters like signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), array geometry, dimensions, and sample size, other factors such as antenna element alignment and polarization significantly impact Direction of Arrival (DOA) estimation algorithms. Conventional methods typically assume identical alignment of all elements, rendering polarization parameters irrelevant to steering vectors. However, under this assumption, specific combinations of DOA angles and polarization states can cause a drastic drop in SNR across the entire array. To prevent such catastrophic failures, antenna elements must be aligned differently. Unfortunately, this approach contaminates steering vectors with polarization effects, rendering most standard DOA algorithms ineffective. To the best of our knowledge, existing literature has not addressed this problem, even in single-user scenarios. This paper investigates that gap by proposing a solution for a circular array with the minimum required elements. We introduce an antenna alignment scheme ensuring that at any given moment, no more than one element experiences a significant SNR drop due to polarization. Furthermore, we develop a low-complexity, closed-form algorithm for estimating DOA angles. Using MUSIC as a baseline, we demonstrate its reliable operation across all possible DOA and polarization conditions. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the performance and computational complexity for both proposed algorithms.

This letter examines the sensing and communication performance of a multiple-input multiple-output downlink integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system. The study investigates three typical ISAC scenarios: sensing-centric, communications-centric, and Pareto optimal designs. For each scenario, the diversity orders and high signal-to-noise ratio slopes for both sensing and communication rates are derived to provide deeper insights. The findings indicate that ISAC offers greater degrees of freedom and a wider rate region compared to existing frequency-division S&C (FDSAC) methods.

We introduce a novel two-component dust geometry framework termed the \textit{Chocolate Chip Cookie} model, in which clumpy nebular structures are situated within a diffuse stellar/interstellar medium disk, analogous to chocolate chips embedded in a cookie. By approximating the binomial distribution of these clumps with a continuous Gaussian function and neglecting dust scattering, we resolve the dust attenuation processes for both emission lines and stellar continua using analytical methods. This model effectively reproduces the inclination-dependent trends of effective dust reddening for both stellar components (derived from stellar population synthesis) and emission lines (characterized by the Balmer decrement) across a large sample of Milky-Way-like disk galaxies from the SDSS main galaxy catalog. Our results indicate that for such galaxies, the clumpy nebular disk is approximately 0.55 times thinner and 1.6 times more extensive than the stellar disk, with individual clumpy regions exhibiting a typical optical depth of $\tau_{\rm{cl,V}} \sim 0.5$ in the $V$ band. Furthermore, after accounting for aperture effects, our model's predictions regarding inclination-dependent dust attenuation align with observational data. Additionally, within this framework, the dust attenuation curve for the stellar population naturally varies with inclination, with its median case matching the classical Calzetti law. Since the modeling constraints rely on optical wavelengths, our approach remains unaffected by optically thick dust components, which might otherwise introduce biases in infrared emission predictions.

We derive compact expressions for the heavy quark structure functions $F^{q\bar{q}}_{2}(x, Q^{2})$ and $F^{q\bar{q}}_{L}(x, Q^{2})$ (where $q = c, b, t$) in electron-proton collisions, accounting for next-to-leading order (NLO) gluon density behavior, and provide the corresponding ratios $R^{q\bar{q}} = F^{q\bar{q}}_{L} /F^{q\bar{q}}_{2}$. These results are achieved by fitting heavy quark coefficient functions for deep-inelastic lepton-hadron scattering across a broad spectrum of $Q^{2}$ values. Furthermore, the calculated numerical values are benchmarked against HERA experimental data, as well as predictions from the KLN model and MSTW2008.

We report comprehensive orbital parameters, radial velocities, and detailed elemental abundances for Patchick~125, a newly identified metal-poor globular cluster (GC) located toward the Galactic bulge. High-resolution near-infrared spectra ($R\sim22,500$) were acquired for two member stars during the second phase of the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment at Las Campanas Observatory, utilizing data from the sixteenth Data Release (DR 16) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Our analysis focused on four chemical species, covering $\alpha$-elements (Mg, Si), Fe-peak elements (Fe), and odd-Z elements (Al). We determined a metallicity range of [Fe/H] $= -1.69$ to $-1.72$, indicating a mean metallicity $\langle$[Fe/H]$\rangle \sim -1.7$. This value signifies a substantial increase in metallicity relative to earlier low-resolution spectroscopic studies. Additionally, we measured a mean radial velocity of 95.9 km s$^{-1}$, approximately 21.6 km s$^{-1}$ higher than previously reported. The stars display $\alpha$-enrichment ([Mg/Fe]$\lesssim+0.20$, [Si/Fe]$\lesssim +0.30$) consistent with typical metal-poor GCs. Furthermore, the aluminum abundance ratios ([Al/Fe]$\gtrsim +0.58$) for the two observed members are enhanced, a hallmark of the "second-generation" stellar population in GCs at comparable metallicities. These findings support the existence of multiple populations within Patchick~125 and confirm its status as a genuine globular cluster. Dynamically, Patchick~125 follows a low-energy, low-eccentricity ($<0.4$) retrograde orbit trapped near the edge of the inner Galaxy. Consequently, we affirm that Patchick~125 is a verified metal-poor globular cluster currently residing in the vicinity of the Milky Way bulge.

This study employs the fractional Taylor series method to identify both the solution and an unknown space-dependent coefficient within a space-time fractional differential equation. A key advantage of this approach is that it does not rely on over-measured data, thereby enabling more precise determination of the solution and the coefficient. The provided examples demonstrate that the method's results align closely with the exact solutions of the corresponding problems. Furthermore, this technique proves to be highly effective and easily implementable when compared to alternative methods.

To address the challenge of data scarcity, we introduce a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework designed for class-imbalanced semantic segmentation. Initially, to enable semi-supervised operation, we developed a confidence-level-based contrastive learning approach that explicitly performs instance discrimination by aligning low-confidence, low-quality features with their high-confidence counterparts. Furthermore, to mitigate class imbalance issues in crack segmentation and road component extraction, we introduced a data imbalance loss to substitute the traditional cross-entropy loss used in pixel-level semantic segmentation. Additionally, we proposed an effective multi-stage fusion network architecture to enhance segmentation performance. Extensive experiments on real-world industrial crack segmentation and road segmentation tasks demonstrate the superior efficacy of our proposed framework. Notably, our method achieves satisfactory segmentation results even when utilizing merely 3.5% labeled data.

We introduce a sample of four emission-line galaxies at redshifts $z=6.11-6.35$, serendipitously identified using commissioning data from JWST/NIRCam's wide-field slitless spectroscopy (WFSS) mode. While one source at $z=6.11$ was previously reported, the remaining three are new discoveries. These objects are defined by secure detections of both [O III] $\lambda$5007 and H$\alpha$ lines, with fainter lines such as [O II] $\lambda$3727, [O III] $\lambda$4959, [N II] $\lambda$6583 tentatively detected in some cases. On the [O III]/H$\beta$ - [N II]/H$\alpha$ Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich diagram, these galaxies align with the parameter space of $z\sim2$ star-forming galaxies, indicating rapid enrichment to sub-solar metallicities ($\sim$0.6 $Z_{\odot}$), comparable to galaxies of similar stellar mass at lower redshifts. The presence of strong H$\alpha$ lines implies a higher ionizing photon production efficiency in early Universe galaxies. We observe a brightening of the [O III] $\lambda$5007 line luminosity function (LF) from $z=3$ to 6, whereas the H$\alpha$ LF shows little to no evolution from $z=2$ to 6. Both LFs are under-predicted by cosmological simulations by a factor of $\sim$10 at $z\sim6$, suggesting a global Ly$\alpha$ photon escape fraction of 5-7% at this redshift, significantly lower than prior estimates derived from comparing UV-based star-formation rate density and Ly$\alpha$ luminosity density. Our sample recovers $88^{+164}_{-57}$% of $z=6.0-6.6$ galaxies within the survey volume with stellar masses exceeding $5\times10^8$ $M_{\odot}$, highlighting the ubiquity of strong H$\alpha$ and [O III] line emitters during the Epoch of Reionization, a trend expected to be further revealed by JWST.

The study examines a direct ${\cal N}=1$ SQCD-like $\Phi$-theory featuring $SU(N_c)$ color symmetry and a flavor count $N_F$ satisfying $3N_c/2 < N_F < 2N_c$, comprising light quarks ${\overline Q},\,Q$. This framework also incorporates $N_F^2$ additional colorless, flavored fields $\Phi_{i}^{j}$ with a large mass parameter $\mu_{\Phi}\gg\Lambda_Q$, which interact with quarks via Yukawa coupling. Concurrently, its Seiberg-dual counterpart, the $d\Phi$-theory, is analyzed, possessing $(N_F-N_c)$ dual colors, $N_F$ flavors of dual quarks ${\overline q},\,{q}$, and $N_F^2$ elementary mion fields $M^i_j$ corresponding to $({\overline Q}_j Q^i)$. In the vacua under consideration, quarks in both theories reside in conformal regimes at scales $\mu<\Lambda_Q$, with mass spectra detailed in sections 4 and 5. The results demonstrate that these spectra differ between the direct and dual theories, contradicting Seiberg's hypothesis regarding their equivalence. Furthermore, within the direct theory, a novel qualitative phenomenon emerges: the ostensibly heavy $\Phi$ fields "return," giving rise to two additional generations of light $\Phi$-particles with pole masses $\mu^{\rm pole}_{2,3}(\Phi)\ll\Lambda_Q$. Finally, the conclusions compare the mass spectra of both theories under parameter values where the direct theory operates in a very strong coupling regime while the dual theory remains in a weak coupling, IR-free logarithmic regime. It is established that their mass spectra are parametrically distinct in this scenario.

Recent advances now allow for self-consistent, full-scale turbulent transport simulations of the scrape-off layer (SOL) and divertor in current tokamaks, enabling direct comparisons between turbulence models and experimental data. This study presents a series of diverted Ohmic L-mode discharges on the TCV tokamak, creating a unique dataset named TCV-X21 designed to validate edge turbulence models. The TCV-X21 dataset integrates measurements from five diagnostic systems, yielding 45 one- and two-dimensional observables across two toroidal magnetic field orientations. Using this dataset, we validate three flux-driven 3D fluid-turbulence codes: GBS, GRILLIX, and TOKAM3X. For each code, we simulated the TCV-X21 scenario, adjusting particle and power source rates to reasonably match the upstream separatrix density and electron temperature. Our findings indicate that simulations align well with experimental profiles at the outer midplane (OMP) regarding both shape and magnitude, though agreement diminishes near the divertor targets. The simulation-experiment match proves sensitive to resistivity, heat conductivities, power injection rates, and sheath boundary condition choices. Furthermore, despite targeting a sheath-limited regime, the discrepancies observed suggest that neutral dynamics must also be incorporated. Overall, these validation results demonstrate that turbulence models can successfully simulate existing devices with reasonable experimental agreement; where mismatches occur, they highlight areas for model improvement. By publicly releasing the TCV-X21 dataset, this work aims to accelerate and guide the development of predictive turbulence simulations for the edge and SOL.

We introduce the application of non-linear representation learning to voxelwise resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) data, utilizing a variational autoencoder (VAE) to achieve non-linear dimensionality reduction that preserves meaningful information. The efficacy of these representations is assessed through downstream tasks involving age regression and sex classification. Results are highly promising; notably, a linear regressor trained on our unsupervised model's representations achieves performance nearly equivalent to a supervised neural network specifically trained for age regression on the same dataset. Furthermore, the model's viability as a dimensionality reduction technique for neuropsychiatric data is tested via schizophrenia diagnosis prediction. These findings underscore the potential of pre-training on large cohorts of healthy individuals to enhance performance in downstream neuropsychiatric tasks. When fine-tuned on a schizophrenia dataset for varying numbers of epochs, the model performs optimally after just one epoch. Consequently, this work not only advances non-linear dimensionality reduction for voxelwise rs-fMRI but also demonstrates that pre-training deep learning models on such datasets significantly boosts performance even on smaller datasets. Future research can leverage the VAE's latent space to analyze the distribution of rs-fMRI time series in heterogeneous disorders like schizophrenia. This analysis can be augmented by the model's generative capabilities, which allow reconstruction of latent points back into brain space, thereby deepening our understanding of the relationships the VAE learns between subjects, timepoints, and individual characteristics.

In the current age of social media, networks have evolved into vital reservoirs of user-generated content online. These resources, rich with public sentiments, opinions, feedback, and reviews, hold immense value for major corporations, markets, political spheres, journalism, and numerous other domains. Politics stands as one of the most prominent and discussed subjects on these platforms today. Many politicians leverage micro-blogging services like Twitter due to their extensive follower bases and supportive communities. Political entities, including parties, organizations, and foundations, utilize social media to engage with citizens proactively. Currently, hundreds of thousands of political groups and leaders employ these networks, where individual politicians and parties often boast millions of followers. These platforms enable leaders to devise innovative strategies for mobilizing public participation in political processes. Moreover, social media aids politicians in diverse decision-making tasks by offering insights such as crafting policies and strategies informed by past data, identifying suitable candidates for specific constituencies, selecting appropriate personnel for party roles, and launching campaigns aligned with public sentiment regarding various issues and controversies. This research specifically examines the application of Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Semantic Analysis (SA) within the Twitter ecosystem to investigate the supporter networks of political leaders, as this approach can enhance decision-making by facilitating predictions regarding their political futures.

The nonlinear evolution of the coupled system involving drift waves (DW) and energetic-particle-induced geodesic acoustic modes (EGAM) is examined through fully nonlinear two-field equations, focusing on soliton-based turbulence spreading and nonlinear energy transfer between the two modes. Four distinct scenarios, varying in EGAM initial amplitudes and linear growth rates, are established to analyze how linear EGAM drive and finite amplitude influence the nonlinear dynamics of DW. When driven by linear energetic particles, soliton propagation intensifies due to the emergence of small radial scale structures. Two conservation laws for this nonlinear system are derived, one of which is energy conservation. Results indicate that DW energy consistently decreases while EGAM energy invariably increases, demonstrating that EGAM regulates DW.

The ALICE collaboration has recently presented high-statistics transverse momentum ($p_t$) spectra from proton-proton collisions at 5 TeV and 13 TeV, aiming to clarify the influence of jets in high-multiplicity events. This study employs a two-component model (TCM), comprising soft and hard components, to analyze ALICE $p_t$ spectra in p-p collisions. Similar to prior TCM investigations of A-B collision systems, this approach successfully disentangles jet and non-jet contributions to the $p_t$ spectra across the full acceptance range. By quantifying the statistical significance of discrepancies between data and the model, the study provides insights into selection biases and the validity of spectral models.
