To support future research, we employed EAZY to derive photometric redshifts (photo-zs) using forced-photometry catalogs for both fields. Our resulting photo-z catalog includes approximately 0.8 million sources across 4.9 deg² in W-CDF-S and a similar number spanning 3.4 deg² in ELAIS-S1. Of these, roughly 0.6 million sources in W-CDF-S and 0.4 million in ELAIS-S1 exhibit signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) exceeding 5 in more than five bands. By comparing our estimated photo-zs against existing spectroscopic redshifts, we have validated the overall reliability of our measurements. This catalog is publicly accessible at \doi{10.5281/zenodo.4603178}.

The Bianchi IX cosmological model (alongside Bianchi I and II) is examined within a generalized uncertainty principle framework, where universal anisotropies are characterized by a deformed Heisenberg algebra. Three primary findings emerge: (i) the Universe fails to isotropize due to deformed Kasner dynamics; (ii) the triangular allowed domain remains asymptotically stationary relative to the particle (Universe), and its bounces against walls proceed without interruption from deformed effects; (iii) no reflection law can be derived because the Bianchi II model loses its analytical integrability.

Metal structures are frequently safeguarded against corrosion through cathodic protection systems utilizing sacrificial anodes, which corrode more readily than the protected metal. Monitoring these anodes during their initial operational phase could provide valuable insights into the degradation of surrounding infrastructure and serve as an early warning system for maintaining critical assets. This paper introduces an Electro-Mechanical Impedance (EMI) technique to quantify zinc anode corrosion without manual intervention. The detection setup features a lead zirconate titanate (PZT) transducer bonded to a circular zinc disc, protected by waterproofing epoxy while submerged in a salt solution for accelerated corrosion testing via impressed current. We developed an analytical model to assess corrosion extent by tracking shifts in the resonance frequency of the disc's in-plane radial expansion mode, which also accurately accounts for the nonlinearity caused by partial delamination of the zinc oxide corrosion layer. The developed model demonstrates strong agreement with both Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and experimental data. Our findings confirm the effectiveness of this technique for monitoring the early-stage health of sacrificial anodes, suggesting its potential for widespread adoption in structural health monitoring applications within the Internet of Things.

Exotic states were theorized both prior to and following the development of QCD. Over recent decades, accelerator experiments have identified these states within the two-heavy-quark sector, specifically at or beyond the quarkonium strong decay threshold, designating them as X, Y, and Z states. These entities provide a singular avenue for exploring the dynamical characteristics of strongly correlated systems in QCD. I will demonstrate how combining nonrelativistic effective field theories with lattice methods enables the study of these states. Specifically, I will outline the prospects and difficulties inherent to lattice QCD in this context and identify the novel tools that require development.

A simple linear loop is defined as a basic while loop characterized by linear assignments and linear loop conditions. When such a loop involves exactly two program variables, we provide a complete algorithm to determine the set of all inputs causing non-termination. However, for loops with more than two variables, we demonstrate that the set of inputs leading to non-termination generally cannot be represented using Tarski formulae.

Quantum chaotic system ensembles are anticipated to display energy eigenvalues characterized by random-matrix-like level repulsion for pairs of energies separated by less than the inverse Thouless time. Recent studies have demonstrated that exact and approximate global symmetries leave distinct marks on these spectral statistics, either boosting the spectral form factor or diminishing level repulsion. This work extends those findings to scenarios involving spontaneous symmetry breaking, revealing the surprising result that such breaking further amplifies the spectral form factor. For both RMT-inspired toy models and systems describable via fluctuating hydrodynamics, we derive formulas quantifying this enhancement across various symmetry breaking patterns, including $Z_n$, $U(1)$, and partially or fully broken non-Abelian symmetries.

We suggest expanding the conventional flow analysis, typically restricted to the transverse $p_x$-$p_y$ plane, to introduce new flow coefficients derived from angular distributions within the $p_x$-$p_z$ and $p_y$-$p_z$ planes. These novel coefficients, designated as $u_n$ and $w_n$ alongside the established $v_n$, demonstrate significant sensitivity to the nuclear Equation-of-State (EoS), offering a more detailed exploration of the EoS than $v_n$ alone permits. To illustrate the impact of the EoS, we employ the Ultra-relativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics (UrQMD) model to analyze 20-30% central Au+Au collisions at an energy of $E_\mathrm{lab}=1.23~A$GeV.

A hybrid observer is proposed for estimating the state of a system defined by $\dot{x} = Ax$ and $y_i = C_ix$ for $i=1,...,m$. The state $x$ is concurrently estimated by $m$ agents, where each agent $i$ utilizes its local measurement $y_i$ and data exchanged with neighbors. These neighbor relationships are modeled by a time-varying directed graph $N(t)$. At discrete event times $t_{i1}, t_{i2}, \dots$, agent $i$ refines its estimate $x_i$ by combining a local continuous-time linear observer with a local parameter estimator that performs $q$ iterations within each interval $[t_{i(s-1)}, t_{is})$ to determine $x(t_{is})$. Under the conditions that $N(t)$ is strongly connected and the system is jointly observable, parameters can be tuned to ensure $x_i$ converges to $x$ at a predetermined rate. This convergence is maintained even with asynchronous communication, provided $N(t)$ evolves slowly. Furthermore, exponential convergence is guaranteed if the agents' event sequences differ slightly, though this requires the observed system to be exponentially stable; however, this constraint reflects a common robustness limitation shared by all open-loop state estimators subject to small modeling errors. Additionally, the proposed approach remains effective despite sudden changes in the number of vertices or edges within the inter-agent communication graph.

Dense areas within networks often signal significant and atypical data, yet current methodologies primarily address simple, undirected, and unweighted structures. Real-world complex networks, however, contain abundant information through asymmetrical edges and categorical or numerical node/edge attributes; consequently, identifying dense subgraphs that account for these features is a critical task with broad applications. Moreover, most existing algorithms overlook higher-order relationships, known as motifs, which are valuable for dense subgraph discovery but difficult to leverage effectively due to the vast diversity of motifs in heterogeneous networks. This study introduces a quark decomposition framework designed to pinpoint dense subgraphs enriched with a specific motif, focusing on networks featuring directed edges and categorical attributes on nodes and edges. For a designated motif, the framework constructs "quarks"—subgraphs of varying quality linked hierarchically. The approach is versatile, efficient, and extensible, with discussions on its limitations, practical implementations, and the role confusion issue inherent in directed networks. An extensive evaluation covers directed, signed-directed, and node-labeled networks across various motifs using real-world datasets. Results demonstrate that quark decomposition outperforms state-of-the-art methods and proves practical and scalable for networks containing up to 101 million edges.

While the non-Bloch band theory effectively describes energy bands in one-dimensional (1D) non-Hermitian systems, extending it to higher dimensions remains a challenging problem. This work establishes a non-Bloch band theory for two distinct classes of two-dimensional (2D) non-Hermitian systems by reducing them to equivalent 1D non-Hermitian models. Within these frameworks, we derive the generalized Brillouin zone for complex wave vectors and examine topological characteristics. Using the non-Hermitian Chern insulator as a case study, we demonstrate the bulk-edge correspondence, linking the Chern number calculated within the generalized Brillouin zone to the emergence of edge states.

This study presents a simplified model for iron corrosion, where ferric cations and electrons evolve within a fixed oxide layer under a self-consistent electrostatic potential. Boundary reactions are described using Butler-Volmer formulas, while electrostatic boundary conditions represent capacitors at material interfaces. Drawing from existing literature but incorporating minor adjustments to ensure thermodynamic consistency and adherence to the second law, we utilize a free energy estimate to prove the global-in-time existence of a solution without restricting physical parameters—a significant advancement over prior works. The proof employs Moser iterations to derive uniform estimates on chemical potentials. Finally, numerical examples illustrate the similarities and distinctions between our proposed model and previous studies.

In a simple connected graph $G$, a hole is defined as a chordless cycle $C_n$ with $n \in \Bbb N$ and $n \geq 4$. The girth of such a graph refers to the length of its smallest cycle, should one exist; notably, all minimal cycles are inherently chordless. Within this context, a cycle $C_3$ is designated as a primitive hole. This paper introduces the concept of the primitive hole number, representing the count of primitive holes within a graph, and calculates this value for various standard graphs. Furthermore, it derives the primitive hole number of the underlying graph of a Jaco graph, $J^*_{n+1}(1)$ (where $n \in \Bbb N, n \geq 4$), recursively based on the underlying Jaco graph $J_n(1)$ containing a prime Jaconian vertex $v_i$. Additionally, the study defines the primitive degree of vertices and determines these degrees for specific graphs.

Since Bitcoin's inception a decade ago, its rising prominence has made it a prime target for various adversaries. Among these, China stands out as a particularly formidable opponent, having adopted hostile stances toward cryptocurrency and demonstrated significant capacity to influence it. This paper examines how China endangers Bitcoin's security, stability, and viability through its dominance within the ecosystem, political and economic regulation of domestic activities, and control over national internet infrastructure. We analyze the China-Bitcoin relationship, outline China's motivations for undermining the currency, and provide a case study illustrating its substantial influence. Furthermore, we categorize the potential attack vectors China can employ to better assess the threat it poses. Our conclusion is that China possesses both the mature capabilities and strong incentives to execute a wide range of attacks against Bitcoin.

We introduce a new scenario where light dark fermions (sterile neutrinos with masses of a few eV) interact with a scalar field, similar to mass-varying neutrino dark energy models. Since these eV-scale sterile states naturally transition to non-relativistic states before Matter Radiation Equality (MRE), we demonstrate that the neutrino-scalar fluid experiences significant perturbative instability, leading to the formation of neutrino-nuggets and the disappearance of early dark energy behavior near MRE. The stability of these nuggets arises from a balance between Fermi pressure and the attractive scalar force; we numerically determine the mass and radius of these heavy, cold nuggets by solving for the static scalar field configuration. Our results indicate that when dark matter nugget density is sub-dominant and most early dark energy converts into scalar field dynamics, the model can potentially resolve the Hubble anomaly. Specifically, if a kinetic energy-dominated phase emerges after the phase transition, the dark energy density dilutes more rapidly than radiation, satisfying the conditions to address the $H_0$ tension. Unlike original early dark energy theories, our scenario controls dark energy density via the (eV) neutrino mass without requiring fine-tuned EDE scales. Through MCMC analysis and confrontation with Planck + SHOES and BAO data, we find evidence for non-zero neutrino-scalar EDE density during MRE. Our findings show that this model is consistent with the SHOES $H_0$ measurement of $74.03 \pm 1.42$ km/s/Mpc at approximately the 1.3$\sigma$ level.

The low-spin configuration of the semimagic 64Ni nucleus has been significantly refined by integrating data from four experiments, which identified multiple 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV and determined their properties. The Monte Carlo shell model successfully reproduces these findings, revealing an unexpectedly intricate landscape of coexisting shapes. Notably, a prolate 0+ excitation was found at a surprisingly high energy of 3463 keV, with a collective 2+ state situated 286 keV above it; this marks the first such observation in Ni isotopes. Furthermore, the shift in the excitation energy of the prolate minimum across the neutron N = 40 subshell gap underscores the influence of the monopole interaction and its strength variations with N.

This study establishes several operator inequalities linked to an extension of the $s$-convex function-based Kantorovich inequality. Furthermore, we present an application concerning the order-preserving power inequality for three variables and derive an improved lower bound for the numerical radius of a positive operator under specific conditions.

Gaussian Process (GP) emulators are extensively employed to approximate the behavior of complex computer models throughout the input space. Driven by the challenge of coupling computer models, recent theoretical advancements have been made regarding networks of interconnected GP emulators. This paper integrates these modern methodological developments with traditional state-space models to build a Bayesian decision support system. This framework establishes a coherent probabilistic model that generates predictions accompanied by uncertainty quantification via two first moments, facilitating the propagation of uncertainty across individual decision components.

We apply this methodology to develop a decision support tool for a UK county council evaluating low-carbon technologies to modernize its infrastructure and achieve net-zero carbon goals. Specifically, we illustrate how to integrate data from an energy model, a heating demand model, and time-series data on gas and electricity prices to quantitatively evaluate the effects of various policy decisions and energy market shifts on operational costs.

In the single-source sandpile model, $N$ sand grains are placed at a central vertex on the 2D integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. We investigate the stabilization of this setup for a stochastic sandpile defined by a parameter $M \in \mathbb{N}$. In this framework, any vertex holding $4M$ or more grains topples, distributing $k$ grains to each of its four neighbors, where $k$ is randomly selected from the set $\{1, \dots, M\}$ according to a distribution $\gamma$. This toppling process repeats, drawing a new $k$ at each step, until a stable state is reached where every vertex contains fewer than $4M$ grains. This approach represents a minor modification of the model proposed by Kim and Wang.

We examine the stabilization dynamics as $N$ grows large (with fixed $M$) across different probability distributions $\gamma$. Our analysis centers on two global metrics: the radius, defined as the maximum distance from the origin reached by sand grains, and the avalanche number, representing the total count of topplings. Simulations indicate that both metrics exhibit relatively straightforward asymptotic behaviors with respect to $\gamma$, $N$, and $M$ as $N \to \infty$. Furthermore, we present a more rigorous analysis for the specific case where $\gamma$ follows a binomial distribution with parameter $p$, particularly as $p$ approaches 1. In this regime, we identify a phase transition occurring at the scale $p \sim 1/N$.

This paper presents a theorem demonstrating an equivalence between the representational assembly conjecture proposed by the author and a rigidity question, specifically for Galois groups that are pro-l groups. In collaboration with R. Joshua, further work will validate this rigidity conjecture, ultimately proving the original conjecture for the case of a pro-l absolute Galois group.

This report, originally written in French, focuses on the special functions most frequently employed in physics. Representing a vast domain within mathematics, theoretical physics, and mathematical physics, these functions emerged in the nineteenth century as solutions to mathematical physics equations, specifically second- and fourth-order partial differential equations. Mastery of these functions is crucial for effectively addressing and comprehending contemporary physics challenges, and they are closely linked to the practice of scientific computing in both physics and mathematics. Widely integrated into computer algebra systems like Matlab, Mathematica, and Maple, special functions are indispensable for solving nearly all current physics problems; consequently, students are strongly urged to engage in this ongoing development. The manuscript is structured into six chapters covering the gamma and beta functions, Bessel functions, Fresnel error and integral functions, exponential, sine, cosine, and logarithmic integrals, orthogonal polynomials, and hypergeometric functions.

Current deep learning-based single image super-resolution (SISR) techniques predominantly train models using clean data, assuming noise-free low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) image pairs derived from bicubic down-sampling. However, this degradation process does not reflect real-world conditions. To address this, we introduce a deep cyclic network structure designed to ensure domain consistency between LR and HR distributions, drawing inspiration from the success of CycleGAN in image-to-image translation. We present the Super-Resolution Residual Cyclic Generative Adversarial Network (SRResCycGAN), which employs a GAN framework for end-to-end LR to HR domain translation. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our approach generalizes effectively to real-world image super-resolution and is readily deployable on mobile and embedded devices. Furthermore, results on the AIM 2020 Real Image SR Challenge datasets show that our method achieves performance comparable to other state-of-the-art approaches.

The conventional explanation for galaxy rotation relies on the tidal-torque theory (TTT), which posits that an ellipsoidal dark-matter protohalo acquires spin through gravitational torques exerted by its surrounding environment. We propose a complementary framework, the "spin from primordial inner motions" (SPIM) concept, which utilizes the velocity field rather than the tidal field, offering a more intuitive link to the distribution of distant matter. Although implicit in TTT derivations, SPIM highlights that angular momentum sourced by gravity within a protohalo's velocity field largely cancels internally, with net spin arising from excess contributions in the aspherical outer regions. Initially, net spin follows linear theory, resembling the conservation of comoving angular momentum, before being conserved in physical coordinates upon collapse. Subsequently, small haloes typically undergo secondary angular momentum exchanges. While TTT remains valuable for analytic approximations, a literal interpretation is often inaccurate without accounting for the smoothing of velocity and tidal fields, a nuance that is crucial for students to avoid misconceptions. Specifically, protohaloes are not perfectly ellipsoidal nor do they torque uniformly as a naive TTT reading suggests; their inner velocity fields retain significant dispersion. Furthermore, given specific initial conditions and boundaries, SPIM provides a more direct and accurate prediction of halo spins than TTT. We also examine the application of SPIM to rotating filaments and the relationship between halo mass and spin, conceptualizing the total spin of a halo as a sum of random contributions.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) offers the promise of revolutionizing engineering site characterization by generating high-resolution 2D and 3D maps of subsurface stiffness through non-invasive imaging. However, the precision of FWI is heavily dependent on the initial model chosen, given the inherent complexity and non-uniqueness of the inverse problem. To address this, we introduce a novel method applying convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to convert experimental seismic wavefields from linear surface sensor arrays directly into robust starting models for 2D FWI. We outline three essential steps in developing the CNN: selecting the network architecture, curating an appropriate training dataset, and executing the training process. The trained CNN's capability to generate effective starting models for 2D FWI was evaluated against standard methods using a classic near-surface scenario involving an undulating two-layer soil-bedrock interface. The study's CNN successfully predicted complex 2D subsurface images directly from seismic wavefields for the test set, achieving an average mean absolute percent error of 6%. Compared to conventional approaches, the CNN-derived starting models resulted in reduced seismic image and waveform misfits, both prior to and following FWI. Furthermore, the CNN's ability to generalize to subsurface structures different from its training data was tested using a more intricate three-layered model. Although predictive performance decreased slightly in this case, the CNN still achieved misfit levels comparable to other common starting models. This research highlights the significant potential of CNNs as a tool for creating high-quality starting models for FWI.

Approximately ten years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya defined $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where each player's payoff function exhibits $\lambda$-Lipschitz continuity relative to other players' actions. They demonstrated that these games possess $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific conditions for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$, but they did not address the computational difficulty of locating such equilibria. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a query-efficient reduction from broader game classes to Lipschitz games. Utilizing this reduction, we establish an exponential query lower bound for any randomized algorithm seeking $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player, binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, where the exponent scales with $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we propose "Multi-Lipschitz games," a generalization allowing player-specific Lipschitz constants, and demonstrate a reduction to standard Lipschitz games, revealing that the critical parameter is the sum of individual Lipschitz values. Finally, we derive an exponential lower bound on the deterministic query complexity required to find $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player, $m$-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games for sufficiently large $\epsilon$, thereby highlighting the necessity of randomized approaches for the aforementioned results. Our proof methodology is notably more straightforward than prior techniques used to achieve similar findings.

This study presents a concise empirical evaluation of iterative term set expansion techniques rooted in centrality and classification within distributional semantic models. In this interactive framework, distributional semantics guides a system to propose candidate terms for labeling after a user identifies terms belonging to a specific set, with the goal of maximizing the discovery of positive examples. Although centrality-based approaches have a well-established history in this domain, this paper contrasts them with classification methods utilizing the Simple Margin technique, an Active Learning strategy employing Support Vector Machines. By assessing the efficacy of diverse centrality and classification methods across multiple distributional models and five distinct term sets, the findings demonstrate that Active Learning-based approaches consistently surpass centrality-based ones.

The looping pendulum is a straightforward physical system comprising two masses linked by a string that runs over a rod. By applying Newtonian mechanics, we derive the equations of motion for this system and demonstrate that numerical solutions effectively describe its dynamics. These numerical results capture the complex behaviors of the looping pendulum and align well with experimental observations.

Taylor-Couette flow frequently serves as a simplified representation of intricate rotating systems found within stars and accretion disks. The dynamics of these systems are significantly affected by magnetic fields. For instance, in conducting fluids, quasi-Keplerian flows within a Taylor-Couette setup become unstable to traveling or standing waves under an external magnetic field, even when the flow remains hydrodynamically stable. This magnetorotational instability precipitates chaotic states and, given sufficiently rapid cylinder rotation, culminates in turbulence. The path to turbulence in this flow can be intricate, featuring coexisting parameter regimes characterized by spatio-temporal chaos and quasi-periodic behavior involving one or two extra modulating frequencies. While unstable modes in periodic flows can be identified through Floquet analysis, this study employs a more adaptable, equation-free, data-driven methodology. We examine data from the transition to chaos in magnetized Taylor-Couette flow, utilizing Dynamic Mode Decomposition to isolate flow structures associated with modulating frequencies; this technique relies on approximating nonlinear dynamics via a linear, infinite-dimensional Koopman operator. Leveraging these identified structures enables the construction of a nonlinear reduced model for the transition.

This study quantitatively examines the dependence of solutions to a fractional differential equation of order $\alpha \in (0,1]$ involving Caputo derivatives on their initial conditions. Focusing on two solutions, $x_1$ and $x_2$, defined over a shared interval $[0,T]$ for the same equation, we derive upper and lower bounds for the difference $x_1(t) - x_2(t)$ across $t \in [0,T]$ that surpass the accuracy of existing literature bounds.

This study provides a theoretical investigation into the Bose-Hubbard realization of the renowned Su-Schrieffer-Heeger topological model, representing a one-dimensional chain of coupled oscillators with dimerization and on-site interactions. We analyze the physical phenomena across the entire spectrum of dimerization strengths, from weak to strong limits. By concentrating on the two-excitation subspace, we systematically identify and characterize the various states resulting from the interplay between oscillator couplings, lattice topology, and interaction intensity. Specifically, we examine the emergence of scattering bands composed of extended states, bound bands containing two-particle pairs (notably "doublons" localized at the same site), and distinct varieties of topological edge states. These findings offer potential realizations in diverse systems, such as photonic cavities and optical lattices, thereby advancing the field of topological many-body physics.

For the first time, the temperature dependence of ultrasound wave absorption in bulk $p$-Cd$_{0.2}$Hg$_{0.8}$Te crystals, free of low-angle grain boundaries, was experimentally investigated within a frequency range of 10--55 MHz and a temperature interval of 150--300 K, with measurement results provided. As the ultrasound frequency increases, the peak absorption coefficient was observed to rise and shift to higher temperatures. These findings are well explained by the Brailsford model, which links ultrasound absorption to the vibrations of thermally activated dislocation kinks. Key parameters for this model in $p$-Cd$_{0.2}$Hg$_{0.8}$Te were calculated, yielding a frequency coefficient $f_{k}\approx $~6\,$\times $\,10$^{\,9}$\,Hz and a kink diffusion activation energy $W_{k}\approx $~0.11\,eV. Additionally, the dislocation concentration was estimated at $\alpha \approx $~2\,$\times$\,10$^{10}$\,m$^{-2}$, a value that aligns with results from the selective etching method (0.7\,$\times $\,10$^{10}$\,m$^{-2}$).

Let $K$ denote a global function field with a fixed place $\infty$. Consider a finite abelian extension $L/K$ where $\infty$ splits completely, known as a real abelian extension. We define a group of elliptic units $C_L$ within $\mathcal{O}_L^\times$ in a manner analogous to Sinnott's cyclotomic units and calculate the index $[\mathcal{O}_L^\times:C_L]$. Furthermore, assuming $L$ is a cyclic extension of prime power degree, we employ techniques developed by Greither and Ku\v{c}era to extract specific roots of these elliptic units, thereby establishing a result concerning the annihilation of the $p$-component of the class group of $L$.

Mutual information serves as a crucial metric for assessing both classical and quantum correlations within quantum information theory and quantum many-body physics, particularly because it adheres to an area law for thermal states and bounds all correlation functions. Despite its significance, exact or approximate calculation often presents practical difficulties. This work explores alternative formulations grounded in Rényi divergences. A primary benefit of these Rényi-based measures over the von Neumann version is that they can be formulated as variational problems, allowing for efficient evaluation of their cost functions across state families such as matrix product operators without sacrificing the essential properties of a correlation measure. Specifically, we demonstrate that these measures satisfy a thermal area law with broad applicability and serve as upper bounds for all correlation functions. Furthermore, we examine their performance on specific tensor network states and classical thermal distributions.

Federated Learning (FL) enables the training of machine learning models on user devices without compromising personal data privacy, as only model updates (such as gradients) are transmitted to a central server for aggregation. Despite this privacy-preserving approach, recent inference attacks that extract sensitive information from gradients have highlighted the urgent need for robust protection mechanisms to facilitate widespread FL adoption. Although server-side defenses exist, client-side protection remains largely unaddressed. In this domain, Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) are a leading solution; however, current frameworks like DarkneTZ necessitate statically embedding a significant portion of the model within the TEE to counter complex or combined attacks. We introduce GradSec, a novel approach that secures only the sensitive layers of a machine learning model within the TEE, either statically or dynamically. This method reduces the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) size and decreases overall training time by up to 30% and 56%, respectively, compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

Accurate segmentation of head and neck (H&N) tumors and the forecasting of patient outcomes are vital for diagnosis and monitoring treatment progress. However, the advancement of robust deep learning models is currently impeded by the scarcity of large-scale, multi-center, multi-modal datasets with high-quality annotations. The MICCAI 2021 HECKTOR challenge was established to facilitate the comparison of segmentation techniques for primary gross target volumes on FDG-PET and CT scans, as well as the prediction of progression-free survival in H&N oropharyngeal cancer. Regarding segmentation, we introduced a novel encoder-decoder network featuring full inter- and intra-skip connections to leverage both low-level and high-level semantic information across all scales. Furthermore, Conditional Random Fields were employed as a post-processing mechanism to refine the resulting segmentation maps. By training multiple neural networks for tumor volume segmentation and ensembling their outputs, we achieved an average Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.75 during cross-validation and 0.76 on the challenge test set. For the progression-free survival prediction task, we developed a Cox proportional hazards regression model that integrates clinical, radiomic, and deep learning features. This survival prediction model attained a concordance index of 0.82 in cross-validation and 0.62 on the challenge testing data.

This article introduces an algorithm designed to efficiently compute the exchange matrix in periodic systems employing Gaussian basis sets and pseudopotentials. While standard algorithms for this task exhibit cubic scaling relative to system size due to the requirement of performing O(N²) fast Fourier transforms (FFTs), our proposed method maintains cubic scaling while drastically reducing the prefactor. This improvement is achieved by removing the need for FFTs during the exchange matrix construction, instead representing products of Gaussian basis functions as a linear combination of auxiliary basis functions, where the number of these functions scales linearly with system size. By storing the potentials generated by these auxiliary functions in memory, the exchange matrix can be calculated without invoking FFTs, though this approach necessitates increased memory usage. Although the concept of utilizing auxiliary functions is established, our algorithm is more cost-effective because it integrates three specific components: (a) a robust Pseudospectral method that achieves high accuracy with a relatively small set of auxiliary basis functions; (b) occ-RI exchange, which avoids constructing the full exchange matrix; and (c) the (interpolative separable density fitting) ISDF algorithm to build the auxiliary basis required for the Pseudospectral method. The resulting algorithm is accurate, with the error in the final energy decreasing exponentially as the number of auxiliary functions increases.

We introduce World of Bugs (WOB), an open platform designed to facilitate research in Automated Bug Detection (ABD) for video games. By addressing existing challenges in ABD and linking them to the platform's architecture, we argue that advancing the field necessitates learning-based approaches. A central component of WOB is its expanding repository of typical video game bugs, which serves as a resource for both training and assessing ABD methodologies.

Collisional plasma shocks arising from supersonic flows play a critical role in various laboratory high-energy-density plasmas and astrophysical environments. Unlike shocks composed of a single ion species, those containing multiple ion species exhibit added complexity, such as interspecies ion separation caused by gradients in electric potential, pressure, temperature, and concentration. This study provides time-resolved measurements of density and temperature for two ion species within collisional plasma shocks generated by the head-on merging of supersonic plasma jets, enabling the calculation of their diffusion velocities. The findings reveal that lighter ions diffuse more rapidly than heavier ones within the shock front, aligning with inter-ion-species transport theory. Furthermore, the experimental results achieve near-quantitative agreement with both theoretical predictions and 1D ion-Fokker-Planck kinetic simulations.

Winter pruning of grapevines is a sophisticated operation demanding skilled laborers to perform accurately. This inherent complexity renders the process time-intensive, typically requiring 80 to 120 hours per hectare; consequently, automation is particularly vital for large-scale vineyards to accelerate the workflow. This paper introduces a new multidisciplinary solution to address this challenge by segmenting grapevine imagery to construct a representative plant model. Subsequently, a series of candidate pruning locations are identified based on this model. The study details: (a) procedures for data collection and annotation, (b) the fine-tuning of a neural network for grapevine segmentation, (c) an image processing technique to generate a vine representation from the segmented data, and (d) the detection and localization of potential pruning points derived from the simplified plant structure. Using this methodology, we can identify a substantial number of candidate pruning sites on the canes, which can then be filtered to determine the final set of actual pruning points.

Estimating ranks from data introduces uncertainty, presenting significant challenges across various applications. Since estimated ranks are deterministic functions of estimated parameters, their uncertainty must stem from the uncertainty in those parameter estimates. This paper provides a comprehensive characterization of this relationship using the linear extensions of a partial order derived from interval estimates of the relevant parameters. Leveraging this framework, we develop a set estimator for the overall ranking, utilize its cardinality to quantify ranking uncertainty, and propose efficient algorithms for several key inquiries. We demonstrate that our set estimator constitutes a valid confidence set and elucidate its connection to a recently proposed joint confidence set for ranks by Klein, Wright, and Wieczorek. Finally, we apply these methods to both simulated and real-world datasets and release the implementation via the R package rankUncertainty.

The rapid expansion of pretrained generative models has rendered it impossible for users to keep track of all available options. To solve this, we propose a content-based model search task: identifying models that best align with a specific query from a vast collection. Since each generative model outputs an image distribution, we frame the search as an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the likelihood of generating a match for the query. We create approximations to ensure the problem remains solvable across diverse inputs, including images, sketches, text descriptions, other models, or combinations thereof. Our method is evaluated on both accuracy and speed using a comprehensive set of generative models. Results show that our approach effectively retrieves suitable models for applications such as image editing and reconstruction, few-shot transfer learning, and latent space interpolation. Finally, we have integrated our search algorithm into our online generative model-sharing platform at https://modelverse.cs.cmu.edu.

This paper investigates a unified framework for Quantum Markov Chains. We explore a novel quantum Markov property that extends the classical definition, introducing Markov states and chains defined on general local algebras with a specific generic algebraic property, encompassing both Boson and Fermi algebras. The central contribution is a reconstruction theorem for quantum Markov chains within these local algebras; this theorem enables the replication of all known examples of quantum Markov chains and their associated states.

We present a hybrid software-hardware platform designed to facilitate research on bridging the sim-to-real gap in robotics and autonomous vehicle engineering. The software, which is operating-system agnostic, comprises three core modules: the Chrono simulation engine for high-fidelity vehicle and sensor modeling, an autonomy stack for algorithm development and testing, and a development environment enabling visualization and hardware-in-the-loop experiments. Complementing this is a 1/6th scale vehicle equipped with reconfigurable mounts for computing, sensing, and tracking. Because this physical vehicle has a corresponding digital twin in the simulation, researchers can evaluate perception, state estimation, control algorithms, and their underlying processors in both virtual and real-world settings. We provide a demonstration illustrating the platform's application in autonomy research. Future efforts will focus on expanding ART/ATK capabilities to support a full-sized Chevy Bolt EUV, which is expected to be made available to the group soon.

Cauchy reals are typically constructed as a quotient of Cauchy sequences of rationals. However, defining the limit of a Cauchy sequence of Cauchy reals by lifting it to a sequence of rational Cauchy sequences requires the axiom of countable choice or the law of excluded middle, both of which are unavailable in homotopy type theory. To overcome this limitation, the Univalent Foundations Program employs a higher inductive-inductive type to define Cauchy reals as the free Cauchy complete metric space generated by the rationals. This approach is generalized to construct the free Cauchy complete metric space for any arbitrary metric space, resulting in a monad within the category of metric spaces and Lipschitz functions; when instantiated with the rationals, it yields the Cauchy reals. Furthermore, leveraging the partiality monad described by Altenkirch and Danielson (2016), a semi-decision procedure for comparing real numbers with rational numbers is established. The complete construction has been formalized in the Coq proof assistant and can be accessed at https://github.com/SkySkimmer/HoTTClasses/tree/CPP2017.

KM3NeT is an ongoing research infrastructure situated beneath the Mediterranean Sea. It comprises two extensive neutrino Cherenkov telescopes: ARCA, positioned 3,500 meters deep off Sicily, and ORCA, located 2,500 meters below sea level off the southern French coast. Both detectors utilize identical detection principles, technologies, and data acquisition systems, differing only in the geometric layout of their optical sensors. This uniformity enables coverage of a broad neutrino energy spectrum and supports a comprehensive scientific agenda, including the investigation of neutrino properties (particularly mass ordering), the identification and analysis of high-energy astrophysical neutrino sources, indirect dark matter searches, and the detection of core-collapse supernovae.

We investigate positive singular solutions, characterized by non-removable singularities, within a system of PDEs governed by $p$-Laplacian operators and featuring an additional nonlinear first-order term. Through the precise application of a recently developed variant of the moving plane method, we establish the symmetry of these solutions. This finding constitutes a novel result even in the scalar context.

Debugging is widely regarded as one of the most challenging and time-intensive activities within the software development lifecycle. Consequently, researchers have dedicated substantial resources to creating automated tools and methods designed to help developers perform these tasks more effectively. Despite notable advancements that have proven the usefulness, efficacy, and efficiency of these approaches, they have yet to achieve widespread adoption in industry settings. This paper examines the commercialization attempts of a specific automated debugging technique, outlines potential reasons for the scarcity of successful implementations, and proposes strategies for future progress.

The magnetization dynamics of an $S=1$ antiferromagnetic chain featuring single-ion anisotropy $D$ and biquadratic interactions are examined through numerical diagonalization. Results indicate that both interaction types stabilize the 2-magnon Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid (TLL) phase throughout the magnetization process. Utilizing various excitation gaps derived from the diagonalization calculations, specific phase diagrams for this process are constructed. These diagrams demonstrate that a spin-nematic-dominated TLL phase emerges at elevated magnetization levels when $D$ is sufficiently negative.

Cervical cancer represents one of the most prevalent and fatal diseases affecting women globally. Although it is entirely curable when detected early, the arduous and expensive nature of current detection methods hinders population-wide screening. To support clinicians, this paper introduces a fully automated framework employing Deep Learning and evolutionary optimization-based feature selection for classifying cytology images. The system extracts deep features from multiple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures and applies a two-stage feature reduction strategy to lower computational costs and accelerate convergence. Features derived from these CNN models create a high-dimensional space, which is compressed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) while retaining 99% of the variance. From this reduced space, the Grey Wolf Optimizer, an evolutionary algorithm, selects an optimal, non-redundant feature subset to enhance classification performance. These selected features then train a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier to produce final predictions. The framework was tested on three public benchmark datasets: the Mendeley Liquid Based Cytology (4-class), Herlev Pap Smear (7-class), and SIPaKMeD Pap Smear (5-class) datasets, achieving accuracies of 99.47%, 98.32%, and 97.87%, respectively, which validates the method's reliability. The source code for this approach is available at: https://github.com/DVLP-CMATERJU/Two-Step-Feature-Enhancement.

Dynamical two-particle susceptibilities play a crucial role in numerous condensed-matter experiments and related fields. However, standard textbooks often omit the derivation of these response functions, likely due to their perceived complexity. While existing literature typically relies on generalized susceptibilities—which are broader but demand even greater sophistication—this study offers a more straightforward derivation using model Hamiltonians that map directly onto impurity models. Additionally, we provide an alternative derivation for the irreducible vertex specifically within the framework of the Falicov-Kimball model.

Understanding how episodic memories are encoded in the brain is crucial for studying neural networks featuring recurrent asymmetric couplings. This study incorporates the experimental finding of a wide synaptic integration window into our model of continuous-time sequence retrieval. We theoretically analyze the model with non-normal neuron interactions by deriving a random matrix theory for the Jacobian matrix governing neural dynamics. The resulting spectra exhibit unique characteristics, including the breaking of rotational symmetry around the origin and the formation of nested voids within the spectral boundary, leading to a highly non-uniform distribution of spectral density in the complex plane. Furthermore, this random matrix theory predicts a transition to chaos, where the edge of chaos offers specific computational advantages for sequential memory retrieval. Our systematic investigation of time-lagged correlations across arbitrary delays aims to inspire future research on diverse memory models and the large-scale analysis of biological time series.

This paper outlines key advancements and future concepts concerning the measurement of astrophysically relevant $(n,\gamma)$ data at CERN's n_TOF facility. It examines a Monte Carlo-assisted analytical approach for employing low-efficiency radiation detectors in time-of-flight neutron-capture experiments, focusing specifically on systematic accuracy. Additionally, recent instrumental innovations are highlighted, including total-energy detectors equipped with $\gamma$-ray imaging for background reduction, and an array of compact organic scintillators designed to leverage the high instantaneous neutron flux available at EAR2. The discussion concludes with astrophysical implications regarding the intermediate $i$ neutron-capture nucleosynthesis process within the framework of the newly established NEAR activation area.

We present a coherent formulation of electromagnetism within the non-relativistic quantum-mechanical framework for interacting charged many-body systems. Employing the mathematical structure and quantization procedures of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), we aim to address widespread misinterpretations, particularly concerning magnetic fields and gauge invariance. These misconceptions stem from the historical evolution of quantum mechanics, which began with the Schrödinger equation for a single particle in fixed electromagnetic fields and progressed to many-body theories involving identical charged particles with only Coulomb interactions. Our approach to non-relativistic QED highlights the significance of gauge invariance and external fields. Furthermore, we extend this theory using a $1/c^2$ approximation to provide a closed description of interacting charged particles without explicit photons. The resulting Hamiltonian matches the quantized Darwin Hamiltonian, which includes both Coulomb and current-current diamagnetic interactions. We illustrate the importance of this extension to many-body theory through several examples.

This report details the first observation of a $B^0$ meson decaying into a purely baryonic final state, specifically $B^0 \to p \bar{p}$. The analysis utilized proton-proton collision data from the LHCb experiment, gathered at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, with a total integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. The measured branching fraction is ${\cal B}(B^0 \to p \bar{p}) = (1.25 \pm 0.27 \pm 0.18 ) \times 10^{-8}$, where the first uncertainty represents the statistical component and the second represents the systematic uncertainty. To date, this represents the rarest observed decay mode for the $B^0$ meson. Additionally, the study examined the $B_s^0 \to p \bar{p}$ decay channel; no signal was detected, leading to an upper limit on its branching fraction of ${\cal B}(B_s^0 \to p \bar{p}) < 1.5 \times 10^{-8}$ at the 90% confidence level.

ImageNet remains the standard benchmark for assessing computer-vision model performance. Currently, the prevailing approach involves training each architecture using a custom, expert-designed and fine-tuned protocol. This paper introduces USI (Unified Scheme for ImageNet), a generalized training framework applicable to any backbone on ImageNet. Built upon knowledge distillation and contemporary techniques, USI eliminates the need for model-specific adjustments or hyperparameter tuning while maintaining training efficiency. We evaluated USI across diverse architectures, including CNNs, Transformers, mobile-oriented networks, and MLP-only models, where it consistently surpassed previous state-of-the-art results. Consequently, USI transforms ImageNet training from an expert-dependent task into an automatic, seamless process. Furthermore, because USI trains any backbone to top-tier performance, it facilitates systematic comparisons and the identification of the most efficient backbones along the speed-accuracy Pareto frontier. The implementation is accessible at: https://github.com/Alibaba-MIIL/Solving_ImageNet

Social scientists and psychologists are keen on analyzing how individuals convey emotions and sentiments during catastrophic occurrences like natural disasters, political instability, and terrorism. The COVID-19 pandemic, a major crisis, has triggered various psychological challenges, including depression, stemming from sudden societal shifts and job losses. Deep learning-based language models have shown great potential for sentiment analysis using social media data, such as that from Twitter. During the pandemic, different nations experienced varying infection peaks; these fluctuations influenced lockdown policies, which in turn impacted the economy and employment. As new COVID-19 cases surged and lockdowns tightened, people increasingly voiced their sentiments on social media, offering valuable insights into human psychology during such crises. This paper introduces a framework utilizing deep learning language models, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks and a global vector embedding, alongside the state-of-the-art BERT model, to analyze sentiment during the initial rise of novel COVID-19 cases in India. We examine sentiments expressed during specific months in 2020, covering the first major peak in the country. Our approach employs multi-label sentiment classification, allowing for the identification of multiple simultaneous sentiments. Our findings reveal that the majority of tweets were positive and optimistic during the surge in cases, though the volume of tweets dropped significantly as the peak approached. Overall, while most individuals remained optimistic, a notable segment of the population expressed frustration with how authorities managed the pandemic.

Currently, 2D barcodes are extensively utilized for advertising, mobile payments, and verifying product authenticity. Nevertheless, in the realm of product authentication, legitimate 2D barcodes can be illicitly duplicated and affixed to counterfeit items to circumvent verification protocols. This study leverages a unique 2D barcode pattern alongside multimedia forensics techniques to examine scanning and printing artifacts generated by copy (rebroadcasting) attacks. We introduce a varied and complementary feature set designed to measure the texture distortions caused by illegal duplication. These proposed features consist of global and local descriptors that respectively characterize multi-scale texture appearance and the distribution of interest points. The efficacy of these descriptors is evaluated against existing texture descriptors and deep learning methods across various scenarios, including cross-dataset and cross-size comparisons. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the method's practical applicability in real-world environments.

Utilizing the London equation with a rotor-free vector potential ${\bf A}$ alongside SQUID current measurements, we have determined the Pearl length $\Lambda$ and coherence length $\xi$ for ultra-thin, ring-shaped MoSi films as functions of thickness $d$ and temperature $T$. Our results indicate that $\xi$ depends on $d$, exhibiting a discontinuity where $\xi \sim d \sim 5$nm. At base temperature, the superconducting stiffness, defined by $1/\lambda^2=1/(\Lambda d)$, increases with $T_c$. This trend mirrors the Uemura plot observed in bulk layered superconductors, though there doping serves as the implicit variable. Additionally, we present the critical exponents for $\Lambda (T)$.

The system of rhenium nitride pernitride (ReN$_2$) has garnered significant interest due to the unusual crystal structure of its high-pressure phase and its exceptional hardness and bulk modulus. This study examines the thermodynamic and electronic characteristics of the P2$_1$/c phase, contrasting them with the C2/m and P4/mbm polytypes proposed in existing literature. Zero-temperature formation enthalpy calculations indicate that the P2$_1$/c phase is the most stable up to 170 GPa, after which the P4/mbm phase becomes stabilized; this theoretical finding was validated by diamond anvil cell synthesis of P4/mbm ReN$_2$ at approximately 175 GPa. Furthermore, applying the quasi-harmonic approximation to account for finite temperature effects at 100 GPa reveals that the P2$_1$/c phase maintains the lowest free energy of formation up to at least 1000 K. Finally, an analysis of the pressure-induced evolution of the electronic structure identifies two topological transitions near 18 GPa. These transitions involve a change in Fermi surface topology, characterized by the emergence of a new electron pocket at the high-symmetry Y$_2$ point and the simultaneous disruption of a neck slightly offset from the $\Gamma$-A line.

Neutron stars within astrophysical binary systems offer promising prospects for multi-messenger astrophysics. While often overlooked, the neutron star ocean—a fluid layer enveloping the star—can generate electromagnetic transients associated with compact binaries. This study establishes a foundation for analyzing tidal waves in these oceans and their implications. We examine how tidal forces during compact binary inspirals and parabolic encounters excite oscillation modes in the neutron star ocean, thereby creating tidal waves. Our findings indicate that these oceans can support tidal waves with frequencies below 100 mHz. We propose that resonant tidal waves in neutron star oceans represent a previously unexplored source of precursor electromagnetic emission before neutron star-black hole and binary neutron star mergers. With energy budgets potentially reaching $10^{45}$ erg, these resonant waves could act as early warning signals (approximately 1–10 years prior to merger) if accompanied by electromagnetic flares. Furthermore, excited ocean tidal waves coincide with parabolic encounters. Depending on the specific ocean model and flare emission scenario, such flares might be observable by Fermi and NuSTAR out to roughly 100 Mpc, with detection rates estimated at $\sim 7$ yr$^{-1}$ for binary neutron stars and $\sim 0.6$ yr$^{-1}$ for neutron star-black hole binaries. Detecting emission from these tidal waves alongside gravitational waves would yield insights into the equation of state at the neutron star surface, the composition of oceans and crusts, and neutron star geophysics.

The question of what constitutes the basic layer of reality is central to philosophy. The conventional view posits that fundamental reality comprises entities like particles, fields, or quantum states, with non-fundamental facts deriving at least partially from these material constituents. This paper proposes an alternative framework termed the "cosmic void," which asserts that the universe lacks any fundamental material ontology. Instead, phenomena such as tables and chairs are derived from a unique class of laws that adhere to strong determinism, ensuring that all non-fundamental facts are fully accounted for by nomic (law-like) facts. The discussion includes a specific application of this framework within a strongly deterministic variant of the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, alongside an examination of philosophical and scientific objections to this perspective, as well as its relationship to ontological nihilism.

Every Thurston map $f\colon S^2\rightarrow S^2$ defined on a 2-sphere $S^2$ generates a pull-back mechanism acting on Jordan curves $\alpha$ contained within $S^2\setminus P_f$, where $P_f$ denotes the map's postcritical set. Crucially, the isotopy class $[f^{-1}(\alpha)]$ (relative to $P_f$) is determined solely by the isotopy class $[\alpha]$. This study focuses on such maps possessing four postcritical points, identifying Thurston obstructions as fixed points of the pull-back operation. We demonstrate that for a map $f$ with a hyperbolic orbifold and four postcritical points, the existence of a Thurston obstruction permits the "blowing up" of specific arcs in the underlying sphere to construct a new map $\widehat f$. This process eliminates the original obstruction, and since no new obstructions emerge, $\widehat f$ is realized by a rational map. Consequently, this method enables the combinatorial generation of a broad class of rational Thurston maps with four postcritical points. Furthermore, we analyze the dynamics of the pull-back operation during iteration, providing a positive resolution to the global curve attractor problem for a specific subclass of these rational maps.

Capsule Networks aim to create a biologically-inspired, explainable neural architecture, with a primary innovation being a routing mechanism that constructs a parse tree to explicitly define relationships between capsules. Despite this, the model's potential for explainability remains unrealized because these relationships are highly heterogeneous and complex to interpret. This paper introduces REM, a technique designed to enhance explainability by minimizing the entropy of the parse tree structure. By employing a pruning mechanism as a proxy to steer model parameters toward low-entropy configurations, we successfully generate static parse trees without sacrificing performance. These results demonstrate that REM enables Capsule Networks to establish more robust relationships between capsules.

This paper presents a probabilistic framework for learning nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), a technique widely utilized for imputing missing data and uncovering latent patterns, where matrix factors serve as latent variables tied to specific data dimensions. To enforce nonnegativity on these factors, we select priors defined over the nonnegative subspace and utilize a Gibbs sampling-based Bayesian inference approach. The model's performance is assessed across multiple real-world datasets, such as MovieLens 100K and MovieLens 1M, demonstrating that our proposed Bayesian NMR GRRN model outperforms existing Bayesian NMF methods by yielding superior predictions and mitigating overfitting.

This study investigates the Fermi surface, defined as the boundary of gapless quasiparticle excitations in momentum space, within a mean-field framework for doped Mott insulators where quasiparticles arise as collective modes. The low-doping pseudogap phase is defined by a two-component resonating-valence-bond (RVB) order that disappears upon overdoping ($\delta > \delta^*$). While a Fermi arc structure naturally exists in the pseudogap state absent superconducting phase coherence, a complete Fermi surface is restored only in the overdoped regime where RVB vanishes. However, we demonstrate that the Luttinger volume enclosed by the gapless quasiparticle contour remains satisfied in both scenarios. The "Fermi arc" observed at $\delta < \delta^*$ is actually attributed to a substantial reduction in spectral weight due to quasiparticle fractionalization into more elementary particles in the antinodal region. Specifically, hot spots manifest as enhanced density of states at the arc endpoints, potentially generating charge-density-wave-like quasiparticle interference patterns. Furthermore, we identify that small Fermi pockets violating the Luttinger volume can emerge if secondary doping-induced RVB order is suppressed independently, such as by strong perpendicular magnetic fields. At the critical doping $\delta^*$ where the primary RVB order vanishes, fractionalized spin excitations lose coherence, indicated by a divergent specific heat. For $\delta > \delta^*$, quasiparticle coherence is maintained uniformly across the entire (large) Fermi surface, despite fractionalization persisting at higher energies or temperatures. Finally, we briefly discuss various mechanisms for the Fermi arc and compare them with experimental data.

Software patching is a standard approach for eliminating vulnerabilities in software components to enhance IT security. However, patching is often unfeasible for critical applications, particularly when vendors guarantee correct operation only within specific configurations. This paper proposes a solution to this challenge by running unpatched and patched application instances concurrently. In this setup, the unpatched instance retains full control, while the patched instance's output serves solely as a comparison mechanism to detect discrepancies caused by potential bugs. To validate this concept, we developed a system for parallel web application execution and evaluated it across three web applications. Experimental results indicate that the approach is technically promising for web applications. Additionally, the paper examines potential limitations of both the system and the underlying idea, including the duration required to probabilistically confirm that a patched version introduces no new errors. It also explores other use cases involving concurrent application instances and discusses the system's applicability to different application types, such as SCADA systems.

This research investigates the formation of a giant component within a spatial network characterized by scale-invariant metric distances between nodes and long-range power-law interactions. Nodes are arranged in metric space via a Lévy flight process, utilizing a scale-invariant step probability density function, followed by connecting node pairs with a probability dependent on their separation distance. The system is analyzed by calculating the total probability of an edge between steps based on their indices, summing over all possible positions. This approach reveals a correspondence between the model and one-dimensional lattice percolation with long-range interactions, enabling the identification of conditions for a percolation transition. Results indicate that the emergence of a giant component and percolation transitions are governed by a complex phase diagram, featuring a transition from weak to strong long-range interactions.

Advances in extensive air shower telescope technology and experimental refinements have allowed for the measurement of Galactic cosmic-ray interactions within the sub-PeV energy range (100 TeV to 1 PeV), opening fresh pathways for investigating dark matter and new physics. Utilizing observations of Galactic diffuse gamma rays from Tibet AS$\gamma$ and HAWC spanning 10 TeV to 1 PeV, we conduct the first search for an axion-like-particle (ALP) induced gamma-ray signal directly connected to the source of IceCube's extragalactic high-energy neutrinos. Since the generation of high-energy neutrinos in extragalactic objects necessitates the simultaneous production of gamma rays at similar energies, these photons can efficiently convert into ALPs within the magnetic fields of their host sources. This conversion allows the ALPs to bypass absorption and travel through intergalactic space, eventually reconverting into gamma rays within the Milky Way's magnetic field, thereby generating an all-sky diffuse high-energy gamma-ray signal in the sub-PeV band. By accounting for established Galactic astrophysical gamma-ray backgrounds from cosmic-ray interactions with gas and radiation, as well as contributions from sub-threshold sources, we establish competitive upper limits on the photon-ALP coupling constant $g_{a\gamma\gamma}$. Our results yield $g_{a\gamma\gamma} < 2.1\times10^{-11}$ GeV$^{-1}$ for ALP masses $m_a \leq 2\times10^{-7}$ eV at 95% confidence, effectively narrowing the mass gap toward the limits set by ADMX.

This study investigates the diffusion of photo-generated holes within a high-mobility mesoscopic GaAs channel characterized by hydrodynamic electron behavior. It demonstrates that injecting holes into this electron system creates a hydrodynamic three-component mixture comprising electrons, photo-generated heavy holes, and light holes. These findings are examined through the lens of ambipolar diffusion, highlighting features akin to viscous flow. Both hole species display comparable hydrodynamic properties. Consequently, the diffusion lengths, ambipolar diffusion coefficient, and effective viscosity of the electron-hole system are calculated.

A thermal relic WIMP continues to be a leading candidate for Dark Matter, especially for heavy candidates ($\gtrsim$ 1 TeV) where constraints are currently weaker. The strongest signals from WIMP annihilations are anticipated in the Galactic Centre (GC), making it an ideal target for current and upcoming gamma-ray observatories to rigorously test the WIMP hypothesis. Although it is well-known that gamma-ray annihilation produces charged secondary particles capable of generating 'delayed' inverse Compton (IC) emission, this contribution is frequently overlooked in indirect Dark Matter searches. This study examines IC emission under the specific conditions of heavy WIMP annihilation in the GC. By utilizing models of the region's magnetic and radiation fields and accounting for the transport of secondary particles, we demonstrate that for TeV-scale WIMPs, the IC component is significant and cannot be ignored. In this scenario, the produced particles cool within the GC rather than propagating outward into the Galaxy. This phenomenon substantially alters the predicted spectral shape, thereby enhancing the detection prospects for heavy WIMPs.

$R^2$ inflation, which extends General Relativity (GR) through quadratic scalar curvature, drives a quasi-de Sitter expansion in the early Universe, characterized by the Ricci scalar acting as an eigenmode of the d'Alembertian operator. This paper derives the most comprehensive gravitational theory accommodating an $R^2$ inflationary solution, revealing it to be a higher-curvature, non-local extension of GR. We provide a detailed analysis of inflationary perturbations within this framework, examining the form factors that yield massless tensor modes and a massive scalar mode (scalaron). We demonstrate that the theory involves a finite set of free parameters determinable via cosmological observations. Our generalized non-local $R^2$-like inflation predicts a scalar spectral index of $n_s\approx 1-\frac{2}{N}$ and permits any tensor-to-scalar ratio $r<0.036$. Furthermore, the tensor spectral index $n_t$ can be either positive or negative ($n_t\lessgtr 0$), violating the standard consistency relation $r = -8n_t$ in a non-trivial manner. We calculate the running of the tensor spectral index and discuss observational strategies to differentiate this model from various single-field scalar inflation scenarios. These predictions enable future CMB and gravitational wave studies to probe the nature of quantum gravity. Finally, we argue that the characteristics of this generalized non-local $R^2$-like inflation lie beyond the scope of established effective field theory approaches for single-field inflation, necessitating a redefinition of our methodology in inflationary cosmology.

We examine the analytic Landau damping problem for the Vlasov-HMF equation by determining the asymptotic behavior of the solution. For this "scattering problem," we employ a novel method that resembles the approach used for the Cauchy problem. This allows us to contrast the outcomes of both frameworks, highlighting the distinct roles of plasma echoes in each. Notably, we establish a non-perturbative result for the scattering problem.

Discourse parsing serves as a critical preliminary step in Natural Language Processing, offering significant benefits for numerous practical applications. However, despite its established importance, contemporary discourse parsers (and the tasks that depend on them) predominantly depend on small, manually annotated discourse treebanks, attempting to generalize discourse structures from scarce data within restricted domains. To address this challenge and enable discourse parsers to learn from extensive, varied, and domain-agnostic datasets, we introduce a framework that produces "silver-standard" discourse trees by leveraging distant supervision through an auxiliary sentiment analysis task.

Although third-generation CMB experiments have produced the initial maps of thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) Compton-$y$ distortion, upcoming missions will enable the mapping of electron gas temperature ($T_{\rm e}$) across the sky by detecting relativistic corrections to the thermal SZ effect. We outline the experimental conditions necessary to resolve the degeneracy between $y$ and $T_{\rm e}$ in observed SZ intensity and introduce a novel component separation method utilizing moment expansion. This approach isolates the $y$ and $T_{\rm e}$ observables of the relativistic SZ effect while reducing foreground contamination. We demonstrate that this method provides a new spectroscopic perspective on clusters, extending analysis across both frequency and temperature domains. Furthermore, we show that the relativistic electron temperature power spectrum constitutes a novel cosmological observable that can complement the Compton-$y$ map power spectrum, helping to alleviate parameter degeneracies in future cosmological SZ studies.

To investigate the surface physical conditions of the near-Earth asteroid (4179) Toutatis, we determined its geometric albedo. Although this asteroid has been extensively examined through ground-based photometric, spectrometric, polarimetric, and radar studies, as well as via the *in situ* observations of the Chinese Chang'e-2 probe, its geometric albedo remains poorly characterized. In April 2018, during an opposition event, we performed V-band photometry using the three southern hemisphere telescopes of the Korea Microlensing Telescope Network (KMTNet). By correcting the observed time-variable cross-section with a radar-derived shape model, we derived a geometric albedo of $p_\mathrm{V} = 0.185^{+0.045}_{-0.039}$, a value characteristic of S-type asteroids. Comparing this result with archival polarimetric data confirms that the polarimetric slope–albedo law yields a reliable albedo estimate for this S-type object. Furthermore, thermal infrared observations yielded consistent results when the asteroid's size was adjusted to align with Chang'e-2 findings. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that Toutatis's surface is composed of grains smaller than those found on near-Sun asteroids such as (1566) Icarus and (3200) Phaethon.

We investigate the dynamics of chiral SU(N) gauge theories, which include Weyl fermions in symmetric or anti-symmetric representations alongside additional fermions in fundamental and anti-fundamental representations. By revisiting an earlier proposal by Bars and Yankielowicz regarding the matching of 't Hooft anomalies with free fermions, we demonstrate that novel and occasionally stringent constraints on the large N dynamics emerge. Furthermore, we examine SU(N) theories augmented by an extra Weyl fermion in the adjoint representation, revealing that all 21 't Hooft anomalies associated with global symmetries correspond to those of a Spin(8) gauge theory. This correspondence implies a non-supersymmetric generalization of the Pouliot and Strassler duality. Finally, we address certain non-supersymmetric dualities involving vector-like matter in SO(N) and Sp(N) gauge theories, along with the restrictions derived from Weingarten inequalities.

Detecting COVID-19 early remains a critical research focus, offering benefits for patient triage, monitoring, and health evaluation while alleviating the operational burden on hospitals during the pandemic. Although various machine learning methods utilizing routine clinical data, such as blood tests and vital signs, have been employed to identify the virus, the associated risks of data breaches and information leakage pose significant reputational and legal threats to healthcare institutions. Despite these risks, safeguarding medical models against the exposure of sensitive information remains an underexplored field. This study investigates two machine learning strategies designed to predict a patient's COVID-19 status using standard, readily available clinical data. By applying adversarial training, we develop robust deep learning architectures specifically engineered to protect demographic attributes from leakage. The proposed models aim to maintain privacy against adversarial attacks and information disclosure. Through experiments utilizing datasets from Oxford University Hospitals, Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, and Portsmouth Hospitals University NHS Trust, we train and evaluate two neural networks that forecast PCR test results based on basic laboratory blood work and vital signs recorded upon hospital arrival. Our assessment demonstrates the privacy levels provided by each model and validates the efficacy and robustness of our proposed architectures against comparable baselines. A primary contribution of this work is the development of effective COVID-19 detection models that incorporate built-in mechanisms to selectively shield sensitive attributes from adversarial attacks.

Corporate research divisions are vital catalysts for organizational innovation. However, as information expands rapidly in both speed and volume, extracting insights, tracking trends, and developing strategies have become increasingly difficult for researchers and executives alike. This paper details a case study of IBM Research, a corporate research community, demonstrating how Semantic Web technologies enable the creation of a unified Knowledge Graph by integrating structured and textual data from diverse applications covering research projects, academic publications, datasets, and accolades. To enhance accessibility for developers, we identified common patterns for leveraging this induced knowledge and exposed them via APIs; these patterns were derived from user research aimed at addressing critical pain points and high-value use cases. We present two distinct business scenarios—recommendations and analytics—and provide a detailed discussion along with an empirical evaluation focused on entity recommendation. Furthermore, the methodologies and lessons learned from this initiative are applicable to other organizations confronting similar challenges.

We introduce a technique for generating mixed quantum states of any dimension $D$ ($D \geq 2$) by encoding them into the discretized transverse position and momentum of single photons passing through an aperture featuring $D$ slits. Building on our prior work, we employ a programmable, phase-only spatial light modulator (SLM) to define the aperture and adjust the complex transmission amplitude of each slit, thereby enabling independent control over the complex coefficients that constitute the quantum state. Because these SLMs allow for the dynamic adjustment of these coefficients during measurement, the method can produce not only pure states but also states representing mixtures of pure states. By varying the apertures over time according to a specific probability distribution, we have experimentally realized $D$-dimensional quantum states with purities that follow a clear analytical relationship with the distribution's parameters, facilitating easy customization. Furthermore, this approach eliminates the need to reconfigure the optical setup when transitioning between pure and mixed states or when increasing the state's dimensionality. Experimental results demonstrate robust performance up to $D=11$, achieving state fidelities $F > 0.98$ across all tested cases.

Soft radiation emission serves as a critical test for the internal consistency of Quantum Field Theory. Consequently, measuring soft photon bremsstrahlung—such as the method proposed for the upcoming ALICE experiment upgrade at the LHC—is of significant importance. This letter investigates the application of recently developed analytic techniques for Next-to-Leading-Power (NLP) soft gluon resummation to the soft photon spectrum. We present a formula for the differential cross-section utilizing shifted kinematics, which is optimized for numerical implementation. Furthermore, we examine how radiative jet functions influence loop corrections to Low's theorem.
