This paper introduces the concept of MAP-independence to capture this notion of relevance and investigates its utility in justifying inference to the best explanation. Furthermore, we formalize several computational problems based on this concept and evaluate their computational complexity.

Astrophysical neutrinos serve as powerful tools for investigating both astroparticle and high-energy physics. Their energies vastly exceed those of neutrinos from the Sun, supernovae, the atmosphere, or accelerators, allowing them to probe fundamental physics across the TeV to EeV range and beyond. These particles reveal phenomena both within and beyond the Standard Model, influenced by their creation processes and their journey across cosmic distances. Furthermore, they provide distinct insights into extreme non-thermal sources by penetrating regions blocked to electromagnetic waves. This white paper outlines the current and future opportunities that observing astrophysical neutrinos presents for astrophysics and high-energy physics.

Distinguishing between similar objects presents a challenge even for humans. This paper demonstrates that class interference, a learning difficulty inherent in the data, affects all deep neural networks and accounts for the majority of their generalization errors. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce cross-class tests, class ego directions, and interference models. We illustrate how these concepts can be used to examine the flatness of minima and the extent of class interference in trained models. Furthermore, we present methods to detect class interference during the training process by observing label dancing patterns and class dancing notes.

Clinical trials increasingly incorporate time-to-event outcomes alongside non-tabular patient data, such as MRI scans and electronic health record text. While recent neural-network solutions have largely focused on binary classifiers, parametric and distribution-free methods that fully leverage survival times and censoring information have received limited attention. This paper introduces Deep Conditional Transformation Models (DCTMs) as a unified framework for both parametric and semiparametric survival analysis. DCTMs facilitate the modeling of non-linear and non-proportional hazards across tabular and non-tabular data, accommodating all forms of censoring and truncation. Empirical evaluations on real and semi-synthetic datasets demonstrate that DCTMs perform competitively against current state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for survival analysis.

Capturing a stellar occultation offers a robust technique for directly determining the physical characteristics of solar system bodies. To ensure reliable and precise outcomes, it is crucial to conduct simultaneous observations from various sites situated across the projected path. Nevertheless, coordinating observing stations, consolidating data, and performing analysis is a laborious and complex process. To address this, we have created the Occultation Portal (OP), a web-based system designed to centrally manage occultation campaigns. This platform systematically archives instrumental and observational details from all participants, along with the corresponding data, in a standardized format. Researchers can then visualize this archived information on a per-event basis. Furthermore, investigators can generate light curves for each dataset by utilizing an integrated reduction pipeline within the portal. This paper provides a comprehensive description of the portal's architecture and its implemented features.

Deep neural networks for semantic segmentation typically depend on extensive datasets with pixel-level annotations, creating a significant bottleneck for practical deployment. To mitigate labeling expenses, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods have been developed to transfer knowledge from labeled synthetic sources to unlabeled real-world targets. Recently, semi-supervised learning techniques integrated into UDA have achieved state-of-the-art results, with entropy minimization being a prominent strategy. However, when applied to UDA for semantic segmentation, the gradient of the entropy term tends to bias the model toward easily transferable samples. To address this and balance the gradients of well-classified target samples, we introduce the maximum squares loss. This approach prevents the training process from being dominated by easy-to-transfer instances in the target domain. Additionally, we incorporate an image-wise weighting ratio to mitigate class imbalance within the unlabeled target data. Experiments on both synthetic-to-real and cross-city adaptation tasks validate the efficacy of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/ZJULearning/MaxSquareLoss.

Coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI) offers a promising approach for capturing three-dimensional hyperspectral images (HSI) via a single coded two-dimensional (2D) measurement, relying on algorithms to solve the resulting inverse problem. However, because this reconstruction task is ill-posed, various regularizers have been applied to recover 3D data from 2D inputs, yet they often fail to meet requirements regarding both accuracy and computational efficiency. A viable solution involves integrating auxiliary information, such as RGB measurements, into the CASSI framework. This paper introduces a novel fusion model for HSI reconstruction based on the combined use of CASSI and RGB data. The method leverages the spectral low-rank property of HSI, which is decomposed into a spectral basis and spatial coefficients; specifically, RGB measurements estimate the coefficients while CASSI data provides the orthogonal spectral basis. Furthermore, a patch processing strategy is proposed to strengthen the spectral low-rank characteristics. Unlike previous approaches, this model avoids non-local processing, iterative procedures, and the need for an RGB spectral sensing matrix. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real HSI datasets demonstrate that the proposed method not only surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in quality but also accelerates reconstruction speeds by more than 5,000 times.

Accurately predicting influenza hospitalizations is essential for public health preparedness, enabling hospitals to manage potential surges in patient volume. While various methods—including mechanistic, auto-regressive, and machine learning approaches—have been employed in real-time for CDC reporting, we hypothesize that combining multiple mechanistic trajectories via machine learning can yield superior forecasts. Specifically, we propose a Tree Ensemble design that leverages individual predictors from the baseline SIkJalpha model, each generated by varying specific hyper-parameters. Deployed for the 2022 FluSight challenge, our fully automated method requires no manual tuning. Results demonstrate that our Random Forest approach outperforms individual predictors and all other submitted models in terms of mean absolute error, coverage, and weighted interval score across all weekly 2022 submissions. Furthermore, analyzing the Random Forest's tree structure provides explainability, offering insights into how this ensemble enhances forecasting accuracy.

Sodium, potassium, and calcium-ion battery electrode materials are promising alternatives to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) due to their natural abundance and low cost. Although MoO2 has been studied as an anode for LIBs, it has not yet been explored for Na and other ion batteries. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the interaction of Na, K, and Ca with MoO2. The metal atoms strongly adsorb at the hexagonal center of the MoO2 lattice, inducing a transition from semiconducting to metallic behavior. The calculated diffusion barriers are exceptionally low (0.13, 0.08, and 0.22 eV for Na, K, and Ca, respectively), resulting in ultrahigh diffusivity. Notably, the maximum storage capacities for the MoO2 monolayer correspond to Na4MoO2, K2.5MoO2, and Ca3MoO2, yielding theoretical specific capacities of 837, 523, and 1256 mAh g-1, respectively. The materials also demonstrate moderate average voltages of 0.30, 0.75, and 0.35 V. These findings indicate that the MoO2 monolayer is a promising anode candidate for next-generation ion batteries, offering high capacity and superior rate performance.

We present the initial direct identification of molecular hydrogen linked to the Galactic nuclear wind. Observations from the Far-Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) of LS 4825—a B1 Ib-II star located at Galactic coordinates $l,b$ = 1.67$^{\circ}$,$-$6.63$^{\circ}$ and a distance of $d$ = 9.9$^{+1.4}_{-0.8}$ kpc, placing it roughly 1 kpc beneath the Galactic plane near the Center—reveal two high-velocity H$_2$ components at $v_\mathrm{LSR}$ = $-79$ and $-108$ km s$^{-1}$. Conversely, the FUSE spectrum of the foreground star HD 167402, situated approximately 0.6$^{\circ}$ away and at $d$=4.9$^{+0.8}_{-0.7}$ kpc, shows no H$_2$ absorption at these specific velocities. More than 60 H$_2$ lines arising from rotational levels $J$ = 0 to 5 were identified within the high-velocity clouds. For the cloud at $v_\mathrm{LSR}$ = $-79$ km s$^{-1}$, we determined a total column density of log $N$(H$_2$) $\geq$ 16.75 cm$^{-2}$, a molecular fraction $f_\mathrm{H_2}$ $\geq$ 0.8%, and rotational excitation temperatures of $T_{01}$ $\geq$ 97 K and $T_{25}$ $\leq$ 439 K. At $v_\mathrm{LSR}$ = $-108$ km s$^{-1}$, the measurements yield log $N$(H$_2$) = 16.13 $\pm$ 0.10 cm$^{-2}$, $f_\mathrm{H_2}$ $\geq$ 0.5%, and excitation temperatures of $T_{01}$ = 77$^{+34}_{-18}$ K and $T_{25}$ = 1092$^{+149}_{-117}$ K. Notably, the excited-state ortho-to-para-H$_2$ ratio is 1.0$^{+0.3}_{-0.1}$, significantly lower than the equilibrium value of 3 expected for gas at this temperature. This non-equilibrium ratio indicates that the $-108$ km s$^{-1}$ cloud was recently excited and has not yet reached equilibrium. Given that the LS 4825 sight line traverses a tilted segment of the Galactic disk, we propose that we are observing a boundary zone where the nuclear wind is stripping gas from the disk.

Various forms of Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimators, including the widely used Maximum Likelihood (ML) approach, are commonly employed to evaluate intricate econometric models where moment or likelihood functions cannot be computed analytically. Since the objective functions for both GMM and ML estimators approximate an integral—specifically, the expected value across real-world data space—a key question emerges: can the approximation of the moment function and the simulation of the full objective function be integrated? Drawing inspiration from popular Probit and Mixed Logit models, we examine double integrals featuring a linking function derived from the specific estimator (such as the logarithm for ML) and utilize sparse tensor product quadrature to minimize the computational burden of approximating this combined integral. Under the assumption of H\"older continuity for the linking function, we demonstrate that this methodology can enhance the convergence rate order of classical GMM and ML estimators by a factor of two, even when dealing with low-regularity integrands or high-dimensional problems. The efficacy of this result is demonstrated through numerical simulations of Mixed Logit and Multinomial Probit integrals, which are estimated using ML and GMM estimators, respectively.

We investigate the link between synchronization and the rate of information exchange among nodes within a spatio-temporal network modeling the dynamics of classical particles under a Remoissenet-Peyrard potential. Furthermore, we demonstrate methods for identifying both phase and complete synchronization in this system. Detecting phase synchronization proves challenging due to the highly non-coherent nature of particle dynamics, which prevents a proper definition of phase behavior. Similarly, identifying complete synchronization is difficult because the spatial character of the potential leads to asymptotic states that are heavily dependent on initial conditions.

The increasing prevalence of machine learning in decision-making has sparked concerns regarding fairness and the need for methods to address discrimination. When an individual receives an unfavorable outcome—such as a loan denial or housing rejection—principles of justice suggest we must be able to determine what changes could lead to a positive result in the future. Furthermore, the capacity to alter one's situation, such as through better education or enhanced credentials, should not be restricted to those with access to costly resources. Consequently, \emph{recourse} for negative decisions should be viewed as a valuable metric that ought to be equitably distributed across demographic groups. This paper outlines a method for constructing models that deliver accurate predictions while ensuring that the penalties associated with negative outcomes do not disproportionately disadvantage specific groups. We define recourse as the distance between an individual and a classifier's decision boundary. To address disparities, we introduce a regularized objective function designed to minimize the difference in recourse across groups. We investigate this approach within linear frameworks and subsequently extend it to non-linear and model-agnostic scenarios where precise boundary distances are unattainable. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to reduce unfairness in recourse without compromising the overall performance of the classifier.

We demonstrate that for any separated algebraic space of finite type over a field, provided its affinization is both connected and reduced, a universal morphism to a para-abelian variety exists. These para-abelian varieties are schemes that become abelian varieties upon extending the base field sufficiently. This result extends classical findings by Serre regarding universal morphisms from algebraic varieties to abelian varieties. Our proof synthesizes facts from the proper case with theories concerning Macaulayfication, singularity removal via alterations, pseudo-rational singularities, ind-objects, and Bockstein maps. Furthermore, we establish that the construction of the Albanese variety commutes with base change up to universal homeomorphisms. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive examination of Albanese maps for algebraic curves and groups, with particular focus on scenarios involving imperfect ground fields.

The emergence of nanoscale memristors has sparked optimism regarding the development of ultra-dense in-memory computing architectures, specifically the CMOL (CMOS/nanowire/molecular) design. In this framework, nanoscale memristors are intended to be placed at nanowire intersections. While the CMOL concept offers potential for neuromorphic hardware by combining lower-density CMOS neurons with massive analog synaptic connectivity provided by post-fabricated nanowire and nanoscale memristor layers, current commercial monolithic CMOS-memristor technologies face significant technical hurdles. First, ensuring reliable forming and programming in large arrays requires a series MOS selector transistor for each memristor, creating 1T1R compound synapses that deviate from the ideal nanowire crossing configuration. Second, memristors currently lack the reliability and stability required for massive analog-weight synapses involving gradual learning. This study presents a pseudo-CMOL monolithic chip core that overcomes these challenges by (a) utilizing a CMOL-inspired geometrical layout to enhance density despite the 1T1R constraint, and (b) employing a binary weight stochastic Spike-Timing-Dependent-Plasticity (STDP) learning rule that leverages the superior reliability of binary memristor memory. Experimental validation is provided for a spiking neural network (SNN) CMOL-core featuring 64 input neurons, 64 output neurons, and 4096 1T1R synapses, fabricated using 130nm CMOS with 200nm Ti/HfOx/TiN memristors. The core utilizes query-driven event read-out to enable computations that are insensitive to memristor variability.

We suggest creating a new TeV-scale collider facility designed for muon-proton and muon-nucleus interactions, which would enable high-precision deep inelastic scattering studies in unexplored regions and support a comprehensive research agenda in nuclear and particle physics. This infrastructure could facilitate or support the advancement of a muon-antimuon collider while utilizing current hadron accelerator resources at sites like CERN, Fermilab, or Brookhaven National Laboratory. The proposal outlines potential energy and luminosity specifications for various configurations and demonstrates scientific potential through analyses of deep inelastic scattering kinematics, as well as the production of Higgs bosons, vector bosons, top quarks, and beyond Standard Model leptoquarks. Additionally, we address detector design requirements and provide a tentative roadmap for the project's development.

We present new tools for controlled variable selection designed for economists. Specifically, we utilize a recently developed aggregation method for false discovery rate (FDR) control to analyze German administrative data, identifying which segments of women's employment histories significantly influence their career outcomes. Our findings indicate that career trajectories can be forecasted using a limited set of variables, including daily earnings, wage growth paired with high educational attainment, employment status, and work experience.

Natural language processing relies heavily on named entity recognition (NER), yet the inner workings of most NER models remain opaque to users. In high-stakes decision-making contexts, enhancing the interpretability of NER methods is both vital and difficult. This paper introduces a novel binary tree model, termed BTPK, which builds upon the existing Deterministic Talmudic Public announcement logic (TPK) framework. We integrate BTPK with two prevalent Bi-RNN architectures to create interpretable variants and subsequently develop a counterfactual verification module to validate this approach. Experiments across three public datasets indicate that BTPK-based learning surpasses two classical Bi-RNNs incorporating self-attention, demonstrating particular superiority on small, simple datasets as well as larger, complex ones. Furthermore, counterfactual verification confirms that the explanations generated by the BTPK-based method are accurate and reasonable for NER tasks. Additionally, the logical reasoning inherent to BTPK elucidates how Bi-RNNs process NER tasks, specifically highlighting the impact of varying distances in public announcements within long and intricate sequences.

Policies, which are essential elements of networking infrastructure utilized in routing tables and firewalls, have been extensively studied. However, theoretical models suggest that the decision tree size for such policies is prohibitively large (O((2n)d), where n represents the number of rules and d the number of packet features examined). If this theory held true, existing algorithms for detecting anomalies, conflicts, and redundancies would be intractable for practical scenarios (e.g., n = 1000, d = 10). This paper resolves this apparent contradiction by introducing the concept of "rules in play" to establish a realistic upper bound on decision tree size. We demonstrate that three practical factors—narrow fields, singletons, and all-matches—render the problem tractable. Furthermore, we illustrate how this concept addresses an open challenge: pruning a policy to its minimum rule count without altering its semantic meaning.

Although model robustness has been widely examined in language understanding, the robustness of Seq2Seq generation has received far less attention. This paper presents the first quantitative analysis of robustness in pre-trained Seq2Seq models, revealing that even state-of-the-art models like BART remain vulnerable, resulting in notable declines in faithfulness and informativeness during text generation. Motivated by these findings, we introduce AdvSeq, a novel adversarial augmentation framework designed to enhance the faithfulness and informativeness of Seq2Seq models by strengthening their robustness. During training, AdvSeq automatically generates two categories of adversarial augmentations: implicit samples created by perturbing word representations and explicit samples formed through word swapping, both of which effectively boost robustness. Extensive experiments across three common text generation tasks demonstrate that AdvSeq significantly improves both faithfulness and informativeness in Seq2Seq generation, as verified by both automatic and human evaluations.

Field theory solitons often possess localized bound states within their linear perturbation spectra, suggesting the potential for long-lived excitations that influence soliton dynamics. We begin by examining these effects in the most basic scenario: a domain wall kink solution within the $1+1$ dimensional $\lambda \phi^4$ theory. Our analysis reveals a single bound state for this solution, and we numerically determine its slow decay rate in flat space. Furthermore, we simulate a cosmological phase transition occurring in an expanding universe to generate these kinks, investigating the amplitude of the resulting excitation. Our findings indicate that formed kinks carry approximately $20\%$ more energy than their ground state. Additionally, we study the interaction between the kink and a thermal bath, calculating the excitation amplitude across varying temperatures. While this amplitude rises with temperature, the excess energy remains capped at the $20\%$ threshold. Finally, we contend that this surplus energy could significantly impact the later evolution of defects observed in numerical simulations.

This study introduces a novel approach for numerically investigating the interaction between a submerged solid structure and a current featuring surface waves. The methodology employs a Navier-Stokes solver utilizing a two-fluid formulation, where the Accurate Conservative Level-set (ACLS) technique tracks the interface. By extending the solver to unstructured grids, the method facilitates a boundary-fitted implementation of Fluid-Solid Interaction (FSI). The analysis focuses on a vertical, partially submerged cylinder moving through a flume containing flowing water and surface waves. Simulation outcomes assess the free surface configuration, air entrapment, wake vorticity generation, and pressure distribution on the solid. These numerical findings are validated against an experiment conducted by the same research team.

A celebrated fundamental identity in number theory relates the degree of an extension of global fields to local data. This paper demonstrates a generalized version of this identity applicable to any Dedekind domain. As an application, we establish that every Japanese Dedekind domain is excellent.

Typically, X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) signals do not appear in antiferromagnets. However, this letter presents the detection of spontaneous XMCD spectra in the chiral antiferromagnet Mn$_{3}$Sn thin film, attributed to the inverse triangular spin structure or the polarization of the cluster magnetic octupole. These findings align with recent theoretical predictions suggesting that such an inverse triangular arrangement can generate finite XMCD signals even without net magnetization [J. Phys. Soc. Jpn. 89, 083703 (2020) and Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 157402 (2021)].

This study investigates the dynamics of a three-dimensional discrete fractional-order eco-epidemiological model featuring a Holling type II functional response. We begin by discretizing a fractional-order predator-prey-parasite system incorporating piecewise constant arguments to analyze its behavior. Using the Jury criterion, we derive analytical conditions for the local stability of various fixed points, which are subsequently validated through multiple examples. Our findings indicate that the stability of the discrete fractional-order system is highly sensitive to both the step-size and the fractional order. Specifically, the critical step-size at which stability transitions occur diminishes as the fractional derivative order decreases. Furthermore, simulation results demonstrate that for larger step-sizes, the discrete fractional-order system can exhibit complex dynamics, including chaos.

Video compression enhances coding efficiency by reusing pixels from prior decoded frames through motion and residual compensation. We categorize hierarchical redundancy in video frames into two levels: 1) first-order redundancy, which exists in pixel space as similarities between neighboring frames and is currently handled by motion and residual compensation, and 2) second-order redundancy, found within motion and residual maps resulting from smooth motion in natural scenes. While current neural video coding research primarily focuses on first-order redundancy, we address the capture of second-order redundancy using predictors. We propose generic motion and residual predictors capable of extrapolating from previously decoded data; these are lightweight and compatible with most neural video codecs to boost rate-distortion performance. Furthermore, whereas RGB is the standard colorspace in existing literature, we introduce general modifications to support the YUV420 colorspace and present corresponding results. Experiments demonstrate that integrating our predictors with a prominent neural video codec achieves 38% and 34% bitrate reductions in RGB and YUV420 colorspaces, respectively, on the UVG dataset.

With the rapid expansion of Graph Neural Networks (GNN), there is an escalating demand for extensive, real-world datasets to train and evaluate new models on complex, realistic scenarios. However, acquiring such data is often difficult or impossible because these graphs frequently originate from online environments with strict privacy constraints. This scarcity limits the availability of benchmark graphs, forcing the research community to depend on a very small set of public datasets. To resolve this issue, we propose the Computation Graph Transformer (CGT), a new generative model capable of learning and replicating the distribution of real-world graphs while enhancing privacy. Our model (1) produces effective benchmark graphs that yield GNN performance comparable to that on the original data, (2) handles large-scale real-world graphs, and (3) ensures user privacy. Comprehensive experiments comparing our approach against numerous existing graph generative models demonstrate that only CGT can successfully create privacy-preserving, synthetic substitutes of large-scale real-world graphs suitable for robust GNN evaluation.

This study addresses the challenge of differentially private selection. Given a finite collection of candidate items and their associated quality scores, we aim to create a differentially private mechanism that selects an item with the highest possible score. While the exponential mechanism is the standard approach for this task, we introduce a novel mechanism derived from a rigorous analysis of privacy constraints. Our method guarantees an expected score that is never lower than that of the exponential mechanism and can achieve up to a two-fold improvement. Furthermore, our mechanism is straightforward to implement and operates with linear time complexity.

**Objective:** The study aims to create and assess a free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D (3D plus respiration) $T_2$-weighted turbo spin echo sequence suitable for radiology and MR-guided radiotherapy applications.

**Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR). This method was designed to match the contrast of conventional linear phase encoding while organizing data into multiple respiratory phases. Low-resolution, respiratory-correlated 4D images were reconstructed via compressed sensing to estimate non-rigid deformation vector fields, which facilitated motion-compensated image reconstruction. The rCASPR sampling technique was compared against linear and CASPR sampling regarding point-spread function (PSF) and image contrast through in silico, phantom, and in vivo studies. A grid search was employed to determine optimal reconstruction parameters for low-resolution 4D-MRI, specifically spatial resolution and temporal regularization. The proposed motion-compensated rCASPR was tested in eight healthy volunteers and benchmarked against free-breathing scans utilizing linear sampling, with image quality assessed both visually and quantitatively using gradient entropy.

**Findings:** rCASPR demonstrated a superior PSF (comparable in ky but narrower in kz) with no significant difference in image contrast relative to linear sampling. Optimal 4D-MRI reconstruction parameters were identified as a spatial resolution of $4.5 \text{ mm}^3$ and $\lambda_t=10^{-4}$. The groupwise average gradient entropy values were 22.31 for linear, 22.20 for rCASPR, 22.14 for soft-gated rCASPR, and 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR.

**Conclusion:** The proposed motion-compensated rCASPR facilitates high-quality free-breathing $T_2$-TSE imaging with negligible alterations to image contrast and scan duration. Consequently, this method allows for the direct adaptation of clinically established 3D TSE sequences to free-breathing protocols.

This study utilizes machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence, to evaluate how discounts on Swiss Federal Railways' "supersaver" tickets influence demand. Analyzing survey data from purchasers of these tickets, we examine which customer and trip attributes—including the discount magnitude—predict specific behaviors: booking previously unrealized trips, choosing first-class over second-class, or rescheduling journeys (such as shifting away from rush hours). Predictive models indicate that factors like passenger age, specific connection demand metrics (e.g., departure time, utilization), and discount levels can forecast purchasing decisions to a notable degree. Additionally, we apply causal machine learning to determine the impact of discount rates on trip rescheduling, a factor particularly relevant given rush-hour capacity limits. Under the assumptions that the discount rate is quasi-random conditional on our extensive characteristic set and that purchase probability increases weakly monotonically with the discount, we isolate the effect on "always buyers"—those who would have traveled regardless of the discount—using survey responses regarding behavior absent of discounts. Our findings reveal that, on average, a one-percentage-point increase in the discount rate raises the proportion of rescheduled trips by 0.16 percentage points among this group. Furthermore, an analysis of effect heterogeneity suggests these impacts are more pronounced for leisure travelers and during peak hours when other variables are controlled.

This work begins by investigating a generalization of Kim-independence and Conant-independence, grounded in Kaplan, Ramsey, and Shelah's concept of "strong Kim-dividing." We propose an axiom regarding stationary independence relations that essentially extends the "freedom" axiom found in certain free amalgamation theories developed by Conant. This axiom establishes the appropriate framework for applying arguments by Chernikov, Kaplan, and Ramsey to $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$ theories relative to a stationary independence relation. Extending Conant's findings on free amalgamation to the boundaries of current knowledge regarding the $\mathrm{NSOP}_{n}$ hierarchy, we utilize methods from Conant and our prior research to demonstrate that any theory satisfying the local conditions of this $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$ variant is either $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$ or $\mathrm{SOP}_{3}$, and either simple or $\mathrm{TP}_{2}$. Furthermore, we note that these theories constitute a significant class of examples where Conant-independence is symmetric, encompassing all of Conant's examples, Shelah's small cycle-free random graphs, and the finite-language $\omega$-categorical Hrushovski constructions by Evans and Wong.

Subsequently, we address a query by Conant, confirming that the generic functional structures defined by Conant and Kruckman serve as instances of non-modular free amalgamation theories. We also establish that every free amalgamation theory is either $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$ or $\mathrm{SOP}_{3}$, and that within the realm of $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$ free amalgamation theories, simplicity occurs if and only if the theory is modular.

Finally, we prove that any theory exhibiting symmetry in Conant-independence must be $\mathrm{NSOP}_{4}$. Consequently, the symmetry of Conant-independence represents the next recognized neostability-theoretic dividing line on the $\mathrm{NSOP}_{n}$ hierarchy beyond $\mathrm{NSOP}_{1}$. We also elucidate the relationship between this finding and several established open questions.

Because the $^4$He dimer possesses only a single weakly bound state with an average interatomic separation significantly exceeding the van der Waals length—and lacks deeply bound states—$^4$He$_N$ clusters for $N>2$ serve as an ideal paradigm for investigating fundamental concepts like large $s$-wave scattering length universality, van der Waals universality, Efimov physics, and effective field theories. This study examines structural characteristics, including pair and triple distribution functions, hyperradial density, the likelihood of locating the $N$th particle at a specific distance from the center of mass of the remaining $N-1$ atoms, and selected contact points. Additionally, it details kinetic energy release, which can be quantified through Coulomb explosion in specialized size-selected molecular beam experiments for small $N$. These structural properties were calculated using three distinct realistic $^4$He-$^4$He interaction potentials and compared against an effective low-energy potential model from existing literature. This model reproduces ground-state energies for $^4$He$_N$ clusters across $N=2$ to $N=\infty$ with approximately 95% accuracy using only four parameters. The investigation was further extended to the unitary regime (infinite $s$-wave scattering length) by artificially reducing the interaction strengths. Beyond aiding in the characterization of small bosonic helium quantum droplets, this work offers valuable insights into the predictability of various structural properties within the effective low-energy theoretical framework.

Post-data statistical inference involves deriving probabilistic statements regarding model parameters given observed data. When prior knowledge exists, Bayesian posteriors offer a convenient framework for such inference. In scenarios lacking prior information, objective Bayes or generalized fiducial inference (GFI) remain viable alternatives. Drawing inspiration from approximate Bayesian computation, we introduce a new characterization of post-data inference utilizing differential geometry. Under appropriate smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that both Bayesian posteriors and generalized fiducial distributions (GFDs) can be described as absolutely continuous distributions defined over the same differentiable manifold. This manifold is uniquely defined by the observed data and the data-generating equation of the fitted model. Our geometric analysis clarifies both the relationships and distinctions between Bayesian inference and GFI, while enabling the sampling of posteriors and GFDs via manifold Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. A repeated-measures analysis of variance example is provided to demonstrate this sampling approach.

This study examines the nonselfadjoint Sturm-Liouville operator subject to either periodic or antiperiodic boundary conditions. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the system of root functions of these operators to form a Riesz basis, expressed through the Fourier coefficients of $q$.

We theoretically introduce and investigate a novel electron-impurity scattering mechanism in heavily dielectrically screened, doped semiconductors. This approach relies on the \textit{vector} nature of lattice distortions induced by point defects located asymmetrically within the unit cell. Consequently, elastic deformations resulting in local lattice compression diminish as $1/r^2$ with distance from the impurity. Scattering of electrons via the standard deformation potential on these defects yields a low-temperature mobility $\mu(n)$ that scales with electron density $n$ according to $\mu(n) \propto n^{-2/3}$, a relationship that aligns closely with experimental data for several pertinent materials.

Modeling non-linear temporal trajectories is crucial across various fields, including longitudinal microbiome studies. While many current methods concentrate on estimating average trajectories, analyzing individual temporal patterns is equally valuable. Sparse Principal Component Analysis (SFPCA) is a valuable tool for evaluating individual variation in non-linear trajectories, yet applying it to real-world data often demands rigorous model selection and diagnostic procedures. This study introduces a Bayesian framework for SFPCA, enabling the use of efficient leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) for model selection. Furthermore, this approach leverages the shape parameter estimated by PSIS-LOO and employs posterior predictive checks for graphical diagnostics. Consequently, this Bayesian implementation facilitates the careful application of SFPCA across a broad spectrum of longitudinal data applications.

This study explores physics beyond the Standard Model by examining the hitherto unobserved Higgs-plus-photon final state at the LHC within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) framework. Leveraging dimension-6 operators, we investigate two distinct interaction classes defined by the Lorentz structures of Higgs couplings to gauge bosons and fermions. Constraints on the associated Wilson coefficients were first established using existing experimental data. Subsequently, we focused on the boosted hadronic decay of the Higgs boson into two bottom quarks, which results in a high-$p_T$ fat-jet recoiling against a hard photon. Building upon a CMS Run II search for a resonance decaying into a Higgs and a photon, we conducted a comprehensive signal and background analysis for this channel to derive limits on the relevant Wilson coefficients. Through a cut-based analysis, we identified specific kinematic observables that differentiate the signal from Standard Model backgrounds. We calculated the minimum Wilson coefficient values required to achieve a $3\sigma$ signal significance at the 14 TeV LHC run with an integrated luminosity of $3000 ~\rm fb^{-1}$. Additionally, a multivariate analysis employing boosted decision trees and jet substructure techniques helped isolate phase space regions where the SMEFT-driven signal contribution is significantly enhanced. Finally, we briefly discuss the dependencies of these parameters and the interpretation of the allowed coefficient values in the context of a specific ultraviolet-complete model, the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM).

Recent advancements in machine learning have enabled the deployment of new model classes for inference on milliwatt-powered IoT devices. While current ML-to-FPGA compilers are optimized for deep neural networks on large FPGAs, general-purpose High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools underperform because they fail to leverage ML-specific characteristics. To address this, we introduce MAFIA, a compilation tool designed for ML inference on compact FPGAs tailored for IoT use. MAFIA natively supports linear algebra operations and accommodates diverse ML algorithms, including state-of-the-art architectures. Our results demonstrate that programs generated by MAFIA achieve an average performance improvement of 2.5x compared to the best-performing variant of a commercial HLS compiler.

We examine the motion of point charges within the background of finite-action vacuum solutions to Maxwell's equations, referred to as knot solutions. Specifically, we utilize a basis of electromagnetic knots produced via the "de Sitter method." Our analysis reveals diverse dynamical behaviors contingent upon the field configuration and chosen parameters. These include electromagnetic acceleration of particles from rest to ultrarelativistic velocities, the rapid convergence of trajectories into narrow asymptotic cones at high coupling values, and significant, coherent twisting and turning of paths. This study contributes to a broader initiative to enhance the comprehension of knotted electromagnetic fields and the resulting charged particle dynamics, with potential implications for experimental applications.

Although automated machine learning has gained significant traction in supervised classification and regression, advancements in unsupervised domains remain constrained. We introduce a new framework for automating outlier detection by utilizing meta-learning derived from historical datasets containing outliers. Our core assumption is that the ideal outlier detection method is contingent upon the intrinsic characteristics of the data distribution. Specifically, we employ optimal transport to identify the dataset with the most analogous underlying distribution and subsequently apply the outlier detection algorithms that have demonstrated superior performance for that specific distribution. Our evaluation confirms the robustness of this approach, showing it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised outlier detection. Furthermore, this methodology can be readily extended to automate other unsupervised tasks.
We provide a basic method for investigating the Euclidean property of rings of $S$-integers in complex quadratic fields relative to the $S$-norm.

Citation Context Analysis (CCA) is a crucial natural language processing task focused on understanding the mechanisms and motivations behind scholarly discussions of others' work. Despite extensive research over decades, traditional CCA frameworks have depended on overly simplistic assumptions regarding citation behaviors, overlooking significant phenomena. For example, academic papers frequently feature detailed discussions of cited works that extend across multiple sentences and convey multiple intents simultaneously. However, CCA is conventionally treated as a single-sentence, single-label classification problem, causing existing datasets to miss these complex discursive elements. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new framework that treats CCA as a document-level context extraction and labeling task. We present MultiCite, a dataset comprising 12,653 citation contexts drawn from more than 1,200 computational linguistics papers. As the largest collection of expert-annotated citation contexts to date, MultiCite uniquely includes multi-sentence, multi-label contexts embedded within full paper texts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while our dataset remains compatible with training traditional CCA models, it also facilitates the development of novel model architectures for CCA that extend beyond fixed-width text classification. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/allenai/multicite.

We transform the calculation of three-point correlation functions involving spinning operators with arbitrary polarizations into a statistical mechanics problem using the hexagon formalism. The hexagon partition function serves as the fundamental component of these correlations. By investigating its analytic properties, we generate perturbative data for spinning three-point functions. For specific polarizations across any coupling strength, we derive the full asymptotic three-point function in determinant form. Having established this integrability framework, we pave the way for exploring the large spin limit, where dualities involving null Wilson loops and integrable pentagons are expected to emerge.

This paper presents InDistill, a unified model compression framework that integrates knowledge distillation with channel pruning to transfer essential information flow paths from a large teacher network to a lightweight student. Unlike prior methods that collapse such information due to a preceding encoding stage, InDistill applies pruning to the teacher's intermediate layers, narrowing them to match the student's width. This strategy enforces architectural alignment, allowing for direct distillation of intermediate layers without an encoding step. Furthermore, the method employs a curriculum learning training scheme that accounts for the specific distillation difficulty of each layer and the critical periods when information flow paths are established. Experimental results demonstrate that InDistill outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on three standard benchmarks—CIFAR-10, CUB-200, and FashionMNIST—by 3.08%, 14.27%, and 1% mAP, respectively, as well as on more demanding datasets like ImageNet and CIFAR-100, achieving improvements of 1.97% and 5.65% mAP, respectively.

Emotions, such as joy and anger, are ubiquitous in everyday software engineering (SE) tasks and serve as key predictors of productivity, including bug-fixing efficiency. However, recent research indicates that applying general-purpose emotion classification models directly to SE datasets yields poor results. Furthermore, within the SE domain, model performance drops substantially when trained on one communication channel (e.g., StackOverflow) but evaluated on another (e.g., GitHub comments). Retaining tool effectiveness by retraining with channel-specific data is costly, as manually annotating large volumes of ground truth data requires significant effort. To tackle this data scarcity issue, this paper proposes automatically generating new training data through data augmentation. By analyzing the specific error patterns of popular SE-focused emotion recognition tools, we tailored our augmentation strategy to enhance classification performance. Our findings demonstrate an average 9.3% increase in micro F1-Score across three existing tools (ESEM-E, EMTk, and SEntiMoji) when utilizing our optimal augmentation approach.

This research addresses a straightforward challenge: estimating the frequency of identical full names within a vast population. Determining name popularity can be achieved through personal name matching in databases and holds significance across various fields. A key characteristic of extensive name datasets is the presence of a high volume of unique entries, which poses difficulties for statistical modeling. We examine several statistical methods and introduce a simple yet efficient approach designed to yield more precise count estimates. Our experiments utilize a dataset comprising approximately 20 million name instances representing roughly 13 million real individuals. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of name counting techniques and a record linkage study driven by these popularity estimates. The results indicate that theoretically grounded methods surpass basic heuristics and offer utility for diverse applications.

Social media posts frequently include contextual annotations and metadata, such as authors, mentions, hashtags, and hyperlinks, which we term Non-Textual Units (NTUs). We argue that NTUs convey social context beyond pure textual meaning and that incorporating them can enhance social media text representations. In this study, we build an NTU-focused social heterogeneous network to jointly embed these units. We then seamlessly integrate these NTU embeddings into a large pretrained language model through fine-tuning that accounts for these additional elements. This approach enriches noisy, short-form social media text. Experimental results demonstrate that NTU-augmented text representations significantly surpass text-only baselines by 2-5% relative improvement on various downstream tasks, underscoring the critical role of context in social media NLP. Furthermore, we find that integrating NTU context into the initial layers of the language model, alongside the text, yields better performance than applying it after text embeddings are generated. Ultimately, our work enables the creation of holistic, general-purpose embeddings for social media content.

On April 11 and 14, 2016, faint meteors were observed using the Tomo-e PM, a wide-field CMOS mosaic camera installed on the 105-cm Schmidt telescope at the University of Tokyo's Kiso Observatory. As a prototype for the Tomo-e Gozen, the Tomo-e PM covers approximately $1.98\,\mathrm{deg^2}$ at a rate of 2\,Hz. The observations recorded 1514 and 706 meteors on the respective dates, all classified as sporadic. These meteors exhibited absolute magnitudes between $+4$ and $+10\,\mathrm{mag}$ in the $V$-band, corresponding to masses ranging from $3.3{\times}10^{-4}$ to $8.3{\times}10^{-2}\,\mathrm{g}$. The derived magnitude distributions align well with a single power-law luminosity function characterized by a slope of $r = 3.1{\pm}0.4$ and a meteor rate of $\log_{10}N_0 = -5.5{\pm}0.5$. These findings highlight the effectiveness of wide-field video telescopic observations in constraining the luminosity function of faint meteors. While the Tomo-e Gozen is expected to achieve roughly double the performance of the Tomo-e PM, a survey using the Gozen will yield a more robust determination of this function.

As a key climate change mitigation strategy, global power grids are becoming more dependent on wind energy. However, wind's inherent variability undermines system reliability, often necessitating curtailment that inflicts significant financial losses on wind farm operators. While Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) can mitigate curtailment by acting as local backups, their auxiliary function can severely limit revenue generation in electricity markets, especially for energy arbitrage in the Spot market and frequency control ancillary services (FCAS). Ideally, BESS scheduling should harmonize curtailment absorption with market trading, but this is challenging due to the stochastic nature of wind and prices, as well as coordination complexities. This study examines the bidding strategy of a co-located wind-battery system participating simultaneously in both Spot and Regulation FCAS markets. We introduce a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach that decouples market participation into two linked Markov decision processes, allowing the BESS to manage onsite curtailment while bidding in wholesale Spot and FCAS markets to maximize total revenue. Validated using realistic wind farm data, our coordinated bidding strategy outperforms optimization-based benchmarks by generating higher revenues and responding more effectively to curtailment. Our findings demonstrate that joint-market participation significantly enhances the financial performance of wind-battery systems compared to participating in individual markets.

Vision models have expanded exponentially in recent years, particularly following the introduction of the Vision Transformer. This trend has spurred the creation of parameter-efficient tuning techniques, such as adapter layers and visual prompt tokens, which train only a small fraction of parameters while freezing the bulk of those derived from pre-training. However, crafting an effective tuning method is challenging; it often involves testing numerous design variations, and specific downstream datasets frequently demand custom solutions. In this paper, we treat existing parameter-efficient tuning methods as "prompt modules" and introduce Neural prOmpt seArcH (NOAH). NOAH is a novel framework that utilizes neural architecture search to automatically determine the optimal prompt module design for large vision models tailored to each downstream dataset. Through extensive experiments on over 20 vision datasets, we show that NOAH (i) outperforms individual prompt modules, (ii) exhibits strong few-shot learning capabilities, and (iii) is domain-generalizable. The code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/Davidzhangyuanhan/NOAH.

Measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDIQKD) represents a groundbreaking protocol due to its physical immunity against all detection-side attacks. Nevertheless, it maintains strict requirements regarding the source, mandating the perfect preparation of four BB84 states to guarantee security. While certain protocols relax some encoding assumptions to enhance practicality, this often leads to a significant drop in performance. This study introduces an MDIQKD protocol that demands less precise knowledge of the encoding system to effectively mitigate modulation errors and fluctuations. We have successfully demonstrated this protocol experimentally, with results indicating both high performance and robust security suitable for real-world applications. Furthermore, its resilience and adaptability make it particularly valuable for complex environments, such as quantum key distribution networks.

Random forests are widely recognized as robust ensemble models in machine learning. By training numerous decision trees with diversity achieved through data and feature subsampling, they offer more stable and reliable predictions than a single tree. However, this benefit reduces interpretability; whereas individual decision trees are easy to understand, random forest predictions are complex due to the majority vote mechanism across hundreds of trees. This paper investigates the underlying reasons why a Boolean random forest classifies an input as positive or negative. We introduce "majoritary reasons," defined as prime implicants shared by a strict majority of trees, as an alternative to traditional sufficient reasons (prime implicants of the entire forest). We analyze the tractability of generating these abductive explanations, specifically addressing the challenges of finding a single reason versus finding the shortest one. Experimental results across various datasets highlight a trade-off between computational runtime and result sparsity. Sufficient reasons, which are DP-complete to identify, are slightly larger than majoritary reasons generated via a simple linear-time greedy algorithm and significantly larger than minimal majoritary reasons approximated by an anytime PARTIAL MAX SAT algorithm.

This paper proposes the Input Constrained Control Barrier Function (ICCBF) as a technique for designing safety-critical controllers for non-linear control affine systems subject to input limitations. By identifying a specific subset of the safe state space, the method constructs a controller that ensures this subset remains forward invariant. The resulting feedback controller is formulated as the solution to a quadratic program, enabling efficient computation for real-time applications. Additionally, the study demonstrates that ICCBFs generalize Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, making them suitable for systems with non-uniform relative degrees. Simulation results are provided to validate the approach on adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous scenarios.

Document Layout Analysis (DLA) involves partitioning document images into distinct region types, a critical function for document content understanding and information extraction systems. Developing DLA methods that require minimal data for effective training is essential for its advancement. This work explores Human-in-the-loop (HITL) collaborative intelligence within DLA, inspired by the concept that HITL enables models to learn from unknown challenges by incorporating a small amount of knowledge-based data. While existing HITL approaches select key samples based on confidence, this metric proves unsuitable for DLA tasks. We introduce the Key Samples Selection (KSS) method, which leverages agent collaboration to more accurately identify key samples in high-level tasks like semantic segmentation, thereby reducing costs. After selection, these samples undergo active labeling by humans, and the model is subsequently updated with the labeled data. Drawing from reinforcement learning principles, we redesigned the learning system with a sample-based agent update strategy that significantly enhances the agent's capacity to assimilate new samples. This approach yields substantial performance gains on two benchmarks: DSSE-200 (improving from 77.1% to 86.3%) and CS-150 (improving from 88.0% to 95.6%) using only 10% of labeled data.

The Moufang loop attributed to Richard Parker serves as a central extension of the extended binary Golay code. It stands as the primary example of a broader category of nonassociative structures called code loops, which have been examined through various algebraic and combinatorial lenses. This expository piece aims to showcase an experimental methodology for computations within code loops, utilizing a blend of minimal precomputed data and the extensive identities satisfied by the loops' twisted cocycles. Additionally, we demonstrate that Parker's loop multiplication can be reconstructed from a limited portion of its twisted cocycle. We also identify relatively large subspaces of the Golay code where Parker's loop decomposes into a direct product.

We begin by building integrable $\lambda$-deformed WZW models grounded in non-semisimple groups, specifically examining the four-dimensional scenario governed by the non-semisimple group $E_2^c$. The associated Lorentzian gravitational backgrounds are plane waves, derivable as Penrose limits of a $\lambda$-deformed $SU(2)$ background multiplied by a timelike coordinate, provided the $\lambda$-matrix is suitably chosen. We present two such integrable deformations that both modify the Nappi-Witten plane wave yet remain inequivalent; however, they share the same underlying symmetry algebra, which arises from a Saletan-type contraction of the algebra for the $\lambda$-deformed $SU(2)$ background with a timelike direction. Furthermore, we derive a plane wave via the Penrose limit of a $\lambda$-deformation applied to the $\nicefrac{SU(2)}{U(1)}$ coset CFT times a timelike coordinate, representing a deformation of a previously constructed logarithmic CFT. Lastly, we briefly explore contractions rooted in the simplest Yang-baxter $\sigma$-models.

We present a novel proof demonstrating that every finite quadratic module can be decomposed into indecomposable components. For each indecomposable finite quadratic module, we construct both a lattice and a positive definite lattice with the minimal possible rank, such that their discriminant modules correspond to the given one. These resulting lattices are explicitly defined through their Gram matrices.

We introduce a protocol for two-parameter estimation using a Bose-Einstein condensate trapped within a symmetric triple-well potential. The process begins by adiabatically preparing a three-mode NOON state. The target parameters are the phase differences across the wells. We analyze the estimation scheme's sensitivity by evaluating both quantum and classical Fisher information matrices. This analysis reveals an optimal method for particle number measurement. Furthermore, under this optimal measurement strategy, the estimation precision achieves Heisenberg scaling.

Typically, materials return to thermal equilibrium after femtosecond-laser excitation, though rare exceptions exist. In this study, we show that a single 100-fs laser pulse can disrupt the standard thermal-equilibrium path in the canonical 3D antiferromagnetic (AFM) material Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, causing the loss of long-range magnetic correlations along one axis and resulting in a glassy state. Furthermore, we identify a "critical-threshold ordering" phenomenon occurring at fluences exceeding approximately 12 mJ/cm$^2$; this threshold aligns with the minimum thermodynamically stable $c$-axis correlation length required to sustain long-range quasi-two-dimensional AFM order. We attribute this behavior to the crystalline anisotropy of magnetic-exchange parameters in Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, which operate on distinct timescales. Consequently, these parameters evolve differently during ultrafast recovery compared to thermal equilibrium processes. Therefore, our findings are likely applicable to various challenges concerning the nonequilibrium dynamics of low-dimensional magnets and similar ordering phenomena.

While neural network architectures vary significantly in performance across different tasks, the relative importance of weight parameters versus architectural design remains a critical question. This study investigates how far architecture alone can encode task solutions without learning any weights. We introduce a search methodology designed to identify architectures capable of performing tasks using only random weights. To evaluate these models, we assign a single shared weight, drawn from a uniform random distribution, to all connections and measure the resulting expected performance. Our results demonstrate that this approach can discover minimal architectures effective for multiple reinforcement learning tasks without weight training. Furthermore, in supervised learning, we identified architectures that achieve accuracy well above chance on the MNIST dataset using random weights. An interactive version of this paper is available at https://weightagnostic.github.io/.

We achieve a full two-loop calculation of the leading-twist contribution to the photon-pion transition form factor $\gamma \, \gamma^{\ast} \to \pi^0$ by utilizing the hard-collinear factorization theorem alongside contemporary multi-loop methods. Our predictions reveal that the two-loop perturbative correction is numerically significant. Furthermore, we show that our findings will be essential for distinguishing among various models of the twist-two pion distribution amplitude, given the anticipated precision at Belle II.

In a recent publication, we presented the chirality-flow formalism, a technique for straightforward and transparent Feynman diagram calculations grounded in the left- and right-chiral $\mathrm{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ properties of spacetime. Building on our prior focus on massless QED and QCD at the tree level, this work extends the chirality-flow formalism to the complete Standard Model at tree level, incorporating massive particles and electroweak interactions—where the chiral nature of $W$ interactions leads to an elegant simplification. We demonstrate how Feynman diagram values can be directly constructed through several representative examples.

We examine the resolution of nonlinear equations involving a single real variable, commonly known as root finding. While this is a longstanding issue, we contend that certain facets of its solution via interval arithmetic remain poorly understood and offer our perspectives on the matter. We maintain that single-variable problems are significantly more straightforward than multi-variable ones and should be addressed with specialized techniques. Furthermore, we have developed an implementation of these concepts in C++ and released the code under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

We calculate the inertial modes for a freely rotating two-layer planetary system featuring an inviscid, ellipsoidal fluid core and a perfectly rigid mantle. We introduce a method to obtain analytical expressions for the frequencies of the Free Core Nutation (FCN) and Chandler Wobble (CW) that remain accurate to all orders of dynamical flattening for both the core and mantle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the FCN and CW represent the direct generalization of the purely fluid Spin-Over mode (SO) and the Eulerian Wobble (EW) to scenarios where the mantle is free to oscillate around a steady rotation state. Finally, using numerical computations for an axisymmetric oblate spheroidal planet, we show that all other inertial modes within the steadily rotating fluid core also function as free modes in this freely rotating two-layer configuration.

Driven by the growing integration of artificial intelligence within the Internet-of-Things (IoT), this paper addresses the challenge of scheduling packets from various sensing sources to a central controller via a wireless network. In this scenario, packets from different sources hold varying degrees of importance for the controller's intelligent decision-making processes, making it essential to deliver timely and high-value information. We propose a parameterized maximum-weight scheduling policy that integrates Age of Information (AoI) metrics with Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) estimates into its weight calculation, governed by a parameter $\eta$. The UCB component is vital for balancing the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in learning, thereby ensuring minimal cumulative regret. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed algorithm limits the running average total age to at most $O(N^2\eta)$ and bounds the cumulative regret over a time horizon $T$ by $O(NT/\eta+\sqrt{NT\log T})$. These results highlight a tradeoff: increasing $\eta$ reduces cumulative regret but concurrently increases the running average total age. Finally, simulations are presented to assess the efficiency of the proposed approach.

This survey examines equivariant harmonic maps that originate from Higgs bundles. It elucidates the non-abelian Hodge correspondence, emphasizing the significance of equivariant harmonic maps within this framework. Following this introduction, we review recent advancements addressing open questions in the study of these maps.

Professional meetings are ubiquitous, yet equipping vocal assistants with sophisticated meeting management capabilities remains difficult. In this setting, active speaker detection offers valuable insights into participant interactions. Driven by the goal of creating advanced meeting assistants, we aim to integrate audio and visual data to maximize performance. This paper introduces two fusion strategies for active speaker detection, combining audio with two visual modalities via neural networks. For comparison, we also employ classical unsupervised methods for audio feature extraction. We hypothesize that visual data focused on participants' faces, specifically capturing lip and facial gestures, is highly effective for voice activity detection. Consequently, our baseline utilizes visual data processed by a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to efficiently encode both appearance and motion. To enhance this system, we integrated audio streams processed by either a CNN or an unsupervised speaker diarization model. Performance was further boosted by incorporating motion data derived from optical flow. Our proposals were evaluated using the AMI corpus, a public, state-of-the-art benchmark. We analyzed each system's contribution to determining current speakers and discussed the resulting outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that adding motion information significantly improves performance within our application context. Furthermore, we observed that attention-based fusion not only enhances performance but also reduces standard deviation.

The self-propelled motion of phoretic colloids drives their accumulation at boundaries and interfaces. This surplus concentration, relative to passive particles, renders the dynamics of phoretic colloids uniquely responsive to boundary conditions and opens pathways for externally manipulating both individual and collective behaviors. This review examines recent theoretical findings regarding the dynamics of phoretic colloids near and adsorbed onto fluid interfaces, with a specific focus on comparing and contrasting these behaviors with those observed at solid-fluid interfaces.

Buddha statues are a significant component of Asian culture and have existed alongside human civilization for over two millennia. Due to historical conflicts, natural disasters, and other factors, records regarding the construction dates of these statues have often been lost, making it a challenging task for historians to determine their ages. This paper proposes a neural network model designed to automatically estimate the construction years of Buddha statues using solely their facial images. Our approach employs a composite loss function comprising three components: an MSE loss to serve as the foundation for age estimation; a KL divergence-based loss to accommodate samples with both precise dates and broader historical ranges (such as dynasties or centuries); and a regularization term that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data under the manifold assumption. By integrating these three elements during training, we demonstrate that our method achieves a mean absolute error of 37.5 years on the test set when estimating construction dates from provided images.

Research in fashion recommendation has expanded significantly, especially within areas like shop-the-look, context-aware outfit generation, and personalized styling. While most existing studies prioritize understanding the complementary relationships between lifestyle items, recent efforts have recognized that style is a crucial factor in compatibility learning and outfit assembly. This paper introduces an end-to-end methodology for creating outfits guided by specific styles or themes, utilizing a novel style encoder network. We provide a comprehensive analysis of our approach through various experiments and offer a demonstration API that illustrates the system's capability to generate outfits based on an anchor item and a chosen style.

We examine an optimal liquidation scenario characterized by instantaneous price impact and stochastic resilience, specifically for small levels of instantaneous impact. Within this modeling structure, as the instantaneous impact factor approaches zero, the optimal portfolio process converges to the solution of an optimal liquidation problem governed by general semimartingale controls. These findings establish a unified framework that integrates the two predominant modeling approaches in liquidation literature, offering a microscopic justification for employing semimartingale liquidation strategies and portfolio processes with unbounded variation. This convergence analysis relies on new results concerning backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with singular terminal conditions, as well as novel representation theorems for BSDEs expressed through uniformly continuous functions of forward processes.

The development of controlled one-dimensional carbon nanostructures on metal substrates involves multiple steps, where the pathway, activation barriers, and intermediate metastable states are highly substrate-dependent. Although gold has been extensively investigated for this process, silver surfaces, which exhibit distinct catalytic properties, have received comparatively less attention. This study combines experimental and theoretical approaches to examine the growth of poly-p-phenylene (PPP) chains and subsequent narrow graphene ribbons from 4,4''-dibromo-$p$-terphenyl precursors deposited on silver. By integrating scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with density functional theory (DFT), we characterize the molecular morphology and organization throughout the growth stages, analyzing the stability and transformation of intermediate species using calculated thermodynamic data. Unlike on gold, the debromination stage on silver yields organometallic molecules and chains, a phenomenon explained by their negative formation energy in the presence of a silver adatom reservoir. Furthermore, at dehydrogenation temperatures, persistent intercalated bromine atoms on silver prevent the formation of well-ordered graphene ribbons observed on gold, resulting instead in only partial lateral coupling of the PPP chains. Numerical calculations reveal significantly different activation energies for bromine desorption from silver versus gold, underscoring the critical role of this process in determining the kinetics of molecular chain and graphene ribbon formation across different metal surfaces.

Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) has long offered significant potential to advance the field, yet creating practical algorithms that realize this promise has proven difficult. To deepen our theoretical grasp of HRL, we examine hierarchical credit assignment through the lens of standard multistep reinforcement learning. We demonstrate that a 1-step "hierarchical backup" is effectively a conventional multistep backup utilizing $n$ skip connections across time, which link subsequent states back to the initial state regardless of intermediate actions. Additionally, we discover that extending hierarchy to multistep return estimation necessitates determining how to segment environment traces to build backup paths. Leveraging these insights, we developed a novel algorithm, Hier$Q_k(\lambda)$, and showed that hierarchical credit assignment by itself can enhance agent performance, even when generalization and exploration are removed. Overall, our research provides fundamental clarity on the mechanics of hierarchical backups and establishes them as a distinct pillar for future reinforcement learning studies.

This research introduces an algorithm for numerically calculating Maass forms and their corresponding eigenvalues for Fuchsian groups with infinite covolume. Leveraging Patterson-Sullivan theory, this approach also enables the computation of the Hausdorff dimensions associated with the limit sets of these groups. To approximate Maass forms, we analyze their Fourier expansions across various coordinate systems. To address fundamental domains of infinite volume, we employ the concept of flare domains. Furthermore, we establish theoretical frameworks regarding Fourier expansions within flare domains, drawing parallels to the classical theory concerning cusps. The paper concludes with detailed applications of the algorithm to symmetric Schottky groups and infinite volume Hecke groups.

We establish that $s_r(K_{k+1}) = O(k^3 r^3 \log^3 k)$, where $s_r(K_k)$ denotes the Ramsey parameter defined by Burr, Erd\H{o}s, and Lov\'{a}sz in 1976. This parameter represents the minimal minimum degree of a graph $G$ such that every $r$-edge-coloring of $G$ yields a monochromatic $K_k$, but no proper subgraph of $G$ possesses this property.

Recent Galactic surveys have uncovered a primordial merger, the Gaia-Saurus-Enceladus (GSE), which dominates our Galaxy's stellar halo. By analyzing chemical abundances and kinematic data from the H3 Survey, we have identified 5,559 halo stars belonging to this merger within a radial distance of $r_{\text{Gal}}=6-60\text{ kpc}$. We modeled the complete H3 selection function to deduce the density profile of this accreted stellar component, employing a general ellipsoid with principal axes that can rotate relative to the Galactocentric frame, combined with a multiply-broken power law. The optimal fit reveals a triaxial ellipsoid with axis ratios of 10:8:7, inclined $25^\circ$ above the Galactic plane toward the Sun, alongside a doubly-broken power law with break radii at 12 kpc and 28 kpc. This finding reconciles conflicting literature estimates regarding the halo's breaking radius, which previously varied between $\sim15\text{ kpc}$ and $\sim30\text{ kpc}$ under singly-broken power law assumptions. Since N-body simulations link breaking radii to apocenter pile-ups of stellar orbits, this double-break offers novel insights into the GSE merger's initial conditions and evolution. Additionally, the halo's tilt and triaxiality suggest that a portion of the underlying dark matter halo may share these characteristics, with significant consequences for both the dynamical mass modeling of the Galaxy and direct dark matter detection experiments.

This research investigates Lyapunov exponents for flat bundles over hyperbolic curves, constructed through parallel transport along the geodesic flow. Treating these exponents as invariants within the space of Hitchin representations, we demonstrate that a strict gap exists between any pair of consecutive values. Furthermore, we identify the uniformizing representation of a Riemann surface as the unique case exhibiting extremal gaps. The proof strategy involves connecting Lyapunov exponents for Anosov representations to other invariants where gap properties are either established or provable. Specifically, we first link these exponents to a foliated variant associated with a foliation Hölder equivalent to the unstable foliation of the unitary tangent bundle of a Riemann surface. Second, we establish a connection to the renormalized intersection product within the thermodynamic formalism framework advanced by Bridgeman, Canary, Labourie, and Sambarino.

Thermal friction presents a viable approach to addressing both the Hubble and large-scale structure (LSS) tensions. By applying an additional frictional force to a scalar field in the early universe, this mechanism transfers the field's energy density into dark radiation, producing effects comparable to early dark energy (EDE) models. Crucially, this dark radiation redshifts at the minimal rate required to alleviate the Hubble tension, while the added radiation component helps mitigate the LSS tension. We analyzed this model using cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillation, and supernova data, specifically incorporating the SH0ES $H_0$ measurement and Dark Energy Survey Y1 data. Our findings reveal a preference for a scenario where the scalar field converts to dark radiation at extremely high redshifts, effectively behaving as an extra self-interacting radiation species rather than an EDE-like injection. In this regime, thermal friction can ease both tensions but fails to fully resolve them. We attribute this outcome to the conflict between CMB data and the linear density perturbations of dark radiation when injected near the epoch of matter-radiation equality.

Music loops are a fundamental component of electronic music production, driving significant demand for pre-recorded loops across diverse styles. Although numerous commercial and community databases exist to satisfy this need, their restrictive licensing often renders them unsuitable for research purposes. We introduce the Freesound Loop Dataset (FSLD), a large-scale collection of expert-annotated music loops sourced from Freesound, a community repository of audio under Creative Commons licenses that permits redistribution. The dataset features comprehensive annotations covering instrument, tempo, meter, key, and genre. This paper outlines the methodology for assembling and annotating the data, details the distribution of tags, and reports on inter-annotator agreement. Additionally, we provide the community with a custom online loop annotation tool. To demonstrate the dataset's utility, we present case studies on estimating tempo and key, generating music tracks, and evaluating a loop separation algorithm. We expect the community to discover further applications for FSLD, ranging from automatic loop characterization to algorithmic composition.

Coherent states based on the Perelomov framework are introduced for infinite, equally spaced homogeneous waveguide arrays exhibiting Euclidean E(2) symmetry, accompanied by novel identity resolutions formulated in both Cartesian and polar coordinates.
